Ita haut absimili modo,quicunque nos in Philosophico stadio & Gymnasterio versamur, optato fine, qui est Ϭεωεία τ ὄντων ἢ πεϱὶ ξὶς τ δεόντων, quibus aliquâ exparte imaginem Dei, lapsu Adami pene abolitam, quoad ejus naturaliter fieri poterit, restaurare annitimur, per sæpe frustamur. Etenim aut non currimus, nec ad eruditionis culmen serio adspiramus; aut si omninò currere certò nobis propositum sit, à legitimo tramite deflectimus, & in devia abripimur, quibus quò longius proc sserimus, eò magis à scopo aberramus; quò celerius festinaverimus, eò citius labyrintho circumducimur inexplicabili. Aut denique licet seria nobis ac destinata ad rerum cognitio-
units.tr: is carried headlong, or is left without the proper provisions and suitable means needed to complete the journey. So too in much the same way, all of us who spend our time in the philosophical arena and gymnasium, though we aim at the goal that is the contemplation of things that are, or of things that ought to be [θεωρία τῶν ὄντων ἢ περὶ τῶν δεόντων], by which we strive to restore, in some measure and as far as it can naturally be done, the image of God, almost abolished by Adam's fall, often fail. For either we do not run at all, nor earnestly aspire to the summit of learning; or, if we are indeed resolved to run, we turn aside from the straight course and are carried off into byways, and the further we go along them, the further we wander from the goal; the faster we hurry, the sooner we are led round into an inextricable labyrinth. Or finally, although our purpose in the knowledge of things is serious and settled,

units.tr: knowledge of things, and though we are still keeping to the genuine road, there presents itself a very great lack, or difficulty, or ignorance, of the means, experiments and other things needed to complete this journey. Once these are removed we grow old entirely and yield to fate, and it is so that [ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή]: life is short and art is long. And although many men, whose breast was formed from better clay, have with truly Herculean daring tried to bring a remedy to this long-standing complaint, not every difficulty has yet been overcome, so that it seems almost insurmountable. Among all the means by which, in this darkness, we aspire to an exact knowledge, as it were, of all things, and to "knowing everything" [τὸ πάντα εἰδέναι] (than which nothing is bittersweet [οὐδὲν γλυκύπικρον]; and with which removed, all reason both of living and of doing business is removed, Cicero, De Finibus 1, and to which

units.la: cui si quis sæpius vacare voluerit, ac sapientiam amare didicerit, jucundam valde reddet vitam, & maximum in tribulatione præstabit solatium:) una est scientia, quæ quòd sit sapientia, sapientes, hoc est, omnium rerum peritos, sui cultores reddat. Hæc est, quæ brevitate succinctâ, ac claritate evidenti cognoscendum exhibet, quidquid aut est, aut dici cogitarive possit; quidquid esse reale, aut rationis habet; Illa autem qui cognoscit, omnia tenet. Hæc est, quæ sui possessorem adeò reddit intemeratum ac rerum omnium gnarum, ut nihil ipsi occurrere, nihil proponi, aut objici possit, de quo dicere necesse habeat, se nihil de eo scire; Quidquid enim in cogitationem, sermonem aut disquisitionem venit, est Deus, vel creatura, Ens, vel ejus affectio & attributum
units.tr: If anyone is willing to give himself often to it, and has learned to love wisdom, it will make his life very pleasant and will afford him the greatest comfort in trouble. There is one science which, because it is wisdom, makes its devotees wise, that is, skilled in all things. This is the science which, in a brief and compact way and with evident clarity, sets forth for knowing whatever either is, or can be spoken or thought of, whatever has real or rational being. Whoever knows it holds all things. This is the science which makes its possessor so unimpaired and so well informed about all things that nothing can occur to him, nothing be put before him or objected to him, about which he would have to say that he knows nothing. For whatever comes into thought, speech or inquiry is either God or creature, being or its affection and attribute.

units.la: tum, aliquid, vel nihil; At de iis omnibus convenienter cogitare ac differere suos ipsa facit cultores. Si quippe Ens fuerit, nôrunt ipsi suam constitutionem, essentiam, unitatem, veritatem, distinctionem, utilitatem &c. convenire; Et si non ens, ipsum illud dici & cogitari, non autem dari, opponi quidem alicui, non autem habere attributa realia, ilicò agnoscunt; Quo ipso hujus scientiæ peritus, reliquarum disciplinarum inferiorum gnaros, longis antecellit parasangis; nulla quippe est scientiarum, quæ omnium pollicetur, aut præstare potest cognitionem: Ex. gr. teneat quis Geometriam, quæratur de Deo, Angelis, purgatorio, quid prosere, quâ Geometra: At hujus scientiæ epopta, de his & aliis omnibus aliquid proferre potest. Hæc scientia, ut generalis est, ita nihil à sua
units.tr: ...whether it is something or nothing. But this science enables its devotees to think and reason about all these things properly. For if a thing is a being, they know that its constitution, essence, unity, truth, distinction, usefulness, and so on belong to it. And if it is not a being, they at once recognise that it can be named and thought of, though not that it exists; that it can be opposed to something, but does not have real attributes. For this reason the expert in this science far surpasses those who know only the lower disciplines by long parasangs. No science promises or can provide knowledge of everything. For example, let someone master geometry and be asked about God, angels, or purgatory: what can he say about them as a geometer? But the initiate of this science can say something about all these things and others too. This science, being general, is therefore not separated from its own...

units.la: à suâ exçludit tractatione, adeoque quam maximè brevitati Studiorum consulit; Prout enim ideo traditur Scientia hominis in communi, ut quod prolixum nimis in singulorum hominum cognitione repetendum esset, simul ac semel tradatur; ac ideo de Animalibus in genere præcipiunt naturalium rerum mystæ, ut unico quasi obtuitu teneatur, quod de singulis speciebus cognoscere & operosum & tædiosum nimis foret; Ita & universalis Entis tradenda est scientia, quæ eô magis brevitati isti consulit, quô magis universalis est, & ad omnia pertinet. Hæc ea est, quæ ideo maximæ inter reliquas necessitatis ac utilitatis est, quod omnes, aut saltem maximè deformes naturæ humanæ defectus, ad pristinam integritatem reducat. Non aliâ ratione, quam reliquis
units.tr: It excludes from its own treatment, and so greatly serves the brevity of studies. For knowledge of man in general is handed down in this way: what would be too lengthy to repeat in the knowledge of each individual man is, once delivered, delivered all at once. For this reason the natural philosophers also prescribe, concerning animals in general, that they be held in a single glance, since to know each species separately would be too laborious and tedious. So too the science of universal being must be handed down, and it serves brevity all the more because it is the more universal and pertains to all things. This is the science which, for that reason, is of the greatest necessity and usefulness among the rest: it restores to their original integrity all the defects of human nature, or at least the most grievous of them. Not by any other method than the rest

units.la: liquis medicamentis, ad pristinam sanitatem corpori restituendam comparatis, illud merito præfertur, quod aut instar panaceæ omnes, aut præcipuos, aut plurimos morbos sanare aptum est. At ubi reliquæ disciplinæ particularem quemdam defectum tollere nituntur, hæc sola omnem universim ausfert; Et reliquis modo has, modò illas succcrescentes infirmitates eradicantibus, sola hæc illam, quæ reliquarum omnium caput & scaturigo est, radicitus evellit. Omnium quippe præstat notitiam; non quidem singularium, sed omnium in generalissimis suis attributis; Non quidem omnium secundum propriissimas ipsorum rationes, sed generalissimas , sub quibus hæ comprehenduntur; Non omnium quidem in sese, sed in principiis & causis suis; Non omnium proxime
units.tr: as with other remedies prepared to restore bodily health to its former state, it is rightly preferred because it is able, like a panacea, to cure all diseases, or the chief or most of them. But whereas the other disciplines strive to remove some particular defect, this one alone removes every defect in general; and while the others eradicate now this and now that weakness as it springs up again, this one alone tears up by the roots that which is the head and fountain of all the rest. For it provides knowledge of all things: not indeed of individual things, but of all things in their most general attributes; not of all things according to their own most proper reasons, but according to the most general reasons under which these are comprehended; not of all things in themselves, but in their principles and causes; not of all things proximately

units.la: ximè & actu; sed remotè, & quasi potentiâ, factâ accuratiori ad singula attentione in actum deducendâ: Adeòque prout semen virtute est tota arbor, ita hæc scientia, tota Philosophia, omnisque studio humano acquisita notitia. Quare & γνωκωτάτη, καθολικὴ, imò & καλ' ἐξοχὴν Philosophia & sapientia merito audit. Hujus igitur Institutiones tradere, apprimè necessarium videbitur; Prout hujus studium maximè est utile; Quamobrem eas breviter adornare, inque Discipulorū usum convertere constitui; idque non tantum viva voce, sed & hacce Ἀφορισμοί, pro ratione gratiæ Divinæ, præstare tentavi: Quam dum publicæ luci, publicis in Academiâ vestrâ Disputationibus, in commodum Studiosorum, qui meis curis se committunt, expono, non potui huncce fru-
units.tr: Not proximately and in act, but remotely and, as it were, in potency, to be brought into act by a more careful attention to particulars. And so, just as the seed virtually is the whole tree, this science is the whole of philosophy and all the knowledge that human study can acquire. Hence it is rightly called most knowing, universal, and even pre-eminently [γνωστικωτάτη, καθολική, καθ' ἐξοχήν] philosophy and wisdom. It will therefore seem especially necessary to hand down the Institutes of this science, since the study of it is most useful. Accordingly I resolved to put them together briefly and to turn them to the use of students, and I have tried to do this not only by spoken word but also in these aphorisms [Ἀφορισμοί], as far as the grace of God allowed. When I set these before the public light in public disputations in your Academy, for the benefit of the students who entrust themselves to my care, I could not withhold this fru-

units.tr: Having received this fruit, which is the product of your fostering, I do not presume to offer it to you (most illustrious and distinguished gentlemen) with a grateful and humble heart, relying above all on your favour towards true lovers of the truth and on your singular goodwill towards me. I therefore hang these Institutes at your altar, and humbly beg that you receive them kindly and protect them from the bites of malicious envy.

units.la: ceptore Johanne Phocylide p.m. Philosophiæ simul fundamenta jaceremus, maximè fuisse alieno; Sed memores utique estis, quam sint δολτίεχι φεοντίδες σοφόπεχ, quodque, quætam rei iniquâ æstimatione, quam cæco præjudiciorum assensu, immaturâ judicii trutinâ sunt approbata, ea demum generosiorum canum n.ore ρινλατῶντες, ac vetera vestigia sagaci odoratu repetentes, sæpe numero rejiciamus, melius, abjecto omnis præjudicii velamine, id quod rei est, pondetantes. Ita quippe facere decet ingenuum, ita judicare æquum, ita intellectum suum rebus conformare Philosophum, ut nihil admittat, tanquam verum quod non prius clarè ac distinctè percipiat; utque si quod receptum sit, vel prava infantiæ & adolescentiæ institutione, vel cæco præceptorum amore, vel & ipsorum sensuum idolis, genuino judicandi modo non conveniens, idem accurationi examine suspensum, denuò æstimetur, factaque æstimatione, secundum distinctam ac evidentem perceptionem judicetur, factumque judicium, tanquam solum congruum retineatur. Quem morem in ιλλεχτικοῖς Philosophis à Lipsio laudatum, ubique me secutum novisti, sæpius vobiscum præjudica-
units.tr: ...when we were laying the foundations of philosophy together under our late teacher John Phocylides, which was most alien to this. But you surely remember how [δολτίεχι φεοντίδες σοφόπεχ], that those things which have been approved by a blind assent and an unfair estimate, by an immature balance of judgment, we often reject, like noble hounds tracking by scent [ρινλατῶντες] and following old traces with keen smell. It is better, with the veil of all prejudice cast off, to weigh what the matter actually is. For so it becomes a free man to act, so it is fair to judge, and so the philosopher should conform his understanding to things, admitting nothing as true that he does not first clearly and distinctly perceive. And if anything has been received, whether through the faulty training of infancy and youth, or blind love of teachers, or the idols of the senses themselves, and does not agree with a genuine way of judging, it should be held in suspense by careful examination and evaluated again. Once it has been evaluated, it should be judged according to distinct and evident perception, and the judgment made should be kept as the only fitting one. This method, praised by Lipsius among the Sceptical [ιλλεχτικοῖς] philosophers, you know I have followed everywhere, often weighing with you opinions by legitimate perception and prior estimation, with

units.la: testas sententias legitimâ perceptione ac æstimatione prævia expendentem. Eundemque in Metaphysicæ causâ me observâsse profiteor. Fateor equidem, me maximo odio ipsam prosecutum, maximaque clade ipsam afficere, & si dis placeret, planè è medio tollere conatum fuisse: Verum exuto præjudiciorum velo, rejectoque Autorum amore vel odio, ipsâque re tantummodo spe-ctatâ, hanc longe aliter se habere compers. Nunc igitur pro turpi exilio gloriosam ipsi molior introductionem, pro abjectâ vilitate summam præstantiam, pro vili servitio fastuosum dominium, pro servili reste, im-periosa sceptra, pro infami contemtu, præ- claras laudes, pro inani jactura, fructuosissimam occupationem, omnibusque cujuscunque ordinis eruditis, summopere necessariam, ipsi subesse existimo; Immensum igitur mutatus ab illo Hectore, qui olim vobiscum fui. Rationem quaeritis? fuit omnimoda ipsius Metaphysicae utilitas, quam dum Lectionibus ac Disputationibus publicis habendis quotidie vacabam, ubique experiebar. Non enim ad subtilitates Disputationum, sed ad utilitates insignes ipsam comparatam esse, in ipsa tractatione, ni fallor satis enodavi. Vestrum igitur erit V.
units.tr: the opinions of authors, and I profess that I have observed the same method in the case of Metaphysics. I admit that I pursued it with great hatred and tried to inflict great ruin upon it, and, if it had pleased the gods, to remove it entirely from the middle. But having cast off the veil of prejudice, and rejected both love and hatred of authors, and looking only at the thing itself, I find that it is quite otherwise. So now, in place of shameful exile, I construct for it a glorious introduction; in place of abject worthlessness, supreme excellence; in place of base servitude, lordly dominion; in place of servile rope, imperial sceptres; in place of infamous contempt, distinguished praises; in place of empty loss, a most fruitful occupation, which I think is most necessary for learned men of every rank. I have therefore changed immensely from that Hector who was once with you. Do you ask the reason? It was the complete usefulness of Metaphysics itself, which I experienced everywhere while I was daily busy giving lectures and public disputations. For, if I am not mistaken, I have sufficiently explained in the treatment itself that it was prepared not for the subtleties of disputations, but for its remarkable uses. It will therefore be yours, V.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM METAPHYSICARUM, Tractatus Primus.
units.tr: INSTITUTIONS OF METAPHYSICS, First Treatise.

units.la: Introitus.
units.tr: Introduction.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: INstitutiones Metaphysicas triplici absolvam tractatu, Proœmiali, Subjectivo & Consequente; Quorum primus Præcognita; secundus Metaphysicæ subjectum, eôque pertinentia; postremus, proxima exinde consequentia exhibet: Adeoque inter hos primus est quasi radix, secundus truncus, tertius fructus.
units.tr: I shall set out the Metaphysical Institutions in three treatises: the Preliminary, the Subjective and the Consequential. Of these, the first sets out the Preliminaries; the second, the subject of Metaphysics and what pertains to it; the last, the things that follow from these immediately. Thus among these the first is as it were the root, the second the trunk, and the third the fruit.

units.la: 2. Tractatus Proœmialis tribus constabit sectionibus; Quarum prima Naturam Philosophiæ in genere: secunda Naturam Metaphysicæ in specie: tertia prærequisita ad notitiam Entis in genere explicat. Sit igitur
units.tr: 2. The Preliminary Treatise will consist of three sections. The first explains the nature of Philosophy in general; the second the nature of Metaphysics in particular; the third the prerequisites for knowledge of Being in general. So let it be.

units.la: SECTIO I.
units.tr: SECTION I.

units.la: DE Natura Philosophia.
units.tr: On the Nature of Philosophy

units.la: 1. LIcet sapientes antiquitus, hodie recentius Phliosophi dicantur, Cognitio tamen humana, cujus natura nunc explicanda, rectius Σοφία & Sapientia appellatur, quam Philosophia; Quod tamen nomen ob vulgarem usum retinebitur.
units.tr: 1. Although the wise were called philosophers in ancient times, and more recently philosophers are so called, human knowledge, whose nature is now to be explained, is more correctly called Sophia [Σοφία] and Sapientia than philosophy. Still, that name will be retained because of common usage.

units.la: 2. Non enim Humana cognitio hic consideranda est, ut habitus mentis, neque ut Systema, libro & codice comprehensum; (nam priori modo jam ab alio aliquatenus possidetur: posteriori possessæ quasi pictura, & utroque multis numeris imperfecta est:) sed in ideâ, præscindendo ab actuali inhæsione, quatenus illam, ut finem, propositam habemus, quâ ratione debitæ perfectionis particeps est.
units.tr: 2. Human knowledge is not to be considered here as a habit of the mind, nor as a system contained in a book or codex. (For in the first way it is already to some extent possessed by another; in the second, it is like a picture of what is possessed, and both are imperfect in many respects.) Rather, it is to be considered as an idea, abstracting from actual inherence, insofar as we hold it proposed as an end, by which the mind partakes of its due perfection.

units.la: 3. Angustiores & latiores vocis Philosophiæ acceptiones, ex habituali ejus inhæsione ortæ, majorem vel minorem ejus possessionem videntur indicare; nisi & genuinæ conditiones ignorentur, quæ ad eam pertinentibus disciplinis convenire debent. Adæquata autem ejus acceptio, exfine, subjecto, objecto, & effectis ejusdem desumenda est.
units.tr: 3. The narrower and broader uses of the word philosophy, arising from its habitual inherence, seem to indicate a greater or lesser possession of it, unless the genuine conditions which the disciplines pertaining to it ought to meet are also ignored. Its adequate meaning, however, is to be drawn from its end, subject, object, and effects.

units.la: 4. Est autem Philosophia, cognitio eorum, quibus mens perficitur ex lumine natu-ræ. Cognitio dicitur, vel & scientia, quatenus hæc latè sumta, fidei & opinioni opponitur. Ad faciliorem hujus captum, brevis habitus delineatio subjicienda.
units.tr: 4. Now philosophy is the knowledge of those things by which the mind is perfected from the light of nature. Knowledge is said, or also science, insofar as this is taken broadly, to be opposed to faith and opinion. For easier understanding of this, a brief outline of the habit is to be added.

units.la: 5. Habitus itaque, qui ordinarius est, cujusque potentia naturaliter inest, (non extraordinarius, qui simul cum potentiâ eminentiori virtute confertur:) pro duplici animæ potentiâ, vel intellectus est, vel voluntatis: Illius generis est Philosophia, non hujus, utpote per se hominem nec bonum, nec malum faciens; non enim aut virtus aut vitium est.
units.tr: 5. A habit which is ordinary, and naturally inherent in each faculty (not the extraordinary kind, which is conferred together with a more eminent power by virtue), belongs to the twofold power of the soul: it is either of the intellect or of the will. Philosophy belongs to the former kind, not the latter, since by itself it makes a man neither good nor bad; for it is neither a virtue nor a vice.

units.la: 6. Is igitur cognitio quædam est; oriturque 1. vel ex nudo intuitu terminorum & conceptuum; idque vel solius apprehensionis gratiâ, dicturque Intelligentia, vel ad θεωρίαν & operationem ordinatur, & observantia sive Συνταηρησις appellari commode potest: vel 2. Testimonio & authoritate fundamenti loco utitur, & fidei nomine venit: vel 3.Ratione & discursu comparatur; atque adeò fit Scientia, si ex certis & indubitatis principiis ea notitia debitè oriatur: At Opinio, si rationes pendulum saltem efficere valeant assensum.
units.tr: 6. This knowledge is therefore a certain kind, and it arises (1) either from the bare intuition of terms and concepts, and this either for the sake of apprehension alone, and is called understanding, or it is directed to contemplation [θεωρίαν] and practice, and may fittingly be called observance or Synteresis [Συνταηρησις]; or (2) it makes use of testimony and authority in the place of a foundation, and comes under the name of faith; or (3) it is acquired by reason and discourse. Thus it becomes science, if that knowledge arises from certain and indubitable principles and rightly; but it is opinion, if reasons are able to produce an assent that is at least hanging.

units.la: 7. Philosophia igitur, cum tota demonstrativa sit, neque ad fidem neque ad opinionem revocari poterit; ab illius enim parte incvidentia,ab hujus autem dubitatio & incertitudo obest.
units.tr: 7. Philosophy, then, since it is wholly demonstrative, cannot be reduced either to faith or to opinion. For on the side of the former, obviousness is lacking; on the side of the latter, doubt and uncertainty stand in the way.

units.la: 8. Intelligentia quidem & Observantia primorum & indemonstrabilium principiorum habitus, Philosophiæ introitum, utpote ejus principia præparant, eam tamen non absolvunt. Negligi tamen prorsus nequeunt; ut quæ ad Sapientiam quam maximè requiruntur.
units.tr: 8. Understanding and observance, the habits of first and indemonstrable principles, prepare the entrance to philosophy, inasmuch as they prepare its principles; yet they do not complete it. Still, they cannot be neglected at all, since they are especially required for wisdom.

units.la: 9. Scientiæ autem hujus tres summæ species sunt. 1. Scientia stricte & καθ’ ἐξοχὴν dicta. 2. Prudentia. 3. Ars. Prima est Entis alicujus, adeoque subjecti necessarii, solius speculationis gratiâ cognitio; adeoque subjecto potissimum & fine à posterioribus distinguitur. Secunda est cognitio eorum, quæ hominem bonum vel malum reddunt, per consultationem ad electionem vel fugam instituta. Tertia est habitus cum rectâ ratione effectivus; sive cognitio eorum, quibus intellectus instrumenta, ad operis alicujus effectionem dirigere & applicare potest.
units.tr: 9. The three chief species of this science are: 1. science strictly and pre-eminently so called [καθ’ ἐξοχὴν]; 2. prudence; 3. art. The first is the knowledge of some being, and so of a necessary subject, pursued merely for the sake of contemplation; and it is chiefly distinguished from the others by its subject and its end. The second is knowledge of those things which make a man good or bad, arranged through deliberation for choice or avoidance. The third is a habit effective with right reason; that is, the knowledge of those things by which the intellect can direct and apply its instruments to the making of some work.

units.la: 10. Ex harum speciebus, tanquam partibus, colliguntur illæ, quæ ad mentis persectionem, ejusque restaurationem à corruptelis lapsus Adamitici, quoad ejus naturaliter fieri potest, requiruntur. Quarum collectio dicitur Sapientia, & Philophia illa modo definita. Quæ proinde merito cognitio dicitur, cum omnes ejus partes cognitiones esse reperiantur.
units.tr: 10. From these species, as parts, are gathered those things which are required for the perfection of the mind, and for its restoration from the corruptions of the Adamic fall, as far as this can naturally be done. The collection of these is called Wisdom, and that philosophy as just defined. Which is therefore rightly called knowledge, since all its parts are found to be cognitions.

units.la: II. Differentia autem Philosophiae, reliquis verbis definitionis contenta, absolvitur 1. Subjecto tractationis. 2. Subjecto inhaesionis & informationis. 3. Causa.
units.tr: II. The difference of philosophy, contained in the remaining words of the definition, is completed by: 1. the subject of treatment; 2. the subject of inherence and information; 3. the cause.

units.la: 12. Subjectum tractationis (uo materiali constat & formali. Materiale est id, quod tractatur & explicatur, quod hic simpliciter & absolute EORUM nomine designatur. Quod si cui nimis remote nec satis determinate fieri videatur, ei dicam, vix propius, magisque determinatum citra copulam dari posse. Quod autem determinationi deesse videtur, id formali satis limitato completur. Sin a copula non abhorreas, loco eorum substituas Res divinas ac humanas: Easdem enim communiori illo modo dicendi, intelligendas volui.
units.tr: 12. The subject of treatment consists of a material and a formal part. The material part is that which is treated and explained, which here is simply and absolutely designated by the name of these things. If anyone thinks this is too remote and not sufficiently determinate, I reply that nothing closer and more determinate can be given without a copula. What seems to be lacking in the determination is supplied by the formal part, which is sufficiently limited. But if you do not shrink from a copula, substitute for "these things" the divine and human things; for I wanted these to be understood in that more common manner of speaking.

units.la: 13. Res autem Divinae sunt, Deus, ejusque opera ordinaria in Natura, ut pote quae admirabilitate sua, nos ad sui contemplationem invitant: Dicunturque aliter necessariae, quod videlicet per arbitrium humanum non fiant, ipsive suum esse debeant. Humanae vero res sunt opera hominis, ab ejusque arbitrio profecta, quae ideo, quod esse & non esse possint, contingentia appellantur. Eorum igitur, id est, Dei, operumque divinorum ac humanorum cognitio est Philosophia
units.tr: 13. Divine things are God, and his ordinary works in Nature, since by their wonder they invite us to contemplate him; and they are called necessary in another way, namely because they are not done by human choice and must be what they are. Human things, however, are the works of man, proceeding from his choice; and because they can be and not be, they are called contingent. Of these, that is, of God and of divine and human works, philosophy is the knowledge.

units.la: 14. Formale Subjectum, est modus id
units.tr: 14. The formal subject is the mode of

units.la: Bl. considerandi, Et in tribus consistit, Fine, perficere. Subjecto inhæfionis, mente. Efficiente, lumine Naturæ. Hæc tria Subjectum materiale, adeoque & ipsam Philosophiam ita constituunt, ut nihil ad mentis perfectionem per naturalia media ipsi queat deesse; ac ita coarctant, ut quidquid ad illam perfectionem per se non requiratur, extra Philosophiæ pomœria relegandum sit.
units.tr: considering it, and it consists in three things: the end, to perfect; the subject of inherence, the mind; the efficient, the light of nature. These three, together with the material subject, constitute philosophy itself in such a way that nothing needed for the perfection of the mind by natural means can be lacking to it; and they limit it so that whatever is not required for that perfection in itself must be banished beyond the boundaries of philosophy.

units.la: 15. Subjectum inhæsionis & informationis cui inhæret, ac quod perficit Philosophia, est Mens, seu anima rationalis, potior hominis pars, quâ scilicet rationalis ac discursivus est; Discursus enim ac ratio omninò ad illam requiruntur. Hinc Brutis animantibus, utpote ratione destitutis, Philosophia erit deneganda, & solum proprium ejus subjectum constituendum Mens humana, aut verò per denominationem, homo.
units.tr: 15. The subject of inherence and information, in which it inheres and which philosophy perfects, is the mind, or rational soul, the nobler part of man, namely that by which he is rational and capable of discourse; for discourse and reason are altogether required for it. Hence philosophy must be denied to brute animals, since they lack reason; and its proper subject must be taken to be the human mind, or else, by denomination, man.

units.la: 16. Nec tamen eodem prorsus respectu Subjectum inhæsionis & informationis est, sed admodum diverso: Dicitur namque inhæsionis, quâtenus Philosophia, ut habitus adeoque & accidens, ipsi inhæret: At informationis, quâtenus mens eâ informatur, hoc est, perficitur, ac quasi novâ formâ, vel pristinâ sanitate, lapsu Adami amissâ, donatur.
units.tr: 16. Yet the subject of inherence and of information is not in the same respect at all, but in quite a different one. It is called the subject of inherence, insofar as philosophy, as a habit and therefore an accident, inheres in it; but it is the subject of information, insofar as the mind is informed by it, that is, is perfected, and is given, as it were, a new form or the original health lost in Adam's fall.

units.la: 17. Causa, in definitione adducta, est lumen Naturæ, quatenus gratiæ ac revelationi Divinæ contradistinguitur. Omnia igitur illa complectitur, quæ ordinario modo mentis informationem procreant ac adjuvant, adeoque universim omnes Philosophiæ causas Efficientes.
units.tr: 17. The cause, in the definition adduced, is the light of nature, insofar as it is distinguished from grace and divine revelation. It therefore embraces all those things which in the ordinary way produce and assist the information of the mind, and so, in general, all the efficient causes of philosophy.

units.la: 18. Causæ enim Philosophiæ potissimum externæ sunt; Nam internæ, materia nempe & forma, utreliquis qualitatibus, ita nec Philosophiæ proprie loquendo conveniunt. Analogice tamen materia Philosophiæ sunt ejus partes, partiumque partes, quot ad ejus complementum requiruntur; Quemadmodum forma, illi respondens, earum partium nexus ac conveniens ordo & dispositio est.
units.tr: 18. For the causes of philosophy are chiefly external; for internal causes, namely matter and form, do not, as with other qualities, apply to philosophy properly speaking. Nevertheless, by analogy, the matter of philosophy is its parts, and the parts of its parts, as many as are required for its completion; just as form, corresponding to this, is the connection of those parts and their fitting order and arrangement.

units.la: 19. Sunt igitur Philosophiæ causæ, vel Efficientes, vel finales. Inter illas una prima est, Deus Opt. Max. qui cum sit ipsissima Sapientia, ejus quoque ratione hominem ad sui imaginem condere voluit. Et ad ejus jam amissæ aliqualem reparationem, largâ suâ benedictione adjuvare. Opera igitur danda, ut ipsius timor, qui Sapientiæ initium à Sapientissimo mortalium depræ dicatur, animis discentium infilleturj, ejusque benedictio seriis ac ardentibus precibus imploretur.
units.tr: 19. Therefore the causes of philosophy are either efficient or final. Among the former, the first is God, Best and Greatest, who, since he is Wisdom itself, willed also by that same reason to make man in his own image, and to help him toward some restoration of what he has now lost, by his generous blessing. Hence efforts must be made that the fear of him, which the wisest of mortals says is the beginning of wisdom, be instilled into the minds of learners, and that his blessing be implored with earnest and fervent prayers.

units.la: 10. Reliquæ Efficientes secundæ, & à Deo dependentes sunt; Æque vel principales, vel minus principales. Illæ duæ sunt, sunt, Natura & Cura.
units.tr: 20. The remaining efficient causes are secondary and dependent on God; equally, they are either principal or less principal. There are two, namely Nature and Diligence.

units.la: 21. Natura hic dicuntur potentia, homini ab ipso ortu indita, sive illæ prima fuerint, sive orta, & à primis fluentes. Prima iterum dua sunt; Intellectus & voluntas.
units.tr: 21. Here nature refers to faculties implanted in man from his very birth, whether they were first or arisen later and flowing from the first ones. The first are again two: intellect and will.

units.la: 22. Intellectus, quatenus cogitationum est principium, & actu meditatur, principalis Philosophiæ dicitur causa; Quoniam omnis humana cognitio quædam de rebus est cogitatio. Voluntas, quatenus cogitationes intellectus ad talia objecta, determinat, easque continuat aut abrumpit, non minus, quam ipse intellectus, ad Philosophiam requiritur. Intellectus enim, ex se indifferens, non magis de rebus Philosophicis cogitat, quam de aliis quibuscunque, nisi voluntas ipsum ad objecta determinet.
units.tr: 22. The intellect, insofar as it is the source of thoughts and actually reflects, is called the principal cause of philosophy, since all human knowledge of things is a kind of thought. The will, insofar as it determines the intellect's thoughts to such objects, and continues or breaks them off, is no less required for philosophy than the intellect itself. For the intellect, indifferent in itself, thinks no more about philosophical matters than about any others, unless the will determines it to the objects.

units.la: 23. Orta potentia, Philosophiæ quoque causæ principales, tres sunt, Apprehensio, Iudicium & Memoria. Apprehensio est potentia percipiendi, quâ res objectas acie intellectûs debitè inspiciemur ac consideramus; Pro cujus majori vel minori excellentia, facilior aut tardior ad rerum cognitionem patet aditus. Hac qui pollent, acuti ac perspicaces ingenio, qui secus hebetes ac stupidi dicuntur.
units.tr: 23. The powers that arise: the principal causes of philosophy are also three: Apprehension, Judgment and Memory. Apprehension is the power of perceiving, by which we rightly look at and consider the objects set before the eye of the intellect. The greater or lesser excellence of this power opens a easier or more difficult way to knowledge of things. Those who excel in it are called keen and perceptive in mind; those who lack it are called dull and stupid.

units.la: 24. Iudicium est potentia æstimandi percepta, quâ debita rei attributa convenire, ac indebita disconvenire statuimus. Hoc itaque perceptionem sive apprehensionem legitimam sequi debet, nec antevertere: Differri tamen nequit, re jam bene perceptâ, ne in continuam fluctuationem ac dubitationem Philosophia degeneret.
units.tr: 24. Judgment is the power of evaluating what has been perceived, by which we decide that what is due belongs to a thing and what is not due does not. It ought therefore to follow upon a proper perception or apprehension, and not to run ahead of it. Yet, once a thing has been properly perceived, it must not be delayed, lest philosophy degenerate into constant wavering and doubt.

units.la: 25. Memoria est potentia retinendi judicata, quâ ea promptè imprimimus, impressa retinemus, ac retentorum recordamur. Hæc ad omnem habitualem cognitionem tam necessaria est, ut per eam doctus ab indocto, peritus ab imperito discernatur.
units.tr: 25. Memory is the power of retaining what has been judged, by which we readily impress things, keep them once impressed, and recall what we have retained. This is so necessary for all habitual knowledge that by it the learned is distinguished from the unlearned, and the skilled from the unskilled.

units.la: 26. Sequitur Cura, altera principalis causa, quâ naturam ejusque potentias promovemus ac adjuvamus. Quorsum pertinent 1. Attentio. 2. Exercitatio. 3. Ordo.
units.tr: 26. There follows Care, the second principal cause, by which we advance and assist nature and its powers. To this belong: (1) Attention; (2) Exercise; (3) Order.

units.la: 27. Attentio est rei cognoscendæ debita consideratio; Debita autem hæc est, si satis acriter, satisque diu circa unamquamque seorsim versetur. Sine hac cogitare, est quasi nihil cogitare; sine hac non fit judicium; nec memoriæ quidquam imprimitur; adeoque quam maximè potentias ratione actuum perficit.
units.tr: 27. Attention is due consideration of the thing to be known. It is due if it occupies us sufficiently keenly and sufficiently long with each thing taken separately. Without it, to think is almost to think nothing; without it no judgment is made, and nothing is impressed on the memory; and so it especially perfects the powers with respect to their acts.

units.la: 28. Exercitatio est frequens actuum, à potentiis fluentium, ut & attentionis repetitio. Hac igitur frequenter attendimus, percipimus, judicamus; & memoriæ mandamus, ut ita repetitis istis actibus facilitatem, & quasi habitum bene attendendi, perpercipiendi, judicandi ac retinendi nobis acquiramus; Quod enim Natura incipit, id exercitatio perficit.
units.tr: 28. Exercise is the frequent repetition of acts flowing from the powers, and likewise of attention. By it we therefore attend, perceive and judge frequently, and commit things to memory, so that by repeating these acts we acquire for ourselves a facility, and as it were a habit, of attending well, perceiving, judging and retaining. For what nature begins, exercise brings to perfection.

units.la: 29. Ordo est, partim debita reliquarum causarum successio; partim earum ad diversa objecta, per debitam successionem applicatio. Duo igitur Ordo praestat, 1. ut supradictae causae secundae inter se connectantur; nempe ut perceptionem sequatur judicium, & hoc memoria, iisque omnibus comites sint Attentio & Exercitatio.
units.tr: 29. Order is, on the one hand, the due succession of the remaining causes; on the other hand, their application to different objects in due succession. Order therefore accomplishes two things: (1) that the aforesaid secondary causes be connected with one another, namely that perception be followed by judgment, and judgment by memory, with attention and exercise as their companions;

units.la: 2. Vt dum per vices modo huic, modo illi objecto applicantur, illa vicissitudo non temere & fortuito, sed certa quadam lege fiat; adeo ut posterius cognoscatur, quod ab alterius notitia pendet.
units.tr: (2) that, while the mind is applied in turn now to this object, now to that, this alternation take place not rashly and by chance, but by a certain fixed law; so that that which depends on the knowledge of another is learned later.

units.la: 30. Has causas omnes debite dirigere & applicare, non videtur nudae esse natura, sed potius artis alicujus, hisce omnibus certas normas ac regulas praescribentis, secundum quas debite instituti ac peragi debeant; ac simul ipsis rebus cognoscendis se applicare docentis. Cujus Artis peritia, non minima est intellectus perfectio; adeoque nec illa extra Philosophiam releg[anda] videtur. Atque hac de causis principalibus.
units.tr: 30. To direct and apply all these causes duly does not seem to be a matter of mere nature, but rather of some art which prescribes certain norms and rules for all of these, according to which they ought to be duly arranged and carried out; and which at the same time teaches us to apply ourselves to the things to be known. Skill in this art is no small perfection of the intellect, and so it does not seem to be banished outside philosophy either. So much for the principal causes.

units.la: 31. Sequuntur minus principales, quae vel impellendo, vel inserviendo, quod suum est, ad Philosophiae acquisitionem conserunt. Inter illas quaedam sunt externa, extra hominem constitutæ, quædam interna, in ipso positæ. Inter externas occurrunt 1. Res ipsæ, quàtenus admirabiles sunt. 2. Homines, tam doĉti & eruditione clari, quibus pares esse nitimur; quam indoĉti & obscuri, quos superare animus est.
units.tr: 31. There follow the less principal causes, which contribute to the acquiring of philosophy, either by impelling or by serving, each in its own way. Among these, some are external, situated outside the man, and some are internal, placed within him. Among the external causes occur: (1) the things themselves, insofar as they are wonderful; (2) men, both those learned and distinguished for erudition, whom we strive to equal, and those unlearned and obscure, whom we intend to surpass.

units.la: 32. Interna radicalis est ignorantia, ex quâ fluit eam detegens admiratio, quam comitatur appetitus ille naturalis cognoscendi, ad attentionem, perceptionem, caterasque causas principales, tanquam media, suo desiderio impellens. Sed harum nexum interse, ac munus, quod præstant, alibi latiùs exposui.
units.tr: 32. The internal radical cause is ignorance, from which there flows the wonder that uncovers it, and which is accompanied by that natural desire of knowing, driving us by its longing toward attention, perception and the other principal causes as means. But I have set out at greater length elsewhere the connection of these among themselves and the office which they perform.

units.la: 33. Inservientes causæ sunt instrumenta, quæ vel necessaria, vel arbitraria sunt. Et necessaria iterum vel sunt conjuncta cum Philosophiâ, vel separata.
units.tr: 33. The causes that serve are instruments, which are either necessary or optional. And the necessary instruments are again either joined with philosophy or separate from it.

units.la: 34. Conjuncti instrumenti munus, una Philosophiæ pars alteri suggerit; sive id fiat per suggestionem modi ac ordinis, quem Logica, Ars illa, thes. 30. indigitata, præscribit; sive per dependentiam materiæ ac rerum, quomodo Metaphysica reliquis omnibus, Mathesis Physicæ, Ethica Oeconomicæ & Politicæ inservit.
units.tr: 34. The office of the joined instrument is that one part of philosophy suggests something to another; whether this happens by suggesting the method and order which Logic, that art already noted in thesis 30, prescribes; or by the dependence of matter and things, as Metaphysics serves all the rest, and Mathematics serves Physics, and Ethics serves Economics and Politics.

units.la: 35. Inter separata instrumenta occurrunt 1. Sensus, quibus res sese manifestant.
units.tr: 35. Among the separate instruments occur: (1) the senses, by which things make themselves manifest.

units.la: 2. Observatio, ea quæ sensibus sunt manifestata colligens, Græcis ἰσοξῖν dicta. A 6 3.Ex-
units.tr: (2) Observation, gathering together those things which have been made manifest to the senses, called [ἰσοξῖν] in Greek.

units.la: 3. Experientia, observationes collectas ad usum applicans. 4. Inductio, ex singularibus experientiis axiomata universalia colligens 5. Discursus sive διάνοια, ignotum ex notis universalibus deducens.
units.tr: (3) Experience, applying the collected observations to use. (4) Induction, gathering universal axioms from singular experiences. (5) Discursus, or [διάνοια], deducing the unknown from known universals.

units.la: 36. Arbitraria instrumenta sunt, quae ad bene esse ab arbitrio eliguntur; Cujus generis sunt, Praeceptores, Libri, Academiae, Scholae &c. Et haec de efficientibus Philosophiae causis
units.tr: 36. The optional instruments are those chosen at will for well-being. Of this kind are teachers, books, academies, schools, etc. And so much for the efficient causes of philosophy.

units.la: 37. Sequitur finis, qui proximus & adaequatus in definitione exprimitur, quod sit mentis humanae ratione debiti objecti ac causae consimilis perfectio, qua ipsi pristina, quoad ejus fieri poterit, integritas, ac a defectibus, primorum parentum lapsu contractis, restauratio conciliatur. Hic tamen finis Deo, ejusque gloriae, tanquam omnium creaturarum fini supremo, ut & ipsi hominis bono ac saluti subordinatur: Et consimiliter plurima Philosophiae effecta, tanquam sui media sibi supposita requirit.
units.tr: 37. There follows the end, which is expressed in the definition as proximate and adequate, namely that it is the perfection of the human mind consimilar to the due object and cause in accordance with reason, by which the original integrity of the mind, so far as it can be, is secured and its restoration effected, the defects contracted through the fall of our first parents being made good. Yet this end is subordinated to God and his glory, as the supreme end of all creatures, and likewise to the good and salvation of man himself. In the same way, it requires many effects of philosophy as means supposed to it.

units.la: 38. Effecta autem illa vel absoluta sunt, vel relata: Quorum illa perse ad illam persectionem pertinent: Haec autem usum Philosophiae istiusque perfectionis circa alia ostendunt. Ambo varia sunt; priora tamen ad duo quasi capita reduci possunt, Voluptatem & Libertatem.
units.tr: 38. These effects are either absolute or relative. Of these, the former pertain to that perfection by itself; the latter show the use of philosophy and of that perfection with respect to other things. Both are various; the former, however, can be reduced to two chief heads, Pleasure and Liberty.

units.la: 39. Voluptas Philosophica, non illa tantum aestimanda, quae sensuum eorumque est appetitus, sive illa [?], sive [?] fuerit, sed potissimum mentis & rationis, quâ mens incomparabili dulcedine, & admirabili delectatione pură ac constanti perfunditur, Vid. 10. Eth. Nicom. cap. 7.
units.tr: 39. Philosophical pleasure is not only to be esteemed as that which belongs to the senses and their appetite, whether it be [?], or [?] it may have been; but chiefly that of the mind and reason, by which the mind is suffused with an incomparable sweetness and a wonderful delight, pure and constant. See Nicomachean Ethics, book 10, chapter 7.

units.la: 40. Haec comites habet. 1. Puritatem.
units.tr: 40. This has companions. (1) Purity.

units.la: 2. Constantiam. 3. Sufficientiam. Puritas Philosophicae voluptatis, est ejusdem cum genuinâ normâ, tam veritatis ejusque modi, quam actionum voluntatis convenientia. Constantia est ejusdem convenientia immutabilitas. Sufficientia verò est opulentia ac debita istius voluptatis affluentia, quâ nihil ipsi possit deesse, nihilque superabundare, eorum quae ad naturalem illam perfectionem requiri possunt. Hinc igitur veritas plurimorum Paradoxorum Stoicorum elucescit.
units.tr: (2) Constancy. (3) Sufficiency. Purity of philosophical pleasure is its agreement with the genuine norm, both of truth and of its mode, and of the actions of the will. Constancy is the unchanging agreement of the same. Sufficiency, however, is the abundance and due flowing in of that pleasure, so that nothing can be lacking to it, nor anything superabundant, of those things which can be required for that natural perfection. Hence the truth of many of the Stoic paradoxes becomes clear.

units.la: 41. Cum his se [?] omnes Philosophiae partes diffundit voluptas; adeoque vel Contemplationis, vel Actionis, vel Effectionis puritatem, constantiam ac sufficientiam singulis convenientem inducit. Voluptas igitur Contemplationis est suavissima mentis laetitia, quâ post debitam admirationis ac ignorantiae ablationem, ipsa variarum ac pulchrarum rerum clarâ ac distinctâ cognitione perfunditur. Actionis verò est consimilis laetitia ac delectatio, orta ex facili & constanti actionum, secundum virtutem directarum, exercitio. Effectionis denique voluptas, oritur ex genuinâ dire-
units.tr: 41. With these, pleasure spreads through all the parts of philosophy; and so it brings about purity, constancy and sufficiency, suited to each, whether of contemplation, of action, or of production. Thus the pleasure of contemplation is the sweetest gladness of the mind, by which, after the due removal of wonder and ignorance, it is suffused with the clear and distinct knowledge of various and beautiful things. That of action is a similar joy and delight, arising from the easy and constant exercise of actions directed according to virtue. Finally, the pleasure of production arises from the genuine direction,

units.la: directione, & applicatione facili & non impedita, eorum actuum, quibus ipsa rerum cognitio comparatur. De his autem actibus vid. supra inter causas.
units.tr: and from the easy and unimpeded application, of those acts by which knowledge of things is acquired. Concerning these acts, see above among the causes.

units.la: 42. Alterum absolutum Philosophiae effectum est Libertas, soli Sapienti à Stoicis tributa, quâ mens humana maximè dicitur sui juris esse, id est, quâ cuncta probando, bona tantum retinet; adeoque facit, non quod libet, sed quod licet. Estque hæc ipsa quoque triplex, Theoretica, Practica & Poëtica.
units.tr: 42. The other absolute effect of philosophy is Liberty, ascribed by the Stoics to the wise man alone, by which the human mind is said most of all to be its own master; that is, by which, testing all things, it retains only what is good, and so does not do what it pleases, but what it may. This too is threefold: Theoretical, Practical and Poetical.

units.la: 43. Theoretica Libertas, in veritatis judicio consistens, est spontaneitas judicii, quâ non nisi post legitimam perceptionem, per certam & infallibilem rationem, sententiam aliquam recipimus. Veram igitur libertatem Philosophi non retinent illi, qui aut re nondum satis perceptâ, aut vî passionum, præjudiciorum, ac præconceptarum opinionum, aut denique solâ auctoritate, sententiæ alicui, licet alias veræ, subscribunt. Hæc enim spontaneitati judicii fibulam imponunt.
units.tr: 43. Theoretical liberty, consisting in the judgment of truth, is the spontaneity of judgment, by which we accept any opinion only after lawful perception, by a certain and infallible reason. Those therefore do not keep the true liberty of philosophers who subscribe to some opinion, though otherwise true, either before the thing has been sufficiently perceived, or under the force of passions, prejudices and preconceived opinions, or finally on authority alone. For these impose a clasp upon the spontaneity of judgment.

units.la: 44. Practica libertas est, quâ solam exercere virtutem, bonosque mores, in quocunque statu, tam publico, quam privato, maximè libitum est, quia tantum hoc licitum. Contrarium enim ei quidquam præstare, libertatis non est inditium, sed verum servitium, adeoque impotentis animi simulachrum.
units.tr: 44. Practical liberty is that by which a person chiefly wishes to practise virtue and good morals, in any state, public or private, because this alone is lawful. For to do anything to the contrary is not a sign of liberty but true slavery, and so an image of a powerless mind.

units.la: 45. Poëtica denique libertas est, quæ quisque per normam Artis Logicæ instructus, liberâ fruitur ratione, adeo ut circa unumquodque cognoscibile actus cognitioni debitos pro libitu applicando, versari possit; eosque actus ex suæ voluntatis beneplacito ad accuratam rerum cognitionem indagandam, instituere. Et hæc de effectis Philosophiæ absolutis: Sequuntur
units.tr: 45. Finally, poetical liberty is that by which each person, instructed by the rules of the Art of Logic, enjoys free reasoning, so that he can apply the acts due to knowledge at his pleasure concerning anything knowable, and can set those acts in motion, at the good pleasure of his will, to investigate an accurate knowledge of things. And this is said of the complete effects of Philosophy. There follows:

units.la: 46. Relata, quibus utilitas Philosophiæ continetur. Ejus autem utilitas ad quatuor capita reduci potest. Usum scilicet præbet 1. in cognitione Dei, 2. in cognitione sui 3. in aliis disciplinis & facultatibus. 4. in communis Vitæ actionibus.
units.tr: 46. The relations in which the usefulness of Philosophy consists. Its usefulness can be reduced to four heads. It is of use (1) in the knowledge of God; (2) in the knowledge of oneself; (3) in other disciplines and faculties; (4) in the actions of common life.

units.la: 47. Ad cognoscendum Deum utilis est Philosophia, non tantum quatenus ipsa naturalem Dei scientiam, tanquam sui partem, nobis suggerit, sed potius, quòd ipsum Deum ejusque attributa, triplici illa via, vel causalitatis, vel eminentiæ, vel negationis, ex operibus ipsius rite cognitis, deprehendamus; simulque exinde amorem ac reverentiam Dei in nobis accendamus ac augeamus.
units.tr: 47. Philosophy is useful for knowing God, not only insofar as it suggests to us the natural knowledge of God, as a part of itself, but rather because we grasp God himself and his attributes, by that threefold way of causality, eminence, or negation, from his works rightly known; and at the same time we kindle and increase in ourselves the love and reverence of God.

units.la: 48. Seipsum cognoscit homo per Philosophiam, non tantum ratione essentiæ & proprietatum, sed etiam ratione suæ dignitatis præ reliquis fermè Creaturis, ut & vilitatis ratione Creatoris; ut dignoscat, quid valeat, quid ad sui conservationem ac debitas actiones requiratur.
units.tr: 48. A man knows himself through Philosophy, not only with respect to his essence and properties, but also with respect to his dignity above almost all other creatures, and to his lowliness with respect to the Creator; so that he may discern what he is capable of, and what is required for his self-preservation and proper actions.

units.la: §9. In aliis discip̄linis tantum præstat Philosophia usum, ut non tantum omnes insigniter promoveat, sed & plerasque ipsarum unicè stabiliat; Quod, ut pateat, in specie breviter ostendendum.
units.tr: §9. Philosophy is of such use in the other disciplines that it not only greatly advances all of them but also establishes most of them uniquely. To make this clear, it must be shown briefly in particular.

units.la: §0. Cum igitur illæ disciplinæ vel liberales sint, ut Theologia, Jurisprudentia, Medicina & Magia Naturalis, vel mechanicæ & quasi serviles, quorsum omnes spectant artes, ad commodum hominis instituta; Nulla inter ipsas excogitari poterit, quæ Philosophiæ insignem non experiatur usum.
units.tr: §0. Since those disciplines are either liberal, such as Theology, Jurisprudence, Medicine and Natural Magic, or mechanical and almost servile, all of which aim at the convenience of man, no discipline can be thought of among them that does not experience the notable use of Philosophy.

units.la: §1. Illum vero usum necessarium in Theologicâ Disciplinâ, tam ad διδασκαλίαν, quam ad ἔλεγχον, tam luculenter ostendit Keckermannus, lib. 1. Præcogn. Philosoph. cap. 4. ut ipsi aliquid superaddere, soli facem accendere merito videri possit. Ut mirandi, vel potius dolendi sint illi, tam qui Pastori futuro, nihil nisi quod ad Cathedram Ecclesiasticam proximè pertinet, discendum aut utile esse, magno suo damno, sive ex odio, sive ignorantiâ, autores sunt; quam qui Philosophiam Theologiæ contrariari ac repugnare clamitant.
units.tr: §1. Keckermann shows that use, which is necessary in theological discipline, both for instruction [διδασκαλίαν] and for refutation [ἔλεγχον], so clearly, book 1, Praecognita Philosophiae, chapter 4, that it may rightly seem that he is adding a torch to the sun. Those are to be wondered at, or rather pitied, who, to their great loss, whether from hatred or ignorance, declare that for the future minister nothing is to be learned or is useful except what pertains most closely to the ecclesiastical chair; and those too who loudly complain that Philosophy is at odds with and opposed to Theology.

units.la: §2. Iurisprudentia, quatenus disciplina est, utilis est Philosophia, non tantum ratione Logica, communis omnium facultatum instrumenti; sed & ratione 1. Metaphysicæ, quatenus hæc principia & Axiomata generalia tradit, ex quibus non solum contemplativæ, sed & practicæ conclusiones speciales sunt educendæ. 2. Physicæ, quâtenus juris naturalis subjectum, objectum & fundamentum ex rerum naturalium cognitione exoritur. Hoc autem jus naturale omnis æquitatis & juris est fundamentum; Quæ enim rerum natura prohibentur, nullâ lege confirmata sunt, leg. 188. §. 1. D. de Reg. Juris. 3. Mathescos, quâtenus justitia tam commutativa, quam distributiva, proportione quâdam utitur, cujus naturam explicare puræ est Mathescos. 4. Ethicæ, Oeconomicæ & Politicæ, utpote quæ secundum jus naturale bonum ac justum à contrariis separant.
units.tr: §2. Jurisprudence, insofar as it is a discipline, is useful from Philosophy not only in respect of Logic, the common instrument of all the faculties, but also in respect of (1) Metaphysics, insofar as it delivers those general principles and axioms from which not only theoretical but also practical special conclusions are to be drawn; (2) Physics, insofar as the subject, object and foundation of natural law arise from knowledge of natural things. This natural law is the foundation of all equity and right: "For those things which are forbidden by the nature of things are not confirmed by any law," Digest, law 188, §1, De regulis iuris; (3) Mathematics, insofar as justice, both commutative and distributive, uses a certain proportion, the nature of which to explain belongs purely to Mathematics; (4) Ethics, Economics and Politics, inasmuch as they separate the good and the just from their contraries according to natural law.

units.la: §3. Medicina tam utilis, imo necessaria est Physica, ut nihil in ipsa sciri cognosci, aut præstari possit, quod ex rerum Naturalium cognitione non deducatur. Quamobrem & nonnulli eam Physicæ subalternatam esse crediderunt; Quod utut ratione principiorum verum sit, subjecti tamen & finis ratione fallit. Eadem quoque necessitas est Logicæ & Metaphysicæ, illius ut instrumenti, hujus ut fundamenti generalis. Considimiliter ipsi utilis est Mathesis, quâtenus sine hac ne quidem consistit Physica. Nolim tamen consimilem utilitatem Astrologiæ judiciariæ ad Medicinam esse existimes. Nimis enim remota, & maximè fallacia illa venditat signa, ubi Medici propinquiora & certiora domi habent.
units.tr: §3. Medicine is so useful, indeed necessary, to Physics that nothing can be known, understood or performed in it that is not deduced from knowledge of natural things. For this reason some have believed it to be subordinate to Physics; which, though true in respect of its principles, is false in respect of its subject and end. The same necessity applies to Logic and Metaphysics, the former as an instrument, the latter as the general foundation. Likewise Mathematics is useful to it, insofar as Physics does not even exist without this. I would not, however, have you think that judicial astrology has a similar usefulness for Medicine. For it offers signs that are too remote and very deceptive, when physicians have nearer and more certain ones at home.

units.la: §4. Magia Naturalis, quorsum & Chymiam refero, occultiores corporum Naturalium virtutes, à Physicâ suggestas, artificio quodam detegens ac applicans, non nisi Physices specialis fructus est; eam igitur, ut radicem & arborem suam, requirit & præsupponit.
units.tr: §4. Natural Magic, to which I also refer Chemistry, which by a certain art uncovers and applies the hidden powers of natural bodies, suggested by Physics, is nothing but a fruit of special Physics; it therefore requires and presupposes Physics as its root and tree.

units.la: §5. Mechanicis Artibus quoque non mediocre confert Philosophia, licet ipsi Artifices id raro advertant. Tota Architectura in varias subordinatas Artes dispersa, non nisi Geometriæ fructus est, quem admodum Statica, Nautica, &c. Ita Venatoriæ omnes Physicæ ope utuntur; probant & Agricultura, Pistoria, ac statuaria: Idem in reliquis experiri non est difficile.
units.tr: §5. Philosophy also contributes no small amount to the mechanical arts, although the craftsmen themselves rarely notice it. All architecture, dispersed into various subordinate arts, is nothing but a fruit of Geometry, as are Statics, Navigation and so on. Thus all hunting uses Physics; agriculture, baking and sculpture also prove it. It is not difficult to experience the same in the rest.

units.la: §6. Denique in communibus Vita actionibus utilitatem quoque suam præstat Philosophia, quatenus ipsa nobis præscribit regulas & leges agendi, operandi, vivendi, prout communes in naturâ notiones, ut mensuræ & regulæ assumi possunt, ad ea mensuranda ac regulanda, quæ ab homine produci debent; Et vicissim, ut ex iis facta, mores & studia hominum exigamus ac æstimemus, videndo an illa his rerespondeant & consentiant, an vero ab iis deflectant & dissentiant. Consimiliter dum Philosophia rerum perfectiones ac dignitates ponderat, ac suo pretio æstimat, multum facit ad deliberationes & consultationes recte instituendas, docens, quid sit eligendum, quid fugiendum, quid laudandum, quid vituperandum. Et quantum confert ad vitæ sustentationem, uxoris electionem, Prolis procreationem, alimentorum ac possessionum comparationem?&c.
units.tr: §6. Finally, Philosophy also offers its usefulness in the common actions of life, insofar as it prescribes for us rules and laws of acting, working and living, since the common notions in nature can be taken as measures and rules, to measure and regulate those things which must be produced by man. And conversely, so that from these we may judge and assess the morals and pursuits of men, seeing whether those things correspond and agree with these, or rather deviate from and disagree with them. Likewise, while Philosophy weighs the perfections and dignities of things and estimates their worth, it does much to conduct deliberations and consultations rightly, teaching what is to be chosen, what avoided, what praised, what blamed. And how much it contributes to the support of life, the choice of a wife, the begetting of offspring, the acquisition of food and possessions, etc.?

units.la: 57. Et cum tam necessarium polliceatur Philosophia finem, quis de usu ejus omnigeno dubius esse poterit? cum nihil debite ab homine fieri posse certum sit, quod mentis quandam perfectionem non sapiat. Et hæc de Definitione & essentia Philosophiæ, sequitur ipsius in partes suas distributio.
units.tr: 57. And since Philosophy promises an end so necessary, who could doubt its use in every respect? For it is certain that nothing can be rightly done by man that does not savour of some perfection of the mind. And so much for the definition and essence of Philosophy; there follows its division into parts.

units.la: 58. Partes autem Philosophiæ vel generales sunt, vel speciales: Illæ sunt, quæ ad omne cognoscibile se extendunt: Hæ vero quæ certam aliquam classem certi ac determinati finis gratia considerant. Generales partes duæ sunt, Metaphysica & Logica; Quarum illa in genere omne Ens, quoad attributa communia suggerit: Hæc vero modum illum cognoscendi, ac intellectum ad rerum cognitionem dirigendi, cujus supra facta est mentio, tradit.
units.tr: 58. The parts of Philosophy are either general or special. The former are those which extend to every knowable thing; the latter are those which consider a certain class of a certain and determined end. General parts are two, Metaphysics and Logic; of which the former sets forth in general every Being, as to its common attributes; the latter, however, delivers that method of knowing, and of directing the intellect to the knowledge of things, of which mention was made above.

units.la: 59. Speciales partes vel intellectum perficiunt, circa Entium cognitionem in specie, adeoque sunt Scientia; vel Voluntatem, circa ea, quæ homini bona vel mala sunt, dirigunt, unde Prudentia appellantur.
units.tr: 59. Special parts either perfect the intellect, concerning the knowledge of beings in particular, and so are Science; or they direct the will, concerning those things which are good or evil for man, and for this reason are called Prudence.

units.la: 60. Scientia autem illæ duplices sunt, pro duplici genere substantiæ, scilicet vel Mentium vel Corporum. Atque illa quidem vel in genere illa subjecta exhibent, vel secundum species. Mentium Scientia in genere Pneumatica vel Pneumatologia, Corporum vero Somatologia appellari commodè poterit.
units.tr: 60. Sciences of this kind are twofold, according to the twofold kind of substance, namely either of minds or of bodies. And the former either set forth those subjects in general, or according to species. The science of minds may conveniently be called Pneumatics in general or Pneumatology, and that of bodies Somatology.

units.la: 61. In specie autem Mentium scientias seu Pneumatologias speciales alii tres faciunt, Theologiam Naturalem, Angelographiam, & Psychologiam; alii vero illas ad Metaphysicam revocant: Sed sicut hi insigniter confusam farraginem Scientiarum generalium & specialium nobis offerunt; ita & illi formale Philosophiæ subjectum, ex fine, subjecto accausa junctum constitutum, violant, dum Angelos, quorum nec essentia, nec existentia naturali ratione lumine innotescit, ad Philosophiæ ambitum revocant. Duæ igitur, videlicet Theologia Naturalis & Psychologia sufficere videntur.
units.tr: 61. In particular, however, some make three special sciences or pneumatologies of minds, namely Natural Theology, Angelography, and Psychology; others, however, refer them to Metaphysics. But just as the former offer us a remarkably confused hodgepodge of general and special sciences, so the latter violate the formal subject of Philosophy, constituted by the end and the subject joined together, while they bring angels, whose essence and existence are not known by the natural light of reason, within the scope of Philosophy. Two, therefore, namely Natural Theology and Psychology, seem to suffice.

units.la: 62. Quæ verò Scientiæ corpus in species, id est, sub certa aliquâ formâ considerant, vel Physica sunt vel Mathematica; illa ipsum cum essentiali forma & natura considerant; Hæ vero cum Accidentali sive mensura. Physica porro scientiæ, alibi à nobis enumeratæ, prout variæ sunt, pro varietate corporum Naturalium, ad unam tamen totalem tanquam partes, nec præter rationem reducuntur.
units.tr: 62. Those sciences which consider the body of science by species, that is, under some particular form, are either Physical or Mathematical. The former consider the thing itself with its essential form and nature; the latter consider it with its accidental aspect, or measure. The physical sciences, which I have listed elsewhere, are many according to the variety of natural bodies, yet they are all reduced to one whole, as its parts, and do not go beyond this one rationale.

units.la: 63. Mathematicæ autem Scientiæ, vel præcise solam illam mensuram considerant; quare & pura sive abstractæ dicuntur; vel illam ipsam ad subjectum suum applicant, ac cum eo ipsam attendunt; unde mixtæ, sive concretæ appellantur. Quia autem illa mensura duplex est Discreta sive numerus, & continua, sive mensura magnitudinis, duæ quoque puræ erunt scientiæ Mathematicæ, Arithmetica, quæ numerum, & Geometria, angustiori voce, quam par est appellata, quæ omne mensurabile continuum tradit.
units.tr: 63. The mathematical sciences either consider that measure alone, precisely; and so they are called pure or abstract; or they apply that same measure to their subject and consider it together with that subject; and so they are called mixed or concrete. Since this measure is twofold, discrete, that is number, and continuous, that is the measure of magnitude, there will likewise be two pure mathematical sciences: Arithmetic, which deals with number, and Geometry, called by a narrower name than it ought to be, which treats of every continuous measurable thing.

units.la: 64. Mistæ autem vel ad ipsum Corpus referunt suam mensuram; Qualis est Cosmographia, cujus partes principaliores sunt; Astronomia & Geographia. (Astrologiam judiciariam, conjecturâ potius, quam ratione sufultam, nec ad perfectionem mentis requisitam, merito omitto:) Vel ad Qualitatem, affectionemve Corporis illam adhibent; qualis est Optica, circa lucem, lumen & Colores, tamquam obiecta per sensibilia, prout certâ mensurâ fiunt, propagantur ac intereunt, occupata. Cui vulgò adjungitur Musica, circa sonum harmonicum, i. e. legitimâ intensione & extensione, sive duratione constantem, versans: sed hæc potius Mathematicæ & Philosophiæ fructus, quam ejus pars æstimanda: Aures quidem demulcet ac animos, sed mentem nihilo perfectiorem reddit, magisque auditoris, quam authoris & posfidentis gratiâ instituitur; Quod in reliquis partibus Philosophiæ omnibus absonum.
units.tr: 64. The mixed sciences either refer their measure to the body itself, as Cosmography does, whose principal parts are Astronomy and Geography (I rightly omit judicial astrology, which rests on conjecture rather than reason and is not required for the perfection of the mind); or they apply it to a quality or affection of the body, as Optics does, occupied with light, luminous things and colours as objects perceived through the senses, insofar as they are produced, propagated and perish by a certain measure. To this is commonly added Music, which deals with harmonious sound, that is, sound that remains constant in lawful intensity and extension or duration. But this is to be regarded as a fruit of mathematics and philosophy rather than a part of it: it indeed soothes the ears and minds, but does not make the mind any more perfect, and it is pursued more for the sake of the listener than of the author and possessor. This would be absurd in all the other parts of philosophy.

units.la: 65. Prudentia, regulam Vitæ, tam communis, ut in Ethicâ, quam speciālis, sive Privatæ, ut in Oeconomicâ, sive Publicæ, ut in Politica, tradentes, quoniam ex lumine Naturæ, ac innato quasi discrimine honesti & turpis, ad mentis perfectionem, ad quam non minus τελείωσις τῶν ἠθῶν, quam Θεωρία τῶν ὄντων requiritur, adspirant, quin Philosophiæ partes sint, dubitari non potest. Attamen quoniam lapsu Adami valde obnubilatum, imò fere extinctum est, istud interioris conscientiæ; sive legis naturalis cordibus inscriptæ, lumen, ejusque rudera saltem circa externos Virtutum actus aliquatenus emicent, nunquam ipsæ ex purâ naturâ perfectionem ac finem, qui est hominis summum bonum adipisci possunt. Quare ad aliud principium revocandæ videntur, ubi adæquata iustius regulæ mensura, forma, finis ac perfectio proponuntur; Scilicet ad Observantiam, Theologiæ revelatæ posteriorem partem. Non secus ac Botanicam & Physiologiam corporis humani Medicinæ ultrò, licet prodigâ nimis liberalitate concedunt, nonnulli ex Philosophis.
units.tr: 65. Prudence, which teaches the rule of life, both general, as in Ethics, and particular, whether private, as in Economics, or public, as in Politics, aspires, since it arises from the light of nature and from an innate sense, as it were, of the honourable and the base, toward the perfection of the mind, which requires the completion of the morals (τελείωσις τῶν ἠθῶν) no less than the contemplation of beings (Θεωρία τῶν ὄντων). That it is therefore parts of philosophy cannot be doubted. Yet, since that inner light of conscience, or of the natural law written in hearts, has been greatly obscured, indeed almost extinguished, by the fall of Adam, and only its remnants shine forth to some extent in the external acts of virtue, they can never attain from pure nature the perfection and end which is man's highest good. Therefore they seem to be referred to another principle, where the adequate measure, form, end and perfection of a more just rule are set forth: namely, to Observance, the later part of revealed theology. Some philosophers, indeed, concede too freely and lavishly that Botany and the Physiology of the human body belong to medicine.

units.la: 66. Atque bisce partibus earumque membris Philosophiæ Corpus absolvitur: Ad hoc autem complendum, certus quidam inter ipsas ordo requiritur, qui potissimum hic Doctrinæ & cognitionis erit. Ordo enim inventionis ex Historiâ Philosophicâ petendus, curiositatem magis, quam hujus loci utilitatem sapit. Et fortean dici posset, eas omnes partes origine simul fuisse; Id sanè in Adamo in statu integritatis collocato obtinuisse videtur; Et licet detrimentum satis insigne lapsu Adami passæ sint, aliquid tamen ex singulis, licet longè imperfectiori modo, in ipso reliquum fuisse, (quamvis nec hoc in cæteris obtingat:) non videtur involvere absurditatem quandam. Sed de his alibi. Ordine autem dignitatis, si hic ex subjecto desumendus sit, Speciales præ Generalibus, Scientia præ Prudentiis, Pneumatica præ Somatologiæ partibus, Physica præ Mathematicis Scientiis, primas obtinent. Licet ratione finis & evidentiæ in quibusdam aliter se res habeat.
units.tr: 66. And with these parts and their members the body of philosophy is completed. To complete it, however, a certain order among them is required, which here will chiefly be the order of teaching and knowledge. For the order of discovery is to be sought from the history of philosophy, and this savours more of curiosity than of usefulness for this place. Perhaps it could be said that all these parts arose at the same time; this seems to have been so in Adam, placed in the state of integrity. And although they suffered considerable damage through the fall of Adam, it does not seem to involve any absurdity that something of each remained in him, though in a far more imperfect manner (although this does not hold for the others). But of these things elsewhere. In the order of dignity, if this is to be drawn from the subject, the special sciences take precedence over the general, science over prudence, pneumatology over the parts of somatology, and physics over the mathematical sciences. Yet in some cases, with respect to end and evidence, the matter stands otherwise.

units.la: 67. Ordo autem Doctrina, vel est in partibus tradendis, vel ipsis addiscendis; Et in discendis quidem, requiritur processus a Generalibus ad speciales partes; Quare omnium prima est Ars Logica, generalem modum cognoscendi suppeditans; cui conjungatur, aut immediatè succedat Metaphysica; Neutiquam enim hæ duæ, quarum una sine altera ne constat quidem, sejungi debent. In specialibus opera danda, ut simul cum scientiis addiscantur Prudentiæ; ne aliàs dum scientiâ sumus tamquam Angeli alati, vitâ reddamur serpentes, humi repentes. Inter Scientias autem Somatologia antecedat Pneumaticam. Mathematica Physicam; Psychologia Theologiam Naturalem, ut ita in Deo, Ente singularissimo, nostræ perfectionis, ipsius respectu satis imperfectæ, quæramus complementum.
units.tr: 67. The order of teaching is either in the parts as they are delivered or in the parts as they are learned. In learning, a progression is required from the general to the special parts. Hence the first of all is the art of Logic, which supplies the general method of knowing; to this should be joined, or immediately follow, Metaphysics; for these two, of which neither exists without the other, ought by no means to be separated. In the special sciences care must be taken that the prudences are learned together with the sciences, lest, while we are like winged angels in knowledge, we become serpents crawling on the ground in life. Among the sciences, somatology should precede pneumatology, mathematics physics, and psychology natural theology, so that in God, the most singular Being, we may seek the completion of our perfection, which is rather imperfect in comparison with him.

units.la: 68. In tradendis verò partibus observetur ordo, huic priori quoad ejus fieri potest convenientissimus; Quare Logicæ subjungatur Metaphysica; & huic omnes scientiæ speciales, adeo ut prudentiis ultimus reservetur locus. Sin cui vix placeat iste ordo, ei dicam, cum Clariss. Kypero p. m. perinde fermè esse, ubi aliquid tractetur, modo bene tractetur. Solent quippe nec omnes omnium partium tractationem suscipere, nec omnes omnium partium noritiam quærere: sed pro libitu, aut majoris commoditatis gratiâ, hanc vel illam partem à reliquis avocare; Prout inpræsentiarum Metaphysicas Institutiones separatim subornare animus fert.
units.tr: 68. In delivering the parts, however, an order should be observed that is as closely as possible in agreement with the former one. Hence Metaphysics is to be subjoined to Logic, and all the special sciences to it, so that the last place is reserved for the prudences. But if anyone scarcely likes this order, I shall tell him, with the most distinguished Kyperus of blessed memory, that it makes almost no difference where something is treated, provided it is treated well. For people usually neither undertake the treatment of all parts nor seek knowledge of all parts; rather, as they please, or for the sake of greater convenience, they detach this or that part from the rest, just as at present my inclination leads me to prepare the Metaphysical Institutes separately.

units.la: SECTIO II. DE Natura Metaphysica.
units.tr: SECTION II. On the Metaphysical Nature.

units.la: I. INter scientiæ cujuscunque præcognita illa potissimum consideranda, quæ ad naturam & constitutionem ipsius pertinent; Quare operæ pretium me facturum existimo, si ante ipsius Entis scientiam, aliquid de ipsâ scientiâ in limine præmoneam. Id autem, post nominis considerationem, commodè ad hæc tria capita revocari poterit, ut inquiratur 1. in ejus existentiam 2. In essentiam 3. in divisionem.
units.tr: I. Among the preliminaries of any science, those are chiefly to be considered which pertain to its nature and constitution. I therefore think it worth while, before the science of Being itself, to say a few things about the science in its introduction. These can conveniently be brought under three heads, after the consideration of the name, so that we inquire 1. into its existence, 2. into its essence, and 3. into its division.

units.la: 2. Variis autem nominibus hæc Entis Scientia appellatur, inter quæ vulgatissimum est Metaphysica: Sed cum omnes disciplinas nomen à Subjecto sive Objecto tractationis, sortiri conveniens sit, non immeritò æstimare quis posset, Generalem hanc Entis scientiam rectius Ontologiam, ut vult Calovius, aut Ontosophiam, ut æstimat Lobkowitz, quam Metaphysicam. cam appellari. Etenim ob compositionem ex praepositione μετά vox non tantum ambigua videtur, modò post, modò supra Physicam constitutam disciplinam, prout Interpretes ajunt, significans: Sed & praeterea vox illa ab oppositi vel diversi negatione defumta est, adeoque ipsius scientiae esse, à subjecto desumto, minimè est conveniens. Et tandem post vel supra aliud esse, relationem aliquam denotat, adeoque aliquid ipsâ scientiâ posterius.
units.tr: 2. This science of Being is called by various names, of which the most common is Metaphysics. But since it is proper for every discipline to take its name from its subject or object of treatment, one might reasonably judge that this general science of Being should be called Ontology, as Calovius wishes, or Ontosophy, as Lobkowitz thinks, rather than Metaphysics.
