For the word, compounded from the preposition meta [μετά], seems not only ambiguous, sometimes meaning after and sometimes above, as the commentators say, of the discipline constituted after Physics. Besides, the word is taken from the negation of an opposite or different thing, and so it is not at all suitable for the science itself when derived from its subject. Finally, to be after or above something else denotes some relation, and so something posterior to the science itself.

units.la: 3. Nolim tamen exinde conjicias, Philosophum suæ tractationi inconveniens nomen tribuisse; Non enim omninò eadem est Metaphysica Aristotelis cum Scholasticorum Metaphysicâ, aut eâ, quam hic tractabimus, Ontologiâ. Philosophus Theologiam tractat, ut patet ex 6 Met. cap. 3. & 11. Metaph. cap. 6. Scholastici farraginem plurium disciplinarum, (quales sunt Ontologia, Angelographia, Psychologia, & Categoriarum seu Praedicamentorum confideratio:) miscent. At nos universalem Entis scientiam proponimus.
units.tr: 3. Yet I would not have you conclude from this that the Philosopher gave a name unsuited to his treatment. For the Metaphysics of Aristotle is not altogether the same as the Metaphysics of the Scholastics, or as the Ontology we shall treat here. The Philosopher treats of Theology, as is clear from Metaphysics 6, chap. 3, and Metaphysics 11, chap. 6. The Scholastics mix together a hodgepodge of several disciplines (such as Ontology, Angelology, Psychology, and the consideration of the Categories or Predicaments). But we propose the universal science of Being.

units.la: 4. Aristotelis itaque Metaphysicæ pulchrè conveniunt nomina & encomia, quibus eam exornavit; Qualia sunt Philosophia, Philosophia prima, Sapientia & Theologia. Ea tamen Ontologiæ accommodari nec omnia, nec tam aptè poterunt, nisi hæc forte Prima Philosophia, aut Sapientia nomine ne aliquando venire possit. Illius quidem, quatenus communissima, quæ & prima dicuntur, attributa considerat, aut quòd reliquis scientiis in accurato ordine præmittatur. Hujus verò, quatenus immediatè ex primis, & solâ terminorum apprehensione notis principiis proximas elicit conclusiones; id est, quâtenus intelligentiam proximè cum scientiâ conjunctam habet. Sed de his, ut & aliis nominibus, quibus Encomia ejus contineri videntur, latius inter ejus proprietates.
units.tr: 4. Thus the names and praises with which Aristotle adorned his Metaphysics fit it beautifully: such as Philosophy, First Philosophy, Wisdom, and Theology. Yet not all of these, nor so aptly, can be applied to Ontology, unless perhaps the names First Philosophy or Wisdom may sometimes apply to it. The former considers the attributes that are most common, which are also called first, or because it is placed before the other sciences in the proper order. The latter, insofar as it draws its conclusions immediately from first principles known from the mere grasp of terms, that is, insofar as it has understanding closely joined with science. But concerning these and the other names by which its praises seem to be contained, I shall speak more fully among its properties.

units.la: 5. Ad rem igitur conversis, primò inquirenda ejus existentia, de quâ quæritur; An necessariò talis aliqua Entis scientia, à reliquis disciplinis distincta, dari debeat? Resp. per affirmationem. Cum enim 1. Generalia generaliter, & specialia specialiter tractanda sint, non minus quoque generalissima, qualia sunt Metaphysica, generalissimo modo sunt consideranda. At quid aliud est, generalissimo modo considerari, nisi in generalissimâ disciplinâ, quæ necessariò scientia erit generalissima, siid tractandum sit τὸ ὄν, sive scientificum. Jam verò Ens in genere sumtum est Ens, & subjectum scientificum generalissimum. Ergo in generalissimâ aliquâ scientiâ, distinctâ à specialibus omnibus, tractari debet. Atilla est Ontologia, vel Metaphysica.
units.tr: 5. Turning, then, to the matter itself, we must first inquire into its existence, which is in question: Must some such science of Being, distinct from the other disciplines, of necessity exist? Answer: Yes. For, first, since general things must be treated generally and special things specially, the most general things, such as Metaphysics, must be considered in the most general way. But what else is it to be considered in the most general way than to be considered in the most general discipline, which must necessarily be the most general science, since being [τὸ ὄν], or what is knowable, is to be treated? Now Being taken in general is Being, and the most general scientific subject. Therefore it must be treated in some most general science, distinct from all the special ones. And that is Ontology or Metaphysics.

units.la: 6. II. Posito uno relatorum, alterum
units.tr: 6. II. When one of two correlatives is posited, the other must be posited too.

units.la: poni necesse est : Quare positis scientiis speciaribus actu & de facto, non debet denegari generalis, utpote ipsis relative respondens: Hujus enim respectu illæ speciales, & illarum hæc generalis appellatur.
units.tr: Therefore, since special sciences exist actually and in fact, a general science, which corresponds to them relatively, must not be denied. For with respect to it those are called special, and it is called the general science with respect to them.

units.la: III. Cum omnis discipl na discursiva ex precedente oriatur cognitione, aut dabitur progressus in infinitum, aut una aliqua prima & universalis scientia, quæ ex infitis,aut saltem solo terminorum contextu & intuitiva apprehensione intellectuali notis principiis, immediatas elicit conclusiones, ex quibus reliqua cognitio discursiva specialis, per succedentes demonstrationes ratiocinando educetur : At quænam erit illa, si Metaphysica expellatur?
units.tr: III. Since every discursive discipline arises from prior knowledge, either there will be a progress to infinity, or there is some one first and universal science which, from principles innate or at least known from the mere context of terms and from intellectual intuitive apprehension, draws immediate conclusions, from which the rest of the special discursive knowledge is reasoned out through successive demonstrations. But what will that science be, if Metaphysics is cast out?

units.la: 7. IV. Omnis conclusio scientifica, etiam specialis, ex immediatis debet oriri præmissis, ipsa conclusione generalioribus: At illæ præmissiæ non possunt esse universalissima, & ex terminis nota principia, si subjectum sit speciale. Non enim universalissimum & speciale immediatè concluduntur. Quare quædam requiruntur principia intermedia, inter demonstrata tamen generalia, proximè ex illis, quæ ex intelligentiâ terminorum fiunt, deducta, quæ ratione ipsius intelligentiæ sunt conclusiones: Atque adeo subjectum habent, & scientifica sunt ; Quæ proinde Subjecti & Scientiæ erunt generalis: Qualis illa nostra præsupponitur.
units.tr: 7. IV. Every scientific conclusion, even a special one, must arise from premises immediate to it and more general than the conclusion itself. But those premises cannot be the most universal principles known from terms if the subject is special. For the most universal and the special are not immediately concluded from one another. Therefore certain intermediate principles are required, demonstrated as general, drawn immediately from those that arise from the understanding of terms, which by the nature of that understanding are conclusions. And so they have a subject and are scientific; these will therefore belong to a general subject and science, such as that of ours which is presupposed.

units.la: 8. V. Et de facto plurimi termini communes in specialibus disciplinis occurrunt, qui tamen per se nõri non sunt, adeoque explicatione opus habent; quæ in singulis specialibus institui, ob tautologiam, & sæpius frustrà iteratam repetitionem, non potest: ac proinde generalis aliqua scientia constituenda, generalium istorum terminorum explicationem, ut propriam, sibi vendicans. VI. Imò & specialibus scientiis sunt sua communia principia, quæ tamen ex naturâ terminorum immediatè non fluunt, adeoque demonstratione quâdam indigent. Quorum tamen demonstratio in specialibus istis institui nequit, ob tautologiam, ac generalium & specialium confusionem. Quare in generali aliquâ & ipsis propriâ scientiâ eorum demonstratio instituenda. Illa igitur ut detur, necesse est.
units.tr: 8. V. In fact, many common terms occur in special disciplines which are not known in themselves, and so need explanation. This cannot be done in each special discipline, because of tautology and the often vainly repeated repetition. Therefore some general science must be set up, claiming for itself as its own the explanation of these general terms. VI. Indeed, the special sciences also have their own common principles, which do not flow immediately from the nature of the terms, and so need some demonstration. Yet their demonstration cannot be carried out in those special disciplines, because of tautology and the confusion of general and special matters. Therefore their demonstration must be carried out in some general science that belongs to them. So it is necessary that such a science exist.

units.la: 9 VII. Et cum quælibet Scientia subjectum suum præsupponat præcognitum; Neque tamen specialis aliqua scientia subjectum ex terminis planè notum obtineat, neque immediatè ex notitiâ terminorum eductum, necessariò concedenda est talis aliqua scientia, in quâ subjecta specialium scientiarum prænoscuntur; quæque, ut vu'gò dicimus, reliquis scientiis sua subsubjecta praescribat; Quae procul omni dubio erit Metaphysica. Hisce rationibus superaddi possunt, aliae aliorum rationes, quae tamen potissimum à subjecto & modo considerandi omnes desumuntur; Adeoque ad unam, miris modis ac formis contortam, revocari possunt: Vt Metaphysicos Autores consulenti manifestum est.
units.tr: 9. VII. And since every science presupposes its subject as already known, and yet no special science has a subject that is wholly known from its terms, nor one drawn immediately from knowledge of the terms, there must of necessity be granted some such science in which the subjects of the special sciences are known beforehand: a science which, as we commonly say, prescribes their subordinate subjects to the other sciences. Without doubt this will be Metaphysics. To these reasons other reasons of other men may be added, but these are drawn chiefly from the subject and the mode of consideration, and so can be reduced to one, twisted into wonderful shapes and forms, as is plain to anyone who consults the Metaphysical authors.

units.la: 10. Unum tamen restare videtur, ut scilicet ostendatur, hanc scientiam ab aliis distinctam esse: Sunt enim qui ad Theologiam, sunt qui ad Logicam referunt; Et quidam ad Theologiam revocari non posse, si non ex allatis rationibus, vel ex detectione causae erroris dilucidè parere poterit. Ea enim haec fuit, quod vulgares Metaphysici etiam de Deo agerent, cujus cognitionem omnem sibi voluerunt vendicare Theologi: Sed nec hi, nec illi recte. Metaphysicae fas non est ad specialia, multo minus ad specialissimum descendere; Nec Theologi, lumen naturae, cum revelatione, quidquid urgeant, unquam confundent.
units.tr: 10. One thing, however, still seems to remain, namely, to show that this science is distinct from the others. For some refer it to Theology, and some to Logic. And some think it cannot be reduced to Theology, unless it clearly follows from the reasons already given, or from the detection of the cause of the error. For the cause was this: the common Metaphysicians also treated of God, and the Theologians wished to claim all knowledge of him for themselves. But neither group does so rightly. Metaphysics may not descend to the special, much less to the most special; nor do the Theologians ever confuse the light of nature with revelation, however they press it.

units.la: 11. Circa Logicam vero major videri posset dubitationis species, quod plurima ipsis sint communia; Utraque enim generalis, & circa omne Ens est; Nec reliquae scientiae sine utraque constant; multaque consimiliter in utraque tractantur. Major tamen inter utramque intercedit diversitas. Differunt quippe 1. Genere, quod Metaphysica est scientia strictè dicta: Logica verò Artis.
units.tr: 11. Concerning Logic, however, there may seem to be a greater kind of doubt, because many things are common to them. For both are general and concern every Being; nor do the other sciences exist without either; and many things are similarly treated in both. Yet a greater difference lies between the two. For they differ, first, in genus: Metaphysics is science strictly so called, while Logic is an Art.

units.la: 2. Subjecto tractationis, quod Metaphysica est Ens omne, quatenus simpliciter Ens est: Logica verò finis suum ipsius subjectum est tractationis, directio scilicet mentis in rerum cognitione. Vide qq. Logicæ Elenchticæ 3. Subjecto operationis & usus, quod Metaphysica nullum: Logica verò omne intelligibile est. 4. Subjecto informationis, quod Metaphysica proprie nullum, Logica verò Mens humana. 5. Fine, qui Metaphysica est nuda Entis contemplatio, Logica autem directio Mentis & operatio. 6. Effectis variis, Metaphysica fundamentum, Logica vero instrumentum reliquis suppeditat; Metaphysica demonstrat, Logica modum demonstrandi tradit; Metaphysica aliis scientiis subjectum præscribit. At tale nihil Logica, &c. 7. Medio demonstrationis & cognitionis, quod in Metaphysica simpliciter demonstrativum, ex proximis & propriis principiis, in Logica autem simpliciter didascalicum. 8. Ordine tractationis, qui in Metaphysica synthuticus, à principiis ad affectiones: in Logica verò analyticus à fine ad media. 9. Latitudine objecti; Metaphysica Ens reale cognoscendum tradit, Logica modum cognoscendi omne intelligibile proponit. Quare diverso modo utraque generalis, & circa omne Ens est, & sine utrâque reliquæ non constant, multaque eadem in utrâque tractantur. Metaphysica generale est fundamentum: Logica instrumentum; Metaphysica est circa omne Ens, ut subjectum tractationis, Logica ut operationis; Reliquæ non constant sine Metaphysicâ, ut fundamento, sine Logicâ, ut instrumento; Ea quæ communiter tractant, uni per se, alteri per accidens sunt adjudicanda. Plura de his, tam differentiis, quam convenientiis in qq. Logicæ Elenchticæ suggeram.
units.tr: 2. In the subject of treatment: Metaphysics is all Being, insofar as it is simply Being; but Logic's subject is direction of the mind in the knowledge of things, its end and subject of treatment. See the Elenctic Questions on Logic, 3. In the subject of operation and use: Metaphysics has none, but Logic is every intelligible thing. 4. In the subject of information: Metaphysics properly has none, but Logic is the human mind. 5. In the end: Metaphysics is the bare contemplation of Being, but Logic is the direction and operation of the Mind. 6. In its various effects: Metaphysics supplies the foundation to the other sciences, Logic the instrument; Metaphysics demonstrates, Logic hands down the method of demonstrating; Metaphysics prescribes the subject to the other sciences, but Logic prescribes nothing of the kind, etc. 7. In the medium of demonstration and knowledge: in Metaphysics it is simply demonstrative, from proximate and proper principles, but in Logic simply didactic. 8. In the order of treatment: in Metaphysics it is synthetic, from principles to affections; but in Logic it is analytic, from end to means. 9. In the breadth of the object: Metaphysics teaches that real Being is to be known, Logic sets forth the mode of knowing every intelligible thing. Therefore, in different ways both are general, and both concern every Being, and the other sciences do not exist without either, and many of the same things are treated in both. Metaphysics is the general foundation, Logic the instrument; Metaphysics is about every Being as the subject of treatment, Logic as the subject of operation; the other sciences do not exist without Metaphysics as their foundation, nor without Logic as their instrument; things treated in common by both are to be assigned to one essentially and to the other accidentally. I shall offer more on these matters, both differences and agreements, in the Elenctic Questions on Logic.

units.la: 12. Venit nunc indaganda essentia Metaphysicæ, ubi expendenda 1. ejus definitio.
units.tr: 12. Next we must examine the essence of Metaphysics, and here its 1. definition must be weighed.

units.la: 2. Proprietates. Definitur autem Scientia Entis, quatenus ens est. In quâ definitione notandum 1. Genus, Scientia. 2. Subjectum tractationis, reliquis definitionis verbis expresse indigitatum.
units.tr: 2. Properties. Metaphysics is defined as the science of being, insofar as it is being. In this definition note: 1. the genus, which is science; 2. the subject of treatment, expressly indicated by the other words of the definition.

units.la: 13. Genus ejus esse scientiam, scilicet strictè dictam, ex definitione scientiæ praeced. sect. thes. 9. satis elucet; Cui adjungi possent, omnes scientiæ proprietates, quales sunt, ordine synthetico tradi, necessarias conclusiones per principia de subjecto ostendere, ex principiis educere affectiones, &c. si id necessitas postularet.
units.tr: 13. That its genus is science, strictly so called, is clear enough from the definition of science in the preceding section, thesis 9. To this could be added all the properties of science: that it is taught in synthetic order, that it demonstrates necessary conclusions from principles concerning its subject, that it draws out affections from principles, and so on, if necessity demanded it.

units.la: 14. Quia igitur scientia est Metaphysica, omnia quoque ipsi conveniunt, quæ ad esse scientiæ in genere requiruntur, sive subjectum inhæsionis, sive causæ, sive effecta, five proprietates omni scientiæ convenientes fuerint; Quæ tamen omnia pro naturâ subjecti ipsi propria ac particularia evadunt. Quare si quæras, cur in definitione Metaphysicæ, æquè ac in definitione Philosophiæ, non fiat mentio causæ efficientis ac finis? Respondebo, eorum generalem mentionem implicitè fieri in posito genere, quod sufficit; Expressè enim poni in definitione speciei, quod ad essentiam generis spectat, Logices præcepta vetant. Specialem verò mentionem ex posito subjecto esse hauriendam. Quoniam igitur demonstrativa est omnis scientia, vel progrediendo ab universalibus ad specialiora, vel regredien- do ab his ad illa, per inductionem demonstrativam, consimilis quoque est Metaphysica, ex naturâ notis principiis generales demonstrans conclusiones, & has vicissim singularium enumeratione comprobans. Unde simul patet, quare in definitione non addatur, Metaphysicam proximè cum intelligentiâ conjunctam esse; Quia enim generalissima est scientia, ut ex subjecto palam est, proximè ad intelligentiam accedere debet.
units.tr: 14. Since Metaphysics is therefore a science, all the things that belong to it and that are required for the being of a science in general also belong to it, whether they are the subject of inherence, or causes, or effects, or properties common to every science. Yet all these things become proper and particular to it, according to the nature of its subject. So if you ask why, in the definition of Metaphysics, just as in the definition of Philosophy, no mention is made of the efficient and final cause, I reply that their general mention is implicitly made in the genus given, which is enough. For the rules of Logic forbid stating expressly in the definition of a species what belongs to the essence of the genus. The special mention is to be drawn from the subject given. Since every science is demonstrative, whether by proceeding from universals to more specific things or by reasoning back from these to those through demonstrative induction, Metaphysics is similar: from notions that are known by nature it demonstrates general conclusions as principles, and in turn confirms these by enumerating the singulars. From this it is also plain why no addition is made in the definition that Metaphysics is most closely joined with intelligence. For since the science is most general, as is evident from its subject, it ought to come close to intelligence.

units.la: 15. Sicut circa Genus hujus disciplinæ vix differsus est inter Philosophos, ita è contra, circa subjectum, cujus est scientia, vix reperies consensum, aliis hoc, aliis aliud statuentibus. In definitione nostrâ
units.tr: 15. Just as there is hardly any disagreement among philosophers about the genus of this discipline, so on the contrary, about the subject of which it is the science, you will hardly find agreement, some positing one thing and others another. In our definition

units.la: dicitur Metaphysica Entis quâtenus Ens est, scientia. In quo subjecto proponitur 1. Materiale. 2. formale. Materiale est Ens, quod nec semper idem significat, nec eodem modo capitur. Significatautem hic tantũ,id quod esse verum,reale ac positivum, id est, proprie dictum, obtinet: non autem omne illud, de quo aliquid affirmatè dici potest;alias enim vel ipsius attributa & affectiones formaliter Entia forent. Et quidem in priori significatu sumitur, vel in actu signato, vel in actu exercito. Priori modo accipitur pro communi aliquâ notione, vicem generis vel quasi generis à suis speciebus abstracti,aut abstracte consideráti, gerente: posteriori autem pro ipsis speciebus ac speciérum speciebus, quotquot in exercitio de istâ notione participant; Quomodo hîc accipi debet. Quare Entis scientia hîc idem est, quam scientia omnium eorum, quae esse tale verum ac positivum habent: Ea autem sunt ipsa singularia, ut in seqq. ostendetur. Omnium igitur singularium, quorum tale est esse, Scientia est Metaphysica.
units.tr: Metaphysics is called the science of being, insofar as it is being. In this subject two things are set out: 1. the material; 2. the formal. The material is being, which does not always mean the same thing nor is taken in the same way. Here, however, it means only that which has true, real and positive existence, that is, properly speaking; not every thing of which something can be affirmatively said, for otherwise the attributes and affections of things would formally be beings. Now it is taken in the former sense, either in the signified act or in the exercised act. In the first way it is understood as some common notion which serves in place of a genus or quasi-genus, abstracted from its species or considered abstractly; in the second way it is understood as the species themselves and the species of species, as many as participate in this notion in actual use, and this is how it must be understood here. Hence the science of being here is the same as the science of all those things that have such true and positive being. These are the singulars themselves, as will be shown in what follows. So the science of all singulars whose being is of this kind is Metaphysics.

units.la: 16. Ab hac igitur Metaphysicâ exulare debent. 1. Quæ verum esse non habent, ut denominationes externa, Relationes, Entia in potentiâ. 2. Quæ non habent esse reale, ut sunt Modi Entium, Entia rationis, Entia ficta, & notiones secunda. 3. Quæ non habent esse positivum, ut privationes, negationes &c. Hæc enim omnia à materiali objecto excluduntur.
units.tr: 16. Therefore these must be banished from Metaphysics: 1. those things that do not have true being, such as external denominations, relations, beings in potency. 2. those things that lack real being, such as modes of beings, beings of reason, fictitious beings, and second notions. 3. those things that lack positive being, such as privations, negations, and so on. For all these are excluded from the material object.

units.la: 17. Alii nominaliter vel participialiter Ens sumi ajunt; Verum 1. nominaliter sumtum ens est, quod potentiam ad esse habet, non verò est. 2. Non potest explicari nisi per participium. 3. Ei non competunt Entis attributa originalia, quæ vulgò principia dicuntur, essentia nempe & existentia. Participialiter sumi ajunt, pro eo quod revera [suum esse habet]; Hic autem nominaliter sumi ajunt, non participialiter. Sed cum hoc ultimum solum Ens sit, ejusque attributa habeat, omnino tantum hujus loci esse debet. Nec obstat, quod singulare sit; nihil enim in rerum natura præter singularia datur, quæ si sine notis hic & nunc considerentur fiunt universalia. Præterquam quod singularitatis forma ab ipsis in Metaphysica auferatur, quoniam sub conceptibus omnium generalissimis considerantur: Hoc enim formale subjectum involvit.
units.tr: 17. Others say that being is taken nominally or participially. But 1. being taken nominally is what has a potency to be but is not. 2. It cannot be explained except through the participle. 3. The original attributes of being, commonly called principles, namely essence and existence, do not belong to it. They say it is taken participially for that which really [has its being]; here, however, they say it is taken nominally, not participially. But since this last alone is being and has its attributes, it ought to belong wholly and only to this place. Nor is it an objection that it is singular; for in the nature of things nothing is given except singulars, and if these are considered without the marks of here and now, they become universals. Besides, the form of singularity is removed from them in Metaphysics, since they are considered under the most general concepts, for this involves the formal subject.

units.la: 18. Circa explicationem autem subjecti formalis, notandum 1. Quare hoc additur? 2. Quid hoc proprie significet? Circa primum videri posset, frustra addi, illud quatenus Ens est, quia æquè Physica scientia, & tamen simpliciter corporis naturalis est; omnis enim scientia simpliciter suum subjectum considerat. Verum enim vero nisi hoc formale adderetur, sola Metaphy‐ sica effet scientia, utpote omnia Entia, fe‐ cundùm omnes suas rationes ac notiones consideranś, quemadmodum omnia illa illo materiali subjecto sunt indigitata. Quare alia ratio est Physicæ, cujus ma‐teriale & formale æquè patent, ac cui ad specialia ac inferiora omnia decendere licet, ac Metaphysicæ, cujus materiale ad omnia fe quidem extendit, at per forma‐ le ad certam quam rationem contrahi‐tur. Additur igitur, ut denotetur modus, quo Metaphysica omnia illa singularia; ve‐rum, reale ac positivum esse habentia, tra‐ctet, ne videlicet quosvis eorum conce‐tus sibi vendicando, panfophias titulum sibi aflumat, reliquasque scientias folio de‐ turbet. Et quidem omnis scientia sim‐pliciter suum subjectum confiderat, sed quâtenus hoc ex materiali & formali suo constat.
units.tr: 18. In explaining the formal subject, note 1. why this is added? 2. what this properly means? As to the first, one might think it added in vain, namely insofar as it is being, since Physics is equally a science and yet is simply the science of natural body; for every science considers its subject simply. Indeed, if this formal element were not added, Metaphysics alone would be a science, since it would consider all beings according to all their grounds and notions, just as all those things are indicated by that material subject. So Physics has a different ground: its material and formal aspects are equally extensive, and it may descend to all special and lower things. Metaphysics, by contrast, extends its material aspect to all things, but through its formal aspect it is restricted to a certain ground. So it is added in order to denote the mode in which Metaphysics treats all those singulars that have true, real and positive being, lest, by claiming for itself any of their concepts, it assume for itself the title of pansophy and dethrone the other sciences. Indeed every science considers its subject simply, but insofar as this consists of its material and formal aspects.

units.la: 19. Quoad fecundum quæritur, quid proprie significetur, hac limitatione, quâ‐tenus Ens est? Vulgò reduplicativè vel spe‐ cificativè, fumi hanc particulam quâ vel quâtenus, Lexici Autores sunt, quod ut avidè fatis arreptum à Metaphysicis, ita tamen non fatis evidenter explicatum ac applicatum; Quare statuendum, hanc par‐ ticulam fumi, ut notet vel sensum compo‐ situm, vel divisum; sensum compositum quidem, quatenus idem ad seipsum limitat & quasi reduplicat, ut homo qua homo: Divisum vero, quando idem per aliud limitat sive specificat, ut homo qua Animal est sentiens. Ex quibus videtur consequi, hanc particulam hic sumendam esse in priore modo, quia scilicet Ens refert ad seipsum. Quod quidem verum esset, si idem denotaret Ens hoc limitans, quod limitatum. Hoc vero in actu exercito sumi supra ostensum est: At limitans in actu signato sumi debet, quatenus videlicet collectionem conceptuum communium denotat; alias enim omnia Entia in specie considerarent quoad proprias rationes Metaphysica. Et si hoc sit reduplicative sumi, omninò negandum videtur, quatenus in hac limitatione reduplicative accipi debere: Quod confirmatur, quia de quatenus reduplicative sumto valet haec regula Logicorum, à quatenus ad omne valet consequentia; adeoque tali modo accipi debet, quando licet ad specialia omnia descendere, ut in Physica. At specificative tum sumitur, quando ad specialia digredi fas non est, ut hic.
units.tr: 19. As to the second point, what is properly meant by this limitation, insofar as it is being? Lexicographers say the particle qua, or quatenus, is commonly taken reduplicatively or specificatively. Metaphysicians have eagerly seized upon this, yet it has not been sufficiently clearly explained or applied. We must therefore establish that this particle is taken to indicate either a composite sense or a divided sense. The composite sense is when it limits and as it were reduplicates the same thing by itself, as man qua man. The divided sense is when it limits or specifies the same thing through something else, as man qua animal is sentient. From these points it seems to follow that this particle must be taken here in the former way, since being refers to itself. That would indeed be true if the limiting being and the limited being were the same. But it has been shown above that this is taken in the exercised act, whereas the limiting element must be taken in the signified act, insofar as it denotes the collection of common concepts. Otherwise all beings would be considered in species, according to their proper grounds, as Metaphysics would then do. And if this is to be taken reduplicatively, it seems altogether to be denied that in this limitation it should be understood reduplicatively. This is confirmed by the rule of the logicians that a consequence holds from quatenus taken reduplicatively to everything. Therefore it must be understood in that way when one may descend to all special things, as in Physics. But it is taken specificatively when it is not lawful to digress to special things, as here.

units.la: 2o. Formale igitur objectum per hanc limitationem excludit quosvis rerum particulares conceptus, quibus vel secundum proprium esse, vel quoque aliquod aliud genericum, non tamen universalissimum, conconcipiuntur. Quare de Deo, Angelis, mente humana, Prædicamentis, cæterisve Entibus in specie Metaphysica agere nequit, citra manifestam ἀμεθοδίαν, & formalis subjecti violationem. At Metaphysica illa cognoscenda tradit, quæ ab aliis scientiis ob nimiam generalitatem excluduntur; adeoque tam ad hanc, quam ad illam specialem pertinerent; in quibus si tractarentur, præter maximum πευτὸ λογίας vitium, nulla quoque scientia determinatum haberet subjectum.
units.tr: 20. Therefore the formal object, through this limitation, excludes any particular concepts of things by which they are conceived either according to their own being or also according to some other generic notion that is not most universal. So Metaphysics cannot treat of God, angels, the human mind, the categories, or other beings in particular, without a manifest unmethodical procedure [ἀμεθοδίαν] and a violation of the formal subject. Rather, Metaphysics teaches those things that are to be known and that other sciences exclude because of their excessive generality, and so they would belong equally to this science and to that special one. If these were treated in it, then, besides the great fault of verbosity [πολυλογίας], no science would have a determinate subject.

units.la: 21. Quandoquidem igitur omnia Entia, quatenus de communi ac generali notione entis participant, Metaphysica considerat, non adæquatum posuêre ejus subjectum I. Qui illud Deum, Ens unicum ac singularissimum esse contendunt. II. Qui Ens creatum illud constituunt; nam nec hoc generale & adæquatum est, nec ipsi omnes affectiones ac divisiones accommodari possunt. III. Qui aut substantiam in communi, aut substantiam immaterialem ponunt, ob easdem scilicet rationes. IV. Qui Ens quâ immateriale faciunt; nam & hoc formale nimis angustum, nec generale est. 2. Planè hoc æquivocum est formale. Quid enim immateriale secundum essentiam & secundum indifferentiam præter nomen habent commune? 3. Et generalia & quædam specialia simul involvit hoc formale. At nulla ratio dari potest, quare de unâ magis quam de alterâ specie generalis disciplina agat. Quemadmodum contra latius debito illud subjectum ponunt, qui omne intelligibile, seu Ens in generalissimâ significatione hujus subjectum esse volunt. Non enim id genus esse potest, ne quidem analogum. 2. Nec per se cognoscibile est, aut communes assectiones obtinet. 3. Præterquam, quod & sic principia & affectiones subjecti nullæ dari possent, de quibus & subjectum formaliter dici non posset. II. Qui omne Ens secundum omnes rationes ac notiones suas etiam singularissimas huc referunt: Confundunt quippe generalia ac specialia, & omnium scientiarum multitudinem, à subjecto desumendam, tollunt.
units.tr: 21. Since Metaphysics considers all beings insofar as they share in the common and general notion of being, those who have assigned it an inadequate subject have done so in the following ways. I. Those who contend that its subject is God, the one and most singular Being. II. Those who make it a created being; for this is neither general nor adequate, and not all its affections and divisions can be applied to it. III. Those who posit either substance in general or immaterial substance, for the same reasons. IV. Those who make it being qua immaterial; for this formal object is too narrow and is not general. 2. Indeed, this formal object is equivocal. For what do immaterial things have in common, according to essence and according to indifference, beyond the name? 3. This formal object also involves general and some special matters at once. Yet no reason can be given why a general discipline should treat of one species rather than another. Conversely, those who posit the subject too broadly, wanting every intelligible thing, or being in its most general sense, to be the subject of this science, err on the other side. For this cannot be a genus, not even an analogous one. 2. Nor is it knowable in itself, nor does it possess common affections. 3. Besides, on this view no principles or affections of the subject could be given, of which the subject itself could not be formally predicated. II. Those who refer every being, according to all its notions and concepts, even the most singular, to this science, confound the general and the special, and remove the multitude of sciences, which ought to be distinguished by their subjects.

units.la: 22. Sequuntur Proprietates Metaphysicæ,ex hac definitione resultantes, quæ vel sunt propria officia & effecta, vel propria attributa. Officia ejus vel generalia sunt vel specialia. Generale officium est, ut quemadmodum omnium reliquarum disciplinarum, naturæ lumine acquisitarum, fundamentum est, ita utilitates istas omnes, supra Philosophiæ concessas, superiori quodam ordine promoveat ac adjuvet, adeò ut ejus usus nullibi deesse possit.
units.tr: 22. There follow the properties of Metaphysics, which result from this definition. These are either its proper offices and effects, or its proper attributes. Its offices are either general or special. Its general office is this: just as it is the foundation of all the other disciplines acquired by the light of nature, so it advances and assists, in a certain higher order, all those uses which are granted beyond philosophy, so that its use can be lacking nowhere.

units.la: 23. Specialia munera ratione scientiarum varia sunt, ita quippe 1. Dum prin-
units.tr: 23. The special functions vary according to the sciences. Thus, indeed, 1. while

units.la: cipia ab aliis scientiis præsuppofita, aut demonstrat, aut immediatè ex conceptibus eruit, reste dicitur ejus officium esse, aliarum scientiarum defendere principia. 2. Et quia ubi aliæ scientiæ incipiunt, hæc definit, aliis subjectum præscribere dicitur. 3. Et quia terminos generales, in specialibus scientiis occurrentes, explicat, mirificè quoque confert tam γνώσεως quam ἀναλύσεως reliquarum scientiarum. Sed de his aliisque Metaphysicæ officiis abundè dicetur, in tractatu tertio, ubi ejus utilitas explicabitur & applicabitur.
units.tr: it either demonstrates the principles presupposed by other sciences, or derives them immediately from concepts, it is rightly said that its office is to defend the principles of the other sciences. 2. And because it sets the limits where the other sciences begin, it is said to prescribe the subject to them. 3. And because it explains the general terms occurring in the special sciences, it also greatly contributes to both the knowledge [γνώσεως] and the analysis [ἀναλύσεως] of the other sciences. But these and the other offices of Metaphysics will be discussed at length in the third treatise, where its usefulness will be explained and applied.

units.la: 24. Inter propria attributa hæc sex potissima sunt. I. Quod sit scientia accuratissima, id est clarissima ac distinctissima; ut pote quæ ex maximè primis principiis deducitur, adeo ut reliquæ scientiæ ejus principia præsupponant; Unde & hac in parte Mathematicas scientias superat, in se & actu signato spectata. Quod enim Mathematicæ demonstrationes evidentiores videantur, quam Metaphysicæ, id non vitio Metaphysicæ, sed incuriâ Metaphysicorum factum est.
units.tr: 24. Among its proper attributes, these six are the chief. I. That it is the most accurate science, that is, the clearest and most distinct, since it is deduced from the most primary principles, so that the other sciences presuppose its principles. Hence in this respect too it surpasses the mathematical sciences, considered in themselves and in their actual exercise. That mathematical demonstrations seem more evident than metaphysical ones is not the fault of Metaphysics, but the result of the negligence of metaphysicians.

units.la: 25. II. Quod sit scientia præstantissima; ubi notandum, scientiæ alicujus præstantiam ex triplici oriri posse fundamento. 1. Ex dignitate subjecti. 2. Ex evidentiâ Medii, seu demonstrationis. 3. Ex fine & usu. Primo modo non est dignissima; nisi etiam ad ipsam referatur Theologia naturalis; Cum alias universalissima minimæ sint entitatis ac dignitatis: At duobus posterioribus modis reliquas superat omnes, ob summam evidentiam ac utilitatem.
units.tr: 25. II. That it is the most excellent science. Here it should be noted that the excellence of any science may arise from a threefold foundation: 1. from the dignity of its subject; 2. from the evidence of its middle term, or demonstration; 3. from its end and use. In the first way it is not the most worthy, unless natural theology is also referred to it, since otherwise the most universal things have the least entity and dignity. But in the latter two ways it surpasses all the rest, on account of its great evidence and usefulness.

units.la: 26. III. Quòd sit Sapientia; non quòd sit integra Philosophia, nisi ratione usus & fundamenti, nec quòd sit præstantissimi subjecti; sed potius 1. quòd aliquo modo omnia cognoscenda tradat. 2. Quòd sit præstantissima scientia. 3. quòd immediatè ex intelligentiâ deducatur.
units.tr: 26. III. That it is Wisdom. Not that it is the whole of philosophy, except in respect of use and foundation, nor that its subject is the most excellent; but rather 1. that in some way it teaches all things that can be known; 2. that it is the most excellent science; 3. that it is deduced immediately from understanding.

units.la: 27. IV. Quòd sit Domina; Dominium autem ejus in summâ utilitate, fundatione, ac quadam dependentiâ inferiorum ab ipsâ constitit.
units.tr: 27. IV. That it is Mistress. Its dominion consists in its great usefulness, its role as foundation, and a certain dependence of the inferior sciences upon it.

units.la: 28. V. Quòd sit ordine naturæ, adeoque & doctrinæ, reliquis omnibus prior. Maximè quippe generalis est adeoque proximè ad intellectum accedit.
units.tr: 28. V. That by the order of nature, and so also of teaching, it is prior to all the rest. For it is the most general and therefore comes closest to the intellect.

units.la: 29. VI. Quòd reliquæ scientiæ ipsi subalternentur. Quod tamen laxiori vocis acceptione intelligendum; Quam ut capias, nota, triplicem esse ordinem scientiarum inter se 1. Coordinationem 2. Subordinationem. 3. Subalternationem. Prima est inter scientias tales, quarum subjecta sunt species unius generis, v. gr. inter θεολογίαν & ἀνθρωπολογίαν. Secunda est inter scientias, quarum unius subjectum est species vel pars alterius subjecti, qualis v. gr. inter Metaphyficam & reliquas omnes. Tertia hanc subordinationem praefupponit, & vel late sumitur vel stricte. Late 1. pro fola fubordinatione. 2. Pro communione mediorum seu principiorum. 3. Pro consensu finium. Stricte vero sumitur, quatenus priores tres modos includit, & simul illi inferiori vel partiali subjecto accidentalem quam differentiam superaddit; Quomodo frænefactoria est subalternata equestri: non autem reliquae scientiae Metaphysicae, ut pote quae & propria habent principia & proprios fines; nec accidentalem, sed essentialem addunt subjecto differentiam; Nec Medicina Physicae, quia subjectum tractationis Medicinae, quod est ejus finis, non continetur, ut species vel pars, sub subjecto Physicae. Et haec de essentia Metaphysicae, sequitur de ejus divisione judicium.
units.tr: 29. VI. That the other sciences are subalternated to it. This, however, must be understood in a looser sense of the word. To grasp it, note that there is a threefold order among the sciences: 1. coordination; 2. subordination; 3. subalternation. The first obtains between sciences whose subjects are species of one genus, for example between theology [θεολογίαν] and anthropology [ἀνθρωπολογίαν]. The second obtains between sciences of which the subject of one is a species or part of the subject of another, as for example between Metaphysics and all the rest. The third presupposes this subordination and is taken either broadly or strictly. Broadly, it means: 1. subordination alone; 2. the sharing of means or principles; 3. agreement of ends. Strictly, it is taken insofar as it includes the former three modes and at the same time adds to that inferior or partial subject an accidental rather than essential difference. Thus the art of bridle-making is subalternated to horsemanship. But the other sciences are not subalternated to Metaphysics, since they have their own principles and their own ends, and they add an essential, not accidental, difference to the subject. Nor is Medicine subalternated to Physics, because the subject of medical treatment, which is its end, is not contained, as species or part, under the subject of Physics. And these things concern the essence of Metaphysics; the judgment about its division follows.

units.la: 30. Recepta quorundam divisio est Metaphysica in partem Generalem & Specialem. Sed quoniam Deus, Angeli, Mentes humanae, aliaeque Entis species, jam alteri foro sunt adjudicatae, & absurdum fit, Scientiae generalis quaerere partem specialem; Et quoque Ens qua Ens, ejus subjectum, respuat species, ut pote ad illas indifferens; ejusque finis sit generalis Entis cognitio, cum species specialem finem requirant; & denique omnino generalitas ad illam scientiam requiratur, quæ proximè ad intelligentiam accedit, sepelienda videtur ista divisio; nisi partem specialem voces illam, quæ usum Metaphysicæ asserit; aut quæ est de generalibus affectionibus singulis; adeò ut generalis sit quæ Ens, ejusque Principia & affectiones in genere tradit. Et hæc de natură Metaphysicæ, sequuntur reliqua prænoscenda, quæ exhibet
units.tr: 30. The division of Metaphysics into a General and a Special part is received by some. But since God, angels, human minds, and the other species of being have already been assigned to another discipline, and since it is absurd for a general science to seek a special part; and since Being qua Being, its subject, rejects the species as indifferent to them; and its end is the general knowledge of being, whereas the species require a special end; and finally, since generality is required of that science which comes closest to understanding, this division seems to be buried. Unless one were to call a special part that which asserts the use of Metaphysics, or that which concerns the individual general affections, so that the general part is that which treats of Being, its principles and affections in general. And with this concerning the nature of Metaphysics, the remaining things to be known beforehand, which it sets forth, follow.

units.la: SECTIO. III.
units.tr: SECTIO. III.

units.la: DE Prærequisitis. CAP. I.
units.tr: On the Prerequisites. CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Ente.
units.tr: On Being.

units.la: 1. PRærequisitum Scientiæ primarium est ejus subjectum, quod ut constituatur præcognitum esse debet 1. Ratione exi-stentiæ, quòd sit, 2. Ratione essentiæ, quâtenus nomine certo ac definitione quâ distinguente exprimitur. 3. Ratione attributorum, quæ ipsi ut sit subjectum convenire debent. Præsupponit quippe omnis scientia suum subjectum esse in rerum naturâ, ididque, aliquâtenus & ex parte cognitum, habere principia quædam & affectiones sibi debitas, quæ nec minus quomodo ad illud subjectum sese habeant, cujusque sint naturæ, prænoscenda.
units.tr: 1. The first prerequisite of a science is its subject, which, in order to be established as known beforehand, must be known (1) with respect to its existence, that it is; (2) with respect to its essence, insofar as it is expressed by a certain name and a distinguishing definition; (3) with respect to the attributes which must belong to it as its subject. For every science presupposes that its subject exists in the nature of things, and therefore that it has, and is in some measure and in part known to have, certain principles and affections proper to it; and these must also be known beforehand, both how they stand in relation to that subject and what their nature is.

units.la: 2. Subjectum autem Metaphysicæ constitutum est Ens, quod dari omni dubio caret, illi, qui seipsum esse, Deinde existentiam necessariam certè & infallibiliter cognoscit; vel si sensuum judicio itare vel-lit, perplurima hinc inde sibi occurrentia advertit.
units.tr: 2. The subject of Metaphysics, however, is set down as Being, which admits of no doubt that it is given, for it is known with certainty and without fail to anyone who knows himself to exist and, next, that necessary existence; or, if he should wish to rely on the judgment of the senses, he notices very many things presenting themselves to him on every side.

units.la: 3. Quid nomine Entis significetur, & quomodo hoc accipiendum, supra ostensum est: Hic tamen repetendum, Ens hic non tam late sumi, ac quid, seu aliquid, sed solum denotare. Ens verum, reale ac positivum. Unde facile dijudicamus, quid sentiendum sit de synonymis Entis, qualia dicuntur esse Aliquid & Res.
units.tr: 3. What is signified by the name of Being, and how this is to be understood, has been shown above; yet it must be repeated here that Being is not taken here so broadly as "what" or "something", but only denotes what is true, real and positive. Hence we can easily judge what is to be thought of the synonyms of Being, such as are said to be Something and Thing.

units.la: 4. Primò enim aliquid aut idem est, quod aliud quid, & sic angustius patet quam Ens; Quia Ens quâ Ens non præsupponit aliud quid existere præter se; alias enim Ens ut sic plurialitatem involveret. Vel aliquid est idem quod quid; omne illud denotans, quod non est omninò nihil, sed de quo aliquid affirmatè potest dici; atque ita latius patet, quam Ens hoc Metaphysicum, significans etiam omnia illa, quæ vel Principii vel affectionum Entis rationem obtinent. Hinc facile solvi potest difficultas, an inter Ens & nihil detur medium? Nempe datur, si Ens Metaphysicum designetur: non datur, si Ens idem sit, quod aliquid.
units.tr: 4. First, "something" is either the same as "some other what", and so it is narrower in scope than Being, since Being as such does not presuppose that anything else exists besides itself; otherwise Being would involve plurality. Or "something" is the same as "what", denoting everything that is not altogether nothing, but of which something can be affirmatively said; and so it is broader in scope than this Metaphysical Being, signifying also all those things which have the character of a principle or an affection of Being. Hence the difficulty, whether there is a middle between Being and nothing, can easily be resolved: there is, if Metaphysical Being is meant; there is not, if Being is the same as something.

units.la: 5. Secundò Res, etiam inter synonyma Entis adducta, aliquando idem est, quod aliquid, denotans scilicet, omne, de quo rerum, & sic Ente Metaphysico latius patet. 2. Res est idem quod singulare aliquod, jam actu existens, cum sua singularitatis forma, id est hic & nunc præcise consideratum, quâ significatione, vulgò passim usitatâ, æquipollet Subjecto Metaphysicæ materiali. 3. Denotat res, quidquid habet essentiam veram, & sic fiėto opponitur, Ensque reale denominat, ac latius eo patet. 4. Notat illud quod per se suum esse habet, & sic opponitur Modis ac relationibus, & penè cum Ente coincidit. Ex quibus liquet, totum illud negotium de synonymis Entis infirmo stare talo, & exigui pretii esse, cum Grammaticum potius, quam Metaphysicum sit.
units.tr: 5. Second, "thing", also adduced among the synonyms of Being, sometimes is the same as "something", namely denoting anything about which something can be said, and so it extends more widely than Metaphysical Being. (2) "Thing" is the same as some singular individual, already actually existing, with its form of singularity, that is, considered precisely here and now; in this sense, commonly used everywhere, it is equivalent to the material subject of Metaphysics. (3) It denotes whatever has a true essence, and so it is opposed to fiction, and names real Being, and extends more widely than it. (4) It signifies that which has its being through itself, and so it is opposed to modes and relations, and nearly coincides with Being. From these things it is clear that the whole business of the synonyms of Being stands on a weak heel and is of little worth, since it belongs rather to grammar than to Metaphysics.

units.la: 6. Quoniam igitur Ens Metaphysicum dicitur, quidquid verum, reale ac positivum esse habens, cum aliis, si quæ sint, conceptu universalissimo & communi convenit, porro inquirendum venit, an illi applicari possint, subjecti genuini requisita? Et quidem 1. Cum unius scientiæ unum dedebeat esse subiectum, dubitatur, numne hoc Ens unum quid dici queat; cum de facto plurima Entia dentur, darive possint? Resp. Ens in actu exercito, prout subiectum materiale est, non unum est, sed multa, unitur tamen ratione istius actus signati, seu conceptus, communiter eo formali quâ Ens, expressis.
units.tr: 6. Since, therefore, Metaphysical Being is said to be whatever has being that is true, real and positive, and agrees with other things, if there are any, in the most universal and common concept, it remains to inquire whether the requirements of a genuine subject can be applied to it? And indeed, (1) since one science ought to have one subject, it is doubted whether this Being can be called one thing, since in fact very many beings exist, or can exist. Answer: Being in exercised act, as it is the material subject, is not one but many; yet it is unified by reason of that signified act, or concept, expressed commonly by the formal aspect by which it is Being.

units.la: 7. Sed datur ne talis conceptus communis? Alii prorsus negant, alii analogum concedunt, alii tantum æquivocum, alii etiam, univocum volunt; Alii formalem conceptum analogum dant, sed objectivum negant. Quæstio igitur spinosis subtilitatibus difficilis reddita.
units.tr: 7. But is there such a common concept? Some deny it altogether, some concede an analogous concept, some only an equivocal one, and some want it univocal; some grant a formal concept that is analogous, but deny that it is objective. The question has therefore been made difficult by thorny subtleties.

units.la: 8. Qui negant omnem prorsus conceptum communem, hoc potissimum ducuntur fundamento, quòd inter infinitum & finitum nulla sit proportio. Verum hoc non impedit, quo minus habeant conceptum communem. Nam si esset extensio infinita æquè ac finita, ex proportionem quidem nullam, communem tamen habebunt conceptum, quo utraque extensio aut quantitas dicatur. Quare potius dicemus, aliquem esse communem Entis conceptum, licet is diversimodè ad inferiora se habeat. Nam vel hoc de omnibus concipimus, quod sint, constituta in suo esse, & ab aliis distincta; unde hæctria ipsis communia assignamus 1. esse, i.constitui in eo: 3.ab aliis distingui, quæ communi illo Entis conceptu includuntur.
units.tr: 8. Those who deny any common concept at all are led chiefly by the ground that there is no proportion between the infinite and the finite. But this does not prevent them from having a common concept. For if there were an infinite extension just as there is a finite one, they would indeed have no proportion, yet they would have a common concept by which each extension or quantity is called such. Therefore we shall rather say that there is a common concept of Being, although it relates to its inferiors in different ways. For we conceive of all things that they are, established in their being and distinct from others; hence we assign these three things to them in common: (1) being, that is, to be established in it; (2) being distinct from others; these are included in that common concept of Being.

units.la: 9. Sed an hæc tria omnibus æqualiter conveniunt, hoc est, an ille conceptus est univocus, an analogus, an æquivocus? Resp. Non est plane æquivocus, quia in æquivoco saltem nomen commune est, & nihil rei. Sed hîc præter nomen communis etiam ratio τῶ εἶναι omnibus convenit; utpote quibus hoc commune est, quod inter se ratione scilicet istorum trium, magis conveniant, quam cum nihilo; Omnibus enim illa tria conveniunt, nihilo nullum. Et quidem nec univocum, sed analogum esse hunc conceptum vulgaris suadet ratio; quia illud esse non omnibus æqualiter convenit, ut pote independenti magis, quam dependenti tribuendum. Quod omninò verum est, commodiusque hoc statuitur, quam univocatio à Stoicis, modum illum essendi omittentibus.
units.tr: 9. But do these three belong to all equally, that is, is that concept univocal, analogous, or equivocal? Answer: It is not plainly equivocal, because in an equivocal term there is at least a common name and nothing in the thing. But here, besides the common name, the reason of to be (τὸ εἶναι) belongs to all, since they share this, namely that among themselves, by reason of those three, they agree more than they do with nothing; for all things share those three, and nothing shares none. And indeed common opinion suggests that this concept is not univocal but analogous, since being does not belong to all equally, as it is to be attributed more to the independent than to the dependent. This is wholly true, and it is stated more conveniently than the univocity of the Stoics, who omit that mode of being.

units.la: 10. Ex dictis denique simul manifestum est, non esse illum conceptum communem tantum formalem & purè intentionalem, sed & objectivum; præterquam enim, quod alias non sufficeret ad unitatem subjecti constituendam, nihil quoque hic concipitur, nisi quod in re sive objecto fundamentum habeat; quod tamen formaliter ab inserioribus distinctum est. Qui enim Ens considerat, quâ Ens, sive in illo actu & conceptu Metaphysico, is illud non considerat, ut substantiam aut accidens; ita namque illud consideraret, ut jam restrictum per differentias, quæ neque substantiæ, neque accidentia sunt, in illo tamen conceptu involvuntur.
units.tr: 10. From what has been said it is finally also plain that this common concept is not merely formal and purely intentional, but objective too; for besides the fact that otherwise it would not suffice to constitute the unity of the subject, nothing is conceived here except what has its foundation in the thing or object, which nevertheless is formally distinct from the inferior things. For he who considers Being as such, or in that act and Metaphysical concept, does not consider it as substance or accident; for he would consider it in that way only as already restricted by differences, which are neither substance nor accidents, yet are involved in that concept.

units.la: 11. II. Nec minus dubium est, an huic Enti etiam sua sint principia & affectiones? Cum enim non-Ens non possit esse Entis principium aut affectio, & præter Ens nihil videatur dari posse, hac in parte deficere subjectum Metaphysicæ videtur. Resp. Illa nec nihil prorsus sunt, nec plane formaliter idem cum Ente: diversimodè tamen ipsum Ens afficiunt; quæ diversitas, ut patefiat, hîc de medio illo, inter ens & nihil intercedente, agere consultum est.
units.tr: 11. II. It is no less doubtful whether this Being also has its own principles and affections? For since non-being cannot be a principle or affection of Being, and nothing seems able to exist besides Being, the subject of Metaphysics seems to be deficient in this respect. Answer: Those things are neither altogether nothing nor plainly formally the same as Being; yet they affect Being itself in different ways; and in order that this diversity may be made clear, it is fitting to treat here of that middle which lies between being and nothing.

units.la: CAPUT. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: DE Medio inter Ens & Nihil in genere.
units.tr: ON THE MEDIUM BETWEEN BEING AND NOTHING IN GENERAL.

units.la: 1. MEdium igitur illud, inter Ens Metaphysicum, id est verum, reale, positivum, ac nihil intercedens, generalem postulat tractationem & specialem: In generali
units.tr: 1. That medium, lying between being (metaphysical, that is, true, real, positive) and nothing, calls for a general and a special treatment. In the general treatment the following must be inquired into here.

units.la: {y} ... norali hic inquirendum. 1. An sit tale medium ? 2. Quo nomine appellandum ? 3. Quid rei subsit ?
units.tr: {y} ... In the general treatment the following is to be inquired here: 1. Whether there is such a medium? 2. By what name it is to be called? 3. What underlies the thing?

units.la: 2. Quantum ad primum: Licet superriori cap. sufficienter hujus medii necessitas sit demonstrata, ex eo quod principia & affectiones Entis ipsum Ens formaliter non sint, nec tamen omnino nihil esse possint, hic tamen propius ejus inter Entia præsentia expendenda venit. Quoniam, igitur I. Multa Entibus tribuuntur, quæ si alia entia forent, cum iis compositionem, aut mutationem, ab ipsorum natura alienam, aut processum in infinitum inducerent, necessario videntur concedenda talia quædam, quæ nec omnino nihil, nec quoque præcise ipsum Ens sunt. Talia autem attributa sunt principia & affectiones Entium; item reliquæ denominationes externæ, relationes ac modi Entium. Quæ ideo plane nihil non sunt, quod & inter se differant, ac de Ente suo modo dicantur; Cum nihil à nihilo non differat, neque de Ente quovis modo dici queat.
units.tr: 2. As for the first question: although the necessity of this medium was sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding chapter, from the fact that the principles and affections of being are not formally being itself, yet they cannot be altogether nothing, its place among present beings must be examined more closely. Therefore, first, many things are attributed to beings which, if they were other beings, would introduce a composition or change alien to their nature, or an infinite regress. So it seems necessary to grant certain things that are neither altogether nothing nor precisely being itself. Such attributes are the principles and affections of beings, likewise the remaining external denominations, relations and modes of beings. These are therefore not nothing at all, since they differ from one another and are predicated of being in their own way; for nothing does not differ from nothing, nor can it be predicated of any being in any way.

units.la: II. Idem de facto ex modis entium, Relationibus, Entibus rationis, denominationibus externis, privationibus &c. ostenditur. Hæc enim nemo sanus suo modo dari negabit, nec tamen Entia esse Metaphysica, supra visum, & infra in specie demonstrandum est; Nec quoque prorsus nihil.
units.tr: II. The same is shown in fact from the modes of beings, relations, beings of reason, external denominations, privations, and so on. No sane person will deny that these exist in their own way, yet, as seen above and as will be demonstrated in detail below, they are not metaphysical beings; nor are they altogether nothing.

units.la: 4. Nomen igitur talis medii in genere quod attinet, credo ipsum proprio ac determinato carere, quare id simpliciter medium inter Ens & nihil appellandum censui, donec ipsi de commodiori titulo prospiciatur. Alibi id appellavi Non-Ens, scilicet comparatè ad Ens Metaphysicum sumtum. Observo quoque id alibi appellari Modum Entis, sed presfiori quam par est denominatione, ut infra patebit. Potius nunc, quid rei ipsi subsit, inquirendum.
units.tr: 4. As to the name of such a medium in general, I believe it lacks a proper and determinate one. I have therefore thought it best to call it simply a medium between being and nothing, until a more suitable title is provided for it. Elsewhere I called it Non-Being, namely in comparison with metaphysical being taken as such. I also note that elsewhere it is called a Mode of Being, but with a more precise label than is fitting, as will become clear below. For now, it is better to inquire what underlies the thing itself.

units.la: 5. Circa rem autem multa investiganda occurrere possent, scilicet, quæ hujus causa, utilitas, ratio &c. sed de his in genere vix certi quid afferri potest, quare in præsentiarum rei considerationem absolvam, indagando. 1. Quid sit hoc medium? 2. Quomodo se habeat ad extrema? 3. Qua divisio, ac differentia?
units.tr: 5. Many matters concerning the thing itself could come up for investigation, namely its cause, use, reason, and so on. But little that is certain can be said about these in general, so for the present I will finish with the consideration of the thing by inquiry. 1. What is this medium? 2. How does it stand in relation to the extremes? 3. What is its division and difference?

units.la: 6. Quid sit in genere hoc medium, difficilius est definitu, quam quid sit Ens aliquod. Hoc enim certo generi jam assignatum, illi verò nondum de classe est prospectum, ac plurima quoque etiam toto genere distantia sub se continet. Quare mihi hoc instanti sufficit hæc descriptio, quâ medium hoc dicitur, aliquid abente distinctum ad illud aliquo modo pertinens. Quæ si generalibus nimis terminis concepta alicui videatur, eum rogatum vellem, ut ad commune Theatrum Metaphysicorum convenientiorem afferat. Hæc equidem hoc medium a nihilo simul & Ente distinguit, ejusque habitudinem ac officium ratione extremorum satis effert.
units.tr: 6. What this medium is, in general, is more difficult to define than what some being is. For a being has already been assigned with certainty to a genus, whereas this medium has not yet been given its class, and it contains under it many things that are even widely distant within the whole genus. So for me at this moment this description suffices, by which the medium is said to be something distinct from what is, and pertaining to it in some way. If this seems to anyone conceived in overly general terms, I would ask him to bring a more suitable one to the common Theatre of the Metaphysicians. Indeed, this description distinguishes this medium from nothing and from being alike, and sufficiently brings out its relation and office with respect to the extremes.

units.la: 7. Extrema autem hujus medii sunt Ens Metaphysicum & Nihil, inter quæ non intercedit, ita ut aliquid ab utroque participet; ita enim nihil & Ens Metaphysicum inter se commisceri, ac unum aliquod junctim constituere deberent. Sed potius ut utrumque extremorum de ipso negetur; Licet enim ratione materiæ seu conceptus materialis & identici illud medium vel ens, vel Nihil sit, ratione tamen formæ & conceptus formalis ab utroque distinguitur, ut non possit hoc de aliquo extremorum dici, aut eorum formam induere. Unde quoque dimetienda distantia ipsius ab utroque extremo: Nam hinc patet, quod omne hoc medium, utpote aliquid ratione formæ, magis accedat ad Ens Metaphysicum, quod etiam aliquid est, quam ad nihil. At ratione materiæ quædam propius ad Ens, ut modi, Relationes &c., quædam propius ad nihil accedunt ut Entia rationis, privationes &c.
units.tr: 7. The extremes of this medium are being (metaphysical) and nothing, between which it does not lie, so that it partakes of something from each. For then nothing and metaphysical being would have to mix with one another and constitute one joint thing. Rather, each of the extremes is to be denied of it. For although, in respect of matter, or of material and identical concept, this medium is either being or nothing, yet in respect of form and formal concept it is distinguished from both, so that it cannot be said of either extreme, nor take on their form. Hence its distance from each extreme must also be measured. For it is clear from this that every such medium, as something in respect of form, comes closer to metaphysical being, which is also something, than to nothing. But in respect of matter, some lie nearer to being, such as modes and relations, and others nearer to nothing, such as beings of reason and privations.

units.la: 8. Quoad differentias: Medium hoc vel positivum est, vel negativum. Positivum, est, quod per se adesse dicitur: Negativum vero, quod adest ob absentiam alterius, adeoque in se non est aliquid, sed nihil.
units.tr: 8. As to the differences: this medium is either positive or negative. Positive is that which is said to be present through itself; negative, however, is that which is present on account of the absence of another, and so is not something in itself but nothing.

units.la: 9. Positivum ergo, quod in se aliquid est, vel internum est, vel externum: internum ad ipsam rem pertinet, eamque immutat, si non re, saltem conceptu, estque modus Entis, scilicet stricte dictus; Nam aliqui omne medium modum appellant. Externum vero est, quod rem nullatenus immutat; Eique primum & radicale Relatio, & Ortum ex primo, Denominatio externa.
units.tr: 9. Positive, therefore, which is something in itself, is either internal or external. The internal pertains to the thing itself and changes it, if not in reality at least in concept, and it is a mode of being, strictly so called; for some call every medium a mode. External, on the other hand, is that which changes the thing in no way. To it belong the first and radical relation, and, derived from the first, external denomination.

units.la: 10. Negativum autem medium, quod per se nihil est, sed cui ab intellectu nostro forma affingitur, triplex est. 1. Ens rationis. 2. Ens in potentia. 3. Privatio. Quorum duo priora in forma sua aliquam perfectionem includunt: at privatio meram imperfectionem involvit.
units.tr: 10. The negative medium, which is nothing in itself but to which a form is attributed by our intellect, is threefold: (1) being of reason; (2) being in potency; (3) privation. Of these, the first two include some perfection in their form, but privation involves mere imperfection.

units.la: 11. Haec tria Negativa media a quibusdam etiam Entia rationis appellantur; nec male, ab intellectu enim, quoad formam dependent, & ratione materiae, sive in se, nihil sunt. Nam quando intellectus noster concipit illud, quod non est, ac si esset, dicitur in specie Ens rationis, quemadmodum si conciperet montem aureum, qui non est, ac si esset. At cum intellectus concipit illud, quod non est, ac si posset esse, dicitur Ens in potentia, ut si pullum, qui non est in ovo, concipiam ac si posset esse ex eo. Denique cum concipit intellectus, id quod nihil est in se, ac si deberet esse, tum id nihil privatio dicitur. Quemadmodum si quis concipiat visum, qui cæco non inest, ac si deberet inesse.
units.tr: 11. These three negative media are also called beings of reason by some, and not badly, for they depend on the intellect as to form, and in respect of matter, or in themselves, they are nothing. For when our intellect conceives that which is not, as if it were, it is called in particular a being of reason, as when it conceives a golden mountain, which is not, as if it were. But when the intellect conceives that which is not, as if it could be, it is called a being in potency, as when I conceive a chick, which is not in the egg, as if it could come from it. Finally, when the intellect conceives that which is nothing in itself, as if it ought to be, then that nothing is called privation, as when someone conceives sight, which is not in the blind man, as if it ought to be in him.

units.la: 12. Quæ differentia simul ordinem in speciali mediorum consideratione instituendum ostendit. Priora quippe sunt positiva negativis, & inter illa interna externis; quemadmodum & inter externa prima ortus, & inter negativa, quæ perfectionem designant, iis quæ meram imperfectionem notant. Et denique inter illa, quæ denotant perfectionem præsentem, iis quæ non præsentem significant. Hoc igitur ordine sibi succedent. 1. Modus Entis. 2. Relatio. 3. Denominatio externa. 4. Ens Rationis. 5. Ens in potentia. 6. Privatio, De quibus ordine.
units.tr: 12. This difference also shows the order to be followed in the special consideration of the media. For the positive come before the negative, and among the former the internal before the external; just as among the external the first in origin comes before the derived, and among the negative those which designate perfection come before those which note mere imperfection. And finally, among those which denote present perfection come before those which signify what is not present. In this order they will follow one another: (1) mode of being; (2) relation; (3) external denomination; (4) being of reason; (5) being in potency; (6) privation. These will be treated in that order.

units.la: CAP. III. De Modis Entium.
units.tr: Chapter III. On the Modes of Being.

units.la: 1. Modus Entis, cui primus locus nunc concessus, considerandus est, 1. Quoad nomen. 2. Quoad rem.
units.tr: 1. The mode of being, which now takes the first place, is to be considered (1) as to its name and (2) as to its reality.

units.la: 2. Quoad nomen. 1. sumitur respective ad omne modificatum, atque ita omne modificans significat, sive hoc sit forma, sive differentia qualiscunque, sive qualitas, sive aliud quodvis accidens. 2. Pro omni medio accipitur, quo pacto etiam Relationes modi sunt. 3. Pro tali modificante, quod formaliter non est Ens, ipsum tamen suo modo limitat; Quâ hic significatione expendendus est.
units.tr: 2. As to the name: (1) it is taken relatively to whatever is modified, and so signifies whatever modifies, whether it is a form, any kind of difference, a quality, or any other accident. (2) It is taken for any intermediate, and in this sense even relations are modes. (3) It is taken for such a modifying thing, which is not formally a being, yet limits it in its own way; it is in this sense that it must be weighed.

units.la: 3. Quoad rei explicationem, inprimis adverto insignem difficultatem hujus, partim ob maximam generalitatem ac latitudinem, partim ob nimiam varietatem modorum, ut non mirum sit ingenia Scholasticorum hoc in negotio maximè se torquisse. Neque ipse hic aliud, quam glaciem frangere ausim, conando exponere 1. Quid sit modus? 2. Quid non sit? 3. Quotuplex sit?
units.tr: 3. As to explaining the thing itself, I note first the notable difficulty of the subject, partly because of its very great generality and breadth, and partly because of the excessive variety of modes, so that it is no wonder that the minds of the Scholastics have exerted themselves so greatly on this matter. Nor do I dare here to do more than break the ice, attempting to set out: (1) What is a mode? (2) What is it not? (3) How many kinds are there?

units.la: 4. Quidditas modi definitione hac exprimitur, quod sit alicujus interna & positiva limitatio. Vbi notandum. 1. Genus 2. Subjectum.
units.tr: 4. The quiddity of a mode is expressed by this definition: that it is an internal and positive limitation of something. Where note: (1) Genus; (2) Subject.

units.la: 5. Genus est Limitatio, id est, determinatio, sive restrictio quædam; effectum enim modorum est modificata limitare, seu determinare, adeo ut quodammodo munere formæ sive differentiæ fungantur. Ea tamen restrictio pro diversâ naturâ modorum varia est. Alio enim modo infiniti & immutabiles modi, alio finiti, alio illi, qui saltem formaliter differunt à re, & alio qui tota natura. Burgersdicio, modus dicitur appendicula. Limitans. Sed Limitatio actiua istius appendiculæ etiam modus est, unde sic nullus modus, nisi mediante alio aliquo, ipsi modificato conuenire posset.
units.tr: 5. The genus is limitation, that is, determination or some kind of restriction. For the effect of modes is to limit or determine what is modified, so that in a way they perform the office of form or difference. This restriction, however, varies with the different nature of the modes: in one way infinite and immutable modes restrict, in another finite ones, in another those which differ from the thing only formally, and in another those which differ in their whole nature. Burgersdijk says a mode is called an appendage, limiting. But the active limitation of this appendage is also a mode, so that no mode could belong to what is modified except through some other thing.

units.la: 6. Ex hoc igitur genere, colligi potest modum esse aliquid; quia scilicet omnis limitatio aliquid est: Et quoque modus accedit & recessu suo mutationem, & suâ præsentiâ aliqualem compositionem efficit.
units.tr: 6. From this genus, therefore, it can be gathered that a mode is something, since every limitation is something. Moreover, a mode by its coming and going brings about a change, and by its presence produces a certain composition.

units.la: 7. Sequitur Subjectum, de quo in genere & in specie agendum. In genere est aliquid; non tantum Res, aut Ens: Modificantur enim & illa, quæ Res non sunt; Dantur quippe & modi modorum.
units.tr: 7. There follows the subject, which must be treated in general and in particular. In general it is something, not only a thing or a being: for even those things which are not things are modified, since there are indeed modes of modes.

units.la: 8. In specie circa subjectum, quæritur 1. An omni Enti conueniat modus? Resp. Omninò; Omne enim Ens ab alio distinguitur; distingui autem, limitari, & limitatio modus est. Non tamen quascunque cuilibet Enti conueniunt, sed unicuique debiti.
units.tr: 8. In particular, concerning the subject, the question is: (1) Does a mode belong to every being? Answer: Absolutely. For every being is distinguished from another, and to be distinguished is to be limited, and limitation is a mode. Yet not every mode belongs to every being, but each belongs to the being it is due to.

units.la: 9. Quæritur 2. An igitur & Deo conveniant modi? Resp. Quidni? ut enim taceam distinctionem trium personarum, modo subsistendi distinctarum: Omnis autem distinctio modum præsupponit; talis quoque modi ipsi convenire debent, qui ut affectiones ac principia Entis Metaphysici evadant, inadæquato conceptu modificato convenire apprehenduntur; Prout quoque propria ipsius attributa, quae in se & sensu identico idem sunt cum ipso Deo, formaliter tamen, & inter se, & à Deo distincta non nisi inadaequati quidam modi considerandi sunt.
units.tr: 9. The second question: Do modes also belong to God? Answer: Why not? To say nothing of the distinction of the three persons, which are distinguished by their mode of subsisting: every distinction presupposes a mode, and such modes must belong to him too. These, in order to become affections and principles of metaphysical being, are apprehended as belonging to the modified thing by an inadequate concept. So too his proper attributes, which in themselves and in identical sense are the same as God himself, are to be considered as formally distinct from one another and from God only by certain inadequate modes.

units.la: 10. Sed obiic. 1. Modi limitant: At Deus limitari non potest. Resp. 1. An & quomodo tres illi modi subsistentiae existentiam Dei limitent, nulla ostendit natura ratio, quare de eo Theologi consulendi. 2. Reliqui illi modi Deum extrinsece limitant ad conceptum, & tamen quia infiniti sunt, hoc praestant citra ullam imperfectionem, aut ipsius essentiae coarctationem.
units.tr: 10. But objection 1: Modes limit, but God cannot be limited. Answer: (1) Natural reason shows nothing as to whether, or how, those three modes of subsistence limit the existence of God; so theologians are to be consulted on this point. (2) The remaining modes limit God extrinsically with respect to concept, and yet, because they are infinite, they do this without any imperfection or confinement of his essence.

units.la: 11. Obiic. 2. Modi faciunt mutationem. At Deus immutabilis. Resp. 1. Immutant modi suo accessu & recessu; At Deo nec accedunt, nec ab ipso recedunt. 2. Immutant modi, si sint finiti & mutabiles: Infinitorum autem alia est ratio. 3. Immutant, si non saltem formaliter, sed & ex rei natura à modificato differant. At Attributa Dei saltem formaliter, id est, definitione & inadaequato conceptu à Deo discrepant.
units.tr: 11. Objection 2: Modes bring change, but God is immutable. Answer: (1) Modes change by their coming and going, but neither do they come to God nor depart from him. (2) Modes change if they are finite and mutable; infinite modes have a different account. (3) They change if they differ not only formally but also in the nature of the thing from what is modified. But the attributes of God differ from God only formally, that is, by definition and inadequate concept.

units.la: 12. Obiic. 3. Modi faciunt compositionem: At Deus nullo modo est compositus. Resp. 1. An illi modi ὑπόξεσις divinae infiniti non faciant compositionem aliquam (utpote quæ aliquam distinctionem involvunt, omnis autem distinctio unitorum facit compositionem: ) nolo in præsentiarum disputare, Theologis quod revelatum est concedens.
