Novi quidem, exinde nullam imperfectionem ad Deum redundare, quia juxta Burgersdicium, compositio ex modis finitis & mutabilibus, non autem ex infinitis immutabilibus imperfectionem infert: Sed præterea hos modos subsistentiæ, non autem immediatè esse ipsius essentiæ, & tales nulla ratione imperfectionem, sed si infiniti sint, infinitam, quæ Dei est, perfectionem præsupponere, ratio dictat. 2. Modi faciunt compositionem, sed non omnes eandem; Quare illi modi considerandi Deum non magis faciunt compositum, quam ipsum Ens: Hoc autem saltem conceptu dicitur compositum ex iis, quæ identicè eadem sunt cum ipso, quæ compositio in reipsa nulla est.
units.tr: 12. Objection 3: Modes make a composition, but God is in no way composite. Answer: (1) Whether those modes of the divine subsistence [ὑπόστασις] do not make some composition (inasmuch as they involve some distinction, and every distinction among things united makes a composition) I am unwilling to dispute at present, granting to the theologians what has been revealed. I know indeed that no imperfection flows from this to God, because according to Burgersdijk a composition of finite and mutable modes, not of infinite and immutable ones, brings imperfection. But reason dictates that these modes of subsistence are not immediately of the divine essence itself, and that such modes bring no imperfection at all; if they are infinite, they presuppose the infinite perfection which belongs to God. (2) Modes make a composition, but not all the same kind; so those modes, when considered, make God no more composite than being itself does. He is called composite only in concept, from those things which are identically the same as himself, and this composition is none in reality.

units.la: 13. Quæritur 3. An modus etiam aliis modis conveniat? Resp. Omninò, nec hoc tantum, sed & modis modorum convenit modus; quemadmodum ex. gr. motui, qui modus est, convenit celeritas & tarditas, & hisce etiam certi gradus. Objic. Atqui sic foret processus in infinitum. Resp.
units.tr: 13. Question 3: Does a mode also belong to other modes? Answer: Entirely so, and not only this, but a mode also belongs to modes of modes, just as, for example, speed and slowness, which are modes, belong to motion, and certain degrees to these in turn. Objection: Yet in that case there would be a process to infinity. Answer:

units.la: 1. Is processus inter Entia negatur: sed an pari modo inter puros modos negari debeat, non ita palam est. 2. Processus in infinitum infertur inter ea, quæ vel realiter, vel tota natura differunt, sed modi modorum, ab illis modis, quorum sunt modi, tali modo non distinguuntur; ita v. gr. celeritas aut tarditas motus non distinguitur ex natura rei à motu, quemadmodum nec gradus celeritatis ab ipsa celeritate. 3. Quod semel atque iterum obtinet, non semper progreditur in infinitum; nisi succedentia parem servent entitatem; At modi modorum continuò exiliores fiunt.
units.tr: (1) That process is denied among beings; but whether it should be denied in the same way among pure modes is not so plain. (2) A process to infinity is inferred among things which differ either really or in their whole nature; but modes of modes are not distinguished from those modes of which they are modes in this way. Thus, for example, the speed or slowness of a motion is not distinguished in the nature of the thing from the motion, just as the degrees of speed are not distinguished from speed itself. (3) What holds once and again does not always proceed to infinity, unless the successive items keep an equal entity; but modes of modes grow continually thinner.

units.la: 14. Quæritur 4. An etiam aliis mediis sui sint modi? Resp. Privationi competere videtur; Quia hæc in subjecto est, idque certo modo. Reliquis verò subjectum non requirentibus non convenit modus.
units.tr: 14. Question 4: Are there also modes of other intermediates of their own? Answer: It seems to belong to privation, since it is in a subject, and in a certain manner. But it does not belong to the others, which do not require a subject.

units.la: 15. Restat inquirendum, quid non sit modus? Et quidem 1. Non est omninò nihil; ut pote, quod nec limitat, nec componit, nec mutat. 2. Modus non est res ipsa formaliter; ab illâ enim, tanquam modificatâ, distingui debet: Præterquam, quod si modus res sive Ens esset, ac omni Enti conveniret; jam aliquod ens conveniet omni Enti; cui iterum conveniet suus modus, & sic processus foret in infinitum. Excip. Licet modus discrepet ab illo Ente, cujus est modus, manebit tamen in se Ens. Resp. Non manebit: Dantur quippe modi & omni Enti, & maximæ ipsius parti convenientes, v. gr. duratio, præsentia, & reliquæ Entis affectiones; Quæ Entia nullatenus fieri possunt.
units.tr: 15. It remains to inquire what a mode is not? And indeed: (1) It is not altogether nothing, inasmuch as it neither limits, nor composes, nor changes. (2) A mode is not the thing itself formally, for it must be distinguished from that thing as modified. Besides, if a mode were a thing or being, and belonged to every being, then some being would belong to every being, and to that again its own mode would belong, and so the process would go on to infinity. Objection: Although a mode differs from the being of which it is a mode, it will remain a being in itself. Answer: It will not remain one. For there are modes that belong to every being and to its greatest part, for example duration, presence, and the other affections of being; and these beings could in no way come to be.

units.la: 16. Quæres 2. Quomodo igitur modi ab Ente distinguuntur? Resp. 1. Si ens in se consideretur, differt toto genere à modis; quia ita sumtum sine modis cognoscitur; At si Ens ut modificatum consideretur, modi non nisi formaliter, non identicè ab ipso distinguuntur, hoc est, definitione & conceptu inadæquato; quia sunt quasi formæ & differentiæ modificati, ut suprà visum.
units.tr: 16. You will ask, secondly, how, then, are modes distinguished from being? Answer 1. If being is considered in itself, it differs from modes in its whole genus, because so taken it is known without modes. But if being is considered as modified, modes are distinguished from it only formally, not identically, that is, by definition and by inadequate concept, because they are, as it were, the forms and differences of what is modified, as was seen above.

units.la: 17. Deinde 3. Modus non est privatio; hæc enim absentiam alicujus, modus autem positivam præsentiam denotat. 4. Nec est denominatio externa; quia hæc subjecto non inest, ut modus. 5. Non est relatio, quia hæc in medio duorum subjectorum est, modus autem præcisè in uno.
units.tr: 17. Then, thirdly, a mode is not a privation, for the latter denotes the absence of something, whereas a mode denotes a positive presence. (4) It is not an external denomination, because the latter does not inhere in the subject as a mode does. (5) It is not a relation, because a relation lies between two subjects, whereas a mode is precisely in one.

units.la: 18. Quoad differentias modorum; has tradere non ita in propatulo est, ob insignem ipsorum varietatem, subjecti latitudinem, ac multitudinem ipsorum in eodem subjecto; Quod tamen constat, communicandum. Igitur differentiæ modorum sunt vel communes, sive accidentales, vel propriæ sive essentiales.
units.tr: 18. Concerning the differences of modes: to set these out is not very plain, on account of their remarkable variety, the breadth of the subject, and the multitude of them in the same subject; yet it is agreed that they should be communicated. Therefore the differences of modes are either common, or accidental, or proper, or essential.

units.la: 19. Inter accidentales 1. à connexione modi cum suo subjecto, vel est essentialis vel accidentalis. Essentialis est, qui ad essentiam sui subiecti pertinet: Accidentalis, qui salva manente essentia tolli potest. Essentialis iterum duplex est, Antecedens, ut sunt Entis principia, vel consequens, ut affectiones.
units.tr: 19. Among the accidental differences: (1) from the connection of a mode with its subject, it is either essential or accidental. Essential is that which pertains to the essence of its subject; accidental is that which can be removed while the essence remains. The essential is again twofold: antecedent, as are the principles of a being, or consequent, as are the affections.

units.la: 20. Eadem ratione, 2. modus est vel separabilis à suo subiecto, ut motus ab homine, vel inseparabilis, ut duratio ab Ente.
units.tr: 20. By the same reasoning, (2) a mode is either separable from its subject, as motion is from a man, or inseparable, as duration is from a being.

units.la: 21. Ratione Status & conditionis, 3. modus est vel immutabilis, vel mutabilis, scilicet ratione sui, non subiecti, alias enim cum praecedente coincideret haec distinctio.
units.tr: 21. By reason of state and condition, (3) a mode is either unchangeable or changeable, namely by reason of itself, not of the subject; otherwise this distinction would coincide with the preceding one.

units.la: 22. Ratione status subiecti 4. modus est vel essendi, vel fiendi: Prior est qui est in re constituta, posteriore vero ipsa constituitur; hic tamen respectu constituentis est essendi; Quemadmodum incubatio ovorum ratione constituendi pulli est modus fiendi: at ratione constituentis gallinae modus essendi.
units.tr: 22. By reason of the state of the subject, (4) a mode is either of being or of becoming. The former is that which is in a thing already constituted; the latter is that by which the thing itself is constituted. Yet this latter, with respect to what constitutes it, is a mode of being: thus the incubation of eggs, with respect to the constituting of the chick, is a mode of becoming, but with respect to the constituting hen, a mode of being.

units.la: 23. Essentiales differentiae modorum & Subiecto proprio desumenda videntur, quare modus sic vel est rei, vel alterius modi; quorum ille immediate rei convenit, hic vero mediante alio modo: Ille denominat subiectam rem, hic vero modum, & non rem ipsam, nisi concrete cum modo modificato sumtam.
units.tr: 23. The essential differences of modes seem to be derived also from the proper subject. Hence a mode is either of a thing, or of another mode; of these, the former belongs to the thing immediately, the latter through another mode. The former denominates the subject thing, the latter the mode, and not the thing itself, unless it is taken concretely, together with the mode which modifies it.

units.la: 24. Modi rerum porro vel Generales sunt, omni Enti convenientes, vel speciales huic & illi tantum competentes. Ad generales refero, Principia & ex affectionibus quasdam (non enim omnes per modum modi, sed & quaedam per modum relationum & denominationum externarum &c. concipiendae sunt:) ipsius Entis.
units.tr: 24. Further, the modes of things are either general, belonging to every being, or special, belonging to this or that alone. To the general I refer the principles and some of the affections of being itself (for not all of them are to be conceived by way of a mode; some also are to be conceived by way of relations and external denominations, etc.).

units.la: 25. Speciales modi vel Infiniti sunt, vel finiti. Illi æterni, inseparabiles, immutabiles, infinitam perfectionem involventes, & à se invicem non distincti, adeoque idem in se & cum subjecto sunt: Quod in finitis non requiritur.
units.tr: 25. Special modes are either infinite or finite. The former are eternal, inseparable, immutable, involving infinite perfection, and not distinct from one another; hence they are the same in themselves and with the subject. This is not required in finite modes.

units.la: 26. Finiti modi vel spirituum sunt, vel Corporum; verum quinam illi præter generales, spiritibus proprii sint modi, nondum plenè constat, negari tamen prorsus nequeunt.
units.tr: 26. Finite modes are either of spirits or of bodies. But which modes, besides the general ones, are proper to spirits is not yet fully established, yet they cannot be denied altogether.

units.la: 27. Corporum modi vel simplices sunt, vel compositi; Simplices quinque sunt: Mensura, Motus, Quies, Situs & Figura.
units.tr: 27. Modes of bodies are either simple or compound. There are five simple ones: measure, motion, rest, situation, and figure.

units.la: 28. Mensura est cujuslibet extensi quà talis limitatio. Adeoque vel quantitatis continuæ est, vel discretæ, & hujus, vel numeri, vel temporis; Gradus intensionis, remissionis & perfectionis in qualitatibus ut numeri se habent.
units.tr: 28. Measure is the limitation of any extended thing as such. Hence it is either of continuous quantity or of discrete, and of the latter either number or time. Degrees of intensity, remission and perfection in qualities behave as numbers do.

units.la: 29. Motus est potentia ad exercitium limitatio; Dicituruque ratione exercentis Actio, at recipientis passio. Manente illa motus definitione, is etiam Spiritibus conconveniet. Quare duæ species erunt actionis, Cogitatio, & motus strictè dictus. Prior Spiritibus, posterior corporibus propria est acto.
units.tr: 29. Motion is the limitation of a power to its exercise. It is called action with respect to the one exercising it, and passion with respect to the one receiving it. This definition of motion remaining, it also belongs to spirits. Hence there will be two species of action: thought, and motion strictly so called. The former is proper to spirits, the latter to bodies.

units.la: 3o. Quies est Entis permansio in potentiâ: Quare totidem modis ac motus, qui ipsi contrariè opponitur, dividi debet.
units.tr: 30. Rest is the permanence of a being in a power. Hence it must be divided into as many modes as motion, which is opposed to it directly.

units.la: 31. Situs est ordo partium vel corporum inter se; Huc ergo pertinent 1. Sex positionum differentiæ: Antrorsum, retrorsum: dextorsum, sinistrorsum: superum, inferum: Quæ quidem strictè loquendo solis animantibus convenient, at latiori acceptione etiam reliquis corporibus. 2. Ad situm spectat, gestus ac habitus corporis.
units.tr: 31. Situation is the order of parts or bodies among themselves. To this belong, (1) the differences of the six positions: forward and backward, right and left, upward and downward; which, strictly speaking, belong only to living things, but in a wider sense to other bodies also. (2) To situation pertain the gesture and the habit of a body.

units.la: 32. Figura est magnitudinis determinatio; quæ vel regularis est vel irregularis; & utraque vel plana vel solida: Ad Regularem planam, pertinent, Triangulum, quadratum, Circulus, Ellipsis: &c. ad solidam, Pyramis, Conus, Cubus, Sphæra, Cilindrus &c. Irregulares, tam planæ, quam solidæ innumerabiles sunt.
units.tr: 32. Figure is the determination of magnitude; it is either regular or irregular, and each either plane or solid. To regular plane figures belong the triangle, the square, the circle, the ellipse, etc.; to solid ones the pyramid, the cone, the cube, the sphere, the cylinder, etc. Irregular figures, both plane and solid, are innumerable.

units.la: 33. Compositus modus est, quando plures simplices inter se coëunt, qualis in pluribus est Qualitatibus.
units.tr: 33. A compound mode is when several simple modes come together, as is the case in many qualities.

units.la: 34. Et hæc de difficili illa materiâ modorum nunc sufficient; Reliquæ, quæ desiderari possent, alibi, si voluerit Ille, supplebo.
units.tr: 34. And these things concerning that difficult matter of modes will suffice for now; the remaining things, which might be wanted, I will supply elsewhere, if he wishes.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: DE Relatione.
units.tr: ON RELATION.

units.la: 1. RElatio à referendo nomen habet, quia in eo quod unum ad aliud referatur consistit. Vulgò latè sumi dicitur tam pro transscendentali, quam pro prædicamentali, tam pro rationis, quam pro reali respectu; Et strictè pro solo prædicamentali & reali. Verùm lata illa acceptio hic retinenda, ea enim, quæ quam maximè generalia sunt, hîc accipienda veniunt. Nec tanta est differentia inter relationes transscendentales ac prædicamentales, ac vulgò exîstimatur, ut infra patebit.
units.tr: 1. Relation (relatio) has its name from being referred (referendo), because it consists in one thing being referred to another. Commonly it is taken broadly, both for the transcendental and for the predicamental, both for relation of reason and for real relation; and strictly only for the predicamental and real. But this broad sense is to be retained here, for it is the most general notions that are to be considered here. Nor is the difference between transcendental and predicamental relations as great as is commonly thought, as will appear below.

units.la: 2. Synonyma ejus sunt apud Latinos quidem 1. Respectus. 2. Ordo, quatenus hic latè sumitur pro omni ordinatione, non stricte pro solâ illâ, quæ fit secundum aliquam successionem. Apud Græcos autem πρός τι i. e. habitudo, quia τὰ πρός τι aliquo modo se ad seinvicem habent.
units.tr: 2. Its synonyms are, among the Latins: (1) respect (respectus); (2) order (ordo), taken here broadly for every arrangement, not strictly for that alone which follows some succession. Among the Greeks, however, it is "pros ti", that is, a habitude (habitudo), because the things "pros ti" stand in some way towards one another [πρός τι].

units.la: 3. In re, Relatio explicanda venit, ut inquiratur 1. Quid sit? 2. Quid non sit? 3. Quæ ejus divisiones?
units.tr: 3. In regard to the thing itself, relation must be explained by inquiring: (1) What is it? (2) What is it not? (3) What are its divisions?

units.la: 4. Quid sit relatio explicatur. 1. definitione.
units.tr: 4. What relation is, is explained first by definition.

units.la: 2. Requisitis, ex definitone deducendis. Definitur autem, habitudo unius ad aliud. Habitudo dicitur, vel & respectus. unde apparet, quod relatio 1. sit aliquid 2. Aliquid positivum. 3. Positivum ratione duorum subjectorum.
units.tr: 2. By the requisites to be deduced from the definition. It is defined as a habitude of one thing to another. Habitude is also called respect. Whence it appears that relation (1) is something, (2) something positive, (3) positive by reason of two subjects.

units.la: 5. Requisita relationis vulgò quinque enumerantur, 1. Relatum. 2. Correlatum. 3. Subjectum. 4. Terminus. 5. fundamentum. Sed haec ipsa neque inter se, neque ab ipsa relatione realiter differunt. Definitio nostra duorum facit mentionem, unius nempe & alterius. Vnum illud est, a quo incipit relatio, quod & ideo terminus a quo dicitur, item subjectum, quia de eo praedicatur Relatio; In quâ praedicatione si concretivè simul cum ipsa relatione consideratur, dicitur Relatum; Unde apparet, subjectum & Relatum non nisi denominatione differre, in re prorsus idem esse.
units.tr: 5. The requisites of relation are commonly listed as five: (1) the relate (relatum); (2) the correlate (correlatum); (3) the subject; (4) the terminus; (5) the foundation. But these do not differ from one another, nor from the relation itself, really. Our definition makes mention of two, namely one and another. That one is that from which the relation begins, and for this reason it is called the terminus from which, and likewise the subject, because the relation is predicated of it. If in that predication it is considered concretely together with the relation itself, it is called the relate. Whence it appears that subject and relate differ only in name and are altogether the same in reality.

units.la: 6. Alterum illud est, ad quod tendit Relatio, diciturque ideo 1. terminus ad quem, & terminus simpliciter. 2. Correlatum, quatenus & hoc à relatione denominatur, & cum eo concretè consideratur: Unde iterum patet, terminum & correlatum in se idem esse, & tantùm denominatione differre. Duo igitur illa re quidem, sed modo & denominatione quatuor in omni relatione requiruntur.
units.tr: 6. The other is that to which the relation tends, and it is therefore called (1) the terminus to which, and simply the terminus. (2) the correlate, insofar as it too is named from the relation and is considered concretely along with it. Whence again it appears that terminus and correlate are the same in themselves and differ only in name. Thus two things, indeed in reality but in mode and name four, are required in every relation.

units.la: 7. Unde consequitur veritas istius effati, omnem Relationem esse inter duo, non inter plura, nec inter pauciora. Cui tamen obstare videtur 1. Quod idem sibi ipsi dicatur simile; Unde est & relatio ejusdem ad seipsum. Resp. Idem quâ idem, hoc est materialiter sumtum, non est sibi ipsi simile; sed quatenus diversas induit formas, secundum quas illa identitas ac convenientia æstimatur; v. gr. cum dicitur hodiernus & hesternus. Vel 2. dici potest, quod idem conveniat cum ideâ, quam in mente expressam habet, aut exprimere apta est; Unde tunc relatio erit inter hominem objectivè & eundem formaliter consideratum.
units.tr: 7. Hence follows the truth of this saying: every relation is between two, not between several, nor between fewer. Yet it seems to be opposed to this that (1) the same thing is said to be like itself; hence there is also a relation of the same to itself. Reply: the same, as the same, that is, taken materially, is not like itself; but insofar as it takes on diverse forms, according to which that identity and agreement is judged; e.g., when we say "today's" and "yesterday's". Or (2) it may be said that the same agrees with the idea which it has expressed in the mind, or is fit to express; whence the relation will then be between the man objectively and the same man formally considered.

units.la: 8. Deinde obstare videtur huic effato, Quod unus sit princeps & plures subditi; unus pater & plures filii; item quod sint plures fratres, Amici &c. Ut & quod testatio intercedat inter testem, testimonium & rem testatam. Resp. 1. In genere; plura possunt esse, si materialiter & absolutè, ut res & entia considerentur: sed duo tantum si formaliter, relationis scilicet formâ denominata, considerentur. Unde 2. Plures illi subditi, unam subjectionis formam recipiunt, quâ ad Principem, tanquam correlatum referuntur. 3. Idem pater est re & materialiter, hoc est quatenus homo est, sed plures suscipit formas seu Paternitates, pro numero nempe filiorum. 4. Plures amici & fratres non unâ relatione, nisi nomine tenus, sed pluribus ad se invicem referuntur. 5. Diversa quoque relatio est inter testem & testimonium, & inter testimonium & rem testatam; prout quoque diversa est inter testem & rem testatam.
units.tr: 8. Further, it seems to be opposed to this saying that there is one prince and many subjects; one father and many sons; likewise that there are several brothers, friends, etc.; and that testimony intervenes between the witness, the testimony and the thing testified. Reply: (1) In general, several things can exist if things and beings are considered materially and absolutely, but only two if they are considered formally, namely under the form of relation. Whence (2) those many subjects receive one form of subjection, by which they are referred to the prince as correlate. (3) The father is the same in reality and materially, that is, insofar as he is a man, but he receives several forms or paternities, namely according to the number of sons. (4) Several friends and brothers are related to one another not by one relation, except in name, but by several relations. (5) There is also a different relation between the witness and the testimony, and between the testimony and the thing testified; just as there is a different relation between the witness and the thing testified.

units.la: 9. Porro de subjecto Relationis duo quaeri possunt 1. An Relationis subjectum debeat esse inhaesionis, quale est accidentium, an vero sufficiat subjectum denominationis? Resp. Relatio nec requirit, nec habere potest subjectum inhaesionis. Nam 1. Respectus inter duo manet, neque utrique, neque alterutri inesse potest.
units.tr: 9. Further, concerning the subject of relation, two questions can be asked: (1) Must the subject of relation be a subject of inherence, as accidents are, or is a subject of denomination sufficient? Reply: Relation neither requires nor can have a subject of inherence. For (1) the respect between two things remains between them, and cannot be in either of them or in one of them alone.

units.la: 2. Si relationes subjectum inhaesionis haberent, deberent id nova relatione (inhaerentia) respicere; quae iterum requireret subjectum inhaesionis, & sic foret processus in infinitum. 3. Accidentia saepe sunt subjecta relationum, v. gr. magnitudo aequalitatis, qualitas similitudinis. At nullum accidens subjectum inhaesionis esse potest. 4. Subjectum inhaesionis mutatur accessu & recessu sui inhaerentis: At subjectum relationis accessu & recessu relationis non mutatur. Quemadmodum nos hic non mutamur, licet forte homo apud Indos nascatur aut moriatur, cum quo similitudo inter nos & ipsum oritur ac perit. 5. Praeterea etiam Deo relatio convenit, nec tamen is, nisi mumutabilis dicatur, subjectum inhæsionis esse potest. 6. Si relatio requireret subjectum inhæsionis, inhæreret, & sic prout essentiam accidentis haberet, verum foret Accidens, & per consequens Ens aliquod, quod absurdum, ut statim ostendetur. Sufficit igitur in relatione subjectum denominationis.
units.tr: 2. If relations had a subject of inherence, they would have to refer to it by a new relation (inherence), which would again require a subject of inherence, and so there would be a process to infinity. 3. Accidents are often subjects of relations, e.g., the magnitude of equality, the quality of similarity. But no accident can be a subject of inherence. 4. A subject of inherence is changed by the arrival and departure of what inheres in it; but the subject of a relation is not changed by the arrival and departure of the relation. Just as we are not changed here, although perhaps a man is born or dies among the Indians, with whom a similarity between us and him arises and perishes. 5. Moreover, relation also belongs to God, and yet God, unless he is called mutable, cannot be a subject of inherence. 6. If relation required a subject of inherence, it would inhere, and so, as it would have the nature of an accident, it would be an accident, and consequently some being, which is absurd, as will be shown at once. A subject of denomination is therefore sufficient in relation.

units.la: 10. II. Quæritur, quodnam sit illud subjectum denominationis, an relatum, an correlatum, an utrumque? Resp. Vtrumque; non quidem ut nonnulli existimant, geminatâ relatione; Quorsum enim multiplicatio illa relationum? Prout igitur unus ille fluxus exercitii actio dicitur & Passio, neque geminatur, ita consimiliter, una est relatio, bina illa subjecta denominans.
units.tr: 10. II. It is asked: what, then, is that subject of denomination, the relate, the correlate, or both? Reply: Both; not indeed, as some think, by a doubled relation; for why should relations be multiplied? Just as that one flow of exercise is called both action and passion and is not doubled, so likewise there is one relation denominating the two subjects.

units.la: 11. Fundamentum Relationis, illud dicitur esse, quo mediante relatio subjecto convenit. Sed an hoc requiritur? Resp. Non ut sit aliquid absolutum ab ipsâ relatione distinctum: Sed ut sit ratio aliqua in ipsâ re fundata, propter quam relatio adsit; quæ tamen realiter à relatione distinguì non debet. Alias enim nova relatio inter fundamentum & relationem fundatam intercederet, quæ denuò fundamentum postulans, processum in infinitum induceret. Et quidem hæc vera sunt de Relationibus realibus; eorum enim quæ rationis sunt, nullum est fundamentum, præter causam.
units.tr: 11. The foundation of relation is that by means of which the relation belongs to a subject. But is this required? Reply: No, not that it be something absolute distinct from the relation itself; but that it be some ground founded in the thing itself, on account of which the relation is present; which, however, ought not to be really distinct from the relation. For otherwise a new relation would lie between the foundation and the founded relation, which again demanding a foundation would lead to an infinite process. And indeed these things are true of real relations; for of relations of reason there is no foundation except the cause.

units.la: 12. Secundum circa Relationem explicandum fuit, Quid non sit illa? Et quidem 1. Non est omnino nihil; quoniam differt à relatione relatio: alio quippe modo se habet Dominus ad servum, alio Pater ad filium; Quæ diversitas licet à fundamento oriatur, adeo ut per illud relationes inter se distinguantur, sufficit tamen, ut Relatio aliquid sit; Nihil enim neque per se, neque per aliud à nihilo differre potest.
units.tr: 12. The second point to be explained about relation was what it is not. And indeed (1) it is not altogether nothing; since relation differs from relation: for the lord stands towards the servant in one way, the father towards the son in another. Although this difference arises from the foundation, so that by it relations are distinguished from one another, it is enough that relation be something; for nothing can differ from nothing either through itself or through another.

units.la: 13. II. Relatio non est Ens. Ratio. 1. Quia in subjecto, nec compositionem aut mutationem facit; Ubi tamen nullus congressus entium citra compositionem, aut regressus sine mutatione concipi aut fieri potest. Sed Objic. Multæ tamen relationes, ex prævia mutatione oriuntur. Resp. Ita est: Sed illa mutatio naturâ prior relatione istâ, & quasi ejus causa est, si in subjecto vel termino eveniat. Aliud autem est mutationem esse causam relationis, quod verum est; aliud relationem esse causam mutationis, quod falsum. 2. Rat. Si relatio esset Ens, nova quâ relatione suum subjectum deberet respicere; Omne enim Ens alteri alicui Enti additum ad illud relationem quamdam obtinet. Sed inter subjectum & Relationem aliam statuere relationem, est 1. Multiplicationem quidditatum, 2. procedere in infinitum admittere. 14.
units.tr: 13. II. Relation is not a being (ens). Reason: (1) Because it makes no composition or change in the subject; whereas no meeting of beings can be conceived or brought about without composition, nor any return without change. But it is objected that many relations arise from a prior change. Reply: So it is; but that change is prior in nature to this relation and is, as it were, its cause, if it occurs in the subject or the terminus. It is one thing for change to be the cause of relation, which is true; another for relation to be the cause of change, which is false. (2) Reason: If relation were a being, it would need another relation by which to refer to its subject; for every being added to another being has a certain relation to it. But to posit a relation between the subject and another relation is (1) to multiply entities, and (2) to admit a process to infinity. 14.

units.la: 14. III. Relatio non est modus Entis, quia nihil in re mutat, aut componit. IV. Nec est privatio; Quia a relatione desumitur quædam perfectio & præsentia, quæ de subjecto prædicatur: Omnis autem privatio imperfectionem & absentiam involvit.
units.tr: 14. III. A relation is not a mode of being, because it changes or composes nothing in the thing. IV. Nor is it a privation, because a certain perfection and presence is derived from the relation and predicated of the subject, whereas every privation involves imperfection and absence.

units.la: 15. Differentiæ relationum ac relatorum variæ passim circumferuntur; suntque vel communes, vel essentiales.
units.tr: 15. The differences of relations and of related things are various and are commonly put forward; they are either common or essential.

units.la: 16. Inter communes primo dividitur, quod sit vel mutua vel non-mutua. Mutua dicitur, quæ geminâ relatione utrique subjecto convenit: Non mutua, cum simplex relatio uni subjecto inhæsivè, alteri denominativè convenit. Sed 1. in nullo respectu gemina est relatio. 2. Neque relatio subjectum inhæsionis requirit. Sed 3. omnis relatio est inter duo, de quibus denominativè tantum dicitur. Unde omnis relatio mutua est. Nec obstat, quod relatio inter Creatorem & creaturam inesse quidem creaturæ, non autem creatori dicatur, adeo ut non esset mutua; Nam neque creaturæ, neque Creatori ea inest, sed tamen hic, quam illa, ab eâ denominatur; quare etiam & illa mutua est.
units.tr: 16. Among the common differences, first, a relation is divided into mutual or non-mutual. A relation is called mutual when it belongs to each of its two subjects by a double relation; non-mutual when a simple relation belongs to one subject as something inhering in it, and to the other as a denomination. But (1) no relation is double in any respect; (2) nor does a relation require a subject of inherence; but (3) every relation is between two things, of which it is predicated only by way of denomination. Hence every relation is mutual. Nor does it count against this that a relation between the Creator and the creature is said to inhere in the creature but not in the Creator, so that it would not be mutual. For it inheres neither in the creature nor in the Creator; yet the one is denominated from it no less than the other, and so it too is mutual.

units.la: 17. Secundò, dividitur relatio; quod sit vel realis vel rationis. Realis est, quæ habet fundamentum in re; ejus igitur duæ sunt conditiones, 1. Ut utrumque ejus relatum fit Ens verum. 2. Ut habitudo inter illa intercedens in ipsâ re fit fundata, & non confista. Unde contra, relatio rationis dicitur 1. cum utrumque relatum est figmentum. 2. Cum alterutrum tale est. 3. Quando habitudo inter Entia vera concipitur, quæ in naturâ talis non est. Dices. Si dentur Relationes reales illæ erunt entia. Resp. Non omne reale statim Ens est: Dicuntur autem relationes reales, non quod ipsæ sint Entia, sed quod reipsa interentia non cogitata intercedant.
units.tr: 17. Secondly, relation is divided into real or of reason. A real relation is one that has its foundation in the thing. Its two conditions, therefore, are: 1. that each of its relata be a true being; 2. that the relation between them be founded in the thing itself and not consist in thought. Conversely, a relation of reason is said to be so (1) when each of its relata is a fiction; (2) when one of them is such; (3) when a relation between true beings is conceived which is not such in nature. Objection: If there are real relations, they will be beings. Reply: Not every real thing is at once a being. Relations are called real not because they are beings themselves, but because they really hold between things that exist, not merely as thought.

units.la: 18. Tertio, Relata dividuntur, quod sint velsecundum dici, velsecundum esse: Hæc dicuntur, quæ eô ipso, quod sint, ad alia referuntur: Illa verò, quæ per se pertinent ad aliud prædicamentum, adeo ut totum ipsorum esse ad aliud non referatur; At hæc distinctio ipsis competit ratione signi, sive nominis, quo appellantur; Quædam enim relata tali efferuntur nomine, quod per se ad aliud nullum prædicamentum pertinet, ut Pater. Quædam verò tali, quod per se ad aliud prædicamentum dirigitur, ut Scientia.
units.tr: 18. Thirdly, related things are divided into those that are related according to being said and those according to being. The former are those which, by the very fact that they exist, are referred to other things; the latter are those which belong in themselves to another category, so that their whole being is not referred to something else. This distinction, however, applies to them by reason of the sign or name by which they are called. For some related things are expressed by a name which in itself belongs to no other category, such as father; while others are expressed by a name which in itself is directed to another category, such as knowledge.

units.la: 19. Quarto, Relatio dividitur, quod fit vel transscendentalis, vel prædicamentalis; Hæc dicitur, quæ est inter talia relata, quæ ratione esse absoluti ad unum aliquod pertinent prædicamentum, ut v. gr. inter patrem & filium. Illa verò, quæ est inter talia relata, quæ vel secundum absolutum esse, ipsis prædicamentis generaliora sunt, ut inter causam & causatum; vel inter talia, quæ sunt diversorum prædicamentorum, ut inter substantiam & accidens; Vel inter talia, quorum unum quidem est prædicamenti alicujus, alterum vero nullius, ut inter creatorem & creaturam. Veruntamen omnis relatio ratione superioris sui generis appellari potest transscendentalis; neque illæ, qui prædicamentales dicuntur, aliquem usum habent, nisi ad transscendentales referantur. Quare magnoperè errant illi, qui illas toto genere distinctas volunt; quippe eadem utrisque convenit definitio, eædemque notæ ac proprietates, ut solidè demonstravit, Clariss. P. Voet. Philos. prim. reform. cap. 28. Interim si cui libeat transscendentales appellare, illas relationes, quæ sunt inter tres personas divinitatis, & reliquas omnes prædicamentales, non inconvenienter faciet; Vix enim illæ aliquid præter nomen cum cæteris commune habent.
units.tr: 19. Fourthly, relation is divided into transcendental or predicamental. The latter is one that holds between such related things as, by reason of their absolute being, belong to one category, for example between father and son. The former is one that holds between such related things as either, in respect of their absolute being, are more general than the categories themselves, as between cause and effect; or between such as belong to different categories, as between substance and accident; or between such of which one belongs to some category while the other belongs to none, as between the Creator and the creature. Yet every relation may be called transcendental by reason of its higher genus, and those called predicamental have no use except as they are referred to transcendental ones. Therefore those who want them to be distinct in their whole genus greatly err; for the same definition applies to both, and the same marks and properties, as the most distinguished Voetius has solidly demonstrated in Philosophia prima reformata, chapter 28. Meanwhile, if anyone prefers to call them transcendental, he will not be wrong to apply that name to the relations which hold between the three persons of the Godhead, and to all the rest of the predicamental relations; for those hardly have anything in common with the others except the name.

units.la: 20. Quinto dividuntur relata, quod sint vel Synonyma, eodem nomine, vel heteronyma, diverso nomine appellata. Sed hæc externa est à signo petita, distinctio; nec novi eam alicujus esse fructus.
units.tr: 20. Fifthly, related things are divided into synonymous, called by the same name, and heteronymous, called by different names. But this distinction is external, taken from the sign, and I do not see that it bears any fruit.

units.la: 21. Sexto relata sunt vel æqualia, vulgò æquiparantiæ dicta, quæ eamdem habent dignitatem; vel inæqualia, diversâ dignitate constantia. Horum autem, quod dignius est, dici solet relatum superpositionis, ut Creator; at indignius suppositionis, ut Creatura.
units.tr: 21. Sixthly, related things are either equal, commonly called correlatives of equal standing, which have the same dignity; or unequal, having different dignity. Of these, the one that is more worthy is usually called the relative of superposition, as Creator; the less worthy is of subposition, as creature.

units.la: 21. Essentiales & summas Relationum differentias tradere solus videtur laborâsse Keckermannus, in tabulâ Prædicam. Relationis, ubi ipsas dividit in duas summas species, ut sint vel καπὰ φύσιν sive naturales, vel καπὰ θέσιν, sive ex instituto. Sed utut magno labore, nec minori emolumento illam tradiderit, nondum tamen in omnibus satisfacit. Nam 1. exulat omnis relatio rationis. 2. Externa saltem divisio est, à causa efficiente petita. 3. Quædam relationes ex parte à naturâ, ex parte ab instituto sunt, ut conjugium. 4. Quædam quoque eodem modo inter relata intercedentes, & consimilem planè habitudinem inter illa ostendentes, modò à natura, modò ab institutione fiunt; prout significatio, inter signum & signatum intercedens, manifestè ostendit. 5: Desideratur quoque dependentiæ altera species, inhærentia nimirum, &c.
units.tr: 21. Keckermann alone seems to have labored to give the essential and highest differences of relations, in his table of the predicament of relation, where he divides them into two chief kinds, namely those according to nature [κατὰ φύσιν], or natural, and those according to placing [κατὰ θέσιν], or by institution. But however great his labor, and however little his benefit in setting this out, he still does not satisfy in every respect. For (1) every relation of reason is left out; (2) it is at least an external division, taken from the efficient cause; (3) some relations are partly from nature and partly from institution, as marriage; (4) some relations which hold between related things and show a plainly similar bond between them arise sometimes from nature and sometimes from institution, as the signification which holds between sign and thing signified clearly shows; (5) the other kind of dependence is also lacking, namely inherence, and so on.

units.la: 23. Alia igitur tradenda videtur, quæ mihi nunc ex reliquis, quas olim tentavi, quam maximè allubescit; quam etiam admonitus corrigam. Est ergo relatio vel realis, vel rationis; eo scilicet sensu, quo suprà explicata est ; Et hæc quidem certas species habere non videtur. Realis autem vel infinita est vel finita. Prior est inter personas divinitatis tantum : Posterior inter reliqua omnia. Ubi & hoc notandum, quod infinitæ tales dicantur, non tantum ratione sui subjecti, sed & ratione proprii esse : Arfinitæ saltem ab alterutro, vel utroque subjecto denominantur ; In se enim nec infinitæ, nec finitæ esse possunt : Quoniam finitas & infinitas Entis proprietates sunt ; plures diversitates inter relationes divinas & reliquas, vid. apud Clariss. Voet. l. d.
units.tr: 23. Another division therefore seems to be needed, which now pleases me more than the rest I once tried, and which I shall correct if I am reminded. Relation is either real or of reason, in the sense explained above; and the latter does not seem to have definite kinds. Real relation is either infinite or finite. The former holds only between the persons of the Godhead; the latter between all the rest. Here it should also be noted that such relations are called infinite not only by reason of their subject, but also by reason of their own being; the finite ones are denominated only from one or both of their subjects. For in themselves they can be neither infinite nor finite, since finitude and infinitude are properties of being. Other differences between divine relations and the rest may be seen in the most distinguished Voetius, in the place cited.

units.la: 24. Vltimi autem generis relatio, vel est prima vel orta ; Prima est, quæ relato citra alterius relationis interventum convenit; Estque vel interna vel externa ; Interna est inter talia, quorum unum est de essentiâ alterius; adeòque vel est Dependentia, vel Vnio. Externa est inter talia, quorum unum non constituit essentiam alterius, estque Appositio, vel Circumstantia. Orta denique relatio, in priore aliquâ fundata, est vel convenientia & disconvenientia, vel ordo.
units.tr: 24. Relation of the last kind is either first or arising. A first relation is one that belongs to the related thing without the intervention of another relation; it is either internal or external. An internal relation is between such things, one of which is part of the essence of the other; and so it is either dependence or union. An external relation is between such things, one of which does not constitute the essence of the other; it is apposition or circumstance. Finally, an arising relation, founded on some prior one, is either agreement and disagreement, or order.

units.la: 25. Et quidem hæ relationes fundamenta sunt omnium respectivarum Entis affectionum ; Unde quoque principia illa prima, quibus specialium Entium affectiones cognoscimus, deducuntur, quare de iis inter affectiones erit dicendum. Et hæc de relatione.
units.tr: 25. Indeed these relations are the foundations of all the respective affections of being. Hence also those first principles by which we know the affections of particular beings are derived; therefore concerning these it will be necessary to speak among the affections. And so much on relation.

units.la: CAPUT. V. D E Denominatione externâ.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On External Denomination.

units.la: 1. Equitur Denominatio externa, aliter etiam attributum externum &, quandoque simpliciter denominatio dicta,ut cum v. gr. dicimus, aliquid rei convenire vel inhæsivè, vel denominativè.
units.tr: 1. There follows external denomination, otherwise also called the external attribute, and sometimes simply so-called denomination, as when we say that something belongs to a thing either inherently or denominatively.

units.la: 2. Circa hujus notitiam, indagandum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quotuplex sit? 3. Quomodo ab aliis differat?
units.tr: 2. For knowledge of this, we must inquire: (1) what it is; (2) how many kinds there are; (3) how it differs from other things.

units.la: 3. Quantum ad primum: Denominatio externa definitur, quod sit attributum denotans ordinem relati externi ad suum correlatum; hoc est, ostendens illud quod extra rem est ad illam pertinere. Unde apparet 1. Quod non sit nuda vox, sed præter hanc aliquid eâ denotatum, ordo nempe inter Relationem & Relata. 2. Apparet, quod non sit ipsa res, à quâ denominatio desumitur, aut quæ denominata est, sed medium aliquod inter utramque; Quemadmodum dicit Philosophus, τὸ ἔχειν, ad prædicamentum habitus pertinens, esse medium aliquod inter vestem & eum, qui eâ indutus est, scilicet vestitum esse; Præterea, mutatâ denominatione externâ non mutatur res, ejusque accessu & præsentiâ in re nulla fit compositio, ut cum v. gr. Deus dicitur Creator, Conservator, &c. Quibus accedit, quod denominatio à Relatione desumatur, eamque ut fundamentum præsupponat: At nec ipsa Relatio Ens vel Res est.
units.tr: 3. As to the first point: external denomination is defined as an attribute denoting the order of an external relative to its correlate; that is, showing that what is outside a thing pertains to it. Hence it appears (1) that it is not a bare word, but over and above the word it signifies something, namely the order between the relation and the related things. (2) It appears that it is not the thing itself from which the denomination is drawn, or which is denominated, but some intermediate between the two. Just as the Philosopher says that to have [τὸ ἔχειν], which belongs to the category of habit, is something intermediate between a garment and the man who is clothed in it, namely being clothed. Moreover, when the external denomination changes, the thing does not change, and by its coming or going no composition arises in the thing, as when God is called Creator, Preserver, and so on. To these is added that the denomination is drawn from the relation and presupposes it as its foundation; yet the relation itself is not a being or a thing.

units.la: 4. Hinc sequitur 3. Quod denominationes externæ non sint plane nihil; Nihil enim de Ente verè dici nequit: At Denominationes externæ verè de Ente affirmantur; ac fundamentum, æquè ac reales relationes, in re nemine cogitante, obtinent; Ac denique Denominationes inter se & ab aliis differunt; quod à nihilo est alienum. Sunt ergo medium aliquod inter Ens strictè dictum, seu Metaphysicum, & inter Nihil.
units.tr: 4. From this it follows (3) that external denominations are not utterly nothing. For nothing can truly be said of a being, yet external denominations are truly affirmed of a being; and they hold in the thing, as do real relations, even if no one is thinking of them. Finally, denominations differ from one another and from other things, which is foreign to nothing. They are therefore some intermediate between a being strictly speaking, or a metaphysical being, and nothing.

units.la: 5. Quantum ad secundum; Variæ differentiæ denominationum externarum sunt, quæ ex termino externæ relationis, utpote ejus fundamento, omnes desumendæ videntur. Notabis tamen Relationem in ternam hîc paulò angustius sumi, ac superiori cap. fuit definita; ibi enim ea, quæ intercedit inter causas externas, earumque causatum, internæ titulo venit, eò quòd causæ illæ ad istius causati essentiam pertineant: Hic tamen excluditur, quoniam causæ illæ non fiunt partes essentiæ istius causati, aut illud, ut accidentia inhærentia penetrant. Quare hic tantum unio & dependentia causativa interna, ut & inhærentia, internæ dicuntur relationes: Reliquæ omnes externæ.
units.tr: 5. As to the second point: there are various kinds of external denominations, and they seem to be all drawn from the term of the external relation, as from its foundation. Note, however, that here relation is taken somewhat more narrowly than it was defined in the previous chapter. For there the relation that obtains between external causes and their effect was counted as internal, because those causes belong to the essence of that effect. Here, however, this is excluded, since those causes do not become parts of the essence of that effect, nor do they penetrate it as inhering accidents do. Hence here only the union and the internal causal dependence, as well as inherence, are called internal relations; all the rest are external.

units.la: 6. Sed ordine ista fundamenta denominationis externæ, addito exemplo, proponenda. Itaque I. Denominatio desumitur a dependentiâ externâ, & quidem 1. à causâ efficiente denominatur effectus, v. gr. Corpus vel Naturale dicitur vel Artificiale, homo filius. 2. Efficiens causa ab effectu, ut Deus Creator, homo Pater. 3. Finis denominatur a medio, ut Pax alia bello, alia supplicatione & pretio pacta. 4. Medium a fine, ut Bellum vel offensivum, vel defensivum.
units.tr: 6. But these foundations of external denomination are to be set out in order, with an example added. So: I. Denomination is drawn from external dependence; and indeed (1) from the efficient cause the effect is denominated, for example a body is called either natural or artificial, a man a son. (2) The efficient cause from the effect, as God is Creator, a man a father. (3) The end is denominated from the means, as one peace is made by war, another by supplication and by payment. (4) The means from the end, as war is either offensive or defensive.

units.la: 7. II. Desumitur extrinseca denominatio, ab Appositione, ejusque speciebus, ut 1. ab adjuncto stricte dicto, homo dicitur Vestitus, Ocreatus, Uxoratus. 2. Ab objecto, ut Lex civilis & Ecclesiastica; homo Rex, vel subditus, Dominus, servus, &c. 3. A signo, ut Orion nimbosus, Cometa minax. III. A circumstantia, tam loci, ut homines Europæi, Asiatici, &c. quam temporis, ut morbus brevis & chronicus, Homo senex, juvenis &c. IV. Ab ordine, Res primæ, secundæ, principales, minus principales, pretiosæ, viles. V. A convenientia & disconvenientia res similes, dissimiles, æquales, inæquales, &c. extrinsecâ denominatione appellantur.
units.tr: 7. II. An extrinsic denomination is drawn from apposition and its species: (1) from an adjunct strictly so called, a man is called clothed, booted, married. (2) From the object, as civil and ecclesiastical law; a man is called a king or a subject, a lord, a servant, and so on. (3) From a sign, as Orion is stormy, a comet threatening. III. From a circumstance, both of place, as Europeans and Asians, and so on, and of time, as a short and a chronic illness, an old man, a young man, and so on. IV. From order: first things, secondary things, principal things, less principal things, precious things, base things. V. From agreement and disagreement, things are called by extrinsic denomination like, unlike, equal, unequal, and so on.

units.la: 8. Quid tandem denominatio externa ab aliis non-entibus differat, nunc videndum; Et quidem 1. differt a Privatione, quia hæc in subjecto est, denominatio verò non inest. 2. Privatio denotat absentiam ejus, quod adesse debet, denominatio ordinem ejus quod præsens est. II. Differt a modis, qui insunt, & accessu & recessu suo subjectum mutant: Denominatio verò nec inest, nec mutat. III. Differt ab Ente rationis, ut quod non est, sed esse concipitur: Denominatio verò est. IV. Tandem a relatione, ut ejus fundamento differt denominatio; quare Relatio prior naturâ est denominatione, eamque mensurat, ac stabilit.
units.tr: 8. It remains now to see how external denomination finally differs from other non-beings. And indeed (1) it differs from privation, because the latter is in a subject, whereas denomination is not in it. Privation denotes the absence of what ought to be present; denomination denotes the order of what is present. II. It differs from modes, which inhere and by their coming and going change the subject; denomination neither inheres nor changes anything. III. It differs from a being of reason, which is what is not but is conceived as being; denomination is real. IV. Finally, denomination differs from relation as from its foundation; hence the relation is prior in nature to the denomination, and measures and establishes it.

units.la: 9. Ex hac de denominatione externâ doctrinâ, varia documenta educi possunt, quorum potissima sunt, quæ sequuntur. 1. Nulla denominatio externa est de rei essentiâ; quoniam nempe ab externo accedit. Vnde quoque denominatio externa 1. nequit esse genus rei, v. gr. Logicæ instrumentum, Philosophiæ Doctrina, aut Disciplina. 2. Nec potest esse rei differentia essentialis, ut in Domino & servo &c. II. Nulla denominatio in re denominatâ facit mutationem; Quoniam scilicet ipsa res non est; fundamentumque habet, quod nec ipsum est Ens, videlicet relationem. Hinc igitur nulla statuenda mutatio in Deo Opt. Max. quòd is dicatur Creator, Conservator, &c. III. Nulla denominatio externa cum re fit compositionem; Non enim magis componet, quam relatio; quæ nec hoc præstare potest. Quare nec ob illas denominationes compositio in Deo sta- tuenda est. IV. Omnis denominatio præsupponit respectum; ut pote relationem, ejus fundamentum. Absoluti igitur quâ talis nulla est denominatio externa. Et hæc de Denominatione breviter dicta sufficient.
units.tr: 9. From this doctrine of external denomination several lessons can be drawn, of which the chief are these. (1) No external denomination belongs to the essence of a thing, since it comes from outside. Hence also external denomination (1) cannot be the genus of a thing, for example a tool of logic, a doctrine of philosophy, or a discipline. (2) Nor can it be the essential difference of a thing, as in lord and servant, and so on. II. No denomination makes a change in the denominated thing; since the thing itself is not, and it has as its foundation something that is not itself a being, namely a relation. Hence no change is to be posited in God, the best and greatest, because he is called Creator, Preserver, and so on. III. No external denomination makes a composition with the thing; for it composes no more than a relation does, and a relation cannot do this either. Hence no composition in God is to be posited on account of those denominations. IV. Every denomination presupposes a respect, since it has a relation as its foundation. Therefore no external denomination is absolute as such. And this brief account of denomination will suffice.

units.la: Cap. VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: D E Ente Rationis.
units.tr: On the Being of Reason

units.la: I. ENs ration's sequitur, ita appellatum, quod in intellectu sedem habeat; què admodum reale dicitur, quod est à parte rei extra intellectum. Diversis autem modis accipitur, & quidem I. Latissimè pro omni eo, quod ad rationem sive intellectum aliquo modo spectat, & ab eodem dependet: Quod quidem triplici modo vulgò fieri dicitur. Quædam enim effectivè à ratione dependent, quorsum pertinent, quæcunque ab arte, aliisque mentis actionibus aut habitibus, opera prodeunt. Alia vero subjectivè, ut Potentiæ, dispositiones ac habitus intellectuales omnes, menti ut suo subjecto inhærentes. Alia denique objectivè, qualia sunt, quæ rebus conveniunt, prout menti objiciuntur, aut quæ omni realitate objectivâ extra mentem carent.
units.tr: I. The being of reason (Ens rationis) is so called because it has its seat in the intellect, just as that is called real which exists outside the intellect in the thing itself. It is taken in various ways. First, most broadly, for everything that in some way pertains to reason or the intellect and depends on it. This is commonly said to happen in three ways. Some things depend on reason effectively, such as all works that come forth from art or from other actions or habits of the mind. Others depend on it subjectively, such as the powers, dispositions and all the intellectual habits, which inhere in the mind as their subject. Finally, others depend on it objectively, such as those qualities that belong to things insofar as they are presented to the mind, or those that lack all objective reality outside the mind.

units.la: 2. Ea quidem, quæ duobus prioribus modis Entia rationis dicuntur, veram habent essentiam, adeoque veræ ac realis existentiæ capacia sunt; Eorum igitur hic consideratio nulla est. At vero postrema Classis Ens rationis latè sumitur, prout & Ens in Potentiâ, & Privatio Entia rationis appellari possunt, ut supra ostensum; At strictè tantum, pro eo quod concipitur vel fingitur ac si esset; Idque vel pro omni eo, adeo ut & Entia ficta & chymærica comprehendat, vel strictè, pro solo eo, quod fundamentum in re habet, ut Notio secunda. Hic igitur pro eo accipi debet, quod ac si esset concipitur, & commune quid est figmentis & Notionibus secundis.
units.tr: 2. Those things which are called beings of reason in the first two ways have a true essence, and so are capable of true and real existence; therefore they are not the subject of this inquiry. But the last class is taken broadly, so that both a being in potency and a privation can be called beings of reason, as was shown above. But it is taken strictly only for that which is conceived or feigned as if it were. This is taken either for everything of this kind, so that it includes both fictitious and chimerical beings, or strictly, for that alone which has a foundation in the thing, such as a second intention. Here, then, it must be understood as that which is conceived as if it were, and it is something common to fictions and second intentions.

units.la: 3. Quo dato duplex ipsius institutenda tractatio, Generalis & specialis. Illa explicabit, 1: An sit? Quid sit? 2 3. Quid ab aliis differat? 4. Quæ nam ejus sint requisita. 5. Quo pacto dividenda? Hæc vero speciesejus (speciatim) proponet.
units.tr: 3. Given this, the treatment of it must be set out in two parts, general and special. The first will explain: (1) whether it is? (2) what it is? (3) how it differs from other things? (4) what its requisites are? (5) in what way it is to be divided? The latter will set out its species in particular.

units.la: 4. Primo igitur quæritur, an sit Ens rationis? Cujus quæsiti duplex potest esse sensus; 1. Quidem an sit à parte rei? Quod negandum; sic enim aut res ipsa foret, aut alialiquid ad illam necessario requisitum; Quomodo essentiæ & existentiæ extra intellectum foret particeps 2. At si quæratur, an sit in ratione? Affirmari potest, si præsupponatur intellectus de eo cogitare, ac id apprehendere. Necessitas autem ejus in genere nulla; Non enim ideo hoc dari debet, quia ens rationis est, sed quia est ta'e aliquod, rebus, prout intellectui objiciuntur, conveniens. Dices forte: Atqui huic Enti rationis affectiones reales tribuuntur, ut v. gr. Regiæ solis, sua materia &c. Resp. Est Simia Entis realis, adeoque analogicè illæ affectiones ipsi potius affinguntur, quam attribuuntur.
units.tr: 4. First, then, it is asked whether there is a being of reason. This question can have a twofold sense. (1) Is there such a thing on the part of the thing itself? This must be denied, for then it would be the thing itself, or something else necessarily required for it, and so would share in essence and existence outside the intellect. (2) But if it is asked whether it is in reason, it can be affirmed, provided it is presupposed that the intellect thinks about it and apprehends it. Its necessity, however, is nil in general. For it need not be granted because it is a being of reason, but because it is some such thing as agrees with things insofar as they are presented to the intellect. You may perhaps say: But real affections are attributed to this being of reason, such as the royal path of the sun, its matter, and so on. Answer: It is an ape of real being, and so those affections are feigned for it by analogy rather than truly attributed to it.

units.la: 5. Secundò, Ens rationis definitur, aliquid ab intellectu conceptum, ac si esset. Aliquid dicitur, quia planè nihil non est; Differunt quippe Entia rationis inter se, nihilum autem à nihilo non differt. Reliqua discriminant hoc Ens rationis potissimum à Privatione & Entæ in potentiâ; illa enim ab intellectu quoque concipiuntur, sed sub aliâ planè formâ, hoc ac si posset, illa ac si deberet esse.
units.tr: 5. Second, a being of reason is defined as something conceived by the intellect as if it were. Something is said because it is in no way nothing; for beings of reason differ among themselves, whereas nothing does not differ from nothing. The rest distinguishes this being of reason chiefly from a privation and from a being in potency. For these too are conceived by the intellect, but under a quite different form: this as if it could be, those as if they ought to be.

units.la: 6. Atque ita quidem simul manifestum est, quid ab illis differat Ens hoc rationis, non tamen æquè perspicuum videtur, quomodo à reliquis distinguatur? Et quidem 1. Relatio etiam ens rationis dici posse videtur, quoniam ipsius forma intellectus opus est ; Et omninò dantur relationes rationis, quæ nullo modo ab Ente rationis distingui posse apparent. Resp. Relationis quidem, ut apprehensæ & æstimatæ, non autem ut fundatæ, forma dependet ab intellectu ; in se igitur Ens rationis dici nequit, ut pote per se suum materiale ac formale possidens, antequam ab intellectu concipiatur ; Præterquam quòd relatio sublatâ cogitatione maneat, manente fundamento : At Entis rationis eâ ablatâ, nihil est reliquum. Relationes rationis quod attinet, si inter figmenta dicantur intercedere, habent sese ad illa, quemadmodum Relatio realis inter Entia, inter quæ verè intercedit, eadem videlicet consequuntur : Conceptis igitur quibusdam, ut Entibus, ordo quidam inter illa vel non attendentibus consequitur. Sed an hoc Ens rationis appellabitur, quòd ens rationis, ut fundamentum sequatur ? Non magis, meo judicio, quam relatio realis ideo Ens reale dicitur, eo quòd Entia realia sequantur. At quid dicendum de illis Relationibus rationis, in quas, ut in objectum formandum per se occupatur ratio, adeoque illas inter vera Entia citra ullum fundamentum intercedere concipit ? Resp. Illæ non concipiuntur ac si essentEntia, sed ac si essent relationes, quare denominatione à causâ efficiente desumtâ, non Entia, sed relationes rationis appellantur: Quoad cætera maximus est consensus.
units.tr: 6. And so it is clear at once how this being of reason differs from those, but it does not seem equally plain how it is distinguished from the rest. And indeed, (1) a relation also seems to be able to be called a being of reason, since its form depends on the intellect; and there are plainly relations of reason which cannot appear to be distinguished from a being of reason in any way. Answer: The form of a relation, as apprehended and estimated, though not as grounded, does depend on the intellect. Therefore it cannot be called a being of reason in itself, since it possesses in itself its matter and form before it is conceived by the intellect. Besides, a relation remains when thought is removed, as long as its foundation remains; but when the thought of a being of reason is removed, nothing remains. As for relations of reason, if they are said to hold among fictions, they stand toward those as a real relation stands among beings between which it truly holds, namely they follow the same things. So when certain things are conceived as beings, some order arises among them, even if one does not attend to it. But shall this be called a being of reason because it follows a being of reason as its foundation? In my judgment, no more than a real relation is called a real being because it follows real beings. But what shall be said of those relations of reason in which the reason, as if in an object to be formed by itself, occupies itself, and so conceives them to hold among true beings without any foundation? Answer: These are not conceived as if they were beings, but as if they were relations; so, taking the name from the efficient cause, they are called relations of reason, not beings. As to the rest there is the greatest agreement.

units.la: 7. Nec forte minus difficile erit, Ens rationis, a modis Entium distinguere, & præsertim illis, qui secundum indæquatam considerationem Enti tribuuntur, quales sunt Principia Entis, ejusque affectiones plurimæ, quæ materialiter idem plane sunt cum modificato, ac secundum identicum sensum de ipso in casu recto prædicantur, adeo ut non nisi ratione distinguantur. Resp. Distinctio facilis & aperta est inter illa: Ens rationis materialiter nihil est, at modus talis materialiter est ipsum Ens. 2. Nullum Ens rationis cum Ente identificari potest, utpote toto genere ab ipso distans: At identificatur talis modus. Distinctio quidem rationis est; sed eo ipso, modus ille distinctus cum Ente coincidit, nec Ens rationis est. Dices: Attamen illa distinctio forma est istorum modorum? Resp. Quid inde? Manent tamen modi in seipsum Ens: At Ens rationis, ut formam à ratione obtinet, ita materialiter & in se nihil est.
units.tr: 7. Nor will it perhaps be less difficult to distinguish a being of reason from the modes of beings, especially those which are attributed to a being according to an inadequate consideration, such as the principles of a being and many of its affections, which are materially the very same as the modified thing, and are predicated of it in the nominative case in the same sense, so that they are distinguished only by reason. Answer: The distinction between these is easy and clear. A being of reason is materially nothing, but such a mode is materially the being itself. (2) No being of reason can be identified with a being, since it is entirely different in kind from it; but such a mode is identified with it. The distinction is indeed one of reason; but by that very fact the distinct mode coincides with the being and is not a being of reason. You may say: Yet is that distinction the form of these modes? Answer: What follows from that? The modes nevertheless remain the being itself. But a being of reason, since it receives its form from reason, is therefore nothing materially and in itself.

units.la: 8. Sequuntur requisita Entis rationis, quæ ad hæctria revocari possunt 1. ut concipiatur. 2. ab intellectu. 3. ac si esset. Primo requisito indigitatur, partim ejus existentiam in actu concipiendi consistere, partim ipsum extra illum conceptum nihil esse. Secundo exhibetur ejus efficiens, intellectus quippe, cujus est cogitando concipere. Et quidem hic humanus potissimum intelligi debet intellectus; inutiles quippe sunt quæstiones, an Deus formet Entia rationis? Et an per intellectum Angelicum formentur? Quæ enim Deus format, ea existentiam veram acquirunt; Nec, alicujus gratiâ ea à Deo prodirent Entia rationis. Angeli, quia finiti sunt spiritus cogitantes, cogitando Ens rationis concipere posse, nihil absurdi, aut quoque difficultatis habet. Tertium requisitum postulat, ut ipsi, tanquam Entis similæ, affingantur vestimenta, id est, principia & assectiones Entis; quæ eo modo sunt, quo ipsum illud Ens rationis, hoc est finguntur.
units.tr: 8. The requisites of a being of reason follow, and these can be reduced to three: (1) that it be conceived; (2) by the intellect; (3) as if it were. The first requisite indicates partly that its existence consists in the act of conceiving, and partly that outside that conception it is nothing. The second sets out its efficient cause, namely the intellect, whose office is to conceive by thinking. And here the human intellect chiefly must be understood; for it is useless to ask whether God forms beings of reason, or whether they are formed through an angelic intellect. For what God forms acquires true existence, nor would beings of reason proceed from God for the sake of anything. Angels, since they are finite thinking spirits, can conceive a being of reason by thinking, and there is nothing absurd or even difficult in this. The third requisite demands that, as to a fictional being, there be attached to it, as garments, its principles and affections, which are in the same way as the being of reason itself, that is, they are feigned.

units.la: 9. Dividitur Ens rationis, quod sit vel rationis ratiocinantis, vel rationis ratiocinata. Primum est, quod fundamentum habet in solo intellectu, quorsum pertinent figmenta, & Chymærica: Posterius est, quod aliquod fundamentum quoque habet in objecto quodam, quod ipsum certo modo mensurat, cujusque gratiâ instituitur: Huc dirigendæ Notiones secundæ. Et hæc fuit Generalis tractatio, sequitur Specialis, quæ primo exhiberet figmenta, si horum tractatio utilis esset; aut magis si ipsa certâ lege, mensurâ, formâ, constarent; Nunc verò pro vago intellectu humano ad libitum immutantur. Sint ergo illa Generali ista consideratione, contenta.
units.tr: 9. A being of reason is divided into that which is of reason reasoning and that which is of reason reasoned. The first is that which has its foundation in the intellect alone, to which belong fictions and chimeras. The latter is that which also has some foundation in an object, which it measures in a certain way and for whose sake it is instituted; to this belong the second intentions. This was the general treatment. The special follows, which would first set out fictions, if their treatment were useful, or rather if they had some fixed law, measure, and form; but now they are changed at will by the vague human intellect. Let these, then, be contented with this general consideration.

units.la: 10. Specialis igitur Entis rationis tractatio, ad notiones secundas se tantum extendit; Quas antequam explicem, in antecessum dubium erit removendum, annon plura sint Entia rationis ratiocinata, quam Notiones secunda? Notiones enim universales primæ, sive universalia omnia formam ab intellectu dependentem habent: At in reipsa nihil esse videntur. Resp. Forma universalium est conceptus, & is ab intellectu concipiente est: At falsum est, quod in reipsa nihil sint; Sunt enim ipsa singularia, ut infra ostendetur. Quare nota duplicem hanc inter universale & Ens rationis differentiam 1. Ens rationis est materialiter nihil: Universale autem ipsum Ens. 2. Ens rationis toto genere ab Ente differt: At universale saltem conceptu.
units.tr: 10. The special treatment of the Entity of reason therefore extends only to second notions. Before I explain these, a doubt must be removed in advance: are there not more Entities of reason which are conceived than second notions? For first universal notions, or all universals, have a form that depends on the intellect, yet they seem to be nothing in reality. Reply: The form of universals is a concept, and it is in the concipient intellect. But it is false that they are nothing in reality, for they are the singulars themselves, as will be shown below. Hence note this twofold difference between the universal and the Entity of reason: (1) the Entity of reason is materially nothing, whereas the universal is itself an Entity; (2) the Entity of reason differs from an Entity in its whole genus, whereas the universal differs from it only in concept.

units.la: 11. Notio igitur secunda consideranda.
units.tr: 11. The notion, then, is to be considered as second.

units.la: 1. Quoad nomen. 2. Quoad rem. Dicitur autem vox Notio a notando, vel notum faciendo, quia scilicet notificat aliquid intellectui, unde est quasi imago intellectui obiectum aliquod repræsentans; quæ dum ab intellectu respicitur, aliter species, vel idea appellatur. Secunda autem dicitur hæc notio, eo quod mediante alia quâ notione rem ipsam repræsentet, utpote imimmediatè notionem primam , ejusque conceptum designans , ad differentiam primæ notionis , quæ immediatè rem ipsam repræsentat, adeoque objectivè est ipsa res. Quamobrem etiam hæc sæpiusculè pro reipsâ sumitur; unde nonnunquam Notio simpliciter hanc secundam denotat.
units.tr: 1. As to the name. 2. As to the thing. The word "notion" is taken from noting, or making known, because it makes something known to the intellect; hence it is, as it were, an image representing some object to the intellect. When the intellect regards it, it is called otherwise a species or an idea. This notion is called second because it represents the thing itself by means of another notion, namely by designating the first notion and its concept immediately, as distinct from the first notion, which represents the thing itself immediately and so is objectively the thing itself. For this reason it is often taken for the thing itself; hence sometimes "notion" simply denotes this second notion.

units.la: 12. Quod rei sive naturæ est notionis, explicabitur hisce articulis, 1. An sit? 2. Quid sit? 3. Quid non sit? 4. Quæ ejus causæ? 5. Quis modus? 6. Quæ divisio?
units.tr: 12. What belongs to the thing or nature of a notion will be explained under these heads: 1. Whether it is? 2. What is it? 3. What is it not? 4. What are its causes? 5. What is its mode? 6. What is its division?

units.la: 13. Ad primum, non difficile est, ait Burgersdicius noster, demonstratu, quoniam præter ea, quæ rebus tribuuntur, prout ipsa sunt in se, etiam quædam rebus conveniunt, prout à nobis apprehenduntur, atque inter se ab intellectu comparantur: Et hæc sunt Entia rationis, sive Notiones secundæ: Aut clarius, intellectus non saltem illa respicit, quæ de rebus dicuntur, sed & ad modum attendit, quo ipsa dicuntur; Ille autem modus notionis secundæ est fundamentum; Cui si accedat actualis istius modi perceptio fit ipsa notio. Quare reipsâ non datur, sed saltem cogitatione sive perceptione.
units.tr: 13. As to the first, our Burgersdijk says, it is not difficult to demonstrate that, besides those things which are attributed to things as they are in themselves, some things also belong to things as they are apprehended by us and compared with one another by the intellect. These are Entities of reason, or second notions. Or, to put it more clearly, the intellect attends not only to those things which are said of things, but also to the mode in which they are said. This mode of the second notion is the foundation; if the actual perception of this mode is added, it becomes the notion itself. Hence it does not exist in reality, but only in thought or perception.

units.la: 14. Ad secundum: Notio secunda est imago ab intellectu concepta ad repræsentandam habitudinem prædicatorum. Quæ definitio genere, efficiente, fine ac objecto constat.
units.tr: 14. As to the second: A second notion is an image conceived by the intellect to represent the relation of predicates. This definition consists of the genus, the efficient cause, the end and the object.

units.la: 15. Tales autem notiones non sunt purum putum nihil, ut ad tertium accedam; utpote quæ imagines sunt alicujus, inter se & ab aliis differunt, à nobis intelliguntur, & officio quodam funguntur; Quorum nullum puro nihilo convenire potest. Nec tamen sunt Entia realia; sunt enim 1. quasi imagines imaginum sive notionum primarum, quæ in suâ formâ, saltem Entium realium conceptus sunt. 2. Mentis & cogitationis beneficio à puro nihilo separantur, atque ita constituuntur. 3. Sunt media, quibus res ac Entia cognoscimus: Atque hæc si Entia forent, aliis mediis ad sui cognitionem opus haberent; quare processus foret in infinitum, ipsumque Ens incognitum maneret; Infinitum enim quâ tale incognitum est.
units.tr: 15. Such notions are not pure nothing, to come to the third point; for they are images of something, they differ from one another and from other things, they are understood by us, and they perform a certain office, none of which can belong to pure nothing. Nor are they real Entities. For (1) they are, as it were, images of images, or of first notions, which in their own form are concepts at least of real Entities. (2) By the benefit of the mind and of thought they are separated from pure nothing and so are constituted. (3) They are the means by which we know things and Entities. If these were Entities, they would need other means to know them, and so the process would go on to infinity, and the Entity itself would remain unknown, for the infinite, as such, is unknown.

units.la: 16. Nec difficili negotio a Privatione & Ente potentiali distingui potest Notio, licet genere cum ipsis conveniat; eo enim modo differt, quo omne Ens rationis. A modis Entium quoque differt, utpote formaliter in ente constitutis, aut per inadæquatum modum conceptis. A Relatione autem, quod ex multis relationibus rationis oriatur, adeo ut sit quasi imago variarum relationum beneficio constituta. Dicitur quippe imago repræsentans convenientiam, id est relationem, prædicatorum, id est eorum, quæ etiam ad aliud referuntur.
units.tr: 16. The notion can be distinguished without difficulty from privation and from potential Entity, although it agrees with them in genus; for it differs in the same way as every Entity of reason does. It also differs from the modes of Entities, since these are formally constituted in an Entity or conceived through an inadequate mode. It differs from relation, which arises from many relations of reason, so that it is, as it were, an image constituted by the help of various relations. For it is called an image representing the agreement, that is the relation, of predicates, that is, of those things which are also referred to something else.

units.la: 17. Causæ Notionum secundarum sunt vel efficiens, vel Materia, vel finis. Forma enim earum ex efficiente & fine componitur.
units.tr: 17. The causes of second notions are either the efficient, or the matter, or the end. For their form is composed of the efficient and the end.

units.la: 18. Efficiens causa earum duplex, Principalis & Minus principalis: Principalis efficiens est intellectus, utpote qui cogitat, & cogitando assimilat. Sunt quippe cogitationis beneficio notiones secundæ. Minus principales sunt diversi illi actus, tam præparantes, quam consummantes, quos instituit intellectus, ut sibi tales imagines efformet; suntque potissimum quatuor. Primo enim format notiones primas. 2. Eas factas inter se comparat, ut scilicet appareat, quo pacto Enti conveniant. 3. Reflectit se ad illam comparationem, ut scilicet illum arctius inspiciat. 4. Percipit modum ex illa comparatione, quo & notiones primæ Enti conveniunt, & inter se, & ab ipso apprehenduntur, cujus perceptio notioni secundæ ultimam manum addit.
units.tr: 18. The efficient cause of them is twofold, principal and less principal. The principal efficient is the intellect, since it thinks, and by thinking it assimilates.
