Second notions are indeed produced by the benefit of thought. The less principal causes are those various acts, both preparatory and completing, which the intellect performs in order to form such images for itself; and there are chiefly four. (1) For first it forms first notions. (2) Having made them, it compares them with one another, so that it becomes clear how they agree with the Entity. (3) It reflects on that comparison, so that it may examine it more closely. (4) It perceives from that comparison the mode in which the first notions agree with the Entity and with one another, and are apprehended by it; this perception adds the final touch to the second notion.

units.la: 19. Materiam notionum constituit partim earum subjectum, quod est ipse intellectus, partim fundamentum, quod duplex est remotum & proximum. Remotum est relatio quædam rerum ac attributorum inter se; Proximum vero modus, quo illa relatio apprehenditur ac concipitur.
units.tr: 19. The matter of notions is constituted partly by their subject, which is the intellect itself, and partly by a foundation, which is twofold, remote and proximate. The remote is a certain relation of things and attributes to one another; the proximate, however, is the mode by which that relation is apprehended and conceived.

units.la: 20. Finis notionum secundarum est repræsentare habitudinem eorum, quæ Enti conveniunt, adeoque ut sint conceptus, il-lum lum quo cognoscimus suâ similitudine admbrantes, atque ita cognitionem nostram non mediocriter promoventes.
units.tr: 20. The end of second notions is to represent the relation of those things which agree with the Entity, and so that they may be concepts, which shadow forth to us, by their likeness, that by which we know, and so promote our knowledge not a little.

units.la: 21. Modus notionum fecundarum, in eo collocandus, quòd ipsæ certâ lege, certoque numero ac ordine fiant. Certâ autem lege fiunt, si intelleƈtus, debito modo aƈtus illos, ad formationem ipsarum requisitos, instituat; atque adeo illam habitudinem ejusque modum, tanquam fundamentum sequatur; Planè secus ac in figmentis, quæ nec debito illo modo ac fundamento, neque insequentibus intelleƈtus aƈtibus opus habent. Debitus numerus in eo consistit, ut, licet multæ uni Enti tribuantur, eo quod ipsum pluribus modis cum aliis ratione prædicatorum comparari possit; illæ tamen certo numero constent, nec prorsus infinitæ sint. Conveniens denique earum ordo requiritur, qui naturali prædicatorum ordini, quoad ejus fieri potest respondeat.
units.tr: 21. The mode of second notions is to be placed in this, that they come about by a certain law, a certain number and order. They come about by a certain law if the intellect performs, in the proper way, those acts required for their formation, and so follows that relation and its mode as a foundation. This is quite unlike fictions, which have no need of that proper mode and foundation, nor of the subsequent acts of the intellect. The due number consists in this: although many things are attributed to one Entity, because it can be compared with others in many ways with respect to predicates, yet those notions should be of a certain number and not wholly infinite. Finally, a suitable order of them is required, which should correspond, as far as possible, to the natural order of predicates.

units.la: 22. Conspicua quidem diversitas, eademque satis insignis, inter notiones secundas est; non tamen æquè manifestum, quo pacto in suas species ac classes dirimendæ sint. Intentatum quippe hoc: Mihi notio secunda vel vocum est vel rerum: Notionis vocum exempla præbent Grammatici. Notio rerum vel est simplicium, vel complexarum, prout vel simplex vel complexum thema repræsentat ; ad illam pertinent , Genus, species, subjectum,prædicatum, &c. Ad hanc autem Propositio, syllogismus, inductio &c. Quibus nunc acquiesco, alibi prolixius examinaturus, quid hæc divisio frugi habeat ; Quo dato reliquas inferiores species enumerabo.
units.tr: 22. There is indeed a clear diversity, and quite a striking one, among second notions; but it is not equally plain how they are to be divided into their species and classes. For this is a question not yet tried: second notions are either of words or of things. Grammarians provide examples of notions of words. Notions of things are either of simple or of complex things, according as the thema represented is simple or complex. To the former belong genus, species, subject, predicate, etc.; to the latter, proposition, syllogism, induction, etc. I rest content with these for now, intending to examine elsewhere more fully what use this division has; once that is granted, I will enumerate the remaining, lower species.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: DE Ente in Potentiâ.
units.tr: ON Being in Potentiality.

units.la: 1. ENs in potentiâ, vel aliter Ens possibile, est, quod cum non sit, concipitur tamen ac si possit esse : sive, quod non quidem existit, ad existendum tamen nullam involvit repugnantiam.
units.tr: 1. Being in potentiality, or otherwise possible being, is that which, although it does not exist, is nevertheless conceived as if it could be; or, that which indeed does not exist, yet involves no contradiction in existing.

units.la: 2. Hoc igitur materialiter nihil est, utpote quod non est, aut existit, neque per se, neque per aliud : formaliter tamen certum genus eorum quæ sunt aliquid, per conceptum nostrum constituit.
units.tr: 2. This, then, is materially nothing, since it neither is nor exists, neither through itself nor through another. Yet formally it establishes, through our concept, a certain genus of those things that are something.

units.la: 3. Formalitas autem illa non repugnantiæ sive possibilitatis ad esse concipitur. 1. Ratione causæ. 2. Ratione objecti possibilis. Illius quidem, quatenus virtus sive potentia alicujus causæ talis & tanta est, ut per illam tale Ens esse acquirat. Hujus vero quatenus ipsum illud talibus constat prædicatis, quæ contradictionem aliquam non involvunt. Et quidem possibilitatem illa duo includere, ex opposito ipsius impossibili apparet; Hoc enim quia nunquam extra causas produci potest, in terminis primo involvit contradictionem fecundo nunquam in virtute cujuscunque causæ esse aut fuisse; Possibile igitur tam contradictionem tollit, quam virtutem in causa præsupponit.
units.tr: 3. That formality, however, is conceived as the absence of contradiction, or the possibility, of existing. (1) By reason of the cause; (2) by reason of the possible object. The former, insofar as the power or potency of some cause is so great that through it such a being is able to acquire existence; the latter, insofar as that thing itself consists of such predicates as involve no contradiction. And that possibility includes these two things is evident from the opposite of the impossible: for the impossible, since it can never be produced outside its causes, first involves a contradiction in its terms, second has never been, and never can be, in the power of any cause. Therefore the possible both excludes contradiction and presupposes power in a cause.

units.la: 4. Quoniam vero duplex virtus est, infinita & finita, duplex quoque poffibilitas statui debet, una absoluta, quâ ejus esse infinitâ virtute procurari potest: Hæc etiam poffibilitas Logica appellari potest, utpote quæ ex terminorum contradictione negatâ æstimatur: Altera comparata, quando aliquid possibile æstimatur ex virtute finita; Hæc vero non tantum non-contradictionem præfupponit, sed & 1. præsentiam subjecti. 2. ejus aptitudinem, tam quæ ordinario cursui objicitur, quam quæ extraordinariæ operationi obedit. Si ordinarius cursus præfupponatur dicitur Ens in potentiâ Physica: Sin alteri isti pareat, in potentiâ obedientiali esse dicitur. Interim nota, etiam aliquando virtutem infinitam extraordinario modo ad subjectum revocari posse, inque eo operari, quæ etiam subjecti aptitudo, quâ illam actionem reciepre potest, obedientialis potentia dicitur : Sed hæc ratione Dei, illa ratione Artis obedire dicitur.
units.tr: 4. Since, however, power is twofold, infinite and finite, a twofold possibility must also be posited: one absolute, by which its being can be brought about by infinite power. This possibility may also be called logical, since it is judged from the denial of contradiction in the terms. The other is comparative, when something is judged possible from finite power. This latter presupposes not only non-contradiction but also (1) the presence of the subject, and (2) its aptitude, both that which is subject to the ordinary course of nature and that which obeys extraordinary operation. If the ordinary course is presupposed, it is called being in physical potentiality; but if it is subject to the other, it is said to be in obediential potentiality. Meanwhile, note that sometimes infinite power can also be applied to a subject in an extraordinary manner and work in it; and this aptitude of the subject, by which it can receive that action, is called obediential potentiality. But this is said to obey God by reason of his power, and that by reason of art.

units.la: 5. Virtus illa si determinetur aut à seipsa, aut aliunde, ut aliquid sibi possibile existere faciat, illud possibile futurum facit ; Quod proinde vel absolutè tale est, ratione scilicet causæ infinitæ, cui nihil obstare potest, vel comparatè, ratione virtutis finitæ, quæ impediri potest: Possibilium verò in se nulla est futuritio antecedenter ad voluntatem Dei decernentem : Licet absolutè futura dicantur, ex hypothesi constantiæ determinationis virtutis divinæ. De Possibilitate autem latius in sequentibus dicendum ˌeô loci, ubi de Persectione agetur.
units.tr: 5. If that power is determined either by itself or from elsewhere to make something possible for itself to exist, it makes that possible future. And this is such either absolutely, namely by reason of an infinite cause, which nothing can hinder, or comparatively, by reason of a finite power, which can be impeded. Yet in itself there is no futurition of possibles antecedent to the decree of the will of God; although they may be called absolutely future, on the hypothesis of the constancy of the determination of divine power. But concerning possibility more will be said at length in what follows, in the place where we shall treat of perfection.

units.la: 6. Vnum tamen hîc inquirendum restat, videlicet, annon hoc Ens possibile, seu in potentiâ, ad subjectum materiale Metaphysices pertineat ? Metaphysica enim ipsum Ens ab existentiâ videtur separare, ut pote illud non præcisè jam existere considerans. Resp. Neutiquam ; Ens enim in potentia ab eo excluditur, ut supra ostensum ; Et quomodo includeretur, cum uno concep-tu communi, cum Ente actuali, illo scilicet, quod Deo & Creaturis commune est, concipi nequit; Non enim hoc habet, sed habere saltem potest, ut existentiam, ita & essentiam, ut quæ individuè cohærent. Metaphysica quidem à determina-toto hîc & nunc auffert suum Ens, non tamen prorsus ab omni ; Singularia enim talia esse relinquit, licet ea communi quodam conceptu consideret, secundum quem non nunc praecisè, sed aliquando sunt.
units.tr: 6. One thing, however, still remains here to be inquired, namely, whether this possible being, or being in potentiality, belongs to the material subject of Metaphysics? For Metaphysics seems to separate being from existence, as considering it not precisely as already existing. Answer: By no means. For being in potentiality is excluded from it, as shown above. And how would it be included, since it cannot be conceived under one common concept together with actual being, namely that which is common to God and creatures? For it does not have existence, but can at least have it, and likewise essence, as things that cohere inseparably. Metaphysics indeed removes its being from this determinate here and now, but not altogether from every such determination; for it leaves singulars to be such, although it considers them under a certain common concept, according to which they are not precisely now, but at some time.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: DE Privatione.
units.tr: On Privation.

units.la: 1. PRivatio sequitur, id quod non est ac si deberet esse repraesentans; etiam, quoad nomen, ac id quod ipsius Entitati subest, consideranda.
units.tr: 1. Privation follows that which is not, as if it ought to be present; it is to be considered also as to its name, and as to that which underlies its entity.

units.la: 2. Ad nomen ambigue dicitur privatio. 1. Late de omni & quàcunque negatione quomodò visu carere lapis dicitur. 2. Angustius, quâtenus etiam privationem includit physicam, hoc est, quatenus id quod adesse potest, & quoque, sed nondum ordinario naturae motu, aderit, quemadmodum in Ovo privario dicitur esse pulli, significat: Atque in hac significatione Privatio Physica dicitur, atque inter generationis principia vulgò numeratur. 3. Adaequatè, quâtenus saltem debitam perfectionem negat, hoc est, quando jam aptum est subjectum habere, & illud quod adesse negatur, haberi, non tamen hoc habetur, nec illud habet, quemadmodum Animali morbus convenit. Atque in hac significatione, prout vera ac preproprie dicta est privatio, ita hic consideranda venit.
units.tr: 2. The word is used ambiguously. 1. Broadly, of every and any negation, as when a stone is said to lack sight. 2. More narrowly, insofar as it also includes physical privation, that is, when that which can be present, and also will be present but not yet by the ordinary motion of nature, is signified, as an egg is said to have the privation of a chick. In this sense Physical Privation is called, and is commonly counted among the principles of generation. 3. Adequately, insofar as it denies at least the due perfection, that is, when the subject is already apt to have it, and what is denied to be present can be had, yet it is not had, nor does the subject have it, as disease belongs to an animal. And in this sense, as true and properly so called privation, it is to be considered here.

units.la: 3. In rei vel quasi rei consideratione, distinguè explicandum, 1. An detur privatio? 2. Quid sit? 3. Quid non sit? 4. Quomodo dividenda?
units.tr: 3. In the consideration of a thing or quasi-thing, we must explain distinctly: 1. Whether there is privation? 2. What it is? 3. What it is not? 4. How it is to be divided?

units.la: 4. I. Dari privationem, ambigendum esse non videtur, cum actu & de facto multa de rebus dicantur, quæ, cum non sint positiva, alicujus perfectionis istis debitæ involvunt negationem, sicut homo dicitur cæcus, ægrotus &c. Attamen vehementer obstare videtur, 1. Quod dari sit idem quod poni in rerum natura, & hoc quod positivum esse; Quare dum privatio non potest esse positiva, nec poni, nec dari quoque posse videtur. 2. Quoniam id quod datur in rerum natura, alicubi præsens esse debet; Atqui præsentia existentiam, & hæc Ens præsupponit; Quare si daretur privatio, ens fore videtur. 3. Et magis, quod datur, productum ut sit oportet; Non Ens autem produci nequit, sed tantum Ens; prout causam habere producentem & existere facientem, ipsi Enti tantum convenit. Resp. Ad decisionem notandum, duo privationis conceptu includi posse, 1.puram absentiam, istius quod adesse debebat, & sic neutiquam datur privatio, sed in se non-Ens & nihil est, Exgr. si cæcitas præcise significet ipsam visus absentiam in oculo humano, non datur, sed dati seu debiti est negatio. 2. Illam dispositionem partium subjecti, quæ, quod ibi fit, ubi ipsi esse non convenit, prava dicitur; Atque ita quidem datur, sed non nisi denominativè est ipsa privatio. Ex gr. sic illa dispositio partium oculi datur quidem, sed quia nunc talis est, ut actiones lædat aut tollat, ideo prava dicitur & morbus, vel privatio, sed non nisi denominativè; ipsa enim illa dispositio positivum quid est, à positivâ etiam causâ factum.
units.tr: 4. I. That there is privation seems not to be in doubt, since in act and in fact many things are said of things which, since they are not positive, involve a negation of some perfection due to them, as a man is said to be blind, sick, and so on. Yet it seems strongly to stand in the way: 1. Because to exist is the same as to be posited in the nature of things, and this is to be positive; wherefore, since privation cannot be positive, it seems it can neither be posited nor exist. 2. Because what exists in the nature of things must be present somewhere; but presence presupposes existence, and this presupposes being; wherefore, if privation were given, it would seem to be a being. 3. And more so, what is given must be produced to be; but non-being cannot be produced, only being; since to have a producing cause and to be made to exist belongs only to being itself. Reply: For the resolution, note that two things can be included in the concept of privation: 1. pure absence of what ought to be present, and so privation is in no way given, but in itself is non-being and nothing; e.g. if blindness precisely signifies the very absence of sight in the human eye, it is not given, but is a negation of what is given or due. 2. That disposition of the parts of the subject which, because it is there where it is not fitting for it to be, is called depraved; and so indeed it is given, but only denominatively is it privation itself. E.g. that disposition of the parts of the eye is indeed given, but because it now is such that it harms or destroys its actions, therefore it is called depraved and disease, or privation, but only denominatively; for that disposition itself is something positive, made also by a positive cause.

units.la: 5. II. Quiddítas Privationis definitione explicanda est; Hanc autem mihi definitionem constitui, quod fit perfectionis debita absentia; Absentia dicitur vel & Negatio, quàtenus hæc absentiæ est index: Attamen licet omnis privatio fit negatio, non tamen vice versâ omnis negatio est privatio: Differunt quippe inter fe 1. subjecto, quod privatio præfupponit, negatio tollit. 2. Objecto, quoniam privatio negat debitam perfectionem, Negatio quamcunque. 3. Modo, quia privatio habilitatem subjecti præfupponit, quam nec curat quidem negatio.
units.tr: 5. II. The quiddity of privation is to be explained by definition; I have settled on this definition for myself: it is the absence of a due perfection. Absence is called or negation, insofar as this is the sign of absence. Yet although every privation is a negation, not conversely is every negation a privation. They differ indeed 1. in subject: privation presupposes a subject, negation removes it. 2. in object: privation denies a due perfection, negation any whatever. 3. in mode: privation presupposes the aptitude of the subject, which negation does not even care about.

units.la: 6. Illud quod per privationem abest & negatur, debita est perfectio. Perfectio dicitur, quàtenus ad complementum rei, tali tempore, ordine & conditione constituendæ requiritur, quæ quoque eò ipso, quòd quasi à subjecto, haberi debeat, habitus appellatur, qui ideoque hîc nihil est, nisi debita istius perfectionis praesentia.
units.tr: 6. That which is absent and denied by privation is a due perfection. Perfection is so called insofar as it is for the completion of a thing, to be constituted at such a time, in such an order and condition, is required; which, also by the very fact that it ought to be had, as if from a subject, is called a habit; which therefore here is nothing but the due presence of that perfection.

units.la: 7. Debita autem hîc dicitur, iftaprivatione negata perfectio, eô quod ipsi subjecto vel natura, vel tempore, vel ordine conveniat. Natura inquam, prout illa persectio ad essentialem rei constitutionem aliquo modo pertinet, prout Animal naturâ suâ visus subjectum est. Tempore autem, quatenus ad illam constitutionem possidendam nonnunquam praerequiritur quaedam praeparatio, aliquo temporis tractu peragenda, quo nondum exspirato, absoluta nondum censetur debita ista persectio; adeoque tum ejus absentia privatio dici nequit. Quemadmodum catuli ante nonum diem non videntes non rectè appellantur caeci; & infantes ante sextum mensem licet dentes non habeant, edentuli tamen non sunt dicendi. Ordine denique quâtenus, aliquâ successio, institutio, aut contractus requiritur ad istam praesentiam, ac perfectionis debitudinem, quibus non extantibus non fit privatio, licet ea persectio non acquiratur. Ita filius Regis non nisi post mortem Patris regno carere dici poterit.
units.tr: 7. Due here is said of that perfection denied by this privation, because it suits the subject either by nature, or by time, or by order. Nature, I say, insofar as that perfection pertains in some way to the essential constitution of a thing, as an animal is by its nature the subject of sight. By time, however, insofar as for possessing that constitution a certain preparation is sometimes required, to be carried out over some stretch of time; before this has elapsed, that due perfection is not yet considered complete, and so its absence cannot then be called privation. Just as puppies that do not see before the ninth day are not rightly called blind; and infants before the sixth month, although they have no teeth, are not to be called toothless. By order, finally, insofar as some succession, institution, or contract is required for that presence and the due-ness of the perfection, without which privation does not arise, although that perfection is not acquired. Thus the king's son can be said to lack the kingdom only after his father's death.

units.la: 8. Ad tertium, 1. Hinc patet privationem non esse purum ac putum nihil, quoniam nihil non est alicujus subjecti. At privatio requirit subjectum. Nihil à nihilo non differt. At à privatione differt privatio, àcæcitate surditas. 2. Nec tamen est res aliqua vel Ens. Hoc enim quid positivum est, ac ponit perfectionem: At privatio negativa & perfectionem tollit. Quinimo si privatio foret Ens, privationis posset dari privatio; adeoque daretur processus in infinitum.
units.tr: 8. As to the third point: hence it is clear that privation is not pure and simple nothing, since nothing belongs to any subject. But privation requires a subject. Nothing does not differ from nothing. But privation differs from privation: blindness from deafness. 2. Nor is it, however, some thing or being. For this is something positive, and posits perfection; but privation is negative and removes perfection. Indeed, if privation were a being, there could be a privation of privation; and so there would be an infinite regress.

units.la: 9. Quarto, Privationis divisio ex opposita habitus sive debitæ perfectionis diversitate petenda. Quare dum perfectio rei vel à natura, vel ab ordine & institutione ipsi convenit, Privatio quoque vel Naturalis erit vel Politica. Priore tollitur perfectio naturæ debita; posteriore ea quæ ab institutione, vel mandato est.
units.tr: 9. Fourth, the division of privation must be derived from the diversity of the opposed habit, or due perfection. Therefore, since the perfection of a thing belongs to it either by nature or by order and institution, privation too will be either natural or political. The former removes the perfection due by nature; the latter that which is due by institution or command.

units.la: 10. Naturalis privatio vel est ipsius essentiæ, vel Proprietatum essentiæ. Illa tota rei natura perit, adeo ut naturali naturæ ordine ab ipsâ non detur regressus, ut à morte ad vitam; quare ea ipsa quoque subjectum illud è tali suo esse destruit.
units.tr: 10. Natural privation is either of the essence itself or of the properties of the essence. The former destroys the whole nature of the thing, so that by the natural order there is no return from it, as from death to life; wherefore this privation itself also destroys that subject from such being as it has.

units.la: 11. Privatio proprietatum, vel est concomitantium, id est, potentiarum, vel consequentium, id est actuum. Illa nunquam fit, nisi simul adsit essentiæ privatio, quare & illa ipsa, æquè ac illa essentiæ totalis appellatur, neque ordine naturali regressum ad habitum patitur. Hæc autem subjectum tali in esse remanere præsupponit, quod tamen vitio organorum aliorumque ad operationem requisitorum, actibus suis fructratur. Quare etiam partialis dicitur, regressumque admittit ad habitum.
units.tr: 11. Privation of properties is either of concomitants, that is, of powers, or of consequents, that is, of acts. The former never occurs unless privation of the essence is present at the same time; wherefore it too, just like that of the whole essence, is called total, and does not admit of return to the habit by the natural order. The latter presupposes that the subject remains in such a state of being, which, however, by the fault of the organs and of other things required for operation, is frustrated in its acts. Wherefore it is also called partial, and admits a return to the habit.

units.la: 12. Hic tamen notandum, illum regressum quidem non admitti à privationibus Essentiæ & proprietatum concomitantium; non tamen proinde ab omnibus partialibus & consequentium proprietatum privationibus admitti debere; Nam & inter has sunt, quæ naturalem regressum excludunt.
units.tr: 12. Here, however, it must be noted that this return is indeed not admitted by privations of the essence and of concomitant properties; yet it must not therefore be admitted for all partial privations and privations of consequent properties, for among these too there are some which exclude natural return.

units.la: 13. Præterea attendendum, nonnunquam aliter accipi Privationem totalem & partialem, ut scilicet totalis non sit, quæ totam essentiam destruit, sed quæ destruit omnem plane actum, ut universa cœcitas: Partialis vero quæ actum depravat, aut imminuit, ut in Myopia, Nyctalopia, & obscuritate visus cerni potest. Atque in hunc sensum nonnulli etiam dicunt à totali privatione non dari regressum; Quod licet in quibusdam obtineat, in nonnullis tamen plane fallit; Ventriculus quippe non solum à Bradypepsia, & Dyspepsia, sed & ab Apepsia ad ordinariam coctionem reduci potest.
units.tr: 13. Besides, it must be noted that total and partial privation are sometimes understood otherwise: namely, that total is not that which destroys the whole essence, but that which destroys every act altogether, as universal blindness; partial, however, is that which depraves or diminishes an act, as can be seen in myopia, nyctalopia, and dimness of sight. And in this sense some also say that from total privation there is no return; which, although it holds in some cases, in others plainly fails, for the stomach can be brought back to ordinary digestion not only from bradypepsia and dyspepsia, but also from apepsia.

units.la: 14. Politica privatio, ita Doctrinæ causa appellata, est defectus istius perfectionis, quæ est ab instituto. Estque vel communis, vel Propria. Illa est defectus à regulâ & normâ, vitæ & actionibus præ-
units.tr: 14. Political privation, so called for the sake of teaching, is the defect of that perfection which is from institution. It is either common or proper. The former is a defect from the rule and norm of life and actions pre-

units.la: E . scriscriptâ; Adeoque est peccatum. Hæc verò est partim carentia graduum dignitatis, affinitatis ac consanguineitatis: partim desectus possessionum ac divitiarum, &c. Et hæc de Privatione, adeoque & reliquis Mediis, pro instituto dicta sufficient.
units.tr: scribed in writing; and so it is sin. The latter is partly the lack of degrees of dignity, affinity and consanguinity, partly the defect of possessions and riches, and so on. And what has been said about privation, and so about the remaining means, according to the plan, is enough.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: Chapter IX

units.la: DE Principiis.
units.tr: On Principles

units.la: 1. IN omni scientiâ tria requiri supra dictum est, Subjectum, ejusque principia ac affectiones, eademque aliquo modo inter se distincta; Quare nec minus illa Metaphysica tribuenda videntur, utpote quæ scientiarum est accuratissima. Fuit quidem consideratum Ens, tanquam ejus subjectum, qualia autem ejus sint principia, qualesque affectiones, ac quomodo se ea ad Ens habeant, præunoscendum nunc restat; Materia satis ardua, ac vix dum ab aliis tentata, in quâ glaciem quasi frangendo, conabor explicare, primo principia, deinde affectiones.
units.tr: 1. As said above, every science requires three things: a subject, its principles, and its affections, and these must be distinguished from one another in some way. Metaphysics, as the most exact of the sciences, should therefore be credited with these too. Being has indeed been considered as its subject. It remains now to establish beforehand what its principles are, what its affections are, and how these stand in relation to Being. This is a rather difficult matter, scarcely yet attempted by others, and in it I will try, as it were, to break the ice and explain: first the principles, then the affections.

units.la: 2. Quantum igitur ad principia, 1. explicanda generalis eorum natura ac diversitas in actu signato. 2. In actu exercito ipsa ad Ens erunt referenda.
units.tr: 2. As for principles, then: first, their general nature and their diversity must be explained in the signate act; second, in the exercised act they must be referred to Being.

units.la: 3. Principium ergo generaliter definitur, quòd sit illud, unde res est, fit ac cognoscitur. Quae definitio ob generalitatem, omnibus modis dependentiae latissimè dictae, adeoque & omnibus causis, tam rei, quam cognitionis accomodari potest; Unde duplex communiter statuitur principium, scilicet essendi, quod etiam principium fiendi sub se continet, & cognoscendi, quorum hoc complexum, eo quòd axiomata constituat, illud autem incomplexum, utpote simplici termino apprehensum, appellatur.
units.tr: 3. A principle is therefore generally defined as that from which a thing is, comes to be, and is known. Because this definition is so general, it can be applied in every way that dependence is broadly understood, and so to all causes, both of the thing and of knowledge. Hence a twofold principle is commonly laid down: that of being, which also includes the principle of becoming, and that of knowing. Of these, the former is called complex, since it constitutes axioms, while the latter is called incomplex, since it is apprehended by a simple term.

units.la: 4. Principium porrò essendi, vel est externum, vel internum. Externa, quae actione aliquâ intercedente aliquid à suâ essentiâ diversum constituunt, Efficiens & finis sunt. Interna autem ipsam essentiam ingrediuntur, eamque intrinsecè constituunt, ita ut ipsa rei essentia evadant, neque ab ipsâ ulterius distingui possint, nisi vel ratione ratiocinatâ, vel conceptu quodam inadæquato, per modum alicujus originatione conceptuum prioris; Qualia corporis naturalis sunt materia & forma.
units.tr: 4. Further, the principle of being is either external or internal. External principles, which, through some intervening action, constitute something different from the essence, are the efficient cause and the end. Internal principles enter into the essence itself and constitute it intrinsically, so that they become the very essence of the thing and cannot be distinguished from it further, except by reasoned reason or by some inadequate concept, after the manner of one of the concepts prior in origin. Of a natural body, matter and form are such principles.

units.la: 5. Ex his igitur enumeratis Enti quaedam convenire debent, aut ipsum omni principio destituetur; Quaenam autem conveniant, quaenam non, in specie videndum. Occurrunt itaque 1. Principia complexa, quae sunt axiomata quaedam, ex solis terminis, eorumque complexione nota. Atque haec quidem ut in omni scientiâ ita quoque in Metaphysica requiruntur; Sed ea non sunt ipsius subjecti, sed cognitionis nostræ principia: Scientiæ autem est, principia sui subjecti statuere. Quare licet adsint illa principia cognoscendi, alia tamen, quæ aliquo modo & essendi sunt principia, Metaphysica ad suum subjectum postulare videtur.
units.tr: 5. Of these enumerated items, then, some ought to belong to Being, or else Being would lack every principle. Which ones belong and which do not must be examined in particular. There occur, therefore: (1) complex principles, which are certain axioms known from the terms alone and their combination. These are required in every science, and so in Metaphysics too; but they are not principles of the subject itself, but of our knowledge, and it belongs to a science to set down the principles of its own subject. Therefore, although those principles of knowing are present, Metaphysics seems to demand others for its subject which are in some way also principles of being.

units.la: 6. Dices: Metaphysica, quoniam Sapientia est, hoc est, ex intelligentia & scientia conflata; etiam complexorum principiorum est cognitio; Quare hæc sufficere videntur. Resp. Ita quidem est: Sed Metaphysica tamen non facit illa principia cognoscendi, ut sint principia sui subjecti: Sed illa ex notionibus suis eruta, vel sui vel alterius scientiæ subjecti cognitioni substernit. Quare nec propterea illa complexa sufficere videntur; Quoniam & illa cognoscendi principia, si proxima fuerint, ab ipsis principiis essendi, eorumque notionibus desumi debent; quatenus nempe axiomata certa & indubitata ex eis circa subjectum colliguntur.
units.tr: 6. You will say: Metaphysics, since it is wisdom, that is, compounded of understanding and knowledge, also has knowledge of complex principles, so these seem sufficient. Reply: It is indeed so; yet Metaphysics does not make those principles of knowing into principles of its subject. Rather, having drawn them from its own notions, it lays them as a foundation for knowledge of its own subject or of the subject of another science. Therefore those complex principles do not seem sufficient on this account either, since those principles of knowing, if they are proximate, must be derived from the principles of being themselves and their notions, namely insofar as certain and indubitable axioms about the subject are gathered from them.

units.la: 7. Deinde inter essendi principia primò occurrunt externa: Sed hisce Ens quà Ens porrùs caret; neque in scientiâ omni requiruntur, utpote extra essentiam subjecti constituta. Ea quippe si enti ut sic velles tribuere, processum in infinitum non evitabis. Principia enim essendi externa, ab Ente realiter deberent distingui, nec tamen minus quidquam esse, quam Ens, utpote virtute suâ Ens continentia. Quare si hæc Entia dicantur, vicissim alia requirerent principia; Quæ, eo quod entia essent, & Ens omne ex hypothesi principia externa haberet, denuò alia requirerent; Et sic manifestus est ille processus. Deinde Deus Ens est, principia tamen talia non habet, ob summam ac infinitam suam persectionem, ac omnimodam independentiam; Quod autem non convenit omni Enti, id quoque Enti, quâ Enti non convenit.
units.tr: 7. Next, among the principles of being, the external ones come first. But these Being as such lacks, and they are not required in every science, since they are constituted outside the essence of the subject. For if you wished to attribute them to Being as such, you would not avoid an infinite regress. External principles of being would have to be really distinct from Being, and yet nonetheless something other than Being, since by their own power they would contain Being. So if these are called beings, they would in turn require other principles; and these, since they too are beings, and every being by hypothesis has external principles, would again require others. Thus that regress is evident. Further, God is a Being, yet he has no such principles, because of his supreme and infinite perfection and his absolute independence. What does not belong to every Being does not belong to Being as such.

units.la: 8. Interna igitur sola restant, quæ vel ideò requiri videntur, quod alias nulla subjecto Metaphysicæ convenirent; adeoque nullæ affectiones aut directè, aut à priori de Ente demonstrari possent. Imò sic nulla axiomata, sive complexa cognitionis principia, debitè formarentur; iis enim ut constet sua veritas, in ipsius Entis fundantur principiis, adeoque aliquid, Enti à priori conveniens, exprimere debent. Quin & principia demonstrationis indirectæ, sive ad impossibile ducentis, (quale est illud: Impossibile est aliquid simul esse, & non esse) utpote negante modo expressa; aliud præsupponunt, cujus modus est affirmans, quale v.igr. est: Necesse est, quodlibet esse vel non esse; quod in ipso Ente ipsum esse præsupponit, tanquam aliquod prius;quemadmodum semper abstractum concreto suo, aliquo signo rationis ad minimum prius concipiendum est.
units.tr: 8. Internal principles therefore remain alone, which seem to be required only because otherwise no affections could belong to the subject of Metaphysics, and so no affections could be demonstrated of Being either directly or a priori. Indeed, in that case no axioms, or complex principles of knowledge, would be properly formed; for their truth to be established they rest on the principles of Being itself, and so must express something belonging to Being a priori. Moreover, the principles of indirect demonstration, or reduction to the impossible (such as It is impossible for something to be and not to be at once), since they are expressed in a negating mode, presuppose another principle whose mode is affirming, such as It is necessary that anything either is or is not. This presupposes being itself in Being, as something prior, just as an abstract thing must always be conceived prior to its concrete thing, by some sign of reason at least.

units.la: 9. Vehementer tamen obstare videtur 1. Quòd Entis principia in genere, etiam Deo, ac attributis divinis accommodari deberent; Nihil enim Enti ut sic, tribui debet, quod iis, de quibus Ens dicitur, repugnet. 2. Quòd videantur illa principia Entia esse debere, adeoque iterum alia requirere principia, quare per ea, æquè ac externa, processus in infinitum induceretur. 3. Quòd sic omne Ens compositum foret, ex illis videlicet principiis, quæ quia sunt interna, videntur nulla alia esse posse, præter materiam & formam. At nihil absurdius, quam Ens quâ Ens dicere compositum, præsertim ex materiâ & formâ. 4. Quod sic Ente aliquid prius concedendum esse videretur, Quoniam principiū omne suo principiato prius est. Verùm enim verò quoniam duplicia sunt principia interna incomplexa, quædam videlicet, quæ simul cum sunt subjecti & affectionum proprie dicta, ideoque re differunt, ab eo cujus principia esse dicuntur: Quædam verò re non distinguuntur, sed saltem sunt rationes sive notiones per modum antecedentiū conceptæ, quibus ad consequentium notitiā venire possumus, quo pacto Deitas est principium infinitatis, quia hæc illam præsupponit. Ea igitur, quæ primi ordinis sunt principia, hic omninò negari debent, ob alias rationes; Quibus tamen posterioris ordinis principia non tolluntur; Vid. Combacchium, lib. 1. Metaph. cap. 3.
units.tr: 9. Yet there seem to be strong objections: (1) that principles of Being in general should also be adapted to God and the divine attributes, for nothing should be attributed to Being as such that conflicts with those things of which Being is predicated; (2) that these principles would seem to have to be beings, and so would again require other principles, so that through them, as through external principles, an infinite regress would be induced; (3) that every Being would thus be composite, namely from those principles which, since they are internal, seem to be possible only as matter and form. But nothing is more absurd than to call Being as such composite, especially of matter and form; (4) that something would thus seem to have to be conceded prior to Being, since every principle is prior to what it principles. But since principles are twofold, internal and incomplex, some of them, namely those which together with the subject are properly called affections, really differ from that of which they are said to be principles. Others, however, are not really distinct, but are at least reasons or notions conceived after the manner of antecedents, by which we can come to know consequents. In this way Deity is the principle of infinity, because the latter presupposes it. Therefore those which are principles of the first order must here be entirely denied, for other reasons; yet principles of the later order are not thereby removed. See Combacchius, Metaphysics book 1, chapter 3.

units.la: 10. Quare ea Entis principia ita erunt constituenda, ut Deo, ejusque attributis non repugnent, ac simul omni Enti conveniant. Non igitur Entia quædam, ab eo Ente, cujus sunt principia, erunt distincta; nedum materia & forma, licet ipsis ratione officii aliquo modo analoga. Quæ proinde processum in infinitum non involvunt, neque Ens compositum aut alio aliquo posterius reddunt, utpote quæ saltem inadæquato modo considerandi, per modum antecedentium in signo rationis, sive secundum originationem conceptuum, de Ente concipiuntur, ac si junctim ipsum Ens constituerent: Quod omninò secundum conceptus ipsorum formales locum habet; à parte enim objecti & rei idem planè sunt, cum ipso Ente.
units.tr: 10. Therefore those principles of Being must be constituted so that they do not conflict with God or his attributes, and at the same time belong to every Being. Not therefore are some beings to be distinct from that Being of which they are the principles, much less matter and form, although these are in some way analogous to them by reason of their function. These principles therefore do not involve an infinite regress, nor do they make Being composite or posterior to anything else, since they are conceived of Being only in an inadequate mode of consideration, after the manner of antecedents in a sign of reason, or according to the origin of concepts, as if together they constituted Being itself. This holds entirely according to their formal concepts; for in respect of the object and the thing they are altogether the same as Being itself.

units.la: 11. In ordine igitur Entitatum ad modos revocanda sunt, quoniam concipiuntur secundum formas suas in ipso Ente esse, illudque constituere. Inadæquatiquippemodi Entis duplicis generis sunt, alii enim per modum antecedentis, qui principia, alii per modum consequentis, qui affectiones dicuntur, ipsi Enti inesse concipiuntur.
units.tr: 11. In the order of entities, therefore, these principles are to be reduced to modes, since they are conceived, according to their forms, to be in Being itself and to constitute it. The inadequate modes of Being are of two kinds: some are conceived as inhering in Being itself after the manner of an antecedent, and these are called principles; others are conceived after the manner of a consequent, and these are called affections.

units.la: 12. Talia autem principia vulgò Essentia & existentia dicuntur: Sed non satis accommodatè. Primò enim illa principia ita constituenda sunt, ut Enti quàtenus esse habet, in omni ratione conveniant, neque ab ipso vel conceptu separari & abesse queant. At Ens nec semper, nec omne, ut præsens suum esse habens, hoc est existens concipitur; Ita enim nunquam sine singularitatis formâ concipi posset. Secundò, essentia non præcisè infert ipsum habere τὸ esse, quod tamen quam maximè ad principii radicalis rationem requiritur, sed præterea certum quem modum, quo illud esse habetur, quare alterutrius principii quasi modus est, & entis potius affectio, quam principium. Tertiò, existentia non nisi modum ipsum esse consequentem, quàtenus scilicet Ens hoc præsens habet, denotat; Quare nec minus quam essentia principii alicujus modus esse debet. Quartò, interna principia Entis analogicè materiæ & formæ, esse naturale corporis naturalis constituentibus, respondere debent. Quemadmodum igitur hæc ipsum esse naturale inferunt, & quidem materia prout illud ipsum simpliciter est naturale; forma verò prout illud tale vel tale est, distinctum à quovis alio: Ita quoque principia Entis, ipsum esse Entis inferre debent, adeo ut unum illud esse constituat, hoc est possideri vel haberi, alterum illud à quocunque alio distinctum dicat.
units.tr: 12. Such principles are commonly called essence and existence, but not very aptly. First, because those principles ought to be constituted so that they belong to Being insofar as it has being, in every respect, and cannot be separated or absent from the concept itself. But Being is not always conceived as having its being present, that is, as existing, nor is every being so conceived, for then it could never be conceived without the form of singularity. Second, essence does not precisely imply that it has the τὸ [the to] being, which is nonetheless especially required for the notion of a radical principle, but it implies in addition a certain mode by which that being is had. So it is a kind of mode of one or other principle, and an affection of being rather than a principle. Third, existence denotes only the mode consequent upon being itself, insofar as it has this present being, and so it should be a mode of some principle no less than essence is. Fourth, the internal principles of Being, analogous to matter and form, which are the constituents of a natural body, should correspond to it. Just as matter and form imply the natural being itself, matter insofar as it is simply natural and form insofar as it is such or such, distinct from anything else, so too the principles of Being ought to imply the being of Being itself, such that one constitutes that being, that is, is possessed or had, while the other says that it is distinct from anything else.

units.la: 13. Cui negotio sufficere existimo, si principia Entis interna statuantur esse Constitutio & Distinctio. Et quidem ut Constitutio sit ipsius esse possessio, hoc est ipsum esse, quatenus possidetur: Distinctio verò ipsius esse separatio, sive ipsum esse, prout ab aliis distinguitur. Quod ut pateat, imprimis notandum, tam constitutionem, quam distinctionem, non semper positivè sensu accipi debere, ac si omne Ens ab alio aliquo esset constitutum, aut ipso actu ab aliis distinctum: sed & quandoque negativè; quomodo & Deus negativè constitutus dici potest, quatenus nihil aliud est, quod ipsum constituat: Et ante mundum creatum, negativè distinctus dici potest, quatenus & tunc æquè ac nunc esse sibi proprium obtinebat. Neuter tamen sensus hic seorsim acceptandus, sed aliquis indifferens ad utrumque.
units.tr: 13. I think it is enough for this task to hold that the internal principles of being are Constitution and Distinction. Constitution is the possession of being itself, that is, being as it is possessed; Distinction is the separation of being itself, or being as it is distinguished from others. To make this clear, it must first be noted that both constitution and distinction are not always to be taken in a positive sense, as if every being were constituted by some other thing or actually distinguished from others; they are sometimes to be taken negatively as well. In this way God may be said to be constituted negatively, insofar as nothing else constitutes him; and before the world was created he may be said to be distinguished negatively, insofar as he then possessed his own being just as he does now. Yet neither sense is to be accepted here by itself; rather, one must be taken as indifferent to both.

units.la: 14. Atque hunc in modum non tantum omni Enti conveniunt Constitutio & distinctio, sed & ex iis absolutæ Entis proprietates seu affectiones omnes deduci ac demonstrari possunt; Cujus gratia Principia Entis potissimum investiganda videbantur. Et hæc de principiis Entis.
units.tr: 14. In this manner, constitution and distinction belong not only to every being, but from them all the properties or affections of absolute being can be deduced and demonstrated. For this reason the principles of being seemed especially to require investigation. And this is enough about the principles of being.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: CAPUT X. DE Affectionibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. ON AFFECTIONS.

units.la: 1. Restant denique investigandæ, ac cum Ente conferendæ, ipsius Affectiones, quæ de ipso per sua principia demonstrantur; Quæ consimiliter explicandæ veniunt, 1. quoad actum signatum; 2. quoad exercitum actum. Adeò ut in priori consideratione generalis affectionum natura ac differentia explicetur: in posteriori verò eædem cum Ente conferantur, ipsíque applicentur.
units.tr: 1. There remain finally to be investigated, and to be compared with Being, its affections, which are demonstrated of it through its own principles. These likewise come to be explained (1) with respect to the signified act and (2) with respect to the exercised act. Thus in the former consideration, the general nature and difference of affections is explained, while in the latter these same affections are compared with Being and applied to it.

units.la: 2. Prior igitur partim nominis, partim rei explicatione absolvitur. Quoad nomen igitur; Affectio ab afficiendo nomen habet, eò quod subjectum, dum de illo prædicatur afficiat. Significat autem modo animi afsectum, qualis est ira, amor &c. modo dispositionem prævia: modò respectum & relationem; modò quodvis accidens: modò denique proprium alicujus seu attributum, ex esse ipsius resultans; idque vel latè, prout etiam tribuitur illis, quæ non-sunt omninò nihil, v. gr. Privationi, Relationi &c. vel strictè, prout soli Enti tribuitur.
units.tr: 2. The first consideration is therefore completed partly by explaining the name and partly by explaining the thing. As to the name: affection comes from affecting, because it affects its subject when it is predicated of it. It signifies, in one sense, an emotion of the mind, such as anger or love; in another, a prior disposition; in another, a respect or relation; in another, any accident; and finally in another, a property or attribute of something, arising from its being. This is taken either broadly, when it is also ascribed to things that are not absolutely nothing, for example privation, relation and the like, or strictly, when it is ascribed to Being alone.

units.la: 3. Et quidem in hac significatione, hic retinendâ, aliter dicitur 1. Proprietas, quòd soli suo subjecto conveniat. 2. Passio, quod Ens in prædicando ab ipsâ quasi patiatur. 3. Attributum, quod quidem aliis, præreliquis, eo quod aliquam impersectionem videantur involvere, maximè allubescit, mihi verò generalius debito esse videtur, eo quod etiam dentur attributa v. g. genus & differentia, quæ tamen affectiones non sunt. Neque ulla, in reliquis apparet imperfectio, nisi quod aliquam passionem seu subjectionem subjecto tribuant, quæ, cum nulla sit, nisi prædicationis, & non strictè dictæ passionis aut inhæsionis, etiam nomine Attributi involvitur.
units.tr: 3. In this sense, which is the one to be retained here, the affection is also called differently: 1. a property, because it belongs to its subject alone; 2. a passion, because Being, in being predicated, as it were suffers it; 3. an attribute, which name is most pleasing to others, because it seems to involve some imperfection. To me, however, it seems too general, since there are also attributes, for example genus and difference, which are nonetheless not affections. Nor does any imperfection appear in the rest, except that they ascribe to the subject some passion or subjection. Since this is nothing but predication, and not passion or inherence in the strict sense, it is included also under the name of attribute.

units.la: 4. In reipsâ videndum 1. Quid sit Afsectio? 2. Quotuplex sit? Quoad primum, Affectio est attributum alicui proprium, ad esse ipsius consequens. Unde conflat, 1. Quod omnis affectio de suo subjecto debeat prædicari; non enim alias foret attributum.
units.tr: 4. In the thing itself we must consider 1. what an affection is, and 2. how many kinds there are. As to the first: an affection is an attribute proper to something, following from its being. Hence it is clear, 1. that every affection must be predicated of its own subject; otherwise it would not be an attribute.

units.la: 2. Quod de subjecto solo debeat dici, quoniam proprium est ipsum consequens: non quidem semper ordine naturæ strictè dictæ, sed etiam ordine originationis conceptuum.
units.tr: 2. That it must be said of the subject alone, since a property is what follows it; not always indeed in the order of nature strictly speaking, but also in the order of the origin of concepts.

units.la: 5. Ad secundum, Affectio vel absoluta est, vel respectiva. Absoluta dicitur, quæ subjecto, per se convenit, adeoque ex
units.tr: 5. As to the second: an affection is either absolute or respective. It is called absolute when it belongs to the subject in itself, and so

units.la: ipsis principiis jam unitè spectatis emanat, adeò ut certus aliquis modus sit, ipsi subjecto conveniens, còquod ex talibus principiis constet. Et hujusmodi affectiones vel accidentales dicuntur, eò quòd etiam abesse possint, vel essentiales, quòd salvo subjecti esse non abśint.
units.tr: flows from the principles already considered together, so that it is a certain mode belonging to the subject itself, because it rests on such principles. Affections of this kind are called either accidental, because they can also be absent, or essential, because they are not absent so long as the subject's being remains.

units.la: 6. Atque hæ essentiales nonnunquam à subjecto suo distinguuntur, non tantum formaliter, quod semper & in omnibus ad minimum requiritur, sed etiam secundum rem ipsam, quia tales affectiones etiam distinctum suum esse, licet à subjecto dependens habeant; Quales v. gr. dicuntur esse propria Accidentia ad series categoriarum reducta. Nonnunquam vero tantum formaliter distinguuntur, suntque nihil aliud, quam inadæquati quidam modi, ipsum subjectum considerandi.
units.tr: 6. These essential affections are sometimes distinguished from their subject, not only formally (which is always and in all cases required at least), but also in reality, since such affections have their own distinct being, although they depend on the subject. Examples are the so-called proper accidents, reduced to the series of the categories. Sometimes, however, they are distinguished only formally, and are nothing other than certain inadequate modes of considering the subject itself.

units.la: 7. Præterea talis affectio, vel est Positiva, vel Negativa; Illa positivam sui modi præsentiam indicat: hæc vero oppositi alicujus negationem; Quod imprimis intelligendum ratione vocis, quæ ob defectum melioris negativa est, aliquid positivum nihilominus in re designans; deinde & ratione conceptûs, quatenus is per remotionem oppositæ, sive imperfectioris, sive perfectioris, positivo conceptu apprehensæ, perfectionem aliquam, aut aliter non comprehensibilem, aut difficultèr exexprimendam, repræsentat.
units.tr: 7. Moreover, such an affection is either positive or negative. The former indicates the presence of its own mode; the latter the negation of some opposite. This must be understood, first, with respect to the word, which, for lack of a better term, is negative, yet nonetheless designates something positive in reality; and secondly with respect to the concept, insofar as, by removing the opposite, whether less or more perfect, it represents through a positive concept some perfection that is otherwise either not comprehensible or hard to express.

units.la: . 8. Respectiva dicitur affectio, quæ subjecto convenit, ob relationem seu respectum ipsius ad aliud; Quæ proinde, quòd ex relatione oriatur, non nisi externè denominat.
units.tr: 8. An affection is called respective when it belongs to the subject on account of a relation, or respect of it to something else. Since it arises from a relation, it therefore only names it externally.

units.la: 9. Sequuntur nunc Affectiones in actu exercito consiederandæ, quâtenus Enti tribuuntur; Quæ & ideo transscendentales appellari possunt, quod species & genera prædicamentalia Entium suâ generalitate superent: Minus rectè tamen, seorsim transscendentia dicuntur; Illa enim appellatio, non minus Enti ejusque synonymis, quam Affectionibus tribuenda, non tantum ratione communitatis significandi, sed & generalitatis conceptuum.
units.tr: 9. Next are to be considered the affections in the exercised act, insofar as they are ascribed to Being. For this reason they may also be called transcendental, because they surpass the species and genera of the categories by their generality. It is, however, less correctly said that they are transcendent by themselves; for that name must be given to Being and its synonyms no less than to the affections, not only because of the commonness of their signification, but also because of the generality of their concepts.

units.la: 10. Affectiones igitur, quâtenus Entis sunt, expendendæ veniunt, inquirendo 1. An Enti conveniant affectiones? 2. Quid sint illæ? 3. Quid Enti superaddant? 4. Quotuplices sint? 5. Quis ordo inter eas de Ente demonstrandas, in genuino Metaphysicæ tractatu, observari debeat?
units.tr: 10. The affections, then, insofar as they belong to Being, come to be examined, by inquiring: 1. Do affections belong to Being? 2. What are they? 3. What do they add to Being? 4. How many kinds are there? 5. What order should be observed among them, in demonstrating them of Being, in a genuine treatise of Metaphysics?

units.la: 11. I. Dari Entis affectiones, utut negandum non videatur, non admodum firmiter tamen alii plerique eas demonstrarunt. Burgersdicius, id non debere esse dubium asserit, quoniam datur medium inter Ens & nihil. Sed non stringit ratio, à positione generis ad positionem determinatæ speciei; qualis est v. gr. hæc: Datur Animal ; Ergo datur homo. Non enim omne medium statim Affectio est Entis. Alii illas dari probant, quia dantur de facto Unitas, veritas &. Sed sic quod inquiritur, desideratur, nempe an unitas, veritas &c. sint Entis affectiones. Alii hoc inde astruunt, quia Metaphysica scientia est, ideoque sui subjecti requirit afsectiones. Sed manifestus sic circulus committendus est ; Antea quippe metaphysicam scientiam esse,probari debet,quia Ens, quod ipsius subjectum est, habet affectiones, & precariò obtineri potest Metaphysicam esse scientiam , donec Entis affectiones ostendantur. Certius igitur eas probari existimo. 1. Dialectice ; Quia multa dantur, quæ de Ente prædicantur in quale, eique soli conveniunt : quod autem in quale de uno solo dicitur, id ejus affectio est. 2. Analytice; Omne habens esse, habet & requisita ad esse ; Ens autem habet esse ; Ergo & requisita ad illud ; Quod verò illa requisita habet, id perfectum est; Et quod perfectum est habet perfectiones, sive affectiones. Firmiores si quis promat, rationes, gratiæ ei non erunt denegandæ.
units.tr: 11. I. That there are affections of Being, though this does not seem to be denied, has not been demonstrated very firmly by most others. Burgersdicius asserts that this ought not to be doubted, since there is a middle between Being and nothing. But this does not follow: from the positing of a genus one cannot infer the positing of a determinate species, as in this example: there is an animal, therefore there is a man. For not every middle is at once an affection of Being. Others prove that they exist because Unity, Truth and so on exist in fact. But this begs the question, since what is in dispute is whether unity, truth and so on are affections of Being. Others argue for it from the fact that Metaphysics is a science, and therefore requires affections of its subject. But this would be a manifest circle: for it would first have to be proved that Metaphysics is a science, because Being, which is its subject, has affections; and it would be assumed without proof that Metaphysics is a science until the affections of Being are shown. I therefore think they are proved more certainly: 1. Dialectically: because many things are predicated of Being as a quality and belong to it alone; and what is predicated as a quality of one thing alone is its affection. 2. Analytically: every thing that has being also has the requisites for being; Being has being; therefore it also has the requisites for it. But whatever has those requisites is perfect; and what is perfect has perfections, or affections. If anyone brings forward firmer arguments, he should not be denied his due credit.

units.la: 12. Verum obstare videtur hisce Entis affectionibus 1. Quod sic Ens quâ Ens compositum foret, ex esse videlicet & afsectionibus. Resp. Negatur consequentia, quia Entis affectiones aut identificantur cum subjecto, neque ab ipso realiter, sed tantum inadæquato conceptu differunt; aut non nisi denominationes sunt externæ, nullam cum subjecto compositionem involventes. Objic. 2. Affectio debet realiter distingui à subjecto suo. Resp. Non semper, ut plurimum enim contrarium obtinet. Instant. 1. Aqui prædicantur affectiones de subjecto in secundo modo per se: Sed quæ ita prædicantur, realiter distinguuntur. Resp. 1. Hoc postremum in plurimis fallit. 2. Ut & Antecedens, quoniam multæ affectiones necessitatem tertii gradus obtinent, ac reciprocè de subjecto prædicantur. Instant. 2. Inter prius & posterius realis requiritur distinctio: At subjectum est prius, & affectio posterior. Resp. Antecedens falsum 1. in ordine naturæ secundum existendi consecutionem, v. gr. Animal prius est homine, non tamen ab ipso realiter distinguitur. 2. In prioritate originationis metaphysicæ, quæ saltem conceptuum inter se est, quo pacto essentia prior dicitur existentiâ, ab ipsâ tamen realiter non distinguitur. Objic. 3. Afsectio non debet dici in quid de suo subjecto: At si affectio esset realiter idem cum Ente, posset quoque de ipso in quid dici. Resp. Ad antecedens: Affectio potest dici de subjecto secundum identitatem realem, non secundum formalitatem conceptûs, quemadmodum & affectiones divinæ de Deo dicuntur.
units.tr: 12. Yet these affections of Being seem to be opposed: 1. that Being, insofar as it is Being, would then be composite, namely of being and affections. Reply. The consequence is denied, because the affections of Being are either identical with the subject and differ from it not really but only in an inadequate concept, or they are merely external denominations, involving no composition with the subject. Objection. 2. An affection must be really distinct from its subject. Reply. Not always; for the contrary usually holds. Counter-objection. 1. Affections are predicated of the subject in the second mode of predication through itself; but what are so predicated are really distinct. Reply. 1. This last point fails in most cases. 2. Also the antecedent, since many affections hold the necessity of the third grade and are predicated of the subject reciprocally. Counter-objection. 2. Between what is prior and what is posterior a real distinction is required; but the subject is prior and the affection posterior. Reply. The antecedent is false: 1. in the order of nature, according to the succession of existence, for example, animal is prior to man, yet is not really distinct from him; 2. in the priority of metaphysical origin, which is at least a priority of concepts among themselves, in the way that essence is said to be prior to existence, yet is not really distinct from it. Objection. 3. An affection should not be said in quid of its own subject; but if an affection were really the same as Being, it could also be said in quid of it. Reply. As to the antecedent: an affection can be said of the subject according to real identity, not according to formal identity of concept, just as the divine attributes are also said of God.

units.la: 13. II. Quid sint affectiones ex applicatâ generali definitione patere potest; si videlicet, ex tali modo Enti dicantur convenire, ac ibi alicui competere dictæ sunt; ut videlicet de Ente solo prædicentur, nec tamen sint formaliter ipsum Ens, sed ipsius saltem consequentia. Non igitur sunt substantiæ aut accidentia, aut in universum aliquod Ens, quia & hisce, ut Entibus suæ forent affectiones, & his utpote denuò Entibus etiam suæ, idque in infinitum.
units.tr: 13. II. What affections are can be seen from the general definition applied to them: namely, that they are said to belong to Being in the manner described, and to pertain to it there. They are predicated of Being alone, yet they are not formally Being itself, but only its consequences. Therefore they are not substances or accidents, nor any Being in general. If they were, they would be affections of beings, and these in turn, being beings themselves, would have their own affections, and so on to infinity.

units.la: 14. III. Quoniam prædicatio Affectionum de Ente non est identica planè & nugatoria, manifestè apparet ab iis Enti aliquid apportari, quod præcise ipsum Ens non est, dubitari potest, quidnam sit illud, quod in tali prædicatione affectiones Enti superaddant? Quod quidem non potest esse, aut Ens, aut substantia, aut Accidens, quia nihil horum sunt affectiones, sed certa aliqua formalitas, quæ ab ipso realiter non distinguatur; Sed velut ipsius modus consideratur, ut Essentia, Existentia, Unitas, Veritas &c. Vel ut denominatio externa, ut Causa, Causatum, Dependens, Independens, &c. Addunt alii etiam Negationem, Privationem, & Ensrationis. Sed priores duæ, licet voce videantur designari, in re tamen perfectionem tollunt; non addunt.
units.tr: 14. III. Since the predication of affections of Being is not plainly identical and idle, it is clearly apparent that they bring to Being something which Being itself precisely is not. It may be asked what that is which affections add to Being in such predication. It cannot be Being, or substance, or accident, because affections are none of these. It is rather a certain formality which is not really distinct from Being, and is regarded as its mode, such as essence, existence, unity, truth, etc. Or it is an external denomination, such as cause, caused, dependent, independent, etc. Others add also negation, privation, and a being of reason. But the first two, although they seem to be designated by a word, in reality take away perfection rather than add anything.

units.la: Posterius autem, Ens rationis puta, fundamentaliter nihil est, cum tamen Entis affectiones eo modo ipsum Ens esse debeant; Quare nec hoc admitti potest, nisi dicamus id ideo fieri, quia plurimæ assectiones ratione formæ ab intellectu concipiantur. Quæ ratio tamen non sufficit, ut illæ Enti, dum de ipso prædicantur, Ens rationis supperaddere dicantur.
units.tr: But the latter, a being of reason, is fundamentally nothing, although the affections of Being ought to make Being to be so in that way. Wherefore this cannot be admitted either, unless we say that this happens because many affections are conceived by the intellect by reason of form. Yet this reason is not sufficient for them to be said to add a being of reason to Being when they are predicated of it.

units.la: 15. IV. Differentiæ affectionum ex legitimis fundamentis eruere, laboratu opus est; Inprimis igitur Entis affectiones vel absolutæ sunt, vel respectivæ; Quarum illæ, ex principiis eruta, definiri possunt, quod sint, certi modi Entis ipsi consequenter tributi, eo quod in esse constitutum ac distinctum sit. Dicuntur autem modi Entis, quia conceptu saltem distinctæ, in ipso esse considerantur; Enti consequenter tribui dicuntur, non tempore, aut naturâ stricte dictâ, sed originatione metaphysicâ conceptuum. Et denique ipsi tribui dicuntur, quod constitutum ac distinctum sit, ut denotetur, eas ex illis duobus principiis deduci ac demonstrari debere. Hæ autem, putâ respectivæ affectiones, Enti convenient propter relationem ad aliud aliquod.
units.tr: 15. IV. The differences of affections must be drawn from legitimate foundations; it is a labour. First, then, the affections of Being are either absolute or respective. Of these, the former, drawn from principles, can be defined as certain modes of Being, consequently attributed to it, inasmuch as it is constituted and distinguished in being. They are called modes of Being because they are considered in being itself as distinct at least in concept; they are said to be attributed consequently, not in time or in nature strictly speaking, but by the metaphysical origination of concepts. And finally they are said to be attributed to it insofar as it is constituted and distinguished, to denote that they must be deduced and demonstrated from those two principles. But respective affections, such as these, belong to Being on account of relation to something else.

units.la: 16. Absolutæ affectiones, licet omnes utrumque Entis principium præsupponant, non tamen semper æque principaliter; Quare secundum illa principia, tanquam sua fundamenta dividi possunt, quod alia oriantur, scilicet principaliter ex constitutione, alia ex distinctione, alia ex utraque. In omni tamen genere una qua si radix est omnium reliquarum, ex ea oriarum: Quemadmodum earum, quæ ex constitutione oriuntur, prima & immediata est essentia: At quæ ex distinctione, existentia; Ex utraque Actus.
units.tr: 16. Absolute affections, although all presuppose both principles of Being, not always equally principally. Wherefore they can be divided according to those principles as their foundations, so that some arise principally from constitution, others from distinction, others from both. Yet in every genus there is one which is as it were the root of all the others, from which they arise: just as of those which arise from constitution, the first and immediate is essence; but of those from distinction, existence; from both, act.

units.la: 17. Ab essentia autem oriuntur tres illæ notissimæ, Vnitas, Veritas, Bonitas, sive perfectio. Vnitati iterum ortum debent. 1. Singularitas & Vniversalitas. 2. Simplicitas & Vnio. Veritati, 1. Necessitas & Contingentia; 2. Mutabilitas & Immutabilitas. 3. Certitudo & Evidentia. Bonitati autem sive perfectioni, Infinitas & finitas, Absolutio & Comparatio.
units.tr: 17. From essence arise those three most well-known: unity, truth, goodness, or perfection. From unity in turn arise: 1. singularity and universality; 2. simplicity and union. From truth: 1. necessity and contingency; 2. mutability and immutability; 3. certainty and evidence. To goodness or perfection: infinity and finitude, absoluteness and comparison.

units.la: 18. Existentia, ex distinctione sola dimanans, præsentia, adeoque localitati sive ubietati, ac durationi ortum præbet. Quemadmodum ab Actu ex utroque principio dimanante, propullulat Vtilitas, sive bonitas externa: Atque hæ absolutæ Entis Afsectiones sunt.
units.tr: 18. Existence, flowing from distinction alone, gives rise to presence, and so to locality or ubiety, and duration. Just as from act, flowing from both principles, springs utility, or external goodness. These are the absolute affections of Being.

units.la: 19. Respectiva affectiones, prout relationem præsupponunt, ita quoque pro diversitate relationum inter se distingui debent; Adeo ut aliæ oriantur à Relatione primâ, aliæ ab orta: a primâ quidem vel interna, vel externa: Ab interna I. à Dependentia fluunt affectiones conjunctæ. 1. Indepen& dependens. 2. Quæ hujus species vel modi sunt, Principium & Principiatum. 3. Causa & Causatum. 4. Subjectum & Accidens. II. Ab unione. 1. Totum & Pars. 2. Completum & Incompletum.
units.tr: 19. Respective affections, insofar as they presuppose relation, must likewise be distinguished from one another according to the diversity of relations; so that some arise from the first relation, others from the one arisen: from the first, either internal or external. From the internal: I. from dependence flow conjoined affections: 1. independent and dependent; 2. those which are species or modes of this: principle and principiate; 3. cause and caused; 4. subject and accident. II. From union: 1. whole and part; 2. complete and incomplete.

units.la: 20. Ab externa relatione consimiliter oriuntur, & quidem I. ab Appositione, 1. Subjectum & Adjunctum strictè dictum. 2. Subjectum & Objectum. 3. Signum & Signatum. 4. Mensura & Mensuratum. II. A Circumstantia: I. Temporis, Antiquum & Novum. 2. Praeteritum, Praesens & futurum. II. Loci, Praesens & Absens. 2. Proximum & Remotum.
units.tr: 20. Similarly from the external relation arise, and indeed I. from apposition: 1. subject and adjunct strictly speaking; 2. subject and object; 3. sign and signified; 4. measure and measured. II. From circumstance: 1. of time, old and new; 2. past, present and future. II. of place, present and absent; 2. near and remote.

units.la: 21. Ab ortis relationibus etiam fluunt affectiones, nomine tamen ab ipsis relationibus nondum distinctas; Quare hic occurrunt, Convenientia & Disconvenientia, cum omnibus suis modis & speciebus, inter quas quoque Oppositio collocanda; Et denique Ordo, cujus species Prioritas, Posterioritas & Simultas; Quemadmodum quoque Principalitas & Minus principalitas. Atque hæ omnes enumeratæ Affectiones Entis respectivæ sunt; An etiam aliæ sint, quæ ad has revocari non possint, nondum constat: Si quæ mihi occurrant, earum in Exercitationibus Metaphysicis, volente Deo, meminero.
units.tr: 21. Affections also flow from the arisen relations, yet not yet distinct from the relations in name. Hence there occur agreement and disagreement, with all their modes and species, among which opposition is also to be placed; and finally order, whose species are priority, posteriority and simultaneity; just as also principality and lesser principality. All these enumerated affections are respective affections of Being. Whether there are others which cannot be reduced to these is not yet settled. If any occur to me, I shall remember them in my Metaphysical Exercises, God willing.

units.la: 22. V. Inter has explicandas ac de Ente demonstrandas ordo, requiritur, qui qualis institui debeat, vix patet, aliis alium sequentibus; Quos ut suo judicio frui permitto, rogatos volo, ut me vicissim meo frui sinant; Atque ita prius agam de Absolutis, deinde de Respectivis; Inter illas primo de iis quæ à constitutione, deinde quæ à distinctione, tertiò, quæ ab utrâque oriuntur; Adeo ut singulæ suis principiis distinctè subnectantur. Inter respectivas disponendas secundum ordinem relationum procedam, ut scilicet fundamentorum ordini respondeat ordo fundatorum. Atque hæc de Affectionibus in genere, adeoque de omnibus Prænognitis, primo tractatu proponendis, dicta sufficient.
units.tr: 22. V. Among these to be explained and demonstrated of Being, an order is required. What kind it ought to be is hardly clear, as different people follow different orders. I permit each to enjoy his own judgement, and I want them, asked in turn, to let me enjoy mine. And so I shall treat first of the absolutes, then of the respectives. Among the former, first of those which arise from constitution, then those from distinction, thirdly, those which arise from both; so that each is distinctly subjoined to its principles. Among the respective ones I will proceed to arrange them according to the order of relations, so that the order of the foundations corresponds to the order of the founded. And this is enough said about affections in general, and thus about all the prolegomena to be set out in the first treatise.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM METAPHYSICARUM, Tractatus Secundus,
units.tr: INSTITUTES OF METAPHYSICS, Second Treatise,

units.la: QUI EST DE Subjecto, seu Trunco. CAPUT. I. DE Constitutione & Essentia.
units.tr: WHICH CONCERNS the Subject, or Trunk. CHAPTER I. ON Constitution and Essence.

units.la: 1. SEcundum ordinem Principiorum & Affectionum, ad calcem superioris tractatus propositum, primum agmen ducit, Constitutio, cum suis affectionibus ex ipsa de Ente demonstrandis. Primò igitur dicendum de Constitutionis, tum nomine, tum re.
units.tr: 1. Following the order of the Principles and Affections proposed at the end of the previous treatise, Constitution leads the first rank, together with its affections, which are to be demonstrated from Being itself. First, then, we must speak of Constitution, both as to its name and as to its thing.

units.la: 2. Nomen à constituendo, & quasi simul ordinando habet, primitus desumtum ab eis, quae ex unione sensibilium partium esse suum obtinebant, unde non secus ac plurimi alii termini ad Metaphysicam traductum, ßum , quamcunque possessionem τῆ εἶναι denotat. Idque non tantum positivè, quâtenus id esse ab aliquo constituente acquiritur, sed& negativè, quâtenus ipsum esse habetur , citra ordinem ad constituens quodcunque ; Adeo ut constitutio, prout hïc accipi debet, ad utrumque modum indifferenter se habeat, posteà tamen in speciali applicatione ipsius esse determinanda.
units.tr: 2. The word constitution is derived from constituting, and at the same time, as it were, from ordering. It was first taken from those things which obtained their being from the union of sensible parts, whence, not otherwise than many other terms, it was transferred to Metaphysics, and denotes whatever possession of being [τῆ εἶναι]. And this not only positively, insofar as that being is acquired from some constituting cause, but also negatively, insofar as being itself is had without any relation to any constituent. So constitution, as it must be understood here, relates to either mode indifferently, to be determined afterwards in the specific application of being.

units.la: 3. Quid sit Constitutio, superiori tractatu dictum est, nempe, Modus Entis quo hoc suum esse habet, seu possidet ; Præter quod, hic notari debent, 1. Ejus Subjectum.
units.tr: 3. What Constitution is was said in the previous treatise: namely, the mode of Being by which a thing has, or possesses, its being. Besides this, the following must be noted here: 1. its Subject.

units.la: 2. Ordo ejus ad illud. 3. Ordo ejus ad Distinctionem. 4. Axiomata, ex ejus naturâ resultantia.
units.tr: 2. Its order to that subject. 3. Its order to Distinction. 4. Axioms resulting from its nature.

units.la: 4. I. Subjectum ipsius omne & solum Ens est ; utpote quod omne & solum esse habet; Cujusque sunt Affectiones, quas Constitutio comites habet. Objic. 1. Sic etiam Deo conveniret Constitutio. Atqui is esse suum habere dici nequit, quoniam ex habente & habito foret compositus : Et deinde non rectè constitutus dicitur. Resp. Etiam Deo convenit; nec proinde fiet compositus, quia habens & habitum non nisi formaliter distinguuntur ; Prout quoque Affectiones & Attributa habere dicitur: Nec quidem rectè constitutus dicitur positivè, nihil tamen vetat, quin negativè dicatur, prout & à se negativè dicitur esse, quâtenus à nullo est alio. Obiic. 2. Etiam non-Entibus,saltem quibusdam, videtur tribuenda Constitutio, quoniam nonnulla ipsorum causam agnoscunt. Resp. Eo modo non-Entibus convenit, quomodo aliqua ipsis Entitas vel quidditas tribuitur ; latè videlicet & analogicè loquendo.
units.tr: 4. I. Its Subject is every and only Being, for it is what every and only being has. The affections which Constitution has as companions belong to each. Objection 1. In this way Constitution would also belong to God. But he cannot be said to have his being, since he would then be composed of the having and the had; and moreover he is not rightly said to be constituted. Answer. It does belong to God too, and yet he is not thereby made composite, because the having and the had are distinguished only formally. In the same way he is also said to have affections and attributes. Nor indeed is he rightly said to be constituted in a positive sense, yet nothing prevents its being said negatively, just as he is also said negatively to be from himself, insofar as he is from nothing else.
