Objection 2. Constitution seems to be ascribed also to non-beings, at least to some of them, since some acknowledge a cause. Answer. It belongs to non-beings in the way that some entity or quiddity is attributed to them; that is, speaking broadly and analogically.

units.la: 5. II. Ab Ente ejusque esse non differt realiter constitutio, sed saltem ratione ratiocinatâ, seu formaliter; cujus distinctionis fundamentum est, distincta apprehensio habiti & habentis, quæ habitionem, vel, ita liceat loqui, habentiam quamdam simul involvunt, quæ est ipsa Constitutionis forma. Quare quoque nihil reale ab Ente diversum ipsi Enti superaddit, sed saltem inadæquatum aliquem modum, seu conceptum, quo Ens, ut aliquid ad suum esse complementum habens consideratur.
units.tr: 5. II. Constitution does not differ really from Being and its being, but only by reasoned distinction, or formally. The foundation of this distinction is the distinct apprehension of the had and the having, which together involve a certain having (or, if one may so speak, a kind of havingness), and this is the very form of Constitution. Hence it adds nothing real, different from Being, to Being itself, but only some inadequate mode, or concept, by which Being is considered as having something for the completion of its being.

units.la: 6. III. A distinctione, suo conprincipio, eodem quoque modo differt, ratione scilicet ratiocinatâ; cujus distinctionis fundamentum est, distincta apprehensio habendi τὸ εἶναι, ac habendi illud proprium ac solum sibi; Realiter igitur hæc duo inter se & cum ente idem sunt; ex hac autem inter utrumque principium distinctione, fluit &altera, quâ differunt, ut prius& posterius secundum originationem conceptuum; Quia prius in signo rationis est, τὸ simpliciter habere esse, quam habere illud proprium.
units.tr: 6. III. It differs from distinction, its co-principle, in the same way, namely by reasoned distinction. The foundation of this distinction is the distinct apprehension of having being [τὸ εἶναι], and of having that as one's own and alone. Really, therefore, these two are the same as each other and as the being. From this distinction between the two principles there also flows another, by which they differ as prior and posterior according to the origin of concepts, because in the order of reason, to have being simply is prior to having that as one's own.

units.la: 7. IV. Axiomata seu Principia & Porismata, ex Constitutionis naturâ elici possunt varia; Quorum hæc sunt præcipua.
units.tr: 7. IV. Various axioms, or principles and corollaries, can be drawn from the nature of Constitution. The following are the chief of these.

units.la: 1. Omnis Constitutio præsupponit esse; vel, cujus nullum est esse, ejus nulla constitutio. Ratio est, quia nihil poterit habere esse, nisi habeat in eo constitutionem; Est enim Constitutio ipsum esse quatenus habetur.
units.tr: 1. Every Constitution presupposes being; or, where there is no being, there is no constitution. The reason is that nothing can have being unless it has a constitution in it, for Constitution is being itself insofar as it is had.

units.la: 2. Quale est aliquujus esse, talis est & ejus constitutio. Quorum igitur esse est dependens, eorum constitutio talis est. 3. Qualis est alicujus constitutio, talis quoque essentia, talesque ejus sunt affectiones reliquæ. Ratio est, quia essentia & cæteræ affectiones ex constitutione emanant, utpote quam ut radicale principium præsupponunt: Cujus igitur infinita & independens est Constitutio, ejus quoque tam essentia, quam affectiones omnes sunt infinitæ; & contrà.
units.tr: 2. Such as the being of anything is, such also is its constitution. Therefore, where a being is dependent, its constitution is such. 3. Such as the constitution of anything is, such also is its essence, and such are its remaining affections. The reason is that essence and the other affections emanate from constitution, since they presuppose it as the radical principle. So whose constitution is infinite and independent, its essence too and all its affections are infinite; and conversely.

units.la: 8. Proximus Constitutionis modus est Essentia; Unumquodque enim, quatenus in esse constitutum est, essentiæ particeps esse dicitur. Hæc igitur nunc consideranda venit, & quidem 1. Quoad nomen. 2. Quoad rem.
units.tr: 8. The next mode of Constitution is Essence, for each thing, insofar as it is constituted in being, is said to partake of essence. This therefore now comes to be considered, and indeed 1. as to name, 2. as to thing.

units.la: 9. In nomine Essentiæ notanda 1. Homonymia & Ambiguitas, 2. Synonymia. Quoad ambiguitatem, varias habet significationes Essentiæ vox, utpote maximè in Scriptis Philosophorum obvia; Et quidem 1. sumitur pro substantiâ. 2. Pro principio formali essentiæ, sive pro formâ, aut quod ejus rationem obtinet. 3. Pro eo, quod rei definitionem constituit; Quod tribus potissimum modis fit, latè, strictè & adæquatè; Latè prout etiam analogicè non-entibus tribuitur: strictè pro naturâ, sive corporum naturalium essentiâ; Adæquatè autem ipsam Constitutionem τᾶς esse realis, veri ac positivi sequitur; Quo pacto hic capienda.
units.tr: 9. In the name Essence, note 1. homonymy and ambiguity; 2. synonymy. As to ambiguity, the word essence has various meanings, as it is most common in the writings of philosophers. Indeed 1. it is taken for substance; 2. for the formal principle of essence, or for form, or for what holds its character; 3. for that which constitutes the definition of a thing. This happens chiefly in three ways: broadly, strictly and adequately. Broadly, as it is also attributed analogically to non-beings; strictly, for nature, or the essence of natural bodies; adequately, however, it follows Constitution itself in the sense of real, true and positive being. It is in this last sense that it is to be taken here.

units.la: 10. Synonymiam quod spectat, dicitur Essentia. 1. Entitas; quæ latè sumta etiam non-entibus tribui potest; at angustius cum essentiâ coincidit; Poterit tamen hic delectus haberi, ut Entitas dicatur, nonEntium quidditas: At Entium essentia. 2. Quidditas; eaque 1. sumitur, prout omni illi convenit, quod non est omninò nihil; 2. strictè capitur, prout solis substantiis & quidem completis, à Philosopho in Prædicamento Substantiæ tribuitur; 3. Adæquatè autem eis tantum tribui videtur, quæ essentiam habent prout illa definitione explicari potest; Atque ita nonnisi essentiæ videtur esse denominatio. III. Essentia etiam dicitur natura; vox φολύσημα, si quæ alia; Inter varias ejus significationes, quæ huc quadrare videntur, hæ potissimæ sunt, 1. Denotat universalem corporum naturalium efficientem, Deo subordinatam. 2. Essentiam corporum naturalium, in quâ à naturâ sunt constituta. 3. Formam talium corporum. 4. Cujuscunque Entis essentiam, prout illa actionibus suis est destinata; Unde sic vel modum, vel denominationem essentiæ superaddere videtur. IV. Essentia quoque aliquando formæ appellatione donatur: Verum forma relationem quamdam dicit, & proprie solis corporibus convenit; De quâ tamen infrà latius.
units.tr: 10. As to synonymy, essence is called: 1. entity, which taken broadly can also be attributed to non-beings, but more narrowly coincides with essence. Yet this distinction may be kept here, so that the quiddity of non-beings is called entity, but that of beings essence. 2. Quiddity, which is taken 1. in the sense that it belongs to all that is not altogether nothing; 2. taken strictly, as the Philosopher in the Predicament of Substance attributes it only to substances, and indeed complete ones; 3. taken adequately, it seems to belong only to those things which have an essence, insofar as it can be explained by that definition, and so it seems to be only a denomination of essence. III. Essence is also called nature, a word [πολύσημα], polysemous if any other is. Among its various meanings which seem to fit here, these are the chief: 1. it denotes the universal efficient of natural bodies, subordinate to God; 2. the essence of natural bodies, in which they are constituted by nature; 3. the form of such bodies; 4. the essence of any being, insofar as it is destined for its actions, whence it seems to add either a mode or a denomination to essence. IV. Essence is also sometimes given the name form; but form expresses a certain relation, and properly belongs only to bodies, of which more below.

units.la: 12. In rei consideratione explicandum.
units.tr: 12. In the consideration of the thing, the following must be explained.

units.la: 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quomodo se ad subjectum habeat? 4. Quid differat ab existentia? 5. Quomodo dividenda? 6. Quaenam ex eâ Axiomata deducantur?
units.tr: 1. What is it? 2. What is its subject? 3. How does it stand to its subject? 4. How does it differ from existence? 5. How is it divided? 6. What axioms are deduced from it?

units.la: 12. I. Quid sit Essentia, ex definitione colligendum: Definitur autem, modus constitutionis, quo Ens simpliciter habet suum esse: Hoc est quo Ens, illud præcise quod definitione ejus explicatur, possidet; In quo distinguitur à constitutione, quæ totum illud quod ad esse pertinet, etiam assectiones definitionem non ingredientes, involvit.
units.tr: 12. I. What Essence is must be gathered from the definition. It is defined as the mode of constitution by which a being simply has its being; that is, the mode by which a being possesses precisely that which is explained by its definition. In this it is distinguished from constitution, which involves everything that pertains to being, including affections that do not enter the definition.

units.la: 13. II. Subjectum Essentiæ est Ens, reale ac positivum; Quoniam enim 1. Modus est constitutionis, quæ ut principium radicale & primum talis Entis tantum concipitur; Non potest alteri convenire nisi cui convenit Constitutio. 2. Essentia in se eadem est cum Constitutione, & hæc cum Ente; At quæ ita se habent, eorum unum extra alterum se non extendit; neque potest esse sine altero. Dum autem Ens dicitur subjectum essentiæ, intelligendum est subjectum prædicationis, conceptu nostro ab essentia sive prædicato distinctum.
units.tr: 13. II. The subject of Essence is Being, real and positive. For since 1. it is a mode of constitution, which is conceived only as the radical and first principle of such a being, it cannot belong to anything except that to which Constitution belongs. 2. Essence is the same in itself as Constitution, and this is the same as Being; but things so related do not extend beyond one another, and neither can exist without the other. When Being is called the subject of essence, however, it must be understood as the subject of predication, distinct in our concept from essence, or the predicate.

units.la: 14. Sed quæres, An omni Enti conveniat essentia? Resp. Sic sanè, ut ex dictis patet. Objic. 1. Non convenit Enti in potentia. Resp. Nec debet convenire; Quia enim hoc simpliciter ens non est, non potest quoque simpliciter suum esse habere. Objic. 2. Deo non convenit essentia: Quia est ipsa sua essentia. Resp. Etiam Deo convenit; licet longè eminentiori modo, quam Creaturis. Nec valet addita ratio; Nam etiam creaturæ à suâ essentiâ non differunt nisi conceptu formali, quomodo etiam essentiam Dei à Deo distinguere possumus; Quatenus Deus considerabatur, ut habens, essentia, ut habita.
units.tr: 14. But you will ask: does essence belong to every being? Answer: Yes, certainly, as is clear from what has been said. Objection 1: It does not belong to a being in potency. Answer: Nor ought it to, for since this is not a being simply, it cannot also have its own being simply. Objection 2: Essence does not belong to God, since he is his own essence. Answer: It belongs to God too, though in a far more eminent way than to creatures. Nor does the added reason hold; for creatures too differ from their essence only by formal concept, just as we can also distinguish the essence of God from God, insofar as God is considered as having, and essence as had.

units.la: 15. Quæres ulterius, An soli enti conveniat essentia? Resp. Ita esse ex allatis rationibus patet. Objic. 1. Essentia est, quod definitione explicatur; quæ igitur definiri possunt habent essentiam. Quoniam igitur definiri possunt, & suprà definita sunt non-Entia, non videtur eis deneganda essentia. Resp. Quod definitione Entis explicatur est essentia, non verò quod cujuscunque definitione explicatur; foret enim alias etiam essentiæ essentia, quia & hæc definita est. Interim verum est, omne definitum habere aliquam Entitatem sive quidditatem, quâ est aliquid; Nihil enim definiri nequit. Resp. 1. Definita sunt illa non-entia, non ac si per se Entitatem haberent, sed cum respectu ad illud quod veram essentiam obtinet. Objic. 2. Quid quid est habet essentiam; Essentia enim ab esse derivatur: At illa nonentia sunt quoque: Habent ergo & essentiam. Resp. 1. Quidquid est, habet essentiam, scilicet late dictam, quæ rectius Entitas, vel Quidditas, quam essentia dicitur. 2. Nec ipsum esse non-entibus convenit proprie & in se, sed vel analogice ut Enti Rationis, & Enti in potentiâ, vel ratione subjecti & materiæ, ut modis, Relationibus, Privationibus &c.
units.tr: 15. You will ask further, does essence belong only to being? Answer: That it is so is clear from the reasons adduced. Objection 1: Essence is what is explained by definition; therefore things which can be defined have essence. Since, then, they can be defined, and non-beings have been defined above, essence should not be denied to them. Answer: What is explained by the definition of being is essence, but not whatever is explained by the definition of something; otherwise there would be an essence of essence as well, since this too is defined. Meanwhile it is true that everything defined has some entity or quiddity by which it is something, for nothing can be defined that is nothing. Answer 1: Those non-beings are defined not as if they had entity in themselves, but in relation to that which possesses true essence. Objection 2: Whatever is has essence, for essence is derived from being. But those non-beings also are; therefore they have essence too. Answer 1: Whatever is has essence, namely essence taken broadly, which is more correctly called entity or quiddity than essence. 2. Nor does being itself belong to non-beings properly and in themselves, but either analogically, as to a being of reason and a being in potency, or by reason of subject and matter, as to modes, relations, privations, and so on.

units.la: 16. III. Sequitur habitudo Essentiæ ad Ens suum subjectum; Quæ explicanda. 1. Per convenientiam. 2. Per disconvenientiam ab eo. Quoad convenientiam, notandum 1. Quod se habeat essentia ad Ens, ut modus principii radicalis interni videlicet constitutionis, quæ non re, sed solo conceptu, ut a constitutione, ita & ab ipso Ente distat. Unde 2. Essentia & Ens realiter idem sunt; foret enim alias Essentia Ens aliquod, ab eo, cujus est essentia distinctum; Quod iterum requireret
units.tr: 16. III. There follows the relation of essence to being, its subject, which must be explained: (1) by agreement; (2) by disagreement from it. As to agreement, note first that essence stands to being as a mode of the radical internal principle, namely constitution, which differs from constitution and from being itself not in reality but only in concept. Hence, 2. essence and being are really the same; for otherwise essence would be some being distinct from that whose essence it is, which again would require its own essence, by which the process would run on to infinity. 3. Wherefore essence stands to being as nature, abstracted by precision, stands to that of which it is the nature, just as the life of a living thing is its essence. Hence 4. it follows that essence adds to being nothing diverse from itself, but only some mode of concept, not accidental but at least distinct in concept, by which being is considered as having and essence as had.

units.la: (Some faint marks and reference letters are present in the text; not transcribed.) reret suam essentiam quo pacto processus in infinitum involveretur.3.quare ita se habet essentia ad Ens, ut natura per praecisionem abstracta, ab eo, cujus est natura, quemadmodum vita viventis est essentia.Hinc4.sequitur, quod essentia Enti nihil diversum à se superaddat, sed modum saltem aliquem conceptûs, non accidentalem, sed conceptu saltem distinctum; Quo Ens consideratur ut habens, essentia ut habita.
units.tr: …would have to have its own essence, by which the process would run on to infinity. 3. Wherefore essence stands to being as nature, abstracted by precision, stands to that of which it is the nature, just as the life of a living thing is its essence. Hence 4. it follows that essence adds to being nothing diverse from itself, but only some mode of concept, not accidental but at least distinct in concept; by which being is considered as having, essence as had.

units.la: 17. Quoad disconvenientiam, notandum primo, quòd non habeat se essentia ad Ens, tanquam forma ad formatum; forma enim 1. dat esse tale: At essentia dat esse simpliciter. 2. forma distinctioni respondet: Essentia Constitutionis modus est.3. Forma non constituit totum esse, sed partem ejus saltem: At Constitutio totam. 4. Forma non absolvit totam definitionem, at essentia totam perficit. Objic. 1. Dicitur tamen forma, tota rei essentia. Resp. 1. Ita dicitur, quia in iis, in quibus locum habet, potissima essentiæ pars est. 2. Et quod esse tale constituat, cum essentia id simpliciter faciat. Objic. 2. Forma est id, per quod res est id, quod est: Sed etiam per essentiam est id quod est. Resp. Forma non est id totum, sed tantum pars, cui ob determinationem totius essentiæ officium tribuitur. Dinde per essentiam non tantum res, id totum est, quod est, sed etiam simpliciter. Secundò notandum, quòd solâ ratione ratiocinatâ, essentia abente distinguatur; Cujus fundamentum multiplex est; Nam 1. Ens ut habens, & concretum, essentia ut habita & abstracta consideratur. 2. Ens includit tam divisionem ab aliis, quam indivisionem in se: At essentia solam indivisionem; &c.
units.tr: 17. As to disagreement, note first that essence does not stand to being as form to formed thing. For form (1) gives such being, whereas essence gives being simply; (2) form corresponds to distinction, whereas essence is a mode of constitution; (3) form does not constitute the whole being, but at least a part of it, whereas constitution constitutes the whole; (4) form does not complete the whole definition, whereas essence perfects all of it. Objection 1: Yet form is called the whole essence of a thing. Answer 1: It is so called because, in those things where it has a place, it is the chief part of the essence. 2. And because it constitutes such being, although essence does this simply. Objection 2: Form is that through which a thing is what it is; but also through essence it is what it is. Answer: Form is not the whole but only a part, to which the office is assigned because of the determination of the whole essence. Further, through essence a thing is not only that whole which it is, but also simply. Secondly, note that essence is distinguished from being by reason alone, reasoned out; the grounds for this are manifold. For 1. being is considered as having and concrete, essence as had and abstract. 2. Being includes both division from others and indivision in itself, whereas essence includes only indivision, etc.

units.la: 18. IV. Quoad habitudinem inter essentiam & existentiam, obiter hic notandum, quod existentia & essentia in se idem sint, utpote quæ citra se invicem dari aut concipi nequeunt; Quare solius rationis intercedit discrimen, de quo latius in tractatione existentiæ infrà cap. 12.
units.tr: 18. IV. As to the relation between essence and existence, it should be noted here in passing that existence and essence are the same in themselves, since they can be neither given nor conceived apart from one another. Hence the distinction is only one of reason, about which more fully in the treatment of existence below, chap. 12.

units.la: 19. V. Differentiæ essentiarum variæ traduntur, suntque potissimum omnes Accidentales tantum; Quarum prima; Essentia est vel Actualis, vel Potentialis; Illa dicitur quæ rei jam actu existenti convenit, Hac verò quæ habitudinem tantum ad esse infert, qualis est rosæ in hyeme. Sed quoniam nulla res est, quin sit actualis, nulla quoque nisi actualis essentia esse poterit. Potentialis enim non est, sed esse potest essentia. Melius Actualis dici poterit, quæ omni potentiâ caret, & semper actum involvit, qualis est essentia solius Dei; Ut potentialis sit, quæ habet potentiam ad non esse, qualis est omnium creaturarum.
units.tr: 19. V. The differences of essences are handed down in various ways, and they are for the most part merely accidental. The first is this: essence is either actual or potential. The former is said to belong to a thing already actually existing; the latter implies only a relation to being, as the essence of a rose in winter. But since no thing exists which is not actual, no essence can be other than actual, for a potential essence is not an essence, but an essence can be. It would be better to call actual that which lacks all potency and always involves act, such as the essence of God alone; and potential that which has the potency toward non-being, such as the essence of all creatures.

units.la: 20. Secundò essentia vel est necessaria vel contingens ; Prior est quæ tolli non potest, sive absolutè, ut essentia Dei, sive comparatè, ad perfectionem universi, ut essentia cœli, Materiæ &c. Contingens verò est, quæ tolli potest, etiam ratione perfectionis universi, ut est essentia singularis Arboris, hominis hujus istiusve.
units.tr: 20. Secondly, essence is either necessary or contingent. The former is that which cannot be removed, either absolutely, as the essence of God, or comparatively, with respect to the perfection of the universe, as the essence of heaven, of matter, etc. Contingent, however, is that which can be removed, even with respect to the perfection of the universe, as the essence of a particular tree, or of this or that man.

units.la: 21. Tertiò, Essentia est vel completa, sive totalis, vel incompleta, sive partialis. Verum hæc comparatè intelligi debet; absolutè enim loquendo, omnis essentia completa & totalis est ejus, cujus est essentia; Licet fortean ratione alterius partialis dicatur, quâtenus ejus essentiam integrè non absolvit; ita v. gr. manus absolutè habet essentiam totalem, per quam est manus, comparatè tamen ad hominem, cujus essentiam integrè non perficit, dicitur habere essentiam partialem.
units.tr: 21. Thirdly, essence is either complete, or total, or incomplete, or partial. Yet these must be understood comparatively; for speaking absolutely, every complete and total essence belongs to that whose essence it is, although perhaps it is called partial with respect to something else, insofar as it does not fully complete that thing's essence. Thus, for example, a hand absolutely has a total essence, by which it is a hand, but in comparison with man, whose essence it does not fully complete, it is said to have a partial essence.

units.la: 22. Quartò, essentia est vel absoluta, vel respectiva; Ita absoluta est per quam homo est homo; & Respectiva per quam est Pater: At verò ultima hæc potius denominatio, quam essentia est? Quis enim diceret Deo convenire essentias plures licet respectivas, quando dicitur, Creator, Conservator, Gubernator &c.
units.tr: 22. Fourthly, essence is either absolute or respective. Thus the absolute essence is that by which man is man, and the respective that by which one is a father. But is this last rather a denomination than an essence? For who would say that many essences, even if respective, belong to God, when he is called Creator, Preserver, Governor, and so on?

units.la: 23. Quintò, Essentia est vel pura, vel modalis; Pura est per quam v. gr. Canis est canis; modalis, per quam est currens. Sed de hac modali idem sentiendum, quod de respectivâ.
units.tr: 23. Fifthly, essence is either pure or modal. The pure is that through which, for example, a dog is a dog; the modal, that through which it is running. But concerning this modal essence the same should be thought as concerning the respective.

units.la: 24. Essentiales differentias si quis petat, eas ex essentiali Entis diversitate petat; Videbitque aliam esse Infinitam, aliam finitam; aliam per se subsistentem, aliam inhærentem; Aliam Spirituum, aliam corporum; Prout ipsum Ens ita essentialiter discriminandum est.
units.tr: 24. If anyone asks about the essential differences, let him seek them from the essential diversity of being; and he will see that one is infinite, another finite; one subsisting through itself, another inhering; one of spirits, another of bodies, since being itself is to be discriminated essentially in this way.

units.la: 25. Axiomata haut pauca, ex essentiæ contemplatione propulluant, inter ea, hæc non videntur inferioris ordinis 1. Quod est habet essentiam, sive, quod non est, non habet essentiam; Quod enim non est, non est constitutum; Et negatâ constitutione negatur ejus modus, essentia videlicet: Eâ autem posità, ponitur ejus modus, ut supra ostensum.
units.tr: 25. Axioms not a few spring from the contemplation of essence, and among them these do not seem to be of lower rank: 1. What is has essence, or, what is not does not have essence. For what is not is not constituted; and with constitution denied, its mode, namely essence, is denied; but with it posited, its mode is posited, as shown above.

units.la: 26. 2. Hinc fluit alterum; Impossibile est, aliquid simul esse, & non esse; Quia impossibile est idem habere & non habere essentiam; esse enim & non-esse contradicunt; Contradictoria autem se mutuò tollunt: Hujus axiomatis insignis est usus, utpote omnis indirectæ demonstrationis fundamenti; Quare etiam nonnullis Principium absolutè primùm dicitur; Præsupponere tamen videtur, ea quæ ex constitutionis naturâ desumta sunt.
units.tr: 26. 2. From this follows a second axiom: It is impossible for something both to be and not to be; because it is impossible for the same thing to have and not to have an essence; for being and non-being contradict each other; and contradictories cancel each other out. The use of this axiom is remarkable, since it is the foundation of every indirect demonstration; for this reason some also call it the principle that is absolutely first. Yet it seems to presuppose those things which are drawn from the nature of constitution.

units.la: 27. 3. Cujuslibet Entis una est essentia; Quia una ejus est constitutio in esse. Capiendum tamen hoc de essentiâ proprie dictâ, id est totali & absolutâ; Partiales enim, respectivæ, & modales plures dari, nihil obstat; Quare nec proprie dictæ essentiæ sunt, ut modò dictum.
units.tr: 27. 3. Of any being there is one essence; because its constitution in being is one. This must be understood, however, of essence properly so called, that is, total and absolute; for that there are several partial, relative and modal essences is no obstacle; hence these are not properly essences, as has just been said.

units.la: 28. 4. Essentia non sunt multiplicanda prater necessitatem; Unius enim Entis saltem una est; hoc axiomate Nominales omnes superfluas Entitates ac essentias eradicare, & herculeo verè ausu quasi abradere ac amputare niteruntur; Unde etiam Novacula Nominalium dicitur.
units.tr: 28. 4. Essences are not to be multiplied beyond necessity; for of one being there is at least one essence. By this axiom the Nominalists strive to eradicate all superfluous entities and essences, and, with a truly Herculean boldness, to scrape them away and cut them off; whence it is also called the Razor of the Nominalists.

units.la: 29. 5. Parte essentiæ [ablatâ], tota interit; Debet enim omnis essentia totalis esse, sicut numerus, cui si vel particula deficiat, ilico ejus essentia perit, & alius fit numerus; Et si essentiæ deficeret pars, non esset completa; Adeoque nulla, quia incompleta constitutioni non satisfacit.
units.tr: 29. 5. If a part of an essence is removed, the whole perishes; for every essence ought to be total, like a number: if even a small part of it were lacking, its essence would at once perish, and it would become another number. And if a part of an essence were lacking, it would not be complete; and so it would be no essence at all, since an incomplete thing does not satisfy the requirements of constitution.

units.la: 30. 6. Hujus consectarium est: Essentia non recipit magis & minus; id est, non non admittit gradus intensionis & remissionis: Ratio est, quia essentia non variatur, non variatâ constitutione; At hæc permanet, permanente ipso Ente. Dices: Quomodo igitur Qualitates dicuntur recipere magis & minus? Resp. Hoc non fit, quia ipsarum essentia modò magis, modò minus talis; (Caloris enim essentia semper uniusmodi est, sive æstate, sive hyeme; ) sed quia ob suam majorem vel minorem præsentiam & quasi extensionem, fortius vel debilius operantur, unde subjecto per magis & minus praedicantur.
units.tr: 30. 6. A consequence of this is: An essence does not admit more and less; that is, it does not admit degrees of intensity and remission. The reason is that an essence does not vary, since the constitution does not vary; and this remains while the being itself remains. You will say: how then are qualities said to admit more and less? Answer: this does not happen because their essence is sometimes more and sometimes less of such a kind (for the essence of heat is always of one kind, whether in summer or in winter); but because, by reason of their greater or lesser presence and, as it were, extension, they act more strongly or more weakly, and so are predicated of a subject as more or less.

units.la: 31. 7. Quod habet essentiam, eádem Ens est, sive, unum quadque est Ens per propriam, & non per alienam, essentiam. Ratio est, quia unumquodque ens propriam habet constitutionem, adeoque & proprium constitutionis modum.
units.tr: 31. 7. What has an essence is a being by that same essence; or, each thing is a being through its own essence and not through another's. The reason is that each being has its own constitution, and therefore its own mode of constitution.

units.la: 32. 8. Qualis est alicujus essentiæ, tales sunt ejus affectiones & operationes. Hæ enim mediante essentia ex Constitutione profluere concipiuntur: Quare cum tales sint affectiones, quale est Ens; & quale hoc, talis ejus constitutio; & qualis ejus constitutio, talis sit & essentia; Erunt quoque tales affectiones, qualis est essentia.
units.tr: 32. 8. Such as the essence of anything is, such are its affections and operations. For these are understood to flow from the constitution through the mediation of the essence. Therefore, since such affections are such as the being is, and such as the being is, such is its constitution, and such as its constitution is, such also is its essence; the affections will likewise be such as the essence is.

units.la: 33. 9. Non-Entis nulla est essentia; Quia nulla est ejus constitutio; utpote quod esse non habet, ideoque in eo constitui nequit.
units.tr: 33. 9. A non-being has no essence; because it has no constitution; since it does not have being, it cannot be constituted in it.

units.la: 34. 10. Cujus nulla essentia, ejus nulla affectiones; Ratio est; Quia mediante essentia rei affectiones tribuuntur; Quare negatâ conditione, sine quâ non, etiam negari debet conditionatum.
units.tr: 34. 10. Whatever has no essence has no affections. The reason is: because affections are attributed to a thing through the mediation of its essence; therefore, when the condition without which something cannot be is denied, the conditioned thing must also be denied.

units.la: 35. Affectiones Enti mediante essentiâ convenientes vel immediatæ sunt vel mediatæ; Immediatæ, citra interventum alterius alicujus, cujus videlicet modi sunt, Enti competentes, tres sunt, Unitas, Veritas, Bonitas. De quibus ordine.
units.tr: 35. Affections that belong to a being through the mediation of its essence are either immediate or mediate. Immediate affections, those that belong to a being without the intervention of any other thing, of which kind there are three, are: Unity, Truth, Goodness. Of these in order.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: DE Unitate.
units.tr: Of Unity.

units.la: I. VNitas ante Veritatem & Bonitatem explicanda videtur, quia propius ad essentiam accedere videtur, adeo, ut veritas & Bonitas ipsam aliquatenus praesupponant; Explicatio vero ejus vel Vocis, vel Rei erit.
units.tr: I. Unity seems to need explaining before truth and goodness, because it seems to come closer to essence, so much so that truth and goodness presuppose it to some extent. Its explanation will be either of the word or of the thing.

units.la: 2. Ambigua vox unitatis est; Notat enim. 1. Solitudinem, adeo ut unum idem sit, quod unicum; qua significatione non est affectio aut proprietas Entis; Unicum enim esse negationem designat: At Affectio Entis ejus perfectionem. Ac deinde non omni Enti ex se convenit unicum esse; Sed soli Deo, ut infra ostendendum. 2. Unitas significat convenientiam duorum in essentia, estque idem quod identitas. 3. Sumitur pro principio numeri. 4. Denotat modum vel affectionem Entis, qua hoc in se indivisum dicitur; Quo pacto hic consideranda est.
units.tr: 2. The word unity is ambiguous, for it denotes: 1. solitude, so that one is the same as unique. In this sense it is not an affection or property of being, for "unique" signifies a negation, whereas an affection of being signifies its perfection. Moreover, being does not belong to everything by its own nature to be unique, but to God alone, as will be shown below. 2. Unity signifies the agreement of two things in essence, and is the same as identity. 3. It is taken for the principle of number. 4. It denotes the mode or affection of being by which it is said to be undivided in itself. It is in this sense that it must be considered here.

units.la: 3. In rei consideratione, explicandum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quaenam habitudo ejus ad subjectum? 4. Quodnam oppositum? 5. Quae differentia?
units.tr: 3. In considering the thing, we must explain: 1. what it is; 2. what its subject is; 3. what its relation to the subject is; 4. what its opposite is; 5. what its differences are.

units.la: 4. I. Vnitas vulgo definitur, Affectio Entis, quâ hoc est indivisum in se, & divisum à quovis alio; Verum sic non est inseparabilis Affectio: non enim necesse est omne Ens actu divisum esse ab alio; Nam ante conditum mundum, inquit Burgersdicius, Deus erat unus, nec tamen à quopiam erat actu divisus: quia nihil erat præter Deum. Præterea, omnis definitio ex prioribus debet constare, & iis quæ definito per se insunt. At divisum esse à quovis alio sequitur essentiam Entis, si nempe plura dentur, nec ipsi propterea per se inest. Nec tamen reliqua, quibus Ens dicitur in se indivisum esse, licet vera sint, genuinam ejus definitionem constituunt. Indivisio namque negatio quædam est, male ad explicandam Affectionem positivam adhibita.
units.tr: 4. Unity is commonly defined as "an affection of being by which it is undivided in itself and divided from every other thing." But in this way it is not an inseparable affection, for it is not necessary that every being be actually divided from another. Before the world was created, says Burgersdijk, God was one, and yet he was not actually divided from anything, because nothing existed besides God. Moreover, every definition ought to consist of prior things, and of those which belong to the thing defined per se. But being divided from every other thing follows from the essence of a being only if several beings exist, and so it does not belong to it per se. Nor do the remaining things by which being is said to be undivided in itself, although they are true, constitute its genuine definition. For indivisibility is a kind of negation, wrongly used to explain a positive affection.

units.la: 5. Rectius igitur unitas definitur, quod sit modus essentiæ, quo ea Enti convenit semel. Dum dicitur modus essentiæ, significatur, quod essentia ut origo & fundamentum unitatis concipiatur; Nam semper talis est unitas, qualis est essentia. Dum porro additur, per unitatem Enti semel convenire essentiam, ponitur ipsa formalis ratio unitatis, quâ ab aliis affectionibus distinguitur; & simul ostenditur, quid ab Ente alienum sit, scilicet essentiam suam habere non-semel, sed vel nunquam, vel pluries.
units.tr: 5. Rather, then, unity is defined as "the mode of essence by which the essence belongs to a being once." When it is said "mode of essence," it is signified that essence is conceived as the origin and foundation of unity, for unity is always such as the essence is. When it is further added "that the essence belongs to a being once through unity," the formal reason of unity itself is laid down, by which it is distinguished from the other affections. At the same time it is shown what is alien to being, namely, to have its essence not once but either never or several times.

units.la: 6. II. Subjectum Vnitatis idem, quod effentia est; Omne scilicet & solum Ens; Quoniam enim Essentiae modus est, ejusdem cum ipsa debet esse subjecti; Imo unitas identice est ipsum Ens; est enim idem realiter cum essentia, & haec cum Ente. Hinc igitur 1. fluit reciprocatio illa inter Ens & unum, quâut omne Ens unum, ita omne unum Ens dicatur. 2. Quod non fit aliqua differentia, per quam Ens tanquam in species dividitur: Et hinc 3. male instituitur Entis divisio in unum. & multa.
units.tr: 6. II. The subject of unity is the same as that of essence: namely every being and only being. For since unity is a mode of essence, it must have the same subject as essence itself. Indeed, unity is identically being itself, for it is really the same as essence, and essence is the same as being. Hence there follows: 1. the reciprocity between being and one, by which every being is called one, and every one is called being. 2. That unity is not some difference by which being is divided, as a genus into species. And hence 3. the division of being into one and many is wrongly instituted.

units.la: 7. III. In habitudine, quam habet Unitas ad Ens, duo consideranda sunt. 1. Quid addat Enti? 2. Quid non superaddat? Addit autem modum aliquem internum, inseparabilem & positivum; Non autem externum, sive externam denominationem, non seperabilem, sine quo Ens esse possit; non negativum, quo aliqua perfectio removeatur. Quare & illius ratio positivo modo explicari debet; Prout ut in definitione praestitum. Non igitur Enti superaddit. 1. aliquod Ens, quia & hujus foret alia unitas, unde processus in infinitum ubique evitandus occurrit. 2. Nec denominationem externam, quia Ens in se est unum, citra ordinem alicujus ad illud. 3. Nec ens rationis, quia Ens rationis vere de Ente dici nequit, praeterquam quod Ens unum sit, etiam nemine cogitante. 4. Nec Relationem, quia Ens & unum forent relata, adeoque opposita, neque de fe invicem prædicabilia; Et magis sic Ens unius foret Ens; Et Unum Entis Unum; Relatorum quippe unum alterius est.. 5. Nec Privationem, 1. quia unitas involvit persectionem: Privatio vero defectum. 2. Oppositum unitatis Multitudo negatio vel privatio quædam est, quare fi unitas effet Privatio, alterius privationis vel negationis erit negatio, cum tamen Privatio privationis non detur. Denique Privatio præsupponit aptitudinem in subjecto, ad habendam privatione negatam perfectionem: sed nullum Ens aptum est, ut fit multum, five ut habeat essentiam suam sæpius repetendam, & non semel. Imo datur Ens, quod non tantum quoad actum, sed & quoad speciem multitudinem respuit, ut Deus. 6. Nec puram negationem; Nequit enim perfectio, vel affectio esse negatio; Imo quia oppositum ejus negativum est, ut ipsa positiva sit oportet.
units.tr: 7. III. In the relation that unity has to being, two things must be considered: 1. what it adds to being; 2. what it does not superadd. It adds some internal mode, inseparable and positive, but not an external mode or external denomination, separable, without which being could exist; nor a negative mode, by which some perfection is removed. Wherefore its nature must also be explained in a positive way, as was done in the definition. It therefore does not superadd to being: 1. some being, for then there would also be another unity of that being, and an infinite regress would arise, which must be avoided everywhere. 2. Nor an external denomination, because being is one in itself, apart from any order of it to something else. 3. Nor a being of reason, because a being of reason cannot truly be predicated of being, apart from the fact that being is one, even if no one is thinking. 4. Nor a relation, because being and one would then be relatives, and so opposites, and not predicable of each other; and further, the one of being would be being, and the being of one would be one, for of relatives one is the other's. 5. Nor a privation: (a) because unity involves perfection, whereas privation involves defect; (b) the opposite of unity, multitude, is a negation or privation of a kind, so if unity were a privation it would be the negation of another privation or negation, whereas a privation of a privation does not exist. Finally, privation presupposes an aptitude in the subject to have the perfection denied, but no being is apt to be many, or to have its essence repeated often and not once. Indeed there is a being that rejects multitude not only in act but also in kind, such as God. 6. Nor a pure negation, for a perfection or affection cannot be a negation; indeed, because its opposite is negative, it must itself be positive.

units.la: 8. V. Oppositum unitatis dicitur multitudo, quæ tamen potius solitudini, quam huic affectioni opponi videtur. Rectius ergo diceretur non-unitas, cui si dicas æquipollere multitudinem; ego eam, ut unitatis genuinum oppositum, assumere non gravabor. Sed dicet quà: Multitudo etiam una dicitur, ut una decas, eicas &c. Resp. Scilicet hoc fuit, quod me de opposito hoc dubitare fecit, ut & quod omnis compositio aliquam habeat multitudinem, & tamen ex eâ unum quid resulter. Responderi quidem potest, multitudinem dici abstractè vel concretè: Abstractè, quatenus certum denotat numerum, aut certam colle&ionem, atque sic unitatis modus est: Concretè verò pro ipsis multis, atque ita non est unum quid, sed multa; vereor tamen an satis accuratè & ad captum. Quomodo enim quod unitati, adeoque Enti, opponitur, in se unitatis aut Entis modus fieri possit, non capio. Sumenda igitur multitudo 1. negativè ut notet non-unitatem. 2. Politivè, ut designet concursum plurium, ad unius constitutionem requisitum. Priori modo non dicitur una; ac unitati opponitur; Posteriori modo verò una dicitur, quâtenus unum constituit, quo pacto ab unione non differt.
units.tr: 8. V. The opposite of unity is said to be multitude, which however seems rather to be opposed to solitude than to this affection. It would be more correct to call it non-unity, and if you say that multitude is equivalent to this, I shall not hesitate to take it as the genuine opposite of unity. But someone will object: multitude too is called one, as one decade, one hundred, and so on. Reply: this is precisely what made me doubt about this opposite, as well as the fact that every composition has some multitude, and yet something one results from it. It may indeed be answered that multitude is spoken of abstractly or concretely: abstractly, insofar as it denotes a certain number or a certain collection, and so is a mode of unity; concretely, however, for the many themselves, and so it is not one thing but many. I fear, however, whether this is accurate enough and within the grasp of the reader. For I do not understand how what is opposed to unity, and so to being, can itself become a mode of unity or of being. Multitude must therefore be taken: 1. negatively, so as to denote non-unity; 2. positively, so as to designate the concurrence of several things required for the constitution of one. In the former sense it is not called one, and it is opposed to unity; in the latter sense, however, it is called one, insofar as it constitutes one thing, and in this respect it does not differ from union.

units.la: 9. Quæres ulterius, quomodo non-unitas, seu multitudo negativè sumta, unitati opponatur? Resp. Aliqui privativè dicunt; Sed non satis rectè, quia sic unitas, ut habitus ab ente posset separari, aut saltem Ens ut non unum considerari, quod absurdum est. Rectius igitur dicendum, opponi contradictoriè; Nam 1. nullum inter unitatem & non-unitatem intercedit medium.
units.tr: 9. You will ask further, how non-unity, or multitude taken negatively, is opposed to unity? Some reply that it is opposed privatively. But this is not quite correct, because then unity would be like a habit that could be separated from being, or at least being could be considered as not one, which is absurd. It must rather be said that it is opposed contradictorily, for 1. no middle lies between unity and non-unity.

units.la: 2. Posità unitate, tollitur multitudo. 3. Vnitas est Ens, identico scilicet sensu: Multitudo non. Verum si multitudinem ipsi unitati opponas, non erit expressa, sed implicita contradictio, quia per hanc tollitur unitas, quæ Enti essentialis est; Eodem enim pacto, quo dicitur rationale brutum, dicitur quoque ens esse multum.
units.tr: 2. Unity being posited, multitude is removed. 3. Unity is being, in the same sense of identity; multitude is not. But if you oppose multitude to unity itself, the contradiction will not be expressed but only implicit, because through multitude unity, which is essential to being, is removed. For in the same way that a brute is called rational, being too is said to be many.

units.la: 10. Differentia unitatis desumendæ sunt partim à diversitate essentiarum, partim quoque à diverso modo considerandi essentiam; Quibus enim & quot modis res habet essentiam, eis & tot modis habet unitatem. Quoniam igitur essentia vel abstracte consideratur vel concrete: Abstracte quidem, quatenus res habet naturam vel esse suum simpliciter: Concrete autem, quatenus simul cum existentia illud esse non solum simpliciter, sed & præsens Enti tribuitur, nata quoque est Vnitatis distinctio in Vniversalem & Singularem: Universalitas quippe & Singularitas duo modi sunt, quibus unitatem consideramus: De his igitur nunc agendum.
units.tr: 10. The differences of unity are to be drawn partly from the diversity of essences, and partly also from the different ways of considering essence. For in as many ways as a thing has an essence, in so many ways it has unity. Since essence is considered either abstractly or concretely: abstractly, insofar as a thing has its nature or being simply; concretely, insofar as, together with existence, that being is attributed to a thing not only simply but as present. Hence the distinction of unity into universal and singular also arises, for universality and singularity are the two modes by which we consider unity. Of these we must now treat.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: DE Singularitate & Universalitate.
units.tr: Of Singularity and Universality.

units.la: 1. Singularitatis vox 1. spectandaest; 2. Res. In voce notanda 1. Ambiguitas.
units.tr: 1. The word singularitas is to be considered first; 2. the thing itself. In the word, notice first its ambiguity.

units.la: 2. Synonymia.
units.tr: 2. Synonymy.

units.la: 2. Quoad ambiguitatem 1. Singulare aliquando idem est, quod rarum & inusitatum. 2. Denotat pretiosum; rara quippe majori in pretio sunt. 3. Idem est quod proprium, ut singulare est homini ridere. 4. Significat id, quod communiter individuum appellamus; quomodo hic accipi debet.
units.tr: 2. As to ambiguity: 1. Singulare sometimes means the same as rare and unusual. 2. It denotes precious, since rare things are held in greater value. 3. It is the same as proper, as being singular is proper to man, to laugh. 4. It signifies what we commonly call individual, and this is how it must be understood here.

units.la: 3. Quoad Synonymiam; Dicitur Singulare aliter 1. Individuum, non prout quamcunque divisionem negat, sed saltem quatenus divisionem in partes subjectivas, de quibus nempe ipsum divisum in quid posset dici, auffert. Quamobrem & 2. Incommunicabile dicitur, eo quod essentiam suam non posset communicare inferioribus.
units.tr: 3. As to synonymy: singular is also called 1. individual, not in the sense that it denies every division whatever, but at least insofar as it excludes division into subjective parts, of which the divided thing could be predicated. For the same reason it is also called 2. incommunicable, because it cannot communicate its essence to inferiors.

units.la: 3. Dicitur etiam singularitas unitas numerica, vel quod singularia tantum numerentur, vel quod singularia, ut quibusdam placet, unius speciei saltem numero a se invicem differant.
units.tr: 3. Singularity is also called numerical unity, either because only singulars are counted, or because singulars, as some think, differ from one another in number alone within a single species.

units.la: 4. In reipsa duo quasi in limine annotanda videntur, 1. Quid sit Singularitas? 2. Quomodo ea distinguatur?
units.tr: 4. Two things seem to need noting at the outset: 1. What singularity is? 2. How it is distinguished?

units.la: 5. Quiddltas singularitatis, commodè hac definitione explicatur: Singularitas est modus unitatis, quo ens habet esse suum semel praesens. Dicitur modus unitatis, quia non nisi conceptu ab eâ differt; Dicitur modus, quo ens habet suum esse; Hoc enim omnibus Affectionibus absolutis, ut & principiis commune est. Additur semel, quod habet singularitas ab unitate; Et tandem subjicitur praesens; hoc enim ab existentiâ habet, cum quâ concretè consideratur essentia, ut fiat singularitas.
units.tr: 5. The quiddity of singularity is conveniently explained by this definition: Singularity is a mode of unity by which a being has its existence once and present. It is called a mode of unity because it differs from unity only in concept; it is called a mode by which a being has its existence, because this is common to all absolute affections, as also to principles. Once is added because singularity has this from unity; and finally present is attached, because it has this from existence, with which the essence is considered concretely, so that singularity comes about.

units.la: 6. Distinguitur autem Singularitas in formalem & Materialem. Formalis dicitur Entibus singularibus convenire ratione communitatis inter se: Materialis autem, quae ipsis convenit, quatenus singularia sunt. Sed nisi per formalem singularitatem, ipsum communem conceptum Singularitatis in actu signato, & per materialem ipsam singularitatem in actu exercito, quatenus inest singularibus, intelligas, inanis videtur distinctio. Nam 1. In omni singularitate res debet habere suum esse praesens: At in formali non habet illud praesens; quia eatenus abstrahitur à differentiis individuantibus. 2. Quod denotat naturam communem non est singulare: Sed singularitas formalis denotat naturam com-mumunem, quia denotat aliquid commune. Petro & Paulo. Dices: Formalis singularitas est Petri humanitas, at materialis est Petreitas; Igitur distinguenda videntur illæ duæ singularitates. Refp. Humanitas Petri & Petreitas idem sunt; quia igitur Petreitas est singularitas materialis, talis quoque erit humanitas Petri. Instabis: At singularis humanitas quoque est in Paulo & aliis. Refp. Recte: Non ergo notat singularitatem, quæ in uno est, sed universalitatem. 2. Singularis humanitas Pauli, non est eadem numero quæ Petri est, sed diversa. Omnis ergo vera singularitas materialis est.
units.tr: 6. Singularity is distinguished into formal and material. Formal singularity is said to belong to singular entities by reason of their commonness among themselves; material singularity is that which belongs to them insofar as they are singular. But unless you understand formal singularity as the common concept of singularity in the signified act, and material singularity as singularity itself in the exercised act, insofar as it inheres in singulars, the distinction seems empty. For: 1. In every singularity the thing must have its existence present; but in the formal the thing does not have that presence, because in that respect it is abstracted from individuating differences. 2. What denotes a common nature is not singular; but formal singularity denotes a common nature, because it denotes something common, as in Peter and Paul. Objection: formal singularity is the humanity of Peter, but material singularity is petreitas; therefore these two singularities seem to be distinct. Reply: the humanity of Peter and petreitas are the same; therefore, since petreitas is material singularity, the humanity of Peter will be such too. Objection again: but a singular humanity is also in Paul and others. Reply: rightly so; it therefore does not denote the singularity which is in one, but the universality. 2. The singular humanity of Paul is not numerically the same as that of Peter, but different. Therefore every true singularity is material.

units.la: 7. Quo demonstrato circa hanc materialem singularitatem distinctè inquirendum, 1. Quodnam ejus Subjectum? 2. Quomodo se ad illud subjectum habeat? 3. Quam compositionem cum subjecto faciat? 4. Quid in illo subjecto efficiat? 5. A quo in subjecto fiat?
units.tr: 7. With this demonstrated, we must inquire distinctly about this material singularity: 1. What is its subject? 2. How does it relate to that subject? 3. What composition does it form with the subject? 4. What does it effect in that subject? 5. By what is it produced in the subject?

units.la: 8. I. Subjectum singularitatis, idem quod Unitatis est; omne videlicet & solum Ens; Omne quidem; Quia unum quodque eo ens est, quo simul cum constitutione distinctum est: omne autem distinctum existit: Quod verò existit singulare est, omne igitur Ens singulare. Solum verò, quia soli Enti convenit existentia; adeoque & singularitas: Latius hæc discussa habes infra, in Subjecto Existentiæ. 9.
units.tr: 8. I. The subject of singularity is the same as that of unity: namely every being and only being. Every, because each thing is a being insofar as it is distinct together with its constitution; but everything distinct exists, and what exists is singular; therefore every being is singular. Only, because existence belongs only to being, and so also singularity. You will have this discussed more fully below, in the subject of existence (9).

units.la: 9. II. Ordo, quem habet singularitas ad Ens suum subjectum, consistit partim in utriusque convenientia, partim in disconvenientia. Convenientia autem Singularitatis cum Ente reali est; Realiter quippe convenit singularitas cum unitate, & haec cum Ente; Quæ vero eadem sunt cum uno tertio, illa inter se eadem sunt.
units.tr: 9. II. The order which singularity has to its subject, being, consists partly in the agreement of each with the other, partly in their disagreement. The agreement of singularity with real being is real: singularity really agrees with unity, and unity with being; and things which are the same as a third thing are the same as each other.

units.la: 10. Differt tamen ab Ente & unitate formaliter & modo considerandi, quo videlicet ipsum esse Enti aliter atque aliter tribuitur; Per Ens enim habet suum esse: per essentiam habet illud simpliciter: per unitatem semel; per singularitatem semel praefens. Non igitur 1. inter Ens & singularitatem intercedit differentia realis, foret enim sic singularitas Ens aliquod ab Ente, cujus est singularitas, distinctum, adeoque aliam sibi requireret singularitatem, cujus eadem esset conditio, idque in infinitum. 2. Nec singularitas Accidens Entis esse potest; Accidens enim potest adesse & abesse: Singularitas abesse nequit. Accidens realiter a subjecto distinctum est. At singularitas realiter idem cum eo. Quin si Accidentia sint Entia, etiam requirent singularitatem; Quæ tum utique Accidens esset; Et sic iterum in infinitum progrediendum esset.
units.tr: 10. Yet singularity differs from being and unity formally and in the mode of considering, namely in that being is attributed to a thing in different ways: through being it has its being; through essence it has it absolutely; through unity, once; through singularity, once and present. Therefore: 1. there is no real difference between being and singularity; for singularity would then be some being distinct from the being of which it is the singularity, and would therefore require another singularity, having the same condition, and so on to infinity. 2. Nor can singularity be an accident of a being; for an accident can be present or absent, whereas singularity cannot be absent. An accident is really distinct from its subject, but singularity is really the same as its subject. Moreover, if accidents are beings, they too would require singularity; which would then be an accident, and so one would have to proceed again to infinity.

units.la: 11. Nec 3. Singularitas est proprietas quædam Entis speciali; proprietates enim ut existentiam, ita & singularitatem sequi debent; Nec. 4. Est Collestio proprietatum; Hæc enim & ipsis proprietatibus posterior; Multò igitur minus, quam una proprietas, singularitatem constituere potest.
units.tr: 11. Nor 3. is singularity some property of a special being; for properties, like existence, must follow singularity as well. Nor 4. is it a collection of properties; for this is posterior even to the properties themselves, and so far less than a single property can it constitute singularity.

units.la: 12. III. Ex his facilè dignosces, quam compositionem Singularitas cum Ente faciat; nullam videlicet aliam præter compositionem rationis, qualis est ex modo essentiali, conceptu distinċto, & modificato: Non autem qualis est ex genere & differentiâ.
units.tr: 12. III. From these points you can easily see what composition singularity forms with being: namely no other composition than that of reason, such as arises from an essential mode, a distinct concept, and a modification, but not such as arises from genus and difference.

units.la: 13. IV. Effectum singularitatis dicitur incommunicabilitas: Verùm hæc non nisi nomine differt à singularitate; Per utramque enim res habet esse suum semel præsens nec in partes subjectivas divisibile.
units.tr: 13. IV. The effect of singularity is called incommunicability; but this differs from singularity only in name; for through both a thing has its being once and present, and is not divisible into subjective parts.

units.la: 14. V. Causa singularitatis Principium individuationis appellatur, anxiè satis à Scholasticis quæsitum: Sed inani labore. Uniuscujusque enim Entitas ipsiusmet est singularitas; Ut enim Ens non est sine essentiâ, ita neque sine unitate; Et prout non est sine unitate, ita nec sine singularitate; Et magis quemamodum essentia est ipsa unitas, & unitas ipsa singularitas, ita singularitas est ipsa essentia. Causa erroris fuit opinio quædam, quòd universalia essent Entia quædam à singularibus distincta, eisque priora, adeoque per aliud distinftinctum fingularizanda;quæ statim falfitatis arguenda. Atque hæc de singularitate sufficient. Sequitur
units.tr: 14. V. The cause of singularity is called the principle of individuation, a question the Scholastics have asked with considerable anxiety, but to no purpose. For the entity of each thing is its very singularity; as a being is not without essence, so neither is it without unity, and insofar as it is not without unity, neither is it without singularity. Indeed, just as essence is unity itself and unity is singularity itself, so singularity is essence itself. The cause of the error was the opinion that universals are certain beings distinct from singulars and prior to them, and so must be individualized by something else; this must be refuted at once as false. And this will suffice concerning singularity. Next follows

units.la: 15. Vniuersalitas, tractanda. 1. Ratione nominis. 2. Ratione Rei. In nomine notari debet 1. diuersa significatio. 2. diuersa appellatio.
units.tr: 15. Universality, to be treated: 1. in respect of the name; 2. in respect of the thing. In the name two things are to be noted: 1. its different signification; 2. its different application.

units.la: 16. Significat autem universale primò transscendens aliquod, generalitate sua omnes species Entium superans, & sic enti, ejusq; synonymis, Principiis & Affectionibus tantùm convenit. Secundo, idem est quod Prædicabile, ejusve modus, atque ita quinque ista Prædicabilia dicuntur universalia. Tertiò, significat quodcunque valde commune, ita dicitur universalis causa. Quartò sumitur pro modo unitatis, singularitati opposito, quâ significatione hîc spectanda est.
units.tr: 16. The word universal signifies, first, something transcendental, which by its generality surpasses all the species of beings, and so belongs only to being, its synonyms, principles and affections. Second, it is the same as predicable, or a mode of it, and in this sense the five predicables are called universals. Third, it signifies whatever is very common; thus we speak of a universal cause. Fourth, it is taken for a mode of unity, opposed to singularity, and it is in this sense that it is to be considered here.

units.la: 17. Appellatur aliter universalitas. 1. Generalitas, quia universalia, ut genera de pluribus in quid dicuntur. 2. Communitas, ratione scilicet essentiæ; universale enim essentiam à præsentiâ aufert, ac ipsi indifferentiam ad repetitam præsentiam addit. 3. Prædicabilitas, quia universalium nota est de pluribus in casu recto prædicari.
units.tr: 17. Universality is also called by other names: 1. generality, because universals, like genera, are predicated of many in answer to the question what; 2. commonness, by reason of its essence; for the universal removes essence from presence, and adds to it indifference to being repeated in presence; 3. predicability, because it is a mark of universals that they are predicated of many in the nominative case.

units.la: 18. In re sex consideranda sunt. 1. Quid sit? 2. Ejus subiectum. 3. Habitudo ejus ad subjectum. 4. Efficiens. 5. Finis. 6. Differentia.
units.tr: 18. Six things are to be considered in the thing: 1. What it is? 2. Its subject. 3. Its relation to the subject. 4. Its efficient cause. 5. Its end. 6. Its difference.

units.la: 19. I. Definitur vulgo universalitas, unitas in multis. Sed qualis sit illa unitas, difficulter explicabitur. 2. Illa unitas multorum est convenientia, quæ non est ipsa universalitas, sed ejus fundamentum tantum. Burgersdicio dicitur quæ convenit rebus, quatenus indivisæ sunt in plures res ejusdem nominis & essentiæ, & aptæ, ut in eas dividantur; Quæ definitio huc in modum contrahi potest, Universalitas est indivisio divisibilis in partes subjectas. Sed non facile inte' ;itur, quid sit illa indivisio divisibilis; non enim termini se mutuo compati videntur, idem quippe est, ac si diceretur, rationalitas potentia irrationalis.
units.tr: 19. I. Universality is commonly defined as unity in many. But what kind of unity that is will be hard to explain. 2. That unity of many is an agreement, which is not universality itself but only its foundation. Burgersdicius defines it as that which belongs to things insofar as they are undivided into several things of the same name and essence, and fit to be divided into them; this definition can be reduced to this form: universality is the undivided divisible into subjective parts. But it is not easy to grasp what that divisible undividedness is; for the terms do not seem to be compatible with each other, for it is the same as saying rationality is irrational in potency.

units.la: 20. Reɑtius igitur, Universalitas est modus unitatis, quo res habet esse suum semel, indifferens ad præsentiam & pluralitatem. Indifferentia illa non designat realem abstractionem à præsentiâ, sed saltem rationis: Unde universalitas reipsâ eadem cum Ente præsente est, licet formaliter per illam indifferentiam distinguatur; singularia quippe ad præsentiam determinata sunt. Additur etiam indifferentia ad pluralitatem, quia universale non tantum indiferens est ad præsentiam; sed & ad repetitam in pluribus præsentiam, quâ scilicet pluribus ejus nominis & naturæ convenit.
units.tr: 20. More correctly, then: Universality is a mode of unity by which a thing has its being once, indifferent to presence and to plurality. That indifference does not signify a real abstraction from presence, but only an abstraction of reason. Hence universality is in reality the same as the present being, although formally it is distinguished from it by that indifference, since singulars are determined to presence. Indifference to plurality is also added, because the universal is not merely indifferent to presence but also to presence repeated in many, by which it belongs to many things of the same name and nature.

units.la: 21. Hinc patet, duas esse universalitatis conditiones, 1. Vt ejus conceptus non necessario involvat præsentiam; Vnde conceptus Dei neque est, neque esse potest universalis, quia necessariò determinatus est ad præsentiam & existentiam. 2. Vt universalitas non possit tribui, nisi quorum conceptui non repugnat pluralitas; Vnde iterum Deus, qui necessariò unicus est, universalitatem respuit: Creaturarum autem conceptus semper indeterminatus & indifferens est ad præsentiam. Quoniam nulla creatura necessariò existit, sed saltem ex hypothesi voluntatis divinæ. Quemadmodum nec creaturarum existentia necessariò determinata est ad singularitatem, sive unum individuum.
units.tr: 21. From this it is clear that there are two conditions of universality: (1) that its concept does not necessarily involve presence. Hence the concept of God neither is nor can be universal, because it is necessarily determined to presence and existence. (2) That universality cannot be attributed except to things whose concept is not repugnant to plurality. Hence again God, who is necessarily one, rejects universality. The concept of creatures, however, is always indeterminate and indifferent to presence, since no creature exists necessarily, but only by the hypothesis of the divine will. Nor is the existence of creatures necessarily determined to singularity, or to a single individual.

units.la: 2 2. Hæc autem indeterminatio sive indifferentia ad pluralitatem omnibus creaturis æqualiter non convenit: Aliæ enim actu habent simul plura individua, ut homo. Aliæ autem saltem potentiam, sive non repugnantiam ad pluralitatem habent; idque dupliciter. 1. Sine repugnantiâ ad pluralitatem simultaneam, ut Sol, Luna &c. Qnæ licet actu in uno singulari reperiantur, non repugnat tamen simul plures dari soles, aut lunas. 2. Cum repugnantiâ ad simultatem pluralitatis, sed cum non repugnantiâ pluralitatis successivæ, ut universum, materia prima, quæ actu multa dari simul nequeunt, successione tamen plura esse possunt.
units.tr: 22. This indeterminacy, or indifference to plurality, does not belong equally to all creatures. For some have actually several individuals at once, as man does. Others have at least a potency, or non-repugnance, to plurality, and this in two ways. (1) Without repugnance to simultaneous plurality, as the sun, the moon, etc. Although these are actually found in one singular, it is not repugnant that several suns or moons should exist at the same time. (2) With repugnance to simultaneous plurality, but without repugnance to successive plurality, as the universe or prime matter: things which cannot actually exist many at once, yet can be many in succession.

units.la: 23. II. Ex quibus haut operosè dignoscitur1, quodnam sit Universalitatis subjectum; Scilicet est Ens, non tamen omne, sed tantum creatum, neque hoc eodem modo ut ex dictis colligi poterit.
units.tr: 23. II. From these points it is not difficult to recognise what the subject of universality is. Namely, it is being, not indeed every being, but only created being, and not in the same way, as can be gathered from what has been said.

units.la: 24. III. Ordo universalitatis ad subjectum consistit. 1. in disconvenientia. 2. in convenientia. Quoad disconvenientiam 1. Universalia non sunt Entium ideæ. Quod assertum ut capias, nota triplicem vocis ideæ significationem; Primo enim notat exemplar rei efficiendæ, in intellectu causæ efficientis constitutum: Secundo essentiam rei, extra rem separatim existentem: Tertio conceptum rei essentialem. Ex quibus colliges, universalia ultimo hoc modo ideas, id est conceptus, vel species, dici posse, non autem secundo; de primo enim non est controversia. Ratio autem asserti ex Burgersdicio hæc colligitur; Quidquid per se exstitit singulare est: Quare si universalia essent tales ideæ, per se ac seorsim a singularibus existentes, essent sane singulares; Quod naturæ universalitatis repugnat. Huic aliæ superaddi possunt. 1. Si universalia essent tales ideæ, sive res separatæ, & quidem creatæ, haberent quoque suam universalitatem à seipsis distinctam; Quæ si iterum idea dicatur, erit processus in infinitum: si negetur esse idea, pari ratione negabitur prima universalitas esse
units.tr: 24. III. The order of universality with respect to its subject consists (1) in disagreement and (2) in agreement. As to disagreement: (1) Universals are not the ideas of beings. To grasp this assertion, note the threefold meaning of the word idea. First, it denotes the pattern of a thing to be made, established in the intellect of an efficient cause; second, the essence of a thing existing separately outside the thing; third, the essential concept of a thing. From these you will gather that universals can be called ideas in the last sense, that is, concepts or species, but not in the second; for there is no controversy about the first. The reason for the assertion is drawn from Burgersdijk as follows: whatever exists by itself is singular. So if universals were such ideas, existing by themselves and apart from singulars, they would certainly be singular, which is repugnant to the nature of universality. Other points can be added to this. 1. If universals were such ideas, or separate things, and indeed created ones, they would also have a universality distinct from themselves; if this in turn is called an idea, there will be an infinite regress; if it is denied to be an idea, by the same reasoning the first universality will be denied to be an idea.

units.la: {1} Ex quibus ... (footnote text as printed at the foot of the column, not further legible) esse idea. 2. Sic quoque universalia proprium suum esse obtinerent; idque vel distinctum ab esse singularium, vel idem cum illo. Non possunt habere diversum, quia sic de singularibus in quid proprie praedicari non possent: Nec idem, quia sic non separatim existerent; Quorum enim idem est esse, ea idem Ens sunt; At idem Ens à seipso separatim existere nequit.
units.tr: {1} From which ... is an idea. 2. In this way universals would also have their own being, and this either distinct from the being of singulars or the same as it. They cannot have a different being, for then they could not properly be predicated of singulars in quid; nor the same, for then they would not exist separately. For things whose being is the same are the same being, and the same being cannot exist separately from itself.

units.la: 25. 2. Universalia non sunt res aliqua, citra operationem intellectus à singularibus distincta. Hoc iterum probat Burgersdicius, hunc in modum: Si quae res per se & absque operatione intellectûs essent universales & unae, vel essent aeternae vel factae. Aeternas illas affirmare nimis est absurdum, cum id soli Deo competat. Si factae, singulares sunt; Quia quidquid per actionem esse incipit, singulare est, cum omnis actio sit singularium. Si dicas, pergit, universalia non fieri per se, sed in & per singularia, ut Accidentia fieri dicuntur: non tollis difficultatem; Nam quidquid fit in & per singularia, id ipsum debet esse singulare. Huic accedere possunt rationes aliae. 1. Quidquid datur in rerum naturâ, habet praesentiam: At quod habet praesentiam, habet & existentiam: At haec singularium tantum est: forent igitur illae res universales, singulares. 2. Quidquid inest singularibus realiter, id ipsum singulare esse debet ; inesse enim notat præsentiam. 3. Quidquid est, habet quoque necessaria τῷ esse requisita : At inter ea est quoque præsentia , tanquam fundamentum, adeoque & singularitas. 4. Si universalia essent res distinctæ à singularibus, realiter deberent distingui , Res enim à re realiter distinguitur : At sic 1. οpponerentur singularibus , neque de ipsis possent prædicari. 2. iterum haberent suam essen-tiam & universalitatem, & sic in infinitum progressus apertus.
units.tr: 25. 2. Universals are not some thing distinct from singulars without the operation of the intellect. Burgersdijk proves this again in this way: if any things were universal and one by themselves, without any operation of the intellect, they would be either eternal or made. To affirm them eternal is too absurd, since this belongs to God alone. If they were made, they are singular, because whatever begins to be through action is singular, since every action belongs to singulars. If you say, he goes on, that universals are not made by themselves but in and through singulars, as accidents are said to be made, you do not remove the difficulty; for whatever is made in and through singulars must itself be singular. Other reasons may be added to this. 1. Whatever is given in the nature of things has presence; but what has presence also has existence; and this belongs only to singulars. Those things would therefore be singular, not universal. 2. Whatever really inheres in singulars must itself be singular, for inherence signifies presence. 3. Whatever is also has the things required for its being; and among these is presence, as a foundation, and so singularity. 4. If universals were things distinct from singulars, they would have to be really distinguished from them, for a thing is really distinguished from a thing. But thus (1) they would be opposed to singulars and could not be predicated of them; (2) again they would have their own essence and universality, and so there is an open infinite regress.

units.la: 26. Objic. 1. Ex Monlorio,tractat. de Universal. Universalia habent omnia requisi-ta ad suam entitatem, ante & citra mentis operationem , videlicet unitatem & communitatem, sive indifferentiam, non igitur opus est , ut solâ ratione à singularibus distinguantur. Resp. 1. Multa hic spe-ciosè in prolixis suis probationibus affert Monlorius, quæ tamen ideo non minus sallere deprehenduntur. Verum quidem est, ad universalitatem sufficere unitatem & indifferentiam ; Ea tamen non sufficiunt, ut universalia citra mentis operationem habeant præsentiam, hoc est , ut dentur ; Quoniam indifferentia illa, tam à præsentiâ quam à non præsentiâ præscinditur. 2. Universalia non habent per se unitatem, sed tantum , quâtenus cum Ente videlicet singulari , realiter coincidunt ; neque tum distinctam habent ab Entitate singulari unitatem, sed eamdem plane. Nullum enim alias singulare unum esse posset. Quoniam distincta una ad esse suum requireret. 3. Communitatem sive indifferentiam ad pluralitem habent non à parte rei, sed à parte rationis, ipsa universalia; Quod enim rei inest, id de facto in universitate dari debet. At talis communitas de facto non datur, neque ut detur necesse est; Non igitur à parte rei, sed saltem conceptus sunt. Instant. 1. At sic non una hominis erit universalitas, sed multiplex, pro numero videlicet individuorum; Si enim universale, homo non differat ab ipso singulari ratione unitatis, multiplicabitur quoque, multiplicatâ singularitate. Resp. Falsa illa consequentia; procedit enim à sensu identico ad formalem; Nam valet tantum, hoc modo, si Animal ratione formalis conceptus idem sit, quod homo, multiplicabitur quoque, multiplicato homine & ejus singulari; non verò si ratione rei & conceptus identici animal & homo idem esse dicantur. Instant. 2. Sic realiter idem esset Petrus & Paulus; Non tantum enim Petrus realiter idem est cum homine, sed & Paulus. Resp. 1. Valeret si Petrus & Paulus tam materialiter quam formaliter cum eodem homine realiter coinciderent. Nunc vero tantum homo formaliter est idem, videlicet cum indifferentia confideratus, non materialiter, quatenus in Petro & in Paulo est; quomodo tamen rationem universalitatis nondum induit.
units.tr: 26. Objection 1, from Monlorius, treatise on Universals. Universals have all the requisites for their entity before and without the operation of the mind, namely unity and communality, or indifference. Therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished from singulars merely by reason. Reply. (1) Monlorius brings forward many things here with a show of learning in his lengthy proofs, yet these are found to be no less deceptive for that. It is true that unity and indifference suffice for universality; yet they do not suffice for universals to have presence without the operation of the mind, that is, to be given; since that indifference abstracts both from presence and from non-presence. (2) Universals do not have unity of themselves, but only insofar as they really coincide with a being, namely a singular one; nor then do they have a unity distinct from the singular being, but plainly the same unity. For otherwise no singular could be one, since a distinct unity would require one of its own for its being. (3) Universals have communality or indifference to plurality not on the side of the thing but on the side of reason; for whatever is in a thing must actually be found in the universe. But such communality is not actually found, nor is it necessary that it be found; therefore universals are not on the side of the thing but are only concepts. Objection again. (1) Then the universality of man will not be one but manifold, according to the number of individuals; for if universal man does not differ from the singular by reason of unity, it will also be multiplied when singularity is multiplied. Reply. That consequence is false; for it proceeds from an identical sense to a formal one. For it holds only in this way: if animal is the same as man in the formal concept, it will also be multiplied when man and his singular are multiplied; but not if animal and man are said to be the same in reality and in an identical concept. Objection again. (2) Thus Peter and Paul would really be the same; for not only is Peter really the same as man, but Paul is too. Reply. (1) That would hold if Peter and Paul coincided really with the same man both materially and formally. But now only man is formally the same, namely considered with indifference, not materially, insofar as he is in Peter and in Paul; and yet he has not yet taken on the character of universality.

units.la: 2. Si statuas hominem esse universalem naturam, à singularibus distinctam, validius retorqueri poterit argumentum: Nam sic aeque Paulus ac Petrus, cum ea, ut pote de ipsis in quid praedicatâ, coincideret, & quidem formaliter aeque ac materialiter; Quare nullum effugium, aut distinguendi Petri à Paulo medium.
units.tr: 2. If you hold that man is a universal nature, distinct from the singulars, the argument can be turned back with greater force. For in that case Paul no less than Peter would coincide with that nature, as predicated of them in quid, and indeed formally no less than materially. So there is no escape here, nor any middle way of distinguishing Peter from Paul.
