units.la: 27. Objic. 2. Scientiae sunt Universalium: At sunt etiam de rebus, & non de conceptibus rationis, quia subjectum ipsorum debet esse τὸ ὂν, αἰδιον ἀγέννητον καὶ ἄφθαρτον. Ergo universalia sunt res. Resp. 1. Per concessionem, sunt res, sed non qua universalia, sed quatenus idem sunt quod singularia. 2. Syllogismus in forma legitima constitui nequit, quin alterutra praemissarum manifestâ falsitate laboret. 3. Scientiae sunt universalium, quatenus sunt de singularibus à singularitatis formâ abstractis, hoc est quatenus propter illum conceptum indifferentia, hoc est universalitas, ad esse concipitur. 4. Scientia est universalium ratione subjecti formalis, non materialis. 5. Scientia est universalium, ratione absolutae veritatis, non ratione uni-
units.tr: 27. Objection 2. Sciences are of universals. But they are also of things, and not of concepts of reason, since their subject must be that which is, eternal, unbegotten and incorruptible [τὸ ὂν, αἰδιον ἀγέννητον καὶ ἄφθαρτον]. Therefore universals are things. Answer 1. I grant that they are things, but not as universals; they are things insofar as they are the same as singulars. 2. A syllogism in legitimate form cannot be constructed without one of the premises being manifestly false. 3. Sciences are of universals insofar as they are of singulars abstracted from the form of singularity; that is, insofar as they are conceived as existing by virtue of that concept of indifference, that is, of universality. 4. A science is of universals by reason of the formal subject, not the material. 5. A science is of universals by reason of absolute truth, not by reason of what is universal and indifferent to many things in nature. For the latter is manifestly absurd in natural theology. The other things that can be objected and answered we reserve for disputations or for metaphysical exercises.

units.la: C versalis ac indifferentis ad plura naturæ; Postremum enim manifestè in Theologia naturali absurdum est. Cætera quæ objici & responderi possunt, aut conflictui, aut exercitationibus Metaphysicis reservamus.
units.tr: universal and indifferent to the many things of nature. For the latter is manifestly absurd in natural theology. The other things that can be objected and answered we reserve for disputations or for metaphysical exercises.

units.la: 28. 3. Vniuersalia non sunt tantum nomina communia. Quoniam & illud, quod nominibus istis significatur, commune esse debet; nisi nomina illa prorsus ἀπλῶς ἐφύλαξ & non significantia fingas. Quid autem illud commune sit, nunc dicendum. Sequitur enim
units.tr: 28. 3. Universals are not merely common names. For that which is signified by these names must also be common, unless you feign those names to be altogether bare [ἀπλῶς ἐφύλαξ] and signifying nothing. What that common thing is, must now be said. For there follows

units.la: 29. Conuenientia Vniuersalitatis cum suo subjecto, quæ in eo consistit, ut sit modus quidam unitatis, ratione nostrâ abstractus à præsentiâ, cum superadditione indifferentiæ ad pluralitatem: Quare realiter idem est, quod Ens singulare, & tantum formaliter sive conceptu ab eo differt.
units.tr: 29. The agreement of universality with its subject, which consists in this, that it is a certain mode of unity, abstracted by our reason from presence, with the addition of indifference to plurality. Hence it is really the same as the singular being, and differs from it only formally or in concept.

units.la: 30. I V. Efficiens universalitatis causa, vel remota est, vel proxima; Remota vulgò fundamentum dicitur universalitatis; estque duplex 1. Convenientia rerum inter se. 2. Indifferentia ad existentiam & pluralitatem. Proxima causa est ratio nostra, illud fundamentum designans, & ab eo Entia denominans. Hinc patet conciliatio Nominalium & Realium, quia universalia sunt aliquid fundamentaliter, ante operationem intellectus: formaliter, hoc est ut sint universalia, debent intellectui.
units.tr: 30. IV. The efficient cause of universality is either remote or proximate. The remote cause is commonly called the foundation of universality, and it is twofold: (1) the agreement of things among themselves; (2) indifference to existence and plurality. The proximate cause is our reason, which designates that foundation and names beings from it. Hence the reconciliation of Nominalists and Realists is evident: universals are something fundamentally, before the operation of the intellect; formally, that is, so that they are universals, they owe their being to the intellect.

units.la: 31. V. Finis Universalitatis est; juvare intellectum in rerum cognitione: Quoniam enim hic ad indefinita aut infinita se non extendit: Singularia autem, quia in abstracto conceptu indifferentiam ad pluralitatem involvunt, ex se determinata non sunt ratione numeri, ideo conceptu universali considerantur, ut quotuscunque numerus accedat, is in illâ consideratione, quod suum est quaerat.
units.tr: 31. V. The end of universality is to help the intellect in knowing things. For since the intellect does not extend itself to the indefinite or infinite, and singulars, because in abstract concept they involve indifference to plurality, are not in themselves determinate with respect to number, therefore they are considered under a universal concept, so that, whatever number is added, it seeks in that consideration what is its own.

units.la: 32. VI. Differentia universalitatis est, quod alia sit Synomia, alia Analogia. Synonymia est universalitas notans indifferentiam ad nomen & rem aequaliter. Analogia vero notat indifferentiam ad nomen & rem quidem, sed inaequaliter. Inaequalitas autem illa vel est in Praedicatione, & dicitur analogia attributionis, sive interna, quae tamen huc potissimum spectat, sive externa; Vel est in Proportione & similitudine quadam officii, quae dicitur Analogia Proportionis. Quibus alii universalitatem homonymias addunt, quando solum nomen indifferens, & nihil rei, neque aequaliter neque inaequaliter: Sed haec tantum communitas est vocis: Alii analogiam attributionis appellant analogiam proportionis, & alteram analogiam proportionalitatis: sed nullo fundamento; Praeterquam, quod sic analogia attributionis ex analogia altera oriri deberet, quemadmodum ex proportionalitate proportio; imò una esset alterius, prout proportionalitas proportionis est, & proportio proportionalitatis. Cætera ex iis quæ de genere univoco & analogo præcipienda sunt, facile dignoscès; Est enim genus, unum ex universalibus, respectivè sive Logicè consideratis. Et hæc de Universalitate.
units.tr: 32. VI. The difference of universality is that one kind is synonymy, another analogy. Synonymy is a universality denoting indifference to name and thing equally. Analogy denotes indifference to name and thing, but unequally. This inequality is either in predication, and is called analogy of attribution, whether internal, which however pertains to this point chiefly, or external; or it is in proportion and a certain likeness of function, which is called analogy of proportion. To these some add homonymy as a universality, when only the name is indifferent and nothing of the thing, neither equally nor unequally; but this is merely a commonness of the word. Others call analogy of attribution analogy of proportion, and the other analogy of proportionality, but on no foundation. Besides, analogy of attribution would then have to arise from the other analogy, just as proportion arises from proportionality; indeed one would be the other, since proportionality is of proportion and proportion is of proportionality. The rest you will easily discern from what must be taught about the univocal and analogous genus, for a genus is one of the universals considered relatively or logically. And these things concerning universality.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: DE Simplicitate & Vnione.
units.tr: ON SIMPLICITY AND UNION.

units.la: 1. Alia differentia Unitatis oritur, ex diversimodâ constitutione, sive pura, sive ex aliorum concursu orta; Licet enim unumquodque Ens constitutum sit, non tamen omne simplex est, aut plurium ad illam constitutionem concursum excludit; Pura fuerit constitutio & unitas, Ens dicitur Simplex: At si ex pluribus coalita constitutio, Ens dicitur unitum; Quare nunc de Simplicitate & Vnione, tanquam ex unitate ortis affectionibus, agendum.
units.tr: 1. Another difference of unity arises from the different kind of constitution, whether it is pure or arises from the concurrence of others. For although every being is constituted, not every being is simple, or excludes the concurrence of several things into that constitution. If the constitution and unity is pure, the being is called simple; but if the constitution is joined together out of several things, the being is called united. Hence we must now treat of simplicity and union as affections arising from unity.

units.la: 2. Simplicitas, si nomen spectemus, plicam, hoc est compositionem, negat, quare vox negativa est, positivam, licet imperfectiorem, affectionem oppositam tollens; quemadmodum apud Græcos ἁπλότης.
units.tr: 2. Simplicity, if we look at the name, denies a fold, that is, a composition. So the word is negative, and while it removes the opposite affection it is a positive, though less perfect, term. So the Greeks have haplotes [ἁπλότης].

units.la: τῆς. tns; & nostrates Belgæ, Een-vuldigheydt, sive enkelheydt dicunt, quasi eensgekeertheydt id est, unius modi versio; vel enckeld, quasi eens geleydt, id est semel sive ex uno positum, non compositum; positivâ quidem sed composita voce. Habent tamen Belgæ vocabulum æquè simplex ac Positivum, quo hanc affectionem exprimant, videlicet Slechtheyt, huic rei sat commodum.
units.tr: And we Dutch call it Een-vuldigheydt or enkelheydt, as if eensgekeertheydt, that is, a turning into one way; or enckeld, as if eens geleydt, that is, placed once, or from one source, not compounded. This is a positive word, though a compound one. The Dutch do have a word that is as simple as the positive, Slechtheyt, which expresses this affection and is quite suitable for the thing.

units.la: 3. Quoad ambiguitatem, nec semper idem denotat Simplicitatis vox. 1. Namque simplex idem est, quod absolutum; & sic simpliciter rem considerare, opponitur considerare respectivè sive comparatè. 2. Simplicitas est puritas à dolo, ut Matthæi, 10. Estote simplices, ut columbæ. 3. Simplicitas est puritas à prudentia, & simplex idem quod imprudens, unde & Belgæ dicunt een simpel Mensch. 4. Simplicitas est puritas à compositione vel unione; idque vel cum respectu ad unionem, ut partes ratione totius simplices dicuntur; vel absolutè, sine aliquo ordine ad compositionem, ut Deus dicitur simplex.
units.tr: 3. As to ambiguity, the word simplicity does not always mean the same thing. (1) Simple can mean the same as absolute; so to consider a thing simply is opposed to considering it relatively or comparatively. (2) Simplicity is purity from deceit, as in Matth. 10: "Be simple as doves." (3) Simplicity is purity from prudence, and simple means the same as imprudent; hence the Dutch say een simpel Mensch. (4) Simplicity is purity from composition or union; and this is either with respect to union, as parts are called simple in relation to the whole, or absolutely, without any reference to composition, as God is called simple.

units.la: 4. Simplicitas aliter appellari posset puritas; Et quidem rectius; Positiva enim vox est puritas, ideoque magis significandæ affectioni positivæ proportionata, quam simplicitas, quæ merè in se negativa est.
units.tr: 4. Simplicity could otherwise be called purity, and more correctly so. For purity is a positive word, and so better suited to signify a positive affection than simplicity, which is merely negative in itself.

units.la: 5. Quod ad rem simplicitatis spectat, ababsolvitur explicatione, 1. Quid sit? 2. Quotuplex sit? 3. Quæ ejus proprietates & axiomata?
units.tr: 5. As far as the thing of simplicity is concerned, it is treated under three heads: 1. What it is; 2. How many kinds there are; 3. What its properties and axioms are.

units.la: 6. I. Simplicitatem definit Burgersdicius, quod sit, unitas carens omni multitudine. Sed 1. negativa est definitio post ivæ assectionis. 2. Fit per oppositum, multitudo enim unitati ac simplicitati opponitur. 3. Nec est adæquata, soli quippe simplicitati divinæ ac absolutæ convenit, omni multitudine carere; Reliquæ vero omnes simplicitates, utpote comparatæ, nec simpliciter simplices, aliquam multitudinem præsupponunt. Convenientius igitur definitur modus unitatis, quo ens habet suum esse semel purum; id est, non unitum, mixtum, aut ex pluribus compositum.
units.tr: 6. I. Burgersdicius defines simplicity, that it is unity lacking every multitude. But (1) this is a negative definition of a later affection. (2) It proceeds by way of the opposite, since multitude is opposed to unity and simplicity. (3) Nor is it adequate, for only the simplicity of God and the absolute simplicity belong to something that lacks all multitude. All the other simplicities, being comparative and not simple without qualification, presuppose some multitude. It is therefore more fittingly defined as the mode of unity by which a being has its existence purely as one, that is, not united, mixed, or compounded out of several things.

units.la: 7. II. Duplex inprimis est Simplicitas, alia absoluta, alia comparata. Absoluta simplicitas est omnimoda puritas essentiæ, quâ omnis prorsus multitudo excluditur, estque solius essentiæ divinæ. Comparata est, quæ licet in se aliquam multitudinem habeat, non tamen habet omnem, cujus ratione adhuc puritas manet; Estque triplex Metaphysica, Logica & Physica. Metaphysica simplicitas varia est: Nam primò est puritas ab Actu & Potentiâ, adeoque puro Actui, Deo videlicet tantum convenit. Secundò est puritas ab Actu & essentiâ, sive à constitutione & esse; & iterum
units.tr: 7. II. Simplicity is first of all twofold: one is absolute, the other comparative. Absolute simplicity is complete purity of essence, by which every multitude whatsoever is excluded, and it belongs to the divine essence alone. Comparative simplicity is that which, although it has some multitude in itself, does not have all of it, and so a purity of some kind still remains. It is threefold: Metaphysical, Logical and Physical. Metaphysical simplicity takes various forms. First, it is purity from act and potency, and so belongs to pure act alone, that is, to God. Second, it is purity from act and essence, or from constitution and being; and again

units.la: Deo convenit, utpote negativè constituto: Non item creaturis, quibus positiva constitutio, ab extrinseco tributa, convenit. Tertiò est puritas ab essentiâ & existentiâ, id est ab esse simpliciter & esse præsentes. Ac iterum Deo convenit tantum, utpote cujus essentia necessaria est, adeoque necessariam ac independentem involvit existentiam. Quartò est puritas à natura & suppositô, id est ab esse jam quidem constituto ac distincto,& simul modo, quo illud independenter à subjecto aut alterius sustentatione, & completè possidetur; Quæ propterea convenit Substantiarum partibus, ut & accidentibus, Christique naturæ humanæ, ut & omnibus universalibus. Hujus simplicitatis longè alia est ratio ac reliquarum omnium; ubi enim reliquæ majorem perfectionem sibi oppositis compositionibus inferunt, hæc contra suâ compositione indignior est. Adeo ut cæteris paribus dignius sit, ex naturâ & subsistentiâ constare, quam earum ratione simplex esse. Imò infinitæ perfectionis nota est, plures subsistentias ac hypostases in unâ essentiâ aut naturâ habere, aliamque naturam completam sustentare, ac in hypostasin ac personalitatem unam assumere.
units.tr: it belongs to God, who is constituted negatively, but not to creatures, to whom a positive constitution given from outside belongs. Third, it is purity from essence and existence, that is, from being simply and from present being. This too belongs to God alone, whose essence is necessary and therefore involves a necessary and independent existence. Fourth, it is purity from nature and supposit, that is, from being already constituted and distinct, and at the same time from possessing that being completely and independently of a subject or of another's support. This therefore belongs to the parts of substances as well as to accidents, to the human nature of Christ, and to all universals. The reason for this simplicity is quite different from that of all the others. For where the others bring greater perfection through compositions opposed to them, this one is made less worthy by its composition. So much so that, other things being equal, it is more worthy to consist of nature and subsistence than to be simple in the manner of the others. Indeed, it is a mark of infinite perfection to have several subsistences or hypostases in one essence or nature, to sustain another complete nature, and to assume it into one hypostasis and personality.

units.la: 8. Quæres, an igitur Deo talis compositio non repugnet? Resp. Neutiquam; Non n. i. est
units.tr: 8. You will ask whether such a composition is therefore not repugnant to God? I answer: by no means. For it is not

units.la: n.1.est ex subjecto & accidente 2.ex diversis rebus.non extalibus quæ se habent per modum potentiæ,& actus; sed ex re modificatâ infinitâ, actribus modis subsistendi infinitis ac immutabilibus.Objic. 1.Sed sic periit absoluta simplicitas Dei modò asserta. Resp. Nihil minus:imò potius asseritur;non perit, quia compositio ex modificato & modis finitis tollit simplicitatem; non verò ex modificato & modis infinitis. Asseritur, quia infinitæ simplicitatis ac perfectionis conditio est, plures modos subsistendi in unâ natura retinere.
units.tr: (1) composed of a subject and an accident, nor (2) of different things, such as those that stand toward one another as potency and act. It is composed of a modified infinite thing, with infinite and unchangeable modes of subsisting. Objection 1. But in this way the absolute simplicity of God just asserted is lost. Answer. Nothing could be further from the truth. Rather, it is asserted; it is not lost. A composition of the modified and finite modes removes simplicity, but not a composition of the modified and infinite modes. It is asserted, because it is a condition of infinite simplicity and perfection to retain several modes of subsisting in one nature.

units.la: 9. Objic. 2. Sic foret mutabilis Deus: Omne enim compositum in sua principia ex quibus coalitum est, resolvi potest, adeoque mutari. Resp. Omne compositum ex principiis mutabile: At hæc non est compositio ex principiis. 2. Negatur consequentia; Modi enim infiniti ac inseparabiles nullam mutationem aut mutabilitatem in modificato inferunt. Vid. plenius hæc docentem Clarissimi Heereboord. lib. 2. Pneumatica. cap. 4. Et infra plenius hæc, quantum pote, enucleanda.
units.tr: 10. Logical simplicity is (1) purity from genus and difference. This also belongs to God, for he cannot be contained under a univocal genus, that is, a genus properly so called, together with finite being. (2) Purity from the denominated and from external denomination. But this external purity hardly belongs to any being.

units.la: 10. Simplicitas Logica est 1. puritas a genere & differentia; Ac etiam Deo convenit, sub univoco enim id est proprie dicto, genere cum Ente finito contineri nequit. 2. Puritas a denominato & denominatione externa: verum hæc externa puritas, ac vix dum ulli Enti convenit.
units.tr: 10. Logical simplicity is (1) purity from genus and difference. This also belongs to God, for properly speaking, under a univocal genus, he cannot be contained with finite being. (2) Purity from the denominated and from an external denomination. But this external purity hardly belongs to any being at all.

units.la: 11. Physica simplicitas quadruplex est; Primò namque est puritas à materiâ & forma, quæ opponitur Compositioni Physicæ, quomodo Spiritus simplices sunt. Secundò est puritas à miscline, quæ Elementis & Cœlo convenit. Tertiò est puritas ab aggregatione, sive plurium perfectorum collectione, quæ singulis corporibus naturalibus seorsim convenit. Quartò est puritas à concretione, sive ex subjecto & accidente cohæsione, quæ absolutè soli Deo convenit.
units.tr: 11. Physical simplicity is fourfold. First, it is purity from matter and form, which is opposed to physical composition, as spirits are simple. Second is purity from mixture, which belongs to the elements and to the heavens. Third is purity from aggregation, or the collection of several complete things, which belongs to each natural body taken separately. Fourth is purity from concretion, or cohesion out of a subject and an accident, which belongs absolutely to God alone.

units.la: 12. III. Axiomata ex naturâ simplicitatis oriunda, hæc potissimum sunt 1. Simplicitas est perfectio positiva. Non enim negat, sed ponit perfectionem. Hinc igitur eminentissimo modo Deo convenire debet. 2. Simplicitas est perfectio absoluta. Non enim ob respectum ad aliud Ens dicitur simplex, sed ob propriam essentiam. 3. Simplicitas denominat Ens intrinsecè. Ratio est, quia idem præstat unitas, cum quâ eadem est simplicitas. 4. Simplicitas est prior compositione; unio enim unienda, quæ sunt simplicia, præsupponit. Estque illa prioritas modò temporis, ut Elementa mistis: modò naturæ, ut materiâ corpore naturali: modò originationis metaphysicæ, ut constitutio Ente prior est. 5. Simplicitas est dignior compositione. Præstat enim habere esse purû per le, quam unitum per plurium concursum. 6. Quò Quo quid simplicius, eo perfectius; Quod, sicut & antecedens, de absoluta (simplicitate, non de comparata partium, intell. gi debet; Alias quippe homo ex anima rationali & corpore suo compositus dignior est, vel anima vel corpore seorsim.
units.tr: 12. III. The axioms arising from the nature of simplicity are these, above all: (1) Simplicity is a positive perfection. For it does not deny but affirms perfection. Hence it must belong to God in the most eminent way. (2) Simplicity is an absolute perfection. For a thing is called simple not because of its relation to another being, but because of its own essence. (3) Simplicity denominates a being intrinsically. The reason is that unity, with which simplicity is the same, has the same effect. (4) Simplicity is prior to composition, for union presupposes the things to be united, which are simple. This priority is sometimes of time, as the elements are prior to mixed bodies; sometimes of nature, as matter is prior to a natural body; sometimes of metaphysical origin, as a constitution is prior to a being. (5) Simplicity is more worthy than composition. For it is better to have being purely in itself than to be united through the concurrence of several things. (6) The simpler a thing is, the more perfect it is. This, like the preceding axiom, must be understood of absolute simplicity, not of the comparative simplicity of parts. Otherwise a human being, composed of a rational soul and a body, would be more worthy than either the soul or the body taken separately.

units.la: 13. Simplicitati essentiae opponitur Unio, quae vel absolute capitur, pro modo unitatis, vel respective pro ordine uniti ad unienda: Priori modo hic consideranda: At posteriori inter affectiones respectivas.
units.tr: 13. Union is opposed to the simplicity of essence. It may be taken absolutely, as a mode of unity, or relatively, as the order of the united parts toward being united. The first sense is to be considered here; the second belongs among the relative affections.

units.la: 14. Eo modo igitur sumpta unio, aliter dicitur compositio, videlicet late dicta; Angustius enim haec si accipiatur, aut notat unionem ex partibus se mutuo penetrantibus omnem, aut saltem eam quae est ex materia & forma. Praeterea unio dicitur 1. Confusio. 2 Mixtio. 3. Aggregatio. 4. Concretio 5. Complexio: Sed haec potius certum aliquem modum, aut speciem unionis significant, quam ut pro ipsius synonymis habeantur.
units.tr: 14. Taken in this way, union is also called composition, namely in the broad sense. For in a narrower sense this term signifies either a union made of parts that mutually penetrate one another entirely, or at least that which arises from matter and form. Moreover, union is called 1. confusion, 2. mixture, 3. aggregation, 4. concretion, 5. complexion. But these words signify certain particular modes or species of union rather than being regarded as its exact synonyms.

units.la: 15. Duo reliant in ipsa re unionis consideranda. 1. Quid sit? 2. Quomodo dividi debeat? I. Est autem unio, modus unitatis, quo ens habet esse suum per concursum plurium, hoc est non purum. Iis igitur convenit, quorum esse ex distinctis quibus coalitionem requirit; Adeoque non omni Enti; Quemadmodum nec simplicitas omni convenit. Et praeterea prout simsimplicitas non differt realiter ab ente simplici, ita nec unio ab Ente unito aut composito. Est quippe simplicitas ipsa essentia simplex & pura, & consimiliter unio ipsa essentia unita & non pura.
units.tr: 15. Two things are to be considered in the very nature of union: 1. What it is? 2. How it ought to be divided? I. Union is a mode of unity by which a being has its existence through the concurrence of several things, that is, not purely. It therefore belongs to those things whose existence requires the coalition of distinct components, and so not to every being, just as simplicity does not belong to every being. And as simplicity does not differ really from the simple being, so union does not differ from the united or composite being. Simplicity is indeed the simple and pure essence itself, and in the same way union is the united and impure essence itself.

units.la: 16. II. Variis modis dividitur unio, & quidem primo vulgata est distributio ejus in Realem, Rationalem & Modalem; Et optima si dextrè accipiantur termini. Pro quo nota 1. Quod realis unio sive compositio dupliciter dicatur, vel stricte, de ea, quæ est ex diversis rebus seu entibus diversum esse habentibus, quomodo hic accipi debet: vel late de eâ quoque, quæ habet fundamentum in re; atque ita etiam modalis realis dici potest. 2. Nota, quod etiam rationalis unio duplìciter sumatur, late videlicet & stricte. Late pro omni, quæ fit ex pluribus reipsa non distantibus quibuscumque, & sic modalem quoque sub se comprehendit. Stricte verò, tantum pro eorum, quæ solâ ratione citra aliquod fundamentum, aut etiam solis conceptibus inadæquatis differunt: Quomodo hic accipi debet.
units.tr: 16. II. Union is divided in various ways. First, the common division is into real, rational and modal union, and it is the best if the terms are taken correctly. On this point note 1. that real union, or composition, is taken in two ways: strictly, of that which arises from different things or beings having distinct existence, which is how it must be understood here; or broadly, also of that which has its foundation in the thing, and in this way a modal union can also be called real. 2. Note also that rational union is likewise taken in two ways, broadly and strictly. Broadly, it is whatever arises from several things that are not really distinct, and so it also includes modal union under itself. Strictly, however, it applies only to those things that differ by reason alone, without any foundation, or only by inadequate concepts; this is how it must be understood here.

units.la: 17. Est igitur in hac distinctione Unio realis, modus unitatis, quo Ens habet essentiam ex plurium rerum unione unitam. Estque vel Actualis, vel Potentialis. Actualis dicitur, quod in ipsâ omnes partes proprium actum seorsim habent, vel potius, quod quod partes actu extra se invicem constitutae habeat. Estque vel Continuatio, vel Aggregatio.
units.tr: 17. In this division, then, real union is a mode of unity by which a being has its essence united from the union of several things. It is either actual or potential. It is called actual when all its parts have their own act separately, or rather when the parts are actually constituted outside one another. It is either continuation or aggregation.

units.la: 18. Continuatio est modus unitatis, quo Ens habet essentiam per plurium rerum concursum, sub una superficie sensibili. Talis est 1. in omni mixto homogeneo, v. gr. Auro, Argento &c. 2. in mixto artificiali liquido, v. gr. Aqua salsa, Crama &c. in quibus sensus distinctas partium superficies non advertit.
units.tr: 18. Continuation is a mode of unity by which a being has its essence through the concurrence of several things under one sensible surface. Such is 1. in every homogeneous mixed body, for example gold, silver, etc.; 2. in an artificial liquid mixture, for example salt water, broth, etc., in which the senses do not notice distinct surfaces of the parts.

units.la: 19. Aggegatio est modus, quo Ens habet essentiam per plurium concursum, sub distinctis partium superficiebus sensibilibus. Estque ordinata, vel inordinata; Ordinata aliter nexus vel connexio dicta, est quando partes sub diversis superficiebus sensibilibus contentae, ad se mutuo proportionem ac habitudinem obtinent, qua ordinate inter se connectuntur, ut fit in corpore humano. Inordinata, quae aliter confusio dici potest, est quando partes nullum ordinem ad se invicem habent, sed saltem ἀταξίας & confuse coacervantur, ut in in acervo lapidum.
units.tr: 19. Aggregation is a mode by which a being has its essence through the concurrence of several things under distinct sensible surfaces of the parts. It is either ordered or unordered. Ordered union, otherwise called nexus or connection, is when the parts contained under different sensible surfaces have a proportion and relation to one another by which they are connected in an orderly way, as happens in the human body. Unordered union, which may also be called confusion, is when the parts have no order to one another, but are heaped together without order (ἀταξία) and confusedly, as in a heap of stones.

units.la: 20. Potentialis unio, est quando pars una habet se per modum potentiae, & altera per modum actus; Vel potius quando partes se mutuo penetrant, adeo ut una extra aliam monstrari non possit, neque ad sensum, neque ad rationem. Vel &, cum una pars est subjectum alterius sive informationis, sive inhæsionis, sive denominationis; unde exsurgit triplex unio potentialis 1. Informatio ut in quocunque corpore naturali, quatenus ex materia & forma constat informante, & hæc strictè dicta est compositio. 2. Inhæsio, quæ & concretio dicitur, estque eorum, quæ exsubjecto & accidente uniuntur. 3. Denominatio, aut unio per denominationem, qualis est in eo qui Dominus, Pater &c. dicitur. Ex his unio per informationem facit essentiam per se, reliquæ per accidens, sive intrinsecè, in inhærentiâ, sive extrinsecè, ut in denominatione, quæ propterea unio potius prædicationis, quam essentiæ appellari debet.
units.tr: 20. Potential union is when one part has itself in the manner of a power and the other in the manner of an act; or rather when the parts mutually penetrate one another, so that one cannot be shown outside the other, either to the senses or to reason. Or again, when one part is the subject of the other, whether of informing, of inherence, or of denomination; from which arises a threefold potential union. 1. Information, as in any natural body, insofar as it consists of matter and informing form; and this, strictly speaking, is called composition. 2. Inherence, which is also called concretion, and is of those things that are united as subject and accident. 3. Denomination, or union by denomination, such as is found in one who is called lord, father, etc. Of these, union by information makes an essence per se, the others per accidens, either intrinsically, by inherence, or extrinsically, as in denomination; which union should therefore be called a union of predication rather than of essence.

units.la: 21. Unio rationalis duplex est, vel respectu partium ratione & conceptu tantum distinctarum, ac reipsâ convenientium, qualis est omnis illa, quæ simplicitati Metaphysicæ & Logicæ opponitur; Vel respectu totius, quod solâ ratione colligitur ex partibus non unitis, sed conceptu aliquo quidditativo tantum convenientibus, qualis est unitas Generis aut speciei.
units.tr: 21. Rational union is twofold: either with respect to parts distinguished only by reason and concept, though really agreeing, which is every union opposed to metaphysical and logical simplicity; or with respect to a whole, which is gathered by reason alone from parts that are not united, but agree only by some quidditative concept, such as the unity of a genus or species.

units.la: 22. Unio modalis est inter rem ejusque modum separabilem & accidentalem; nec non à naturâ absolutâ modificati distinctum, qualis est ex homine & sessione in homine sedente.
units.tr: 22. Modal union is that between a thing and its separable and accidental mode, and also distinct from the absolute nature of the thing modified; such as that of a man and sitting in a man who is seated.

units.la: 23. Deinde unio est velper se, cum omnes partes concurrentes ad esse persectum totius requiruntur, ut ad hominem requiruntur corpus humanum & anima rationalis ; velper accidens, cum isti toti essentialiter constituto, aliquid superadditur, ut homini doctrina.
units.tr: 23. Further, union is either per se, when all the parts concurring are required for the perfect being of the whole, as the human body and rational soul are required for man; or per accidens, when something is added to a whole already essentially constituted, as learning is added to a man.

units.la: 24. Denique Vnio est vel Metaphysica, vel Logica, vel Physica ; prout quoque talis fuit simplicitas; Singularum igitur species ex oppositis simplicitatis speciebus hauriri possunt. Atque his simplicitatis ac Unionis, adeoque universa unitatis doctrina, absolvitur.
units.tr: 24. Finally, union is either metaphysical, logical, or physical, just as simplicity also was; therefore the species of each may be drawn from the opposed species of simplicity. And with these the doctrine of simplicity and union, and so the whole doctrine of unity, is completed.

units.la: CAPUT. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: DE Veritate.
units.tr: Of Truth.

units.la: 1. SEquitur secunda ex essentia orta afsectio, veritatis nomine appellata, cum suis modis, consideranda, quoad nomen & quoad rem.
units.tr: 1. There follows the second affection arising from essence, called truth, to be considered with its modes, both as to name and as to thing.

units.la: 2. Quoad nomen. 1. Opponitur figmento, ita dicitur verus Deus, quatenus vere & non fictè est. 2. Opponitur errori, ita verè id cognoscitur, in quo nullus error est. 3. Opponitur mendacio, ita verè loquimur, quæ menti convenienter dicimus. 4. Opponitur falsitati complexæ, ita vera dicitur propositio, quæ conjungit conjungenda & disjungit disjungenda. 5. Sumitur pro certo modo essentia, seu affectione ex essentia orta, videlicet ortu conceptuum. Quo pacto hic accipienda venit.
units.tr: 2. As to the name: 1. It is opposed to fiction; thus God is called true (verus Deus) insofar as He truly is and is not feigned. 2. It is opposed to error; thus that is truly known in which there is no error. 3. It is opposed to lying; thus we speak truly when we say what agrees with the mind. 4. It is opposed to false complex statement; thus a proposition is called true when it joins what should be joined and separates what should be separated. 5. It is taken for a certain mode of essence, or an affection arising from essence, namely from the origin of concepts. It is in this sense that it must be understood here.

units.la: 3. Alii aliter hasce significationes enumerant, dividentes veritatem in simplicem & complexam; quarum illa est, quæ simplici intellectus apprehensioni respondet: Hæc vero quæ ratione compositionis terminorum & conceptuum consideratur: atque duplex est, mentis & verborum; prout videlicet illa compositio & divisio vel solâ mente absolvitur, vel etiam vocibus effertur. Veritas igitur mentis illa est, quæ erori opponitur: Error quippe est, si intellectus ea quæ conjuncta sunt, judicet disjungenda, & disjuncta conjungenda. Veritas verborum etiam duplex est, Ethica & Logica. Prior est convenientia sermonis cum intellectu, eique opponitur mendacium; posterior est nuda convenientia sermonis cum rebus, eique opponitur falsitas Logica. Ex hac distinctione solvitur tritum illud paradoxon, quod aliquis verum dicens mentiri possit; Et contra falsum dicens non mentiri. Non enim mendacium committit, qui profert sermonem suo intellectui convenientem, dicet is falsus sit, si rebus applicetur.
units.tr: 3. Others list these meanings differently, dividing truth into simple and complex. The former corresponds to the simple apprehension of the intellect; the latter is considered by reason of the composition of terms and concepts. And it is twofold, of the mind and of words, insofar as that composition and division is either carried out by the mind alone or is also expressed in vocal sounds. The truth of the mind is therefore that which is opposed to error: for error occurs if the intellect judges things that are joined to be separated, and things that are separated to be joined. The truth of words is also twofold, ethical and logical. The former is the agreement of speech with the intellect, and lying is opposed to it; the latter is the bare agreement of speech with things, and logical falsity is opposed to it. From this distinction is resolved the familiar paradox that someone speaking the truth may lie, and conversely that someone speaking falsehood does not lie. For he who utters a speech agreeing with his own intellect does not commit a lie, even if that speech is false when applied to things.

units.la: 4. Verùm quoniam simplex veritas afsectio
units.tr: 4. But since simple truth is an affection

units.la: feftio est Entis, ideo hic sola acceptanda, reliquis ad proprium forum transmissis. Videtur autem hæc aliquando fumi concreté five materialiter, simul cum suo subjecto, quomodo scientia dicitur veritatis indagatrix : aliquando autem abstractè five formaliter, quatenus accipitur pro forma ratione formali, propter quam Ens verum dicitur.
units.tr: of Being, it is to be taken here alone, the other senses being sent over to their proper place. It seems that truth is sometimes taken concretely, or materially, together with its subject, as when science is called the investigator of truth; but sometimes abstractly, or formally, insofar as it is taken for the formal reason by which a being is called true.

units.la: §. Igitur in formali illâ consideratione videndum 1. Quid sit Veritas? 2. Ejus subjectum. 3. Oppositum. 4. Quinam sint ejus modi?
units.tr: §. Therefore in this formal consideration we must examine: 1. What truth is? 2. Its subject. 3. Its opposite. 4. What are its modes?

units.la: 6. I. Est autem Veritas modus essentia, quo Ens habet esse sibi debitum : hoc est tale cum talibus attributis, quale & quæ ad illud Ens requiruntur : Ita scilicet verum dicitur aurum, quod habet tale esse ac attributa talia, quod & qualia ad id, quod aurum esse debet, requiruntur.
units.tr: 6. I. Truth is a mode of essence, by which a being has the being that is due to it: that is, it is such with such attributes as, and as many as, are required for that being. Thus gold is rightly called true when it has such being and such attributes as are required for what gold ought to be.

units.la: 7. Unde formalis ratio veritatis, prout Enti intrinsecè convenit ; est debitudo quædam inter ens ejusque esse: Solet autem illa debitudo aliter ac aliter ab Autoribus exigi æstimari, unde natæ sunt diversæ illæ de veritatis ratione opiniones, quæ tamen facilè & inter se & nobiscum conciliari possunt. Debitudo enim illa æstimatur vel interne, vel externe. Interne æstimatur ex nudâ terminorum apprehensione, quod quidem evenit dupliciter,
units.tr: 7. Hence the formal reason of truth, as it belongs intrinsically to a being, is a certain due relation between a being and its being. Now that due relation has been estimated by authors in different ways, whence arose the various opinions about the nature of truth; yet these can easily be reconciled both among themselves and with us. For that due relation is estimated either internally or externally. It is estimated internally from the bare apprehension of terms, which happens in two ways:

units.la: 1. Ratione forma. 2. Ratione subjecti. Priori modo æstimatur secundum cujuscunque Entis conceptum formalem, qui est quasi imago ac exemplar illam debitudinem repræsentans, unde etiam idea appellatur. Atque ita verum est, veritatem esse convenientiam rei cum ideâ; Quatenus videlicet idea non significat essentiam separatam, nec etiam exemplar rei ab opifice aliquo constituendæ, sed cujuscunque rei conceptum essentialem. Neque aliud refutant rationes, quibus illa ideæ ratio infirmari videtur.
units.tr: 1. By reason of form. 2. By reason of subject. In the first way it is estimated according to the formal concept of any being, which is like an image and pattern representing that due relation, whence it is also called an idea. And so it is true that truth is the agreement of a thing with its idea; insofar, that is, as the idea does not signify a separate essence, nor a pattern of a thing to be made by some craftsman, but the essential concept of any thing whatever. Nor do the arguments by which this notion of idea seems to be weakened refute anything else.

units.la: 8. Posteriori modo, ratione subjecti, hoc pacto æstimatur veritas : Quoniam idea sive conceptus ille est in intellectu, & sæpissimè intellectus concretè pro seipso & simul ideâ receptâ accipitur, non male quoque illa debitudo veritatis ex intellectu. æstimari dicitur. Atque ita verum est, Veritatem esse convenientiam cum intellectu, Neque ferit ratio, quæ in contrarium adduci posset, quod nempe res vera dicatur, sine ullo respectu ad intellectum : Aliud enim est rem esse veram, & aliud eam veram æstimari. Est quidem vera per internam illam debitudinem, æstimatur autem per intellectum.
units.tr: 8. In the second way, by reason of subject, truth is estimated thus: since that idea or concept is in the intellect, and the intellect is very often taken concretely for itself together with the idea received in it, it is not wrongly said that this due relation of truth is estimated from the intellect. And so it is true that truth is the agreement with the intellect. Nor does the argument that could be brought to the contrary strike home, namely that a thing is called true without any reference to the intellect. For it is one thing for a thing to be true, and another for it to be estimated true. It is indeed true through that internal due relation, but it is estimated through the intellect.

units.la: 9. Externe æstimatur debitudo, cum exigitur ad externam aliquam imaginem, quâ ipsius esse significatur : Talis verò imago est definitio, adeòque nec in universum illi culpand sunt, qui statuunt veritatem esse convenientiam rei cum suâ definitione. Quamvis in eo erent, quod ipsum formale veritatis in eâ convenientiâ ponant, cum saltem ad æstimationem pertineat : Ut & in eo, quod volunt, idem esse rem convenire cum suâ definitione, & ipsum convenire cum suis principiis essentialibus: Hæc enim sunt ipsum esse, at definitio ipsum esse sequitur. Ex dictis igitur sequitur, Autores Metaphysicos non eodem modo Veritatem capere, licet exinde prognatæ diversæ ipsorum positiones amicè conciliari possint.
units.tr: 9. Due relation is estimated externally when it is demanded by some external image by which its being is signified. Such an image is a definition; and therefore those who hold that truth is the agreement of a thing with its definition are not to be blamed in general. Though they would be in error in placing the formal element of truth in that agreement, since it pertains at least to estimation; and likewise in what they maintain, that the same thing agreeing with its definition is the same as it agreeing with its essential principles: for these are the being itself, whereas the definition follows the being. From what has been said it follows that metaphysical authors do not all take truth in the same way, although their diverse positions arising from this can be amicably reconciled.

units.la: 10. II. Subjectum veritatis est omne Ens; Quidquid enim est, illud est, quod esse debet; Cum igitur nihil præter Ens habeat esse, nihil quoque præteripsum veritatem habebit. Dices: At veritas etiam est in conceptibus, imò & vocibus. Resp.
units.tr: 10. II. The subject of truth is every being; for whatever is, is what it ought to be. Since, then, nothing has being except a being, nothing apart from being will have truth. You will object: But truth is also in concepts, and indeed in words. Reply.

units.la: 1. Horum duplex est consideratio: vel secundùm esse reale, quâtenus sunt qualitates vel actiones, quo pacto etiam Entia dici possunt; vel secundum repræsentationem, quâtenus signa & exemplaria rerum, quomodo neque Entia sunt, neque veritatem habent, nisi externam illam in convenientiâ signi & signati constitutam. 2. Resp. Conceptus & voces non habent veritatem in se, sed in significatis tantum. 3. Resp. Veri dicuntur conceptus, quoniam per eos veritas æstimanda est; non quod in se veritatem habeant.
units.tr: 1. This is considered in two ways: either according to real being, insofar as they are qualities or actions, in which respect they too can be called beings; or according to representation, insofar as they are signs and patterns of things, in which respect they are neither beings nor have truth, except that external truth constituted in the agreement of sign and thing signified. 2. Reply. Concepts and words do not have truth in themselves, but only in what they signify. 3. Reply. Concepts are called true because by them truth is to be estimated, not because they have truth in themselves.

units.la: II. Atque hinc patet. 1. Formalem Veritatis rationem non consistere in alijuo respectu ad extrinsecum quodcunque, sed ipsi enti, eo quod esse habeat intimè convenire. Quare nec formalis ratio erit conformitas cum rationibus formalibus sive ideis Entium, in intellectu divino constitutis; Ita enim non nisi extrinseca denominatione Ens verum dici posset. Quamvis hoc verum sit, illas formales rationes in intellectu divino positas, adæquatam esse mensuram, illam veritatem Entium exigentem, ac singulis esse debitum tribuentem.
units.tr: II. From this it is evident: 1. That the formal reason of truth does not consist in any relation to some extrinsic thing whatever, but belongs to the being itself, since it intimately agrees with the being it has. Hence the formal reason will not be conformity with the formal reasons or ideas of beings established in the divine intellect; for in that case a being could be called true only by an extrinsic denomination. Although it is true that those formal reasons placed in the divine intellect are the adequate measure that demands the truth of beings and assigns to each its due.

units.la: 12. Patet 2. Veritatem se ita habere ad Ens, ut ab ipso realiter non distinguatur, ipsique nihil aliud superaddat, nisi positivum aliquem modum, solâ ratione ab Ente distinctum.
units.tr: 12. It is evident 2. That truth so relates to being that it is not really distinct from it, and adds nothing to it except some positive mode, distinct from the being only by reason.

units.la: 3. III. Oppositum Veritatis est falsitas, quæ totidem modis ac veritas accipi potest. Prout autem nunc consideratæ veritati opponitur, describi potest, quod sit, modus non-Entis, quo id habet non-esse sibi non-debitum. Unde patet ipsam Enti contradictorie opponi; quoniam posito ente ejusque veritate, non-ens ejusque falsitas tollitur. Cui tamen obstare videtur 1. Quod unaquæque res possit dici vera, quatenus esse sibi debitum habet, quodque eadem possit dici falsa, quatenus non habet esse alteri debitum. Quemadmodum orichalcum verum est orichalcum, & falsum aurum. Resp. Orichalcum proprie loquendo falsum aurum dici nequit; Falsum enim est, quod habet non esse sibi non debitum: At orichalcum habet esse sibi debitum: Illudque non-esse aurum ipsi est debitum, quare etiam non-aurum dicitur, non vero non-debitum; Quod requireretur, ut salsum diceretur aurum. 2. Obstare videtur, quod in privatione esse debitum tollatur, adeoque falsitas cū accedat subjecto, quod Ens est; quare etiam falsitas in Ente videtur dari. Resp. 1. Si esse debitum privatione tollatur, eo ipso aliud esse debitum accedit, neutiquam vero non-esse nondebitum. 2. Falsitas non est comparata quadam non-debitudo, sed absoluta; quare licet tollatur aliqua debitudo Enti ratione speciei debita, non tollitur tamen absoluta debitudo, ut fiat plane non debitudo.
units.tr: 3. III. The opposite of truth is falsity, which can be taken in as many ways as truth. Insofar as it is opposed to the truth now considered, it can be described as a mode of non-being by which a thing has non-being that is not due to it. Hence it is evident that falsity is contradictorily opposed to being; since, when a being and its truth are posited, non-being and its falsity are removed. Yet the following seems to stand in the way: 1. That any single thing can be called true insofar as it has the being due to it, and the same thing can be called false insofar as it does not have a being due to another. Thus orichalcum is true orichalcum, and false gold. Reply. Strictly speaking, orichalcum cannot be called false gold; for that is false which has a non-being not due to it. But orichalcum has the being due to it; and its non-being as gold is due to it, which is why it is called non-gold, not non-due; and it is non-due that would be required for it to be called gold falsely. 2. It seems to stand in the way that in privation a due being is removed, and so falsity arises in the subject, which is a being; hence falsity seems to exist in a being too. Reply. 1. If a due being is removed by privation, then by that very fact another due being arises, but by no means a non-being that is not due. 2. Falsity is not a certain comparative non-duty but an absolute one; therefore, although some duty is removed from a being by reason of its species, the absolute duty is not removed, so that it becomes plainly not-due.

units.la: 14. Modi veritatis varii sunt, quorum tamen non-nulli complexae, vel externae veritati potius, quam incomplexae & interna, conveniunt; quos tamen omnes breviter enucleandos existimo. Sunt igitur vel interni & absoluti, vel externi & respectivi. Interni modi veritatis duo sunt 1. Gradus.
units.tr: 14. The modes of truth are various. Some of them belong to complex truth, or rather to external truth, rather than to incomplex and internal truth; yet I think all of them should be briefly set forth. They are therefore either internal and absolute, or external and relative. The internal modes of truth are two: 1. Degree.

units.la: 2. Status. Gradus veritatis est ipsius dedebitudinis intensio, quae si firmior sit, dicitur Necessitas, si debilior Contingentia, quae nunc cum suis oppositis explicari debent.
units.tr: 2. Status. The degree of truth is the intensity of the very indebitedness itself, which, if it is firmer, is called necessity, and if weaker, contingency; these must now be explained together with their opposites.

units.la: CAP. VI. DE Necessitate & Contingentia.
units.tr: CHAP. VI. Of Necessity and Contingency.

units.la: 1. Necessitas si nomen spectetur, quibusdam dicitur à ne & cessando, quia in necessariis cunctandum non est: aliis autem necesse dicitur id, sine quo nec esse possumus, adeo ut indigentia quae illo nomine significari videatur.
units.tr: 1. Necessity, if the word itself is considered, is said by some to derive from "ne" and "cessando" (not ceasing), because one must not delay over necessary things. Others say that necessary is that without which we cannot exist, so that the word seems to signify need.

units.la: 2. Quoad significationes, quatuor hoc vulgari disticho continentur. Vtile, perpetuum, sustentans & violentum: Quatuor exprime, vox denotat ista necesse.
units.tr: 2. As to meanings, four are contained in this common couplet: "Useful, perpetual, sustaining, and violent: express the four, this word 'necessary' denotes."

units.la: Ex quibus secundum potissimum huius loci, adeo ut perpetuitatem quamdam denotare videatur: Atque ita tribuitur vel Entibus, vel eorum connexioni, vel orationi.
units.tr: Of these, the sense most important for this place is the one that seems to signify a certain perpetuity. Thus it is attributed either to beings, or to their connection, or to speech.

units.la: 3. Necessitas Entium est eorum quaedam constantia ac firmitas, quae proprie Metaphysica & huius loci est. Necessitas connexionis est necessaria & constans rerum cohaesio, vel quod una ad alterius pertineat essesentiam, quomodo homo necessariò est animal; vel quòd unum sine altero esse nequeat, quomodo 1. Effectus necessariò arguit causam. 2. Pars totum. 3. Accidens Subjectum. 4. Consequens Antecedens, &c. Necessitas orationis, consistit in necessaria ac constanti convenientiâ terminorum essentialium inter se; Cujus gradus sunt καλὰ πανῖος, καὶ αὐτὸ & καὶ ὅλως πεφυκὸς; Sed de hisce consulendi erunt Logici.
units.tr: 3. The necessity of beings is a certain constancy and firmness of things, which properly belongs to metaphysics and to this place. The necessity of connection is the necessary and constant cohesion of things, either because one belongs to the essence of the other, as a man is necessarily an animal, or because one cannot exist without the other, as 1. an effect necessarily implies a cause; 2. a part, the whole; 3. an accident, a subject; 4. a consequent, an antecedent, and so on. The necessity of speech consists in the necessary and constant agreement of essential terms with one another; its degrees are "universally" [καλὰ πανῖος], "in itself" [καὶ αὐτὸ] and "altogether by nature" [καὶ ὅλως πεφυκὸς]. But on these the logicians should be consulted.

units.la: 4. Synonyma penè necessitatis sunt 1. Perpetuitas. 2. Incorruptibilitas. 3. Immutabilitas. Non tamen proprie idem valent, quod necessitas: nam 1. perpetuitas ejus modus est, ut pote necessitas durationis potissimum. 2. Incorruptibilitas non tam notat firmitatem ac constantiam, quam res habet in se, quam quòd ab alio destrui nequeat. 3. Immutabilitas statum veritatis notat, sive Entis in esse debito perseverantiam, non præcisè præsentem firmitatem aut necessitatem.
units.tr: 4. The synonyms of necessity are, almost, 1. perpetuity; 2. incorruptibility; 3. immutability. They do not, however, strictly mean the same as necessity. For 1. perpetuity is a mode of it, being chiefly a necessity of duration. 2. Incorruptibility does not so much denote the firmness and constancy that a thing has in itself, as that it cannot be destroyed by another. 3. Immutability denotes the state of truth, that is, the perseverance of a being in the being that is due to it, not merely present firmness or necessity.

units.la: 5. Rei consideratio, absolvitur inquirendo 1. Quid sit necessitas? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quænam differentia? 4. Quodnam oppositum?
units.tr: 5. The consideration of the thing is completed by inquiring 1. What necessity is? 2. What is its subject? 3. What is its difference? 4. What is its opposite?

units.la: 6. I. Definitur necessarium, quod non potest aliter se habere: sed 1. negative. 2. Ut potius quid nominis, quam quid rei explicetur. Aliis definitur, quod non potest non esse. Vere quidem: sed non sufficienter pro genuinâ rei definitione. Rectius, quod sit, modus veritatis, quo ens habet esse sibi debitum firmiter.
units.tr: 6. I. The necessary is defined as that which cannot be otherwise; but this is 1. negative, and 2. it explains the meaning of the name rather than the nature of the thing. Others define it as that which cannot not be. This is true, but not sufficient as a genuine definition of the thing. More correctly, it is the mode of truth by which a being has firmly the being that is due to it.

units.la: 7. II. Quoad subjectum; Prout omne ens est verum, ita quoque est necessarium; Vnde quia multi gradus sunt veritatis, erunt quoque multi modi necessitatis; Quorum unus summus est, Deo soli conveniens. Reliqui variis intervallis ab ipso declinantes, semper aliquid contingentia involvunt, plus minusve pro majori vel minori accessu & recessu ad illud primum necessarium.
units.tr: 7. II. As to the subject: just as every being is true, so too it is necessary. Hence, since there are many degrees of truth, there will also be many modes of necessity. Of these one is the highest, belonging to God alone. The others, departing from it at various intervals, always involve something of contingency, more or less according to their greater or lesser approach to and withdrawal from that first necessary being.

units.la: 8. III. Differentia Necessitatis varia sunt, imprimis notanda illa, quâ dividitur in necessitatem Internam & Externam. Illa est firmitas interna ab ipso esse debito orta, adeoque potissimum affectio Entis interna. Estque duplex, absoluta, locum habens in iis, quorum non esse implicat contradictionem, sive simpliciter, quomodo necessarius est Deus, sive ex connexione terminorum, ut necessarium est hominem esse animal; vel relata, locum habens in omnibus illis, quorum non-esse contradictionem non implicat, adeoque ab alio aliquo ista debitudine excidere possunt, sive à Deo, ut in ortu solis; sive ab alio quoque agente, ut in descensu gravium.
units.tr: 8. III. The differences of necessity are various, and the chief one to note is that by which it is divided into internal and external necessity. The former is the firmness arising from the very being that is due, and so is chiefly an internal affection of the being. It is twofold: absolute, which holds in those things whose non-being implies a contradiction, either simply, as God is necessary, or from the connection of terms, as it is necessary that a man be an animal; or relative, which holds in all those things whose non-being does not imply a contradiction, and which therefore can lose that due condition by some other cause, either from God, as in the rising of the sun, or from another agent also, as in the falling of heavy bodies.

units.la: 9. Externa necessitas rebus vel rerum connexioni tribuitur, propter conditionem aliquam externam. Quomodo quæ in se & simpliciter considerata contingentia sunt, posità tamen illâ conditione necessaria dicuntur. Talia autem in sensu diviso, hoc est, seorsim sine illâ conditione spectata, dicuntur contingentia: At in sensu composito, hoc est, simul cum posità illâ conditione considerata, sunt necessaria; ita videlicet, loqui in se contingens est, at ex hypothesi finis, ad significandum animi sensum, est necessarium.
units.tr: 9. External necessity is attributed to things, or to the connection of things, on account of some external condition. Thus things which, considered in themselves and simply, are contingent, are nevertheless called necessary when that condition is posited. Such things, taken in the divided sense, that is, considered separately without that condition, are called contingent; but in the composite sense, that is, considered together with that condition posited, they are necessary. Thus, to speak is in itself contingent, but on the hypothesis of the end of expressing the mind's feeling, it is necessary.

units.la: 10. Illa autem conditio, quæ rei in se contingenti necessitatem tribuit, triplex est, Antecedens, Consequens, Connexa. Antecedens, vel tantum est antecedens, vel etiam causa. Tantum antecedens, est v. gr. decretum, præscientia ac prædictio Dei, ita igitur necesse erat, ossa Christi in cruce non frangi, quia hoc à Deo præscitum, & à Prophetis prædictum erat. Conditio antecedens, quæ simul causa, est, vel Coactio, vel Determinatio. Coactio est violenta impulsio, adeoque necessitatem affert effectui ejus, qui cogitur; Quod enim coacte quis & per vim facit, id non potest non facere; omne igitur violentum, etiam necessarium. Determinatio est, agentis contingentis ad unum oppositorum necessitatio: Posità igitur hac, agens non potest non agere, & si ad speciem tendat, non potest nisi illius speciei actionem producere; Sic voluntas, ab ultimo intellectus practici judicio determinata, necessario agit; & quidem hoc, ad quod determinata est, non aliud. Conditio consequens vel est finis, vel Eventus; Priori necesse fuit Christum in mundum venire, ut genus humanum redimeret. Posteriori non possunt non fieri haereses, ut (scilicet δοκιμοι manifestentur. Conditio connexa est, quaecum re cohaeret, ac tempore simul est; ita videlicet necesse est aliquid esse dum est, v. gr. hominem ambulare dum ambulat; Et non esse, dum non est v. gr. hominem non ambulare, dum non ambulat. Quae optime hoc pacto distinxit Burgersdicius, quem sequi consultum duxi.
units.tr: 10. The condition that gives necessity to a thing contingent in itself is threefold: antecedent, consequent, connected. The antecedent condition is either merely antecedent or also a cause. Merely antecedent is, for example, the decree, foreknowledge and prediction of God: so it was necessary that the bones of Christ not be broken on the cross, because this had been foreknown by God and foretold by the prophets. The antecedent condition which is also a cause is either coercion or determination. Coercion is violent impulsion, and so brings necessity to the effect in the one who is compelled; for what someone does under compulsion and by force, he cannot but do; therefore everything violent is also necessary. Determination is the necessitation of a contingent agent to one of two opposites: given this, the agent cannot but act, and if it tends toward a species, it cannot produce anything but an action of that species. Thus the will, determined by the final judgment of the practical intellect, acts necessarily, and indeed it acts toward that to which it is determined, not toward anything else. The consequent condition is either the end or the event. For the former, it was necessary for Christ to come into the world in order to redeem the human race. For the latter, heresies cannot but arise, so that (namely) the approved [δόκιμοι] may be made manifest. The connected condition is that which coheres with the thing and is simultaneous with it in time; thus it is necessary that a thing be while it is, for example, that a man walks while he walks; and that he not be while he is not, for example, that a man does not walk while he does not walk. Burgersdijk distinguished these very well in this way, and I have thought it advisable to follow him.

units.la: II. Deinde necessitas dividitur, quod sit incomplexa, vel complexa: Prior est in essentia ac veritate rei, posterior in praedicatione, & veritate orationis; Estque non nisi nominis distinctio.
units.tr: II. Next, necessity is divided into that which is incomplex and that which is complex: the former is in the essence and truth of the thing, the latter in predication and the truth of a proposition; and this is only a difference of name.

units.la: 12. Tertio distinguitur, quod sit vel ad esse, vel ad bene esse: Estque non universae necessitatis, sed saltem externa ex hypothesi finis, ad quem media quaedam absolute sunt necessaria; quaedam saltem utilia.
units.tr: 12. Thirdly, it is distinguished as necessity for being or for well-being. This is not of universal necessity, but at least external, on the hypothesis of an end, for which certain means are absolutely necessary, and certain others only useful.

units.la: 13. Quarto, necessitas vel est naturae, vel violentiae; Prior rei conveniens est, ut descensus lapidis sursum projecti: posterior vero inconveniens, ut ipsa projectio lapidis sursum.
units.tr: 13. Fourthly, necessity is either of nature or of violence. The former is agreeable to the thing, as the falling of a stone; the latter disagreeable, as the very throwing of a stone upward.

units.la: 14. Quintò, necessitas vel est consequentis, vel consequentia: Prior est interna & ipsius rei: posterior externa, & connexionis rei cum conditione.
units.tr: 14. Fifthly, necessity is either of the consequent or of the consequence. The former is internal and belongs to the thing itself; the latter is external, and belongs to the connection of the thing with its condition.

units.la: 15. IV. Oppositum necessitatis est impossibilitas, quæ consimiliter ac necessitas tributuit 1. rebus. 2. connexioni rerum inter se. 3. Orationi.
units.tr: 15. IV. The opposite of necessity is impossibility, which, in the same way as necessity, is attributed 1. to things, 2. to the connection of things with one another, 3. to speech.

units.la: 16. Impossibilitas rerum, est earum repugnantia ad esse, vel ad existere: Prior est repugnantia in attributis essentialibus, ut impossibile est hominem esse irrationalem:posterior est repugnantia ad præsentiam, ut impossibile est præteritum esse præsens.
units.tr: 16. The impossibility of things is their repugnance to being or to existing. The former is repugnance in essential attributes, as it is impossible for a man to be irrational; the latter is repugnance to presence, as it is impossible for the past to be present.

units.la: 17. Impossibilitas autem hæc vel absoluta est, vel ex hypothesi. Prior est eorum, quæ implicant contradictionem; ut impossibile est non esse Deum; opponiturque hæc necessitati absolutæ. Quod enim absolutè necessarium est, ejus oppositum est absolutè impossibile; ut quia homo necessario est animal, ideo eum non esse animal, absolutè est impossibile.
units.tr: 17. This impossibility is either absolute or on a hypothesis. The former belongs to those things which imply a contradiction, as it is impossible that God not be; and this is opposed to absolute necessity. For what is absolutely necessary, its opposite is absolutely impossible; thus, because a man is necessarily an animal, it is absolutely impossible for him not to be an animal.

units.la: 18. Posterior, ex hypothesi, sive hypothetica impossibilitas, est repugnantia ex posità conditione, quâ sublatâ illud impossibile fit possibile, quia nempe in terminis nulla est repugnantia aut contradictio. Ita impossibile est, hominem esse alatum, quia alas habere repugnat conditioni humanae, tam ratione antecedentis, quia Deus noluit hominem esse alatum; quam ratione connexi, quia homo brachia habet; quam ratione consequentis seu finis, quia homo alarum non indiget. Eis autem conditionibus sublatis, possibile erat hominem esse alatum.
units.tr: 18. The latter, hypothetical impossibility, is repugnance arising from a posited condition, with which removed that impossibility becomes possible, because in the terms themselves there is no repugnance or contradiction. Thus it is impossible for a man to be winged, because to have wings is repugnant to the human condition: both by reason of the antecedent, since God did not will man to be winged; and by reason of the connected, since man has arms; and by reason of the consequent or end, since man has no need of wings. These conditions being removed, it would have been possible for a man to be winged.

units.la: 19. Hinc patet 1. conditionem illam hypotheticae impossibilitatis, non minus ac conditionem necessitatis hypotheticae, vel antecedentem, vel connexam, vel consequentem esse. 2. Patet, impossibile ex hypothesi reipsa idem esse, quod possibile, sed alio plane respectu. 3. Patet, possibilitatem non praesentibus, sed futuris tantum tribui posse.
units.tr: 19. From this it is clear, first, that the condition of hypothetical impossibility, no less than that of hypothetical necessity, is either antecedent, connected, or consequent. Second, it is clear that the impossible, under a hypothesis, is actually the same thing as the possible, but in a quite different respect. Third, it is clear that possibility can be ascribed only to things future, not to things present.

units.la: 20. Impossibilitas connexionis, aliter contradictio in adjecto dicta, est conjunctio eorum quae disjungi repugnant: Quomodo impossibile est, duo opposita eidem secundum idem convenire, & effectum esse sine causa, totum sine partibus, accidens sine subjecto: Estque haec, non minus ac prior absoluta vel hypothetica; cujus declaratio ex supradictis petipotest.
units.tr: 20. The impossibility of a connection, otherwise called a contradiction in terms, is the conjunction of things that cannot be disjoined. Thus it is impossible for two opposites to belong to the same thing in the same respect, or for an effect to exist without a cause, a whole without parts, or an accident without a subject. This impossibility, no less than the earlier absolute or hypothetical kind, is a conjunction; its explanation can be gathered from what has been said above.

units.la: 21. Impossibilitas orationis, est sententiae omnimoda falsitas, ex impossibilitate rerum & connexionis ortum trahens. Et haec de necessitate ejusque oppositio
units.tr: 21. The impossibility of a proposition is the complete falsity of a statement, arising from the impossibility of the things and of their connection. And so much for necessity and its opposite.

units.la: 22. Contingentia, quæ ratione nominis quatuor potissimum habet significationes; 1. Tribuitur omni illi quod fit, atque sic omnes Creaturæ contingentes sunt. 2. Opponitur ei, quod necessario fit, ita contingens est, hominem ambulare. 3. Opponitur ei, quod impetu natura fit, estque idem in re quod libertas. 4. Contingens est, quod raro fit, sive impetu naturæ, & dicitur casus, sive præeunte aliquâ electione, & dicitur fortuna. Harum significationum tres priores potissimum hujus loci sunt; ultima autem non nisi analogicè.
units.tr: 22. Contingency, which in terms of its name has four main meanings: (1) It is ascribed to everything that comes to be, and in this sense all creatures are contingent. (2) It is opposed to what comes to be by necessity; in this sense it is contingent that a man walks. (3) It is opposed to what comes to be by natural impulse, and in fact it is the same in reality as liberty. (4) Something is contingent if it happens rarely, whether by natural impulse, and then it is called chance, or by some preceding choice, and then it is called fortune. Of these meanings the first three are chiefly relevant here; the last applies only by analogy.

units.la: 23. Hæc consimiliter ac necessitas tribuitur 1. rebus. 2. earum connexioni. 3. orationi: Quarum prima hic potissimum consideranda, ut inquiratur, 1. Quid sit?
units.tr: 23. This, like necessity, is ascribed (1) to things; (2) to their connection; (3) to propositions. Of these, the first is to be considered here above all, so that we may inquire: (1) What is it?

units.la: 2. Quænam ejus opposita? 3. Quomodo dividenda sit?
units.tr: 2. What are its opposites? 3. How is it to be divided?

units.la: 14. I. Est autem Contingentia modus veritatis, quo ens habet suum esse sibi debitum infirmiter. Idque oppositè ad necessitatem, cujus aliqua negatio est contingentia, quare vix positivè eam explicari posse credo. Infirmiter autem habere suum sibi debitum esse, est illud possidere ad libitum aut potestatem alterius, quo deficiente ipsum esse, cum suâ infirmitate, perit.
units.tr: 14. I. Contingency is a mode of truth, by which a being has its own being owed to it, but weakly. It is opposed to necessity, of which contingency is in some sense a negation; so I hardly think it can be explained positively. To have one's owed being weakly is to possess it at the pleasure or power of another, and when that other fails, the being itself perishes together with its weakness.

units.la: 15. II. Opponitur autem primò necessitati, idque contrariè, ambæ enim in se popositivæ sunt affectiones sibique tantum eodem pacto opponuntur, neque una est alterius. Secundò opponitur possibilitati, utpote quæ futuro esse, non præsenti, convenit; idque privativè; ut contingentia per possibilitatem negetur, cum habitudine ad illam, in eodem subjecto. Tertiò opponitur impossibilitati, idque contradictorie; Nam in omni contingentiâ præsupponitur aliquod esse, quod per impossibilitatem prorsus auffertur.
units.tr: 15. II. Contingency is opposed, first, to necessity, and that contrarily; for both are positive affections in themselves, and they are opposed only in the sense that neither is the other. Second, it is opposed to possibility, since possibility belongs to what is future, not present; and this opposition is privative, so that contingency is denied of the same subject by possibility, in relation to it. Third, it is opposed to impossibility, and that contradictorily; for every contingency presupposes some being, which is wholly removed by impossibility.

units.la: 26. III. Licet verò contrariè opponatur contingentia necessitati, non tamen propterea in absolutam & conditionatam dividi potest; absoluta enim contingentia, ut pote nullum esse, ejusve necessitatem habens, est ipsa impossibilitas: Omnis igitur conditionata aut hypothetica est, aliquam necessitatem involvens. Quare quem admodum absoluta necessitas, omnem respuit contingentiam, ita conditionata aliquam præsupponit.
units.tr: 26. III. Although contingency is indeed contrary to necessity, it cannot for that reason be divided into absolute and conditional; for absolute contingency, since it is no being and has no necessity, is simply impossibility. Every conditional or hypothetical contingency therefore involves some necessity. Just as absolute necessity rejects all contingency, so conditional necessity presupposes some.

units.la: 27. Contingentia connexionis est eorum, quæ cum conjuncta sunt, dissolvi possunt, ut paries & albedo, homo & doctrina: aut cum disjuncta sunt uniri, ut divitiæ & Philosophus. Contingentia orationis est sententiæ veræ mutabilis veritas, quæ propositionem contingentem in Logicis denominat.
units.tr: 27. The contingency of a connection belongs to those things which, when joined, can be dissolved, such as a wall and whiteness, or a man and learning; or which, when disjoined, can be united, such as riches and a philosopher. The contingency of a proposition is the changeable truth of a true statement, which in Logic names a contingent proposition.

units.la: 28. Possibilitas, quæ contingentia opponitur, est modus non-entis, quo illi non repugnat esse : Hæc igitur Ens in potentiâ denominat ; Quare de eâ, quantum huic negotio sufficit, supra actum : infra tamen latius explicanda est.
units.tr: 28. Possibility, which is opposed to contingency, is a mode of non-being by which being is not repugnant to it. It therefore names being in potency. Hence, so far as this business requires, it has been treated above in act; it is, however, to be explained more fully below.

units.la: 29. Ex his autem, quæ de Necessitate, Contingentiâ, earumque oppositis, dicta sunt, varia axiomata ac documenta desumi possunt ; Quorum hæc præcipua. I. Necessitas absoluta caret omni contingentiâ. Hinc in Deo nulla infirmitas, dependentia &c. locum habere potest. II. Necessitas hypothetica est ipsa contingentia, sed alio respectu : Conditio enim affert necessitatem, quæ rei in se infirmæ & contingenti per se non aderat. Hinc absolutè loquendo, omnes creaturæ contingentes sunt. III. Nulla est contingentia sine aliquâ necessitate : Esset enim alias impossibilitas. IV. Non datur contingentia absoluta, id est nullam necessitatem involvens. Quando igitur res in se dicuntur contingentes, præsupponitur jam illis adesse aliqua conditio necessitatis : alias enim res non forent. V. Idem diverso respectu necessarium & contingens esse potest: Ita necesse est homines loqui, dum loquitur; contingens tamen, quia homo quà homo sine illa determinatione consideratus potest non loqui. VI. Omne liberum quà tale contingens est: Dicitur quà tale, quia determinata liberlibertas fit necessitas. Quod igitur in se liberum & contingens est, id in sensu composito cum conditione & determinatione sive externâ & non vitali, sive interna & vitali, z̃ dicitur necessarium: Atque hoc pacto libere agit homo in sensu diviso & in se: necessariò quatenus & seipsum determinat, & à Deo determinatur; Non ergò hic pugna est necessitatis & libertatis. Sed de his alibi prolixius, in doctrinâ de causa Efficiente.
units.tr: 29. From these things that have been said about necessity, contingency, and their opposites, various axioms and rules may be drawn, of which the following are the chief. I. Absolute necessity is free of all contingency. Hence no weakness, dependence, and so on, can have a place in God. II. Hypothetical necessity is itself contingency, but in another respect: for a condition brings in a necessity which was not present in the thing itself, which is weak and contingent of itself. Hence, speaking absolutely, all creatures are contingent. III. There is no contingency without some necessity: otherwise it would be impossibility. IV. There is no absolute contingency, that is, one involving no necessity. When things are said to be contingent in themselves, it is presupposed that some condition of necessity already belongs to them; otherwise the things would not exist. V. The same thing can be necessary and contingent in different respects: thus it is necessary that men speak while they are speaking, yet contingent, because a man, considered as a man and without that determination, can fail to speak. VI. Everything free, as such, is contingent: it is said "as such" because a free liberty, when determined, becomes necessity. What is free and contingent in itself is therefore called necessary in a composite sense, with the condition and determination either external and non-vital, or internal and vital. In this way a man acts freely in the divided sense and in himself, necessarily insofar as he also determines himself and is determined by God. There is therefore no conflict here between necessity and liberty. But these matters are treated more fully elsewhere, in the doctrine of the efficient cause.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: DE Statu, seu Mutabilitate & Im- mutabilitate.
units.tr: ON STATE, OR MUTABILITY AND IMMUTABILITY.

units.la: 1. Equitur Status, qui est Entis in esse debito perseverantia: Res autem in esse perseverat, vel immutabiliter sine aliquo defectu, vel mutabiliter cum defectu: à priori modo res dicitur immutabilis, à posteriori vero mutabilis.
units.tr: 1. It follows that a state is the perseverance of a being in the being due to it. A thing persists in being either immutably, without any defect, or mutably, with defect. In the first way a thing is called immutable; in the second, mutable.

units.la: 2. Immutabilitas igitur est modus veritatis, quo Ens habet esse suum sibi debitum, citra defectum perseverans: Quæ per negationem oppositæ differentiæ concipitur definitio, quòd positivæ voces non occurrant.
units.tr: 2. Immutability, therefore, is the mode of truth by which a being persists in the being due to it, without defect: a definition conceived through the negation of the opposite difference, since positive words do not occur.

units.la: 3. Est autem immutabilitas vel absoluta, vel hypothetica. Prior ex se nullum agnoscit defectum, adeoque soli Deo, Enti summe necessario ac immutabili non convenit; Posterior ex se agnoscit defectum Entibus tamen ex hypothesi decreti divini convenit.
units.tr: 3. Immutability is either absolute or hypothetical. The former acknowledges no defect in itself, and so does not belong to God alone, the supremely necessary and immutable Being. The latter acknowledges defect in itself, yet belongs to beings by the hypothesis of the divine decree.
