units.la: 4. Reliquis igitur omnibus praeter Deum ex se convenit mutabilitas, sed alio ac alio modo, qui ex speciebus mutationis colligi potest.
units.tr: 4. Mutability, then, belongs of itself to all things other than God, but in different ways, which can be gathered from the kinds of change.

units.la: 5. Est autem duplex mutatio, alia essentia, alia consequentium essentiae: Mutatio essentiae est, qua ens esse suum acquirit vel amittit; Quod dupliciter fieri potest.
units.tr: 5. There are two kinds of change: one of essence, and another of the consequences of essence. Change of essence is that by which a being acquires or loses its being. This can happen in two ways.

units.la: 1. Simpliciter, ex nullo antecedente & in nullum consequens; dicitur talis acquisitio creatio, & amissio annihilatio: ac sola divina virtute praestari potest.
units.tr: 1. Simply, from no antecedent and into no consequent. Such an acquisition is called creation, and such a loss annihilation; these can be effected by divine power alone.

units.la: 2. Secundum quid, ex praejacente nimirum aliquo, & in consequens; dicitur generatio, ratione ejus quod fit ac suum esse acquirit: at corruptio, ratione ejus quod interit; Unde tantum in corporibus locum habet: non item in spiritibus, utpote qui nec generari aut corrumpi dici possunt.
units.tr: 2. In a certain respect, namely from something preceding and into something consequent. It is called generation with regard to what comes into being and acquires its being, but corruption with regard to what perishes. Hence it takes place only in bodies, not in spirits, which cannot be said to be generated or corrupted.

units.la: 6. Mutatio ratione consequentium vel interna est, vel externa: prout illa quae consequuntur, vel externa vel interna sunt. Interna mutatio, vel est in quantitate, vel in qualitate. Mutatio quantitatis, vel est á minori ad majorem, & dicitur augmentatio; vel á majori ad minorem, & dicitur diminutio; iisque tantum conveniunt, quorum est quantitas, corporibus videlicet. Mutatio Qualitatis dicitur alteratio, quæ varia est, pro diversitate mutabilium qualitatum. Habetque locum in corporibus potissimum: aliquo tamen etiam modo in spiritibus.
units.tr: 6. Change with respect to consequents is either internal or external, according as the consequents are external or internal. Internal change is either in quantity or in quality. Change of quantity is either from less to greater, and is called augmentation; or from greater to less, and is called diminution. These belong only to things that have quantity, namely bodies. Change of quality is called alteration, which is various, according to the diversity of the changeable qualities. It takes place chiefly in bodies, yet in some way also in spirits.

units.la: 7. Externa mutatio vel Loci est vel temporis. Prior motus latiori vocis acceptione dici potest, quoniam eâ transfertur res ex unâ præsentiâ in aliam. Posterior Successio appellanda est, eâ quippe Ens à præterito per præsens transit ad futurum. Atque ita ambæ omni Enti creato conveniunt.
units.tr: 7. External change is either of place or of time. The former, motion in the broader sense of the word, can be called so because by it a thing is transferred from one presence to another. The latter should be called succession, for by it a being passes from the past through the present to the future. And so both belong to every created being.

units.la: 8. Nulla harum mutationum Deo tribui potest; quoniam omnes imperfectionem ab Ente infinitè perfecto alienam, involvunt: At præter has nulla alia mutatio excogitabilis videtur; Quare in universum Deus immutabilis censendus: Quare si aliquid mutationem sapiens ipsi tribui videatur id ἀνθρωπωπαθῶς accipi & θεοπρεπῶς explicari debere, optimè Theologi monent. Et hæc de statu
units.tr: 8. None of these changes to God can be attributed, since all of them involve an imperfection alien to the infinitely perfect Being. Beyond these, no other change seems conceivable. In general, then, God is to be judged immutable. So if anything wise seems to be ascribed to him as a change, it must be understood anthropopathōs [ἀνθρωπωπαθῶς] and explained theoprepōs [θεοπρεπῶς], as the theologians rightly advise. And so much concerning state.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: DE Certitudine & Evidentiâ.
units.tr: Of Certitude and Evidence

units.la: 1. HI modi fuerunt interni veritatis; Sequuntur externi, Enti non nisi ob respectum ad aliud convenientes, adeoque ipsi saltem externam denominationem afferentes, quales sunt certitudo & evidentia, de quibus pauca admonenda sunt.
units.tr: 1. Those were the internal modes of truth. There follow the external ones, which belong to a being only by reference to something else and so give it only an external denomination; such are certitude and evidence, concerning which a few things must be noted.

units.la: 2. Certitudo est firmitas quaedam, ejus cui tribuitur: tribuitur autem 1. Rebus. 2. cognitioni. 3. orationi.
units.tr: 2. Certitude is a certain firmness belonging to that to which it is attributed. It is attributed (1) to things, (2) to knowledge, (3) to speech.

units.la: 3. Certitudo rerum est modus veritatis, quo ens esse sibi debitum firmiter habet; sive est firmitas esse debiti, adeoque reipsa concidit cum necessitate, ut ex definitione patet; ut & ejus divisione, quâ dispescitur in absolutam & conditionatam: Eâ enim nihil aliud quam necessitatis divisio infertur.
units.tr: 3. The certitude of things is the mode of truth by which a being firmly possesses the existence that is due to it; or it is the firmness of what ought to be, and so in fact it coincides with necessity, as is clear from the definition, and also from its division into absolute and conditional; for from this division nothing else follows than a division of necessity.

units.la: 4. Certitudo cognitionis est firmitas judicii, quâ non hæsitanter & sine metu oppositi aliquid judicamus. Opponitur igitur 1. Dubitationi, quâ in utramque partem æque inclinamus. 2. Opinioni, quâ magis inclinamus in alteram partem, cum metu tamen opposita.
units.tr: 4. The certitude of knowledge is the firmness of judgement by which we judge something without hesitation and without fear of the opposite. It is therefore opposed (1) to doubt, by which we incline equally to either side, and (2) to opinion, by which we incline more to one side, though with fear of the opposite.

units.la: 5. Certitudo orationis est firma conve-niennientia orationis, tanquam signi, cum re, tanquam signato; adeoque est illa ipsa veritas orationis, aut ejus gradus, necessitas dictus, à quo Propositio necessariò vera dicitur; De hac igitur suprà dictum.
units.tr: 5. The certitude of speech is the firm agreement of speech, as of a sign, with the thing, as with the thing signified; and so it is that very truth of speech, or its degree called necessity, by which a proposition is said to be necessarily true. Of this, therefore, we have spoken above.

units.la: 6. Evidentia rebus tribuitur, quatenus clarè ab intellectu cognosci possunt; Quare etiam perspicuitas dicitur; Quæ vox proprie significat qualitatem corporis, quâ id pellucidum, ac lumen transmittere, non emittere aut reflectere, dicitur; Unde refertur ad intellectum, ut ita significet, quod ab intellectu facilè cognosci potest: Sive illa facilitas sit ex ipsis rebus, sive ex earum signis, conceptibus videlicet & vocibus.
units.tr: 6. Evidence is attributed to things insofar as they can be clearly known by the intellect; for this reason it is also called perspicuity. This word properly signifies a quality of a body by which it is said to be transparent, transmitting light and neither emitting nor reflecting it. Hence it is referred to the intellect, so as to signify that which can easily be known by the intellect, whether that ease arises from the things themselves or from their signs, namely concepts and words.

units.la: 7. Triplex igitur evidentia sive perspicuitus dicitur esse; 1. in rebus: 2. in conceptibus. 3. in vocibus.
units.tr: 7. Evidence or perspicuity is therefore said to be threefold: (1) in things; (2) in concepts; (3) in words.

units.la: 8. Perspicuitas in rebus, est facilitas illa cognoscendi: Res autem facilè cognoscuntur, si intellectui sint proportionatæ; non excedentes, ut infinitum; non deficientes, ut nihil. Huic evidentiæ opponitur subtilitas, & admirabilitas, quâ res difficulter cognoscuntur.
units.tr: 8. Perspicuity in things is that ease of knowing. Things are easily known if they are proportioned to the intellect: not exceeding it, like the infinite, nor falling short of it, like nothing. To this evidence is opposed subtlety and admirability, by which things are known with difficulty.

units.la: 9. Perspicuitas in conceptibus est clara ac distincta rei apprehensio; oriturque vel à consuetudine distinctè apprehendendi, ac distinctos conceptus formandi, vel à legitimâ perceptione, vel & ab infusione.
units.tr: 9. Perspicuity in concepts is the clear and distinct apprehension of a thing; and it arises either from the habit of apprehending distinctly and forming distinct concepts, or from lawful perception, or also from infusion.

units.la: Huic evidentiæ opponitur confusio & imperfectio conceptûs, quâ hic rem obscurè aut imperfectè repræsentat.
units.tr: To this evidence is opposed confusion and imperfection of a concept, by which it represents the thing obscurely or imperfectly.

units.la: 10. Perspicuitas in vocibus, est vel in iis seorsim, vel in earum connexione, seu integrâ propositione: In vocibus seorsim est 1. ipsarum distinctio, cui opponitur ambiguitas. 2. Vsitatio, cui opponitur insolentia, sive illa nimis obsoleta, aut nimis recens fuerit. In enuntiatione oritur perspicuitas partim ex singulis vocibus, partim ex integro sensu. Sed de his latius consulendi Logici.
units.tr: 10. Perspicuity in words is either in the words taken singly or in their connection, that is, in the whole proposition. In words taken singly it consists in (1) their distinctness, to which ambiguity is opposed; and (2) their common usage, to which unfamiliarity is opposed, whether the word is too obsolete or too recent. In a statement, perspicuity arises partly from the individual words and partly from the whole sense. But the logicians should be consulted on these matters at greater length.

units.la: CAPUT. IX. DE Bonitate seu Perfectione.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On Goodness or Perfection.

units.la: 1. SEquitur tertia affectio Entis, immediatè ex essentiâ orta, sub titulo bonitatis sive perfectionis. Hujus autem tractatio apud Metaphysicos obscurior videtur, quoniam inter se non conveniunt, quid proprie bonitas dici debeat. Hic tamen (missō prolixiori sententiarum examine:) breviter agendum. 1. de Voce. 2. De Re ipsâ.
units.tr: 1. There follows the third affection of Being, arising immediately from its essence, under the title of goodness or perfection. Its treatment among the Metaphysicians seems rather obscure, since they do not agree on what goodness ought properly to be called. Here, however (setting aside a lengthier examination of opinions), it must be dealt with briefly: 1. concerning the word; 2. concerning the thing itself.

units.la: 2. Sumitur autem bonitas primò intrinsecè, pro internâ Entis perfectione. 2. Extrinsecè, pro debitâ Entis convenientiâ, cum alio aliquo.Priori modoBonitas & persectio aequipollent: posteriori vero res conveniunt vel cum voluntate Dei, tanquam antecedente quâdam suæ bonitatis mensurâ, quæ convenientia etiam bonitas simpliciter dici potest, & hic quoque post perfectionem tractanda videtur; vel cum alio aliquo Ente, tanquam consequente, atque ita nihil aliud est, quam utilitas, ex actu rei proveniens, de quâ infra agendum erit, cap. 16.
units.tr: 2. Now goodness is taken first intrinsically, for the internal perfection of Being; and secondly extrinsically, for the due agreement of a Being with some other thing. In the former sense, goodness and perfection are equivalent. In the latter sense, things agree either with the will of God, as with a certain prior measure of their goodness, and this agreement may also be called goodness simply, and it seems that it too should be treated after perfection; or with some other Being, as a consequence, and so it is nothing other than the usefulness arising from the activity of a thing, which will have to be treated below, in chapter 16.

units.la: 3. Perfectum ratione vocis, sumitur vel ut nomen, sine respectu aut ordine, quo quod perfectum est antea fuerit imperfectum; quomodo etiam hic accipi debet: vel ut participium, & sic indigitatur ordo, quo ex imperfecto existit perfectum; Et talis imperfectio nihil aliud est, quam potentiâ, ut perfectio sit actus & potentiæ consummatio. Ex quibus apparet, de persecto vi participii accepto agendum esse sub titulo actus, infrà cap. 15.
units.tr: 3. The word perfect (perfectum), so far as the word is concerned, is taken either as a noun, without reference or order to what was previously imperfect, which is how it must be understood here; or as a participle, and then the order is indicated by which the perfect comes into existence out of the imperfect. Such imperfection is nothing other than potency, since perfection is the act and the completion of potency. From these things it appears that the perfect, taken in the sense of the participle, is to be treated under the title of act, below in chapter 15.

units.la: 4. Porrò perfectum pro nomine sumtum vel absolutè capitur, vel comparatè: priori modo omne Ens perfectum: posteriori autem alia aliis perfectiora ac digniora judicantur. Perfectio autem hîc tractanda interna & absoluta est affectio: Comparata igitur alterius erit loci, quare de eâ agendum in doctrina de ordine cap. ultimo.
units.tr: 4. Further, perfect taken as a noun is understood either absolutely or comparatively. In the former way, every Being is perfect; in the latter, some things are judged more perfect and more worthy than others. But perfection to be treated here is internal and absolute, an affection. The comparative sense therefore belongs to another place, and so it is to be discussed in the doctrine of order, in the last chapter.

units.la: 5. Agendum autem de eâ, quæ hujus loci est, perfectione, exponendo 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quam habeat ad subjectum habitudinem? 4. Quodnam ejus oppositum? 5. Quomodo dividenda? 6. Quænam ejus axiomata?
units.tr: 5. We must treat of that perfection which belongs to this place by setting out: 1. What it is? 2. What is its subject? 3. What relation it has to the subject? 4. What is its opposite? 5. How is it divided? 6. What are its axioms?

units.la: 6.I. Perfectum communiter dicitur id, cui nihil deest: Quod licet verum sit, non tamen, quia negative efferetur, legitimam ejus definitionem constituere potest; Rectius igitur perfectio definitur, modus essentia, quo Ens habet omnia sui esse requisita; Eo ipso enim, quia omnia habet, nihil ipsi deest.
units.tr: 6. I. The perfect is commonly called that to which nothing is lacking. Although this is true, it cannot constitute a proper definition, since it is stated negatively. Perfection is therefore more correctly defined as the mode of essence by which a Being has all the requisites of its existence; for by the very fact that it has all of them, nothing is lacking to it.

units.la: 7. II. Subjectum Bonitatis est Ens. Est enim modus essentiæ: at hujus modus semper cum ipsâ ejusdem est subjecti; ac deinde requisita essendi habere, omnis & solius Entis esse debet.
units.tr: 7. II. The subject of goodness is Being. For it is a mode of essence, and a mode always belongs to the same subject as the essence itself; and to have the requisites of existing must belong to every Being and to Being alone.

units.la: 8. Sed quæres 1. An omni Enti conveniat perfectio? Resp. Omninò: quemadmodum enim absurdum, ens fingere sine essentiâ, ita non minus absurdum est, Ens esse, & non habere suæ essentiæ requisita: Errant igitur illi, qui Ens in perfectum & imperfectum distribuunt.
units.tr: 8. But you may ask: 1. Does perfection belong to every Being? Answer: Altogether so. For just as it is absurd to imagine a being without essence, so it is no less absurd for a Being to exist without having the requisites of its essence. Those therefore err who divide Being into perfect and imperfect.

units.la: 9. Objic. 1. Dantur quædam, quæ hoc quòd sunt, imperfecta sunt: & quorum essentia in imperfectione est posita, ut materia prima, puncta, & id genus alia. Resp. Antecedens plane falsum est, ut ex supradictâ ratione manifestè colligi popotest. Materia prima Ens in se perfectum est, ac sibi debita habet requisita, licet comparatè loquendo incompletum sit corpus naturale: Puncta Mathematica Entia rationis sunt, nullam igitur perfectionem, utpote ipsis indebitam requirunt: Puncta Physica minima corpuscula sunt, ac debitæ sibi perfectionis participia; Consimilia alia non reperio.
units.tr: 9. Objection 1. There are some things which, in being what they are, are imperfect, and whose essence consists in imperfection, such as prime matter, points, and other things of that kind. Answer: The antecedent is plainly false, as can be clearly gathered from the reason given above. Prime matter is a Being perfect in itself, and has the requisites due to it, although, speaking comparatively, a natural body is incomplete. Mathematical points are beings of reason, and therefore require no perfection, since none is due to them. Physical points are minute corpuscles, and participate in the perfection due to them. I find no other similar cases.

units.la: 10. Objic. 2. Solus Deus perfectus: Omnis itaque Creatura imperfecta. Resp. Deus solus perfectus est, infinitâ scilicet ac independenti perfectione, sed ideo non neganda est creaturis perfectio dependens & finita, utpote ipsis debita.
units.tr: 10. Objection 2. Only God is perfect; therefore every creature is imperfect. Answer: God alone is perfect, namely with infinite and independent perfection; but for that reason dependent and finite perfection must not be denied to creatures, since it is due to them.

units.la: 11. Objic. 3. Accidentia sunt Entia imperfecta, & propè non-entia. Resp. Habent tamen requisita sibi debita, licet respectu substantiarum imperfectiora judicari debeant, non enim hîc quæstio est de comparatâ, sed de absolutâ perfectione.
units.tr: 11. Objection 3. Accidents are imperfect beings, and almost non-beings. Answer: Nevertheless they have the requisites due to them, although they must be judged more imperfect with respect to substances; for the question here is not about comparative but about absolute perfection.

units.la: 12. Objic. 4. Sic nullæ forent privationes, & homo claudus æquè perfectus esset, ac sanus. Resp. Pervertitur iterum status quæstionis; nam comparatâ perfectione sanus perfectior est, non absolutâ, quâ tam claudus, quam sanus, omnia sui esse, claudi scilicet & sani, habet requisita. Idem responderi potest reliquis objectionibus, quæ ab infantibus, ovis, semine &c. desumuntur. Nam & illa in se perfecta sunt absoluta perfectione, licet respectu alterius imperfecta dici possint.
units.tr: 12. Objection 4. In that case there would be no privations, and a lame man would be just as perfect as a healthy one. Answer: The state of the question is again perverted; for in comparative perfection the healthy man is more perfect, but not in absolute perfection, in which the lame man, no less than the healthy, has all the requisites of his being, namely of being lame or of being healthy. The same answer can be given to the remaining objections, which are drawn from infants, eggs, seed, and so on. For these too are perfect in themselves with absolute perfection, although they may be called imperfect with respect to something else.

units.la: 13. Quæres 2. An soli Enti conveniat persectio? Resp. Sic sane, ob supra allatam rationem. Modis igitur, denominationibus externis, relationibus &c. nulla tribuenda est perfectio, licet analogicè ratione subiectorum, cum quo identificantur, aliquam ipsis tribui non absurdum videatur.
units.tr: 13. Question 2: Does perfection belong to Being alone? Answer: Certainly so, for the reason given above. Therefore no perfection is to be attributed to modes, external denominations, relations, and so on; although, by analogy, given the subjects with which they are identified, it does not seem absurd to attribute some perfection to them.

units.la: 14. III. Quoad habitudinem, quam habet perfectio ad Ens, 1. non est Entis synonymum, ut Burgersdicius exstimavit: Sed ejus affectio, realiter ab ipso non discrepans, sed tantum modo inadæquato considerandi & formaliter; quemadmodum de unitate & veritate supra dictum est. Non igitur perfectio entis est relatio, nec denominatio externa, nec modus externus & separabilis; neque tale quid Enti superaddit, cum de ipso dicitur.
units.tr: 14. III. As to the relation which perfection has to Being: 1. it is not a synonym of Being, as Burgersdijk thought. Rather it is an affection which does not really differ from Being itself, but is considered only by an inadequate mode and formally, as was said above concerning unity and truth. Perfection of Being is therefore not a relation, nor an external denomination, nor an external and separable mode, nor does it add anything of that kind to Being when it is predicated of it.

units.la: 15. Perfectioni opponitur imperfectio, quæ est modus non-entis, quo id nulla habet requisita; atque ita ipsi contradictoriè opponitur, nec alicui Enti convenire potest: sed quemadmodum perfectio est ipsum Ens, ita imperfectio est ipsum nihil. Sumitur tamen imperfectio aliquando respectivè, atque ita Enti tribui potest, non quatenus Ens est, sed quatenus aliquo requisito caret, quod ipsi secundum speci-cm, em, aut naturæ ordinem convenire poterat; Et sic privativè opponitur perfectioni, imò est ipsa privatio.
units.tr: 15. Imperfection is opposed to perfection; it is the mode of non-being by which a thing has none of the requisites. It is thus opposed to it contradictorily, and cannot belong to any Being. But just as perfection is Being itself, so imperfection is nothing itself. Imperfection is however sometimes taken relatively, and in that way can be attributed to a Being, not as far as it is a Being, but as far as it lacks some requisite which could belong to it according to the order of its species or nature; and in this sense it is opposed to perfection by privation, indeed it is privation itself.

units.la: 16. I. Perfectio variis modis dividitur; Et quidem 1. alia est essentialis, alia accidentalis. Prior est secundum quam Enti attributa suæ speciei essentialia conveniunt: Posterior verò quâ Ens debita habet accidentia, quæ duplex est extensiva & intensiva. Extensiva perfectio, aliter Partium dicitur, respicitque legitimum partium numerum: Intensiva aliter Graduum perfectio dicta, respicit legitimam qualitatum temperiem, aut sufficientem ad operationes debitas virtutem. Atque hæc quidem, si absolutæ sit perfectionis divisio, est totius in partes quasi integras: at si comparatæ dicatur, etiam specifica dici potest.
units.tr: 16. I. Perfection is divided in various ways. First, one kind is essential, another accidental. The former is that by which the essential attributes of its species belong to a Being; the latter is that by which a Being has the accidents due to it. The latter is twofold: extensive and intensive. Extensive perfection, otherwise called perfection of parts, regards the proper number of parts; intensive perfection, otherwise called perfection of degrees, regards the proper temperament of qualities, or the power sufficient for the due operations. If this is a division of perfection taken absolutely, it is the division of a whole into what are as it were integral parts; but if it is taken comparatively, it may also be called specific.

units.la: 17. II. Perfectio est vel Substantia vel accidentis, pro differentia scilicet essentiarum: item 3. dependens vel independens: Et 4. Ratione modi vel finita vel infinita. Quæ ultima novam Enti affectionem superaddit, quare de eâ mox latius dicendum.
units.tr: 17. II. Perfection is either substantial or accidental, according to the difference of essences; likewise, 3. dependent or independent; and 4. with respect to mode, either finite or infinite. This last adds a new affection to Being, and so it must be discussed more fully shortly.

units.la: 18. VI. Inter axiomata præcipua hæc sunt 1. Omne Ens perfectum est. Ratio suprà data. 2. Quod non est perfectum, non est Ens, perfectione scilicet sibi debitâ & absolutâ; utpote sine quâ essentiam non haberet. 3. Quò magis aliquid perfectum, eò magis est Ens: Quoniam plura ad suum esse requisita obtinet. Hac ratione substantiæ primæ magis dicuntur esse substantiæ, quam secundæ. 4. Perfecto nihil addi potest; videlicet quod ad illam perfectionem requiratur: Hinc illud, perfectum additum persecto, facit Ens per accidens. 5. A persecto nihil potest tolli, videlicet eorum, quæ ad tale esse requiruntur; Unde homo cœcus a quo ablata videndi potentia secunda, ulterius perfectus absolutè dici nequit, licet perfectus maneat, quoniam omnia cœci hominis habet requisita. 6. Perfectio infinita omni caret imperfectione, etiam relpectivâ. 7. Perfectio infinita omnem habet perfectionem; Unde verum illud, in Deo sunt omnium rerum perfectiones; idque eo pacto, quo infinitæ perfectioni non repugnant; Quare quædam formaliter, quædam eminenter, quædam virtualiter illi convenire dicuntur. 8. Finita perfectio aliquam habet respectu alterius imperfectionem; Quoniam omnis perfectionis capax non est; vel illa incapacitas pro imperfectione æstimanda. 9. Perfectio independens causa & mensura est omnis reliquæ. Atque hæc de Perfectione; sequitur
units.tr: 18. VI. Among the principal axioms are these: (1) Every Being is perfect. The reason was given above. (2) What is not perfect is not a Being, namely with the perfection due to it and absolute; for without it, it would not have an essence. (3) The more perfect a thing is, the more it is a Being, since it possesses more of the requisites for its existence. On this ground, first substances are said to be substances more than second substances are. (4) Nothing can be added to the perfect, namely of what is required for that perfection; hence a perfect thing added to a perfect thing makes a Being by accident. (5) Nothing can be taken away from the perfect, namely of those things which are required for such being; hence a blind man, from whom the second power of seeing has been removed, cannot be called absolutely more perfect, although he remains perfect, since he has all the requisites of a blind man. (6) Infinite perfection lacks all imperfection, even relative imperfection. (7) Infinite perfection has every perfection; hence the true saying that in God are the perfections of all things, and this in such a way as does not conflict with infinite perfection; wherefore some things are said to belong to him formally, some eminently, and some virtually. (8) Finite perfection has some imperfection with respect to another, since not every thing is capable of every perfection; or that incapacity must be reckoned as imperfection. (9) Independent perfection is the cause and measure of all the rest. So much concerning perfection; there follows

units.la: 19. Bonitas simpliciter dicta, in convenientiâ cum aliquo antecedente constituta: Illud autem antecedens regula aut mensura quædam esse debet, quâ perfectio illa interna æstimanda est; adeo ut propter illam convenientiam perfectionis cum regulâ, res dicatur bona: Unde talis bonitas est convenientia Entis cum voluntate divinâ.
units.tr: 19. Goodness taken simply is constituted in agreement with some antecedent. That antecedent must be a kind of rule or measure by which the internal perfection is judged, so that a thing is called good because its perfection agrees with the rule. Such goodness is therefore the agreement of a Being with the divine will.

units.la: 20. Subjectum sive terminus à quo hujus bonitatis est Ens: Hoc quippe affectiones habet, at quod habet affectiones, id convenientiam habet, & potest habere. Idem Scriptura, Genef. 1. verf. ult. ostendit, asserens omnia valdè bona fuisse, eô quod visioni, hoc est, voluntati divinæ, essent conformia.
units.tr: 20. The subject, or terminus from which, of this goodness is Being. For Being has affections, and whatever has affections has agreement and can have it. Scripture likewise shows this in Gen. 1, last verse, where it affirms that all things were very good because they were in conformity with the divine vision, that is, with the divine will.

units.la: 21. Quæres autem, An omne Ens hujus bonitatis sit particeps? Resp. Id quidem rationes dictæ evincunt. Objic. 1. Ante promulgationem istius approbationis, res non potuissent dici bonæ. Resp. 1. Imò potuissent, si non formaliter, quatenus illa forma erat offensa, saltem fundamentaliter, quoniam illud ipsum, ex quo approbatio desumenda esset, ipsis inerat. 2. Erant & antea res bonæ, ut potè ad Dei beneplacitum & voluntatem factæ. Objic. 2. Sic voluntas divina non posset dici bona, non enim ipsa sibi ipsi conformis dici posse videtur. Resp. 1. Non requiritur, ut voluntas Dei eo modo dicatur bona, quoreliqua; Est enim ipsa omnis reliquæ bonitatis mensura. 2. Etiam sibi ipsi mensura dici potest, non quidem positivè, acsi seipsam positivo actu mensuraret, sed negagativè, quoniam nihil aliud est, quo mensuretur.
units.tr: 21. Question: Does every Being partake of this goodness? Answer: The reasons given above indeed prove that it does. Objection 1. Before this approval was declared, things could not be called good. Answer 1. Indeed they could have been, if not formally, at least fundamentally, insofar as that form was offended, since that very thing from which the approval was to be derived was already in them. 2. Things were also good before, since they were made for God's good pleasure and will. Objection 2. In this way the divine will could not be called good, for it does not seem that it can be conformed to itself. Answer 1. It is not required that the divine will be called good in the same way as other things, for it is itself the measure of all other goodness. 2. It can also be called a measure of itself, not indeed positively, as if it measured itself by a positive act, but negatively, since there is nothing else by which it is measured.

units.la: 22. Objectum, sive terminus ad quem, hujus bonitatis est voluntas divina, ipsum esse rerum mensurans & approbans; idque probatur 1. Mensura bonitatis debet esse prima & maxima bonitas: Atqui talis est voluntas Dei. 2. Illa est mensura bonitatis, quæ tribuit Enti bonitatem, sive debitudinem omnium requisitorum, in quovis statu & conditione: Sed voluntas DivinaEnti mutabili tribuit bonitatem mutabilem, immutabili immutabilem, actuali actualem. 3. Per voluntatem divinam habent Entia quòd sint, & quòd hoc sint: At hoc est mensurare Entium bonitatem.
units.tr: 22. The object, or terminus to which, of this goodness is the divine will, which is the being of things measuring and approving them. This is proved as follows. 1. The measure of goodness must be the first and greatest goodness. But such is the will of God. 2. That is the measure of goodness which gives to a Being goodness, or the due possession of all that is required in any state and condition. But the divine will gives to a mutable Being mutable goodness, to an immutable Being immutable goodness, and to an actual Being actual goodness. 3. Beings have through the divine will both that they are and that they are what they are. But this is to measure the goodness of Beings.

units.la: 23. Objic. 1. Mensura & mensuratum debent esse ejusdem generis: sed alterius generis est voluntas Divina; non igitur potest illa mensurare bonitatem. Resp. Axioma valet de genere Mathematico, non de genere Physico, aut Metaphysico; At in eodem genere mensuræ voluntas Divina & bonitas sunt: utraque enim bonitas est, una mensurans, altera mensurata. Objic. 2. Mensura debet esse æqualis mensurato. Resp. Valet in mensurâ univocâ, non in proportionali: Quemadmodum & recta linea mensura curvæ est.
units.tr: 23. Objection 1. The measure and the thing measured must be of the same kind. But the divine will is of another kind. Therefore it cannot measure goodness. Answer. The axiom holds for the mathematical kind, not for the physical or metaphysical kind. But in the same kind of measure the divine will and goodness are found, for each is goodness: one measures, the other is measured. Objection 2. The measure must be equal to what is measured. Answer. This holds for a univocal measure, not for a proportional one, just as a straight line is also the measure of a curve.

units.la: 24. Hæc igitur bonitas talem habet ad Ens habitudinem, ut non sit affectio aut modus ei formaliter inhærens, sed tantum relatio & respectus, realis quidem, utpote ipsum esse rerum pro fundamento habens, & non nisi externè denominans.
units.tr: 24. This goodness therefore has such a relation to Being that it is not an affection or mode formally inhering in it, but only a relation and respect, real indeed, since it has for its foundation the very being of things, and it names the thing only externally.

units.la: 25. Dividi potest hæc bonitas, quod sit vel essentialis, vel Moralis. Verùm moralis hujus loci non est. Est quippe tantum convenientia actionis cum lege Dei, adeoque actiones ac vitam, non ipsum Ens, pro subjecto habet.
units.tr: 25. This goodness can be divided into essential and moral. But the moral kind does not belong to this place. It is merely the agreement of an action with the law of God, and so it has for its subject actions and life, not Being itself.

units.la: 26. Bonitati huic opponitur malitia; quæ diversis capitur modis. 1. Enim sumitur vel absolutè, vel relatè. Absolutè sumta malitia est differentitas cum voluntate divina, atque ita Bonitati contradictorie opponitur, estque ipsum non-ens: Quare talis malitia nulla dari potest. Sed Objic. Datur malitia naturalis, ut privationes, morbi &c. atque illa absolutè sumta esse videtur. Resp. Illa dicuntur mala 1. non absolutè, sed respectivè, quatenus respectivâ impersectionem involvunt, ad speciem vel partes, vel gradus relatam. 2. Non quod discrepent à voluntate Dei, sine quâ nihil est, eorum quæ sunt, sed respectu usus & utilitatis, quæ malitia bonitati consequenter sumtæ opponitur.
units.tr: 26. Opposed to this goodness is malice, which is understood in different ways. 1. It is taken either absolutely or relatively. Malice taken absolutely is discrepancy from the divine will, and so it is opposed to goodness contradictorily, and it is non-being itself. Hence no such malice can exist. Objection. There is natural malice, such as privations, diseases, and so on, and this seems to be taken absolutely. Answer. These are called evils 1. not absolutely, but relatively, insofar as they involve a relative imperfection, referred to a species, or to parts, or to degrees. 2. Not because they differ from the will of God, without which nothing of what exists is, but with respect to use and usefulness, which malice, taken consequentially, is opposed to goodness.

units.la: 26. Malitia respectivè sumta, vel positive capitur, vel privativè. Positiva malitia est perfectio rei alicujus, alteri noxam asse-
units.tr: 26. Malice taken relatively is understood either positively or privatively. Positive malice is the perfection of some thing which brings harm to another...

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: 2. Agendum vero primo de finitate, ut ex hac aliquatenus apprehendatur ratio infinitatis, ex se incomprehensibilis. Videndum ergo. 1. Quid sit finitas? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quaenam ejus axiomata?
units.tr: 2. We must treat first of finitude, so that from this some account of infinity, incomprehensible in itself, may be grasped. Let us therefore consider: 1. What finitude is? 2. What is its subject? 3. What are its axioms?

units.la: 3. I. Est autem finitas, modus perfectionis, quo Ens habet omnia sua attributa limitate. Non igitur finitas ab Ente aliquod debitorum attributorum, seu convenientium perfectionum aliquam auferet, sed eis limites tantum praescribit; Et quidem non huic aut illi saltem, sed omnibus plane, quae isti Enti conveniunt, ut latius inter Axiomata ostendetur.
units.tr: 3. I. Finitude is a mode of perfection by which a Being has all its attributes limited. Finitude therefore does not take away from a Being any of the attributes or perfections due to it, but only prescribes limits for them. And this applies not merely to this or that one, but plainly to all the attributes that belong to that Being, as will be shown more fully among the axioms.

units.la: 4. I I. Subjectum ipsius est Ens, utpote habens perfectionem, cujus finitas modus est. Non tamen omni Enti convenit finitas, sed solum illi, cujus esse limitatum ac positivo actu constitutum est; quale est omne dependens & creatum. Enti enim independenti, & negati e saltem constituto, nulla limitatio convenit, adeoque in ipso nihil finiti excogitari potest, prout in finito nihil infiniti.
units.tr: 4. II. The subject of finitude is Being, inasmuch as it has the perfection of which finitude is the mode. Finitude does not belong to every Being, but only to that one whose existence is limited and constituted in positive act, such as every dependent and created being. For to an independent Being, and one that is at least negatively constituted, no limitation belongs, and so nothing finite can be conceived in it, just as nothing infinite can be conceived in the finite.

units.la: 5. Istius vero Entis Creati finitas non est accidens essentiae superadditum, sive proprium sive commune, aut aliud aliquod ab ipsa essentia distinctum, sed ipsissima ejus essentia. Est quippe finitas ipsa perfectio finita, & perfectio ipsa essentia: Distinguitur tamen ab ipso formaliter & concep-tu inadæquato, quo Ens ut habens, persectio ut habita consideratur.
units.tr: 5. The finitude of this created Being is not an accident added to its essence, whether proper or common, or anything else distinct from the essence itself, but is its very essence. For finitude is itself finite perfection, and perfection is the essence itself. It is nevertheless distinguished from it formally and by an inadequate concept, by which Being is considered as having, and perfection as had.

units.la: 6. III. Axiomata sat copiosa, nec minus illustria, ex finitatis naturâ colliguntur; Quorum hæc non videntur negligenda.
units.tr: 6. III. Axioms, quite numerous and no less illustrious, are gathered from the nature of finitude, and the following are not to be neglected.

units.la: 1. In finito omnia sunt finita: Sive quod huic æquivalet, finitum non est capax infiniti. Certitudo hujus axiomatis perplurimis rationibus demonstrari potest; I. Metaphysicè: In finito omnia sunt limitata, ex definitione finitatis. II. Geometricè 1. Contentum infinitâ proportione non est majus continente. 2. Finito non nisi finita adduntur: At nullum finitum finitis adjectis recipit infinitum. III. Arithmeticè; Omnis numerus omnis numeri, minor majoris aut pars est aut partes, Eu-clid. 4. 7. Nullus igitur perfectionum numerus in finito dari potest, quin sit finiti numeri pars aut partes. At infinitum finiti majus minoris pars est nequit. IV. Logicè; omne receptum recipitur per modum recipientis; Quare si finitum recipiens, etiam tale debet esse receptum. Estque hoc axioma, quasi caput omnium reliquorum.
units.tr: 1. In the finite all things are finite; or, what amounts to the same thing, the finite is not capable of the infinite. The certainty of this axiom can be demonstrated by very many reasons. I. Metaphysically: In the finite all things are limited, from the definition of finitude. II. Geometrically: 1. What is contained by an infinite proportion is not greater than what contains it. 2. Only finite things are added to the finite. But no finite thing, when finite things are added to it, receives the infinite. III. Arithmetically: Every number is a part or parts of every greater number, Euclid 4, 7. No number of perfections, therefore, can exist in the finite without being a part or parts of a finite number. But the infinite cannot be a part of a finite that is less than it. IV. Logically: Whatever is received is received according to the mode of the recipient. Hence, if the recipient is finite, what is received must also be of that kind. And this axiom is, as it were, the head of all the others.

units.la: 7. 2. Finiti finita est constitutio & essentia. Ratio ex primo desumitur: & implicaret, finitum esse, & habere essentiam infinitam, quoniam talia consequentia debent esse, quale est antecedens: & tale semper est Ens, qualis ejus essentia. Habere autem finitam constitutionem dicitur, quod actu positivo ad suum esse opus habet.
units.tr: 7. 2. The constitution and essence of the finite are finite. The reason is drawn from the first axiom. It would be contradictory for what is finite to have an infinite essence, since consequences must be of the same kind as their antecedents, and every Being is such as its essence is. A thing is said to have a finite constitution when it needs a positive act for its being.

units.la: 8. 3. Omne finitum est dependens; Quia ejus constitutio finita est, & actu positivo perfecta; A quo actu necessario dependet finitum. Et ab opposito, si finitum esset independens, esset à nullo alio, adeoque summè perfectum, atque ita infinitum.
units.tr: 8. 3. Every finite thing is dependent. Because its constitution is finite and perfected by a positive act, the finite thing depends necessarily on that act. And conversely, if the finite were independent, it would depend on nothing else, and so would be supremely perfect, and thus infinite.

units.la: 9. 4. A finito nil nisi finitum; Nam quod à finito est, ab ipso dependet? At absurdum est dependens toto genere esse dignius suo independente. Et nihil potest esse in eo, quod est à finito, quod non ante sit in ipso finito: Atqui in finito omnia finita; Ergo & à finito omnia finita.
units.tr: 9. 4. Nothing comes from the finite except the finite. For whatever comes from the finite depends on it. But it is absurd for a dependent thing to be in every respect more worthy than its independent source. And nothing can be in what comes from the finite that was not previously in the finite itself. But in the finite all things are finite. Therefore all that comes from the finite is also finite.

units.la: 10. 5. Finiti finita est virtus. In finito enim omnia finita; Et frustra esset infinita virtus, à qua non nisi actio finita speranda. Hinc igitur nullius creaturæ virtus, se solâ sufficiens est, ut citra concursum Dei agere possit.
units.tr: 10. 5. The power of the finite is finite. For in the finite all things are finite, and it would be vain for there to be an infinite power from which only finite action could be expected. Hence no creature's power is by itself sufficient to act without the concurrence of God.

units.la: 11. 6. Finiti finitæ sunt operationes; Ratio ex quarto petatur: Omnes igitur Entis finiti ac creati operationes dependentes esse debent; Neque propterea supernaturales actiones & infinitæ ab ipso expectandæ.
units.tr: 11. 6. The operations of the finite are finite. The reason is to be taken from the fourth point: all operations of a finite and created being must therefore be dependent, and so supernatural and infinite actions are not to be expected from it.

units.la: 12.7. Finitifinita est præsentia: Nulla igitur Creatura ubique præsens fingi potest.
units.tr: 12.7. The presence of the finite is finite: therefore no creature can be imagined to be present everywhere.

units.la: 8. Finiti finita est duratio; Nulla igitur creatura æterna sse potest; Et quod esse suum continuet, non sibi ipsi, sed alteri debet. Sed de his duobus infra latius.
units.tr: 8. The duration of the finite is finite; therefore no creature can be eternal, and whatever continues its existence owes this not to itself but to another. But of these two more will be said at length below.

units.la: 13. 9. Finitum non necessariò est numero unum. Ratio est, quia finitum non habet omnes perfectiones actu vel potentiâ; Et quas habet, eas finitas habet: At tale ut ad ex stentiam, ita ad pluralitatem indifferens est.
units.tr: 13. 9. The finite is not necessarily one in number. The reason is that the finite does not have all perfections, either actually or potentially; and the perfections it does have, it has as finite. But such a thing is indifferent to plurality just as it is to existence.

units.la: 14. 10. Finito nunquam tot addi potest, ut fiat infinitum. Ratio est, quia ex finitis non fit infinitum: At quod finito additur est finitum; quare simul cum priori finito infinitum non constituit.
units.tr: 14. 10. No number of things can ever be added to the finite so that it becomes infinite. The reason is that from finites no infinite is made. What is added to a finite is finite; therefore, together with the former finite, it does not constitute an infinite.

units.la: 15. 11. Finitum infinito infinities minus est; Adeoque nulla inter finitum & infinitum est proportio. Ratio ex decimo patet. Et quod finito numero finito tantum majus est, id est finitum. &c.
units.tr: 15. 11. The finite is infinitely less than the infinite; and so there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. The reason is clear from the tenth point. And what exceeds a finite by a finite amount is itself finite, etc.

units.la: 16. Sequitur Infinitas, ante cujus explicationem nota, duplex vulgò dici, actu videlicet & potentiâ. Illud dicitur, quod habet partes æquales uni certæ, quarum si una post aliam sumatur, eademque non repetatur, nunquam tot sumi possunt, quin adhuc plures sumendæ restent. Hoc verò, quod habet aut partes inæquales, ad quarum extimam difficulter cogitatio nostra pervenit; aut quod habet illas sibi invicem succedentes, ad quarum extimam cogitatio non pervenit: Prior hæc descriptio corporis ac materiæ partibus, posteriòr numero convenit; Sed utraque hæc potius indefinitæ quam infinitas appellenda esset; utpote non absolutè sine terminis constituta, sed saltem sine talibus, ad quos finitus intellectus aut non, aut difficulter eos assignando pervenit.
units.tr: 16. Next comes Infinity. Before explaining it, note that it is commonly said to be of two kinds, namely actual and potential. The first is that which has parts equal to some one certain part, and if these are taken one after another, with no repetition, they can never be taken so many times that more do not still remain to be taken. The second is that which has either unequal parts, whose outermost our thought reaches only with difficulty, or parts succeeding one another, whose outermost thought does not reach. The former description fits the parts of a body or of matter, the latter fits number. But both of these would more properly be called indefinite than infinite, since they are not constituted absolutely without limits, but only without such limits as the finite intellect either cannot reach, or reaches only with difficulty in assigning them.

units.la: 17. Actualis Infiniti descriptio, licet Mathematica sit, non obscurè tamen infiniti Metaphysici rationem indigitat, si loco partium perfectiones substituantur; Quare illam ita reformo & illustro: Infinitum est, quod habet perfectiones (modo nostro considerandi abipso distinctas) æquales uni certæ (infinitæ; quare & omnes infinitæ) quarum (perfectionum infinitarum) si una) inadæquato quodam conceptûs modo) post aliam (à priori consimiliter distinctam) sumatur (& summo conatu cogitandi retineatur) nunquam tot (certo, etiam maximo quovis excogitabili numero) sumi (excogitari & enumerari (possunt; quin adhuc plures (æquè ac priores infinitæ, adeoque nullo numero comprehensibiles) restent, & in singulis perfectionibus nunc acceptis, & denuò accipiendis totidem, id est infinitæ.
units.tr: 17. The description of actual infinity, although it is mathematical, nonetheless points clearly enough to the nature of metaphysical infinity if perfections are substituted for parts. I therefore reform and illustrate it thus: The infinite is that which has perfections (distinct from it in our mode of considering) equal to some one certain (infinite, so all are infinite) of which (infinite perfections) if one (by a certain inadequate mode of conceiving) is taken after another (similarly distinct from the first) and is held by the utmost effort of thinking, can never be taken so many (by any certain number, even the greatest that can be thought) times (conceived and counted) that more (just as many as the former, infinite, and so comprehensible by no number) do not remain, and in each of the perfections now received, and to be received again, as many, that is, infinite.

units.la: 18. Brevius tamen describitur Infinitas, quod sit, modus perfectionis, quo Ens habet omnes perfectiones, omnimodò perfectas; Elt igitur quasi perfectionum omnium universitas; Ejus quippe ratio est, 1. habere omnes perfectiones, id est omnia attributa positiva vel cogitabilia, perfectionem involventia. 2. Habere illas persectiones omni prorsus modo perfectas, & in nullo defectuosas, hoc est infinitas.
units.tr: 18. More briefly, however, Infinity is described as the mode of perfection by which a Being has all perfections, perfect in every mode. It is therefore, as it were, the totality of all perfections. Its reason is: 1. to have all perfections, that is, all positive attributes or conceivable ones, involving perfection; 2. to have those perfections perfect in every way and defective in nothing, that is, to be infinite.

units.la: 19. Subjectum infinitatis Deus Opt. max. est, qui solus absolutè independens, adeoque infinitæ perfectionis capax est; Estque adeo infinitas ipsissima Dei infinita essentia. Quoniam verò infinitatis est, habere omnes perfectiones; non immeritò hic quaeritur, an & quomodo in Deo sint omnium rerum perfectiones? Et esse quidem in Deo omnium rerum perfectiones, ex ratione infinitatis, patet, quæ omnes vel cogitabiles absolutè præsupponit. Et quia infinitum illimitatas ac independentes habet perfectiones, ideò & necessariò omnes habebit; Quia nihil dici aut fingi potest, quod ipsum ad aliquas saltem limitet. Imò si quæ perfectio esset in finito, & non in infinito, statim aliquâ perfectione destitueretur infinitum, adeoque nec infinitum maneret. Ac denique perfectio omnimoda, nullo pacto aliquo destituta esse potest. At infiniti perfectio est omnimoda. Omnes igitur perfectiones in Deo sunt.
units.tr: 19. The subject of infinity is God, the best and greatest, who alone is absolutely independent and therefore capable of infinite perfection. Infinity is thus the very infinite essence of God. Since it belongs to infinity to have all perfections, it is not unreasonable to ask here: whether and how the perfections of all things are in God? That the perfections of all things are in God follows from the nature of infinity, which absolutely presupposes all perfections that can be conceived. And since the infinite has unlimited and independent perfections, it will necessarily have all of them, because nothing can be said or imagined that would limit it, even in some respect. Indeed, if some perfection were in the finite and not in the infinite, the infinite would at once lack some perfection and so would not remain infinite. Finally, a perfection that is wholly complete can in no way be lacking anything. But the perfection of the infinite is wholly complete. Therefore all perfections are in God.

units.la: 20. Modus autem ille, quo omnes perfectiones Deo inesse dicuntur, non est unicus, sed pro diversâ naturâ perfectionum diversus. Cum enim in infinito nil nisi infinitum esse possit; illæ autem perfectiones Entium finitorum sint finitæ, non poterunt præcisè secundum eamdem rationem ac modum Deo convenire ac reliquis Entibus. Quæ verò infinitæ sunt perfectiones, ex Deo citrà ullam exceptionem formaliter, hoc est, & secundùm nomen & secundum definitionem conveniunt; idque etiam aliquâtenus eminenter, id est perfectissimo ac summo gradu. Atque hæ neutiquam virtualiter ipsi insunt, quò posset eas creaturis communicare. Tales sunt æternitas, omnipotentia, ubiquitas.
units.tr: 20. The mode in which all perfections are said to be in God, however, is not single, but diverse according to the diverse nature of the perfections. For since in the infinite nothing can be except the infinite, while the perfections of finite beings are finite, they cannot belong to God in exactly the same way and mode as they belong to other beings. Those perfections which are infinite belong to God formally, without any exception, that is, both in name and in definition; and also to some extent eminently, that is, in the most perfect and highest degree. But these are by no means virtually in him, so that he could communicate them to creatures. Such are eternity, omnipotence, and ubiquity.

units.la: 21. Earum verò, quæ in Creaturis finitæ sunt, alia ex se & in proprio actu consideratæ, ad illam finitatem & participatam ac dependentem rationem, indifferentes sunt, adeoque etiam sine illâ potentialitate ac dependentiâ considerari possunt, ut essentia, potentia, intellectus, voluntas. Alia verò in actu proprio & formali etiam imperfectionem involvunt, quales sunt, sensus, nutritio, motus localis, affectus. Priores etiam formaliter Deo insunt, secundum nomen & definitionem forormalem, licet non secundum illam dependentem rationem, quâ in creaturis reperiantur. Quare & illæ ipsi proprie eminenter, hoc est summo gradu perfectionis, eo quo in creaturis sunt, infinities superiori, conveniunt. Quæ & ideo quod Creaturis suo modo communicabiles sint, etiam in Deo sunt virtualiter, quatenus virtute suâ Deus illas Creaturis tribuit. At posteriores in Deo formaliter dari nequeunt, ob imperfectionem & dependentiam, quam involvunt; Quemadmodum nec hæ eminenter Deo inesse possunt; Quod enim in conceptu formali omnimodam dependentiam ac limitationem involvit, id nullo, vel eminentissimo gradu, ab illa liberari potest. Sunt tamen in Deo virtualiter, quoniam illas Deus in rebus creatis efficit. Confer Clariss. Voët, Theol. Nat. reform. cap. 4. §. 2.
units.tr: 21. Of those perfections which are finite in creatures, some, considered in themselves and in their proper act, are indifferent to that finiteness and to the participated and dependent character, and so can be considered even without that potentiality and dependence: such are essence, power, intellect, and will. Others, however, in their proper and formal act also involve imperfection: such are sense, nutrition, local motion, and emotion. The former are also formally in God, in name and in formal definition, though not according to that dependent character by which they are found in creatures. Hence they belong to God properly and eminently, that is, in the highest degree of perfection, infinitely above that in which they are in creatures. And because they can be communicated to creatures in their own way, they are also in God virtually, insofar as God by his power bestows them on creatures. The latter, however, cannot be in God formally, on account of the imperfection and dependence they involve; nor can these be in God eminently. For what in its formal concept involves complete dependence and limitation cannot be freed from it, at any degree, however eminent. Nevertheless they are in God virtually, since God produces them in created things. Compare the most distinguished Voët, Theol. Nat. reform. chap. 4, §2.

units.la: Axiomata sive documenta varia, nec minus utilia, ex hac infinitatis doctrinâ desumi possunt, qualia inter alia sunt, sequentia: 1. In infinito omnia sunt infinita: Quia omnia illimitata sunt, & omnimodè perfecta. Et si in infinito esset aliquod finitum, ejus ratione ad extremum & ultimum alicujus perfectionis liceret pervenire; atque adeo infinitum foret finitum. Imò finitum illud aut toti inesset infinito, aut ejus certæ ac limitatæ parti: prius si dicas, finitum infinito æquaretur, adeoque aut finitum foret infinitum, aut infinitum finitum, quod utrumque est impossibile, & contra hypothesin. Posterius si velis, in infinito erunt partes limitatæ, ac ideo finitæ, & sic foret iterum finitum. Cujus enim partes, saltem quædam, finitæ sunt, id totum finitum est. De hoc si dubites, en demonstrationem. Cujus quædam partes finitæ sunt, illius hæ incipiunt, ubi reliquæ desinunt, aut desinunt, ubi reliquæ incipiunt: Ideo quippe finitæ dicuntur, quia ultra fines ac terminos suos se non extendunt, adeoque aliarum limites non ingrediantur: At si reliquæ incipiant ac desinant, etiam finitæ erunt. Hoc axioma, ut omnium reliquorum fermè caput est, ita præclaram habet utilitatem: Hinc quippe à Deo removenda Accidentia, Materia, & quæcunque finitatem involvunt.
units.tr: Axioms, or various teachings no less useful, can be drawn from this doctrine of infinity, among which are the following: 1. In the infinite all things are infinite: because all things are unlimited and perfect in every mode. And if there were some finite thing in the infinite, one could by its measure reach the extreme and ultimate limit of some perfection, and so the infinite would be finite. Indeed, that finite thing would either be in the whole infinite, or in some certain limited part of it. If you say the first, the finite would be equal to the infinite, and so either the finite would be infinite or the infinite finite, both of which are impossible and contrary to the hypothesis. If you prefer the second, there would be limited parts in the infinite, and so finite ones, and again it would be finite. For whatever has finite parts, at least some of them, is itself finite. If you doubt this, here is a demonstration. Of whatever has some finite parts, these begin where the others end, or end where the others begin; for they are called finite precisely because they do not extend beyond their own ends and boundaries, and so do not enter the limits of the others. But if the others begin and end, these too will be finite. This axiom, as it is almost the head of all the rest, has this excellent use: hence accidents, matter, and whatever involves finitude are to be removed from God.

units.la: 23. 2. Infiniti infinita est constitutio ac essentia.
units.tr: 23. 2. The essence and constitution of the infinite is infinite.

units.la: Omnia quippe in ipso infinita: Etquia infinitas infiniti, est ipsius essentia infinita, & hæc ejusdem constitutio, non poterit quoque ipsi infinitas tribui, nisi essentia & constitutio infinitæ dicantur. Quare infinitum nullo actu positivo ad constitutionem suam opus habet, sed à seipso tantum negativè constituitur.
units.tr: For since everything in it is infinite, and since the infinity of the infinite is its own essence, and this is its constitution, infinity cannot be attributed to it unless its essence and constitution are also called infinite. Hence the infinite needs no positive act to constitute it, but is constituted solely negatively, by itself.

units.la: 24. 3. Infinitum necessariò est independens deus; Nihil enim ipsum constituit, adeoque nec limitat: Et si dependens foret infinitum, ab alio infinito penderet: At plura dari infinita repugnat. Prout & dependens omne limitatum & posterius est independente suo; Quare illud infinitum dependens foret finitum, quia limitatum, & non æquè perfectum, quia posterius, adeoque nec sic infinitum. Quoniam igitur æternum proprie est infinitum, absurda est ejus distributio in æternum per se & per participationem.
units.tr: 24. 3. God, the infinite, is necessarily independent. For nothing constitutes him, and so nothing limits him. And if the infinite were dependent, it would depend on another infinite; but for several infinites to exist is contradictory. Moreover, whatever is dependent is limited and posterior to its independent source. Therefore a dependent infinite would be finite, because limited, and not equally perfect, because posterior, and so it would not be infinite in that way either. Since therefore the eternal is properly the infinite, the distinction of the eternal into what is eternal through itself and what is eternal through participation is absurd.

units.la: 25. 4. Ab infinito nil nisi infinitum: intellige 1 quod ex naturæ necessitate, & non ab ipsissimâ libertate ejus prodit. 2. Secundum modum ac virtutem producendi, & non secundum opus ipsum, in iis quæ liberè prodeunt. Priori modo filius æternus necessario & ab æterno à Patre genitus, etiam necessariò infinitus est: Posteriori, omnia quidem opera ad extra producta finita sunt, modo tamen ac virtute ad suam productionem, conservationem ac operationem infinitâ indigent.
units.tr: 25. 4. Nothing but the infinite comes from the infinite. Understand this in two ways: 1. that which proceeds from the necessity of nature, and not from his most free will; 2. according to the mode and power of producing, and not according to the work itself, in those things that proceed freely. In the former way the eternal Son, begotten by the Father from eternity by necessity, is also necessarily infinite. In the latter way, all works produced outside God are indeed finite, yet in their mode and power they need an infinite power for their production, conservation and operation.

units.la: 26. 5. Infiniti infinita est virtus? Quia nihil inest ipsi, quin sit infinitum; & virtus rei, maxima ejus perfectio est: Quare si perfectio infiniti sit infinita, etiam quam maximè ejus virtus talis esse debet. Hinc itaque Deus seipso est agens, seque in agendo continuare potest; nec minus omnium finitorum virtutes activas reddere, & ad agendum determinare ac applicare.
units.tr: 26. 5. The virtue of the infinite is infinite? Because nothing in it is not infinite; and the virtue of a thing is its greatest perfection. Therefore, if the perfection of the infinite is infinite, its virtue too must be most of all such. Hence God is himself the agent, and can continue himself in acting; and equally he can render the active powers of all finite things, and determine and apply them to act.

units.la: 27. 6. Infiniti infinita sunt operationes. Modus enim operandi, sequitur modum essendi; & infinita virtus non nisi infinitas edit operationes. Quare Deus à nullo alio ad agendum determinari aut limitari potest, aut vult; Corruit itaque distinctio voluntatis ipsius, in antecedentem & consequentem.
units.tr: 27. 6. The operations of the infinite are infinite. For the mode of operating follows the mode of being, and an infinite virtue produces only infinite operations. Hence God cannot be determined or limited to act by anything else, nor does he wish to be; thus the distinction of his will into antecedent and consequent falls away.

units.la: 28. 7. Infiniti infinita est praesentia, quâ totum hic, totum extra, & totum in quocunque assignabili, hoc est ubique, est. Tales quippe debet esse essendi modus, quale est ipsum esse. 8. Infiniti infinita, id est, æterna est duratio, Cujus enim esse est independens & illimitatum, id ipsum in continuatione sui esse determinari nequit, aut eam alicui alteri debet. Ac denique infinitè perfecti perfectiones sunt perfectissimæ absolutæ: at æterna duratio omnium perfectissima est.
units.tr: 28. 7. The presence of the infinite is infinite, by which it is wholly here, wholly outside, and wholly in whatever can be assigned, that is, it is everywhere. For the mode of being must be such as is being itself. 8. The duration of the infinite, that is, is eternal. For that whose being is independent and unlimited cannot be determined in the continuation of its being, nor owe it to anything else. And finally, the perfections of the infinitely perfect are absolutely most perfect; but eternal duration is the most perfect of all.

units.la: 29. 9. Infinitum necessario est unicum; Perfectiones enim perfectissimas omnes possidere ad unum saltem pertinet; Si enim in pluribus essent non essent perfectissimæ; Quemadmodum in polycratia in singulis imperfectum est imperium. Et omnino imperfectionis est habere eas perfectiones, quas etiam alterum aliquod habet: Prout perfectius est, solum in illo genere antecellere, quam plura æquè excellentia admittere. Quare necessariò unicus est Deus, qui nequidem plures constituere potest.
units.tr: 29. 9. The infinite is necessarily one. For to possess all the most perfect perfections belongs at least to one being; for if they were in several, they would not be most perfect, just as in a polyarchy dominion is imperfect in each part. And it is altogether a mark of imperfection to have those perfections which another also has; whereas it is more perfect to excel alone in that kind than to admit several equally excellent beings. Therefore God is necessarily unique, who cannot even be made several.

units.la: 30. 10. Infinitum necessariò datur. Illi enim omnes perfectiones conveniunt. At huic ad minimum existentia, quæ & persectio & radix præsentiæ reliquarum omnium est, convenire debet. Et si finitum & limitatum aliquod dari concedas: Etiam infinitum & limitans negare nequis.
units.tr: 30. 10. The infinite necessarily exists. For all perfections belong to it. But to this one, at the least, existence must belong, which is both a perfection and the root of the presence of all the rest. And if you grant that some finite and limited thing exists, you cannot deny that an infinite and limiting being exists too.

units.la: 31. 11. Ab infinito nunquam tot auferri potest, ut fiat finitum. Ratio ex definitione infiniti patet. Imò 12. Ab infinito nihil prorsus adhuc tolli potest: Si enim à persecto ut sic nihil demi possit, multo minus hoc fiet ab infinito infinitè perfecto. Quare 13. Infinitum immutabile est. Mutatur quippe id, cui aliquid ante præsentium negatur.
units.tr: 31. 11. From the infinite nothing can ever be taken away so that it becomes finite. The reason is plain from the definition of the infinite. Indeed, 12. nothing at all can yet be removed from the infinite: for if nothing could be taken from the perfect as such, much less can this be done to the infinitely perfect infinite. Therefore 13. the infinite is immutable. For that is changed to which something previously present is denied.

units.la: 32. 14. Infinitum finito infinities majus est; Finito quippe tantum superaddi nequit, ut 1. ipsum fiat æquale infinito; ut 2. ad infinitum acquirat proportionem: Atqui inter quæ nulla proportio, inter illa infinita distantia. Et si infinitum finito numero perfectionum majus esset finito, esset 1. finitum in infinito. 2. ipsum infinitum finitum, utpote finito numero constans. Mitto plura brevitatis ergo adducere; Quoniam quibus bene hæc pensitans, non difficulter ea eruit. Et hæc de Infinitate & finitate.
units.tr: 32. 14. The infinite is infinitely greater than the finite. For nothing can be added to the finite so that 1. it becomes equal to the infinite, or so that 2. it acquires an infinite proportion to it; but between things with no proportion there is an infinite distance. And if the infinite were greater than the finite by a finite number of perfections, then 1. the finite would be contained in the infinite, and 2. the infinite itself would be finite, since it would consist of a finite number. I pass over further arguments for the sake of brevity, since whoever weighs these well will not find it hard to draw them out. And so much on infinity and finitude.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: DE Absoluto & Comparato.
units.tr: On the Absolute and the Comparative.

units.la: 1. PErfectio ad mensuram suam applicata, atque ex eâ æstimata, invenitur vel rei in se convenire, vel in ordine ad aliud: Priori modo perfectio absoluta dicitur, posteriori comparata: ac exinde Ens absolutum & comparatum appellatur. Qui termini, ut multiplicem usum habent, hic explicandi videntur.
units.tr: 1. Perfection, when applied to its measure and judged by it, is found either to belong to a thing in itself or in relation to something else. In the first way it is called absolute perfection, in the second comparative, and accordingly a being is called absolute or comparative. Since these terms have many uses, they seem to need explanation here.

units.la: 2. Dicitur autem absolutum, quòd ab alio solutum ac liberum sit: Quia verò multis modis unum ab altero liberum dicitur, fieri non potuit, quin variis quoque modis absolutum caperetur. Primo igitur absolutum dicitur, quod ex inchoato nunc consummatum est; atque ita idem est quod perfectum, vi participii sumtum. Secundò, absolutum dicitur, quod liberum est a conditione aliquâ, quo pacto necessitas absoluta opponitur conditionatæ, & decreta Dei absoluta dicuntur. Tertiò, absolutum opponitur respectivo, quomodo accidentia vel absoluta vel respectiva dicuntur. Quartò opponitur comparato: atque ita absolutum est, quod ex se rei convenit, citra comparationem cum alio, ut doctum esse absoluté homini docto convenit, at doctiorem, vel doctissimum per comparationem ad alios. Tres ultimæ significationes aliquam convenientiam inter se habere, adeoque & huc aliquâtenus quadrare videntur: quare de singulis ordine pauca.
units.tr: 2. Now it is called absolute because it is loosed from another, that is, free. Since being free from another is said in many ways, it could not but be that the absolute is also taken in various ways. First, then, that is called absolute which, having been begun, is now completed; in this sense it is the same as perfect, taken as a participle. Second, that is called absolute which is free from some condition; in this way absolute necessity is opposed to conditional necessity, and the decrees of God are called absolute. Third, the absolute is opposed to the relative, as accidents are called either absolute or relative. Fourth, it is opposed to the comparative: thus the absolute is what belongs to a thing of itself, without comparison with another. Thus being learned belongs absolutely to a learned man, but being more learned or most learned belongs to him by comparison with others. The last three meanings seem to have some affinity with one another and so to fit this topic to some extent; therefore I shall take each of them briefly, in order.

units.la: 3. I. Absolutum, prout conditionato opponitur, est liberum à conditione. Estque vel à conditione interna, vel ab externâ. Prius est, quod non opus habet distinctis quibusdam ad suum esse requisitis: Quemadmodum Deus absolutus est, ab omni compositione distinctorum, spiritus absoluti à materiâ & formâ. Posterius est, quod solutum est ab externis ad suum esse requisitis. Estque hoc admodum diversum pro varietate externorum istorum; Quædam tamen species exemplorum gratiâ adducendæ.
units.tr: 3. I. Absolute, as opposed to the conditional, is free from condition. It is free either from an internal condition or from an external one. The former is what has no need of certain distinct things for its being: just as God is absolute, free from all composition of distinct parts, and a spirit is absolute, free from matter and form. The latter is what is loosed from external requisites for its being. This is very various according to the variety of these external things; yet some kinds may be brought forward as examples.

units.la: 4. Est itaque 1. absolutum à conditione externâ antecedente, sive illa sit causa, sive nudum antecedens: Utroque modo Deus absolutus: Priori vero nulla creatura; nec posteriori si voluntas & decretū Dei ipsius antecedens dicatur. Antecedens autem illud vel tantum naturâ prius, vel duratione vel ordine. Naturâ tantum, ut subjectum ratione accidentium absolutum dicitur: Duratione, ut at aurora ratione diei: Ordine, ut primus ratione secundi, &c.
units.tr: 4. Thus, first, a thing is absolute with respect to an external antecedent condition, whether that is a cause or a mere antecedent. In both ways God is absolute; in the first way no creature is, and in the second none is either, if the will and decree of God itself is called antecedent. That antecedent may be prior either merely in nature, or in duration, or in order. In nature only, as a subject is called absolute with respect to its accidents; in duration, as dawn is with respect to day; in order, as the first is with respect to the second, and so on.

units.la: 5. 2. Est absolutum à conditione consequente, sive fuerit effectus, ut homo in se absolutus est ab agendo; sive objectum, ut bruta absoluta sunt à lege Dei hominibus lata; sive adjunctum, ut Dominus à servo, coelebs ab uxore, &c.
units.tr: 5. 2. Something is absolute with respect to a consequent condition, whether that condition is an effect, as man is absolute in himself with respect to acting; or an object, as beasts are free from the law of God given to men; or an adjunct, as a lord is free from a servant, a bachelor from a wife, and so on.

units.la: 6. 3. Absolutum est à conditione connexa, si illa abesse possit; ut hodiernus dies absolutus est à pluviis in se, licet jam pluat; ita & homo absolutus à poenâ, à culpâ, à contractu, dicitur &c.
units.tr: 6. 3. Something is absolute with respect to a connected condition if that condition can be absent. Thus today is absolute in itself with respect to rain, although it may already be raining; so too a man is said to be absolute from punishment, from guilt, from a contract, and so on.

units.la: 7. Conditionatum, huic absoluto oppositum, est quod conditionem suæ præsentiæ habet; sive illa sit interna, sive externa; & hæc vel antecedens, vel consequens, vel connexa, vel & alia aliqua, in absoluti consideratione non enumerata.
units.tr: 7. The conditional, opposed to this absolute, is that which has the condition of its presence, whether that condition is internal or external. External conditions are either antecedent, consequent or connected, or some other kind not listed in the consideration of the absolute.

units.la: 8. II. Absolutum respectivo oppositum, est aliquid habens perfectionem in se alteri alicui non debitam. Atque hoc triplex dicitur esse, 1. Ratione causæ sive interna sive externa; Quomodo quod nullam suæ perfectionis causam agnoscit, absolutum dicitur; atque ita ratione omnium causarum Deus, ratione internarum Nôss absoluti dicuntur. 2. Ratione subjecti, quomodo per se subsistere est absolutum esse à subjecto, ac omnibus substantiis convenit. 3. Ratione termini, quo pacto quantitas & qualitas absoluta accidentia dicuntur, licet non tantum causam, sed & subjectum præsupponant. Tertiæ huic speciei de commodiori appellatione si prospiciatur, illam distinctionem omnino retinendam existimo. Licet commodius ex opposito respectu sive relatione ejus diversitas desumi possit; ut absolutum sit vel à respectu primo, vel ab orto; Et illud vel ab interno, vel ab externo; atque ita deinceps, prout suprà de relatione dictum est.
units.tr: 8. II. The absolute, opposed to the respective, is something having in itself a perfection not owed to some other thing. This is said to be threefold. (1) By reason of cause, whether internal or external: thus what acknowledges no cause of its perfection is called absolute. So God is absolute with respect to all causes, and the notions are called absolute with respect to internal causes. (2) By reason of subject: to subsist through itself is to be absolute, being free from a subject, and this belongs to all substances. (3) By reason of term*: so quantity and quality are called absolute accidents, although they presuppose not only a cause but also a subject. If one looks for a more convenient name for this third kind, I think this distinction should be retained entirely; though its diversity could more conveniently be drawn from the opposite respect or relation, so that the absolute is either from a first respect or from one derived, and that either from an internal or from an external thing; and so on, as was said above about relation.

units.la: 9. Unum tamen monendum videtur, videlicet quædam suâ naturâ aliquem respectum includere, qualia sunt omnia dependentia à causa sive à subjecto; quorum oppositum in se necessariò absolutum esse debet, quoniam in ipsâ consideratione istis respectivis prius est, eisque & quòd sint, & quòd cum tali respectu sint, tribuit. Ita creatura omnis, utpote dependens, in suâ naturâ respectum includit, ejusque oppositum, Creator, in se absolutum quid esse debet. Atque hinc patet veritas distinctionis Scholasticæ, quâ dividitur respectus in respectum in & respectum ad. Quod enim in ipso esse respectivum aliquâtenus est, dicitur habere respectum in se. At illud, quod respicit, dicitur habere respectum ad, quoniam hoc in suâ naturâ absolutum est.
units.tr: 9. One thing, however, seems worth warning: some things by their nature include some respect, such as all dependents on a cause or on a subject. Their opposite must necessarily be absolute in itself, since in the very consideration it is prior to these respective things, and grants to them both that they are and that they are with such a respect. Thus every creature, as dependent, includes a respect in its nature, and its opposite, the Creator, must be something absolute in itself. From this appears the truth of the Scholastic distinction by which respect is divided into respect in and respect to. For what is somehow relative in itself is said to have respect in itself; but that which regards something is said to have respect to, since this is absolute in its nature.

units.la: Unde pari ratione, quoniam omnis respectus, utpote absoluto posterior, aliquam imperfectionem involvit, id intelligi debere, de respectu, quem res in se, non de illo, quem ad aliud tantum habet, concludendum videtur. Quare Deus, licet respiciat creaturas, ut Creator, nulla ideo imperfectio tribuenda, sed potius perfectio; quoniam per illum respectum, illas ut à se dependentes respicit.
units.tr: Hence, by the same reasoning, since every respect, as posterior to the absolute, involves some imperfection, it seems to be concluded that this must be understood of the respect which a thing has in itself, not of that which it has only to another. Therefore God, although he regards creatures as Creator, is not on that account to be ascribed any imperfection, but rather perfection, since by that respect he regards them as dependent on himself.

units.la: 11. Respectivum, huic absoluto quod opponitur, quoniam idem est, quod relativum, ex iis, quae de relatione dicta sunt, cognosci potest.
units.tr: 11. The respective, which is opposed to this absolute, is the same as the relative, and can be known from what has been said about relation.

units.la: 12. III. Sequitur absolutum, comparato oppositum; quod nihil aliud est, quam ipsum Ens, quatenus habet attributa & perfectiones suas simpliciter, prout ipsi sunt debitae; adeoque modum perfectionis, si non ipsam Enti addit; omnique Enti, prout & perfecto, convenit. Nihil enim potest habere esse, nisi ad minimum in ipso tantum sit absoluti, quantum ad illud esse, ejusque perfectionem requiritur.
units.tr: 12. III. There follows the absolute, opposed to the comparative. This is nothing other than Being itself, insofar as it has its attributes and perfections simply, as they are due to it; and so it adds, if not the perfection itself to being, at least the mode of perfection, and it belongs to every being, as also to a perfect one. For nothing can have being unless there is in it at least as much of the absolute as that being and its perfection require.

units.la: 13. Comparatum igitur est Ens, quatenus certo gradu perfectiones suas, altero plus minusve obtinet. Gradus ille vel in ascendendo, vel in descendendo ponitur, & utrobique vel positivus, vel comparativus, vel superlativus est.
