units.tr: 13. The comparative, then, is a being insofar as it possesses its perfections at a certain degree, more or less than another. This degree is placed either in ascending or in descending, and in either case it is positive, comparative, or superlative.

units.la: 14. Gradus in ascendendo positivus est, quo Enti tribuitur nudè ac praecise perfectio, in ordine ad perfectiora & perfectissiVeritatis, Perfectionis, ac reliquarum exinde ortarum affectionum. Et haec de Absoluto ac Comparato; adeoque omnibus, ex sola essentia & constitutione ortis affectionibus.
units.tr: 14. The positive degree in ascending is that by which perfection is ascribed to a being simply and precisely, without reference to more perfect or most perfect things, of truth, of perfection, and of the other affections arising from these. This is what is said about the absolute and the comparative, and so about all the affections arising from essence and constitution alone.

units.la: CAP. XII. D E Distinctione & Existentia.
units.tr: CAP. XII. Of Distinction and Existence.

units.la: 1. SEquitur secundum Entis Principium, ejusque affectiones, quae mediante eo enti conveniunt, videlicet Distinctio, quae 1. sumitur pro modo quodam Entis, quo hoc esse suum sibi proprium habet, quomodo hic consideranda est. 2. Pro diversitate Entis ab alio, quomodo relatio est, ac in sequentibus tractanda, cap. 32.
units.tr: 1. There follows the principle of Being and its affections, which belong to a being through it, namely Distinction. This is taken (1) for a certain mode of Being, by which this thing has its own being peculiar to itself, and in this sense it is to be considered here; (2) for the diversity of one Being from another, as relation is, and it is to be treated in what follows, chapter 32.

units.la: 3. Pro prædicatione partium omnium de toto, sive divisione actu institutâ: Quo- modo ad Logicam spectat.
units.tr: 3. For the predication of all the parts of a whole, or division actually carried out, which belongs to Logic.

units.la: 2. Quoad rem videndum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quam habitudinem ad subjectum habeat? 4. Quomodo se habeat ad constitionem? 5. Quænam axiomata ex eâ educi possint?
units.tr: 2. As to the thing itself, we must examine: (1) What it is? (2) What is its subject? (3) What relation to the subject it has? (4) How it stands with respect to the constitution? (5) What axioms can be drawn from it?

units.la: 3 I. Distinctio est modus Entis, quo id habet esse suum sibi proprium; hoc est, sibi soli conveniens: alioqui formæ quodammodo responder. jus esse alteri communicari nequeunt. 3. Quorum esse sunt distincta, illa quoque disconveniunt, hoc est non sunt unum & idem &c.
units.tr: 3. I. Distinction is the mode of Being by which a thing has its own being peculiar to itself; that is, belonging to it alone. Otherwise it would in some way correspond to a form, and could not be communicated to another. 3. Things whose being is distinct, those also disagree; that is, they are not one and the same, and so on.

units.la: 8. Affectio immediatè ex distinctione orta est Existentia, quæ hic consideranda. 1. quoad nomen. 2. quoad rem.
units.tr: 8. The affection arising immediately from distinction is Existence, which is to be considered here: (1) as to the name; (2) as to the thing.

units.la: 9. Nomen habet existentia ab existendo sive extra sistendo, quod sit rei status sive manifestatio in universo. Sumiturque modo stricte pro solâ existentiâ substantiarum, quomodo inexistentiæ opponitur; modo latius, prout & hanc complectitur, quo pacto hic accipienda est.
units.tr: 9. Existence takes its name from existing, that is, standing out, which is the state or manifestation of a thing in the universe. It is taken strictly for the existence of substances alone, as opposed to inexistence; more broadly, insofar as it also embraces that, and in this sense it is to be understood here.

units.la: 10. Quoad rem considerandum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quomodo se habeat ad subjectum? 4. Quomodo se habeat ad essentiam? 5. Quænam ejus differentia? 6. Quænam axiomata ex eâ fluant?
units.tr: 10. As to the thing, we must consider: (1) What is it? (2) What is its subject? (3) How does it stand with respect to the subject? (4) How does it stand with respect to essence? (5) What is its difference? (6) What axioms flow from it?

units.la: 11. I. Est autem existentia modus distinctionis, quo Ens habet proprium suum esse præsens. Esse præsens habere, est illud alicubi & aliquando habere: Vulgò definitur, actus quo res ponitur extra suas causas: Sed ita existentiæ Dei non convenit, ut pote cujus nullæ sunt causæ. Scheiblerus pronomen reciprocum suas omittit: Sed manet sic definitio negativa: Et Deus extra causas dicitur esse, quod eas non habuerit, & creaturæ, quod eas habuerint, rint, qui duo modi toto genere discrepant.
units.tr: 11. I. Existence is the mode of distinction by which a Being has its own being present. To have present being is to have it somewhere and at some time. It is commonly defined as the act by which a thing is placed outside its causes. But in this way it does not apply to the existence of God, since God has no causes. Scheibler omits the reciprocal pronoun "suas", but the definition remains negative: God is said to be outside causes because he has never had any, and creatures because they have had them; these two modes differ entirely in kind.

units.la: 12. II. Subjectum hic dicitur illud, quod habet existentiam, de quo videndum, primo quid sit? Secundò, quid non sit? Ratione prioris hoc expendendum 1. in genere, 2. in specie.
units.tr: 12. II. The subject here is called that which has existence. Concerning it we must ask, first, what it is? Secondly, what it is not? For the first question, this must be weighed (1) in general, (2) in particular.

units.la: 13. In genere, existentia omni Enti convenit: nam 1. omne Ens distinctum est & constitutum; Quod autem tale est, id existit quoque. 2. Omne Ens habet essentiam: at habere essentiam dicitur id quod habet esse proprium; Et hoc existens. 3. Alias non Entis forent affectiones. Objic. Universalia sunt Entia, sed non habent existentiam; juxta tritum illud, universalium est esse, singularium vero existere. Resp. Sunt Entia, sed non distincta à singularibus, verum eadem cum ipsis sola præsentiâ horum operatione mentis sublatâ; quare eamdem quoque cum singularibus habent existentiam.
units.tr: 13. In general, existence belongs to every Being. For (1) every Being is distinct and constituted, and whatever is such also exists. (2) Every Being has an essence; but that which has its own being is said to have essence, and this is existing. (3) Otherwise there would be no affections of Being. Objection. Universals are beings, but they do not have existence, according to the common saying: universals have being, singulars exist. Reply. They are beings, but not distinct from singulars; rather they are the same as singulars, and differ only in that the presence of the singulars is removed by the operation of the mind. Hence they also have the same existence as singulars.

units.la: 14. In specie circa subjectum quæritur 1. An Deo conveniat existentia? Resp. Omninò, & quidem quam maximè; Dei enim essentia absolutè necessaria est, neque unquam ut possibilis concipi potest, sed semper ut actu præsens apprehendi debet. Objic. At sic compositio erit in Deo ex essentiâ & existentiâ. Resp. 1. Illa compositio non est realis, sed rationis, quæ rei simplicitatem adstruit, non destruit.
units.tr: 14. In particular, concerning the subject, we ask (1) does existence belong to God? Reply. Entirely, and indeed most of all. For God's essence is absolutely necessary; it can never be conceived as merely possible, but must always be apprehended as actually present. Objection. But then there would be a composition in God of essence and existence. Reply. (1) That composition is not real but of reason, which asserts the simplicity of the thing and does not destroy it.

units.la: 2. In creaturis concepta essentia, non necessario concipitur praesentia, unde si illa accedat, intellectus concipit compositionem, ex esse simpliciter & esse praesenter: At in Deo essentia & existentia cogitatione sejungi non possunt; quia in conceptu essentiae divinae manifeste involvitur ejus existentia.
units.tr: 2. In creatures, an essence when conceived is not necessarily conceived as present; so if presence is added, the intellect conceives a composition of simply being and being present. But in God essence and existence cannot be separated in thought, because existence is clearly involved in the concept of the divine essence.

units.la: 15. Quaeritur 2. An creaturis conveniat existentia? Resp. Convenit; Nam 1. Entia sunt. 2. Constituta & distincta sunt. 3. Essentiam habent. 4. Obtinent praesentiam. Objic. Creaturae dependent a Deo in esse, fieri & operari; Ergo videntur existentia propria carere. Resp. 1. Negatur consequentia: Sequitur quippe hoc saltem, quod habeant existentiam dependentem, quod lane verum est. 2. Imo quia dependent in esse, habent quoque suam praesentiam: Non enim dependerent, nisi praesentiam haberent: Praesentia autem est ipsa existentia. Sed haec objectio validius in vulgaram definitionem acui poflet.
units.tr: 15. We ask (2) does existence belong to creatures? Reply. It does. For (1) they are beings; (2) they are constituted and distinct; (3) they have essence; (4) they possess presence. Objection. Creatures depend on God in being, becoming and acting; therefore they seem to lack existence of their own. Reply. (1) The consequence is denied. It follows only that they have a dependent existence, which is indeed true. (2) Indeed, because they depend in being, they also have their presence; for they would not depend unless they had presence, and presence is existence itself. But this objection could be pressed more sharply against the common definition.

units.la: 16. Quaeritur 3. An accidentibus existentia fit tribuenda? Resp. Affirmative; posito, quod Entia sint. Objic. Accidentia non existunt, sed inexistunt. Resp. 1. Quia inexistunt, etiam existunt. 2. Inexistentia stricte, non adaequate dictae existentiae opponitur.
units.tr: 16. We ask (3) is existence to be attributed to accidents? Reply. Affirmatively, given that they are beings. Objection. Accidents do not exist but inexist. Reply. (1) Because they inexist, they also exist. (2) Inexistence is opposed strictly, not adequately, to existence.

units.la: 17. Quaeritur 4. An materia fit tribuenda da existentia? Resp. Ita sanè, quia Ens est‥ & in rerum naturâ suam præsentiam ha‥ bet, utpote à Deo condita. Objic. 1. Ma‥teria est pura potentia, at hujus nulla exi‥ stentia. Resp. Materia absolutè & in se con‥ siderata non est pura potentia, sed saltem respectu determinati corporis naturalis. Objic. 2. Forma est actus materiæ. Resp. Falsum hoc; Habet enim materia esse suum ante considerationem formæ: Forma quippe præsupponit eam esse subje‥ ctum: At quod subjectum est, id patitur, & quod patitur, id præsens est.
units.tr: 17. We ask (4) is existence to be attributed to matter? Reply. Certainly, since it is a being and has its presence in the nature of things, as created by God. Objection (1). Matter is pure potency, and of this there is no existence. Reply. Matter considered absolutely and in itself is not pure potency, but only with respect to a determinate natural body. Objection (2). Form is the act of matter. Reply. This is false; for matter has its being before form is considered, since form presupposes it as its subject. But what is a subject undergoes, and what undergoes is present.

units.la: 18. Quaeritur 5. An etiam partibus sit tribuenda existentia? Resp. Omninò; Habent enim per se suam essentiam ac esse proprium, suâque naturâ priores sunt toto: Quæ autem priora sunt naturâ, etiam eodem ordine prius habent suam præsentiam. Habent ergo partes suam existentiam, antequam totum præsens concipiatur. Objic. 1. Sic in unâ re essent plures existentiæ. Resp. Verum hoc quidem: sed illæ non sunt totales istius rei, sed partiales. Quemadmodum corpus humanum habet existentiam suam propriam, & consimiliter mens humana, constituunt tamen unum totalem existentiam hominis. Objic. 2. Sic ex duobus Entibus actu fieret unum per se. Resp. Axioma Philo‥ sophicum, cui hoc repugnare videtur sufumi debet, in sensu composito. Nam ex duobus hominibus actu, non fit unus homo per fe: fit tamen unus per fe ex tanibus, quæ propriam quidem habent existentiam, sed non habent totalem hominis. Et hæc de Subjecto existentiæ in specie.
units.tr: 18. We ask (5) is existence to be attributed also to parts? Reply. Entirely. For they have their own essence and proper being through themselves, and by nature they are prior to the whole. What is prior by nature also has its presence prior in the same order. So the parts have their existence before the whole is conceived as present. Objection (1). Thus there would be several existences in one thing. Reply. True indeed, but these are not the total existences of that thing, but partial ones. Just as the human body has its own existence, and likewise the human mind, yet together they constitute one total existence of the man. Objection (2). Thus from two beings there would actually come to be one being per se. Reply. The philosophical axiom which seems to oppose this must be understood in the composite sense. For from two men actually there does not come one man per se; yet one thing per se does come from things which indeed have their own existence, but not the total existence of man. And these things concerning the subject of existence, in particular.

units.la: 19. Nunc videndum, quid non sit ejus subjectum, sive quibus non conveniat: Non autem convenit alicui non-enti, cujuscunque ordinis illud fuerit. Objic. 1. Privationibus tribuitur existentia, quia de eis dicitur esse secundi adjecti. Resp. 1. Privatio sumitur materialiter, pro ipsa dispositione subjecti, & sic eamdem cum subjecto habet existentiam; vel formaliter, pro negatione ejus, quod in subjecto esse debebat, & sic præsentiæ est negatio. 2. Esse secundi adjecti dicitur de privatione, non per positionem, sed per remotionem, quia ipsa privatio remotio quædam est. Objic. 2. Entibus rationis etiam tribuitur esse secundi adjecti. Resp. Tribuitur ipsis, sed ficta; nam prout ipsa ficta sunt, ita & fictam requirunt existentiam; quæ non magis, imò minus vera est existentia, quam homo pictus homo.
units.tr: 19. Now we must consider what its subject is not, or to what it does not belong. Existence does not belong to any non-being, of whatever order it may be. Objection (1). Privations are attributed existence, because of them we say they "are" as a second adjective. Reply. (1) Privation is taken materially, for the very disposition of the subject, and so it has the same existence as the subject; or formally, for the negation of what ought to be in the subject, and so it is a negation of presence. (2) "To be" as a second adjective is said of privation not by positing but by removal, because privation itself is a certain removal. Objection (2). Beings of reason are also attributed "to be" as a second adjective. Reply. It is attributed to them, but feigned. For insofar as they are feigned, they require a feigned existence, which is no more true existence, indeed less so, than a painted man is a man.

units.la: 20. III. Quoad habitudinem, quam ad subjectum habet, notandum. 1. Quod existentia idem sit realiter cum Ente: Est quippe reipsa idem cum distinctione, & hæc cum Ente. Quæ autem idem sunt cum uno tertio, illa inter se idem sunt. Objic. Sic ridicula foret propositio Ens habet exister tiam, æquivaleret enim huic, Ens habet Ens & seipsum. Resp. Negatur consequentia; Non enim ridicula est hæc, Deus habet omnipotentiam, licet Deus & omnipotentia realiter idem sint. 2. Ut unum dicatur alterum habere, sufficit distinctio formalis & rationis ratiocinatæ, sive conceptuum inadæquatorum; Quomodo etiam dicitur homo habere animam & corpus, inter quæ & hominem, cujus partes sunt, non nisi formalis est distinctio.
units.tr: 20. III. As to the relation it has to the subject, note: 1. That existence is really the same as being. For it is in fact the same as distinction, and distinction is the same as being. Things that are the same as one third thing are the same as each other. Objection: on this view the proposition "Being has existence" would be absurd, since it would amount to "Being has being and itself." Reply: the inference is denied. "God has omnipotence" is not absurd, even though God and omnipotence are really the same. 2. For one thing to be said to have another, a formal distinction, or a distinction of reason ratiocinated (that is, of inadequate concepts), is enough. So too man is said to have a soul and a body, and between these and the man of whom they are parts there is only a formal distinction.

units.la: 21. Notandum 2. Quod existentia differat ab Ente conceptu & modo considerandi; Ens enim dum consideratur, concipitur totum illud, quod omni modo esse habet: Sed consideratâ existentiâ, concipio saltem modum inadæquatum istius esse, quo præsens dicitur.
units.tr: 21. Note 2: existence differs from being in concept and in the mode of considering it. For when being is considered, there is conceived the whole that has being in every way; but when existence is considered, I conceive at least an inadequate mode of that being, by which it is said to be present.

units.la: 22. Unde notandum 3. Existentiam nihil diversi Enti superaddere, non modum externum & separabilem, non denominationem externam, non relationem, nec ens rationis, sed saltem esse inadæquatum ejus conceptum.
units.tr: 22. Hence note 3: existence adds nothing different to the being. It is not an external and separable mode, not an external denomination, not a relation, nor a being of reason, but at least an inadequate concept of its being.

units.la: 23. IV. Sequitur habitudo cjus ad essentiam, ubi notandum 1. quod existentia & essentia non differant realiter, sed in se idem sunt, quia utraque eadem est cum ente; Unde sequitur primò, existentiam non esse rem aliquam ab essentiâ diversam; quia si res esset, aliam haberet existentiam, & sic manifestus foret progressus in infinitum. Secundò sequitur, quod existentia non sit modus externus essentiæ superadditus; quia omnis res negato modo externo, ut completa concipi potest: at res essentiam habens, negatâ existentiâ concipi nequit; nam nec tribui potest essentia, nisi quatenus habet existentiam.2. Notandum, quod indissolubili nexu essentia & existentia inter se cohæreant; Quia videlicet idem nunquam est sine se ipso: at existentia est ipsa essentia.
units.tr: 23. IV. Next comes its relation to essence, where note 1: existence and essence do not differ really, but are the same in themselves, because each is the same as being. Hence it follows, first, that existence is not some thing distinct from essence; for if it were a thing, it would have another existence, and so an infinite regress would be plain. Secondly, it follows that existence is not an external mode added to essence. For every thing can be conceived as complete with its external mode removed; but a thing having essence cannot be conceived with existence removed, for essence cannot be attributed except insofar as it has existence. 2. Note that essence and existence cohere by an indissoluble bond, namely because the same thing is never without itself; but existence is essence itself.

units.la: 24. V. Nunc videndæ ejus differentiæ, quæ potissimum hæ sunt. 1. Existentia est vel momentanea vel successiva. Momentanea dicitur, quæ indivisibili puncto durationis permanet, atque ita vel eadem est cum permanente, vel nulla, vix enim punctum tantæ parvitatis concipere possumus; quin adhuc minus concipi queat, quare nunquam indivisibilis illa duratio dari posse videtur; quoniam enim illud punctum semper divisibile concipitur, etiam semper durationi isti partes erunt tribuendæ, atque ita successiva evadet.
units.tr: 24. V. Now let us see its differences, which are chiefly these. 1. Existence is either momentary or successive. That is called momentary which lasts through an indivisible point of duration; and so it is either the same as the permanent, or nothing. For we can scarcely conceive a point of such smallness; indeed even less can it be conceived, so that such indivisible duration seems never to be possible. For since that point is always conceived as divisible, parts will always have to be attributed to duration too, and so it turns out to be successive.

units.la: 25. 2. Existentia vel est permanens, vel successiva. Prior est, quæ habet omnes partes suæ præsentiæ simul, unde soli Deo
units.tr: 25. 2. Existence is either permanent or successive. The former is that which has all the parts of its presence together, whence it belongs to God alone;

units.la: convenit, qui ubicunque est, totus est, & totus ubique, cuique omnia sunt præsentia, nihil præteritum aut futurum. Posterior est, quæ habet partes suæ præsentiæ post se invicem, ut est omnium creaturarum existentia. Objic. At angeli, & animæ rationales permanebunt in sæcula; Ergo habent existentiam permanentem. Resp. Est fallacia homonymiæ in voce permanere, quæ in antecedente opponitur destructioni, at in consequente denotat, partes suæ durationis simul habere. Licet igitur nunquam intereant angeli & animæ rationales, non tamen omnia ipsis præsentia sunt, quod ad permanentem existentiam requiritur.
units.tr: who, wherever he is, is whole, and whole everywhere, to whom all things are present and nothing past or future. The latter is that which has the parts of its presence one after another, as is the existence of all creatures. Objection: but angels and rational souls will remain for ever; therefore they have permanent existence. Reply: there is an equivocation in the word "remain". In the antecedent it is opposed to destruction, but in the consequent it denotes having all the parts of its duration together. Although angels and rational souls never perish, not all things are present to them, which permanent existence requires.

units.la: 26. 3. Existentia vel est per se, vel in alio: Hæc accidentium est, & inhærentia dicitur: Illa autem quæ [illegible, ~2 letters] substantiarum est, vel completa est, quæ dicitur subsistentia, vel incompleta, & simpliciter existentia per se dicitur. Completa porro existentia, sive subsistentia, vel est simpliciter talis, vel personalitas, quæ quasi modum priori superaddit, quatenus illi intellectum jungit.
units.tr: 26. 3. Existence is either per se or in another. The latter belongs to accidents and is called inherence. The former belongs to substances, and is either complete, which is called subsistence, or incomplete, and is simply called existence per se. Complete existence, or subsistence, is either simply such, or personality, which as it were adds a mode to the former, insofar as it joins it to intellect.

units.la: 27. 4. Existentia est vel dependens, vel independens, quarum definitiones exterminis desumi possunt Et 5. Est vel necessaria vel contingens. Illa absolute sumta solius Dei est, comparatè tamen etiam quandoque aliis tribuitur.
units.tr: 27. 4. Existence is either dependent or independent, whose definitions can be drawn from the terms themselves. And 5. It is either necessary or contingent. The former, taken absolutely, belongs to God alone, though comparatively it is sometimes attributed to others too.

units.la: 28. VI. Axiomata hæc potissimum ex exsistentia oriuntur. 1. Quidquid habet existentiam habet & essentiam; Et contrà. Ratio est, quia idem sunt realiter, Usus est in redarguendis illis, qui rei essentiam cognoscere volunt, quam exsistere nondum compertum est, quales sint, qui unicornu, Phœnicem, Paradisum hodiernum terrestrem, cantum cygnorum, aureos dentes, describunt, licet ignorent, an illa exsistentiam habeant.
units.tr: 28. VI. These axioms arise mainly from existence. 1. Whatever has existence has essence too; and conversely. The reason is that they are really the same. It is used in refuting those who want to know the essence of a thing whose existence is not yet established, such as those who describe the unicorn, the Phoenix, the present earthly Paradise, the song of swans, or golden teeth, although they do not know whether those things have existence.

units.la: 29. II. Qualis est exsistentia, talis est & essentia; ob eandem scilicet rationem; Hinc redarguendi illi, qui Deum throno quasi includunt, ejusque omnipræsentiam negant: Si quippe habeat exsistentiam permanentem, talem quoque ut habeat essentiam oportet. III. Vnius entis una est exsistentia. Ratio est, quia unum sibi ipsi unum, non multiplex est. IV. Qualis est alicujus exsistentia, talis & ejus duratio; Ratio est, quia duratio est ipsa exsistentia, aut ejus modus; Quoniam igitur Deus permanentem, independentem ac necessariam habet exsistentiam, talem quoque obtinet durationem. Et hæc de exsistentiâ.
units.tr: 29. II. Such as existence is, such also is essence, for the same reason. Hence those are refuted who, as it were, enclose God in a throne and deny his omnipresence; for if he has permanent existence, he must also have such essence. III. Of one being there is one existence. The reason is that one is one to itself, not manifold. IV. Such as the existence of anything is, such also is its duration. The reason is that duration is existence itself, or its mode. Since therefore God has permanent, independent and necessary existence, he also obtains such duration. And these things concerning existence.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: DE Ubietate.
units.tr: Of Ubiety.

units.la: 1. Existentia sive præsentiæ, duo modi sunt inadæquati, quibus ea tota absolvitur; omne enim quod præsens est, alicubi est & non nullibi, & aliquando est, & non nunquam; A priori oritur affectio Entis, ubietas sive localitas dicta: à posteriori, Duratio.
units.tr: 1. Existence, or presence, has two inadequate modes by which it is wholly accounted for. For everything that is present is somewhere and not nowhere, and is at some time and not at no time. From the first arises the affection of being called ubiety or locality; from the second, duration.

units.la: 2. Vbietas, ab ubi nomen habens, aliquando strictè sumitur, & solí finitæ præsentiæ tribuitur, aliquando latius, prout omni illi convenit, quod non est nullibi, quomodo hic accipienda: Aliter etiam localitas dicitur, quæ à loco denominata, modò strictè sumta solis corporibus tribuitur; modò latius accepta ubietati æquipollet.
units.tr: 2. Ubiety, taking its name from "ubi" (where), is sometimes taken strictly and assigned only to finite presence, and sometimes more broadly, so that it belongs to everything that is not nowhere. It is in this broader sense that it is to be understood here. Locality is also used in another sense, named from "locus" (place). Taken strictly, it belongs only to bodies; taken more broadly, it is equivalent to ubiety.

units.la: 3. Circa hujus naturam, investigandum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quomodo dividenda? 4. Quodnam ejus oppositum?
units.tr: 3. Concerning its nature, four things are to be investigated: 1. What it is? 2. What is its subject? 3. How is it to be divided? 4. What is its opposite?

units.la: 4. I. Definitur ubietas, quod sit modus existentia, quo Ens alicubi est præsens. Dicitur modus existentia, quia ex eâ immediatè emanare concipitur, imò quia est ipsa existentia, quatenus ad hanc quasi sui partem restringitur: Dicitur per illam
units.tr: 4. I. Ubiety is defined as the mode of existence by which a being is present somewhere. It is called a mode of existence because it is conceived to flow immediately from existence; indeed, it is existence itself, insofar as it is restricted to this as a kind of part of itself. It is called by that definition

units.la: Ens alicubi praesens, quod capiendum non respective, quatenus ibi est, ubi alia sunt, sed absolute, ut ibi habeat localitatem & praesentiam, ubi est ejus existentia, sive ibi etiam alia sint, sive non, & non nullibi.
units.tr: a being present somewhere, which is to be understood not relatively, insofar as it is there where other things are, but absolutely, so that it has locality and presence where its existence is, whether other things are there too or not, and is not nowhere.

units.la: 5. II. Subjectum ejus est omne Ens; Idem enim existentiae & modi ejus subjectum esse debet: Atqui omne Ens est subjectum existentiae; Ergo & ubietatis. Quare prout localitas non differt realiter ab existentia, ita nec realiter differt ab Ente, sed tantum modo quodam considerandi. Quare etiam ubietas nunquam ab Ente separari potest.
units.tr: 5. II. Its subject is every being. For the subject of existence and of its mode should be the same. But every being is a subject of existence; therefore it is also a subject of ubiety. Hence, just as locality does not differ really from existence, so it does not differ really from being, but only in a certain manner of considering it. For this reason ubiety can never be separated from being.

units.la: 6. Quaeritur 1. An omni Enti conveniat, etiam Deo? Resp. Omnino; Nam prout Deus quam maxime existit, ita quam maxime praesentiam & ubietatem, tanquam necessaria existentiae requisita habet. Objic. Sic etiam Deus erit in loco, & non ubique. Resp. Est in loco generaliter dicto, cui ubiquitas non opponitur, sed cujus species est ubiquitas. Eatenus enim tantum dicitur esse in loco, quatenus non est nullibi. Quaeritur. 2. An & Accidentia sint in loco? Resp. Vtique si sint Entia: sed quia sunt Entia in alio, non requirunt quoque distinctum ab illo alio ubi.
units.tr: 6. The question is: 1. Does it belong to every being, including God? Answer: Certainly. For God, who exists in the highest degree, has presence and ubiety in the highest degree as requisites of his existence. Objection: In this way God will also be in a place, and not everywhere. Answer: He is in place in the general sense, to which ubiquity is not opposed, but of which ubiquity is a species. For he is said to be in place only insofar as he is not nowhere. The question is: 2. Are accidents also in place? Answer: Certainly, if they are beings. But because they are beings in another thing, they do not also require a place distinct from that other thing where they are.

units.la: 7. III. Quoad divisiones, Vbietas vel est infinita; vel finita: Infinita, alias ubi-quiquitas dicitur, estque modus existentiæ infinita, quo ens ubicunque est, totum est, & totum extra, & totum in quocunque assignabili; Ea igitur solius Dei est; Et inanem videntur alere subtilitatem, qui possibilem alicujus corporis ubiquitatem somniant; licet enim omne impleat spatium, non tamen ubique dici potest, quia in quâcunque istius spatii parte totum non est; nec totum in quocunque affignabili.
units.tr: 7. III. As to divisions, ubiety is either infinite or finite. Infinite ubiety, otherwise called ubiquity, is the infinite mode of existence by which a being, wherever it is, is wholly there, and wholly outside, and wholly in whatever place can be assigned. This therefore belongs to God alone. Those who dream of a possible ubiquity of some body seem to nourish an empty subtlety. For although a body may fill a space, it cannot be said to be everywhere, because in any part of that space it is not wholly present, nor wholly in whatever part can be assigned.

units.la: 8. Finita localitas est modus existentiæ finitæ, quoEns tantum totum est ubi est, non vero totum extra, aut totum in quocunque assignabili; Estque hæc omnium creaturarum; Quare nulla creatura ubique esse potest, nec simul in pluribus locis tota; repugnat enim id existentiæ, adeoque & essentiæ finitæ.
units.tr: 8. Finite locality is the mode of finite existence by which a being is wholly only where it is, and not wholly outside, or wholly in whatever place can be assigned. This belongs to all creatures. Hence no creature can be everywhere, nor wholly in several places at once. For this contradicts existence, and so also finite essence.

units.la: 9. Sed duplex est hæc finita ubietas, videlicet ubietas stricte dicta, & localitas stricte dicta. Prior est præfentia individibilis, quâ creatura omnes suæ essentiæ partes intra fe invicem obtinet, estque intelligentiarum: Posterior est, quâ creatura per partes extra fe invicem positas præfens est; Estque corporum. Unde patet 1. Spiritus non replere spatium extensum. 2. Ipfofeffe penetrabiles. 3. Corpora replere spatium extensum; Adeoque 4. non posse penetrari, sed semper alia corpora excludere.
units.tr: 9. But this finite ubiety is twofold: ubiety in the strict sense, and locality in the strict sense. The former is an indivisible presence by which a creature holds all parts of its essence within itself, one within another, and it belongs to intelligences. The latter is that by which a creature is present through parts placed outside one another, and it belongs to bodies. From this it is clear: 1. Spirits do not fill extended space. 2. They are not penetrable in themselves. 3. Bodies fill extended space; and so 4. they cannot be penetrated, but always exclude other bodies.

units.la: 10. V. Oppositum ubietatis est nullibi, seu ratione corporum vacuum, quod nonenti convenit, & ubietati contradictioni opponitur.
units.tr: 10. V. The opposite of ubiety is nowhere, or, with respect to bodies, void. This belongs to non-being and is opposed to ubiety as a contradiction.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: D E
units.tr: ON

units.la: Duratione.
units.tr: Duration.

units.la: I. SEquitur Duratio, quae est modus existentiae, quo ens habet esse suum aliquando praesens. Aliquando hic non capiendum respectivè, acsi Ens esse suum haberet, quando alia suum quando obtinent, nec etiam prout semper esse opponitur: Sed absolutè, prout opponitur nunquam esse.
units.tr: 1. Next comes duration, which is the mode of existence by which a being has its being present at some time. Here at some time is not to be taken relatively, as if a being had its being when other things have theirs, nor even as opposed to always being; it is to be taken absolutely, as opposed to never being.

units.la: 2. Subjectum ejus est omne Ens, ob easdem rationes, circa ubietatem allegatas; Unde etiam saltem modo considerandi ab Ente, ejusque existentia differt; Est enim ipsa existentia continuata.
units.tr: 2. Its subject is every being, for the same reasons alleged above concerning ubiety. Hence it also differs from the being and its existence, at least in the mode of considering them; for duration is existence itself continued.

units.la: 3. Dividitur vulgo in momentaneam & successivam: Sed cum non detur existentia momentanea, hoc est indivisibilis, non datur quoque duratio unius indivisibilis momenti; Licet enim quodcunque minimum momentum fingamus, illud ipsum continuò minus ac minus concipi potest. Nec rectè Deo duratio successiva tribui potest, utpote qui partes suae durationis simul possidet; neque momentanea, ut-pote pote iis tantum debita, quæ eodem quo fiunt puncto, simul intereunt.
units.tr: 3. It is commonly divided into momentary and successive. But since there is no momentary existence, that is, no indivisible existence, there is also no duration of a single indivisible moment. For however small a moment we imagine, it can always be conceived as smaller and smaller. Nor can successive duration rightly be attributed to God, since he possesses all the parts of his duration at once; nor momentary duration, since that belongs only to things which perish at the very point at which they come to be.

units.la: 4. Præterea duratio dividitur, quod sit vel infinita, vel finita. Infinita, aliter æternitas dicta, est modus exsistentiæ infinitæ, quo Ens habet omnes partes suæ durationis finitas; adeoque tali modo duranti nihil præteritum aut futurum est. Omne enim præteritum aliquando determinatè fuit, & omne futurum aliquando erit determinatè. At omne aliquando determinatum incidit in partem aliquam quasi infinitæ durationis, quas hæc simul habet; Omne igitur præteritum ac futurum ipsi præsens est. Talis autem Duratio solius Dei est.
units.tr: 4. Moreover, duration is divided into being infinite or finite. Infinite duration, otherwise called eternity, is the mode of infinite existence by which a being has all the parts of its duration present at once; and so for a thing enduring in this mode there is nothing past or future. For everything past was at some determinate time, and everything future will be at some determinate time. But everything determinate at some time falls within some part of an infinite duration, which this being has all at once; therefore everything past and future is present to it. Such duration belongs to God alone.

units.la: 5. Finita duratio est modus exsistentiæ finitæ, quo Ens habet suæ durationis partes post se invicem: Estque omnium Creaturarum; in quibus momenta, sive partes, durationis à se invicem non dependent, quoniam priores & posteriores sunt: Et omne posterius à priori ut dependet, ita illud ab hoc independens est; Unde quia jam sunt Creaturæ, non necessariò sequenti momento futuræ sunt. Hinc igitur ipsis præteritum & futurum in duratione & existentia convenit, & à præterito in futurum, ope infinitè durantis, conservari debent.
units.tr: 5. Finite duration is the mode of finite existence by which a being has the parts of its duration one after another. It belongs to all creatures, in whom the moments or parts of duration do not depend on one another, since they are earlier and later. And as every later part depends on an earlier one, so the earlier is independent of the later. Hence, since creatures already exist, they are not necessarily going to exist in the following moment. Thus past and future belong to them in duration and existence, and they must be preserved from past into future by the operation of the infinitely enduring God.

units.la: 6. Est autem duplex finita duratio, æviternitas videlicet & tempus. Æviternas illis tribuitur, quæ suæ durationis, carent fine, ut Angelis &c. Tempus vero quae & principium & finem habent, ut corporibus naturalibus.
units.tr: 6. Now finite duration is of two kinds, namely aeviternity and time. Aeviternity is attributed to those things which lack an end of their duration, such as the angels etc. Time, however, belongs to those which have both a beginning and an end, such as natural bodies.

units.la: 7. Tempus vel pro ipsa tali duratione sumitur, vel promensura, quâ ista duratio ejusque partes numerantur; Priori modo hic capienda est. Posterior enim rebus denominationem externam tribuit; Illa autem mensura, vel est activa, vel passiva. Activa mensura est in mensurantibus aliis durationibus; Tales autem durationes potissimum motu aliquo generali commensurantur, qualis est primi mobilis, utpote certissimi, aequabilis & generalissimi; quare sic recte definitur tempus a Philosopho, numerus motus secundum prius & posterius. Estque haec primaria, cui multae secundaria tam naturales, quam artificiales, subserviunt. Naturales quidem, ut motus lunae, & reliquorum planetarum. Artificiales vero ut motus horologiorum, tam rotulariorum, quam sciatericorum. Passiva mensura est ipse ille motus, in certa interstitia distinctus, atque ita durationi applicatus, quales sunt annus, dies &c. Sed de his latius in Physicis.
units.tr: 7. Time is taken either for such duration itself, or for the measure by which that duration and its parts are counted. It is the former sense that must be understood here. For the latter attributes an external denomination to things. That measure is either active or passive. The active measure lies in other durations which measure; and such durations are chiefly measured by some general motion, such as that of the primum mobile, as being most certain, uniform and most general. Hence the Philosopher rightly defines time as the number of motion in respect of before and after. This is the primary measure, which many secondary measures, both natural and artificial, serve. Natural ones, indeed, such as the motion of the moon and of the other planets; artificial ones, such as the motion of clocks, both wheel clocks and sundials. The passive measure is that very motion itself, divided into fixed intervals and so applied to duration, such as the year, the day, etc. But more on these matters in Physics.

units.la: 8. Addunt nonnulli aliam speciem durationis, quae principio carens, finem habere: At talis dari nequit. Nec est, quod Decreta Dei inferant, illa enim, prout ab aeterno sunt, sunt ipse Deus, adeo-que que desinere non possunt.
units.tr: 8. Some add another kind of duration, one which lacks a beginning but has an end. But such cannot exist. Nor is there any reason to infer it from the decrees of God; for those decrees, as they are from eternity, are God himself, and so cannot cease.

units.la: 9. Durationi opponitur nunquam esse: idque contradictorie; quia subjectum durationis, Ens, & subjectum ejus, quod nunquam est, nihil, contradictorie opponuntur: Et quemadmodum duratio realiter coincidit cum ente, ita nunquam esse cum nihilo. Haec autem de Existentia ejusque affectionibus sufficient.
units.tr: 9. Duration is opposed to never being, and that contradictorily; because the subject of duration, being, and the subject of that which never is, nothing, are contradictorily opposed. And just as duration really coincides with being, so never being coincides with nothing. These remarks on existence and its affections will suffice.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: DE Actu & Potentia.
units.tr: OF ACT AND POTENCY.

units.la: 1. ENs in suo esse constitutum ac distinctum, omnes suas perfectiones praesentes habet; quae praesentia actus nomine insignitur: quare vel actus vel actu dicitur esse ens. Actus quidem, quatenus hic concretive sumtus illud ipsum, quod actum, hoc est suarum perfectionum praesentiam, habet, significat: Actu vero, prout abstractive illa praesentia ens esse dicitur. Et si illa praesentia necessitatem absolutam non involvat, impurus dicitur actus, eo quod potentiam praesupponat, qua Ens illam praesentiam non obtineret, cum aptitudine illam obtinendi. Nunc igitur, post explicationem affectionum, vel seorsim a constitutione, vel a distinctione ortarum, agendum est de actu ex utráque simul resultante, ut & de Potentiâ, ejus oppositio ex parte.
units.tr: 1. A being (ens) established and distinct in its own existence has all its perfections present to it. The presence of these is called act, so a being is said to be either act or in act. "Act" taken concretely signifies the thing that has act, that is, the presence of its perfections. "In act" taken abstractly signifies that the being is through that presence. If this presence does not involve absolute necessity, the act is called impure, because it presupposes a potency by which the being would not possess that presence, though it has the aptitude to obtain it. Now, after the explanation of the affections, whether arising from the constitution or from the distinction of the being, we must treat of act as it results from both together, and of potency, its opposite on the other side.

units.la: 2. Actus, nomen ab agendo habens, primitus usurpatus videtur, ad denotandam actionem, ejusve præsentiam: postea verò etiam adhibitus fuit ad reliquarum omnium perfectionum præsentiam denotandam. Sive absoluta esset illa præsentia, quo modo Deus actus purissimus dicitur, sive ad potentiam, cujus sit perfectio, relata, qualiscunque etiam illa fuerit. Quin & hinc illud, quod quasi emanativa causa istius præsentiæ est, actus nomine venit; quomodo, & forma dicitur actus, eo quod suâ præsentiâ potentiam materiæ perficit: Unde & ipsa existentia actus dicitur, quia ipsi Enti jam tributa, nihil præterea desiderari videatur.
units.tr: 2. The word actus (act), having its name from agere (to act), seems to have been used first to denote an action or its presence. Later it was also applied to denote the presence of all the other perfections, whether that presence is absolute, as when God is called pure act, or related to a potency of which it is the perfection, whatever that perfection may be. Indeed, from this usage, that which is the emanative cause of such a presence is also called act. In the same way, form is called act because by its presence it perfects the potency of matter. Hence existence itself is called an act, since, once attributed to the being, nothing further seems to be wanting to it.

units.la: 3. Actus Græcè ἐντελέχεια dicitur, vocabulo magis rei significandæ idoneo, utpote quo actualis perfectionis possessio significatur. Apud Latinos simplex aliud, quo idem denotetur non occurrit, nisi cum Barbaro barbara perfectihabita in civitatem latinam recipiatur.
units.tr: 3. Act is called entelecheia [ἐντελέχεια] in Greek, a term better suited to the thing signified, since it signifies the possession of actual perfection. In Latin there is no single word that denotes the same, unless the barbarous term perfectihabita is admitted into the Latin city.

units.la: 4. Circa rem actûs explicandum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quomodo dividi debeat? 3. Oppositum ejus. 4. Quenam axiomata?
units.tr: 4. In explaining the nature of act, we must consider: (1) What it is? (2) How it ought to be divided? (3) Its opposite? (4) What axioms hold of it?

units.la: 5. I. Quoniam tam diversa actus denotare videtur, difficile erit generalem ejus cuderet definitionem: Sufficiet igitur hæc ejus descriptio, quod sit actualis persectionum possessio; vel, modus constitutionis & distinctionis, quo Ens habet esse sibi proprium præsens, cum omnibus ad illud requisitis. Atque ita omnium perfectionum collectivè iumtarum præsentiæ convenit; cum distributivè sumta, etiam quælibet possessa perfectio actus dicatur, qui quasi totalis pars, aut inadæquata ratio æstimandus est.
units.tr: 5. I. Since act seems to denote things so diverse, it will be difficult to frame a general definition of it. It will suffice, therefore, to give this description: it is the actual possession of perfections; or, the mode of constitution and distinction by which a being has its own proper existence present, together with all that is required for it. This belongs to the presence of all perfections taken collectively; but taken distributively, any single perfection possessed is also called an act, and is to be regarded as a kind of total part, or an inadequate notion, of act.

units.la: 6. Ex quibus clarum fit, actum ab Ente realiter non distingui, neque ipsi aliquid à suis perfectionibus distinctum superaddere; quoniam saltem formaliter & inadæquato modo considerandi, perfectio & ejus possessio præsens distinguuntur.
units.tr: 6. From these points it is clear that act is not really distinct from being, and adds nothing to it that is distinct from its perfections. For perfection and its present possession are distinguished at least formally and in an inadequate mode of consideration.

units.la: 7. II. Quoad differentias, actus est vel absolutus vel respectivus: Absolutus, etiam purus dictus; eô quòd ipsi nulla respondeat potentia, per quam posset non esse præsens, est infinitæ perfectionis possessio, adeoque soli Deo convenit; Neque alius aliquis actus purus extra Deum, imaginabilis videtur. Objic. Angeli etiam actus puri dicuntur. Resp. Hoc fit comparatè ad corpora naturalia, quæ actum ex unione materiæ & formæ requirunt, qualis in angelis non datur: non absolutè, quia ipsorum puritas adhuc infinitis intervallis à puritate simpliciter & absolutè dictâ, declinat.
units.tr: 7. II. As to differences, act is either absolute or relative. Absolute act, also called pure, is the possession of infinite perfection, because no potency corresponds to it by which it could fail to be present. It therefore belongs to God alone, and no other pure act outside God seems conceivable. Objection: angels too are called pure acts. Reply: this is said comparatively, in relation to natural bodies, which require act from the union of matter and form, which is not found in angels; it is not said absolutely, since their purity still falls short, by infinite intervals, of purity simply and absolutely so called.

units.la: 8. Actus respectivus est potentia per-sectio; sectio; hoc est præsentia talis perfectionis, quæ potentiam ad non esse habebat. Estque hic duplex, prout illa perfectio, quæ actu isto præsens esse dicitur, vel actione, vel passione in subjecto se manifestat, activus videlicet & passivus.
units.tr: 8. Relative act is the perfection of a potency, that is, the presence of such a perfection as formerly was in potency to non-being. This is twofold, according as the perfection said to be present by that act shows itself in the subject by action or by passion: namely active and passive.

units.la: 9. Actus activus est præsentia actionis, quâ perficitur potentia actíva suo exercitio: Cujus variæ sunt differentiæ; nam 1. ratione istius virtutis sive activæ potentiæ, est vel infinitus vel finitus. Infinitus est præsentia actionum divinarum: finitus vero actionum à creaturis profectarum. Prioris igitur ordinis sunt actus creandi, conservandi &c. Posterioris actus cogitandi, intelligendi, volendi, movendi, generandi, &c. 2. Ratione principii, actus hic vel elicitus est, vel imperatus. Prior est ipsa præsentia actionis, prout ab ipsâ rei essentiâ profluit: posterior vero, quâtenus instrumento debito, ipsi essentiæ conjuncto, peragitur. Sic præsentia risus est actus elicitus ratione essentiæ humanæ: at imperatus ratione oris & reliquarum partium. 3. Ratione subjecti, actus hic vel est immanens, vel transiens. Immanens est præsentia actionis in eodem cum suâ virtute subjecto, qualis est cogitationis. Transiens autem talis est actionis, quæ in aliud subjectum transit, ut motio, calefactio &c.
units.tr: 9. Active act is the presence of an action by which an active potency is perfected in its exercise. Its differences are various. (1) By reason of this power, or active potency, it is either infinite or finite. Infinite act is the presence of the divine actions; finite act is the presence of actions proceeding from creatures. Of the former order are the acts of creating, conserving, and so on; of the latter, the acts of thinking, understanding, willing, moving, generating, and so on. (2) By reason of the principle, this act is either elicited or commanded. The former is the presence of the action as it flows from the very essence of the thing; the latter is the presence of the action as it is carried out by a suitable instrument joined to that essence. Thus the presence of laughter is an elicited act by reason of human essence, but a commanded act by reason of the mouth and the other parts. (3) By reason of the subject, this act is either immanent or transient. Immanent is the presence of an action in the same subject as its power, as thinking is. Transient is an action that passes over into another subject, such as motion, heating, and so on.

units.la: 10. Actus passivus est praesentia passionis quâ videlicet potentia passiva perficitur: Dicitur autem hic actus passivus, non per contradictionem in adjecto, ut primâ fronte apparere posset, quoniam actio & passio opponuntur. Sed hic actus idem est, quod ενέργεια, adeoque & passionem sub se continet: Necnovum hoc; solet quippe non raro significatio actionis ampliari, ut & passioni tribuatur, ut fit in divisione actus in primum & secundum satis recepta; & in hoc axiomate, omnis res est propter actionem suam, quod nisi & de passione intelligeretur, in materiâ falsum esset.
units.tr: 10. Passive act is the presence of a passion by which, namely, a passive potency is perfected. This act is called passive not through a contradiction in the term, as might appear at first sight, since action and passion are opposites. Rather, this act is the same as energeia [ἐνέργεια], and so contains passion within it. Nor is this novel. The meaning of action is often extended so as to include passion as well, as happens in the division of act into first and second, which is well established, and in this axiom, every thing exists for the sake of its action, which would be false in matter unless it were also understood of passion.

units.la: 11. Estque hic actus duplex, vel existentia, vel receptionis: Prior est praesentia rei, quatenus virtute suarum causarum existit, eique opponitur potentia objectiva. Posterior vero est praesentia receptionis alicujus, ad quam ens suâ essentiâ dispositum erat, opponiturque subjectivae potentiae.
units.tr: 11. This act is twofold: either existence or reception. The former is the presence of a thing as, by the virtue of its causes, it exists; it is opposed to objective potency. The latter is the presence of some reception for which the being was disposed by its essence; it is opposed to subjective potency.

units.la: 12. Actus existentiae vel est entitativus, qui est simplicis rei praesentia; vel formalis, qui est praesentia rei compositae ex materiae partibus, ac formâ illas uniente. Hinc solvitur Quaestio illa, an materiae ex se fit actus aliquis? Est nempe entitativus, non formalis.
units.tr: 12. Act of existence is either entitative, which is the presence of a simple thing, or formal, which is the presence of a thing composed of the parts of matter and the form uniting them. Hence that question is resolved: whether matter, of itself, becomes some act? It is indeed entitative, not formal.

units.la: 13. Actus receptionis vel naturalis est, vel praeter naturalis. Naturalis est praesentia receptionis, rei pu r ordinariam aliquam actionem convenientis ; qualis actus est luminis in aëre. Estque duplex, essentialis & accidentalis: Prior est præsentia aptitudinis recipiendi in se essentiam aliquam, qualis est præsentia potentiæ, quâ in materiâ recipi possunt rerum naturalium formæ. Posterior est præsentia aptitudinis, quâ recipi potest accidens aliquod; qualis est in aquâ, quâ recipere apta est calorem & frigus; Atque hic naturalis actus physicæ potentiæ opponitur.
units.tr: 13. Act of reception is either natural or preternatural. Natural act is the presence of a reception suited to some ordinary action of a thing, such as the act of light in air. It is twofold, essential and accidental. The former is the presence of the aptitude to receive some essence in itself, such as the presence of the potency by which the forms of natural things can be received in matter. The latter is the presence of the aptitude by which some accident can be received, as water has the aptitude to receive heat and cold. This natural act is opposed to physical potency.

units.la: 14. Præternaturalis actus est præsentia aptitudinis, qua Ens ab extraordinario quo agente aliquid recipere potest, ad quod à naturâ non videbatur ordinatum. Qualis est præsentia aptitudinis, quâ ex lapidibus fieri possunt filii Abrahæ, ex ligno lestica, & hic potentiæ obedientiali opponitur.
units.tr: 14. Preternatural act is the presence of an aptitude by which a being can receive something from an extraordinary agent, to which it did not seem ordained by nature. Such is the presence of the aptitude by which children of Abraham could be made from stones, or a log could become a statue; this is opposed to obediential potency.

units.la: 15. Dividitur quoque actus, quod fit vel primus vel secundus: Primus dicitur præsentia aptitudinis essentiæ, quâ ea actionibus aut passionibus est destinata; unde in iis, quæ formam obtinent, dicitur esse ipsa forma, aut potius ejus præsentia, ad quam consequi potest operatio aut passio. Atque ita secundus erit præsentia ipsius actionis vel passionis, ab illâ priori præsentiâ fluentis. Hæc distinctio usum habet in doctrinâ proprii, quod secundùm actum primum inseparabile est, ut posse loqui, ridere, licet actus fecundus, hoc est praefentia loquelae & risus, auferatur. Ex quibus patet, actum primum omnino ad receptivum pertinere, & fecundum ad activum, ratione fluentis operationis, ad receptivum vero ratione passionis. Ita v. gr. praefentia potentiae humectandi & calefiendi primus actus ac receptivus ipsius aquae est: At ipsa humectationis praefentia actus fecundus & activus est; & ipsius calefactionis passivae praefentia itidem actus fecundus, sed receptivus est.
units.tr: 15. Act is also divided into first and second. First act is called the presence of the aptitude of an essence, by which it is destined for actions or passions. Hence, in things that have a form, it is said to be the form itself, or rather its presence, to which the operation or passion can follow. So the second act will be the presence of the action or passion itself, flowing from that first presence. This distinction has its use in the doctrine of a property: that which is inseparable from a thing according to first act, such as being able to speak or laugh, remains even when the second act, that is, the actual presence of speaking and laughing, is removed. From these points it is plain that first act pertains wholly to the receptive subject, and second act to the active subject, with respect to the operation that flows from it, but to the receptive subject with respect to passion. Thus, for example, the presence of the power of wetting and heating is the first act and receptive act of water. But the actual presence of wetting is second and active act, and the actual presence of being heated, as a passion, is likewise second act, but receptive.

units.la: 16. Dividitur etiam actus, quod fit vel effentia vel existentia, quatenus hujus istiusve praefentia enti tribuitur. Utraque enim entis perfectio est, quare non immerito earum praefentia actus appellatur. Actus autem essentiae est praefentia rei, quatenus ejus esse definitione exprimi potest: at existentiae, quatenus ipsum esse praefens est. Sed haec distinctio omni actui non convenit, nisi reliquarum perfectionum praefentiam, ut consequentium, ad hasce referre velimus: quo pacto tamen actus activus, utpote fecundus, difficulter eo trahi poterit.
units.tr: 16. Act is also divided, into essence or existence, according as the presence of this or that is attributed to a being. For both are perfections of a being, so it is not wrongly that their presence is called act. The act of essence is the presence of a thing insofar as it can be expressed by the definition of its being, but the act of existence is the presence of being itself. However, this distinction does not apply to every act, unless we wish to refer the presence of the remaining perfections, as consequences, to these two. In that way, though, active act, as fruitful, could hardly be brought under them.

units.la: 17. Denique dividitur actus, quod fit vel signatus, vel exercitus. Signatus actus est praefentia perfectionum in idea, id est communi quadam forma aut entitate spectatarum: Exercitus vero praefentia earumrumdem in ipsis rebus, ut præsentibus spectatis. Quare non malè describitur signatus, quod sit actus à singularibus abstractus; & exercitus in singularibus multiplicatus, vid. Iacob. Martin. Disp. 2. Met. th. 60. Usus hujus distinctionis haut mediocris est; ita quippe de essentiâ, causis, effectis &c. agit Metaphysica in actu signato, hoc est signat vel definit, quid illa sint; at Physica in actu exercito, hoc est ea specialiter in corporibus naturalibus inquirit. Et dum quæritur, an genus & individuum definiri possint? Respondendum, posse in actu signato, non in exercito. Plura exempla vide apud Scheiblerum; lib. I. Met. cap. 14. tit. 4. art. 5.
units.tr: 17. Finally, act is divided into signate and exercised. Signate act is the presence of perfections in the idea, that is, as considered in some common form or entity. Exercised act is the presence of the same perfections in the things themselves, as present and observed. So it is not badly described: the signate is act abstracted from singulars, and the exercised is act multiplied in singulars; see Jacob Martin, Disp. 2, Met. th. 60. The use of this distinction is no small one. Metaphysics treats of essence, causes, effects and so on in signate act, that is, it signifies or defines what these things are; but Physics treats of them in exercised act, that is, it inquires into them specifically in natural bodies. And when it is asked whether a genus and an individual can be defined, the answer is that they can be defined in signate act, not in exercised act. For more examples see Scheibler, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 14, tit. 4, art. 5.

units.la: 18. III. Oppositum actus est abstentia sive negatio præsentiæ perfectionum, quæ ipsi actui contradictorie opponitur, adeoque est non-ens, ac dari prorsus nequit; Atque hæc tam actui absoluto, quam respectivo opponitur: Huic autem præterea quasi relative opponitur potentia, quæ ab absoluto plane abest, ob summam ac infinitam, quam præsupponit, perfectionem.
units.tr: 18. III. The opposite of act is privation, or the denial of the presence of perfections, which is contradictorily opposed to act itself, and so is a non-being and cannot exist at all. This is opposed to absolute act as well as to relative act. To this, however, potency is, as it were, relatively opposed, and it is wholly absent from absolute act, on account of the supreme and infinite perfection which that act presupposes.

units.la: 19. Potentia igitur ratio ac natura penitius enucleanda, quare videndum 1. ejus nomen. 2. quid ipsa in suâ entitate contineat?
units.tr: 19. Potency's nature and essence must therefore be investigated more closely, so we must consider 1. its name; 2. what it itself contains in its own entity.

units.la: 20. Nomen potentia a posse habet, quod est quasi virtute pollere, quare sic primò aptitudinem agendi, sive actionis præsen-tiæ tiæ denotat; atque deinde quamcunque aptitudinem, tam ad patiendum, quam ad agendum, denotat, atque ita ipsi Græcum δωάμεως respondet. Dicitur quandoque & potestas, quæ tamen vox potius jus vel autoritatem in agendo designat, sive vires sufficiant, sive secus, hoc est sive adsit potentia, sive desit; Huic quippe æquivalet Græcum ἐξουσία, λὰ τῆ ἰξεσι, licitum est, nomen habens.
units.tr: 20. The word potency comes from posse, which is, as it were, to be strong in power. So first it denotes the aptitude for acting, or the presence of action; and then it denotes any aptitude, whether for suffering or for acting, and so corresponds to the Greek [δυνάμεως]. It is sometimes also called potestas, though this word rather designates right or authority in acting, whether or not the powers are sufficient, that is, whether or not potency is present. For to this corresponds the Greek ἐξουσία, it is permitted [ἔξεστι], which has the sense of "it is lawful."

units.la: 21. In re ipsâ explicandum, Primò, quid sit? Secundo, quomodo dividenda sit?
units.tr: 21. In the thing itself it must be explained: first, what it is; second, how it is to be divided.

units.la: 22. Primò, definitio potentiæ non minus difficilis videtur, ac fuit ipsius actus, quia omni actui, solo absoluto excepto, opponitur, adeoque latissimè vagatur: describitur autem, quod sit aptitudo agendi vel patiendi; Quo designatur, ipsam 1. negare actum hoc est præsentiam actionis, & passionis. 2. includere aptitudinem & non repugnantiam ad illam præsentiam. 3. non esse nisi illius actus, eui illa non repugnantia subest, non omnis.
units.tr: 22. First, the definition of potency seems no less difficult than that of act itself, since it is opposed to every act except absolute act, and so ranges very widely. It is described as an aptitude for acting or suffering. By this it is indicated that it 1. denies act, that is, the presence of action and of passion; 2. includes an aptitude and a non-repugnance to that presence; 3. is not of every act, but only of that act to which that non-repugnance belongs.

units.la: 23. Secundò, divisio potentiæ est, quod sit, vel activa vel passiva. Activa est aptitudo ad præsentiam actionis, adeoque omni actui activo opponitur. Estque infinita, vel finita. Infinita, aliter omnipotentia dicta, est aptitudo ad præsentiam actionum divinarum, sive illæ ordinariæ fuerint, sive extraordinariæ.
units.tr: 23. Second, the division of potency is that it is either active or passive. Active potency is an aptitude for the presence of action, and so it is opposed to every active act. It is either infinite or finite. Infinite potency, otherwise called omnipotence, is an aptitude for the presence of divine actions, whether these are ordinary or extraordinary.

units.la: 24. Finita potentia creaturarum est ; Quæ varia admodum : Et quidem primò vel rationalis est, vel irrationalis. Rationalis, quæ creaturarum intelligentium est, vel intellectus, vel voluntas est. Irrationalis est potentia, quâ reliqua corpora naturalia actionibus suis præsunt ; Talis igitur est potentia calefaciendi in sole & igni, trahendi ferrum in magnete, purgandi bilem in Rhabarbaro ; Possuntque tales distingui, quod sint vel animatæ vel inanimatæ; prout vel viventibus, vel aliis corporibus conveniunt. Secundò potentia finita vel est nativa, vel adventitia. Nativa simpliciter potentia dicitur, adventitia verò dispositio, vel habitus, si rei intelligenti accedat.
units.tr: 24. Finite potency belongs to creatures, and it is very varied. First, it is either rational or irrational. Rational potency belongs to the intelligent creatures, and is either of the intellect or of the will. Irrational potency is that by which the remaining natural bodies are capable of their actions. Such is the potency of heating in the sun and in fire, of drawing iron in a magnet, of purging bile in rhubarb. Such potencies can be distinguished as either animate or inanimate, according as they belong to living things or to other bodies. Second, finite potency is either native or acquired. Native potency is called simply potency, while acquired potency is a disposition or habit, if it comes to an intelligent thing.

units.la: 25. Passiva potentia est aptitudo patiendi, omnique actui passivo opponitur, quare & secundum ejus divisiones distinguitur, quòd sit vel existendi, vel recipiendi. Potentia existendi est non-repugnantia ad præsentiam existentiæ, ac aliter dicitur 1. Potentia objectiva, quia per illam, quod non est, fieri potest objectum agentis alicujus, ipsum existere producentis. 2. Potentia Logica, quia ex non contradictione terminorum ex parte æstimatur. 3. Potentia non-subjectiva, quia subjectum non præsupponit prius, sed saltem simul cum ipsâ actione, quâ & subjectum & ipsius actus existit. Est igitur hæc illa potentia, secundum quam aliquid absolutè dicitur possibile, quare impotentia, illi oppofita, ipsa est impoffibilitas.
units.tr: 25. Passive potency is aptitude for suffering, opposed to every passive act; and so it is distinguished, according to its divisions, as being either of existing or of receiving. The potency of existing is non-repugnance to the presence of existence, and it is otherwise called 1. objective potency, because through it what is not can become the object of some agent producing its existence; 2. logical potency, because it is judged from the non-contradiction of the terms; 3. non-subjective potency, because it does not presuppose a subject beforehand, but only together with the very action by which both the subject and its act exist. This, then, is that potency by which something is said absolutely to be possible, so that impotence, opposed to it, is itself impossibility.

units.la: 26. Potentia recipiendi est nonrepugnantia, five aptitudo, aliquid in fe actione alterius acquirendi, diciturque alias fubjectiva, quod subjectum prius præfupponat, in quo agens agendo aliquid efficiat. Estque hæc duplex, naturalis & præternaturalis: Prior est aptitudo, quâ rei substare potest actioni ordinario naturæ cursu ipsi debitæ, qualis est in materiâ ad recipiendas formas naturales, à naturâ; Hæc igitur Physica dicitur potentia, quod fecundum naturam perfici possit. Posterior est aptitudo, quâ res substare potest actioni extraordinariæ alicujus agentis, five Dei, five artificis, qualis est in lapidibus, ut jussu Dei fieri possint panes, & in æstre, ut ex eo fiat statua. Aliter hæc obedientialis dicitur potentia, quia per illam res apta est obedire eminentiori alicui agenti: Quin & Metaphysica dici potest, quâtenus ratione unius fui modi supernaturali jussu Dei completur.
units.tr: 26. The potency of receiving is non-repugnance, or aptitude, for acquiring something in itself by the action of another, and it is otherwise called subjective, because it presupposes a prior subject in which the agent, by acting, produces something. It is twofold, natural and preternatural. The former is an aptitude by which a thing can undergo the action due to it in the ordinary course of nature, as matter has it for receiving natural forms, from nature. This is therefore called physical potency, because it can be perfected according to nature. The latter is an aptitude by which a thing can undergo the extraordinary action of some agent, whether God or an artisan; such is the aptitude of stones, that bread may be made from them at God's command, and of bronze, that a statue may be made from it. This is otherwise called obediential potency, because through it the thing is apt to obey some higher agent. Indeed it can also be called metaphysical, insofar as by one of its supernatural modes it is completed at God's command.

units.la: 27. IV. Axiomata ex hac doctrina prognata, hæc videntur potissima. 1. Actui infinito nulla respondet potentia; videlicet passiva; eo quippe non auffertur ab ipso potentia activa, quâ ipse efficax fit, ea tamen ipsi non respondet, ut per illam actus fiat. Ratio axiomatis, ex ipsa definitione actus puri seu infiniti desumitur. Hinc igitur Deus 1. non potest non-esse. 2. non potest mutari. 3. à nullo extrinseco pati aut determinari. 4. nullum accidens recipere &c.
units.tr: 27. IV. The axioms that follow from this doctrine seem to be the chief ones. 1. To infinite act no potency corresponds, namely passive potency. For it is not removed from it by active potency, by which it is made effective; yet passive potency does not correspond to it, so that act might come about through it. The reason for this axiom is drawn from the very definition of pure or infinite act. Hence God 1. cannot not-be; 2. cannot be changed; 3. cannot suffer or be determined by anything external; 4. cannot receive any accident, and so on.

units.la: 28. II. Finito actui respondet potentia. Ratio est, quia omnis talis actus respectivus est. Hinc igitur Creaturæ possunt 1. non-esse. 2. mutari. 3. ab extrinseco pati ac determinari. 4. accidentia recipere. Et 5. ab extrinseco fieri ac conservari debent.
units.tr: 28. II. Finite act corresponds to potency. The reason is that every such act is relative. Hence creatures can 1. not-be; 2. be changed; 3. suffer and be determined from outside; 4. receive accidents. And 5. they must be made and preserved from outside.

units.la: 29. III. Quod non potest esse actus, ejus nulla est potentia. Dicit quippe potentia aptitudinem & non-repugnantiam ad præsentiam sive actum, quare negatâ hac aptitudine, negatur & ipsa potentia. Hinc igitur, quia creatura actu esse nequit æterna, nullam quoque æternitatis habet potentiam; Huic æquivalet & hoc, impossibilis non est actus; Est enim impossibile, cujus nulla est potentia.
units.tr: 29. III. That of which there cannot be act, of it there is no potency. For potency denotes an aptitude and non-repugnance to presence or act, so when this aptitude is denied, potency itself is denied. Hence, since a creature cannot actually be eternal, it has also no potency of eternity. This amounts to the same as saying an act is not impossible; for that is impossible of which there is no potency.

units.la: 30. IV. Posito actu præsupponitur potentia. Fluit id ex tertio; nihil igitur fit, nisi quod possibile ante à erat.
units.tr: 30. IV. Posited act presupposes potency. This follows from the third axiom; nothing therefore comes to be except what was previously possible.

units.la: 31. V. Propter actum est potentia; non contra, actus propter potentiam; Persectio quippe est actus, at hæc finis est, propter quem sint media oportet. Hinc igitur propter victoriam imperator milites colligit, non victoriam parat propter milites: Et consimiliter propter doctrinam exercendum ingenium, non ingenii gratia doctrina.
units.tr: 31. V. Potency exists for the sake of act, not the reverse, act for the sake of potency. For act is perfection, and this is the end for the sake of which the means must exist. Hence a commander gathers soldiers for the sake of victory; he does not prepare victory for the sake of the soldiers. Similarly, the mind is exercised for the sake of learning, not learning for the sake of the mind.

units.la: 32. VI. Actus melior est potentia. Ratio est, quia finis praestantior mediis, & perfectio praestantior ejus absentia. Hinc exercitium virtutis habitu praestantius est; Habitus quippe potentia saltem exercendi est.
units.tr: 32. VI. Act is better than potency. The reason is that the end is more excellent than the means, and perfection is more excellent than its absence. Hence the exercise of a virtue is more excellent than the habit; for a habit is, at least, the potency of exercising it.

units.la: 33. VII. Potentia prior est actu, videlicet in genesi: Cum in intentione & analysi actus prior sit potentia; intellige hoc de actu & potentia, prout se mutuo respiciunt, alias quippe absolute actus prior est omni modo potentia.
units.tr: 33. VII. Potency is prior to act, namely in genesis: since in intention and in analysis potency is prior to act. Understand this of act and potency as they stand in relation to each other; for otherwise, absolutely speaking, act is prior to potency in every respect.

units.la: 34. VIII. Nihil in potentia existens, seipsum educit in actum. Ratio est, quia idem seipso non est praestantius, adeoque sibi ipsi non confert perfectionem, quam non habuit, sed saltem habere potuit. Hinc itaque creaturae se ipsis agere non possunt, quia ad actiones suas sunt in potentia, quare requiritur praecursus causae primae, illam potentiam ad actum applicans &c. Et haec de Actu & potentia dicta sufficient.
units.tr: 34. VIII. Nothing existing in potency educes itself into act. The reason is that the same thing is not more excellent than itself, and so it does not confer on itself a perfection which it did not have but could only have had. Hence creatures cannot act of themselves, because for their actions they are in potency; therefore the prior action of a first cause is required, applying that potency to act, etc. And let what has been said about act and potency suffice.

units.la: CAP. XVI. DE Utilitate, seu Boni- tate externa.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. On Utility, or External Goodness.

units.la: 1. ENS actu habens suas perfectiones si referatur ad aliud aliquod, ei conveniens esse judicatur, adeo ut ipsi aliquod commodum praestare possit, unde tunc ens bonum, externa videlicet & relata ad consequens aliquod bonitate, dicitur. Commodius tamen haec bonitas utilitas dicitur; vel & amabilitas, quae tamen potius est utilitatis quaedam denominatio, quatenus ob ejus perceptionem, in objecto oritur desiderium & appetitus, vel complacentia quaedam circa ens, utilitatem illam praestans.
units.tr: 1. A being that actually possesses its perfections, if it is referred to some other thing, is judged to be suitable (conveniens) to that thing, so that it can render some advantage to it; then the being is called good, that is, good in an external sense and in relation to some consequent benefit. This goodness is more commonly called utility; or also amiability, which, however, is rather a certain denomination of utility, insofar as on account of its perception there arises in the object a desire and appetite, or a certain complacency towards the being that renders that utility.

units.la: 2. Missa autem hac denominatione, utilitas explicanda hisce titulis 1. Quid sit?
units.tr: 2. Setting aside this designation, utility is to be explained under the following headings: 1. What it is?

units.la: 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quid illi subjecto superaddat? 4. Quaenam ejus differentia? 5. Quaenam axiomata? 6. Quodnam ejus oppositum.
units.tr: 2. What is its subject? 3. What does it add to that subject? 4. What are its differences? 5. What are its axioms? 6. What is its opposite?

units.la: 3. I. Definitur utilitas, convenientia Entis cum alio: sed non satis distincte; convenientia enim non semper est consensus rerum ad finem. Rectius igitur, utilitas est exercitium actus, alteri commodum asse-rens. rens. Dicitur, exercitium, actus, quia persectiones actu possessæ non dicuntur utiles, nisi exerceantur: dicitur, alteri commodum afferens, quia ideo dicitur quid alteri utile, quia vel ipsius tanquam finis medium est; vel simul cum ipso ad alium finem communem conspirat.
units.tr: 3. I. Utility is defined as the agreement of a being with another; but not distinctly enough, for agreement is not always the consensus of things towards an end. More rightly, therefore, utility is the exercise of an act, conferring an advantage on another. It is said "the exercise of an act" because perfections possessed actually are not called useful unless they are exercised; it is said "conferring an advantage on another" because something is called useful to another either because it is a means to that other's end, or because it cooperates together with that other towards another common end.

units.la: 4. II. Subjectum utilitatis est vel primarium vel secundarium. Illudque vel ultimatum sive formale, vel non-ultimatum, sive materiale. Formale est illa ipsa ratio, propter quam Ens convenire aut commodum præstare censetur. Materiale autem est ipsum ens, illam rationem in se habens, hoc est actum illum possidens. Neque hoc unquam potest esse non-ens, utpote quod ignotum est: ignoti autem nulla cupido. Et 2. subjectum illud debet commodum alteri præstare; atque nil nisi ens usum præstat. 3. Debet illam rationem in se continere, quod solius entis est. Subjectum secundarium sunt modi & actiones, quibus, tanquam mediis, usus haberi potest.
units.tr: 4. II. The subject of utility is either primary or secondary. And the primary is either ultimate, or formal, or non-ultimate, or material. The formal is that very reason on account of which a being is judged to be suitable or to render an advantage. The material is the being itself, having that reason in itself, that is, possessing that act. This can never be a non-being, since that is unknown, and nothing unknown is desired. And, second, that subject ought to render an advantage to another; and only a being renders use. Third, it must contain that reason in itself, which belongs only to a being. The secondary subject are the modes and actions by which, as means, use can be had.

units.la: 5. Objectum hujus utilitatis stricte si velis sumere, est illud tantum, quod ipsum bonum ad se redundans cognoscit, ac sibi conveniens judicat; Omne enim hoc mo- do bonum sive utile, finis aut medii rationem habet: At finis & medium, non nisi ab intelligente cognoscuntur. At si latius capias, erit omne illud, cui usus aliquis accommodatur, sive illum cognoscat, sive non.
units.tr: 5. If you wish to take the object of this utility strictly, it is only that which recognises the good flowing back to itself and judges it suitable to itself; for every good or useful thing of this kind has the character of end or means, and ends and means are recognised only by an intelligent being. But if you take it more broadly, it will be everything to which some use is adapted, whether or not it recognises it.
