units.la: 6. Hæc igitur bonitas non est Entis affectio interna, quia juxta hanc nihil per se ipsum bonum est; nec est modus, utpote nullam mutationem afferens, sed nudus respectus aut relatio, cujus fundamentum est indigentia aut voluptas quædam, quæ isto usu solvitur.
units.tr: 6. This goodness, therefore, is not an internal affection of a being, since according to this nothing is good in itself; nor is it a mode, since it brings about no change, but is a bare respect or relation, whose foundation is need or some pleasure that is satisfied by this use.

units.la: 7. Differentiæ variæbono assignatæ sunt, Et quidem 1. est vel verum, vel apparens. Verum est, quod ita se habet, ut esse judicatur : Apparens autem, quod usum illum, qui ab ipso exspectatur, præstare nequit. Sed hæc divisio non est accipienda, ac si bonum aliquod esset, quod non appereret; Nam si id bonum dicatur, quod bonum judicatur, omne bonum apparens dici potest, sive id appareat uti est, ut verum; sive secus, ut apparens strictè dictum.
units.tr: 7. Various differences have been assigned to the good. First, it is either true or apparent. The true is that which is such as it is judged to be; the apparent is that which cannot render the use that is expected from it. But this division is not to be understood as if there were some good that does not appear; for if that is called good which is judged good, every good can be called apparent, whether it appears as it is, as true, or otherwise, as apparent strictly speaking.

units.la: 8. 2. Bonum est vel per se, vel per accidens; Prius est, quod usum speratum præstat: Posterius verò, quod ex inopinato aliquod commodum præber, ut sunt casualia ac fortuita.
units.tr: 8. Second, the good is either per se or per accidens. The former is that which renders the hoped-for use; the latter, however, is that which provides some advantage unexpectedly, as things that are accidental and fortuitous do.

units.la: 9. 3. Bonum est vel materiale, vel formale: Illud est, quod rei inanimatæ & non intelligenti aliquod commodum præbet: Hoc verò, quod homini & intelligenti usum præstat; Estque hoc duplex, internum corpori & animæ hominis usum necessarium suppeditans; & externum, quorsum pertinent divitiæ, honores &c.
units.tr: 9. Third, the good is either material or formal. The former is that which provides some advantage to a thing that is inanimate and not intelligent; the latter, which renders use to a man and an intelligent being. And this is twofold: internal, supplying the use necessary to the body and soul of man; and external, to which belong riches, honours, etc.

units.la: 10. 4. Bonum est vel honestum, vel utile, vel jucundum: Honestum ad mores & vitam spectat, adeoque aut virtus, aut virtutis est actio; utile dicitur, quod requiritur ad bene esse, quemadmodum jucundum ad melius esse.
units.tr: 10. Fourth, the good is either honourable, or useful, or pleasant. The honourable concerns morals and life, and so is either a virtue or an action of virtue; the useful is said of what is required for well-being, just as the pleasant is for better being.

units.la: 11. 5. Bonum est vel summum, vel medium. Summum est, quod ultimi finis rationem habet: Medium vero, quod ad illum finem dirigitur, sive necessario, & dicitur bonum absolutum; sive ex hypothesi & conditione, & dicitur bonum hypotheticum & arbitrarium.
units.tr: 11. Fifth, the good is either supreme or intermediate. The supreme is that which has the character of ultimate end; the intermediate is that which is directed to that end, either necessarily, and is called absolute good; or by hypothesis and condition, and is called hypothetical and arbitrary good.

units.la: 12. Inter axiomata hæc sunt potissima.
units.tr: 12. Among the axioms these are the chief.

units.la: 1. Finis & bonum convertuntur. Ratio est, quia sicut bonum usus gratia, ita & finis propter eundem expetitur. Hinc igitur, objectum voluntatis semper est bonum. 2. Omne bonum est sui communicativum: videlicet ratione suæ utilitatis, non ratione essentiæ. Ratio est, quia omne bonum commodum præstare debet. Non igitur bonum dicendum, quod nulli rei usum præstat. 3. Omne bonum est appetibile; Ratio est, quia finis rationem habet. 4. Quo bonum superius, eo melius. Ratio est, quia id magis appetitur; majoremque usum sum praestat. Hinc igitur summum bonum est optimum & infinitum.
units.tr: 1. End and good are convertible. The reason is that just as the good is desired for the sake of use, so too the end is desired on the same account. Hence, therefore, the object of the will is always good. 2. Every good is communicative of itself: namely by reason of its utility, not by reason of its essence. The reason is that every good ought to render some advantage. Therefore that should not be called good which renders use to no thing. 3. Every good is desirable; the reason is that it has the character of an end. 4. The higher the good, the better. The reason is that it is more desired and renders greater use. Hence the supreme good is best and infinite.

units.la: 13. Malitia huic bonitati opposita, aliter inutilitas dicitur, estque difconvenientia Entis cum alio, quâ illi non tantum usum nullum, sed & damnum praestat; Ac bonitati contrariè oppanitur. Quare hoc modo ens dividi potest in bonum & malum, sive in utile & inutile, ratione videlicet alterius alicujus entis, cui vel usum vel noxam infert. Atque hinc patet malum hoc iisdem modis dividi posse ac bonum.
units.tr: 13. Malice, opposed to this goodness, is otherwise called uselessness, and is the disagreement of a being with another, by which it renders to that other not only no use but also harm; and it is contrary to goodness. Hence in this way a being can be divided into good and evil, or into useful and useless, namely with respect to some other being to which it brings either use or harm. And hence it is evident that evil can be divided in the same ways as good.

units.la: 14. Dubium tamen est, an prout summum datur bonum, omnibus usum praestans, etiam summum detur malum, omnibus nocens? Resp. Si summum malum dicatur, quod nullius respectu bonum est, ita nullum datur: At si illud accipiatur, quod summam huic vel illi perniciem affert, ita negandum non videtur: Ita mors animantis ut sic, summum malum, & aeterna condemnatio ipsis impiis. Atque haec de Utilitate, seu bonitate externâ.
units.tr: 14. It is doubtful, however, whether, if a supreme good is given that renders use to all, a supreme evil is also given that harms all. Answer: if the supreme evil is taken to be that which is good in respect of nothing, then none is given; but if it is taken to be that which brings the greatest ruin to this or that thing, it does not seem to be denied: thus the death of a living creature as such is the supreme evil, and eternal condemnation for the impious themselves. And these things concerning Utility, or external goodness.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: DE Dependente & Independente.
units.tr: Of the Dependent and the Independent.

units.la: 1. FUerunt hactenus affectiones maximâ ex parte absoluta, sequuntur respe-ctiva Ξίvα, Enti ob respectum ad aliud aliquod tributæ, quæ supra allato ordine breviter pertexendæ veniunt, ac ex relationibus suis eruendæ. Primò autem occurrit dependentia, quæ primitus corporibus tributa videtur, quorum unum alteri annexum aut alligatum, ab ipso, aliàs dilabendum, sustentatur, postea autem à Metaphysicis ad significandam fuftentationem unius Entis ab alio ratione τῆ εἶναι potissimum, adhibita fuit.
units.tr: 1. Hitherto we have had affections, for the most part absolute; there follow the respective ones, attributed to a being on account of its relation to something else. These must be set out briefly in the order given above and drawn out from their relations. First comes dependence, which was originally attributed to bodies, where one body, attached or tied to another, is held up by it lest it otherwise fall apart. Later, however, the Metaphysicians adopted it, chiefly to signify the sustaining of one being by another with respect to its being [τῷ εἶναι].

units.la: 2. Sumitur autem vel pro denominatione, vel pro relatione: Priori modo opponitur independentia, atque ita nihil aliud est, quam positiva constitutio, quemadmodum independentia est negativa: Posteriori verò est ipse ordo, inter positivè conftitutum, ejusque constituens, intercedens, quomodo hîc accipi debet.
units.tr: 2. It is taken either as a denomination or as a relation. In the former sense it is opposed to independence, and so it is nothing other than a positive constitution, just as independence is negative. In the latter sense it is the order itself, lying between what is positively constituted and that which constitutes it, and it is in this sense that it must be understood here.

units.la: 3. Est autem dependentia, relatio interna, inter talia, quorum unum alteri debet suum esse; sive quorum unum alterum exigit ad suum esse. Quoniam igitur relatio est, præcisè subjecto sive Enti alicui non inhæret, sed potius inter duo Entia intercedens, utrumque denominat, & quidem extrinsecè plerumque.
units.tr: 3. Dependence is an internal relation between such things, one of which must owe its being to the other; or of which one requires the other for its being. Since, therefore, it is a relation, it does not inhere precisely in some subject or being, but lies between two beings and denominates both, and indeed for the most part extrinsically.

units.la: 4. Locum habet, positâ entium multitudine, quemadmodum & omnis relatio ordinaria; non verò, si Ens unicum absolutè consideretur: Quare negata crea-
units.tr: 4. It holds where there is a plurality of beings, as does every ordinary relation; but not if a single being is considered absolutely. Hence with the creature denied,

units.la: creaereaturâ, negatur dependentia.
units.tr: dependence is denied.

units.la: 5. Axiomata utilissima hinc oriuntur, quorum hæc potissima, I. In omni dependentiâ sunt duo; Ratio est, quia debet esse unum, quod debet alteri suum esse, & alterum cui debet. Hinc igitur, idem non est sui ipsius causa, quia sic à seipso dependeret, & dependentia esset sine duobus.
units.tr: 5. Very useful axioms arise from this, of which these are the chief. I. In every dependence there are two. The reason is that there must be one which owes its being, and another to which it is owed. Hence the same thing is not the cause of itself, for in that case it would depend on itself, and the dependence would be without two.

units.la: 6. II. In omni dependentia est aliquis ordo; Quia omnis dependentia relatio est; Et quo pacto sine ordine unum alteri esse concederet? Unde negato omni prorsus ordine, negatur & dependentia.
units.tr: 6. II. In every dependence there is some order. Because every dependence is a relation; and how could one thing grant its being to another without order? Hence, once all order is denied, dependence is denied too.

units.la: 7. III. In omni dependentia est aliquod primum; Ratio est, quia in omni est ordo, & in omni ordine est aliquod primum. Hinc igitur in serie causarum & effectorum vitandus omnis in infinitum progressus; Et consimiliter hinc una ali-qua causa erit prima.
units.tr: 7. III. In every dependence there is something first. The reason is that in everything there is order, and in every order there is something first. Hence, in the series of causes and effects, every infinite progression must be avoided; and similarly, some one cause will be first.

units.la: 8. IV. In omni dependentia est independens, & dependens. Ratio est, quia duo requiruntur, quorum unum primum est, adeoque independens, alterum postremum & dependens. Illud autem independens & primum, vel absolute est tale, quod nullâ ratione fit dependens, estque ipse Deus, qui omnis Entis dependentis causa est independens prorsus: Vel in suo genere, qualia sunt, quæ principii, L causæ, vel subjecti rationem inter creaturas induunt.
units.tr: 8. IV. In every dependence there is an independent and a dependent. The reason is that two are required, of which one is first and so independent, the other last and dependent. That independent and first thing is either absolutely such, being that which in no respect becomes dependent, and this is God himself, who is wholly independent and the cause of every dependent being; or it is so in its own kind, as are those things which take on the character of principle, cause, or subject among creatures.

units.la: 9. V. Nihil est in dependente, quod non prius fuerit in independente, vel virtute, vel eminentiâ, vel formâ. Ratio est, quia quod tribuit esse, tribuit quoque omnia consequentia ad esse: Nihil autem alteri tribuit, quod ipsum non habet. Hinc igitur effectum toto genere dignius non est suâ causâ; Et nemo plus juris alteri concedere potest, quam ipsemet habuit.
units.tr: 9. V. Nothing is in the dependent which was not first in the independent, either virtually, eminently, or formally. The reason is that what grants being also grants all the consequences of being; but nothing is granted to another that the granter does not itself have. Hence an effect is not more worthy than its cause in its whole kind; and no one can concede to another more right than he himself has had.

units.la: 10. VI. Posito dependente, ponitur independens, ipsi proportionatum. Ratio est, quia dependens non est sine suo esse: At hoc debet independenti; Hinc positâ creatura ponendus Creator independens.
units.tr: 10. VI. Given the dependent, the independent proportioned to it is posited. The reason is that the dependent is not without its being; but this it owes to the independent. Hence, given a creature, a Creator who is independent must be posited.

units.la: 11. Ab hac dependentiâ Ens vel independens vel dependens dicitur; Independens autem vel absolutè vel relativè: Absolutè independens est, quod alteri esse non debet; idque vel positivè, quomodo solus Deus independens est; vel negativè, quomodo non-ens nulli sum esse, utpote quod non habet, debet; Atque ita mera est negatio, utpote ipsum nihil. Relativè independens est, quod alteri esse tribuit, & hic potissimum attenditur. Estque vel primum & summum, vel secundum & medium, prout illud esse tribuit, ita ut illud alteri quoque debeat, vel non.
units.tr: 11. From this dependence a being is called either independent or dependent. The independent is either absolutely or relatively so. That is absolutely independent which does not owe its being to another; and this is either positively, as God alone is independent; or negatively, as non-being owes its being to nothing, since it does not have it, and so is mere negation, being nothing. That is relatively independent which grants being to another, and this is chiefly what is in view here. It is either first and highest, or second and intermediate, according as the being it grants is itself owed to another or not.

units.la: 12. Dependens Ens est, quod alteri suum esse debet, Quale est omne creatum ; finitum, mutabile ; Hoc autem, quod esse suum alteri debet,etiam debet esse sui continuationem', & operationem, utpote quae consequuntur ad esse; Quare omne creatum dependens est, ut in fiendo, ita & in essendo, & operando.
units.tr: 12. A dependent being is that which owes its being to another, such as every created thing: finite, mutable. And what owes its being to another must also owe the continuation of its being and its operation, since these follow upon being. Hence every created thing is dependent, in becoming, in being, and in acting alike.

units.la: 13. Dependentia variis modis dividitur: & quidem primo, quod sit vel essentialis, vel naturalis: Prior dicitur, qua ens debet suum esse, ita ut sine illa exigentia ne quidem divina virtute esse possit: posterior, qua naturam debet, adeo ut illa exigentia Dei virtute tolli possit. Sed absurditatum plena distinctio, in patrocinium foedi erroris, de conservatione Accidentis extra subjectum, conficta. Nam 1. Omnis dependentia est essentialis. 2. Etiam naturalis est essentialis, quoniam natura & essentia dependens idem sunt. 3. Implicat, respectivum ac dependens in esse, fieri absolutum ac independens.
units.tr: 13. Dependence is divided in various ways. First, into essential or natural. The former is that by which a being owes its being, so that without that requirement it cannot exist even by divine power; the latter is that by which it owes its nature, so that the requirement can be removed by divine power. But this distinction is full of absurdities, devised in defence of the foul error concerning the conservation of an accident outside its subject. For: 1. Every dependence is essential. 2. Even the natural is essential, since the nature and essence of the dependent are the same. 3. It implies that what is relative and dependent in being becomes absolute and independent.

units.la: 14. Secundo dividitur dependentia, quod sit, vel a priori, vel a posteriori; Prior est, qua Ens dependet a priori aliquo: Posterior, qua a consequente aliquo. Sed ultima haec dependentia est membrum divisio repugnans; Omnis etenim dependentia a priori, ut pote ab independente est.
units.tr: 14. Secondly, dependence is divided into that which is from a prior or from a posterior. The former is that by which a being depends on some prior thing; the latter, on some consequent thing. But this last dependence is a member of a division that contradicts itself, for every dependence on a prior is on something independent.

units.la: 15. Tertio dispescitur in dependentiam absolutam, & contractam, sive relatam. Quarum illa personis S. S. Trinitatis tribuitur. Verùm inter has nulla dependentia locum habet, utpote ubi talis posserioritas ac prioritas exulat. Neque dari potest eo modo dependentia absoluta, quoniam omnis independens præsupponit.
units.tr: 15. Thirdly, it is divided into absolute and contracted, or related, dependence. Of these, the former is attributed to the persons of the Holy Trinity. Yet no dependence has a place among these, since there such posteriority and priority are absent. Nor can absolute dependence exist in that way, since every dependent presupposes an independent.

units.la: 16. Quartò dependentia alia est causativa, alia subjectiva. Illa est, quâ aliquod dependet a sua causâ, diciturque causalitas. Hæc verò, quâ dependet a subjecto, diciturque inhærentia; quibus communis est dependentia Principialis, inter Principium & principiatum intercedens. Additur à nonnullis dependentia objectiva, quâ Relationes dependere dicuntur à fundamentis & terminis. At illa admittenda non videtur, quoniam dependentia Entium est affectio: Sed relationes entia non sunt. Aut si Entia dicuntur, accidentia erunt, adeòque inhærentia, sive subjectivâ dependentia contentæ esse deberent. Atque hæc de Dependentiâ.
units.tr: 16. Fourthly, one dependence is causative, another subjective. The former is that by which something depends on its cause, and it is called causality; the latter, by which it depends on a subject, and it is called inherence. Common to both is the principial dependence, which lies between a principle and what is derived from it. Some add objective dependence, by which relations are said to depend on foundations and terms. But this does not seem admissible, since the dependence of beings is an affection, whereas relations are not beings. Or if they are called beings, they will be accidents, and so should be contained within inherence or subjective dependence. So much on Dependence.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: DE Principio & Principiato.
units.tr: On Principle and Principiate.

units.la: 1. Quoniam omnis dependentia inter prius & posterius, hinc ab ipsâ Ens dicitur principii, quod prius est, & Principiatū, quod posterius est. Solet tamen Principii appellatio etiam latius extendi, ad denotandam quamcunque originationem, quæ tamen semper dependentiam non admittit; Quâ tamen hîc tractandum videtur Principium, ut generalis ejus notio declaretur.
units.tr: 1. Since every dependence holds between the prior and the posterior, the being itself is therefore called the principle (principium) insofar as it is prior, and the principiate insofar as it is posterior. Yet the name "principle" is commonly extended more broadly, to denote any origination whatever, though this does not always admit of dependence. Here, however, the principle seems to be treated in that sense, so that its general notion may be made clear.

units.la: 2. Dicitur autem Principium quasi primarum partium capium, quòd prioris alicujus rationem plerumque obtineat; Quare & cujuslibet quantitatis terminus primus, ultimo, qui finis appellatur, oppositus, Principium dicitur, sive hoc fiat, positive, ita ut etiam reliquæ partes adsint, sive negative, ut nulla alia extremitas admittatur; Quomodo primus est sol, licet unicus sit. Eâ tamen significatione hîc explicandum non est, quoniam nullam ea infert connexionem inter hoc & principiatum, aut illud cujus est principium.
units.tr: 2. A principle is said to be, as it were, "the captain of the first parts" (quasi primarum partium capium), because it mostly holds the place of something prior. Hence also the first term of any quantity, opposed to the last, which is called the end, is called a principle, whether this happens positively, so that the remaining parts are also present, or negatively, so that no other extremity is admitted; thus the sun is first, although it is unique. This sense, however, need not be explained here, since it implies no connection between this and the principiate, or between that and what it is the principle of.

units.la: 3. Missis autem variis ipsius vocis significationibus, angustioribus & latioribus, Principium hîc est, à quo aliquatenus priori aliquid cum ipso cohærens procedit. Quæ definitio generalis admodum est, ut quæ non tantum principio dependentiæ, sed etiam originationis, in quo Principium & id cujus est principium realiter idem sunt, convenire debet.
units.tr: 3. Setting aside the various meanings of the word, narrower and wider, a principle here is that from which something coheres with the prior thing and proceeds from it in some way. This general definition is quite broad, since it ought to apply not only to the principle of dependence but also to that of origination, in which the principle and that of which it is the principle are really the same.

units.la: 4. Ex hac autem definitione generalia documenta, sive axiomata deduci possunt; Qualia sunt. 1. Omne principium aliquo modo prius est, eo cujus est principium. Nam principium, ab eo cujus est principium praesupponitur: At omne praesuppositum est aliquo modo prius praesupponente. Dicitur autem aliquo modo; non enim requiritur, ut sit prius vel tempore, vel natura stricte dicta: sed sufficit si prius sit originatione, ut supra circa Entis principia notatum fuit. Dicitur autem potius prius eo cujus est principium, quam principiato; Quoniam haec vox soli principio dependentiae ex communi usu loquendi opponitur; Unde licet Pater in S.S. Trinitate dicatur Principium filii, non tamen Filius dicitur principiatum; Et quamvis Constitutio & distinctio dicantur Entis principia, non tamen Ens recte dicitur principiatum.
units.tr: 4. From this definition, general rules or axioms can be deduced, which are as follows. 1. Every principle is in some way prior to that of which it is the principle. For the principle is presupposed by that of which it is the principle; but everything presupposed is in some way prior to what presupposes it. It is said "in some way," for it is not required that it be prior either in time or in nature strictly speaking; it is enough if it is prior in origination, as was noted above concerning the principles of being. It is said, moreover, that it is prior to that of which it is the principle rather than to the principiate, since this word is opposed, in common usage, only to the principle of dependence. Hence, although the Father in the Holy Trinity is called the Principle of the Son, the Son is not called a principiate; and although constitution and distinction are called principles of a being, a being is not rightly called a principiate.

units.la: §. II. Ab omni principio aliquo modo est id, cujus est principium. Nam alias nulla ratio dari posset, quare hoc potius, quam illud esset principium. Dicitur autem aliquo modo a principio esse, id cujus est principium, non semper omni modo, aut stricto illo, quo ab aliquo esse, vel efficienti tantum, vel & omni principio dependentiae tribuitur.
units.tr: §. II. Everything that is the principle of something is in some way from that principle. For otherwise no reason could be given why this should be the principle rather than that. It is said that that of which it is the principle is in some way from the principle, not always in every way, nor in that strict sense in which something is from something, namely only as efficient cause, or as the principle of dependence in general is ascribed.

units.la: §. III. Ab omni principio procedit aliquo modo id, cujus est principium. Ratio est quia in eo distinguitur modo definitum principium, a principio terminationis, quod hoc talem processum non inferat. Hinc igitur non omne prius statim principium est.
units.tr: §. III. Everything that is the principle of something in some way proceeds from that of which it is the principle. The reason is that in this case the principle, defined in a certain way, is distinguished from the principle of termination, which does not imply such a procession. Hence, then, not every prior thing is at once a principle.

units.la: 7. IV. Omne principium aliquo modo connexum est cum eo cujus est principium. Ratio in tertio manifesta est.
units.tr: 7. IV. Every principle is in some way connected with that of which it is the principle. The reason is clear from the third point.

units.la: 8. Differentia principiorum, supra obiter propositiæ, hic penitius enucleandæ sunt; Est autem Principium vel rei, vel cognitionis: A priori aliquo modo est Ens: à posteriori vero cognitio, quod ideo minus hic locum habet, quia hic spectatur Principium, ut est Entis affectio; præterquam quod principia rei etiam sint principia prima cognitionis: Aut, si ipsa cognitio Ens dicatur, etiâ sua ex principiis Entis petere potest principia.
units.tr: 8. The differences between principles, touched on above in passing, are to be unfolded more fully here. A principle is either of a thing or of knowledge. The a priori is in some way a being; the a posteriori, however, is a cognition, which therefore has less place here, since here the principle is regarded as an affection of being; besides, the principles of a thing are also the first principles of cognition; or, if cognition itself is called a being, it can also derive its principles from the principles of being.

units.la: 9. Principium igitur rei, vel est originationis, vel dependentiæ; Originationis est, à quo aliquid procedit reipsâ idem cum suo principio: Dependentiæ vero, à quo procedit aliquid ab ipso principio distinctum.
units.tr: 9. The principle of a thing, therefore, is either of origination or of dependence. The principle of origination is that from which something proceeds, being really the same as its principle; the principle of dependence, however, is that from which something proceeds, distinct from the principle itself.

units.la: 10. Principium originationis est vel personalitatis, vel conceptuum. Prius in personis S. S. Trinitatis tantum locum habet: Posterius vero est inadæquatus modus considerandi, reipsâ abeo, cujus est modus, non distinctus, per modum prioris & antecedentis rei tributus; cujus generis sunt Entis Principia. Atque huic principio originationis non recte videtur opponi principiatum; ut modò dictum.
units.tr: 10. The principle of origination is either of personality or of concepts. The former has place only in the persons of the Holy Trinity. The latter, however, is an inadequate mode of considering, not really distinct from that of which it is the mode, attributed by way of a prior and antecedent thing; of this kind are the principles of being. And it does not seem rightly opposed to this principle of origination to speak of the principiate, as has just been said.

units.la: 11. Principium dependentiæ, vel est causalitatis, vel inhærentia. Prius est quælibet causa, ratione sui causati: Posterius vero subjectum ratione accidentium ipsi inhærentium.
units.tr: 11. The principle of dependence is either of causality or of inherence. The prior is any cause, by reason of its effect; the posterior, however, is the subject, by reason of the accidents inhering in it.

units.la: 12. Porrò, Principium causalitatis vel internum est, vel externum, pro ratione videlicet causarum; Inhærentia vero vel emanationis, vel acquisitionis est. Prius est subjectum ratione inseparabilis & proprii accidentis: Posterius vero ratione cujuscunque communis, & quasi in ipso acquisiti.
units.tr: 12. Further, the principle of causality is either internal or external, according to the kind of causes, namely; inherence, however, is either of emanation or of acquisition. The prior is the subject by reason of an inseparable and proper accident; the posterior, however, by reason of any common accident, and as it were acquired in it.

units.la: 13. Denique Principio dependentiæ omnia conveniunt axiomata, superiori capite ex natura dependentiæ deducta; non enim nisi nomine differt independens, & principium dependentiæ, prout nec dependens & Principiatum.
units.tr: 13. Finally, all the axioms deduced above from the nature of dependence apply to the principle of dependence; for the independent and the principle of dependence differ only in name, just as neither does the dependent differ from the principiate.

units.la: 14. Principiatum, licet a principio nomen habeat, tamen omni principio relative opponi non videtur, sed tantum principio dependentiæ: Si quis tamen non vereatur, omne id, cujus est aliquod principium, appellare principiatum, ampliatâ ejus significatione, magis forte an verbis, quam reipsa offendet. Præstabit tamen loqui, prout usus fert, utpote quem penes arbitrium est & jus & norma loquendi.
units.tr: 14. The principiate, although it takes its name from the principle, does not seem to be relatively opposed to every principle, but only to the principle of dependence. If anyone, however, does not hesitate to call everything of which there is some principle a principiate, extending its meaning, he will perhaps offend more in words than in fact. It will nevertheless be better to speak as usage bears, since usage holds the right and the rule of speaking.

units.la: 15. Æstimandæ autem ejus differentia, ex oppositi Principii divisionibus valet enim quam maximè in relativè oppositis, quòd vulgo dicitur, tot modis unum oppositrum dici, quot modis alterum. Et hæc de Principio & Principiato.
units.tr: 15. Its difference is to be estimated from the divisions of the opposed principle; for it is worth most in relatively opposed things, as is commonly said: one opposite is named in as many ways as the other. And so much concerning Principle and Principiate.

units.la: CAP. XIX. D E Causa & Causato, in genere.
units.tr: CAP. XIX. Of Cause and Caused, in general.

units.la: 1. PRima dependentia species sequitur, causalitas appellata, quòd sit respectus inter causam & causatum, sive dependentia hujus ab illâ. Est igitur hæc ratio formalis, per quam causa est causa, & secundum idem ad idem, aliam inducere non potest relationem. Sed quid in re sit ipsa causalitas, prout valde controversum est, ita nec minus explicatu difficile.
units.tr: 1. The first species of dependence is called causality, because it is the relation between a cause and what is caused, or the dependence of the latter on the former. This is therefore the formal ground by which a cause is a cause, and which, in the same respect and toward the same thing, cannot induce any other relation. But what causality is in reality is much disputed, and it is hard to explain.

units.la: 2. Philosopho est quæstio propter quid, quare tot dicit esse causas, quot sunt quæstiones propter quid. Sed 1. hæc quæstio index quidem posset esse, consequenter ostendens causalitatem, non verò, ipsa causalitas. 2. Propter quid strictè si sumatur, soli fini tribuitur: at latè omne dependens propter suum independens est, prout accidens propter subjectum suum. Aliis est dependentia: Sed nunc ostensum, non tantum causatum à causa, sed & accidens à subjecto dependere. Aliis est influxus rei esse esse in aliud: Sed i. omni dependentiæ quoque convenit; Nam & subjectum habet suum influxum ad esse accidentis. 2. Et quid hoc est influere esse in aliud: Et ut verbis Clariss. Voet, Philos. prim. reform. cap. 20. f. 1. n. 3. dicam: Mala phrasis est, locutio inepta, sensus non genuinus. Ipsi Clariss. Voet, est influentia per se in esse aliud. Sed etiam subjectum in esse aliud, videlicet accidentis, influit: ita enim accidens non est sine dependentia à subjecto, quod ipsi esse dat. Mihi hactenus placuit actio, aut prout in actu primo consideratur, vis sive virtus activa; juxta axioma, quod non agit, non est causa; aut vulgatam definitionem, causa est, cujus vi res est. Sed non videtur sufficere; Nam actio si stricte & Physicè sumatur, prout ad Prædicamentum actionis spectat, solius est efficientis: at latius prout omne verbum activum Grammaticè dictum comprehendit, si accipiatur, omnibus quidem causis convenit, sed non solis; nam etiam subjectum recipit suum accidens, æquè ac materia formam, ejusque unionem, ut & efficientis actionem. At quoniam manifesta diversitas est inter receptionem Subjecti & Materiæ, exinde actio illa generaliter dicta, aliquo modo limitanda est; Quare existimo, tutò dici posse, causalitatem, sive formalem rationem omnis causæ, esse actioactionem constituentem, quâ videlicet causa agendo aliud aliquid in suo esse constituit. Nec est, quòd dicas, etiam subjectum, recipiendo accidens, illud in suo esse constituere; nam recipere materiæ non est propriè ejus constituere, quoniam ad hoc etiam requiritur, ut sit ipsius constituti pars; Quare recipiendo constituere propriè est 1. recipere in se actionem efficientis & externè constituentis. 2. Recipere unionè partium & formam. 3. Fieri ipsius constituti partem. Quæ multùm distant à nudâ receptione.
units.tr: 2. The Philosopher poses the question "on account of what", and so says there are as many causes as there are "on account of what" questions. But (1) this question could indeed be a sign, consequently showing causality, but it does not show causality itself. (2) Taken strictly, "on account of what" is assigned only to the end; but broadly, every dependent exists on account of its independent, as an accident does on account of its subject. Another view is that there is dependence: but it has now been shown that not only the caused depends on its cause, but also an accident on its subject. Another view is that the influence of one thing's being is the being of another flowing into it: but this (i) belongs to all dependence too, for even a subject has its influence on the being of the accident. (ii) And what does it mean for being to flow into another being? To use the words of the most distinguished Voet, Philos. prim. reform. cap. 20. f. 1. n. 3.: it is a bad phrase, an inept expression, not a genuine sense. For the most distinguished Voet himself, it is influence per se into another's being. But the subject too flows into another's being, namely the accident's; for thus an accident is not without dependence on its subject, which gives it being. Hitherto I have preferred action, or as it is considered in first act, active power or virtue, following the axiom that what does not act is not a cause, or the common definition, that a cause is that by whose power a thing is. But this does not seem sufficient. For action, if taken strictly and physically, as it belongs to the category of action, belongs only to the efficient cause; but if taken more broadly, as it includes every active verb in the grammatical sense, it does belong to all causes, but not only to them; for the subject too receives its accident, just as matter receives form, and their union, and also the action of the efficient. But since there is a clear difference between the reception of a subject and of matter, that action taken in general must be limited in some way. Therefore I think it can safely be said that the causality, or formal ground of every cause, namely action constituting, by which, that is, a cause by acting constitutes something else in its being. Nor can you say that the subject too, by receiving its accident, constitutes it in its being; for for matter to receive is not properly to constitute, since for that it is also required that it be a part of what is constituted. Hence to constitute by receiving is properly (1) to receive into itself the action of an efficient cause that constitutes from outside; (2) to receive the union of parts and form; (3) to become a part of what is constituted. These differ greatly from bare reception.

units.la: 3. Ea igitur actio constituens retinenda, donec commodior explicatio affulgeat: intercedit autem hæc inter causam & causatum; Prout in omni actione est agens, & constitutum, actione illâ productum; Unde Ens agendo constituens dicitur causa, & actione constitutum, Causatum, de quibus breviter in genere, & deinde quoque in specie.
units.tr: 3. That constituting action, then, is to be retained until a more convenient explanation appears. It lies between cause and caused, as in every action there is an agent and something constituted, produced by that action. Hence the being that constitutes by acting is called a cause, and the thing constituted by action is called the caused. We shall treat these briefly in general, and then also in particular.

units.la: 4. In genere Causa consideranda est, quoad nomen, & quoad rem. Nomen dici videtur, quasi cavissa, à cavendo, quia per cognitionē causarū caveri possunt omnes errores; vel quasi cauta, quia cognitis causis cauti sumus & circumspecti; Ratio etymologiæ eadem; magis tamē ultima placet, quia vox illa usurata est, & literæ t & (satis Ἀρίσταξλυτοί.
units.tr: 4. In general, a cause is to be considered both as to name and as to thing. The name seems to come, as it were, from cavissa, from cavendo (to take care), because all errors can be guarded against by knowing causes; or as if from cauta, because once we know causes we are cautious and circumspect. The reasoning of the etymology is the same; still, the latter pleases more, because that word is in use, and because of the letters t and & (enough [ἀρίσταξλυτοί]).

units.la: 5. Acceptiones ejus variæ sunt, latitudine potissimum differentes, nam strictè stristè sumitur pro solà efficiente, utpote maximè excellenti causa. 2. Latè pro quocunque principio, tam terminationis, quomodo privatio, 12. Met. cap. 2. etiam dicitur causa, quam processionis, quopacto in scriptis Patrum sæpius Pater Filii in S. S. Trinitate dicitur causa, quod hodiè, mutatâ vocis significatione, tolerandum non videtur. Atque in hac significatione omnis ratio, propter quam alia adsunt, causa appellari potest, ut Rhetores genera sua causarum habent, &c. 3. Adæquatè pro principio dependentiæ actione suâ dependens aliquod constituente; Quæ hu-ius loci est significatio.
units.tr: 5. Its senses are various, differing chiefly in breadth. (1) Strictly, it is taken for the efficient cause alone, as the most excellent cause. (2) Broadly, for any principle whatever, of termination as well as of procession. Thus privation is also called a cause, 12. Met. cap. 2. In this way, in the writings of the Fathers, the Father is often called the cause of the Son in the Holy Trinity, which today, with the meaning of the word changed, does not seem tolerable. In this sense any reason on account of which other things are present can be called a cause, as rhetoricians have their kinds of causes, etc. (3) Adequately, for the principle of dependence which, by its action, constitutes something dependent on it; which is the sense of this place.

units.la: 6. In reipsa videndum. 1. Quid sit? 2. Quænam ejus axiomatâ 3. Quæ affectiones? 4. Quæ differentiæ?
units.tr: 6. In the thing itself, the following are to be considered: 1. What is it? 2. What are its axioms? 3. What are its affections? 4. What are its differences?

units.la: 7. I. Est autem causa, Principium à cujus actione constituente dependet aliud; Vel brevius, cujus vi res est: Quæ omnia ex antedictis satis manifesta sunt.
units.tr: 7. I. A cause is a principle on whose constituting action another depends; or, more briefly, that by whose power a thing is. All of these are sufficiently clear from what has been said above.

units.la: 8. II. Axiomata copiosa ex naturâ causæ oriuntur, qualia sunt 1. Omnis causa prior causato est, naturâ & cognitione. Ratio est, quia omne independens prius est tali ordine suo dependente. 2. Nihil est in causato, quod non prius fuerit in causâ. Quia nihil est in dependente, quod non prius fuerit in independente, 3. Causatum non est dignius suâ causâ. Ratio ex antecedente patet. 4. Posito causato, ponitur causa; Quia posito dependente ponitur independens. 5. Nihil fit sine causa. Ratio est, quia quod fit, actione constituitur. 6. Quod non agit non est causa. Quia causa non est sine suo esse, at hoc est agendo constituere. 7. Quod magis agit id magis est causa. Ratio est, quia illi magis notio causae convenit. 8. Nihil est causa sui ipsius; Ratio, quia in omni dependentia sunt duo.
units.tr: 8. II. Many axioms arise from the nature of a cause, such as: 1. Every cause is prior to its effect, in nature and in knowledge. The reason is that whatever is independent is prior, in its order, to what depends on it. 2. Nothing is in the caused that was not first in the cause. Because nothing is in the dependent that was not first in the independent. 3. The caused is not more worthy than its cause. The reason is clear from the preceding. 4. Posit the caused, and the cause is posited; because, posit the dependent, and the independent is posited. 5. Nothing comes to be without a cause. The reason is that what comes to be is constituted by action. 6. What does not act is not a cause. Because a cause is not without its being, and this is constituting by acting. 7. What acts more is more a cause. The reason is that the notion of cause belongs to it more. 8. Nothing is the cause of itself; the reason is that in every dependence there are two things.

units.la: 9. III. Affectiones causae sunt 1. Ordo 2. Modus 3. Gradus. Ordo est habitudo plurium causarum inter se & causatum. Ordo causarum inter se est vel Subordinatio, vel Coordinatio.
units.tr: 9. III. The affections of a cause are 1. Order, 2. Mode, 3. Degree. Order is the relation of several causes to one another and to the caused. The order of causes among themselves is either subordination or coordination.

units.la: 10. Subordinatio est ordo causarum, quae plures ejusdem generis, ejusdemque speciei, ad idem concurrunt causatum diverso ordine. Adeoque est quaedam dependentia causarum inter se, qua posteriores omnes a prioribus dependent.
units.tr: 10. Subordination is the order of causes when several of the same kind and species concur to the same caused in a different order. And so it is a certain dependence of causes on one another, by which all the later causes depend on the earlier.

units.la: 11. Dividitur Subordinatio, quod sit vel per se, vel per accidens; Subordinatio per se dicitur, cum omnes causae qua tales ad causatum sunt destinatae: Per accidens vero, cum una causa qua talis non ordinatur ad effectum. Sed haec ultima non est vera subordinatio, utpote in qua requiritur, ut ad idem causatum omnes qua tales, hoc est, qua causae istius, sint ordinatæ. Nulla igitur subordinatio est inter Patrem & Filium furtireum, quoniam pater non facit filium causam furti. Dices: Locum tamen illa subordinatio per accidens habet inter Deum & voluntatem humanam, peccaminosum quid patrantem, nisi Deus etiam peccati causa dicatur. Resp. Deus causa est actionum voluntatis, & quidem per se; At quod illæ sint peccaminosæ, non habent ex se, sed ex defectu congruitatis cum lege hominibus præscriptâ; Defectus autem causæ inferioris, ut non imputatur superiori, ita nec ratione istius inferior superiori est subordinata. Omnis igitur vera subordinatio per se est.
units.tr: 11. Subordination is divided into per se and per accidens. Subordination is called per se when all causes as such are directed to the caused. Per accidens, indeed, is when one cause as such is not ordered to the effect. But this last is not true subordination, since in true subordination it is required that all causes, as such (that is, as causes of that thing), be ordered to the same caused. Therefore there is no subordination between a father and a son who is a thief, since the father does not make the son a cause of theft. You will say that such subordination per accidens does hold between God and the human will, which performs something sinful, unless God is also called a cause of sin. I reply: God is the cause of the actions of the will, and indeed per se; but that these are sinful they do not have from themselves, but from their lack of conformity with the law prescribed to human beings. And as the defect of the inferior cause is not imputed to the superior, so the inferior is not subordinate to the superior on account of it. Every true subordination is therefore per se.

units.la: 12. Ex hac subordinationis doctrinâ, utilissima hæc pullulant axiomata 1. In subordinatione causarum semper est aliqua prima. Ratio est, quia in omni dependentia est aliquod primum: At subordinatio est causarum inferiorum à superiori dependentia: prout inferior à superiori depender, quatenus est causa. 2. In subordinatione causarum non datur progressus in infinitum. Ratio est, quia datur aliqua causa prima; Hinc igitur ex cujuscunque finiti actione, certissimè evinci potest, dari Ens primum & infinitum. 3. In subordinatione causarum, quò quæ superior, eò potentior est: Quia nempe reliquæ ab ipsâ dependere debent. Nihil autem est in dependente, quod non prius sit in independente 4. In causis subordinatis suprema potentissima est & infinita. Ratio est, quia absolutè debet esse independens. 5. Causarum subordinatarum superiorest inferiorum causa. Quia hæ ab illâ dependent, quâtenus sunt causæ. 6. Quod est causa causæ etiam est causa causati. Ratio est, quia quod est causa independentis alicujus, idipsum est causa ejus, quod ab illo dependet: Quoniam nihil in hoc esse potest, nisi quod prius in illo sit; Atqui in hoc nihil est, nisi quod prius fuerit in ipsius causâ. Intelligendum tamen hoc in sensu composito, ut sensus sit, quod facit ut causa sit causa, id quoque est causa causati: non verò, quod facit ut aliquid tantum sit, id causa est ejus, quod ab illo quâ causa dependet.
units.tr: 12. From this doctrine of subordination, the following most useful axioms spring forth: 1. In a subordination of causes there is always some first. The reason is that in every dependence there is something first; but subordination is the dependence of inferior causes on the superior, insofar as the inferior depends on the superior as a cause. 2. In a subordination of causes there is no progress to infinity. The reason is that some first cause is given; hence from the action of any finite thing it can most certainly be proven that a first and infinite being exists. 3. In a subordination of causes, the higher the cause, the more powerful it is, since the rest must depend on it. Nothing, however, is in the dependent that was not first in the independent. 4. In subordinate causes the supreme is most powerful and infinite. The reason is that it must be absolutely independent. 5. The superior of subordinate causes is the cause of the inferiors. Because these depend on it insofar as they are causes. 6. What is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the caused. The reason is that what is the cause of some independent thing is the same cause of what depends on it, since nothing can be in the latter except what was first in the former; and nothing is in the latter except what was first in its cause. This must be understood in the compound sense: what makes a cause to be a cause is also the cause of the caused. It does not follow that what merely makes something to be is the cause of what depends on it as a cause.

units.la: 13. Coordinatio est ordo causarum inter se, quo plures ejusdem generis, ejusdem speciei, ejusdemque ordinis ad idem causatum concurrunt. Distinguitur igitur à subordinatione, quod in illâ diverso ordine, hoc est, non æquè proximè, in hac verò eodem ordine, sive æquè proximè, ad effectum plures causæ conspirent.
units.tr: 13. Coordination is the order of causes among themselves, by which several causes of the same kind, the same species, and the same order converge on one and the same effect. It is distinguished from subordination in this way: in subordination several causes work to the effect in a different order, that is, not equally proximately, whereas in coordination they work together in the same order, that is, equally proximately.

units.la: 14. In coordinatione singulæ causæ sufficientem virtutem non conferunt, sed partialem tantum , quæ junctim totalis ac sufficiens evadit ; Vnde patet 1. Plus posse esse in causato, quam in singulis causarum coordinatarum ; quoniam junctis viribus, plus possunt, quam solutis & separatis. 2. Multitudinem ejus quod minus est, posse prævalere magnitudini ejus quod majus est. Nam ex multitudine partium minimarum ingens massa constitui potest.
units.tr: 14. In coordination, the individual causes do not confer sufficient power but only partial power, which together becomes total and sufficient. Hence it is clear, first, that more can be in the effect than in any single one of the coordinate causes, since with their powers joined they can do more than when loosened and separated. Second, the multitude of what is less can prevail over the magnitude of what is greater. For a huge mass can be built up from a multitude of very small parts.

units.la: 3. Inter illas causas coordinatas requiri conspirationem & concordiam ; quoniam ad idem effectum concurrere debent ; Hinc igitur veritas istius politici : Concordia res parvæ crescunt, discordia dilabuntur maximæ.
units.tr: 3. Among those coordinate causes, agreement and harmony are required, since they ought to concur in the same effect. Hence the truth of that political saying: by concord small things grow, by discord the greatest things fall apart.

units.la: 15. Ordo causarum ad effectum constitit in majori minorive accessu earum ad causatum : Illæ autem accedentes causæ, ut sint subordinatæ, requiritur.
units.tr: 15. The order of causes with respect to the effect consists in the greater or lesser approach of the causes to the effect. Those causes that approach are required to be subordinate.

units.la: 16. Modus causæ est aliqua ejus limitatio, quâ in eâdem specie aliter ac aliter ad effectum referetur : Additur in eadem specie, quia alias diversæ species diversum causandi modum præsupponunt; Verùm is essentialis est, hic verò accidentalis, sine quo etiam causa esse posset, & quidem talis speciei. Tales sunt 1. necessitas & contingentia: 2. Per se & Per accidens, &c.
units.tr: 16. The mode of a cause is some limitation of it, by which, within the same species, it is related to the effect in one way or another. It is added "within the same species" because different species presuppose different modes of causing. The mode is, however, essential to the species, whereas this is accidental, and without it the cause could still be a cause, and indeed of the same species. Such modes are: (1) necessity and contingency; (2) per se and per accidens, and so on.

units.la: 17. Gradus causarum est earum in virtute & actione præaliis valor minor, vel mamajor, ac locum habet in causis coordinatis, aliquo modo in eodem genere connexis. Hic gradus à Keckermanno vis ejus appellatur, cum efficientem dividi dicit, ex vi efficiendi.
units.tr: 17. The degree of causes is the lesser or greater value they have in power and action compared with others. It holds among coordinate causes, which are connected in some way within the same genus. Keckermann calls this degree the vis (force) of the cause, when he says that the efficient is divided according to the force of efficiency.

units.la: 17. IV. Ex his affectionibus variæ fluunt causarum differentiæ communes; Et quidem primo à subordinatione; Causa est vel prima vel secunda; Prima causa est à quâ in quocunque genere reliquæ dependent, ut ipsa à nullâ aliâ in eodem genere dependeat. Secunda autem est, quæ à priori aliquâ dependet. Hujus igitur ratio est, ut in operando à primâ determinetur ac dependeat, ut statim probatum.
units.tr: 17. IV. From these affections various common differences of causes arise. First, from subordination: a cause is either first or second. A first cause is one on which all the others in any genus depend, while it itself depends on nothing else in that genus. A second cause, however, is one that depends on some earlier cause. The reason for this is that in acting it is determined and depends on the first, as will be shown presently.

units.la: 18. Secundò à coordinatione, causa est vel Totalis, vel Partialis. Totalis est, quæ totum in suo ordine constituit causatum; Hæc igitur alias coordinatas non admittit, aliterque solitaria, quòd sola in suo ordine sit, appellatur. Partialis verò est, quæ cum aliis causis ejusdem ordinis causatum producit; Dicitur quoque aliter socia, quòd cum reliquis coordinatis societatem & concordiam servet.
units.tr: 18. Second, from coordination, a cause is either total or partial. A total cause is one that by itself constitutes the whole of the effect in its order; it therefore admits no coordinate causes, and is otherwise called solitary, because it alone is in its order. A partial cause, however, is one that produces the effect together with other causes of the same order; it is also called social, because it keeps fellowship and harmony with the other coordinate causes.

units.la: 19. Tertiò, ab ordine ad causatum, causa est vel Proxima, vel Remota. Prior est, quæ immediatè ipsum attingit causatum, nullâ aliâ causâ ejusdem speciei intercedente; Posterior verò, quæ mediato attingit, intercedente unâ, vel pluribus causis ejusdem speciei. Huic æquipollet divisio causæ in immediatam & mediatam.
units.tr: 19. Third, from the order to the effect, a cause is either proximate or remote. The former is one that reaches the effect immediately, with no other cause of the same kind intervening; the latter reaches it mediately, with one or more causes of the same kind intervening. The division of a cause into immediate and mediate is equivalent to this.

units.la: 20. Quarto à modo 1. causa est vel neceffaria vel contingens. Prior est, fine quâ causatum nullâtenus esse potest: Contingens verò, fine quâ esse potest. 2. Est vel per fe, vel per accidens. Illa est cujus actio per fe ordinata est ad tale causatum: Hæc verò, cujus actio primò instituta non erat ad tale causatum, licet illi hoc vitio aliquo intercedente imputari debeat. Intelligi autem debet hæc divisio, ratione primæ inter causas fecundas ordinationis non ratione executionis, quoniam hac nulla causa per accidens dari potest; Omnis quippe producit effectum sibi conveniens, integra integrum, vitiata vitiatum.
units.tr: 20. Fourth, from the mode: (1) a cause is either necessary or contingent. The former is one without which the effect cannot in any way exist; the latter is one without which it can exist. (2) It is either per se or per accidens. The former is one whose action is ordained per se to such an effect; the latter is one whose action was not originally instituted for such an effect, although it must be imputed to the cause on account of some fault intervening. This division ought to be understood with respect to the primary ordering among secondary causes, not with respect to their execution, since in execution no cause can act per accidens: every cause produces an effect suited to itself, whole producing whole, and defective producing defective.

units.la: 21. Quæres, an in omni genere causarum fecundarum, talis aliqua à primâ ordinatione dari possit recessus? Resp. Omninò; nam inprimis circa efficientem & finem nullum est dubium; Et in materiâ ovum est materia primitus ordinata ad pullum: Per accidens fit materia alimenti, & monstri; Et fi in materia id locum habeat, de formâ dubium esse non debet, licet exempla non ita præsto sint; quoniam etiamnum in obscuro latent rerum formæ.
units.tr: 21. You may ask whether, in every genus of secondary causes, some such deviation from the primary ordering can occur. Answer: certainly. For there is no doubt about the efficient and the final cause in particular. And in matter, the egg is matter primarily ordered to the chick; by accident it becomes the matter of nourishment or of a monster. And if this holds in matter, there should be no doubt about form, although examples are not so readily at hand, since the forms of things still lie hidden in obscurity.

units.la: 22. Quintò à gradu virtutis, causa est vel Principalis vel minus principalis ; Quarum illa per se requiritur, hæc propter illam. Specialiores harum descriptiones infra in specie proponendæ.
units.tr: 22. Fifth, from the degree of power, a cause is either principal or less principal. The former is required for its own sake, the latter for the sake of the former. More specific descriptions of these will be given below, in their proper place.

units.la: 23. Causæ relativè opponitur causatum, barbarè defectu melioris, ita appellatum, quod à causis depender; Dicitur que effectum à potissimâ ipsius specie; Hoc totidem modis dicitur & dividitur, ac causa.
units.tr: 23. The effect is relatively opposed to the cause; it is so called, by a barbarous word for lack of a better one, because it depends on causes. It is also said to be the effect of its most powerful species. This is said and divided in as many ways as the cause is.

units.la: 24. Essentialiter causa dividitur in externam, quæ manet extra causati essentiam, quam constituit; & internam, quæ illam essentiam ingrediendo, ejus pars fit. Dicitur autem externa & interna ratione essentiæ causati, non ratione loci; ut quâ etiam efficiens interna esse potest.
units.tr: 24. Essentially, a cause is divided into external, which remains outside the essence of the effect that it constitutes, and internal, which, by entering into that essence, becomes a part of it. It is called external or internal with respect to the essence of the effect, not with respect to place; for the efficient cause too can be internal.

units.la: 25. Externa causa est vel efficiens vel finis; Et interna vel materia vel forma; Adeo ut quatuor summa genera causarum statuantur, non plura, nec pauciora; Cujus genuina ratio, ex causalitate desumta; est, quia totidem actione constituente genere diversa, ad constitutionem causati concurrunt. Non quòd omnium Entium sine quatuor causæ, sed quòd illud, quod ob dependentiam alterius ab ipso causa dicitur, ad aliquod ex hisce generibus pertineat.
units.tr: 25. An external cause is either efficient or final; an internal cause is either matter or form. Thus four highest genera of causes are established, neither more nor fewer. The genuine reason for this, drawn from causality, is that there are exactly as many constituting actions of different kinds that concur in constituting the effect. Not that all beings lack the four causes, but that whatever is said to be a cause of something through its dependence on it belongs to one of these genera.

units.la: 26. Ut autem pateat, non plures causas dari posse, primo instituenda demonstratio, secundo, illæ quæ aliquam similitudinem habere videntur examinandæ. Quoad primum: Actio constituens vel Physica est & externa, vel Grammatica tantum, & late dicta. Actio Physica, sive realis, est exercitium potentiae activae, quâ causatum extrinsecè constituitur; adeo ut illud exercitium ad causatum terminetur. Estque hæc duplex directa & obliqua. Directa est, quæ quasi per lineam rectam terminatur in causatum: Estque causa efficientis: Obliqua verò, quæ indirectè tendit ad effectum, adeò ut prius terminetur in aliam causam directè agentem, adeò ut potius aliam causam, quam causatum videatur producere; Qualis actio est impulsio vi desiderii ac appetitus, in efficientem terminata, ac per illam obliquo ductu ad Causatum; atque hæc est ipsius finis.
units.tr: 26. To make clear that there cannot be more causes, two things must be done: first, a demonstration must be set out; second, those causes that seem to have some similarity must be examined. As to the first: a constituting action is either physical and external, or grammatical only, and broadly speaking. A physical, or real, action is the exercise of an active power by which the effect is constituted outside the agent, so that this exercise terminates in the effect. And this is twofold, direct and oblique. The direct is that which terminates in the effect as if along a straight line; it is the cause of the efficient. The oblique, however, is that which tends to the effect indirectly, so that it first terminates in another directly acting cause, and so seems rather to produce another cause than the effect. Such an action is the impulse of desire and appetite, which terminates in the efficient and through it leads by an oblique course to the effect; and this is the cause of the end.

units.la: 27. Actio Grammatica in concursu potissimum ad unionem partium causati constituit; unde quoque causæ internæ, quasum causalitas talis actio est, non nisi illorum sunt Entium, quorum esse per partium unionem constituitur. Ille autem concursus ad unionem absolvitur r.eo quod unionem illam in suis partibus recipit, ac per illam pars fit essentiae causati, estque Materia. 2. Ipso uniente proximè & interne, quod, à materiâ receptum, immediatè ipsius partes unit, ac seipsam cum materiâ copulans, altera fit pars essentiae compositi, estque nihil aliud quam forma. Quare liquidò satis patet, quaternarium istum numerum, non solâ authoritate, sed & non contemnendâ niti ratione.
units.tr: 27. A grammatical action constitutes chiefly in concurrence to the union of the parts of the effect. Hence also internal causes, whose causality is such an action, belong only to those beings whose being is constituted by the union of parts. This concurrence to union is completed in one way, in that it receives that union in its parts, and through it becomes a part of the essence of the effect; and this is matter. In another way, the uniting agent, proximately and internally, which, once received by the matter, immediately unites its parts and, joining itself to the matter, becomes another part of the essence of the composite, is nothing other than form. Hence it is quite clear that this number of four rests not on authority alone, but also on no contemptible reason.

units.la: 28. Quoad secundum, similitudinem aliquam cum causis videntur habere 1. Causa exemplaris 2. Causa instrumentalis 3. Causa sine quâ non.. 4. Subjectum. 5. Circumstantia loci & temporis; Quare quoque de iis dubitatur, annon distincta genera causarum constituant. Verùm nullum horum est, quin aut ad priora genera possit revocari, aut planè omni actione constitutivâ destituatur. Quod in specie breviter ostendendum.
units.tr: 28. As to the second: certain things seem to have some similarity with causes, namely (1) the exemplary cause, (2) the instrumental cause, (3) the sine qua non, (4) the subject, and (5) the circumstances of place and time. Hence it is also doubted whether these constitute distinct genera of causes. But none of these is such that it either can be reduced to the earlier genera or is entirely deprived of any constituting action. This must be shown briefly in each case.

units.la: 29. I. Causam exemplarem, sive exemplar quod attinet, aut notat certam formam in intellectu conceptam, secundum quam efficiens agit, ut illi opus suum conforme reddat. Atque ita triplici modo potest considerari, primò ut sit simpliciter præparatio ac dispositio in efficiente requisita; atque ita ejus nulla est actio, nedum constituens: sed pro causâ sine quâ non haberi debet: Secundò, prout in intellectu existens, efficientem non solum præparat, sed etiam incitat ac impellit ad actionem, quo pacto quidem causa est, sed ad efficientem minus principalem impellentem pertinet: Tertiò, prout illa incitatio ac impulsio secum habet aliquod desiderium, quo efficiens moveatur: atque ita nihil aliud est, quam finis, concretè cum suo objecto consideratus. Aut exemplar notat formam sive imaginem extra mentem constitutam, secundum quam, non secus ac secundum regulam, efficiens agit; atque sic causa est inserviens & instrumentalis, adeoque ad efficientem pertinet.
units.tr: 29. I. The exemplar, or exemplar cause, either denotes a certain form conceived in the intellect, according to which the efficient acts so as to make its work conform to it. It can be considered in three ways. First, as merely a preparation and disposition required in the efficient; in this sense it has no action at all, much less a constituting one, and should be regarded as a cause without which not. Second, insofar as it exists in the intellect, it not only prepares the efficient but also stirs up and drives it to act; in this way it is indeed a cause, but it belongs to the less principal efficient that drives. Third, insofar as that stirring and impulse carries with it some desire by which the efficient is moved; and so it is nothing other than the end, considered concretely together with its object. Or the exemplar denotes a form or image constituted outside the mind, according to which the efficient acts, just as according to a rule; and so it is a serving and instrumental cause, and thus belongs to the efficient.

units.la: 30. II. Instrumentum sive instrumentalis causa commodè satis ad efficientem reduci potest; agit quippe inserviendo, & quidem directè in ipsum causatum; nec obstat, quod ejus actio sit servitium; nam ad efficientem non requiritur, ut ejus virtus & actio semper causato æqualis sit, aut eo major, sed sufficit, si virtus ejus directè sit terminata in effectum.
units.tr: 30. II. The instrument, or instrumental cause, can quite conveniently be reduced to the efficient. It acts by serving, and indeed acts directly upon the caused thing itself. Nor does it matter that its action is a service; for it is not required of the efficient that its power and action should always be equal to the effect, or greater than it, but it is enough if its power is directly terminated in the effect.

units.la: 31. III. Causa sine quâ non est conditio quædam ad causandum requisita (qualis est v. gr. potentia & virtus præsens, desectus obstaculi, præsentia objecti &c.) quæ improprie causa dicitur, eò quòd nulla ejus sit actio. Nec obstat, sine eâ non fieri causatum; nam illa ratio sola non sufficit, quoniam etiam requiritur, ut actionem suam conferat.
units.tr: 31. III. A cause without which not is some condition required for causing (such as, for example, present power and capacity, the absence of an obstacle, the presence of the object, etc.), which is called a cause improperly so called, because it has no action of its own. Nor does it matter that the effect does not come about without it; for that reason alone is not sufficient, since it is also required that it contribute its own action.

units.la: 32. IV. Subjectum, licet recipiendo accidens, illud à se dependens habeat, non tamen causa est, quoniam illa receptio non est actio constitutiva, quâ ipsum dependentis accidentis pars essentialis fiat, quod ad causalitatem requiritur internam, ut modò dictum.
units.tr: 32. IV. A subject, although by receiving an accident it has that accident depending on itself, is nevertheless not a cause, because that reception is not a constituting action by which it becomes an essential part of the dependent accident. Internal causality requires this, as has just been said.

units.la: 33. V. Circumstantiæ loci & Temporis, aut simpliciter sic spectantur, pro præsentia causationis in loco & tempore, atque sic quidem ad causandum requiruntur in dependentibus, nullam tamen actionem conferunt, adeoque non nisi causæ sine quibus non, id est, improprie dictæ, dici debent. Aut notant aliquam εὐκαιρίαν & opportunitatem, quæ in illis se offendat, quâ allicitur & impellitur efficiens ad agendum, & sic ad efficientem minus principalem impellentem spectant. Adeo ut nullum horum, distinctum Genus causæ constituere possit.
units.tr: 33. V. The circumstances of place and time, either are regarded simply as such, as the presence of the causation in place and time; and in this sense they are indeed required in dependent things for causing, yet they contribute no action, and so ought to be called only causes without which not, that is, improperly so called. Or they denote some opportunity [εὐκαιρία] and convenience which presents itself in them, by which the efficient is enticed and driven to act; and so they pertain to the less principal efficient that drives. So that none of these, as a distinct kind, can constitute a genus of cause.

units.la: 34. Ab altera parte numerus causarum imminuendus videtur; ita quidem ut reducto fine ad efficientem impulsivam, materia & forma potius principia vel partes causati, quam ipsius causæ dicantur. Verum finem quod attinet, licet nullum absurdum sequeretur, si ad efficientem reduceretur, quoniam tamen multum distinguitur actio illa obliqua desiderii finis, ab actione directa efficientis, commodius & consuetudini & rationi ab efficiente distinguendus videtur. Materiam autem & formam si principia dicas & non causas, nimis augustè vocem causæ accipies, quam ut ea usui familiaris sit. De his tamen infra latius suis locis erit dispiciendum. Et hac de Causa & Causato in genere.
units.tr: 34. On the other hand, the number of causes seems to need reducing; so that, with the end reduced to the driving efficient, matter and form would be called principles or parts of the caused thing rather than causes of it. But as for the end, although no absurdity would follow if it were reduced to the efficient, since nevertheless that oblique action of the desired end is much distinguished from the direct action of the efficient, it seems more conveniently and according to both usage and reason to be distinguished from the efficient. If, however, you call matter and form principles and not causes, you would be taking the word cause too narrowly for it to be familiar in use. These matters will be examined more fully below in their proper places. And so much on cause and effect in general.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: DE Efficiente & Effectu.
units.tr: ON THE Efficient and the Effect.

units.la: 1. ORdinem tractandi hæc quatuor genera causarum, alii alium faciunt; Convenientissimè videtur initium ab efficiente sumi; tum quòd hæc inter reliquas causas prima extiterit; tum quod omni Enti conveniat; tum denique, quòd pluribus conveniat ab efficiente constitui, quam à materiâ & forma. Consideranda igitur hæc primò, quoad nomen; secundò quoad rem.
units.tr: 1. Authors differ over the order of treating these four kinds of cause. It seems most fitting to begin with the efficient: first, because it has come first among the other causes; second, because it belongs to every being; and third, because it can be made to apply to more things than the material and formal causes. These things are therefore to be considered first as to the name, and second as to the thing.

units.la: 2. Nomen ab efficiendo habet, quod est, quasi existere facere, quoniam hæc causa potissimum suâ actione existentiam causati constituit: Aliis efficere videtur dici, quasi extra se facere, ut ita saltem convenia t causæ transeunti, ac effectum extra se producenti palpabilem & sensibilem, ut ajunt: Sed nimis angusta erit Etymologia, utpote omni causæ efficienti non conveniens.
units.tr: 2. The name "efficient" comes from "to effect," which is, as it were, "to make to exist," since this cause above all establishes the existence of the caused thing by its action. Others think it is called "to effect" as if it were "to make outside oneself," so that it might at least suit a transient cause that produces an effect outside itself, palpable and sensible, as they say. But that etymology would be too narrow, since it does not fit every efficient cause.

units.la: 3. Ambiguitate caret, quod mireris, nisi fortean angustam illam significationem, ab angustiori illâ etymologiâ petitam, ipsi tribuendam censeas, quæ & fundamento, & authoritate, quantum perspicere potui, cæret.
units.tr: 3. It is free from ambiguity, which you would wonder at, unless perhaps you think that narrower meaning, taken from that narrower etymology, is to be attributed to it; and as far as I could see, this meaning lacks both foundation and authority.

units.la: 4. Dicitur aliter Causa agens, eo quod sola inter reliquas directa actione Physica causatum constituat; item simpliciter causa idque καὶ ἐξοχὴν, quod præstantissima inter reliquas ut causa; imo quod reliquæ omnes in tantum sint causæ, quatenus aliquid, plus minus, de ipsius causalitate participent.
units.tr: 4. It is called otherwise the acting cause, because it alone among the others constitutes the caused thing by direct physical action; likewise it is called simply the cause, and that καὶ ἐξοχὴν ("and preeminently"), because it is the most excellent of the causes; indeed, all the others are causes only insofar as they share, to a greater or lesser degree, in its causality.

units.la: 5. In re ipsa videndum 1. Quid sit? 2. Quænam ejus Proprietates? 3. Quæ differentiæ? 4. Quodnam ejus correlatum?
units.tr: 5. As to the thing itself, we must consider: 1. What it is? 2. What are its properties? 3. What are its differences? 4. What is its correlative?

units.la: 6. I. Est autem efficiens, causa externa à cujus actione directa reali dependet causatum; Vbi præter genus, de quo nullum dubium est, notari debet ejus differentia, partim ex ipsius causalitate, partim ex formulâ & particulâ, quâ ea profertur æstimanda. Causalitas ejus est, actio directa ac realis, qualis est illa, quæ in exercitio virtutis, sive potentiæ activæ, consistit; Unde quoque potissima ipsius axiomata ex illâ virtute fundamentum haurire debent. Particula, quâ illa causalitas explicatur est præpositio à vel ab, variis quidem modis acceptâ, propriissimè tamen, prout in patiente denotat receptionem exercitii virtutis activæ; quomodo & hic sumitur; adeò ut causatum esse à causa efficiente, nihil aliud sit, quam causatum passum esse, hoc est recepisse exercitium potentiæ activæ efficientis, quâ ipsum constitutum est.
units.tr: 6. I. The efficient cause is an external cause on whose direct real action the caused thing depends. Here, besides the genus, about which there is no doubt, its difference must be noted, to be judged partly from its causality and partly from the formula and particle by which it is expressed. Its causality is a direct and real action, such as consists in the exercise of a virtue, or active power; hence its chief axioms must draw their foundation from that virtue. The particle by which that causality is explained is the preposition from (à or ab), taken in various ways, but most properly, as it denotes in the thing acted upon the receiving of the exercise of an active virtue; and it is taken in this sense here. So that for the caused thing to be from an efficient cause is nothing other than for the caused thing to be acted upon, that is, to have received the exercise of the active power of the efficient, by which it is constituted.

units.la: 7. II. Proprietates, sive axiomata, ut dictum, potissimum à conditione potentiæ activæ desumuntur, suntque potissimum, quæ sequuntur. 1. Nulla efficiens agit ultra suum posse; Quia non agit nisi per virtutem suam, quæ est ipsummet posse. 2. Qualis efficiens, talis ejus actio; Ratio est, quia talis est efficiens, qualis est virtus ejus; At qualis virtus talis actio. Hinc igitur, si efficiens necessaria, actio est necessaria; si libera, actio libera; si infinita, actio infinita, &c. 3. Nulla efficiens agit in distans; sive omnis efficiens actionem suam causato debet applicare. Ratio est, quia nulla virtus agit in distans, hoc est ultra sphæram activitatis suæ; intra quam si aliquid sit, id non distare, sed adstare dicitur. 4. Posita efficiente, ponitur virtus; Quia hæc fundamentum est ejus causalitatis, sive est ipsa efficientia. Hinc posito movente, ponitur virtus movendi. 5. Aucta virtute, potentior est efficiens: Et contra; diminuta virtute, debilior fit efficiens. Aucto enim vel diminuto eo, per quod efficiens est efficiens, etiam major vel minor fit ejus efficientia & actio.
units.tr: 7. II. The properties, or axioms, as has been said, are drawn chiefly from the condition of active power, and they are chiefly the following. 1. No efficient cause acts beyond its power; because it acts only through its virtue, which is itself its power. 2. Such as the efficient cause is, such is its action; the reason is that the efficient is such as its virtue is, and such as the virtue is, such is the action. Hence, if the efficient is necessary, the action is necessary; if free, the action is free; if infinite, the action is infinite, and so on. 3. No efficient cause acts at a distance; or every efficient cause must apply its action to the caused thing. The reason is that no virtue acts at a distance, that is, beyond the sphere of its activity; within which, if something is, it is said not to be distant but to be present. 4. Once the efficient cause is posited, the virtue is posited; because this is the foundation of its causality, or is itself the efficiency. Hence, once a mover is posited, the power of moving is posited. 5. When the virtue is increased, the efficient cause is more powerful; and conversely, when the virtue is diminished, the efficient cause becomes weaker. For when that by which the efficient is efficient is increased or diminished, its efficiency and action also become greater or less.

units.la: 8. Differentia causæ efficientis, varia sunt, ac variis passim distinctionibus proponuntur, quæ ex tribus illis affectionibus desumuntur, & quidem 1. Ab ordine. 2. A modo. 3. A gradu.
units.tr: 8. The differences of the efficient cause are various, and are proposed in various distinctions here and there, which are derived from those three affections, namely: 1. From order. 2. From mode. 3. From degree.

units.la: 9. Ordo vel efficientium inter se est, vel communis ad effectum; Et ille vel Subordinatio, vel Coordinatio, ut supra in genere notatum.
units.tr: 9. The order is either of the efficients among themselves, or common to the effect; and the former is either subordination or coordination, as noted above in general.

units.la: 10. I. A subordinatione efficiens vel Prima est vel Secunda: Illa est, quæ non pendet à priori, sed à quâ reliquæ secundæ pendent; Hæc vero, quæ à priori dependet. Prima autem vel absolute talis, quæ à nulla prorsus alia pendet, ut Deus Opt. max. vel in suo genere, quæ in certo ordine primitatem obtinet, ut in naturalibus, natura, licet absolute ab aliâ adhuc dependeat.
units.tr: 10. I. From subordination, the efficient is either first or second. The first is that which does not depend on another prior cause, but on which the other secondary causes depend; the second is that which depends on a prior cause.
