The first is either absolutely such, which depends on nothing at all else, as God, the best and greatest; or in its own kind, which holds the primacy in a certain order, as nature among natural things, although it still depends absolutely on something else.

units.la: 11. Quoniam igitur inter efficientem primam & secundam intercedit dependentia & subordinatio, omnes quoque generales proprietates, supra subordinationi tributæ, inter Deum, tanquam causam primam, omnesque creaturas, ut causas secundas, intercedere debent; adeo ut Deus infinities potentior sit causa, utpote potentissima, quam est aliqua Creaturarum; Et ut sit causa omnium causarum inferiorum, easdem non tantum ut sint, producendo, & ut permaneant, conservando, sed & cum iis ad omnes earum actiones, etiam in specie
units.tr: 11. Since, therefore, dependence and subordination lie between the first and the second efficient, all the general properties ascribed above to subordination must also hold between God, as the first cause, and all creatures, as secondary causes; so that God is infinitely more powerful than any creature, as the most powerful cause; and so that, being the cause of all inferior causes, He not only produces them so that they may be, and conserves them so that they may remain, but also concurs with them in all their actions, even in species and individual, and determines them to act.

units.la: M 6 & & individuo concurrendo, easque ad agendum determinando. Quoniam enim omnis causa inferior & secunda in fieri à Deo dependet, dependebit quoque ab ipso in esse; adeo ut subtracto illo influxu conservationis divinæ, confestim ad non esse sit relapsura, neque ad minutiam horæ sese conservare possit (nam alias per parem sui potentiam sese in æternum posset conservare:) Et prout in fiendo & essendo dependet, ita etiam in operando; cum impossibile sit id operari à se; quod & sit & est per participationem ac dependentiam; In dependenti enim constitutione & essentia, omnia sunt dependentia.
units.tr: For since every inferior and secondary cause depends on God in becoming, it will also depend on Him in being; so that, if that influx of divine conservation were withdrawn, it would at once relapse into non-being and could not preserve itself even for the least moment of an hour (for otherwise, by its own equal power, it could preserve itself for eternity). And just as it depends in becoming and being, so also in acting; since it is impossible for that to act of itself which both is and exists through participation and dependence. For in a dependent constitution and essence, all things are dependent.

units.la: 12. Et quoniam omnis causa secunda finita est ac dependens, nulla quoque talis causa esse potest, eorum quæ infinitâ actione ad sui productionem opus habent; Qualis enim virtus, talis & actio, & talis causa: At impossibile est, ut sit in finito virtus infinita; cum in finito omnia sint finita. Sed de his latius dicendum, Tractatu III.
units.tr: 12. And since every secondary cause is finite and dependent, no such cause can be among those which need an infinite action for their own production; for as the virtue is, so is the action and the cause; but it is impossible for a finite thing to have an infinite virtue, since in the finite all things are finite. But these matters are to be discussed more fully in Tractate III.

units.la: 13. II. A coordinatione efficiens est, vel totalis, sive solitaria, à quâ solâ in suo ordine & specie totum effectum dependet; vel partialis sive socia, quæ cum aliis ejusdem ordinis, ejusdemque speciei efficientibus junctim effectum producit, adeò ut unicuique istarum pars saltem effectûs debeatur, non totum, quod effectui inest. Ex quibus colligi potest, esse 1. Perfectius esse causam totalem, quam partialem. 2. Deum non posse esse causam partialem, utpote a quo omnis imperfectio removenda; cum & sic aliquid esset, a Deo non dependens. 3. Creaturam quidem cum creatrice, si in eodem ordine eademque specie sit, posse esse causam partialem, nunquam vero cum Deo; Quoniam partialitas locum habet inter coordinatas, non autem subordinatas causas. 4. Posse quidem plures causas principales & totales ad idem numerum effectum concurrere, si sint subordinatae: non vero si sint coordinatae, nam sic partiales fiunt.
units.tr: 13. II. From coordination, the efficient is either total, or solitary, on which alone the whole effect depends in its own order and species; or partial, or joint, which together with other efficients of the same order and the same species produces the effect, so that to each of them is owed only a part of the effect, not the whole that is in the effect. From these things it may be gathered: 1. A total cause is more perfect than a partial cause. 2. God cannot be a partial cause, since every imperfection must be removed from Him; for otherwise something would exist that does not depend on God. 3. A creature may indeed be a partial cause along with the Creator, if it is in the same order and of the same species, but never with God; since partiality takes place among coordinated, not subordinated, causes. 4. Several principal and total causes may indeed concur to produce the same single effect, if they are subordinated; but not if they are coordinated, for then they become partial.

units.la: 14. III. Ab ordine ad effectum, efficiens est vel remota vel proxima. Illa est, a qua intercedente alia causa ejusdem speciei dependet effectum. Haec vero, a qua nulla alia ejusdem speciei intercedente effectum dependet. Unde colligi potest 1. In omni effectu efficientem proximam requiri: Quia aliqua esse debet, quae nullam intercedentem ejusdem speciei admittit. 2. Posse quidem alterius speciei causas intercedere, instrumentales videlicet & inservientes, ut tamen maneat causa proxima; Ita v. gr. Scriptor suae scripturae causa est proxima, licet calamus ut instrumentum intercedat.
units.tr: 14. III. From order to the effect, the efficient is either remote or proximate. The remote is that on which the effect depends with another cause of the same kind intervening. The proximate is that on which the effect depends with no other cause of the same kind intervening. Hence it may be gathered: 1. In every effect a proximate efficient is required, since there must be some cause that admits no intervening cause of the same kind. 2. Causes of another kind may indeed intervene, namely instrumental and subservient ones, yet the proximate cause remains; thus, for example, the writer is the proximate cause of his writing, although the pen intervenes as an instrument.

units.la: 15. IV. A modo varie dividitur efficiens;
units.tr: 15. IV. The efficient cause is also divided in various ways according to its mode.

units.la: Et quidem primò prout se habet in effectu, quod sit vel Procreans vel Conservans. Illa est, quæ effectui dat fieri & initium τῆς εἵναι: Hæc verò, à quâ in esse continuatur. Hæc divisio non ab omnibus æquè æstimatur; alii quippe omnem causam procreantem existimantes, conservantem eliminant; alii corrumpentem five destruentem præterea addunt: Alii utramque quidem admittunt, sed conservantem in eo collocant, quod ea non destruat effectum. Sed ubique secus ac fert veritas. Nam 1. Conservans causa verè agendo effectum constituit, dum illum in esse continuat, eâdem videlicet actione, aut homogeneâ, quâ erat primò productus. Dixi eâdem actione, quemadmodum Deus eâdem actione, id est continuatâ creatione, creaturam conservat; vel homogeneâ, quemadmodum parentes suos conservant liberos, eos sustentando, eisque de victu & amictu prospiciendo. 2. Corrumpens causa, si referatur ad corruptum, est deficiens, & opus non habet actione positivâ: at si ad id quod ad corruptionem illam sequitur, revera est procreans. Ex. gr. Qui destruit ædificium, ratione ædificii nihil positivè agit, at si referatur ad id, quod post destructionem illam sequitur (v. gr. ad acervum lapidum, struem lignorum ac rudera) ejus omninò est causa efficiens & quidem procreans. 3. Cum omnis efficientis sit positivè ac realiter agere, etiam id conservanti convenit; Quare si quod dicatur rem conservare, eo quòd non destruat, cùm destruere posset, & nihil præterea conferat, immeritò causa conservans dicitur; Quemadmodum immeritò, quis dicitur conservare arborem, cujus exscindendæ potestatem habet, si illam non amputet.
units.tr: Firstly, according to how it stands with respect to the effect, an efficient cause is either producing or conserving. The former is that which gives the effect its coming into being and its beginning of being [τῆς εἶναι]; the latter is that by which it is continued in being. This division is not valued equally by all. Some, thinking every cause to be producing, eliminate the conserving one; others add a corrupting or destroying cause besides. Others admit both, but place the conserving cause in this, that it does not destroy the effect. But everywhere it is otherwise than truth bears. For 1. a conserving cause, by truly acting, constitutes the effect while it continues it in being, namely by the same action, or by a homogeneous one, by which it was first produced. I say by the same action, as God, by the same action, that is, by continued creation, conserves the creature; or by a homogeneous one, as parents conserve their children by sustaining them and providing for their food and clothing. 2. A corrupting cause, if it is referred to the thing corrupted, is deficient and has no need of positive action; but if it is referred to what follows upon that corruption, it is truly producing. For example, one who destroys a building does nothing positive with respect to the building; but if referred to what follows that destruction (for example, the heap of stones, the pile of timber and the rubble), he is wholly its efficient cause, and indeed a producing one. 3. Since every efficient cause acts positively and really, this also belongs to the conserving cause. Therefore, if something is said to conserve a thing because it does not destroy it, though it could destroy it, and contributes nothing further, it is wrongly called a conserving cause; just as one is wrongly said to conserve a tree, which he has the power to cut down, if he does not cut it.

units.la: 16. Secundò à modo dividitur efficiens in emanativam & activam. Illa dicitur quæ suâ præsentiâ, citra intercedentem actionem producit effectum: Hæc verò, quæ intercedente actione eum producit. Sed cum omnis efficiens intercedente actione, tamquam causalitate suâ, sine quâ esse nequit, effectum producat, illa quæ emanativa dicitur, admittenda inter causas efficientes non videtur; Neque aliquod commodum ipsius exemplum proferri potest; Ut plurimum enim sunt subjecta ratione propriorum accidentium, neque hactenus aliud sese mihi obtulit. Quare etiam supra emanationem speciem dependentiæ subjectivæ feci.
units.tr: 16. Secondly, according to its mode, the efficient cause is divided into emanative and active. The former is that which produces its effect by its presence, without any intervening action; the latter is that which produces it by an intervening action. But since every efficient cause produces its effect by an intervening action, as by its causality, without which it cannot exist, the cause called emanative does not seem to be admitted among efficient causes. Nor can any suitable example of it be put forward; for for the most part such things are subjects, by way of proper accidents, and so far no other has presented itself to me. Hence also above I treated emanation as a species of subjective dependence.

units.la: 17. Tertiò à modo dividitur efficiens in immanentem & transeuntem. Prior est, quæ producit effectum in se: Posterior, quæ producit extra se: Divisio ex terminis nota; Dubium tamen est 1. Annon cum recirecipere sit pati, causa immanens sit patiens? Resp. Est quidem, sed non qua causa essectum producens, sed qua subjectum, effectum recipiens; nec implicat, idem diverso respectu ejusdem esse causam & subjectum; Quemadmodum mens cogitat, & cogitationes, quas format, in se recipit.
units.tr: 17. Thirdly, according to its mode, the efficient cause is divided into immanent and transient. The former is that which produces its effect in itself; the latter, that which produces it outside itself. The division is clear from the terms. A doubt remains, however: 1. Since to receive back is to suffer, is an immanent cause a suffering cause? Answer: it is indeed, but not as a cause producing the effect; rather as a subject receiving the effect. Nor is it contradictory for the same thing to be cause and subject of the same thing in different respects, just as the mind thinks and receives in itself the thoughts it forms.

units.la: 2. An causa transeuntis effectum, ut extra ipsam est, semper sit permanens? Resp. Non semper hoc requiritur; quoniam sufficit, si extra ipsam sit, dum producitur; Ita sonus a transeunte fit causa, non tamen perennis est.
units.tr: 2. Does the cause of a transient effect always remain, as the effect is outside it? Answer: this is not always required, since it is enough that the effect be outside the cause while it is being produced. Thus a sound is made by a transient cause, yet it is not perpetual.

units.la: 18. Quarto a modo efficiens vel necessaria est, vel libera. Illa est, quae ad unum oppositorum determinata, eodem modo agit quando & quantum potest. Haec vero, quae ad opposita indifferens, agit, quando, quantum & quomodo lubet. Ex quibus patet 1. Causam necessariam ex se determinatam esse ad agendum; Quare & agit praesente objecto. 2. Illam semper agere ex se objecto praesente. 3. Nec posse differre actionem; Quoniam determinata est in se. 4. Agere ad extremum virium, id est, quantum potest. 5. Agere semper eodem modo. Tales igitur causae sunt omnes, quae purae naturales sunt, neque aliquem delectum in agendo, ob defectum rationis habent; Quarte etiam aliis dignitate multum cedunt.
units.tr: 18. Fourthly, according to its mode, an efficient cause is either necessary or free. The former is that which, determined to one of two opposites, acts in the same way when and as much as it can. The latter, which is indifferent to opposites, acts when, as much as, and in whatever way it pleases. From these points it is clear: 1. that a necessary cause is determined of itself to act, and so acts when the object is present; 2. that it always acts of itself when the object is present; 3. that it cannot defer its action, since it is determined in itself; 4. that it acts to the utmost of its powers, that is, as much as it can; 5. that it always acts in the same way. Therefore all such causes are purely natural, and since they lack reason they have no choice in acting; hence they also yield much in dignity to others.

units.la: 19. At libera causæ longè potiores sunt partes ; utpote quæ 1. indifferens est ad varias actiones & effecta, nec determinata ex se ad hoc vel illud oppositorum. 2. Agit quando lubet. 3. Quantum lubet. 4. Quomodo lubet, idque omninò præeunte mentis judicio & consentiente voluntate: Adeoque voluntaria est.
units.tr: 19. But free causes are far superior in their roles, inasmuch as they 1. are indifferent to various actions and effects, and not determined of themselves to this or that of the opposites; 2. act when they please; 3. act as much as they please; 4. act in whatever way they please, and that wholly with the judgment of the mind going before and the will consenting. Hence they are voluntary.

units.la: 20. Cum igitur voluntariè agentia causæ efficientes liberæ dicantur; Et voluntas esse non possit, nisi ubi sit & intellectus, sequitur omnes efficientes liberas simul esse intelligentes; neque ullam aliam esse posse. Cum igitur inter Entia, Deus, Angeli & homines intelligant; Illi tantum liberè agentes dicit debent.
units.tr: 20. Since, therefore, agents acting voluntarily are called free efficient causes, and the will cannot exist unless the intellect is also present, it follows that all free efficient causes are at the same time intelligent; nor can there be any other kind. Since, therefore, among beings God, angels and men understand, these alone should be called free agents.

units.la: 21. Consistit autem libertas 1. in indifferentiâ & indeterminatione, quâ agens ex se, id est in sensu diviso, indifferens est ad agendum vel non agendum, & ad agendum hoc vel aliud. 2. in lubentiâ quâdam, quâ agens secundum electionem agit, vel non agit, & hoc vel aliud agit. Electio autem illa ex intellectu oritur, ejusque spontaneitate, quare eousque se extendit causæ liberæ libertas, quousque spontaneitas illa, quæ non æquales in quocunque intellectu habet terminos; prout nec semper in eodem intellectu in quocunque statu æquales obtinet. Quare longè, imò infinities major Dei est libertas, quam An- gegelorum ac hominum; Et longe major hominum in statu integritatis, quam in statu hoc corrupto. Sed de hoc negotio pleniusin exercitationibus Metaphys. dicam; interim conser Clariss. Heereboord Volum.
units.tr: 21. Freedom consists 1. in indifference and indetermination, by which an agent of itself, that is, in the divided sense, is indifferent to acting or not acting, and to acting this or that; 2. in a certain willingness, by which an agent acting according to choice acts or does not act, and acts this or that. That choice arises from the intellect and its spontaneity; hence the freedom of a free cause extends only as far as that spontaneity does, which does not have equal limits in every intellect, just as it does not always keep equal limits in the same intellect in every state. Hence the freedom of God is far, indeed infinitely, greater than that of angels and men; and the freedom of men in the state of integrity is far greater than in this corrupt state. But I shall speak more fully about this matter in my Exercitations on Metaphysics; meanwhile consult the most distinguished Heereboord, volume 1, as well as the rest.
1. Disp. 46 and 47, and volume 2, disp. 14.

units.la: 22. Quintò à modo, efficiens est vel univoca, vel æquivoca: Vnivoca dicitur, cujus effectus ejusdem secum speciei est; Quare etiam causa generans dicitur, quoniam locum saltem habet in viventibus, sibi simile quoad speciem generantibus. Æquivoca est, cum effectus specie distat ab ipsa; ac locum habet in omnibus reliquis causis; Dicitur hæc etiam virtualis, quia procedit à virtute quâdam activâ, & non à formâ viventis.
units.tr: 22. Fifthly, according to its mode, an efficient cause is either univocal or equivocal. It is called univocal when its effect is of the same species as itself; hence it is also called a generating cause, since it has its place at least among living things, which generate what is similar to themselves in species. The equivocal cause is one whose effect differs in species from itself; it has its place in all other causes. It is also called virtual, because it proceeds from a certain active power and not from the form of a living thing.

units.la: 23. Sextò efficiens est vel per se, vel per accidens. Prior est, quæ producit effectum, ad quem vel naturâ vel intentione ordinata est; Posterior verò, quæ effectum producit, ad quem vel naturâ vel intentione non erat ordinata. Si natura non fit ordinata, dicitur efficiens casualis, ut lapis decidens hominem prætereuntem ferit. Sin intentione non fit destinata, dicitur fortuita, ut fodiens vineam repperit Thesaurum.
units.tr: 23. Sixthly, an efficient cause is either per se or per accidens. The former is that which produces an effect to which it is ordained, either by nature or by intention; the latter is that which produces an effect to which it was not ordained, either by nature or by intention. If it was not ordained by nature, it is called a casual cause, as a falling stone strikes a passing man. If it was not destined by intention, it is called fortuitous, as one digging a vineyard found a treasure.

units.la: 24. Sed dubium est 1. An detur effectum per accidens? Resp. Non datur absolutè loquendo adeo ut præter omnem naturam vel intentionem aliquid evenire possit; ratione Dei enim, ut causæ primæ, omnia ex intentione agunt: Sed comparatè, ad caufam aliquam fecundam, quâtenus ipsa naturalis ipsius ordinatio, aut prima intentio effectuum non respondet; Cum tamen in executione ille effectus etiam à causâ per fe dependeat, quâtenus cum circumftantiis suis spectatur, fine quibus dicitur efficiens per accidens. Ita lapis decidens illo tempore & loco, quo ibi est homo, neceffariò illum ferit; per accidens autem, ratione casus, absque circumstantiis confiderati.
units.tr: 24. But there is doubt: 1. Is there an effect per accidens? Answer: it is not given absolutely, so that something could happen beyond all nature or intention; for with respect to God as first cause, all things act from intention. But comparatively, with respect to some second cause, insofar as its natural ordination or primary intention does not correspond to the effect, it can happen. Yet in execution that effect also depends on the cause per se, insofar as it is viewed together with its circumstances, without which it is called an efficient cause per accidens. Thus a stone falling at the time and place where a man is standing necessarily strikes him; but per accidens, by reason of chance, when considered apart from its circumstances.

units.la: 25. 2. Dubium est, an etiam efficiens per accidens causis efficientibus annumerandus fit? Refp. omninò; Quia verè facit; efficit, ac producit effectum. Sed dices, sic Deus cum fit causa per accidens peccati, etiam erit efficiens ejusdem. Refp. Negatur Antecedens; Deus enim nullâtenus est peccati causa, nequidem per accidens; nullo enim modo illud producit aut efficit; Et fi produceret per accidens, etiam præter intentionem produceret, quod ipfius infinitæ sapientiæ repugnat.
units.tr: 25. 2. There is doubt: whether an efficient cause per accidens is also to be counted among the efficient causes? Answer: altogether, because it truly acts, effects and produces the effect. But you will say: so God, since he is the cause per accidens of sin, will also be its efficient cause. Answer: the antecedent is denied; for God is in no way the cause of sin, not even per accidens, since in no way does he produce or effect it. And if he produced it per accidens, he would also produce it beside his intention, which is repugnant to his infinite wisdom.

units.la: 26. V. A gradu virtutis, efficiens est vel Principalis, vel minus principalis: Illa est, à quâ dependet effectus propriâ ac per fe efficaci in suo ordine virtute. Hæc verò cujus virtus in producendo effectu per fe efficax ac proportionata non est. Principalis igitur citra minus principales effectum producere potest, ut Deus mundum creavit: At neutiquam minus principalis sine principali; Negata enim sufficiente virtute, negatur actio :. Et negata actione sufficiente, negatur effectus.
units.tr: 26. V. According to the degree of power, an efficient cause is either principal or less than principal. The principal cause is one on which the effect depends through its own power, which is essentially efficacious within its own order. A less than principal cause is one whose power is not essentially efficacious and proportionate to producing the effect. A principal cause, therefore, can produce an effect without less than principal causes, as God created the world. But a less than principal cause can by no means act without a principal one: when sufficient power is denied, action is denied, and when sufficient action is denied, the effect is denied.

units.la: 27. Minus principalis causa vel impellens est, vel inserviens. Impellens est, quae sua virtute, ad effectum producendum insufficiente, incitat principalem efficientem ad agendum. Estque interna in ipsa principali constituta; & externa extra ipsam constituta. Prior etiam προηγούμενον dicitur, & posterior ἀντικαταλεκτικός; Sed minus commode; nisi aliter hic termini accipiantur, ac a Medicis (apud quos utraque haec principalis est causa) & ipsa vocum significatio prae se fert. Non enim omnis interna impellens συνεργητικόν & antegrediens est. Nec externa semper ἀντικαταλεκτικόν & praeincipiens. Ita convitium datum antegrediens est, & tamen externa; ira autem, ex convitio orta, interna est, & tamen praeincipiens vindictae inferendae: In nonnullis tamen exemplis retineri posse videntur appellationes illae Medicae, Vid. Strigel. in Dialect. Melanth. lib. 4. pag. m. 1000. Ad internam impellentem referuntur habitus, passiones, inclinationes, temperamenta &c. Ad externam occasiones loci & temporis, exempla, hortationes, minae &c.
units.tr: 27. A less than principal cause is either impelling or serving. An impelling cause is one which, by its power, insufficient to produce the effect, incites the principal efficient cause to act. It is either internal, situated in the principal cause itself, or external, situated outside it. The former is also called prior [προηγούμενον, proēgoumenon], and the latter posterior [ἀντικαταλεκτικός, antikatalektikos]; but these are less fitting terms, unless the terms are taken in another sense, as physicians use them (among whom both are principal causes), and as the meaning of the words themselves suggests. For not every internal impelling cause is cooperative [συνεργητικόν, synergētikon] and goes before, nor is every external cause consequent [ἀντικαταλεκτικόν, antikatalektikon] and precedes. Thus a reproach given goes before, and yet is external; but anger, arising from the reproach, is internal, and yet precedes the infliction of vengeance. In some examples, however, those medical terms seem to be retained: see Strigel. in Dialect. Melanth. lib. 4. pag. m. 1000. To the internal impelling cause are referred habits, passions, inclinations, temperaments, etc. To the external cause are referred occasions of place and time, examples, exhortations, threats, etc.

units.la: 28. Inserviens causa est, quæ virtute sua insufficiente principali ipsam elevanti, ac applicanti, inservit: Dicituerque instrumentum; Cujus differentiæ sunt 1. Quòd fit vel Actívum vel Passivum: Actívum est, quod insitâ virtute simul se movet: Passivum vero, quod a principali tantum movetur. Ita actívum instrumentum est manus scripturæ, passivum vero calamus. Sed dum passivum dicitur, id intelligi debet non absolutè, ac fi nihil conferat actionis: sic enim efficiens non effet, sed comparatè, quatenus actionem suam non edit, nisi motum ab alio. 2. Quod fit vel conjunctum vel separatum. Illud est, quod principali unitum est: Hoc vero quod non est unitum; Quæ unio ratione suppositi potissimum est intelligenda: Virtualis enim unio in omnibus est causis; multò magis in instrumento & principali, ipsius instrumenti virtutem movente, dirigente ac adjuvante. Nec Politica exempla, quæ afferri possent de Legato vel Vicerege &c. probant, instrumentum ratione virtutis separatum esse. Nam & virtus illa politica est, quam confert Dominus & Princeps suis instrumentis, etiam extra subjectum, cum in nudo consensu consistat. Conjunctum instrumentum plerumque est pars efficientis, unde etiam semper actívum est: In naturalibus omnia separata passiva sunt: In Politicis, autem activa.
units.tr: 28. A serving cause is one which, by its power insufficient to lift up and apply the principal cause itself, serves it; and it is called an instrument. Its differences are these: 1. It is either active or passive. An active instrument is one which, by its inherent power, moves itself at the same time; a passive one is moved only by the principal cause. Thus the hand is an active instrument of writing, and the pen a passive one. But when an instrument is called passive, this must be understood not absolutely, as if it contributed nothing to the action (for then it would not be an efficient cause), but comparatively, in so far as it does not produce its action unless moved by another. 2. It is either conjoined or separated. The conjoined instrument is one united to the principal cause; the separated one is one that is not united. This union is to be understood chiefly in terms of the subject: for a virtual union is found in all causes, and much more in the instrument and the principal cause, which moves, directs and assists the instrument's power. Nor do the political examples which might be brought forward, of an envoy or a viceroy, etc., prove that an instrument is separated in respect of power. For that political power, too, is conferred by the lord or prince upon his instruments, even outside the subject, since it consists in bare consent. A conjoined instrument is for the most part a part of the efficient cause, whence it is also always active. In natural things all separated instruments are passive; in political things, however, they are active.

units.la: 3. Quod sit vel animatum, vel inanimatum. Illud est, quod animam & principium motus in se habet; adeoque idem quod activum, & vel conjunctum est, vel in Politicis tantum separatum; in naturalibus quippe nullum animatum instrumentum separatum est. Hoc vero motum ab alio habet, adeoque passivum est. 4. Quod sit vel necessarium, sine quo efficiens non potest agere; vel arbitrarium, sine quo non potest æque commodè agere.
units.tr: 3. An instrument is either animate or inanimate. The animate one is that which has a soul and a principle of motion within itself; and so it is the same as the active instrument, and is either conjoined or, in political matters only, separated; for in natural things no animate instrument is separated. The inanimate one has its motion from another, and so is passive. 4. It is either necessary, without which the efficient cause cannot act, or arbitrary, without which it cannot equally act conveniently.

units.la: 29. Correlatum efficientis dicitur effectum, idque potissimum ratione principalis; nam ratione impulsivæ internæ scopus, & optatum quoque dici potest. Est autem, effectum; quod ab efficiente dependet; Dependet autem variis modis, prout insignis diversitas est causarum efficientium; Quæ tamen in effectu ex ipsis causis æstimari potest. Et hæc de Efficiente & Effectu.
units.tr: 29. The correlate of the efficient cause is called the effect, chiefly in relation to the principal cause; for in relation to the internal impelling cause, the aim and the thing desired may also be so called. The effect is that which depends on the efficient cause. It depends in various ways, according to the striking diversity of efficient causes; which, nevertheless, can be estimated in the effect from the causes themselves. And these things on the Efficient and the Effect.

units.la: CAP. XXI. D E Fine & Medio.
units.tr: CAP. XXI. Of the End and the Means

units.la: 1. Altera causa externa finis est, qui efficientem sequitur, non tantum, quod externa sit causa, sed potius, quòd & omni Enti conveniat suo modo finem esse, & & omnia finis alicujus gratia sint condita; Adeo ut & materia & forma propter finem sint.
units.tr: 1. The second external cause is the end, which follows the efficient cause. It is an external cause not merely because it lies outside the thing, but rather because every being in its own way has an end, and all things are made for the sake of some end, so that even matter and form exist for the sake of an end.

units.la: 2. Nomen ipsi a fiendo tribuitur: quòd omnia alicujus finis gratiâ fiant. Sumitur autem vel pro extremo rei cujuscunque termino, prout suprà notatum est, vel pro usu rei, ut finis calcei est munire pedem; vel pro objecto, cui ipse usus applicatur, dicitur finis cui; vel pro ipso opere intento, ita finis in executione ipsum est effectum, seu opus; vel pro eo, quod in intentione est efficientis, eamque suâ appetibilitate ad agendum incitat. Quâ acceptione hic potissimum considerandus est; in reliquis enim vel nullam exercet causalitatem, vel saltem aliquid ad hanc significationem ex parte spectans obtinet.
units.tr: 2. The name end is derived from doing, since all things are done for the sake of some end. It is taken either for the extreme limit of any thing, as was noted above; or for the use of a thing, as the end of a shoe is to protect the foot; or for the object to which the use itself is applied, which is called the end to which; or for the work itself intended, so that in execution the end is the effect itself, or the work; or for that which is in the intention of the agent and moves it to act by its desirability. It is in this last sense that the end must be considered here above all, for in the other senses it either exercises no causality or at least obtains something of causality only indirectly.

units.la: 3. Verùm nondum superata omnis difficultas, nondum quippe constat, quid sit illud, quod dictam illam incitationem suâ appetibilitate instituit; Quò ut perveniam, distinctè inquirendum. 1. An finis sit causa? 2. An sit causa distincta ab efficiente? 3. Quænam ipsius causalitas? 4. Quod sit illud, quod illam causalitatem exercet?
units.tr: 3. But not every difficulty is yet overcome, for it is not yet clear what it is that moves the agent by its desirability in the way just described. To reach this, we must inquire under four heads: 1. Is the end a cause? 2. Is it a cause distinct from the efficient cause? 3. What is its causality? 4. What is that which exercises this causality?

units.la: 4. 1. An finis causa sit, affirmare non detrectandum; Cum enim 1. vi desiderii ac appetitûs ipsam efficientem impellat, ac obliquè per illam effectum constituat; & 2. media à quibus causarum dependet, à se dependentia habeat, utique causa esse debet; facit quippe ut media sint media, hoc est ut revera ipsum causatum producant; At quid hoc aliud est, quam actione constituente, licet indirecte causatum causari?
units.tr: 4. As to the first: that the end is a cause should not be denied. For, first, by the force of desire and appetite it impels the efficient cause itself and through it constitutes the effect indirectly; and second, the means on which causes depend have their dependence from the end. Surely, then, it must be a cause, since it makes the means to be means, that is, really produces the caused thing. And what is this other than a constituting action, by which the caused thing is caused, though indirectly?

units.la: 5. Objic. 1. Finis causalitas est motio Metaphorica; Atqui omne Metaphoricum improprie dictum est: Erit ergo causa improprie dicta. Resp: Dicitur motio Metaphorica, non quod proprie non sit motio; nam & impulsio vera est actio & motio, sed quod sit indirecta & obliqua, per lineam rectam ad causatum non transiens. Neque aliud intellexit Philosophus, dum 1. Gen. & Corr. cap. 7. dixit, finem non esse τοιοῦτον εἶ μὴ ηκητε μεθοφορεν.
units.tr: 5. Objection 1: the causality of the end is a metaphorical motion; but everything metaphorical is improperly so called; therefore the end will be a cause improperly so called. Reply: it is called a metaphorical motion not because it is not really a motion (for impulsion too is a true action and motion), but because it is indirect and oblique, not passing by a straight line to the caused thing. The Philosopher meant nothing else when, in Gen. and Corr. book 1, chapter 7, he said that the end is not something that can be called metaphorically [τοιοῦτον εἶ μὴ ηκητε μεθοφορεν].

units.la: 6. Objic. 2. Nec in intentione est causa, quoniam eo saepe frustramur; neque omnia agentia illum intendere possunt; neque sic est aliquid reale, aut actuale, cum omnis causa, ut rei est & actu agere debet, realem ac actualem requirat praesentiam; Et impossibile sit aliquid reale, ab eo quod rationis & intentionis est, prodire, quoniam causatum toto genere dignius esset causa. Neque in executione, quia est ipsum effectum, quod finita causatione demum existit; Cum vero causa esse debet, dum fit causatio, nihil enim agit, dum nondum est: Etiam finis deberet esse, dum fit causatio. Resp. Est causa in intentione; Licet verò usu sæpe frustremur, non tollit hoc actionem & causalitatem finis, sed impotentiam nostram arguit, ac defectum mediorum; Quo casu præstat, quod potest. Nec requiritur, ut omnia agentia illum intendant, satis enim est, si ob intentum finem, vel à se vel ab alio, cujus vi causæ sunt, agant. Et falsum est, quod non sit aliquid reale & actuale; non enim omne quod in intellectu est, statim est Ens rationis, nisi objectivè insit, ut superiori tractatu ostensum est: At finis, qui causa est, non inest objectivè, sed ille tantum qui in executione erit, utpote qui est ipsum effectum. Verum quidem est, causatum, ut est in se Ens, superare dignitatem finis, quia illud non à solo fine dependet, sed etiam à reliquis suis causis: At axioma loquitur saltem de totâ συμπλοκῇ & complexione omnium causarum, non de hac & illâ seorsim; nisi etiam causatum consideretur, secundum illam rationem, quâ præcisè ab illâ causâ dependet; Atque ita causatum, prout finitum & à fine dependens est, etiam finis dignitatem non superat. Manet igitur inter Causas jure merito finis. •
units.tr: 6. Objection 2: the end is not a cause in intention, since we are often frustrated by it; nor can all agents intend it; nor is it something real or actual, since every cause, in order to act as a thing and actually, requires a real and actual presence; and it is impossible for something real to proceed from what belongs to reason and intention, since the caused thing would be more worthy than its cause by an entire genus. Nor is it so in execution, since the end is itself the effect, which exists only when the causation is finished; but a cause ought to exist while the causation is taking place, for nothing acts while it does not yet exist; so the end too would have to exist while the causation is taking place. Reply: the end is a cause in intention. Although we are often frustrated in practice, this does not take away the action and causality of the end, but reveals our impotence and the lack of means; in such a case what is possible is done. Nor is it required that all agents intend it; it is enough if they act for the sake of the intended end, either of themselves or by another whose power they act through. And it is false that it is not something real and actual; for not everything that is in the intellect is at once a being of reason, unless it is present objectively, as was shown in the earlier treatise. But the end, which is a cause, is not present objectively; only that which will be in execution, namely the effect itself, is. It is true that the caused thing, as a being in itself, surpasses the dignity of the end, because it depends not on the end alone but also on its other causes. But the axiom speaks at least of the whole combination [συμπλοκῇ] and complex of all causes, not of this one or that one separately; unless the caused thing is also considered under that aspect by which it depends precisely on that cause. And so the caused thing, as finished and dependent on the end, does not surpass the dignity of the end. Therefore the end rightly remains among the causes.

units.la: 7.II. Sed, an distincta sit ab illâ causâ quam efficientem impellentem superiori capite diximus, olim fuit dubitatum ; & nunc varii dubitant. Et licet non multum referre videatur, probabilius tamen est, cum toto genere ab efficiente impulsivâ distingui ; Nam nec externa esse potest, nec interna ; non externa impellens, quia illa extra efficientem est constituta : at finis est in ipsâ. Non interna, quia longè alio modo incitat, ac illa impulsiva: Finis quippe 1. sui amore ac desiderio movet : at interna efficiens suâ præsentiâ saltem disponendo incitat. 2. Desiderium finis fluit ab ejus cognitione : At interna impellens nullam præsupponit cognitionem. 3. Finis impellit ad sui acquisitionem : At altera illa ad alterius toto genere & formâ ab ipso diversi. 4. Finis ex impellente sæpe oritur ; At nunquam ex fine impellens. Quæ differentiæ in quocunque exemplo manifestæ sunt, ita ex. grat. Avarus, avaritiâ, tanquam causâ impellente incitatus, acquisitionem bonorum ac divitiarum appetit ; Ubi avaritia intrinsecè ipsum disponendo impellit : At cognitio utilitatis divitiarum ipsum amore ac desiderio earum acquirendarum, ut causa finalis incitat. Avaritiæ cognitio nihil hic præstat : At cognitio finis sui desiderium excitat. Avaritia ad avaritiam non impellit : Sed possessio bonorum cognita ad possessionem bonorum invitat. Ex avaritiâ
units.tr: 7. II. But whether it is distinct from that cause which we called the impelling efficient cause in the previous chapter, was once disputed, and now various people doubt it. And although it may seem not to matter much, it is nevertheless more probable that it is distinguished from the impelling efficient cause by an entire genus. For it can be neither external nor internal. Not external and impelling, because that is constituted outside the efficient cause, whereas the end is within it. Not internal, because it moves in a quite different way from that impelling cause. The end moves by the love and desire of itself: the internal efficient cause incites only by its presence, by disposing. The desire for the end flows from its knowledge; the internal impelling cause presupposes no knowledge. The end impels toward its own acquisition; the other impels toward something else, different from it in genus and form. The end often arises from the impelling cause; the impelling cause never arises from the end. These differences are evident in any example. For instance, the miser, driven by avarice as an impelling cause, seeks the acquisition of goods and riches: here avarice impels him by disposing him within. But the knowledge of the usefulness of riches incites him, as a final cause, by the love and desire of acquiring them. The knowledge of avarice does nothing here; the knowledge of the end arouses desire for it. Avarice does not impel toward avarice; but the known possession of goods invites toward the possession of goods. From avarice there arises the desire for known possession; but from that desire and love there does not arise avarice.

units.la: 1, 2, 3, 4 : section markers in the text. tiâ oritur possessionis cognitæ desiderium: at ex desiderio ac amore illo non fit avaritia.
units.tr: 1, 2, 3, 4: section markers in the text. From avarice there arises the desire for known possession; but from that desire and love there does not arise avarice.

units.la: 8- Quare mirari non desino, Clarissimi Voet, Philos. Prim. reform. cap. 20. sect. 4. tam facilem commisisse à consuetâ viâ recessum, secus ac hypotheses ejus, quas defensioni formarum substantialium, sect. 3. præmiserat, ferre valent: Dicit primò finem non aliter esse causam, quam si cum causâ procatarcticâ aut procegumenâ confundatur: quia alias concipietur esse in idea. Resp. Minor falsa est; neque aliter concipitur esse in ideâ, sed vel ipsa est idea, ut pote quia, est ipsa cognitio objecti desiderati; quæ utique verè est. 2. Et quid obstaret, si dicatur esse in ideâ, sive in intentione, id enim potissimum de objecto ipsius finis, quod demum erit causatum intelligi debet, non autem de ipsâ causa finali. Dicit secundò: non esse excogitabilem ullam realem causalitatem, aut modum causalitatis (videlicet externæ) distinctum à causalitate causæ efficientis. Resp. Ea jam data est: quod sit actio obliqua, cum Efficientis sit actio directa; Quæ actio obliqua & realis est causalitas, ac satis à causalitate efficientis distinct. Dicet: Etiam causa impulsiva obliquè agit; prius in efficientem principalem, ac per illam in effectum. Resp. Quin potius didirectè agit in ipsum effectum causa impulsiva; Quod ut capi possit, notandum est, illam valdè remotam esse causam, adeo ut & finis sæpe ab eâ ortum habeat; At remotæ causæ etiam directè agunt, licet in proximas prius agant, quoniam quod illæ agunt, rectà quasi lineâ ad essectum per alias causas transit, quia videlicet ipsarum causatum formale est, aliquid directè ad causatum materiale pertinens. Ita coquus coctionis cibi est efficiens remota, & tamen directè dicitur cibum coquere, licet ipsum ignem applicatione cibi, ut sit causa, disponat. Adeo ut ipsius effectum formale sit; cibi ad ignem applicati custodia, directè ad cibum coctum pertinens. Consimiliter causatum formale causæ impulsivæ directè tendit ad effectum, licet ad hoc per alias causas transeat: Ita dum spes impunitatis furem ad furtum commovet, ejus causatum formale est, furtum clanculum à fure factum, directè ad ipsum furtum tendens. At formale causatum finalis causæ est medium sive destinatum ad finem, ad quod directè tendit, & saltem per hoc obliquè ad effectum. Ex quibus colligi potest, finali causæ satis esse, si media quærat, ordinet & applicet: At hoc non sufficit impulsivæ, utpote quæ etiam partem effecti constituit, licet minus principaliter. Manet igitur insignis distantia inter causalitatem causæ finalis, & impellentis; Quæ magis patere potest, si unam eamdemque rem consideremus, prout est vel impulsiva, vel finalis causa, de quo vide Burgerfdic. l. 1. log. cap. 18. Theor. 2. com. 1.
units.tr: 8. Hence I cannot cease to wonder that the most distinguished Voet, Philos. Prim. reform. chap. 20, sect. 4, made so easy a departure from the usual way, a departure which his hypotheses, premised in sect. 3 in defence of substantial forms, cannot bear. He says first that the end is a cause only if it is confused with a procatarctic or procegumenal cause, since otherwise it would be conceived as being in the idea. Reply: the minor premise is false; nor is it conceived otherwise than as being in the idea, or rather it is itself the idea, inasmuch as it is the knowledge of the desired object, which is certainly real. Second, what would prevent it from being said to be in the idea, or in the intention? For this must be understood chiefly of the object of the end itself, which will be the caused thing, and not of the final cause itself. He says second: that no real causality, or mode of causality (namely external causality), distinct from the causality of the efficient cause, can be conceived. Reply: this has already been granted: it is an oblique action, whereas the action of the efficient cause is direct; and this oblique action is a real causality, and sufficiently distinct from the causality of the efficient cause. He will say: the impelling cause too acts obliquely, first upon the principal efficient cause and through it upon the effect. Reply: on the contrary, the impelling cause acts directly upon the effect itself. To understand this, it must be noted that the impelling cause is a very remote cause, so that the end often has its origin from it. But remote causes too act directly, although they act first upon the nearer causes, because what they do passes in a straight line, as it were, to the effect through other causes, since, that is, their formal caused thing is something belonging directly to the material caused thing. Thus the cook is the remote efficient cause of the cooking of food, and yet he is said to cook the food directly, although by applying the food to the fire he disposes the fire to be a cause. So the formal effect of the cook is the keeping of the food applied to the fire, which belongs directly to the cooked food. Similarly, the formal caused thing of an impelling cause tends directly toward the effect, although it passes through other causes to reach it. Thus, when the hope of impunity moves a thief to theft, its formal caused thing is the secret theft committed by the thief, which tends directly toward the theft itself. But the formal caused thing of a final cause is the means, or what is destined for the end, toward which it tends directly, and toward the effect only indirectly through that. From this it can be gathered that it is enough for a final cause to seek, arrange and apply the means; but this does not suffice for an impelling cause, which also constitutes a part of the effect, though less principally. Therefore a striking distance remains between the causality of the final cause and that of the impelling cause, which can be made clearer if we consider one and the same thing as either an impelling or a final cause; on this see Burgersdijk, Logic, book 1, chapter 18, Theorem 2, commentary 1.

units.la: 9. III. Causalitas igitur finis, ut ex dictis patet, in actione obliquâ consistit; Quæ nihil aliud est, quam vi desiderii ac appetitus sui objecti, quod est futurum effectum, movere efficientem, ad conquisitionem mediorum, legitimâ quantitate, qualitate ac ordine constantium, eorumque applicationem; Ita cognitio conveniens judicata sanitatis vim desiderii excitat, unde movet ægrum ad expetenda, conquirenda, ac applicanda debita medicamenta.
units.tr: 9. III. Causality of the end, as is clear from what has been said, consists in indirect action: this is nothing other than the power of desire and appetite for its object, which is the future effect, moving the efficient cause to seek out the means, which are of the proper quantity, quality and order, and to apply them. Thus a suitable cognition of health, once judged, arouses the force of desire, and so moves the sick man to desire, seek out and apply the proper medicines.

units.la: 10. IV. Quid vero sit illud, quod illam causalitatem exercet, patebit, si distinguamus, finem ab ipsa finali causa. Finis quippe est vel ipsum effectum, vel ejus fruitio: At finalis causa est illa, quæ media ad effectum, ejusque fruitionem inquirit, ordinat, ac applicat: Quare ipse finis ita sumtus non potest illam causalitatem exercere; Sed causa finalis; quæ itaque, nihil aliud est, quam cognitio objecti, convenientis judicati, adeoque & desiderati; ubi 1. occurrit objectum, quod ratione finis est causa sine quâ non; at ratione efficientis sæpe impulsiva. 2. Cognitio ejusdem, primum gradum ad causam finalem æternens. 3. Iudicium convenientiæ, cognitionem illam complens, adeoque secundum gradum constituens. 4. Desiderium, latè videlicet dictum, quatenus denotat voluntatem, (ab ultimo judicio intellectûs practici determinatam; Atque hoc est quasi formalis ipsius finis ratio; Adeo ut vel solum pro finali causa haberi possit.
units.tr: 10. IV. What it is that exercises this causality will become clear if we distinguish the end from the final cause itself. For the end is either the effect itself or its enjoyment; but the final cause is that which seeks out, orders and applies the means to the effect and its enjoyment. Hence the end, taken in this way, cannot exercise that causality; it is the final cause that does so, and this is nothing other than the cognition of an object, a suitable judged thing, and therefore also desired thing: (1) the object presents itself, which with respect to the end is a cause without which nothing happens, but with respect to the efficient cause is often impulsive; (2) the cognition of it, which begins the first stage toward the final cause; (3) the judgement of suitability, which completes that cognition and so constitutes the second stage; (4) desire, taken broadly, insofar as it denotes the will determined by the last judgement of the practical intellect; and this is as it were the formal reason of the end itself, so that it can be regarded as the final cause alone.

units.la: II. Quamvis autem desiderium potissimum causalitatem finis exerceat, non tamen ab ipso ejus æstimatio desumitur, sed potius ab ejus objecto, utpote à quo originem & denominationem habet. Atque hinc factum est, ut omnia quæ de finali causa præcipiuntur, de ipsâ concretè cum suo objecto consideratâ intelligenda veniant. Quare & eo modo nostra conformanda elt institutio.
units.tr: 11. Although desire chiefly exercises the causality of the end, it is not, however, derived from the estimation of the end itself, but rather from its object, from which it takes its origin and name. Hence it has come about that all the things taught about the final cause are to be understood as said of it when considered concretely with its object. Therefore our exposition too must be arranged in this way.

units.la: 12. Circa finem igitur inquirendum. 1. Quid sit? 2. Quænam ejus axiomata & Proprietates? 3. Quænam differentiæ? 4. Quodnam ejus correlatum?
units.tr: 12. Concerning the end, then, the following is to be investigated: 1. What it is? 2. What are its axioms and properties? 3. What are its differences? 4. What is its correlate?

units.la: 13. I. Est autem finis, causa externa actione indirectâ efficientem ad agendum incitans. Quæ definitio, quoad omnes partes, ex antedictis manifesta est. Dicitur etiam causa, cujus gratiâ, aut propter quam, res est; Quæ definitio non tam causæ finali, quam usui ac utilitati convenit ; Omnis enim res propter usum suum fit. Retineri tamen potest, prout finem in concreto, id est causam sinalem, simul cum objecto suo cognito, explicat.
units.tr: 13. I. The end is an external cause that moves the efficient to act by indirect action. This definition, in all its parts, is clear from what was said above. It is also said to be the cause for whose sake, or on account of which, a thing exists; this definition fits use and utility rather than the final cause, for every thing is made for its use. It may nevertheless be retained, insofar as it explains the end in the concrete, that is, the final cause, together with its known object.

units.la: 14. II. Axiomata ex natura finis oriunda hæc potissimum sunt. 1. Omnis finis habet rationem boni. Ratio est, quia ex ejus cognitione, amor oritur, quo efficientem movet. Sed dubitari potest, anne etiam malum possit induere rationem finis? Resp. Si quâ tale consideretur nunquam; at si speciem boni intellectui perperàm judicanti offerat, finis fieri potest. Dices: At multi ebrietatem malam judicant: At nihilominus Baccho dediti sunt? Resp. Judicant ebrietatem utilem esse, aut genio, aut naturæ suæ, licet eam moraliter malam existiment; non enim voluntas, præsertim humana, bonum morale præ naturali, licet falso, eligit. Dices 2. Multi quoque quæ naturaliter mala ac naturæ destructiva judicant, nihilominus prosequuntur, juxta illud Medeæ: Video meliora proboque, deteriora sequor. Resp. Judicant illa quidem mala esse absolutè, & in thesi, at sibi in hypothesi ea utilia, aut saltem utiliora æstimant; manet igitur aliqua in illis apparens bonitas.
units.tr: 14. II. The axioms arising from the nature of the end are chiefly these. 1. Every end has the character of good. The reason is that love arises from its cognition, and this love moves the efficient. But it may be doubted whether evil too can take on the character of an end. Answer: if it is considered as evil, never; but if it offers the appearance of good to an intellect that judges wrongly, it can become an end. You will object: many judge drunkenness to be bad, and yet give themselves over to Bacchus? Answer: they judge drunkenness to be useful, either to their temperament or to their nature, although they think it morally bad; for the will, especially the human will, does not choose the moral good over the natural good, even if falsely. You will object secondly: many also pursue what they judge to be naturally bad and destructive to nature, in accordance with the saying of Medea: "I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse." Answer: they indeed judge those things to be bad absolutely and in theory, but in the particular case they esteem them useful, or at least more useful; so some apparent goodness remains in them.

units.la: 15. 2. Quo superior est finis, eò melior.
units.tr: 15. 2. The higher the end, the better it is.

units.la: Ratio est, quia inferiores fines à superioribus dependent, adeoque ab ipso partici- patam habent bonitatem; Quemadmodum enim in subordinatione causarum efficientium superior semper est potentior, ita in subordinatione finium superior semper melior; quandoquidem vis ac causalitas finis ex illâ præstantiâ oritur, prout efficientis à potentiâ actiVâ.
units.tr: The reason is that the lower ends depend on the higher ones, and so have their goodness from them; for just as in the subordination of efficient causes the higher is always the more powerful, so in the subordination of ends the higher is always the better, since the force and causality of the end arise from that excellence, just as the efficient's from its active power.

units.la: 16. 3. Finis summus est summum ac infinitum bonum. Ratio ex antecedente patet; Nam quia summus est, nullus eo melior; & quia nulli alteri subordinatus, ideò omnibus bonitatem tribuit, utpote ab ipso dependentibus. Ex quibus patet summum bonum esse Deum, ejusque, quantum à Creaturâ possibile, perfectissimam fruitionem; Adeoque hoc in hac vitâ nunquam persectum, sed saltem inchoatum est; ideoque mediis opus habet ex purâ naturâ non fluentibus, sed speciali Dei benedictione concessis. Consimiliter hinc liquet omnium rerum finem esse Deum ejusque gloriam; Quoniam omnium rerum fines supremo fini subordinari debent.
units.tr: 16. 3. The highest end is the supreme and infinite good. The reason follows from the preceding: for because it is highest, nothing is better than it; and because it is subordinate to no other, it gives goodness to all, which depend on it. From these things it is clear that the supreme good is God, and the most perfect enjoyment of him, so far as it is possible for a creature; and therefore in this life it is never perfect, but at most begun; and so it needs means that do not flow from pure nature but are granted by the special blessing of God. Similarly, it is evident from this that the end of all things is God and his glory, since the ends of all things must be subordinated to the supreme end.

units.la: 17. 4. Omnis actiafit propter finem. Ratio est, quia omnis est propter Deum, utpote quæ etiam est ab ipso. At nihil fieri potest à Deo, nisi propter seipsum; Præstantissimum enim agens præstantissimum sibi finem proponit: Sed finis præstantissimus est infinitus; At nihil praeter Deum infinitum est. Hinc fluit, Deum & Naturam nihil facere frustra.
units.tr: 17. 4. Every action is done for an end. The reason is that every action is for God, since it also comes from him. But nothing can be done by God except for himself; for the most excellent agent proposes to himself the most excellent end. But the most excellent end is infinite, and nothing other than God is infinite. Hence it follows that God and Nature do nothing in vain.

units.la: 18. 5. Finis ponit mediis modum, mensuram ac ordinem: Hoc est, tribuit ipsis legitimam qualitatem, quantitatem ac ordinem. Legitima qualitas consistit in bonitate ac amabilitate, quam finis mediis conciliat: Ratione bonitatis hoc est effatum: finis boni etiam media sunt bona, videlicet per se ad finem requisita. Ratione amabilitatis hoc: Qui vult finem, vult etiam media propter finem. Vult videlicet, non quadam velleitate ac languido appetitu, sed serio. Legitima quantitas mediorum est eorum debita magnitudo ac numerus conveniens; Quare finis omnem in mediis praecavet desectum vel excessum. Legitimus mediorum ordo consistit in debita eorum successione: Succedunt autem sibi debite, si quae in intentione & appetitu erant priora, in executione & genesi fiant posteriora, & contra; juxta regulam: Quo finis prior in intentione, eo posterior in executione. Ratio principalis axiomatis est, quia finis est causa mediorum, quatenus media sunt: At sine legitimo modo, ordine, debitaque mensura media non sunt media.
units.tr: 18. 5. The end gives the means their mode, measure and order: that is, it gives them their proper quality, quantity and order. The proper quality consists in the goodness and lovableness which the end confers on the means. From the goodness comes this saying: the means to a good end are also good, namely those required in themselves for the end. From the lovableness comes this: whoever wills the end also wills the means for the sake of the end. He wills it, that is, not with some half-hearted velleity or languid appetite, but seriously. The proper quantity of the means is their due magnitude and fitting number; so the end guards against every defect or excess in the means. The proper order of the means consists in their due succession: they follow one another duly if what was earlier in intention and desire becomes later in execution and generation, and conversely; according to the rule: the earlier the end in intention, the later in execution. The main reason for the axiom is that the end is the cause of the means insofar as they are means; but without proper mode, order and due measure, means are not means.

units.la: 19. III. Differentiae finium variae sunt; Et quidem primo, vel internus est, vel externus. Prior est usus rei, ex ipsius natura tură resultans, qualis vestimentorum est, tegere nuditatem corporis: Externus, qui exre ab intendente externo elicitur, ut vestimentorum st ornatus. Hæc divisio omnibus reliquis præmitti debet, quia speciales reliquæ denominationes, non semper ex rei natură, sed & ab agente externo, ejusque intentione desumuntur; neque semper conspirant agens externum cum suâ intentione, & naturæ destinatio.
units.tr: 19. III. The differences of ends are various. First, an end is either internal or external. The former is the use of a thing, arising from its own nature, as the use of clothing is to cover the nakedness of the body; the latter is drawn from an external agent, as the ornament of clothing. This division must be placed before all the others, because the remaining special designations are taken not always from the nature of the thing but also from the external agent and his intention; nor do the external agent with his intention and the destination of nature always agree.

units.la: 2o. Secundò; uterque finis, tam internus, quam externus, est vel principalis; vel minus principalis. Principalis internus est, qui principaliter ex rei naturâ oritur; sive ad quem res suâ naturâ quam maximè est ordinata; Qualis est Physicæ, rerum naturalium cognitio.Minus principalis internus est, qui vel simul cum principali adest, vel ex eo fluit, adeo ut præcipuè propter eum res non fit, ut est Physicæ, Medica sanitatis restitutio. Externus principalis est, qui præcipuè in operatione ab agente intenditur, ut si quis Physicam addiscat, ut sit promptior ac expeditior in medicinâ faciendâ: Minus principalis verò est, qui vel propter alium, vel saltem minus præcipuè ab agente intenditur, ut ratione prioris est Cognitio Physica, ratione ejus, qui illam propter usum medicum sibi acquirit. Ex quibus simul liquet, sæpius differsum esse inter internum finem ac externum.
units.tr: 2. Second, each end, both internal and external, is either principal or less principal. The principal internal end is that which arises principally from the nature of the thing, or to which the thing by its nature is most of all ordered; such is the knowledge of natural things for physics. The less principal internal end is that which either is present together with the principal, or flows from it, so that the thing is not done chiefly for its sake; such as, for physics, the restoration of health for medicine. The principal external end is that which the agent intends chiefly in the operation, as when someone learns physics so that he may be readier and quicker in practising medicine; the less principal is that which is intended either for the sake of another or at least less chiefly by the agent, as with physics, which is a cognition for the sake of the first, and for the one who acquires it for the medical use. From these things it is also clear that the internal end and the external end often differ.

units.la: 21. Tertiò finis ratione subordinationis est vel Proximus, vel Remotus. Ille est, qui immediatè ex medio oritur: Hic verò, qui mediante fine propiore ex medio elicitur. Ita proximus finis Logicæ est dirigere mentem in rerum cognitione: Remotus autem ipsa rerum cognitio, quæ per directionem mentis habetur.
units.tr: 21. Thirdly, an end with respect to subordination is either proximate or remote. The former is that which arises immediately from the means; the latter is that which is drawn out from the means through a nearer end. Thus the proximate end of Logic is to direct the mind in the knowledge of things; the remote end, however, is the knowledge of things itself, which is attained through the direction of the mind.

units.la: 22. Quartò, eâdem ratione est vel ultimus, vel intermedius. Ille ad ulteriorem non refertur; sive absolute, ut Deus ejusque gloria, sive in suo genere, ut est pax belli. Hic verò ad superiorem refertur, adeoque subalternus & subordinatus quoque dicitur, ad quem pertinent, omnes reliqui præter Deum fines.
units.tr: 22. Fourthly, by the same reasoning an end is either ultimate or intermediate. The former is not referred to a further end, either absolutely, as God and his glory, or within its own kind, as the peace that is the aim of war. The latter, however, is referred to a higher end, and so is also called subordinate or subaltern; to this class belong all ends other than God.

units.la: 23. Quintò est vel totalis, vel partialis. Prior est, qui totam rei utilitatem complectitur, ut est Logicæ disputare, aut docere alios.
units.tr: 23. Fifthly, an end is either total or partial. The former is that which embraces the whole usefulness of a thing, as the aim of Logic is to dispute or to teach others.

units.la: 24. Sextò est vel opus, vel operis fruitio. Prior finis ipsum effectum, ac posterioris medium est; adeoque hæc divisio æquipollet fermè tertiæ; ita v. gr. Calceus est opus, finis propior; at munitio pedis, ejus fruitio, remotior est finis.
units.tr: 24. Sixthly, an end is either the work or the enjoyment of the work. The former end is the effect itself, and is the means to the latter; so this division almost coincides with the third. Thus, for example, a shoe is the work, the nearer end; but the protection of the foot, its enjoyment, is the more remote end.

units.la: 25. Septimò finis est vel Cujus vel Cui; Prior est quem efficiens assequi intendit, sive sit opus, sive ejus fruitio, qualis est sanitas Medici; ejus enim, consequendæ gratiâ Medicus operatur. Posterior verò est illud objectum, cui opus vel usus ejusdem applicatur; ut v. gr. est ægrotus, cui Medicus sanitatem restituere intendit. Estque hic duplex indigentia & assimilationis; Ille est, qui eo opere, ejusve usu, ad sui persectionem indiget, ut ægrotus sanitatis restituendæ, intellectus humanus, logicæ eum dirigentis, finis indigentiæ est. Hic vero est, quo opus habent media, ut in sui operatione ipsi quadantenus assimilari queant; Estque Deus. Verum hæc distinctio nominis potius, quam rei est, ut supra notatum.
units.tr: 25. Seventhly, an end is either "that for the sake of which" or "that to which." The former is what the efficient cause intends to attain, whether it be the work or its enjoyment, as the health of the patient is the end of the physician; for the physician acts in order to attain it. The latter, however, is the object to which the work or its use is applied, as, for example, the sick person is the one whom the physician intends to restore to health. This end is twofold, of need and of assimilation. The first is that which the thing needs, by that work or its use, for its own perfection: as the sick man needs restoration to health, so the human intellect, which logic directs, is the end of the need. The second is that for which the means are needed, so that by their working they may in some measure be made like it; and this is God. Yet this distinction concerns the name rather than the thing, as noted above.

units.la: 16. IV. Correlatum finis est Medium, ita appellatum, quòd in medio finis & intendentis intercedat; aliter destinatum dicitur, quòd ad finem exequendum ordinatum sit; Estque in se nihil aliud, quam causa efficiens, in quam directè actio finalis causæ tendit; Quare vel necessarium est, vel arbitrarium: Proximum vel Remotum; Principale vel inservions; solitarium vel socium, prout consimiles differentiæ sunt causæ efficientis, ex quibus horum definitiones supplendæ. Et hæc definè & Medio.
units.tr: 16. IV. The correlate of the end is the means, so called because it lies between the end and the one who intends it; otherwise it is said to be "destined," because it is ordained for carrying out the end. In itself it is nothing other than an efficient cause, toward which the final action of the final cause is directly aimed. Hence it is either necessary or arbitrary; proximate or remote; principal or subservient; solitary or associated, according as the corresponding differences of the efficient cause, from which their definitions are to be supplied. And this concludes the chapter on End and Means.

units.la: CAP. XXII. D E Materiâ, Formâ & Compositô.
units.tr: CAP. XXII. Of Matter, Form and Composite.

units.la: 1 CAusæ interna sequuntur, quæ per suam constitutionem etiam partes causati fiunt. Suntque materia & forma, de quibus ordine.
units.tr: 1 The internal causes come next, which by their own constitution become also the parts of the thing caused. They are matter and form, which we take up in order.

units.la: 2. Materia sumitur vel pro eâre, quæ materia à causalitate, quam exercet, denominatur; Atque ita Materia idem in naturalibus est, quod corpus, quoniam hoc solum causalitatem materiæ primæ in Physicis exercet; Vel pro ipsa denominatione à causalitate illâ desumptâ; Quomodo iterum vel analogicè sumitur, vel proprie. Priori modo, vel pro subjecto, ac dicitur materia in quâ, vel pro objecto, dicitypque materia circa quam: Posteriori vero, vel stricte pro sola materia corporum naturalium, & quidem in primis pro prima, quæ & absolutè corpus est. Vel latè pro omni parte collectivâ, ex quâ per modum collectionis etiam accidentariæ res componitur; vel adæquatè pro omni eo, quod causalitatem materiæ exercet, sive in naturalibus, sive in artificialibus, sive in corporeis, sive in iis, quæ ex intelligibus partibus componuntur; Quomodo hic accipienda venit.
units.tr: 2. Matter is taken either for the thing which is named matter from the causality it exercises, and so matter in natural things is the same as body, since body alone exercises the causality of prime matter in physics; or for the very denomination drawn from that causality. This in turn is taken either analogically or properly. In the former way it is taken either for the subject, and is called matter in which, or for the object, and is called matter about which. In the latter way it is taken either strictly for the sole matter of natural bodies, and especially for prime matter, which is also body absolutely; or broadly for every collective part, out of which a thing is put together by way of accidental collection too; or adequately for everything that exercises the causality of matter, whether in natural things, in artificial things, in corporeal things, or in those things which are composed of intelligible parts. It is this last sense that is to be understood here.

units.la: 3. In re ipsa videndum 1. Quid sit materia?
units.tr: 3. In the thing itself, we must consider: 1. What matter is?

units.la: 2. Quaenam ejus diversitates?
units.tr: 2. What are its kinds?

units.la: 4. 1. Est autem materia causa interna, ex cujus partium unione res est, vel ex quâ res est. Materiam causam esse supra oftensum est; Et revera cum res materiata à materiâ dependeat; aut id fiet causativâ, aut subjectivâ dependentiâ. At non fit ultimâ hac; quoniam res materiata ipsi materiæ non inhæret, prout accidens suo subjecto. Dependebit igitur dependentiâ causativâ.
units.tr: 4. 1. Matter is the internal cause, from the union of whose parts a thing is, or the thing from which a thing is. That matter is a cause has been shown above. And indeed, since the material thing depends on its matter, this will happen either by causal or by subjective dependence. It does not happen by the latter, since the material thing does not inhere in its matter as an accident in its subject. It will therefore depend by causal dependence.

units.la: 5. Objic. 1. Omnis causa actu influere, adeoque & ens actu esse debet: At materia non est Ens actu, quia est Ens in potentiâ; imo pura potentia. Resp. Falsum est, materiam non esse Ens actu; habet enim ex se actum ac præsentiam suam citra formæ considerationem; Quando autem Ens in potentiâ aut pura potentia dicitur, hoc 1. intelligendum respectu corporis naturalis; Philosopho enim, qui illam ita sæpius appellavit, Ens in Physicis idem est, quod corpus naturale. 2. Hoc intelligendum de potentiâ subjectivâ, non objectivâ: At subjectiva potentia rem actu & absolutè existere præsupponit; est enim potentia ad respectum. Sed respectus semper absolutum aliquod infert.
units.tr: 5. Objection 1. Every cause must actually influence, and so must actually be a being; but matter is not an actual being, because it is a being in potency, indeed pure potency. Answer. It is false that matter is not an actual being; for it has actuality and presence of its own, apart from any consideration of form. When it is called a being in potency or pure potency, this must first be understood with respect to the natural body, since the Philosopher, who so often called it this, takes being in physics to be the same as natural body. Second, this must be understood of subjective potency, not objective potency; but subjective potency presupposes that a thing exists actually and absolutely, for it is a potency of relation, and a relation always implies something absolute.

units.la: 6. Objic. 2. Quod non agit, non est causa: At materia, quia est principium passivum ac receptivum, agere nequit. Resp. 1. Imò agit quoque, non quidem actione Physicâ, sed latè dictâ, ut suprà dictum. 2. Dicitur principium passivum, ratione motûs, cujus non est causa, sed subjectum tantum.
units.tr: 6. Objection 2. What does not act is not a cause; but matter, because it is a passive and receptive principle, cannot act. Answer. 1. Indeed it does act too, not by physical action, but by action taken broadly, as was said above. 2. It is called a passive principle by reason of motion, of which it is not the cause but only the subject.

units.la: 7. Causalitas Materiæ particulâ ex vulgò, nec præter rationem, exponitur. Ea autem variis modis accipitur; nam 1. tributur causæ efficienti, ut ex convictio fit pugna; & Matthæi, cap. 1. v. 20, Christus conceptus dicitur ex Spiritu S. 2. Fini, ut exinde operamur, id est illius finis gratiâ. 3. Formæ, ut ex animâ & corpore constat homo. 4. Toti, ut versus recitare ex Æneiade. 5. Antecedenti, tam negativo, ut ex nihilo Deus creavit mundum; quam positivo, ut ex nocte fit dies, ex puero vir. 6. Speciei, ut homo est aliquid ex genere bipedum. 6. Proprie Materia tributur, ejusque habitudinem ad compositum denotat; quemadmodum verbum παρατίθημι cum præpositione εκ, significat τὸ ὅλην τὴν ὕλην, juxta Scaligerum. Atque hoc pacto, ex aliquo esse, nihil aliud est, quam partes suas conferre, ex quarum unione, per formam, fit compositum.
units.tr: 7. The causality of matter, through the particle ex, is commonly explained, and not without reason. It is taken in various ways. For 1. it is ascribed to the efficient cause, as a fight arises from a quarrel; and in Matthew 1.20 Christ is said to be conceived from the Holy Spirit. 2. To the end, as we work from a motive, that is, for the sake of that end. 3. To the form, as man consists of soul and body. 4. To the whole, as one recites verses from the Aeneid. 5. To the antecedent, both negative, as God created the world out of nothing, and positive, as day comes from night and a man from a boy. 6. To the species, as man is something from the genus of two-footed creatures. Properly, matter is ascribed to the thing and denotes its relation to the composite, just as the verb paratithēmi [παρατίθημι] with the preposition ek [εκ] signifies to contribute the whole matter [τὸ ὅλην τὴν ὕλην], according to Scaliger. In this way, to be from something is nothing other than to contribute one's parts, from whose union, through form, the composite comes to be.

units.la: 8. II. Differentia variæ sunt, & quidem 1. Ratione ordinis dicitur vel Prima vel secunda. Prima est informis, id est, sine aliquâ formâ consideratâ; Adeoque tantum est materia. Secunda verò, quæ in
units.tr: 8. II. There are various differences, and indeed 1. by reason of order matter is called either prime or second. Prime matter is formless, that is, without any form considered in it, and so is merely matter. Second matter, which

units.la: {y} Eadem sunt. in suo esse aliquam formam involvit; adeoque non tantum est materia. Hæc divisio, licet à variis variè impetita, ac explicata, retinenda tamen est; Non ut per materiam primam intelligamus, aut atomos, aut elementa, aut Chaos, aut simile aliquod jam formatum, sed hoc, quod tantum est materia, hoc est partes unibiles habet, quale in corpore naturali est, corpus simpliciter dictum. Atque ita materia secunda, ex priori illa constituta per certam partium unionem, à forma profectam, est, in quâ forma quædam simul adest, cum partibus jam unitis, ad aliam tamen formam ordinata; Adeoque nunquam est sine prima, & in reipsa non magis ab ipsa distinguitur, quam homo vestibus indutus à nudo; differt tamen denominatione, à forma, quam recipit, defumta, ut & ordine.
units.tr: {y} These are the same. in its being involves some form, and so is not merely matter. This division, though variously attacked and explained by various people, must nonetheless be retained; not so that by prime matter we understand atoms, or elements, or Chaos, or any similar thing already formed, but that which is merely matter, that is, has parts capable of union, as is found in the natural body, namely body simply so called. And so second matter, constituted from that former matter by a certain union of parts proceeding from form, is that in which some form is present at the same time as the parts already united, yet ordered to another form. Hence it is never without prime matter, and in reality it is not distinguished from it any more than a man clothed is distinguished from a naked man; it differs, however, by the denomination taken from the form it receives, and also by order.

units.la: 9. 2. Ratione ordinis ad materiatum, est vel remota, vel proxima. Illa dicitur, inter quam & materiatum alia materia intercedit, ratione videlicet denominationis à forma, ut Elementa sunt corporis humani, Arbor Mensæ: At proxima est, ex quâ simul cum formâ est ipsum materiatum. Diciturque alias materia compositionis & in facto esse, quemadmodum prior Generationis & in fieri; Proxima igitur materia sunt ipsius partes quantitatis & integrantes.
units.tr: 9. 2. By reason of order to the material thing, matter is either remote or proximate. Remote matter is that between which and the material thing another matter intervenes, namely by reason of the denomination from form; thus the elements are the matter of the human body, and wood is the matter of a table. Proximate matter, on the other hand, is that from which the material thing itself is together with the form. It is also called the matter of composition and of being in fact, just as the former is the matter of generation and of becoming. Proximate matter, therefore, is the parts of quantity and the integral parts themselves.

units.la: 10. 3. Ratione durationis est, vel permanens, vel transiens; Hæc quæ aliam denominationem ac essentiam habet in & extra compositum, adeoque semper remota est, licet non omnis remota transiens sit; Talis est ovum pulli, semen caninum canis. Illa vero est, quæ priorem essentiam ac denominationem in & extra materiatum retinet, qualis est lignum lectiçæ, æs statuæ.
units.tr: 10. 3. By reason of duration, matter is either permanent or transient. The former, which has a different denomination and essence inside and outside the composite, and so is always remote, though not every remote matter is transient, is such as the egg of a chick or the seed of a dog.
