The latter is that which retains its earlier essence and denomination inside and outside the material thing, such as the wood of a bed or the bronze of a statue.

units.la: 11. 4. Ratione coordinationis, est vel Totalis, vel Partialis; Illa est ex quâ omnes rei partes quantitativæ sunt desumtæ, ut est ovum pulli, hæc vero, ex quâ non omnes partes sunt desumtæ, ut lapides ædificii. Hæc iterum vel est æqualis, quæ cum reliquis partibus eundem habet dignitatis gradum; vel inæqualis, quando à reliquis diversum præstantiæ gradum obtinet. Atque tum vel est Principalis, quæ in superiori quodam præstantiæ gradu; vel minus principalis, quæ in inferiori gradu est. Sed de hâc differentiâ latius inter partes.
units.tr: 11. 4. By reason of coordination, matter is either total or partial. The former is that from which all the quantitative parts of a thing are drawn, as the egg is for a chick; the latter is that from which not all the parts are drawn, as the stones of a building. The latter in turn is either equal, which has the same degree of dignity as the other parts, or unequal, when it holds a different degree of excellence from the others. And then it is either principal, which is in a higher degree of excellence, or less principal, which is in a lower degree. But this difference is discussed more fully under parts.

units.la: 12. §. Ratione Entitatis materiati, vel est sensibilis, quæ corporum est; adeoque vel naturalis est, ex quâ per naturam fit materiatum: vel artificialis, ex quâ ars opus suum producit. Vel est intelligibilis, ex quâ res aliæ, in quibus partes distinctæ annotantur, constant: Qualis sunt literæ vocis, termini & propositiones syllogismi.
units.tr: 12. §. By reason of the entity of the material thing, matter is either sensible, which belongs to bodies, and so is either natural, from which the thing is made by nature, or artificial, from which art produces its work. Or it is intelligible, from which other things, in which distinct parts are noted, are composed; such are the letters of a word, and the terms and propositions of a syllogism.

units.la: 13. Altera Causa interna, Forma dicitur, fortean à Graeco μορφὴ per metathesin literarum φ & μ, & degenerationem τὲ φ Graecorum in Flatinorum, qualis est in φήμη fama, & φαύνομαι, unde fit fenestra; quoad cætera voces plane æquipollentes sunt.
units.tr: 13. The other internal cause is called form, perhaps from the Greek morphē [μορφὴ] by metathesis of the letters φ and μ, and the change of the Greek φ into the Latin f, as in phēmē, fame, and phainomai, whence comes fenestra, window; in other respects the words are plainly equivalent.

units.la: 14. Sumitur autem vox formæ 1. Pro rei effentiâ. Atque ita æquipollent, essentia, Forma, Natura & Quiddittas, ac unum & idem designant, aliquo tamen intercedente discrimine modali, vel respectivo: Dicitur quippe essentia, prout rem constituit in suo esse: Forma, prout per eam res distinguitur: Natura quatenus operationibus suis edendis idonea est: Quidditas prout definitione explicari potest. 2. Pro differentiâ, prout compositio ex genere & differentiâ, dicitur esse ex materiâ & formâ logicâ. 3. Pro Ente simplici, propter aliquam analogiam; ita Deus forma purissima dicitur, idque non relative, acsi aliquid informet, sed absolute; quia Deus cum nullo alio inter inferiora majorem videtur habere convenientiam, quam cum formâ, ratione essentiæ immaterialis. 4. Pro figurâ, externâque lineamentorum corporis dispositione, quomodo & μορφὴ apud Graecos idem denotat; quemadmodum Christus duobus discipulis apparuisse dicitur, ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ, Marc. 16. 12.
units.tr: 14. The word form is taken 1. for the essence of a thing. In this sense essence, form, nature and quiddity are equivalent and designate one and the same thing, though with some modal or relative distinction between them: it is called essence insofar as it constitutes the thing in its being; form insofar as the thing is distinguished by it; nature insofar as it is fit to produce its operations; quiddity insofar as it can be explained by definition. 2. For the difference, since a composite of genus and difference is said to be made of logical matter and form. 3. For a simple being, by some analogy; thus God is called the purest form, and this not relatively, as if he informed something, but absolutely, because among inferior things God seems to have the greatest affinity with form, by reason of his immaterial essence. 4. For the figure and external arrangement of the lineaments of the body, in which sense the Greek morphē [μορφὴ] also denotes the same; thus Christ is said to have appeared to two disciples in another form [ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῇ], Mark 16.12.

units.la: Et in monte Tabor μεταμορφώθη videlicet ἐνσωματῶς, ratione externæ figuræ, non ἀσωμάτως & interné. 5. Propulchritudine, tanquam commendabili figurâ externâ, aggregatim cum debitâ magnitudine, legitimoque colore acceptâ. 6. Pro externo motore,quomodo intelligentiæ, orbium cœlestium motrices, Philosophi formæ dicuntur. 7. Pro causâ internâ, unionem partium materiæ præstans, eâdemque seipsam cum materiâ uniente, quomodo hîc capi debet.
units.tr: And on Mount Tabor he was transfigured [μεταμορφώθη], that is, bodily [ἐνσωματῶς], in respect of his external figure, not incorporeally [ἀσωμάτως] and in his inner nature. 5. For beauty, as a commendable external figure, received in the aggregate with due magnitude and proper colour. 6. For the external mover, in the way the philosophers call the intelligences, the movers of the heavenly spheres, forms. 7. For the internal cause, which effects the union of the parts of matter and, by uniting itself with the matter, does so in the same act; this is the sense to be understood here.

units.la: 15. Atque in hac significatione ratione officiorum aliter quandoque appellatur ; Et quidem 1. αὸ& sive species, vel quod speciosa, pulchra, ac appetibilis sit, præ materiâ; vel potius, quod per illam materia ad certam speciem materiatorum pertineat, ad quam per se indifferens erat. 2. Λόγος τῆς οὐσίας, ratio essentiæ & quiditatis, quòd potissima pars sit essentiæ, à quâ ejus specificatio & denominatio dependet. 3. Ἐντελέχεια, actus & realis persectionis possessio; quia ejus præsentia compositum actu suas perfectiones obtinere dicitur. 4. Terminus, vel ratione generationis, quam terminat, adeo ut introductâ formâ, cesset generatio; vel ratione materiæ, quam actuat ac determinat, non ut simpliciter sit, sed ut sit in tali specie. Vel ratione accidentium, quæ in mamateriâ determinat; prout ipsi certam quantitatem, figurationem; ac reliqua ex iis orta accidentia, tribuit.
units.tr: 15. In this sense, by reason of its functions, it is also called otherwise at times. Indeed: (1) species [εἶδος], either because it is beautiful, fair and desirable compared with matter, or rather because through it matter belongs to a certain species of material things, to which it was in itself indifferent; (2) reason of the essence [λόγος τῆς οὐσίας], ratio essentiae and quiddity, because it is the chief part of the essence, on which its specification and denomination depend; (3) actuality [ἐντελέχεια], actus, and the possession of real perfection, because by its presence the composite is said to obtain its perfections actually; (4) terminus, either in respect of the generation it terminates, so that once the form is introduced, generation ceases; or in respect of matter, which it actuates and determines, not so that it merely is, but so that it is in such a species; or in respect of accidents, which it determines in matter, since it gives matter a certain quantity and figuration, and the other accidents arising from these.

units.la: 16. Prolixior hæc nominis fuit consideratio, quâ ut plurimum, ob formarum obscuritatem, totus earum tractatus absolvi- ; Circa rem ipsam tamen aliquid tentan.m est, ut explicetur 1. Quid sit forma?
units.tr: 16. This consideration of the name has been rather lengthy, and by it, for the most part, on account of the obscurity of forms, their whole treatment is usually completed. Yet something must be attempted concerning the thing itself, so that it may be explained. 1. What is a form?

units.la: 2. Quænam ejus differentiæ?
units.tr: 2. What are its differences?

units.la: 17. I. Quid sit forma dupliciter enodandum, 1. Quid sit in generali suâ notione, &, ut ajunt, in actu signato? 2. Quid sit in actu exercito, seu quodnam sit illud, cui illa notio convenit, quodque requisita ad formam exequitur?
units.tr: 17. The question what a form is must be answered in two ways: 1. What it is in its general notion and, as they say, in the abstract act; 2. What it is in the concrete act, that is, what that is to which the notion applies, and which fulfils the requirements of a form.

units.la: 18. Prius absolvitur partim definitione, partim officiorum enumeratione. Definitur forma causa interna, per quam res est. Quæ definitio ut capiatur, 1. Examinandum Genus, 2. Differentia.
units.tr: 18. The former is settled partly by definition, partly by enumeration of its functions. A form is defined as the internal cause through which a thing is. To understand this definition, 1. the genus must be examined; 2. the differentia.

units.la: 19. Genus formæ est causa, quoniam ab ipsa dependet actione constituente causatum, ex materiâ & ipsâ constans; Agit quippe, dum immediatè partes materiæ, seque eodem actu cum illis unit. Sed Obiic. 1. Omnis causa prior naturâ est causato: At forma simul cum ipso; quoniam, ipsâ præsente, productio & causatio cessat. Resp. Simul est forma tempore cum causato, sed prior naturâ, vel illâ saltem ratione, si pars quod neutiquam negandum, sit causati. 2. Verum est, præsente formâ cessare causationem, quia ipsius præsentia est intrinseca partium unio, unde ipsa constitutio, nullo alio actu intercedente, sequitur: Sed inde non sequitur, ipsam naturâ priorem non esse; Cum & partes sint priores naturâ suo toto, quæ tamen eâdem unione, quâ partes fiunt, & nullius alterius interventu, totum constituunt.
units.tr: 19. The genus of form is cause, since the composite, made of matter and form, depends on the form in the action that constitutes it. For it acts while it immediately unites the parts of matter, and in the same act joins itself to them. But objection 1: every prior cause is prior in nature to what it causes; but form is simultaneous with the composite, since when form is present production and causation cease. Reply: the form is simultaneous with the composite in time, but prior in nature, or at least in that respect, since it is a part of the composite, which by no means must be denied. 2. It is true that when the form is present causation ceases, because its presence is the intrinsic union of the parts, from which the constitution itself follows with no other act intervening. But it does not follow that the form is not prior in nature; for the parts too are prior in nature to their whole, which nevertheless, by the same union through which the parts become parts, and without the intervention of anything else, constitutes the whole.

units.la: 2o. Objic. 2. Si forma sit causa, vel erit materiæ, vel compositi; Sed non materiæ, quia ea saltem efficientem requirit, & prior est naturâ suâ formâ, utpote quam in suis partibus recipit; nec compositi; quia causa compositi est causa omnium ejus partium, (cum compositum nihil aliud sit, quam suæ partes:) At in composito non est, nisi materia, cuius causa esse nequit, & forma, cujus quoque causa esse non potest, nisi sui ipsius causa dicatur. Resp. Est causa compositi, & per consequens omnium cjus partium, sed quatenus partes sunt, non quatenus absolutum esse habent; Est igitur causa materiæ, quatenus pars est compositi, est quoque causa sui ipsius, quatenus seipsam partem facit. Dum enim partes materiæ unit, eàdemque actione seipsam materiæ jungens, compositum constituit, quid minus præstat, quam ut & materiam & seipsam partem faciat. faciat? Nec mirum hoc? Homo se ipsum partem Collegii, Civitatis facit, seipsum collegio aut civitati associando.
units.tr: 20. Objection 2: if form is a cause, it will be the cause either of the matter or of the composite. But not of the matter, since matter requires at least an efficient cause, and is prior in nature to its form, which it receives in its parts; nor of the composite, since the cause of the composite is the cause of all its parts (the composite being nothing other than its parts). But in the composite there is nothing except matter, whose cause cannot be the form, and the form, whose cause cannot be anything but itself. Reply: it is the cause of the composite, and consequently of all its parts, but insofar as they are parts, not insofar as they have absolute being. It is therefore the cause of the matter insofar as matter is a part of the composite; it is also the cause of itself, insofar as it makes itself a part. For while it unites the parts of matter, and by the same action joins itself to the matter, it constitutes the composite. What does it accomplish less than making both the matter and itself a part? Is this strange? A man makes himself a part of a college or a state by associating himself with the college or the state.

units.la: 21. Objic. 3. Si forma esset causa, ideo esset quia informaret: At cum non nisi materiam informet, idque non per modum causæ, sed adjuncti, non poterit ullatenus causa esse. Resp. Omninò est causa, quia informat, & quidem materiam; Sed ipsam informando, licet ejus dicatur adjunctum, partes tamen ejus inter se, ac illas secum unit, adeoque illa informatione composita causa fit. Maneat igitur forma inter causas.
units.tr: 21. Objection 3: if form were a cause, it would be so because it informs; but since it informs only matter, and that not by way of cause but as an adjunct, it cannot be a cause at all. Reply: it is altogether a cause, because it informs, and indeed informs matter. But in informing it, although it is said to be the adjunct of matter, it unites the parts of matter with one another and with itself, and so by that very informing it becomes a composite cause. Let form therefore remain among the causes.

units.la: 22. Differentia explicatio potissimum ex recta acceptione præpositionis per dependet, quæ cum sit ambigua, paucis ejus ambiguitas discutienda. Notat autem 1. Efficientem quamcunque, ut per exercitationem acquiritur doctrina. 2. Instrumentum, ut ignis cibos coquit per calorem. 3. Medium quodcunque, ut cum dicimus, transfire per ignem, demonstrare per causas, genus, adjuncta. 4. Subjectum, ut corpus coloratum est per superficiem. 5. Perfectionem intrinsecam; Quo pacto aliquid per hoc dicitur esse, quod ipsius partes uniendo ipsum intrinsecè constituit, ac absolvit; nec non ad certam, ac determinatam speciem reducit; Quomodo hic accipi debet. Adeo ut per formam ideo dicatur res esse, quòd hanc per unionem partium constituat, absolvat, ac determiner, ipsiusque adeo fiat pars essentialis, intimè partibus materiæ præsens.
units.tr: 22. The explanation of the difference depends chiefly on the correct understanding of the preposition per [through], which, since it is ambiguous, its ambiguity must be briefly discussed. It denotes: (1) any efficient cause, as knowledge is acquired through practice; (2) an instrument, as fire cooks food through heat; (3) any medium, as when we say to pass through fire, or to demonstrate through causes, genus or adjuncts; (4) a subject, as a body is coloured through its surface; (5) an intrinsic perfection, in which sense a thing is said to be through this, which by uniting its parts intrinsically constitutes and completes it, and also reduces it to a certain and determinate species. This is how it must be understood here. So a thing is said to be through form because form, through the union of its parts, constitutes, completes and determines it, and so becomes an essential part of it, intimately present to the parts of matter.

units.la: 23. Officia formæ, ut varia sunt, ita ad unum generale reduci possunt, quod est informare: Hoc autem est partes informando permeare, ut sit tota in toto informando & tota in quacunque ejus parte; quoniam eo ipso unionem partium præstat: Atqui illa unio tota est in omnibus partibus, & tota in quacunque; quare vel una sublata, unio tollitur; Est quippe respectus ad omnes partes pertinens.
units.tr: 23. The functions of form, though they are various, can be reduced to one general function, which is to inform. This means permeating the parts by informing them, so that the form is whole in the whole by informing it and whole in any part of it; for by that very fact it effects the union of the parts. But that union is whole in all the parts and whole in each, so that if one part is removed the union is destroyed, since it is a relation pertaining to all the parts.

units.la: Ex hac autem informatione fluit. 1. Quod debeat unire partes materiæ, non extrinsecè, prout efficiens unit partes, sed intrinsecè, ut ipsis intimè & sit & maneat præsens. 2. Quod se ipsam debeat unire istis partibus, eâdem intrinseca unione, quâ partes facit partes, & has simul secum partes constituit essentiales ipsius compositi. 3. Quod debeat constituere compositum: Consimiliter intrinsecè, adeò ut ipsius pars sit. 4. Quod debeat composito speciem tribuere, prout aliam atque aliam unionem præstat. 5. Quod debeat compositum distinguere ab omnibus aliis; quia ejus saltem partes unit, non alterius. 5. Quod debeat ipsi composito tribuere, omnes ad ipsum pertinentes per-
units.tr: From this informing there flows: 1. that it ought to unite the parts of matter not extrinsically, as an efficient cause unites parts, but intrinsically, so as to be and remain intimately present to them; 2. that it ought to unite itself to these parts by the same intrinsic union by which it makes the parts parts, and together with them constitute the essential parts of the composite; 3. that it ought to constitute the composite, likewise intrinsically, so that it is a part of it; 4. that it ought to give the composite its species, as it effects one union or another; 5. that it ought to distinguish the composite from all others, since it unites only its own parts and not those of another; 5. that it ought to give to the composite itself all the perfections pertaining to it, both the first ones, established in the powers, and the second ones, to be completed by the due operations.

units.la: sectiofelliones, tam primas, in potentiis conftitutas, quam fecundas, operationibus debitis absolvendas.
units.tr: perfections, both first ones, established in the powers, and second ones, to be completed by the due operations.

units.la: 24. 2. Quid autem illud fit, quod diftam definitionem recipiat, ac enumerata officia præstet in excercitio, dudum multorum fatigavit animos & calamos. Vix tamen etiamnum quid, præter nomen fine re, ostensum fuit. Nota est in homine Anima rationalis, quæ tamen multis modis à reliquis formis, omnium consensu, distinguitur; Licet in eo conveniat, quod ipsius forma fit, non tamen ex unione partium resultat, neque ab illâ unione dependet. Præter hanc nomina Animæ sentientis & vegetantis, Brutis animantibus & simpliciter nutritivis debitæ, frequentia admodum sunt sermone, sed disparuère explicatione. Quid dicam? Egone anfer inter olores strepam? Subscribam receptæ sententiæ, quam temerè rejiciendam non existimo, licet ipsam difficilem δυσνοήτην, multisque spinis circumseptam videam. Sint ergo formæ substantiæ quædam sui generis, (materiales intelligo) à materiâ in esse, fieri ac operari dependentes; ex ipsius potentiâ, id est, legitimâ ipsius partium unione, resultantes. Quod hic dixisse sufficiet; Alibi autem, si Deus cum vitâ occasionem det, hanc sententiam latius deducam.
units.tr: 24. The second question, what that thing is which receives the said definition and in actual exercise performs the enumerated functions, has long wearied the minds and pens of many. Yet hardly anything has been shown beyond the name without the thing. The rational soul in man is well known, which nevertheless, by the agreement of all, is distinguished from the other forms in many ways; although it agrees with them in this, that it is the form of its body, it does not result from the union of parts, nor depend on that union. Besides this, the names of the sentient and vegetative soul, proper to brute animals and to the merely nutritive, are very frequent in speech, but have vanished under explanation. What shall I say? Shall I, a goose, hiss among the swans? I shall subscribe to the accepted opinion, which I do not think should be rashly rejected, although I see that it is difficult, hard to understand [δυσνόητον], and surrounded with many thorns. Let there be, then, certain forms of a kind of their own substance (material ones, I mean), dependent on matter for their being, coming-to-be and operation, and resulting from its power, that is, from the lawful union of its parts. This will be enough to have said here; elsewhere, if God grants life and opportunity, I shall develop this opinion more fully.

units.la: 25. II. Differentia formarum varia sunt. Nam dividitur 1. quòd fit vel Substantialis, vel Accidentalis; cujus termini tribus modis accipi possunt; nam primò substantialis dicitur, quæ constituit substantiam in suo esse. Et Accidentalis, quæ esse accidentis absolvit: Sed sic nulla datur accidentalis; nam cum accidentia non habeant materiam, formæ quoque incapacia sunt. Secundò, Substantialis dicitur, quæ constituit substantiam absolutè, ut sit idem quod essentialis: Accidentalis verò, quæ substantiam constituit in concreto cum Accidente. Sed nec sic concedenda accidentalis: Omnis enim forma essentiam rei absolvere debet; Et homo albus, non per formâ nisi improprie, sed propter accidens ipsi inhærens, dicitur. Tertiò Substantialis dicitur, quæ cum ipsa sit substantia, essentiam rei absolvit: Accidentalis verò, quæ in se est accidens, rei tamen, cui inest essentiam largiens; Quibus significationibus hujus divisionis termini accipi debent, ut inter se opponantur.
units.tr: 25. II. The differences of forms are various. For they are divided (1) into substantial or accidental, and these terms can be taken in three ways. First, a form is called substantial when it constitutes a substance in its being, and accidental when it completes the being of an accident. But in this sense no accidental form is granted, for since accidents do not have matter, they are also incapable of forms. Second, a form is called substantial when it constitutes a substance absolutely, so that it is the same as essential, and accidental when it constitutes a substance in the concrete together with an accident. But neither in this sense should an accidental form be granted: every form ought to complete the essence of a thing, and a white man is called white not by a form, properly speaking, but on account of the accident inhering in him. Third, a form is called substantial when, being itself a substance, it completes the essence of a thing, and accidental when it is itself an accident, yet gives essence to the thing in which it inheres. These meanings are the ones by which the terms of this division should be taken, so that they are opposed to one another.

units.la: 26. 2. Dividitur forma in naturalem & Artificialem. Prior est, quæ ab ordinario agente in materiâ ordinariâ fit: Posterior verò, quæ ab extraordinario agente in materiâ, obediente virtuti extraordinariæ, producitur. Unde patet, duplex discrimen intercedere inter hasce formæ species; Unum a causa à causâ efficiente, alterum à subjecto petendum. Prioris enim causa est Natura, & subjectum materia, prout ordinariam suam habet recipiendi potentiam: Posterioris verò Ars causa est, & Materia, obedientialem obtinens potentiam, subjectum. Naturalis autem forma vel Simplex est, vel mixta; Et haec vel animata, vel inanimata, prout tali modo ab ipsa corpora naturalia denominantur. Artificialis quoque est vel sensibilis, qualis est Mensae, vel intelligibilis, qualis est Syllogismi.
units.tr: 26. 2. A form is divided into natural and artificial. The former is that which is produced by an ordinary agent in ordinary matter; the latter is produced by an extraordinary agent in matter obeying an extraordinary power. Hence it is clear that there is a twofold distinction between these species of form: one to be sought from the efficient cause, the other from the subject. For the cause of the former is Nature, and its subject is matter, insofar as matter has its ordinary capacity for receiving it; but the cause of the latter is Art, and its subject is matter possessing an obediential power. A natural form is either simple or mixed, and either animate or inanimate, according as natural bodies are named from it in such a way. An artificial form is also either sensible, such as the form of a table, or intelligible, such as the form of a syllogism.

units.la: 27. 3. Forma est vel prima vel Secunda. Prima dicitur, quae tantum forma est: Secunda verò, quae est talis & talis; Prima ergo est, per quam corpus simpliciter formatum est; altera verò, per quam est, mixtum, animatum &c. Distinguuntur tamen potius consideratione, quam re, quemadmodum & supra de materiâ prima & secundâ dictum est.
units.tr: 27. 3. A form is either first or second. The first is called that which is merely a form; the second is that which is such and such. The first, then, is that through which a body is simply formed; the second is that through which it is mixed, animate, and so on. Yet these are distinguished by consideration rather than in reality, just as was said above about first and second matter.

units.la: 28. 4. Forma est vel proxima, vel remota; Prior dicitur, quae nulla alia intercedente constituit, ut anima sentiens animal; Remota verò, quae intercedente alia, ut forma mistî animal. Sed iterum non nisi consideration is est distinctio; Anima enim sentiens in animali etiam forma mistî est; Dicitur tamen haec remota, eo quod ob communitatem etiam aliis talis forma conveniat.
units.tr: 28. 4. A form is either proximate or remote. The former is called that which constitutes a thing without any other intervening, as the sentient soul makes an animal. The remote form is that which constitutes a thing with another intervening, as the form of a mixed body makes an animal. But again this distinction is only one of consideration, for the sentient soul in an animal is also the form of a mixed body. It is called remote, however, because such a form belongs also to other things by reason of their commonality.

units.la: Forma est Generica, Specifica, vel numerica; Generica dicitur, per quam res constituitur in genere: Specifica, per quam in specie: Numerica per quam res est singularis. Sed eadem planè cum praecedenti; Nam in Bucephalo sola ipsius anima vera forma est; Quæ ideo, quod ejusdem naturæ in Hirpino aliisque equis reperiatur, Specifica; & quòd per ipsam Bucephalus ad Brutum & animal tanquam Genus pertineat, Generica dicitur. Numerica igitur proxima est: Reliquæ remotæ.
units.tr: Form is generic, specific, or numerical. A generic form is that through which a thing is constituted in a genus; a specific form, that through which it is constituted in a species; a numerical form, that through which the thing is singular. But these are plainly the same as the preceding. For in Bucephalus his soul alone is the true form; because it is found of the same nature in the Hirpinian and other horses, it is called specific, and because through it Bucephalus belongs to the brute and to animal as to a genus, it is called generic. The numerical form is therefore proximate, and the others are remote.

units.la: Forma est, vel informans, vel assistens: Sed est nominis distinctio: Assistens enim non nisi analogicè forma dicitur; Omnis quippe vera forma informans est.
units.tr: Form is either informing or assisting, but this is a distinction of name only. For an assisting form is called a form only analogically, since every true form is informing.

units.la: Forma est vel immaterialis, quæ in esse, fieri & operari a materia non dependet; Qualis est anima rationalis; vel materialis, quæ ex potentia materiæ educta, ab ipsa in esse, fieri & operari dependet; Quales omnes reliquæ.
units.tr: Form is either immaterial, which does not depend on matter in its being, becoming, or operating, such as the rational soul; or material, which, drawn out of the potency of matter, depends on matter in its being, becoming, and operating, as do all the others.

units.la: Forma est vel Principalis, vel Disponens. Prior dicitur quæ per se rem constituit: Posterior verò, quæ prioris gratia in materia prærequiritur. Sed revera omnis forma in suâ materiâ principalis est, utpote quam principaliter informat. Alterius tamen respectu eadem disponens dici poterit, quâtenus per hanc materia disposita est, ad aliam formam recipiendam: Ita forma ovi, ratione sui subjecti principalis est; ratione tamen formæ pulli dicitur disponens.
units.tr: Form is either principal or disposing. The former is called that which constitutes the thing through itself; the latter is that which is required beforehand in matter for the sake of the former. But in reality every form is principal in its own matter, since it principally informs that matter. With respect to another form, however, the same form can be called disposing, insofar as through it matter is disposed to receive another form. Thus the form of the egg is principal with respect to its subject, but with respect to the form of the chick it is called disposing.

units.la: 33. 9. Forma est vel totalis, vel partialis. Prior est per quam totum est id quod est: Partialis vero, per quam aliquid est pars alterius. Ita totalis est anima sentiens animalis, at partialis, per quam cor ipsius cor est, & non alia aliqua pars.
units.tr: 33. 9. A form is either total or partial. The former is that through which the whole is what it is; the partial is that through which something is a part of another. Thus the sentient soul is the total form of the animal, but the partial form is that through which the heart is heart, and not some other part.

units.la: 34. Causatum, ex materia & forma jun-ctim resultans, compositum dicitur; quoniam illæ ut causæ internæ ejus partes fiunt, adeòque ipsum ingredientes constituunt. Sed de hoc supra latius dictum. Atque hæc de Causis dicta sunto.
units.tr: 34. That which results from matter and form joined together is called composite, since those two become its internal parts as causes and so constitute what enters into it. But this has been discussed more fully above. And let these things be said concerning causes.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: DE Subjecto & Accidente.
units.tr: ON Subject and Accident.

units.la: 1. SEquitur inhærentia, altera dependentia species, quæ, prout & dependentia, primitus tributa videtur corporibus, quorum unum in cavitate alterius suspensum est; At exinde à Metaphysicis assumta, dependentiam accidentis, quâ in subjecto suo est penetrativè, denotat: Unde quoque denominativè dicitur, pro ipsa illâ dependente essentiâ Accidentis; Quomodo accipitur cum essentia Accidentis inhærentia esse dicitur.
units.tr: 1. Next comes inherence, the other species of dependence. Like dependence in general, it seems to have been first attributed to bodies, one of which is suspended in the cavity of another. Metaphysicians then borrowed the term to denote the dependence of an accident, by which it is penetrated within its subject. Hence it is also used in an abstract sense for the dependent essence of the accident itself. When it is taken this way, the essence of the accident is said to be inherence.

units.la: 2. Est autem inhærentia, sive dependentia subjectiva, respectus, quo unum alteri debet suum esse, per receptionem ipsius in se. Ex quâ definitione sequitur 1. Nullum inhærens esse, sine eo cui inhæret; Quia nullum dependens est sine suo independente; ut & nihil quod esse debet, sine eo, cui hoc debet. 2. Nullum inhærens extra illud esse posse, cui inhæret? Quia independens in inhærentiâ esse tribuit dependenti, per receptionem in se. 3. Nullum inhærens potest transire ex eo cui inhæret, in aliud. Ratio est; Quia per receptionem esse suum debet; in transitu autem illo recipi non potest; quare tunc esse deberet sine receptione, adeoque & sine eo, cui inhæret; quod impossibile est. Non potest autem in transitu recipi, quia vel reciperetur, in eo ex quo transit, vel in eo, in quod transit, vel in utroque: Sed non in eo ex quo transit; Quia illud relinquitur; neque in eo in quod transit; quia sic frustraneus transitus, si nunc ipsi inhæreat; Neque in utroque; quoniam vel totum in utroque inhæret; vel pars in hoc, & pars in illo. Non potest totum inhærens in utroque simul inhærere; Quia non unum, sed duplex foret; bis quippe reciperetur, ac bis esse suum deberet per receptionem. Neque pars in hoc & pars in illo; Quod enim ex se partes non habet, quomodo per diversas sui partes inhærebit? Ac deinde altera illa pars, secundo, in quod transfit inhærens, in transitu suo, (quoniam enim alteri jam inhæret, adeoque & transfisse supponitur :) vel fuit in eo ex quo, vel in eo, in quod transfit, vel in utroque; adeo ut eadem difficultas in transitu illo partis maneat, quæ suit in transitu totius. 4. Ex hac definitione sequitur, idem inhærens non posse simul duobus distinctis realiter inhærere. Cujus ratio nunc dicta est.
units.tr: 2. Inherence, or subjective dependence, is the relation by which one thing owes its being to another by receiving it into itself. From this definition the following follow. 1. No inherent thing can exist without that in which it inheres, because nothing dependent exists without its independent, just as nothing that owes its being can exist without that to which it owes it. 2. No inherent thing can exist outside that in which it inheres, because the independent thing gives its being to the dependent by receiving it into itself. 3. No inherent thing can pass from that in which it inheres into another. The reason is this: it owes its being to the subject by receiving it, but in such a transit it cannot be received, so it would have to exist without reception and therefore without that in which it inheres, which is impossible. Nor can it be received in such a transit, because it would be received either in that from which it passes, or in that into which it passes, or in both. Not in that from which it passes, because it is left behind. Not in that into which it passes, since then the transit would be pointless, as it would already inhere there. Not in both: either the whole inheres in both, or a part inheres in one and a part in the other. The whole cannot inhere in both at once, because it would not be one but double, for it would be received twice and owe its being twice over by reception. Nor can a part inhere in one and a part in the other, for what has no parts in itself, how could it inhere through different parts of itself? Moreover, that other part which passes over into the second subject, in its transit (since it already inheres in one and is supposed to have passed over), either was in that from which it came, or is in that into which it passes, or in both. So the same difficulty about the transit of a part remains as existed for the transit of the whole. 4. From this definition it follows that the same inherent thing cannot inhere really in two distinct things at once. The reason for this has just been given.

units.la: 3. Dividitur inhærentia, quod sit vel Actualis vel Potentialis; Quarum illa est, per quam actu inhærens debet alteri per receptionem suum esse: Hæc vero, per quam potest recipi. Sed ultima est σύνεχόξυλον: Inhærentia quippe actum notat, & præsentiam debitudinis, non saltem aptitudinem ad debitudinem; Eò ipso enim quia aliquid inhærens, hoc est dependens, dicitur, esse suum actu debet, & non potest solum posse debere; Ac prout causatum nunquam dicitur, quod potest dependere à causa, sed quod actu dependet; Ita nec inhærens dicitur, quod potest tantum inhærere, sed quod actu inhæret. Et denique si sufficeret ista inhærentia potentiam tentialis, etiam inhærens posset esse, sine eo cui inhæreat, quod impossibile nunc dictum. Et contradictionem implicat, esse inhærens, & non inhærens, hoc est posse inhærere: Esse dependens & non esse dependens, sive posse dependere: Esse suum debere alteri, & non debere, sed posse debere.
units.tr: 3. Inherence is divided into actual and potential. The former is that by which the inherent thing actually owes its being to another by reception; the latter is that by which it can be received. But the latter is a contradiction in terms. Inherence denotes an act and the present state of owing, not merely the aptitude to owe. For by the very fact that something is called inherent, that is, dependent, it must actually owe its being and cannot merely be able to owe. Just as a caused thing is never called one that can depend on a cause, but one that actually depends on it, so an inherent thing is not called one that can merely inhere, but one that actually inheres. Finally, if potential inherence were enough, an inherent thing could exist without that in which it inheres, which we have just shown to be impossible. It also involves a contradiction to be inherent and not inherent, that is, able to inhere; to be dependent and not dependent, or able to depend; to owe one's being to another and not to owe it, but only be able to owe it.

units.la: 4. In inhærentiâ, quod inhæret, dicitur Accidens: id autem cui inhæret, Subjectum. Quorum consideratio nunc instituenda. Subjectum igitur quoad nomen 1. idem est quod subditum, ut parcere subjectis, 6. Æneid. 2. Significat substantiam. 3. opponitur prædicato, diciturque prædicationis subjectum. 4. Opponitur Adjuncto, ac adhæsionis appellatur. 4. Opponitur objecto, & occupationis subjectum nuncupatur. 6. Opponitur Accidenti, ut hic sumi debet. Prout enim adjuncto opponitur, de eo agendum cap. 26. & prout referTur ad objectum, cap. 27.
units.tr: 4. In inherence, that which inheres is called the accident, and that in which it inheres is the subject. We must now consider these. As to the name, the subject 1. is the same as what is subjected, as in to spare the conquered (Aeneid 6). 2. It signifies substance. 3. It is opposed to the predicate, and is called the subject of predication. 4. It is opposed to the adjunct, and is called the thing adhering. 5. It is opposed to the object, and is called the subject of occupation. 6. It is opposed to the accident, which is the sense in which it must be taken here. For as opposed to the adjunct it will be treated in chapter 26, and as related to the object in chapter 27.

units.la: 5. Quoad rem Subjecti 1. Videndum, Quid sit? 2. Quænam ejus axiomata? 3. Quæ differentiæ?
units.tr: 5. As to the thing itself, the subject: 1. we must see what it is; 2. what its axioms are; 3. what its differences are.

units.la: 6. I. Est autem subjectum, cui aliquid præter essentiam inhæret, sive, à quo aliquid per receptionem in se dependet; Dicitur ipsi inhærere aliquid præter essentiam, videlicet constituentem, quæ proprie loquendo essentia est; licet quandoque id ininhærens accidens essentiale dicatur, quod ex essentiâ constituente emanet, aut eam sequatur. Idem dicitur, per receptionem in se; ideo enim inhærens, non est essentia subjecti; quia sic idem seipsum recipere in se; quod impossibile.
units.tr: 6. I. The subject is that to which something other than its essence inheres, or that on which something depends by receiving it into itself. It is said that something other than its essence inheres in it, namely its constituent essence, which properly speaking is the essence. Sometimes, though, the inhering thing is called an essential accident, because it flows from the constituent essence or follows it. The phrase by receiving it into itself is used because the inherent thing is not the essence of the subject; for then the same thing would receive itself into itself, which is impossible.

units.la: 7. Il. Axiomata, ex hac definitione deducta, hæc sunt 1. Subjectum naturâ prius est accidente. Ratio est, quia independens naturâ prius suo dependente; Et recipiens suo recepto. 2. Subjectum toto genere dignius Accidente. Ratio est, quia omni ex parte independens toto genere est præstantius dependente: Sed Subjectum omni ex parte à subjecto independens est; igitur toto genere dignius eo, quod dependet à subjecto: Et quemadmodum id quod omni ex parte à causis est independens, toto genere excellentius est eo, quod à causa pendet; ita & hic, quod nullâtenus dependet à subjecto, præstantius est eo, quod dependet. 3. Omne subjectum est substantia: Ratio est, quia independens à subjecto, hoc est per se subsistens, esse debet. Omne enim, à quo aliquid dependet, ratione istius independens esse debet: Ergo à quo aliquid dependet, ut à subjecto, id à subjecto independens esse debet. Adeo ut hic non sit par ratio inhærentiæ ac causalitatis; nam in hac, quod semel est independens, id non continuò est tale, sed etiam potest. esse dependens, nisi sit absolutè independens. At in inhærentiâ, quod semel independens, id nunquam fit dependens; Quia quod independens est, id per se subsistit: At hoc nunquam nulliusque respectu inhærere potest. Ratio diversitatis est; Quia continuò in inhærentiâ Subjectum & accidens toto genere differunt; cùm in causatione non semper toto genere causa à causato differat.
units.tr: 7. II. The axioms, deduced from this definition, are these. 1. The subject is prior in nature to the accident. The reason is that the independent is prior in nature to its dependent, and the receiver to what it receives. 2. The subject is more worthy than the accident in its whole genus. The reason is that what is independent in every respect is more excellent in its whole genus than what depends. But the subject is independent of the subject in every respect, so it is more worthy in its whole genus than what depends on the subject. And just as what is independent of causes in every respect is more excellent in its whole genus than what depends on a cause, so here what in no way depends on the subject is more eminent than what depends. 3. Every subject is a substance. The reason is that what is independent of the subject, that is, subsists through itself, must exist. For whatever something depends on must, by reason of that dependence, be independent, so what something depends on, as on a subject, must be independent of that subject. Thus the case of inherence is not the same as that of causality. In causality, what is once independent is not always such, but can also be dependent, unless it is absolutely independent. In inherence, however, what is once independent never becomes dependent, because what is independent subsists through itself, and this can never inhere in anything's respect. The reason for the difference is that in inherence subject and accident always differ in their whole genus, whereas in causation the cause does not always differ from the caused in its whole genus.

units.la: 8. 4. Omne subjectum aliquo modo est imperfectum ; Quia aliquid in se præter suam essentiam recipit; quod vel perficit essentiam; & sic non satis erat perfecta; vel illam imperfectiorem reddit, atque adeò non erat summè perfecta. 5. Omne subjectum est Ens finitum. Ratio est, quia est aliquo modo imperfectum. 6. Sublato Subjecto tollitur Accidens; Quia sublato independente, tollitur dependens.
units.tr: 8. 4. Every subject is in some way imperfect, because it receives into itself something beyond its essence, which either perfects its essence, and so it was not sufficiently perfect, or makes it more imperfect, and so it was not supremely perfect. 5. Every subject is a finite being, because it is imperfect in some way. 6. When the subject is removed, the accident is removed, because when the independent is removed, the dependent is removed.

units.la: 9. III. Quoad differentias, Subjectum 1. est vel absolutum, vel limitatum. Prius est, quod secundum omnes partes recipit accidens; Unde & subjectum formale dicitur, & Subjectum quo, ut & inhæsionis. Posterius verò, quod in certâ sui parte recipit accidens, sive cui accidens inest per partium limitationem & restrictionem: Dicitur que aliter Subjectum materiale, quod & denominationis.
units.tr: 9. III. As to its differences, the subject 1. is either absolute or limited. The former is that which receives the accident in all its parts. Hence it is called the formal subject and the subject by which, as also the subject of inhesion. The latter is that which receives the accident in a certain part of itself, or in which the accident inheres through the limitation and restriction of its parts. It is also otherwise called the material subject, which is also the subject of denomination.

units.la: 10. 2. Subjectum est vel proprium, vel commune. Illud dicitur, cui soli inest accidens, adeo ut extra illud non pateat, ut est homo risibilitatis: Hoc vero, extra quod patet accidens, ut ipsi soli non insit, ut homo albedinis.
units.tr: 10. 2. The subject is either proper or common. The former is that in which the accident inheres alone, so that it does not extend beyond it, as risibility is in man. The latter is that beyond which the accident extends, so that it does not inhere in that thing alone, as whiteness is in man.

units.la: 11. Accidens sequitur, quod ratione nominis, 1. idem est, quod casuale & fortuitum. 2. Opponitur subjecto cuicunque, quomodo & adjunctum rei accidens dicitur. 3. Opponitur substantiae, & subjecto inhaesionis, diciturque Accidens praedicamentale. 4. Sumitur pro accidente communi tantum, & proprio opponitur, atque sic accidens praedicabile appellatur. Hic consideranda acceptio tertia.
units.tr: 11. The word "accident," taken according to its name, has four senses: (1) it is the same as "casual" and fortuitous; (2) it is opposed to subject, in whatever sense an attribute of a thing is called an accident; (3) it is opposed to substance and to the subject of inherence, and is called a predicamental accident; (4) it is taken only for a common accident, opposed to a proper one, and so is called a predicable accident. Here the third sense is to be considered.

units.la: 12. In re ipsa videndum 1. Quid sit Accidens? 2. Quaenam ejus Axiomata? 3. Quae differentiae?
units.tr: 12. In the thing itself we must examine: (1) what an accident is; (2) what its axioms are; (3) what its differences are.

units.la: 13. 1. Est autem Accidens, aliquid substantia praeter essentiam inhaerens; sive, quod per receptionem ab alio dependet; Quodque adeo per inhaerentiam ac receptionem illam suum obtinet esse. Ejus itaque essentia est ipsa inhaerentia; non quidem illa, quae respectus est, sed quae ob illum respectum denominat accidens. Atque hujus ratio est. 1. Illud est essentia accidentis, quod immediate ab ejus constitutione ortum, omni & soli accidenti convenit. Sed inhaerentiae talis est ratio; nam
units.tr: 13. (1) An accident is something inhering in a substance beyond its essence; or, it is what depends on another by way of receiving, and so obtains its being through that inherence and reception. Its essence is therefore inherence itself: not indeed that inherence which is a relation, but that which, on account of that relation, names the thing an accident. The reason for this is: (1) that is the essence of an accident which arises immediately from its constitution and belongs to every accident and to accidents alone. Such is the nature of inherence; for

units.la: [Remaining marks in the margin are not legible as text.] nam primò inhærentia immediatè oritur ex accidentis constitutione; Est autem ejus constitutio, productio ejus in subjecto, seu possessio sui esse in subjecto; à quâ immediatè oritur, aut cum quâ realiter eadem est, inhærentia. Et secundò omni accidenti & soli convenit, ut infrà latius deducendum. 2. Quemadmodum Ens creatum pro generali suâ essentiâ habet dependentiam à causâ, quatenus hæc denominatio est; Ita quoque accidens, ut dependens à subjecto, pro generali suâ essentiâ habet dependentiam à subjecto, sive inhærentiam, quatenus pro denominatione sumitur, ac relationis est fundamentum. 3. Quibus accedit, nullam aliam essentiam Accidenti in genere tribui posse, si ea non dicatur Entitas per inhærentiam, sive denominata inhærentia; Cui præterea & omnes conditiones ad essentiam requisitæ conveniunt. Adeo ut nihil deesse manifestè pateat.
units.tr: first, inherence arises immediately from the constitution of the accident. Its constitution is its production in the subject, or the possession of its being in the subject, from which inherence arises immediately, or with which it is really the same. Secondly, it belongs to every accident and to accidents alone, as will be deduced more fully below. (2) Just as a created being has, as its general essence, dependence on a cause, insofar as this is a designation, so also an accident, as dependent on a subject, has as its general essence dependence on the subject, or inherence, insofar as it is taken as a denomination and is the foundation of a relation. (3) To this is added that no other essence can be attributed to an accident in general, unless that is called an entity through inherence, or inherence taken as a denomination; and moreover all the conditions required for an essence agree with it. So it is clearly evident that nothing is lacking.

units.la: 14. Objicit, non-nemo; Oportet ut rei cujuscunque positiva & realis essentia primò à nobis concipiatur absoluta esse, antequam dicatur aliquid cum respectu ad aliud. Ergo oportet, ut Accidens habeat primò suum esse absolutum, antequam habeat esse in ordine ad subjectum. Resp.
units.tr: 14. Someone objects: it is necessary that the positive and real essence of any thing be conceived by us first as absolute, before it is said to be something in relation to another. Therefore an accident must first have absolute being, before it has being in relation to a subject. Answer:

units.la: 1. Antecedens verum esse de illa tantum re, quæ esse absolutum habet, non de eâ, quæ esse suum per dependentiam habet, sive quæ in suo esse absoluta non est. Quemadmodum non oportet aliam absolutam essentiam Creaturæ in genere investigare, præterquam ejus dependentiam à Creatore, quæ ipsam in suo esse constitutam immediatè consequitur. Quoniam Creatura in suo esse plane absoluta non est. Sed quemadmodum hæc internum relationis fundamentum pro suâ essentiâ habet; ita & Accidens à subjecto quoad esse dependens, non requirit aliud esse absolutum, præter suam inhærentiam, quæ internum ipsi est relationis fundamentum. 2. Non statuitur ipsa relatio esse ejus essentia, sed actus inhærendi, sive inhærentia denominata, quæ relationis fundamentum est. 3. Quemadmodum in absoluto quâ tali & suâ naturâ omnia absoluta: ita in respectivo quâ tali & suâ naturâ omnia respectiva; Quis igitur sanæ mentis esse generale absolutum quæret Accidentis; quod quâ tale & suâ naturâ respectum ad independens involvit. 4. Transscendentale esse, ex hypothesi, quod Accidens sit Ens sui generis, licet in se respectum non inferat, restrictum tamen illum necessario admittit: Adeo ut nihil absoluti dici possit de ipso secundum essentiam: sed saltem secundum indifferentiam. Hoc tamen attributum illud est, quod ante illum respectum investigandum est.
units.tr: 1. The antecedent is true only of that thing which has absolute being, not of that which has its being through dependence, that is, which is not absolute in its being. Just as it is not necessary to investigate any other absolute essence of a creature in general, besides its dependence on the Creator, which immediately follows upon its being constituted in existence, since a creature is not wholly absolute in its being; so, although this dependence has the internal ground of relation as its essence, an accident, which depends on the subject as to its being, does not require any other absolute being besides its inherence, which is its internal ground of relation. 2. It is not affirmed that relation itself is its essence, but the act of inhering, or inherence taken as a denomination, which is the ground of relation. 3. Just as in the absolute, as such and by its nature, all things are absolute, so in the relative, as such and by its nature, all things are relative. Who then of sound mind would seek an absolute genus of accident, which, as such and by its nature, involves respect to the independent? 4. Transcendental being, on the hypothesis that accident is a being of its own kind, although it does not itself imply relation, nevertheless necessarily admits it in a restricted way; so that nothing absolute can be said of it according to its essence, but at least according to its indifference. Yet this attribute is the one which must be investigated before that relation.

units.la: 15. Objic. 2. Vnumquodque accidens proprie dictum, in se consideratum, habet essentiam denotatam per definitionem propriam, sine ordine ad hoc, aut illud subjectum, cui diceretur inexistere. Ergo non est de parte essentiæ cujusvis accidentis ipsa inhærentia. Et manifestum hoc fit exemplo. Si hoc aut illud accidens in specie definiatur, nullius subjecti in definitione continebitur designatio. &c. Resp. Antecedens apprime falsum; Nullum quippe definiri unquam poterit accidens, sine ordine ad subjectum. Nec obstat exemplum: licet enim expressa in definitione hujus vel illius accidentis, non fiat subjecti mentio, sit tamen implicita; neque debet expressa fieri. Vetant enim regulæ definitionis, ne id, quod ad essentiam Generis pertinet, exprimè repetatur in definitione speciei; Quare dum albedo definitur, quòd sit color nimiùm disgregans visum, implicatur subjectum in genere, quod est Color, qui dum est qualitas, & hæc Accidens proprie dictum, de cujus essentia est inhærentia; etiam inhærentia illa præsupponitur in definitione Qualitatis, & Coloris, adeoque & Albedinis.
units.tr: 15. Objection 2. Each accident properly so called, considered in itself, has an essence denoted by its proper definition, without reference to this or that subject in which it is said to inhere. Therefore inherence is not part of the essence of any accident. This is made plain by example: if this or that accident is defined in particular, no designation of any subject is contained in the definition, etc. Answer: The antecedent is wholly false, for no accident can ever be defined without reference to a subject. Nor does the example stand in the way. Although mention of the subject is not expressed in the definition of this or that accident, it is nevertheless implicit, and need not be expressed. For the rules of definition forbid that what belongs to the essence of the genus be expressly repeated in the definition of the species. Hence when whiteness is defined as a colour that strongly disperses the sight, the subject is implied in the genus, which is colour; and since colour is a quality, and this is an accident properly so called, whose essence includes inherence, that inherence is also presupposed in the definition of quality and of colour, and so of whiteness.

units.la: 16. Objic. 3. Tum in essentiâ accidentis plura involverentur, quam in essentiâ substantiæ; adeoque ipsum accidens præter subsistentiæ perfectionem, etiam includeret
units.tr: 16. Objection 3. Then more would be involved in the essence of an accident than in the essence of a substance, and so the accident itself, besides the perfection of subsistence, would also include

units.la: O
units.tr: O

units.la: omnem suam perfectionem, ut distinctam à perfectione substantiæ. Resp. Nulla species hujus consequentiæ unquam oftendi poterit; imò contrarium potius sequitur; Quid? An quia accidens habet suum esse per dependentiam à subjecto, sive substantiâ, ideone & ipsius substantiæ persectio, quæ est subsistentia per se, convenit accidenti, cui accedens ipsa inhærentia, multiplicat perfectiones Accidentis, præ perfectionibus substantiæ? An quia creatura dependet à Creatore, ut à causa essetribuente, ideòne plures perfectiones erunt creaturæ quam Creatoris? An potius contrarium sequitur? Ita suadet ratio; Quia dum dependens posterius est independente, nunquam fit ipsum independens; Et dum independens dependenti tribuit esse, non ideo seipsum tribuit; sed manet independens.
units.tr: all its own perfection, as distinct from the perfection of substance. Answer: No form of this consequence can ever be shown; indeed the contrary rather follows. How so? Is it because an accident has its being through dependence on a subject, or substance, that therefore the perfection of substance itself, which is subsistence through itself, belongs to the accident, to which inherence itself adds, multiplying the perfections of the accident beyond the perfections of substance? Or because a creature depends on the Creator, as on the cause giving it being, will the creature therefore have more perfections than the Creator? Or rather does the contrary follow? Reason so suggests: because while the dependent is posterior to the independent, it never becomes independent itself; and while the independent gives being to the dependent, it does not thereby give itself to it, but remains independent.

units.la: 17. Objic. 4. Sequeretur ex hac sententiâ, omne accidens in se & suâ naturâ consideratum esse, substantiam accidens; Ratio consequentiæ est; Quia ex illâ sententiâ, accidens includeret in suo conceptu essentiali ipsum subjectum. Resp. Ejusdem generis hæc cum præcedente est consequentia; An creatura in se consideratâ dicenda est Creator creatura; ideo quia esse suum debet Creatori? Addita ratio prave detorquetur; Nam aliud est esse concep‐tum ptum essentialem, aliud de conceptu effentiali. Subjectum non est ipse conceptus essentialis, five definitio, sed de illo conceptu; Quia enim natura prius est accidente, & definitio ex natura prioribus constare debet, illius quoque pars fit. Sed non illico, quod est pars definitionis, hoc est pars essentiæ. Definias Civem Franckeranum; nonne integræ civitatis in definitione mentio fieri debet? Sed estne civitas pars civis unius? Definias actionem; & ingredietur ejus definitionem vel agens, vel virtus ejus: Sed hæc neutiquam partes sunt actionis. Quando igitur accidens in suo conceptu dicitur includere subjectum, hoc intelligendum, non quod subjectum sit pars ejus essentiæ, sed quod subjectum requiratur, ut accidenti esse concedat.
units.tr: 17. Objection 4. It would follow from this opinion that every accident, considered in itself and by its nature, is a substance-accident; the reason for the consequence is that by that opinion the accident would include the subject itself in its essential concept. Answer: this consequence is of the same kind as the preceding one. Is a creature, considered in itself, to be called Creator because it owes its being to the Creator? The added reason is wrongly twisted, for it is one thing to be the essential concept, another to be of the essential concept. The subject is not the essential concept itself, or definition, but belongs to that concept; for since nature is prior to the accident, and a definition must consist of prior things, the subject also becomes a part of it. But it does not follow at once that what is part of a definition is part of the essence. Define a citizen of Franeker: must not mention of the whole city be made in the definition? But is the city a part of one citizen? Define an action: its agent or its power will enter the definition, yet these are by no means parts of the action. So when an accident is said to include the subject in its concept, this must be understood not as meaning that the subject is a part of its essence, but that the subject is required so that it may grant being to the accident.

units.la: 18. Objic. 5. Est communis Philosophorum sententia, quâ statuitur, accidens nunquam perfectè definiri, in quantum definitur mentione subjecti; Quandoquidem nunquam subjectum de rei essentiâ poterit esse. Resp. 1. Quorum Philosophorum illa sententia? Reformatorum ne? (Pontificii enim ac Lutherani hic suspectæ fidei sunt:) nondum potui rescisccere. 2. Imò perfectè definitur accidens pro suâ entitate, mentione subjecti. Quod enim illud ut prius respicit, id per illud satis persectè definitur. 3. Cur subjectum non est de essentiâ accidentis? Nonne ipsi esse tribuit? Nonne ipsum confervat? Et quid habet accidens, quod subjecto non debeat? Non quidem ipsius genus est, subjectum, neque differentia, sed inhærentia in ipso abstracta ratio essentiæ accidentis fit. Sed plusquam satis huic novæ sententiæ repositum, quod non ægre feret, qui à Veterum sententiis temerè recedere crimen existimat.
units.tr: 18. Objection 5. It is the common opinion of the philosophers that an accident can never be perfectly defined insofar as it is defined by mention of a subject, since the subject can never belong to the essence of a thing. Answer: 1. Which philosophers hold that opinion? The Reformed ones? (For the Papists and Lutherans are of suspect faith here.) I have not yet been able to find out. 2. Indeed an accident is perfectly defined with respect to its entity by mention of the subject, for what respects the other as prior is sufficiently perfectly defined through it. 3. Why is the subject not of the essence of an accident? Does it not give it being? Does it not preserve it? And what does an accident have that it does not owe to its subject? The subject is indeed not its genus, nor its difference, but inherence, considered abstractly, becomes the essential ground of the accident. But enough has been replied to this new opinion, which those who think it a rash crime to depart from the opinions of the Ancients will not take ill.

units.la: 19. II. Axiomata ex hac definitione Accidentis oriunda sunt, primò, Nullum accidens extra subjectum esse potest. Ratio est 1. quia est inhærens: At hoc non est sine eo cui inhæret, vid.th. 2. 2. Accidens nunquam est sine suâ essentia: At illa est inhærentiâ, quæ semper actualis est, ut supra ostensum. 3. Quod non inhæret actu, id si sit, per se subsistit: Sublatò enim uno immediatè oppositorum, ponitur alterum: At quod per se subsistit, id substantia est: At accidens, ex hypothesi, manet accidens. Secundò, Accidens non potest transfire de subjecto in subjectum; Ratio est, quia nullum inhærens transit, ut d. 1. ostensum. Tertiò, Accidens non potest simul esse distinctis subjectis; Pertinet enim & hoc ad inhærentis naturam. Objectiones, quæ adversus hæc axiomata moventur, passim apud Reformatos Logicos ac Metaphysicos solutas habes.
units.tr: 19. II. The axioms arising from this definition of accident are these. First, no accident can exist outside its subject. The reason is (1) that it is inherent, but this is not possible without that in which it inheres, as shown in th. 2. (2) An accident is never without its own essence, and that essence is inherence, which is always actual, as shown above. (3) What does not inhere actually, if it did exist, would subsist of itself, for when one of two immediate opposites is removed, the other is posited; but what subsists of itself is a substance, whereas the accident, by hypothesis, remains an accident. Second, an accident cannot pass from one subject to another; the reason is that no inherent thing passes over, as shown in d. 1. Third, an accident cannot be at the same time in distinct subjects, for this too belongs to the nature of what inheres. You will find the objections brought against these axioms answered in many places among the Reformed logicians and metaphysicians.

units.la: 20. III. Differentias quod attinet; Accidens dividitur, quod sit vel proprium, vel commune; Illud est; quod foli illi subjecto inhaeret: Hoc vero, quod etiam aliis. Prius est vel imperfectum, quod licet soli inhaereat, non tamen omni subordinato, aut licet omni, non tamen semper inhaeret; vel perfectum, quod soli, omni subordinato ac semper inhaeret.
units.tr: 20. III. As for the differences: an accident is divided into being either proper or common. The former is that which inheres in that subject alone; the latter is that which inheres also in other things. The proper accident is either imperfect, which, although it inheres in the subject alone, does not inhere in every subordinate thing, or, although it inheres in every subordinate thing, does not always inhere; or it is perfect, which inheres in the subject alone, in every subordinate thing, and always.

units.la: 21. De hoc proprio accidente litigant Philosophi & Theologi, an etiam possit commune fieri alii subjecto, realiter ac specie à suo subjecto distincto. Respondeo cum Reformatis. 1. Non potest communicari secundum rem, sed secundum denominationem; idque non formali, sed materiali denominatione, prout potentia urendi secundum denominationem tribuitur ferro, non formaliter, quod ipsum urat; sed quod denominetur urere, ob ipsi inexistentes particulas igneas. 2. Non potest communicari, per strictè dictam κοινωνίαν, quâ proprium maneret in proprio subjecto, & idem numero etiam in communicativo efficitur; Quod ipsius communicationis Patroni & volunt, & ad palliandum suum errorem, de ubiquitate corporis Christi, necessario velle debent. Licet aliqua latè dicta communicatio fiat, sive per μέθεξιν & participationem, quando unum realiter idem est cum à causâ efficiente, alterum à subjecto petendum. Prioris enim causa est Natura, & subjectum materia, prout ordinariam suam habet recipiendi potentiam: Posterioris vero Ars causa est, & Materia, obedientialem obtinens potentiam, subjectum. Naturalis autem forma vel Simplex est, vel mixta; Et hæc vel animata, vel inanimata, prout tali modo ab ipsa corpora naturalia denominantur. Artificialis quoque est vel sensibilis, qualis est Mensæ, vel intelligibilis, qualis est Syllogismi.
units.tr: 21. Philosophers and theologians dispute about this proper accident, whether it can also become common to another subject, distinct from its own subject both in reality and in species. I answer with the Reformed: (1) it cannot be communicated in reality, but only in name; and this by a material, not a formal, denomination, just as the power of burning is attributed to iron by denomination, not formally, so that the iron itself burns, but so that it is said to burn because of the fiery particles inhering in it. (2) It cannot be communicated by a strictly so-called koinonia [κοινωνία], by which the proper accident would remain in its proper subject and would also become the same in number in the subject receiving the communication. The defenders of this communication want this, and to cover up their error about the ubiquity of Christ's body they must necessarily want it. Some communication, broadly speaking, does take place, either by methexis [μέθεξις] and participation, when one thing is really the same as another and is to be sought from its efficient cause, or from its subject. For the cause of the former is Nature, and its subject is matter, insofar as matter has its ordinary power of receiving; but the cause of the latter is Art, and its subject is matter, which has an obediential power. Natural form is either simple or mixed, and the latter is either animate or inanimate, according as natural bodies are named from it in this way. Artificial form is also either sensible, such as the form of a table, or intelligible, such as the form of a syllogism.

units.la: 27. 3. Forma est vel prima vel Secunda. Prima dicitur, quæ tantum forma est: Secunda verò, quæ est talis & talis; Prima ergo est, per quam corpus simpliciter formatum est; altera verò, per quam est, mixtum, animatum &c. Distinguuntur tamen potius consideratione, quam re, quemadmodum & supra de materiâ primâ & secundâ dictum est.
units.tr: 27. (3) Form is either first or second. That is called first which is merely form; second is that which is such-and-such. The first, then, is that by which a body is simply formed; the second is that by which it is mixed, animate, and so on. Yet these are distinguished more by consideration than in reality, just as was said above of first and second matter.

units.la: 28. 4. Forma est vel proxima, vel remota; Prior dicitur, quæ nullâ aliâ intercedente constituit, ut anima sentiens animal; Remota verò, quæ intercedente aliâ, ut forma mistî animal. Sed iterum non nisi considerationis est distinctio; Anima enim sentiens in animali etiam forma mistî est; Dicitur tamen hæc remota, eò quod ob communitatem etiam aliis talis forma conveniat.
units.tr: 28. (4) Form is either proximate or remote. The former is called that which constitutes without any intervening form, as the sentient soul constitutes the animal; the remote is that which constitutes with another intervening, as the form of a mixed body constitutes the animal. But again this distinction is only one of consideration; for the sentient soul in an animal is also the form of a mixed body. It is called remote, however, because such a form belongs also to other things by commonness.

units.la: 29. 5. Forma est Generica, Specifica, vel numerica ; Generica dicitur, per quam res constituitur in genere: Specifica, per quam in specie: Numerica per quam res est singularis. Sed eadem planè cum præcedenti ; Nam in Bucephalo sola ipsius anima vera forma est ; Quæ ideo, quod ejusdem naturæ in Hirpino aliisque equis reperiatur, Specifica ; & quòd per ipsam Bucephalus ad Brutum & animal tanquam Genus pertineat, Generica dicitur. Numerica igitur proxima est : Reliquæ remotæ.
units.tr: 29. (5) Form is generic, specific, or numerical. It is called generic when by it a thing is constituted in a genus; specific when by it in a species; numerical when by it a thing is single. But these are plainly the same as the preceding. For in Bucephalus the soul alone is the true form; it is called specific because it is found of the same nature in the Hirpinian and other horses, and generic because through it Bucephalus belongs to the brute and to animal as a genus. The numerical form is therefore the proximate one; the rest are remote.

units.la: 30. 6. Forma est, vel informans, vel assistens: Sed est nominis distinctio: Assistens enim non nisi analogicè forma dicitur; Omnis quippe vera forma informans est.
units.tr: 30. (6) Form is either informing or assisting. But this is a distinction of name only: for the assisting form is called form only analogically, since every true form is informing.

units.la: 31. 7. Forma est vel immaterialis, quæ in esse, fieri & operari a materia non dependet; Qualis est anima rationalis; vel materialis, quæ ex potentia materiæ educta, ab ipsâ in esse, fieri & operari dependet; Quales omnes reliquæ.
units.tr: 31. (7) Form is either immaterial, which in its being, becoming, and operating does not depend on matter, such as the rational soul; or material, which is drawn out of the potency of matter and depends on it in its being, becoming, and operating, as all the others do.

units.la: 32. 8. Forma est vel Principalis, vel Disponens. Prior dicitur quæ per se rem constituit: Posterior verò, quæ prioris gratiâ in materiâ prærequiritur. Sed revera omnis forma in suâ materiâ principalis est, utpote quam principaliter informat. Alterius tamen respectu eadem disponens dici potest, quatenus per hanc materia disposita est, ad aliam formam recipiendam: Ita forma ovi, ratione sui subjecti principalis est; ratione tamen formæ pulli dicitur disponens.
units.tr: 32. (8) Form is either principal or disposing. The former is called that which constitutes the thing of itself; the latter is that which is required beforehand in matter for the sake of the former. But in truth every form is principal in its own matter, since it informs it principally. In relation to another, however, the same form can be called disposing, insofar as by it the matter is disposed to receive another form. Thus the form of an egg is principal with respect to its subject, but with respect to the form of the chick it is called disposing.

units.la: 33. 9. Forma est vel totalis, vel partialis. Prior est per quam totum est id quod est: Partialis vero, per quam aliquid est pars alterius. Ita totalis est anima sentiens animalis, at partialis, per quam cor ipsius cor est, & non alia aliqua pars.
units.tr: 33. (9) Form is either total or partial. The former is that through which the whole is what it is; the partial is that through which something is a part of another. Thus the sentient soul is the total form of the animal, but the form by which the heart is a heart, and not some other part, is partial.

units.la: 34. Causatum, ex materia & forma junctim resultans, compositum dicitur; quoniam illæ ut causæ internæ ejus partes fiunt, adeoque ipsum ingredientes constituunt. Sed de hoc supra latius dictum. Atque hæc de Causis dicta sunto.
units.tr: 34. That which results from matter and form joined together as a caused thing is called a compound, since those become its internal parts as causes, and so constitute the thing that enters into them. But this was discussed more fully above. And let these things said about causes stand.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: DE Subjecto & Accidente.
units.tr: Of the Subject and the Accident.

units.la: 1. SEquitur inhærentia, altera dependentia [species], quæ, prout & dependentia, primitus tributa videtur corporibus, quorum unum in cavitate alterius suspensum est; At exinde à Metaphysicis assumta, dependentiam accidentis, quâ in subjecto suo est penetrativè, denotat; Unde quoque denominativè dicitur, pro ipsa illâ dependente essentiâ Accidentis; Quomodo accipitur cum essentia Accidentis inhærentia esse dicitur.
units.tr: 1. There follows inherence, the other dependence [species], which, like dependence, seems first to have been attributed to bodies, one of which is suspended in the cavity of another. Metaphysicians have since taken it over, and it denotes the dependence of an accident by which it is penetratively in its subject. Hence it is also named by a denomination for that very dependent essence of the accident; and when it is taken in this way, the essence of the accident is said to be inherence.

units.la: 2. Est autem inhærentia, sive dependentia subjectiva, respectus, quo unum alteri debet suum esse, per receptionem istius in se. Exquâ definitione sequitur 1. Nullum inhærens esse, sine eo cui inhæret; Quia nullum dependens est sine suo independente; ut & nihil quod esse debet, sine eo, cui hoc debet. 2. Nullum inhærens extra illud esse posse, cui inhæret? Quia independens in inhærentia esse tribuit dependenti, per receptionem in se. 3. Nullum inhærens potest transfire ex eo cui inhæret, in aliud. Ratio est; Quia per receptionem esse suum debet; in transitu autem illo recipi non potest; quare tunc esse deberet sine receptione, adeoque & sine eo, cui inhæret; quod impossibile est. Non potest autem in transitu recipi, quia vel reciperetur, in eo ex quo transit, vel in eo, in quod transit, vel in utroque: Sed non in eo ex quo transit; Quia illud relinquitur; neque in eo in quod transit; quia sic fructraneus transitus, si nunc ipsi inhæreat; Neque in utroque; quoniam vel totum in utroque inhæret; vel pars in hoc, & pars in illo. Non potest totum inhærens in utroque simul inhærere; Quia non unum, sed duplex foret; bis quippe reciperetur, ac bis esse suum deberet per receptionem. Neque pars in hoc & pars in illo; Quod enim ex se partes non habet, quomodo per diversas sui partes inhærebit? Ac deinde altera illa pars, secundo, in quod transfit inhærens, in transitu suo, (quoniam enim alteri jam inhæret, adeòque & transisse supponitur :) vel fuit in eo ex quo, vel in eo, in quod transfit, vel in utroque; adeo ut eadem difficultas in transitu illo partis maneat, quæ suit in transitu totius. 4. Ex hac definitione sequitur, idem inhærens non posse simul duobus distinctis realiter inhærere. Cujus ratio nunc dicta est.
units.tr: 2. Inherence, or subjective dependence, is the relation by which one thing owes its being to another through the reception of the former into itself. From this definition the following follows: (1) Nothing inherent can exist without that to which it inheres, because nothing dependent exists without its independent, and nothing that ought to be has being without that to which it owes it. (2) Nothing inherent can exist outside that in which it inheres, because the independent, through receiving the dependent into itself, gives it inherence. (3) Nothing inherent can pass from that in which it inheres into another. The reason is this: it owes its being through reception, but in such a transit it cannot be received, and so it would have to exist without reception, and therefore without that in which it inheres, which is impossible. Nor can it be received in the transit, since it would be received either in that from which it passes, or in that into which it passes, or in both. Not in that from which it passes, because it is left behind; nor in that into which it passes, because then the transit would be pointless, since it would already inhere there; nor in both. For either the whole inheres in both, or part in one and part in the other. The whole cannot inhere in both at once, since it would not be one but double: it would be received twice and would owe its being twice through reception. Nor part in one and part in the other, for what has no parts in itself, how will it inhere through its different parts? Moreover, that other part, which passes into the new subject, must have been either in that from which it passes, or in that into which it passes, or in both, when it is transferred (since it already inheres in one, and is supposed to have passed over). So the same difficulty remains for the part in that transit as existed for the whole. (4) From this definition it follows that the same inherent thing cannot inhere really in two distinct things at once. The reason for this has just been given.

units.la: 3. Dividitur inhærentia, quod sit vel Actualis vel Potentialis; Quarum illa est, per quam actu inhærens debet alteri per receptionem suum esse: Hæc vero, per quam potest recipi. Sed ultima est ἀδηρόξυλον: Inhærentia quippe actum notat, & præsentiam debitudinis, non saltem aptitudinem ad debitudinem; Eò ipso enim quia aliquid inhærens, hoc est dependens, dicitur, esse suum actu debet, & non potest solum posse debere; Ac prout causatum nunquam dicitur, quod potest dependere à causa, sed quod actu dependet; Ita nec inhærens dicitur, quod potest tantum inhærere, sed quod actu inhæret. Et denique si sufficeret ista inhærentia potenstentialis, etiam inhærens posset esse, sine eo cui inhæreat, quod impossibile nunc dictum. Et contradictionem implicat, esse inhærens, & non inhærens, hoc est posse inhærere: Esse dependens & non esse dependens, sive posse dependere: Esse suum debere alteri, & non debere, sed posse debere.
units.tr: 3. Inherence is divided into that which is actual and that which is potential. The first is that by which an inherent thing must actually owe its being to another through reception; the second is that by which it can be received. But the latter is an ugly word [ἀδηρόξυλον]. Inherence indeed denotes an act and the presence of a debt, not merely the aptitude for a debt. For by the very fact that something is called inherent, that is, dependent, it must actually owe its being, and it cannot merely be able to owe. Just as a caused thing is never called that which can depend on a cause, but that which actually depends, so a thing is not called inherent because it can merely inhere, but because it actually inheres. Finally, if this potential inherence were enough, an inherent thing could exist without that to which it inheres, which we have just shown to be impossible.
