It also involves a contradiction to be inherent and not inherent, that is, to be able to inhere; to be dependent and not dependent, or able to depend; to owe one's being to another and not to owe it, but only to be able to owe it.

units.la: 4. In inhærentia, quod inhæret, dicitur Accidens: id autem cui inhæret, Subjectum. Quorum consideratio nunc instituenda. Subjectum igitur quoad nomen 1. idem est quod subditum, ut parcere subjectis, 6. Æneid. 2. Significat substantiam. 3. opponitur praedicato, diciturque praedicationis subjectum. 4. Opponitur Adjuncto, ac adhæsionis appellatur. 4. Opponitur objecto, & occupationis subjectum nuncupatur. 6. Opponitur Accidenti, ut hic sumi debet. Prout enim adjuncto opponitur, de eo agendum cap. 26. & prout refertur ad objectum, cap. 27.
units.tr: 4. In inherence, that which inheres is called the accident, and that in which it inheres is the subject. These now need to be considered. As to its name, subject (1) is the same as subordinate, as in to spare the subjects, Aeneid 6. (2) It signifies substance. (3) It is opposed to predicate, and is called the subject of predication. (4) It is opposed to adjunct, and is called the subject of adhesion. (5) It is opposed to object, and is called the subject of occupation. (6) It is opposed to accident, as it must be taken here. For as opposed to adjunct it is treated in chapter 26, and as related to object in chapter 27.

units.la: 5. Quoad rem Subjecti 1. Videndum, Quid sit? 2. Quænam ejus axiomata? 3. Quæ differentiæ?
units.tr: 5. As to the thing, concerning the subject: (1) What it is? (2) What are its axioms? (3) What are its differences?

units.la: 6. I. Est autem subjectum, cui aliquid præter essentiam inhæret, sive, à quo aliquid per receptionem in se dependet; Dicitur ipsi inhærere aliquid præter essentiam, videlicet constituentem, quæ proprie loquendo essentia est; licet quandoque id ininhærens accidens essentiale dicatur, quod ex essentia constituente emanet, auteam sequatur. Idem dicitur, per receptionem in se; ideo enim inhærens, non est essentia subjecti; quia sic idem seipsum recipere in se; quod impossibile.
units.tr: 6. I. The subject is that to which something inheres besides its essence, or that on which something depends through reception into itself. Something is said to inhere in it besides its essence, namely its constituting essence, which properly speaking is the essence. Although sometimes an inhering accident is called essential when it flows from the constituting essence yet follows it. The phrase through reception into itself is used because an inherent thing is not the essence of the subject; for then the same thing would receive itself into itself, which is impossible.

units.la: 7. II. Axiomata, ex hac definitione deducta, hæc sunt 1. Subjectum naturâ prius est accidente. Ratio est, quia independens naturâ prius suo dependente; Et recipiens suo recepto. 2. Subjectum toto genere dignius Accidente. Ratio est, quia omni ex parte independens toto genere est præstantius dependente: Sed Subjectum omni ex parte à subjecto independens est; igitur toto genere dignius eo, quod dependet à subjecto: Et quemadmodum id quod omni ex parte à causis est independens, toto genere excellentius est eo, quod à causa pendet; ita & hic, quod nullâtenus dependet à subjecto, præstantius est eo, quod dependet. 3. Omne subjectum est substantia: Ratio est, quia independens à subjecto, hoc est per se subsistens, esse debet. Omne enim, à quo aliquid dependet, ratione istius independens esse debet: Ergo à quo aliquid dependet, ut à subjecto, id à subjecto independens esse debet. Adeo ut hic non sit par ratio inhærentiæ ac causalitatis; nam in hac, quod semel est independens, id non continuò est tale, sed etiam potest esse dependens, nisi sit absolutè independens. At in inhærentiâ, quod semel independens, id nunquam fit dependens; Quia quod independens est, id per se subsistit: At hoc nunquam nulliusque respectu inhærere potest. Ratio diversitatis est; Quia continuò in inhærentiâ Subjectum & accidens toto genere differunt; cùm in causatione non semper toto genere causa à causato differat.
units.tr: 7. II. The axioms deduced from this definition are these. (1) The subject is prior in nature to the accident. The reason is that the independent is prior in nature to its dependent, and the receiver to what it receives. (2) The subject is in its whole genus more worthy than the accident. The reason is that what is independent in every respect is in its whole genus more excellent than what depends. But the subject is independent in every respect of what is subject to it; therefore it is in its whole genus more worthy than what depends on it. Just as what is independent of causes in every respect is more excellent in its whole genus than what depends on a cause, so here what in no way depends on the subject is more excellent than what depends. (3) Every subject is a substance. The reason is that what is independent of the subject, that is, subsisting through itself, must exist. For whatever something depends on must be independent by reason of that dependence. Therefore that on which something depends as on a subject must be independent of the subject. Hence the case of inherence is not parallel to that of causality. In causality, what is once independent is not always such, but may also become dependent unless it is absolutely independent. But in inherence, what is once independent never becomes dependent, because what is independent subsists through itself, and it can never inhere in any respect. The reason for the difference is that in inherence the subject and the accident always differ in their whole genus, whereas in causation the cause does not always differ from the caused in its whole genus.

units.la: 8. 4. Omne subjectum aliquo modo est imperfectum ; Quia aliquid in se præter suam essentiam recipit; quod vel perficit essentiam; & sic non satis erat perfecta; vel illam imperfectiorem reddit, atque adeò non erat summè perfecta. 5. Omne subjectum est Ens finitum. Ratio est, quia est aliquo modo imperfectum. 6. Sublato Subjecto tollitur Accidens; Quia sublato independente, tollitur dependens.
units.tr: 8. (4) Every subject is in some way imperfect, because it receives something in itself besides its essence, which either perfects its essence, and so it was not sufficiently perfect, or renders it more imperfect, and so it was not supremely perfect. (5) Every subject is a finite being, because it is in some way imperfect. (6) When the subject is removed, the accident is removed, because when the independent is removed, the dependent is removed.

units.la: 9. III. Quoad differentias, Subjectum 1. est vel absolutum, vel limitatum. Prius est, quod secundum omnes partes recipit accidens; Unde & subjectum formale dicitur, & Subjectum quo, ut & inhæsionis. Posterius verò, quod in certâ sui parte recipit accidens, sive cui accidens inest per partium limitationem & restrictionem: Dicituresque aliter Subjectum materiale, quod & denominationis.
units.tr: 9. III. As to differences, the subject (1) is either absolute or limited. The former is that which receives the accident in all its parts; hence it is called the formal subject, and the subject by which, and of inherence. The latter is that which receives the accident in a certain part of itself, or in which the accident inheres through a limitation and restriction of its parts. It is also called the material subject, which is also that of denomination.

units.la: nam primò inhærentia immediatè oritur ex accidentis constitutione ; Est autem ejus constitutio, productio ejus in subjecto, seu possessio sui esse in subjecto ; à quâ immediatè oritur, aut cum quâ realiter eadem est, inhærentia. Et secundò omni accidenti & soli convenit, ut infrà latius deducendum. 2. Quemadmodum Ens creatum pro generali suâ essentiâ habet dependentiam à causâ, quâtenus hæc denominatio est ; Ita quoque accidens, ut dependens à subjecto, pro generali suâ essentiâ habet dependentiam à subjecto, sive inhærentiam, quâtenus pro denominatione sumitur, ac relationis est fundamentum. 3. Quibus accedit, nullam aliam essentiam Accidenti in genere tribui posse, si ea non dicatur Entitas per inhærentiam, sive denominata inhærentia ; Cui præterea & omnes conditiones ad essentiam requisitæ conveniunt. Adeo ut nihil deesse manifestè pateat.
units.tr: For, first, inherence arises immediately from the constitution of the accident. Its constitution is its production in the subject, or the possession of its being in the subject, from which inherence immediately arises, or with which it is really the same. Secondly, it belongs to every accident and to accidents alone, as will be deduced more fully below. 2. Just as a created being has, as its general essence, dependence on a cause, insofar as this is a denomination, so too an accident, as dependent on a subject, has as its general essence dependence on the subject, or inherence, insofar as it is taken as a denomination and is the foundation of a relation. 3. To this is added that no other essence can be attributed to the accident in general, unless it is called entity through inherence, or inherence as a denomination. Moreover, all the conditions required for an essence also belong to it. So nothing is manifestly lacking.

units.la: 14. Objicit, non-nemo ; Oportet ut rei cujuscunque positiva & realis essentia primò à nobis concipiatur absoluta esse, antequam dicatur aliquid cum respectu ad aliud. Ergo oportet, ut Accidens habeat primò suum esse absolutum, antequam habeat esse in ordine ad subjectum. Resp.
units.tr: 14. Objection, from someone: the positive and real essence of any thing must first be conceived by us as absolute, before it is said to be something in relation to another. Therefore an accident must first have absolute being before it has being in relation to its subject. Reply.

units.la: 1. Antecedens verum est de illa tantum re, quæ esse absolutum habet, non de eâ, quæ esse suum per dependentiam habet, sive quae in suo esse absoluta non est. Quemadmodum non oportet aliam absolutam essentiam Creaturae in genere investigare, praeterquam ejus dependentiam a Creatore, quae ipsam in suo esse constitutam immediate consequitur. Quoniam Creatura in suo esse plane absoluta non est. Sed quemadmodum haec internum relationis fundamentum pro sua essentia habet; ita & Accidens a subjecto quoad esse dependens, non requirit aliud esse absolutum, praeter suam inhaerentiam, quae internum ipsi est relationis fundamentum. 2. Non statuitur ipsa relatio esse ejus essentia, sed actus inhaerendi, sive inhaerentia denominata, quae relationis fundamentum est. 3. Quemadmodum in absoluto qua tali & sua natura omnia absoluta: ita in respectivo qua tali & sua natura omnia respectiva; Quis igitur sanae mentis esse generale absolutum quaeret Accidentis; quod qua tale & sua natura respectum ad independens involvit. 4. Transscendentale esse, ex hypothesi, quod Accidens sit Ens sui generis, licet in se respectum non inferat, restrictum tamen illum necessario admittit: Adeo ut nihil absoluti dici possit de ipso secundum essentiam: sed saltem secundum indifferentiam. Hoc tamen attributum illud est, quod ante illum respectum investigandum est.
units.tr: 1. The antecedent is true only of that thing which has absolute being, not of that which has its being through dependence, that is, which is not absolute in its being. Just as we need not look for any other absolute essence of a creature in general, apart from its dependence on the Creator, which immediately follows upon its being constituted in existence, since a creature is not wholly absolute in its being; so too an accident, which depends on its subject as to its being, does not require any other absolute being besides its inherence, which is for it the internal ground of relation. And just as the creature has this dependence as the internal ground of relation for its essence, so the accident has its inherence. 2. It is not asserted that relation itself is its essence, but the act of inhering, or inherence taken as a denomination, which is the ground of relation. 3. As in the absolute, as such and by its nature, all things are absolute, so in the respective, as such and by its nature, all things are respective. Who then of sound mind would seek a general absolute of an accident, which as such and by its nature involves respect to the independent? 4. Transcendental being, on the hypothesis that the accident is a being of its own kind, although it does not imply respect in itself, nevertheless necessarily admits it in a restricted way; so that nothing absolute can be said of it according to its essence, but at least according to indifference. Yet this attribute is the one that must be investigated before that respect.

units.la: {*} Note: marginal reference mark at left of line 7 (not transcribed as text).
units.tr: {*} (marginal reference mark, not text)

units.la: 15. Objic. 2. Vnumquodque accidens proprië dictum, in se consideratum, habet essentiam denotatam per definitionem propriam, sine ordine ad hoc, aut illud subjectum, cui diceretur inexistere. Ergo non est de parte essentiæ cujusvis accidentis ipsa inhærentia. Et manifestum hoc fit exemplo. Si hoc aut illud accidens in specie definiatur, nullius subjecti in definitione continebitur designatio. &c. Resp. Antecedens apprimè falsum; Nullum quippe definiri unquam poterit accidens, sine ordine ad subjectum. Nec obstat exemplum: licet enim expressa in definitione hujus vel istius accidentis, non fiat subjecti mentio, sit tamen implicita; neque debet expressa fieri. Vetant enim regulæ definitionis, ne id, quod ad essentiam Generis pertinet, expresse repetatur in definitione speciei; Quare dum albedo definitur, quòd sit color nimium disgregans visum, implicatur subjectum in genere, quod est Color, qui dum est qualitas, & hæc Accidens proprië dictum, de cujus essentia est inhærentia; etiam inhærentia illa præsupponitur in definitione Qualitatis, & Coloris, adeoque & Albedinis.
units.tr: 15. Objection 2. Every accident properly so called, considered in itself, has an essence denoted by its proper definition, without reference to this or that subject in which it is said to inhere. Therefore inherence is not part of the essence of any accident. This is made clear by example: if this or that accident is defined in particular, no designation of any subject is contained in the definition, etc. Reply: The antecedent is quite false, for no accident can ever be defined without reference to a subject. Nor does the example stand in the way: although mention of the subject is not expressed in the definition of this or that accident, it is nonetheless implicit, and it need not be expressed. For the rules of definition forbid that what belongs to the essence of the genus be expressly repeated in the definition of the species. Hence when whiteness is defined as a colour that disperses the sight too much, the subject is implied in the genus, which is colour; and colour, as it is a quality, and quality is an accident properly so called, whose essence is inherence, presupposes that inherence in its definition, and so also does whiteness.

units.la: 16. Objic. 3. Tum in essentiâ accidentis plura involverentur, quam in essentiâ substantiæ; adeoque ipsum accidens præter substantiæ perfectionem, etiam includeret omnem suam perfectionem, ut distinctam à perfectione substantiæ. Resp. Nulla species hujus consequentiæ unquam oftendi poterit; imò contrarium potius sequitur; Quid? An quia accidens habet suum esse per dependentiam à subjecto, sive substantiâ, ideone & ipsius substantiæ persectio, quæ est subsistentia per se, convenit accidenti, cui accedens ipsa inhærentia, multiplicat perfectiones Accidentis, præ perfectionibus substantiæ? An quia creatura dependet à Creatore, ut à causa esse tribuente, ideòne plures perfectiones erunt creaturæ quam Creatoris? An potius contrarium sequitur? Ita suadet ratio; Quia dum dependens posterius est independente, nunquam fit ipsum independens; Et dum independens dependenti tribuit esse, non ideo seipsum tribuit; sed manet independens.
units.tr: 16. Objection 3. Then more would be involved in the essence of an accident than in the essence of a substance, so that the accident itself, besides the perfection of substance, would also include all its own perfection as distinct from the perfection of substance. Reply: No form of this consequence can ever be shown; indeed the contrary rather follows. What? Because an accident has its being through dependence on a subject, or substance, is the perfection of substance, which is subsistence through itself, therefore attributed to the accident, and does inherence itself multiply the perfections of the accident beyond the perfections of substance? Or because a creature depends on the Creator as on the cause giving it being, will there therefore be more perfections in the creature than in the Creator? Or does the contrary rather follow? Reason suggests so: since the dependent is posterior to the independent, it never becomes independent; and when the independent gives being to the dependent, it does not thereby give itself anything, but remains independent.

units.la: 17. Objic. 4. Sequeretur ex hac sententiâ, omne accidens in se & suâ naturâ consideratum esse, substantiam accidens; Ratio consequentiæ est; Quia ex illâ sententiâ, accidens includeret in suo conceptu essentiali ipsum subjectum. Resp. Ejusdem generis hæc cum præcedente est consequentia; An creatura in se considerata dicenda est Creator creatura; ideo quia esse suum debet Creatori? Addita ratio prave detorquetur; Nam aliud est esse concepptum essentialem, aliud de conceptu essentiali. Subjectum non est ipse conceptus essentialis, sive definitio, sed de illo conceptu; Quia enim natura prius est accidente, & definitio ex natura prioribus constare debet, illius quoque pars fit. Sed non ilico, quod est pars definitionis, hoc est pars essentiæ. Definias Civem Franekeranum; nonne integræ civitatis in definitione mentio fieri debet? Sed estne civitas pars civis unius? Definias actionem; & ingredietur ejus definitionem vel agens, vel virtus ejus: Sed hæc neutiquam partes sunt actionis. Quando igitur accidens in suo conceptu dicitur includere subjectum, hoc intelligendum, non quod subjectum sit pars ejus essentiæ, sed quod subjectum requiratur, ut accidenti esse concedat.
units.tr: 17. Objection 4. From this opinion it would follow that every accident, considered in itself and by its nature, is a substance-accident. The reason for the consequence is that by that opinion the accident would include the subject itself in its essential concept. Reply: This consequence is of the same kind as the previous one. Is a creature, considered in itself, to be called a Creator-creature because it owes its being to the Creator? The added reason is wrongly twisted, for it is one thing to be the essential concept, another to be part of the essential concept. The subject is not the essential concept itself, or definition, but is part of that concept; for since nature is prior to accident, and a definition must consist of things prior by nature, the subject is also a part of it. But it does not follow at once that what is part of a definition is part of the essence. Define a citizen of Franeker: must not mention of the whole city be made in the definition? But is the city a part of the citizen? Define an action: its agent or its power will enter the definition, yet these are in no way parts of the action. When therefore an accident is said in its concept to include the subject, this is to be understood not as meaning that the subject is part of its essence, but that the subject is required in order to grant it being.

units.la: 18. Objic. 5. Est communis Philosophorum sententia, quâ statuitur, accidens nunquam perfectè definiri, in quantum definitur mentione subjecti; Quandoquidem nunquam subjectum de rei essentiâ potest esse. Resp. 1. Quorum Philosophorum illa sententia? Reformatorum ne? ( Pontificii enim ac Lutherani hic suspectæ fidei sunt: ) nondum potui resciscere. 2. Imò perfectè definitur accidens pro suâ entitate, mentione subjecti. Quod enim illud ut prius respicit, id per illud satis persectè definitur. 3. Cur subjectum non est de essentiâ accidentis? Nonne ipsi esse tribuit? Nonne ipsum conservat? Et quid habet accidens, quod subjecto non debeat? Non quidem ipsius genus est, subjectum, neque differentia, sed inhærentia in ipso abstracta ratio essentiæ accidentis fit. Sed plusquam satis huic novæ sententiæ repositum, quod non ægrè feret, qui à Veterum sententiis temerè recedere crimen existimat.
units.tr: 18. Objection 5. It is the common opinion of the philosophers that an accident can never be perfectly defined insofar as it is defined by mention of a subject, since the subject can never belong to the essence of a thing. Reply: 1. Which philosophers hold that opinion? The Reformed? (For the Papists and the Lutherans here are of suspect faith.) I have not yet been able to find out. 2. Indeed an accident is perfectly defined with respect to its entity by mention of the subject. For what it refers to as prior, by that it is defined sufficiently perfectly. 3. Why is the subject not of the essence of the accident? Does it not give it being? Does it not preserve it? And what does the accident have that it does not owe to the subject? It is not indeed its genus, subject, nor its difference, but inherence in it, taken abstractly, becomes the formal reason of the essence of the accident. But more than enough has been replied to this new opinion, which he will not take amiss who thinks it a crime to depart rashly from the opinions of the Ancients.

units.la: 19. II. Axiomata ex hac definitione Accidentis oriunda sunt, primò, Nullum accidens extra subjectum esse potest. Ratio est 1. quia est inhærens: At hoc non est sine eo cui inhæret, vid.th. 2. 2. Accidens nunquam est sine suâ essentia: At illa est inhærentia, quæ semper actualis est, ut supra ostensum. 3. Quod non inhæret actu, id si sit, per se subsistit: Sublatò enim uno immediatè oppositorum, ponitur alterum: At quod per se subsistit, id substantia est: At accidens, ex hypothesi, manet accidens. Secundò, Accidens non potest transfire de subjecto in subjectum; Ratio est, quia nullum inhærens transit, ut d. 1. ostensum. Tertiò, Accidens non potest simul inesse distinctis subjectis; Pertinet enim & hoc ad inhærentis naturam. Objectiones, quæ adversus hæc axiomata moventur, passim apud Reformatos Logicos ac Metaphysicos solutas habes.
units.tr: 19. II. Axioms arising from this definition of accident are these. First, no accident can exist outside its subject. The reason is: 1. because it is inhering, but this is not without that in which it inheres, see th. 2. 2. An accident is never without its essence, but that essence is inherence, which is always actual, as shown above. 3. What does not inhere actually, if it were, would subsist through itself; for when one of two immediately opposed things is removed, the other is posited. But what subsists through itself is a substance, whereas an accident, by hypothesis, remains an accident. Second, an accident cannot pass from subject to subject; the reason is that no inhering thing passes over, as shown in d. 1. Third, an accident cannot inhere in distinct subjects at the same time, for this too belongs to the nature of what inheres. You will find the objections that are raised against these axioms solved in many places among the Reformed logicians and metaphysicians.

units.la: 20. III. Differentia quod attinet; Accidens dividitur, quod sit vel proprium, vel commune; Illud est; quod soli illi subjecto inhaeret: Hoc vero, quod etiam aliis. Primus est vel imperfectum, quod licet soli inhaereat, non tamen omni subordinato, aut licet omni, non tamen semper inhaeret; vel perfectum, quod soli, omni subordinato ac semper inhaeret.
units.tr: 20. III. As to difference, an accident is divided into being either proper or common. The former is that which inheres in that one subject alone; the latter inheres in others also. The first is either imperfect, which, though it inheres in that subject alone, does not inhere in every subordinate, or though in every one, does not always inhere; or perfect, which inheres in that alone, in every subordinate, and always.

units.la: 21. De hoc proprio accidente litigant Philosophi & Theologi, an etiam possit commune fieri alii subjecto, realiter ac specie à suo subjecto distincto. Respondeo cum Reformatis. 1. Non potest communicari secundum rem, sed secundum denominationem; idque non formali, sed materiali denominatione, prout potentia urendi secundum denominationem tributur ferro, non formaliter, quod ipsum urat; sed quod denominetur urere, ob ipsi inexistentes particulas igneas. 2. Non potest communicari, per strictè dictam <bl>κοινωνίαν</bl>, quâ proprium maneret in proprio subjecto, & idem numero etiam in communicativo efficitur; Quod ipsius communicationis Patroni & volunt, & ad palliandum suum errorem, de ubiquitate corporis Christi, necessariò velle debent. Licet aliqua latè dicta communicatio fiat, sive per <bl>μέθεξιν</bl> & participationem, quando unum realiter idem est cum altero, quomodo proprietates generi communicantur speciebus; sive per συνδυασμόν, quatenus ipsum subiectum simul transit, quomodo proprietates Elementorum mistis, & partium toti communicantur; in quâ tamen semper denominationis seu limitatum est subiectum.
units.tr: 21. Philosophers and theologians dispute whether this proper accident can also become common to another subject that is really and specifically distinct from its own subject. I answer with the Reformed. (1) It cannot be communicated in the thing itself, but only by denomination. And this is not a formal but a material denomination: just as the power of burning is attributed to iron by denomination, not formally, so that the iron itself burns, but so that it is said to burn because of the fiery particles inhering in it. (2) It cannot be communicated by what is strictly called communion [κοινωνίαν], by which the proper accident would remain in its proper subject and would also become the same in number in the subject receiving it. The patrons of this communication both want this and, to cover up their error about the ubiquity of Christ's body, must want it. Some communication in a loose sense does take place, either through participation [μέθεξιν], when one thing really is the same as another, as the properties of a genus are communicated to its species; or through combination [συνδυασμόν], insofar as the subject itself passes over at the same time, as the properties of the elements are communicated to mixed bodies, and the properties of the parts to the whole. In this case, however, the subject always remains limited to a denomination.

units.la: 3. Licet, quod impossibile esse ratio dictitat, propria accidentia possent communicari; non tamen pari ratione possent communicari proprietates divinæ, ut quæ 1. citra ullam exceptionem sunt ipsissima Dei essentia, quare communicatis istis proprietatibus, etiam communicaretur ipsa essentia; atque sic essentia humana foret divina. Quæque 2. infinitæ sunt; adeoque à nullo finito capi possunt. At si communicandæ essent, nulli nisi finito, communicari possent. Et 3. à seinvicem sejungi nequeunt, quoniam realiter inter se idem sunt; adeoque unâ atque alterâ earum communicatâ omnes communicari deberent; Quod ut impossibile vel ipsi Adversarii admittunt.
units.tr: 3. Even if proper accidents could be communicated, which reason declares impossible, the divine properties could not be communicated by the same reasoning. (1) Without any exception they are the very essence of God, so if these properties were communicated, the essence itself would also be communicated, and thus human essence would be divine. (2) They are infinite and so cannot be grasped by anything finite; yet if they were to be communicated, they could be communicated only to something finite. (3) They cannot be separated from one another, since they are really the same among themselves; so if one or another of them were communicated, all of them would have to be communicated. Even the adversaries themselves admit that this is impossible.

units.la: 22. Dividitur quoque Accidens, quod sit vel separabile; sine quo subiectum esse potest; vel inseparabile, sine quo non esse potest; Quæ divisio non plane eadem est, cum præcedenti; ut nonnullis visum est: Sed diversa; nam licet accidens proprium sit inseparabile, non tamen omne infeparabile est proprium. Separari nequit nigredo ab Æthiope, ut maneat Æthiops, humiditas, ab aqua, ut maneat aqua; &c. Nec quoque omne proprium inseparabile, sed solum perfectum; Doctum esse, licet hominis sit proprium, separari tamen potest. Et hæc de Subjecto & Accidente, adeoque de afsectionibus ex dependentia ortis, dicta pro instituto sufficient.
units.tr: 22. An accident is also divided into separable, without which the subject can exist, and inseparable, without which it cannot exist. This division is not altogether the same as the preceding one, as some have thought, but a different one. For although a proper accident is inseparable, not every inseparable accident is proper. Blackness cannot be separated from an Ethiopian and the Ethiopian remain; moisture cannot be separated from water and water remain; and so on. Nor is every proper accident inseparable, but only the perfect kind: being learned is a property of man, yet it can be separated from him. These points concerning subject and accident, and hence concerning affections arising from dependence, are sufficient for our present purpose.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: DE Toto & Partibus.
units.tr: Of the Whole and the Parts.

units.la: 1. ALtera relatio interna, ex qua Entis respectivæ affectiones oriuntur, est Vnio, quæ est, concursus plurium ad constituendam unum; Vnum hoc totum, plura illa concurrentia Partes dicuntur: de quibus nunc agendum.
units.tr: 1. The other internal relation, from which the respective affections of being arise, is union, which is the coming together of several things to make one. This one thing is called the whole, and those several things that come together are called the parts. We must now treat of these.

units.la: 2. Totum ratione nominis, aliquando absolute capitur, prout partes non respicit; atque sic est idem quod perfectum, cui nihil deest; sive sit pars alterius, ut Anima dicitur esse tota in toto corpore, & tota in singulis partibus, sive nullatenus sit alterius pars, ut Deus ὅλως ὅλον π, totaliter totum quid dicitur. Aliquando vero respective, ut partibus opponitur, capitur; Atque ita varias habet latitudines, prout vel plures, vel pauciores ejus species conce-denuntur: Dua autem præ cæteris sunt notandæ, quarum primâ latissimè sumitur, pro omni quâcunque ratione divisibili, quomodo & causa ratione diversorum causatorum, & causatum ratione causarum, Accidens ratione subjectorum, & subjectum ratione variorum accidentium, locatum ratione locorum, & locus locatorum &c. totum dicitur; Atque ita totum per accidens, simul cum toto per se comprehendit: Secundâ adæquatè sumitur, pro solo toto, per se dicto.
units.tr: 2. The word whole is sometimes taken absolutely, insofar as it does not regard parts, and in this sense it means the same as perfect, that to which nothing is lacking. This holds whether it is a part of something else, as the soul is said to be whole in the whole body and whole in each of its parts, or in no way a part of something else, as God, who is called [ὅλως ὅλον], wholly a whole thing. Sometimes, however, it is taken relatively, as opposed to parts, and in this sense it has various scopes, according as more or fewer of its kinds are admitted. Two of these are to be noted above the rest. The first is taken most broadly, for any divisible thing in any way at all. In this sense a cause is called a whole with respect to its various effects, and an effect with respect to its causes; an accident with respect to its subjects, and a subject with respect to its various accidents; a thing located with respect to places, and a place with respect to the things located, and so on. Thus the whole by accident is included together with the whole per se. The second is taken strictly, for the whole alone, called per se.

units.la: 3. Totum autem est, quod unione plurium (tanquam partium) constat. Ex quâ definitione constat,1. Totum esse aliquo modo unum, ut quod unione constat. 2. Esse aliquo modo multum, utpote plura ad suam unionem postulans.3. Non differre realiter à partibus, quâ talibus; Quæ enim simul ponuntur ac tolluntur, quorum unum constituit interne essentiâ alterius, ejusque definitionem ingreditur; & quæ ne quidem cogitatione à seinvicem separari possunt, illa realiter inter se minimè differunt. Quod verum est, non tantum de partibus simul sumtis, sed & de singulis seorsim, modò maneant partes.
units.tr: 3. The whole, however, is that which consists of the union of several (as parts). From this definition it is clear: 1. that the whole is in some way one, since it consists of a union; 2. that it is in some way many, since it needs several things for its union; 3. that it does not differ really from its parts, as such. For things which are posited and removed together, one of which constitutes the other intrinsically in its essence and enters into its definition, and which cannot even be separated from one another in thought, do not differ really from one another at all. This is true not only of the parts taken together, but also of each of them singly, provided they remain parts.

units.la: 4. Objic. 1. Partes sunt priores toto: Prius autem à posteriore realiter differt. Resp. Antecedens falsum est in sensu composito; Partes enim quâ partes sunt simul cum toto. Objic. 2 Constituens & constitutum differunt realiter: At partes sunt constituentes, & totum constitutum. Resp.
units.tr: 4. Objection 1. The parts are prior to the whole. But what is prior differs really from what is posterior. Reply. The antecedent is false in the compound sense, for the parts, as parts, are together with the whole. Objection 2. The constituent and the constituted differ really. But the parts are constituents and the whole is constituted. Reply.

units.la: 1. Antecedens in constitutione intrinseca fallit. 2. Fallit in constituentibus per emanationem. 3. Falsum est in constitutione reciproca. At hic 1. est intrinseca constitutio, quia partes totius essentiam ingrediuntur. 2. Emanativa, quia positis partibus, sine actione interveniente ponitur totum. 2. Est reciproca; nam prout partes constituunt totum, ita vicissim totum ipsas partes constituit.
units.tr: 1. The antecedent fails in intrinsic constitution. 2. It fails for constituents through emanation. 3. It is false in reciprocal constitution. But here (1) there is intrinsic constitution, because the parts enter into the essence of the whole; (2) there is emanative constitution, because, with the parts posited, the whole is posited without any intervening action; (3) there is reciprocal constitution, for just as the parts constitute the whole, so in turn the whole constitutes the parts.

units.la: §. Totum varie à variis dividitur; convenientissimè (ut mihi videtur, salvo aliorum judicio) in Prædicabile, quod de suis partibus in quid dicitur, & integrale, cujus partes totum in quid de se dici non permittunt; Quæ ex contradictoriis adeoque immediatè oppositis terminis differentias habent; adeòque aut reliquas, ab aliis addictas species, excludunt, aut sub se continent.
units.tr: §. The whole is divided variously by various people. Most conveniently (as it seems to me, saving the judgement of others), it is divided into the predicable, which is said in quid of its parts, and the integral, whose parts do not allow the whole to be said in quid of them. These have differences from contradictory and therefore immediately opposed terms, so that they either exclude the remaining species, which others assign, or contain them under themselves.

units.la: §. Alii autem addunt 1. Totum essentiale: Sed omnes partes, ideo partes sunt, quia totius essentiam constituunt: At quâtenus essentiale totum significat rem aliquam, quæ ex partibus quantitativis, tanquam materiâ, earumque unione, indeque resultante formâ, constat, eâtenus ad integrale totum pertinet, ut quod de partibus, ex quibus coalescit, in quid dici nequit. II. Alii addunt totum perfectionale quale est Deus; Verum hoc partes non respicit, adeoque tantum nomine tenus, quatenus & hoc quod perfectum est denotat, totum dici potest. III. Alii addunt totum Potestativum, quale est anima ratione suarum potentiarum, secundum quas dicitur esse tota in toto; Sed tale totum potius est subjectum rationis propriorum accidentium, aut causa respectu effectuum, adeoque totum improprie & per accidens dictum. IV. Alii addunt totum numericum, quale est numerus ratione partium ex quibus colligitur: Sed hoc totius integralis species est. V. Alii addunt totum individuale; quod tamen inter tota praedicabilia pars est: Aut si materialiter consideretur, totum est integrale, quatenus res illa singularis ex partibus suis constat. VI. Alii denique addunt totum formale, quod esset species ratione generis & differentiae, quibus definitur. Sed 1. Species revera generis pars est. 2. Et quoniam genus & differentia se mutuo penetrant, ad essentiale strictè dictum revocari potest.
units.tr: §. Others, however, add: I. The essential whole. But all parts are parts because they constitute the essence of the whole. Now insofar as the essential whole signifies some thing which consists of quantitative parts as matter, and of their union and the form resulting from it, to that extent it belongs to the integral whole, since it cannot be said in quid of the parts of which it is made up. II. Others add the perfectional whole, such as God. But this does not regard parts, and so it can be called a whole only in name, insofar as it denotes that which is perfect. III. Others add the potestative whole, such as the soul with respect to its powers, in virtue of which it is said to be whole in the whole. But such a whole is rather the subject of its proper accidents, or the cause with respect to its effects, and so is called a whole improperly and by accident. IV. Others add the numerical whole, such as a number with respect to the parts from which it is gathered. But this is a species of the integral whole. V. Others add the individual whole. This, however, is a part among the predicable wholes; or, if it is considered materially, it is an integral whole, insofar as that singular thing consists of its parts. VI. Finally, others add the formal whole, which would be a species with respect to the genus and difference by which it is defined. But 1. a species is really a part of the genus; and 2. since genus and difference penetrate one another, it can be traced back to the essential whole, strictly speaking.

units.la: 7. Praedicabile si nomen spectetur, quandoque notat omne id, quod quávis ratione de alio dici potest; quandoque, modum aliquem, quo aliquid de alio dicitur, quomodo vulgò quinque Praedicabilia dicuncuntur Genus, Species, Differentia, Proprium & Accidens. At quandoque & quidem cum adjectione totius,quod in quid, hoc est fynonymicè, & in casu recto dici de inferioribus potest, quomodo hîc accipiendum.
units.tr: 7. The predicable, if the name is considered, sometimes denotes everything which can be said of another in any way; sometimes a certain mode by which something is said of another, as the five predicables are commonly called: genus, species, difference, property and accident. But sometimes, with the addition of whole, it means what can be said in quid, that is, synonymously, and can be said in the nominative case of inferiors. This is the sense to be understood here.

units.la: 8. Aliis totum Vniversale dicitur ; Verum 1. nomen id magis ambiguum est ; 2. Non omne, quod universale & de multis dici aptum, est statim totum prædicabile, hoc est, vel genus vel species, dici potest, 3. gr. intelligibile, aliquid &c. 3. Partes huic toti oppositæ, fubjectivæ dicuntur ; Subjici autem prædicari, & non æquè univerfali opponitur.
units.tr: 8. By others the whole is called universal. But 1. that name is more ambiguous; 2. not every thing that is universal and fit to be said of many is at once a predicable whole, that is, something that can be said to be either a genus or a species, for example intelligible, something, and so on; 3. the parts opposed to this whole are called subjective. But being subjected to predication is not equivalent to being opposed to the universal.

units.la: 9. Est autem totum prædicabile, quod de partibus suis in quid dici potest. Estque duplex, Genus respectu specierum, & species, respectu individuorum.
units.tr: 9. The predicable whole is that which can be said in quid of its parts. It is twofold: the genus with respect to its species, and the species with respect to its individuals.

units.la: 10. Sed addubitatur hîc, an Genus specierum possit dici totum, quoniam fit pars definitionis speciei? Resp. Omninò genus est totum; est enim 1. ex speciebus, tanquam partibus unitum; 2. Aliquo modo multum. 3. Plura includit, quam singulæ species. 4. Neque à speciebus realiter differt. Ad oppositam rationem, nego consequentiam; Non enim quod est pars definitionis alicujus, id statim ejus pars est, ut thef. 17. præced. cap. ostensum. Quin & in cujuscunque partis definitiotionem ingreditur ejus totum, quod tamen ideo suæ partis pars non evadit.
units.tr: 10. But it is doubted here whether the genus of its species can be called a whole, since it is part of the definition of the species. Reply. The genus is wholly a whole. For it is (1) united out of the species as parts; (2) in some way many; (3) it includes more than the individual species; (4) and it does not differ really from the species. To the opposing argument I deny the consequence. For what is part of some definition is not at once a part of that thing, as shown in thesis 17 of the preceding chapter. Indeed, the whole of anything enters into the definition of each of its parts, and yet it does not for that reason become a part of its part.

units.la: 11. Generis variæ sunt significationes, inter quas communissima, quæ hic retinenda est, quâ sumitur, pro eo toto, quod de pluribus essentiâ differentibus in quid prædicatur; Quodque proinde in partes sub se comprehensas, essentiâ specificâ differentes, divisibile est. Partes autem sub toto comprehensæ, a'iter subjectivæ dictæ, sunt illæ, de quibus singulis totum in quid dici potest.
units.tr: 11. Genus has various meanings. The most common of these, and the one to be kept here, is that by which it is taken for the whole which is said in quid of several things differing in essence; and which therefore is divisible into the parts contained under it, differing in specific essence. The parts contained under the whole, called subjective in another sense, are those of which the whole can be said in quid, each one singly.

units.la: 12. Ex quibus colligitur, 1. Genus non posse conservari in unâ specie: Quoniam de pluribus prædicari debet. 2. Species insimas ratione individuorum non esse genera; quoniam invidua specie non differunt. 3. Eandemque ob causam, 1. Colorem ratione temporis & fervoris. 2. Hominem ratione maris & fæminæ, juvenis & senis. 3. Deum ratione trium Personarum, non posse esse genus. 4. Nihil inesse generi, quod non infit quoque speciebus; quoniam de iis in quid dicitur; At quidditas est ipsa essentia, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: 12. From these points it follows: 1. that a genus cannot be preserved in a single species, since it must be predicated of several; 2. that the lowest species are not genera with respect to individuals, since individuals do not differ in species; 3. and for the same reason, (1) colour cannot be a genus with respect to time and intensity, (2) man cannot be a genus with respect to male and female, young and old, (3) God cannot be a genus with respect to the three Persons; 4. nothing is in the genus that is not also in the species, since the genus is said of the species in quid; but the quiddity is the essence itself, as said above.

units.la: 13. Dividitur Genus 1. ratione distantiæ à speciebus, in proximum & remotum. Illud dicitur, quod immediatè (id est nullo alio genere intercedente) de specie dicitur, ut Animal de homine. Hoc verò, quod mediatè (id est mediante & intercedente alio genere: ) dicitur de specie, ut vivens de homine.
units.tr: 13. Genus is divided, (1) according to its distance from the species, into proximate and remote. The proximate is that which is said of the species immediately, that is, with no other genus intervening, as animal is said of man. The remote is that which is said of the species mediately, that is, with another genus intervening, as living thing is said of man.

units.la: 12. 2. Dividitur Genus ratione ordinis ad alia, quod sit vel summum, vel subalternum. Illud dicitur, quod alterius ratione nunquam fit species: Hoc vero, quod ratione inferiorum quidem genus est,at ratione superiorum fit species. Atque hic notandum 1. hanc divisionem non esse generis formaliter, hoc est quatenus genus est, consideranti; nam sic genus nunquam fit species, adeoque semper summum est. 2. Si tamen duo genera ratione alicujus inferioris æstimentur, unum summum dici potest, quia nullum superius de eo ut inferiori dici potest;& alterum subalternum, quia dum genus dicitur, adhuc superius aliquod admittit. 3. Summum genus ratione inferiorum duplex esse; ita aliud est Entium, aliud Prædicamentorum seu τῶν κατηγορεμένων. Summum Genus Entium, est ipsum Ens, prout in formali Metaphysicæ subjecto sumitur; idque absolutè: Respectivè autem vel est substantiæ; & in hac, aliud Spirituum, aliud corporum; vel Accidentium, posito, quod hæc Entia sint. Summum Genus Prædicamentorum, vel est de Substantiâ primâ, quorsum spectant decem illa Prædicamenta; vel de Actione, quorsum spectant hæc septem: Quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis,
units.tr: 12. 2. A genus is divided by its ratio of order to other things, as either highest or subaltern. The highest is that which never becomes a species in relation to anything else. The subaltern is that which is indeed a genus in relation to its inferiors, but becomes a species in relation to its superiors. Here note: (1) this division does not concern a genus formally, that is, considered only as a genus, for so a genus never becomes a species and is therefore always highest. (2) If, however, two genera are considered in relation to some inferior, one may be called highest, because no higher genus can be predicated of it as of an inferior, and the other subaltern, because, while it is called a genus, it still admits something higher. (3) The highest genus is of two kinds in relation to its inferiors: one is the genus of Beings, the other that of the Predicaments, or τῶν κατηγορουμένων [tōn katēgoroumenōn]. The highest genus of Beings is Being itself, as taken in the formal subject of Metaphysics, and this absolutely. Relatively, however, it is either of substance, and within this, one genus is of spirits and another of bodies; or of accidents, on the supposition that these are beings. The highest genus of Predicaments is either of first substance, to which the ten predicaments belong, or of action, to which these seven belong: who, what, where, by what aids,

units.la: liis, cui, quomodo, quando? Et fortè etiam relationum, modorum, &c. summa, καθηγορεμένων genera dari possunt. Sed de eis latius in Logicâ differendum, ad cujus curam illa genera καθηγορεμένων pertinent.
units.tr: to whom, how, when? And perhaps the highest genera of relations, modes, etc., may also be given as καθηγορουμένων [katēgoroumenōn] genera. But these are to be discussed more fully in Logic, to whose care those genera of κατηγορουμένων belong.

units.la: 13. 3. Dividitur Genus in univocum & Analogum. Illud est, quod secundum nomen & definitionem aequaliter de speciebus dicitur: Hoc verò quod inaequaliter. Quare & minus proprie Genus est, ut Ens respectu substantiæ & Accidentis; Substantia respectu increatæ & creatæ. Scotistæ æqualitatem istam non attendentes, omne genus, etiam cujus nunc proposita exempla, univocum esse volunt; Sed minus commodè; quoniam dependentia unius speciei ab altera, manifestam inæqualitatem in participatione essentiæ involvit: Sed quoniam controversia est de notione generis univoci, potius ea de nomine, quam de re censenda est quæstio.
units.tr: 13. 3. A genus is divided into univocal and analogous. The univocal is that which is predicated of its species equally according to name and definition; the analogous is that which is predicated unequally. Hence Genus is also used less properly, as Being with respect to substance and accident, or substance with respect to uncreated and created. The Scotists, not attending to this inequality, want every genus, including those whose examples have just been given, to be univocal; but this is less convenient, since the dependence of one species on another involves a plain inequality in the participation of essence. But since the controversy concerns the notion of a univocal genus, the question should be judged by the term rather than by the thing.

units.la: 14. Species inter varias significationes, tres huc aliquo modo facientes habet; Nam 1. sumitur, pro omni eo, quod generi subjectum est; atque ita & individua species infimæ dicuntur; quæ significatio Ramo ejusque affectis propria videtur. 2. Refertur ad superius aliquod, & dicitur species subjicibilis, quæ tamen ab individuo, ut superior distinguitur, quomodo est pars subsubjectiva. 3. Refertur ad inferius, cujus totum est, ac species praedicabilis dicitur, quomodo hîc consideranda est.
units.tr: 14. Species, among its various meanings, has three that bear on this somehow. (1) It is taken for everything that is subject to a genus, and in this way even the individuals of the lowest species are called species; this meaning seems proper to Ramus and his followers. (2) It is referred to some superior, and is called a subjectible species, which, however, is distinguished from the individual as the superior is, and is a subsubjective part. (3) It is referred to an inferior, of which it is the whole, and is called a predicable species; this is the one to be considered here.

units.la: 15. Est autem species totum praedicabile, numero differentibus tantum conveniens. Dicitur totum, quod totam individuorum, numero differentium, essentiam includat; adeòque ex iis collectis, si plura sint, resulter. Sed quid fiet, dices, si unum saltem sit individuum, an in eo conservabitur species? Resp. Conservabitur, licet tunc non nisi negativè totum dici possit illa species, prout fuit in Adamo ante creatam Evam conservata species humana. Quomodo enim totum positivè dici posset, cujus una tantum pars est; adeò ut pars & totum æquè late paterent? Negativè tamen totum dici potest, quoniam non est pars alterius speciei; Aliud igitur est species, aliud ipsam ut totum conservari. Dicitur totum praedicabile, eo quòd de suis partibus, prout & genus de speciebus, in quid dici potest. Dicitur convenire numero differentibus, pluribus, si proprie sit totum, uni autem, si improprie tale sit. Dicitur eis tantum convenire, ut distinguatur à genere, quod quoque singularibus convenit, & quandoque proximè, sed non tantum, quia etiam speciebus essentiâ differentibus tribuitur.
units.tr: 15. A species is a predicable whole, belonging only to things differing in number. It is called a whole because it includes the entire essence of the individuals differing in number, and so results from them when collected, if there are several. But, you will ask, what happens if there is only one individual; will the species be preserved in it? I reply: it will be preserved, although that species can then be called a whole only negatively, just as the human species was preserved in Adam before Eve was created. For how could it be called a whole positively when it has only one part, so that part and whole would have equal extent? Yet it can be called a whole negatively, since it is not a part of another species. Thus it is one thing for a species to exist, and another for it to be preserved as a whole. It is called a predicable whole because, like a genus with respect to its species, it can be predicated of its parts in quid. It is said to belong to several differing in number if it is a whole properly, but to one if it is such a whole improperly. It is said to belong only to these so that it may be distinguished from a genus, which also belongs to singulars, and sometimes immediately, but not only to them, since it is also attributed to species differing in essence.

units.la: 16. Dividi potest hæc species, quod sit vel μονάδικ, vel πολλάδικ; quarum illa uni, hæc verò pluribus convenit individuis: Capienda verò hæc distinctio potius materialiter, de iis quæ species dicuntur, quam formaliter, ut ipsæ sint totum aliquod: Alioquin enim μονάδικ species improprie totum est.
units.tr: 16. This species can be divided into what is monadic [μοναδικόν] and what is polyadic [πολλαδικόν]; the former belongs to one individual, the latter to several individuals. This distinction, however, should be taken materially, with respect to the things that are called species, rather than formally, as if the species themselves were some whole; otherwise a monadic species would be a whole only improperly.

units.la: 17. Sequitur integrum, sive totum integrale; Hoc autem aliquando idem est, quod perfectum, & mutilo sive incompleto opponitur; Unde quoque per Metaphoram ad animum transfertur, ut integer vitæ &c. Aliquando omne id integrum dicitur, quod non est pars materialis, sive id partes habeat, ut quodcunque totum, sive non, ut dicitur integra essentia. Deinde sæpius pro solo toto quantitativo sumitur, ac toti essentiali stricte dicto opponitur. At denique rectius, non minus quam latius à Ramæis, prout & essentiale sub se comprehendit; Atque ita est illud totum, quod de partibus suis in quid dici nequit.
units.tr: 17. Next comes the integral, or integral whole. This sometimes is the same as perfect, and is opposed to what is maimed or incomplete; whence also it is transferred by metaphor to the mind, as in integrity of life, etc. Sometimes everything is called integral that is not a material part, whether it has parts, as any whole does, or not, as when we speak of an integral essence. Further, it is more often taken for the quantitative whole alone, and is strictly opposed to the essential whole. But finally, and more correctly, and not less broadly than the Ramists do, it also comprehends the essential under itself; and so the whole is that which cannot be predicated in quid of its parts.

units.la: 18. Est autem hoc duplex; Quantitativum, cujus partes sunt extra se invicem; & Essentiale, cujus partes se mutuo penetrant.
units.tr: 18. This whole is twofold: the quantitative, whose parts are outside one another, and the essential, whose parts mutually penetrate one another.

units.la: 19. Quantitativum 1. est vel continuum, vel discretum: Continuum est, cujus partes communi termino retinentur; Estque vel homogeneum, vel heterogeneum; Illud partes ejusdem, hoc diversi nominis ac naturæ habet. Et hoc ideo vel est aequale, cum partes omnes aequalem habent dignitatem, vel inaequale, cum diversam habent dignitatem.
units.tr: 19. The quantitative whole is, first, either continuous or discrete. The continuous is that whose parts are held together by a common term. It is either homogeneous or heterogeneous: the former has parts of the same name and nature, the latter of different name and nature. And the latter again is either equal, when all parts have equal dignity, or unequal, when they have unequal dignity.

units.la: 20. Discretum totum est numerus quilibet, sive absolutus & numerans, sive comparatus & numeratus, ex unitatibus, tamquam partibus, communi termino non retentis, constans.
units.tr: 20. The discrete whole is any number whatever, whether absolute and numbering, or compared and numbered, consisting of units as parts, which do not keep a common term.

units.la: 21. 2. Totum quantitativum vel est ordinatum, vel inordinatum. Ordinatum est, cujus partes communem habitudinem ad se & totum habent; aliterque totum Physicum dici potest, quale est corpus humanum, Arbor, &c. ratione suarum partium. Inordinatum est, cujus partes ad se & ad totum communem ordinem non habent; ac aliter aggregatum, artificiale, vel & Politicum totum dici potest, quale est v. gr. Philosophia, Domus, Sylva, collegium &c. ratione suarum partium.
units.tr: 21. (2) A quantitative whole is either ordered or unordered. The ordered is that whose parts have a common relation to one another and to the whole; it may also be called a physical whole, such as the human body, a tree, etc., with respect to its parts. The unordered is that whose parts do not have a common order to one another or to the whole; it may also be called an aggregate, artificial, or even political whole, such as philosophy, a house, a forest, a college, etc., with respect to its parts.

units.la: 22. Essentiale autem totum, est quodvis compositum ex materia & forma propria; Et analogice quoque, quicquid ex iis, quae aliquo modo cum materia & forma convenient, componitur; quorsum spectat 1. Omne concretum ex subjecto & accidente. 2. Quidquid ex denominante & denominato confluit. 3. Quod ex genere & differentia constat; Quia in his omnibus partes se mutuo penetrant.
units.tr: 22. An essential whole, however, is any compound of matter and proper form. And analogically, whatever is compounded of those things that in some way agree with matter and form is also called such; to this belong (1) every concrete composed of subject and accident; (2) whatever flows from a denominating and a denominated thing; (3) whatever consists of genus and differentia, because in all of these the parts mutually penetrate one another.

units.la: 23. Sequitur Pars, quæ 1. latè accipitur, pro omni eo, in quod quâcunque ratione aliquid divisibile est; atque ita & partem per accidens comprehendit. 2. Strictè capitur, pro solâ parte quantitativâ; Prout formæ dicuntur non esse partibiles, hoc est, non habere partes. 3. Adæquatè sumitur, pro omni eo, quod ad essentiam totius propriè dicti constituendam requiritur; Atque ita definitur, quæ cum aliis sibi junctis totum constituit.
units.tr: 23. Next comes the Part, which is taken (1) broadly, for anything into which a thing is divisible in any way at all, and so it also includes an accidental part; (2) strictly, for the quantitative part alone, in which sense forms are said not to be partible, that is, not to have parts; (3) adequately, for whatever is required to constitute the essence of a whole properly so called, and in this sense a part is defined as that which, together with other things joined to it, constitutes a whole.

units.la: 24. Differentia Partium, ex totius divisionibus non obscurè patent; ideoque vel est subjectiva, vel integralis. Illa est, de quâ totum in quid dici potest; Hæc verò, de quâ non potest; Quæ differentiæ immediatè opponuntur, alias reliquas partes, aut spurias, aut ad has revocandas esse, satis evincunt.
units.tr: 24. The differences of parts are clear enough from the divisions of the whole; hence a part is either subjective or integral. The former is that of which the whole can be predicated in quid; the latter is that of which it cannot. That these differences are immediately opposed, and that the other remaining parts are either spurious or must be reduced to these, is sufficiently proved.

units.la: 25. Duplex autem est subjectiva pars, vel species subjicibilis, vel individuum. Species subjicibilis est, in quam subse comprehensam dividitur genus; Vel est pars subjectiva Generis, essentialiter ab oppositâ parte distans; Utraque commoda est definitio. Nec mireris, hic iterum de specie agi, cum & paulò antè de ipsâ sit actum; ejus enim causa est diversus, imò oppositus, respectus, inter speciem ut partem, eamdemque ut totum. Quantò magis illi peccant, qui duplicem illum respectum agnoscentes, unicâ tamen definitione speciem explicare conati sunt.
units.tr: 25. A subjective part is twofold: either a subjectible species or an individual. A subjectible species is that into which a genus is divided as contained under it; or it is a subjective part of the genus, essentially distant from the opposite part. Either is a serviceable definition. Nor should you be surprised that species is treated here again, since it was discussed a little earlier; for the cause of this is the different, indeed opposite, relation of the species as a part and the same species as a whole. How much more do those err who, recognizing this double relation, have nonetheless tried to explain species by a single definition!

units.la: 26. Dividitur hæc species 1. in Proximam & Remotam ; illa est, in quam genus immediatè dividitur: Hæc verò in quam dividitur Genus mediante alio. 2. In subalternam & specialissimam ; Quarum illa ratione inferiorum fit Genus ; Hæc autem fit species prædicabilis; ubi nota 1. hoc intelligi debere ratione materiæ & rei, quæ admodum v. gr. corpus vivens species est corporis naturalis, at Genus animalis: non autem ratione formæ, ut corpus vivens sic genus, quâtenus species est. 2. Nota; quod hæc species specialissima reipsa idem sit, cum specie prædicabili infimâ supra tradita; licet respectu, hoc est formâ, maxime ab ipsâ differat. Ex. gr. Petri & Pauli species prædicabilis est homo; atque idem quoque species subjectiva specialissima est, non tamen Petri & Pauli, sed animalis respectu.
units.tr: 26. This species is divided (1) into proximate and remote. The proximate is that into which the genus is divided immediately; the remote is that into which it is divided through an intermediate. (2) Into subaltern and most specific. Of these, the former becomes a genus with respect to its inferiors, while the latter becomes a predicable species. Here note (1) that this must be understood in terms of matter and thing: thus living body is a species of natural body, but a genus of animal. It is not understood in terms of form, so that living body is a genus in the same way that it is a species. (2) Note that this most specific species is in fact the same thing as the lowest predicable species given above, although in respect, that is in form, it differs greatly from it. For example, the predicable species of Peter and Paul is man; and the same thing is also the most specific subjective species, not of Peter and Paul, but with respect to animal.

units.la: 27. 3. Dividitur species in univocam & analogam; illa dicitur, quæ cuim opposita sibi æqualiter de genere participat; At hæc quæ inæqualiter; Atque cum una magis participat, & dicitur analogata prior; altera minus, & dicitur analogata posterior.
units.tr: 27. Species is divided (3) into univocal and analogous. The former is called that which participates in the genus equally with what is opposed to it; the latter is that which participates unequally. When one participates more, it is called the prior analogate; the other, which participates less, is called the posterior analogate.

units.la: 28. Individuum est pars subjectiva speciei, alteri inferiori prorsus incommunicabilis; hoc est, de nullis inferioribus sub se contentis praedicabilis; Adeoque est omne Ens, prout singulare est & existens; unde & supra cap. 12. ejus differentiae traditae sunt.
units.tr: 28. An individual is a subjective part of a species, wholly incommunicable to any other inferior; that is, it is not predicable of any inferiors contained under it. Hence every being, insofar as it is singular and existing, is an individual; and its differences were given above, in chapter 12.

units.la: 29. At ratione nominis, sive signi, quo explicatur,vel determinatum est, vel vagum Illud est, quando signum aeque ac individuum est determinatum, sive hoc fiat nomine proprio; sive appellativo, pronomine vel, adverbio demonstrativo addito, determinato; sive communi nomine, per descriptionem & περιφερειαν limitato; sive propter excellentiam de uno intellecto. Hoc vero est, quando nomen non aeque est determinatum, sed indefinitè propositum, vel per se, vel cum addito signo particulari, aliquod individuum & singulare denotat. Sed de hoc consulendi Logici.
units.tr: 29. With respect to the name, or sign, by which it is explained, a species is either determinate or vague. It is determinate when the sign, like the individual, is determinate, whether this is done by a proper name, or by an appellative with a demonstrative pronoun or adverb added, or by a common name limited by description and periphrasis, or by excellence applied to one thing understood. It is vague when the name is not equally determinate but is put forward indefinitely, either by itself or with an added particular sign, and denotes some individual and singular thing. But on this matter consult the logicians.

units.la: 30. Pars integralis quoque, non secus ac totum integrum, duplex est, vel essentialis, vel quantitativa. Essentialis est, quae non est extra oppositam partem, sed vel ipsam penetrat, vel ab ipsa penetratur; Quaenam autem tales sint, modo indicatum est. Notandum hic, partes essentiales numero semper duas esse, penetrantem & penetratam; quarum haec natura prior est illa.
units.tr: 30. An integral part, no less than an integral whole, is twofold: either essential or quantitative. An essential part is one that is not outside the opposite part but either penetrates it or is penetrated by it. What such parts are has just been indicated. It should be noted here that essential parts are always two in number, the penetrating and the penetrated; of these the latter is prior in nature to the former.

units.la: 31. Pars quantitativa est, quae extra sibi coordinatas est; Estque 1. continua, quae communi termino cum reliquis copulata est ; & discreta , quæ termino communi cum reliquis non continetur. 2. Est vel similaris, vel diffimilaris ; prout eamdem naturam, ac idem nomen cum reliquis & toto habet, vel non habet. Ideoque diffimilaris, est vel æqualis, ejufdem cum reliquis dignitatis, vel inæqualis & diversæ dignitatis. Quæ proinde vel Principalis est, vel minus principalis, prout præstantiâ reliquas antecellit ,vel ab iis superatur.
units.tr: 31. A quantitative part is one that lies outside its coordinate parts. It is (1) continuous, if it is joined to the others by a common term, and discrete, if it is not contained with the others by a common term. (2) It is either similar or dissimilar, according as it has the same nature and the same name as the others and the whole, or does not. Hence a dissimilar part is either equal, of the same dignity as the others, or unequal and of different dignity. Of these, the one is principal or less principal, according as it surpasses the others in excellence or is surpassed by them.

units.la: 32. Fundamentum autem istius præftantiæ, quâ partes fe mutuò superant, non femper idem est ; nam modò est copia & magnitudo partis, quomodo lapides ædificii principales sunt partes ; modò est usus major, quomodo Cor præcipua est corporis humani ; modò est conservatio reliquarum partium, quomodò domûs est fundamentum ; modò arbitrariaquædam pretiositas, quomodo Gemma annuli potiffima pars dicitur &c. Et hæc de Toto & Partibus.
units.tr: 32. The foundation of this excellence, by which parts surpass one another, is not always the same. Sometimes it is the quantity and size of the part, as the principal stones are the chief parts of a building. Sometimes it is greater use, as the heart is the chief part of the human body. Sometimes it is the preservation of the other parts, as a foundation is the basis of a house. Sometimes it is some arbitrary preciousness, as the gem is called the chief part of a ring, and so on. And so much on the whole and its parts.

units.la: CAP. XXV. DE Completo & Incompleto.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. On the Complete and the Incomplete.

units.la: 1. Totum, fi omnes partes, ipsi fecundum speciem debitas, haberat, com- pletum dicitur : At fi ipsi quædam desint, inincompletum ; Prout & singulæ partes totius respectu incompletæ dicuntur ; De his igitur affectionibus nunc dicendum.
units.tr: 1. A whole, if it has all the parts that are due to it according to its kind, is said to be complete; but if some parts are missing from it, it is said to be incomplete. In the same way, the single parts are called incomplete with respect to the whole. Let us therefore now speak of these affections.

units.la: 2. Completum autem aliquando idem est, quod perfectum, prout nonnulli Autores indifferenter terminis Completi ac Perfecti utuntur ; Atque sic incompletum idem est, quod imperfectum : Attamen perfecti & imperfecti alia est ratio, ut cap.9.ostensum. Aliquando vero completum dicitur, quod ex incompleto vi actionis intercedentis, tale est, ut antea fuerit incompletum ; Atque tunc participii significationem habet. Aliquando id, quod omnes partes habet, non attendendo, an prius fuerit incompletum, nec ne. Aliquando quoque idem est, quod consummatum, ut tunc incompletum idem fit, quod inchoatum. Quæ tres ultimæ acceptiones hic conjungenda sunt ; quoniam totum ex partibus revera constans, fi aliquis horum modorum deíit, incompletum dicitur ; at iis præfentibus completum est.
units.tr: 2. Now "complete" is sometimes the same as "perfect", since some authors use the terms complete and perfect interchangeably; and so "incomplete" is the same as "imperfect". Yet the account of perfect and imperfect is different, as was shown in chapter 9. Sometimes, however, "complete" is said of what has become so from being incomplete through the force of an intervening action, so that it previously was incomplete; in this sense it has the force of a participle. Sometimes it means that which has all its parts, without regard to whether it was previously incomplete or not. Sometimes too it is the same as "finished", and then "incomplete" becomes the same as "begun". These last three senses are to be joined here: since a whole, consisting in reality of parts, is called incomplete if it lacks any one of these modes, but is complete when they are all present.

units.la: 3. Est igitur completio modus totius, quo id habet omnes partes, sibi secundum speciem debitas. Quare non realiter differt a toto, sed idem plane cum ipso est, quemadmodum perfectio cum Ente.
units.tr: 3. Completeness, then, is the mode of a whole by which it has all the parts due to it according to its kind. Hence it does not really differ from the whole, but is plainly the same thing as it, just as perfection is the same as being.

units.la: 4. Dices: At sic Deus & Angeli non possent dici completi, utpote qui ob persectionem suam partes respuunt. Resp. Di-cuncuntur completi, eodem pacto ac toti; id est, quatenus totum & completum idem, quod perfectum denotat: non vero per ordinem & respectum ad partes.
units.tr: 4. You will object: but in that case God and the angels could not be called complete, since on account of their perfection they have no parts. I answer: they are called complete in the same way as they are called whole; that is, insofar as "whole" and "complete" denote the same thing as "perfect", and not by an order or relation to parts.

units.la: 5. Quoniam autem idem est totum & completum, hoc quoque eodem modo ac illud dividi poterit. Notandum tamen potius totum integrale, quam praedicabile completum dici; Quare hinc completum potissimum est vel essentiale, vel quantitativum; & hoc magnitudinis & numeri respectu, vel continuum, vel discretum.
units.tr: 5. Since "whole" and "complete" are the same, the complete can also be divided in the same way as the whole. It should be noted, however, that a whole is rather called integral than the complete is called predicable. Hence the complete is chiefly either essential or quantitative; and the quantitative, with respect to magnitude and number, is either continuous or discrete.

units.la: 6. Essentiale completum dicitur totum ex materia & forma constans. Continuum completum consistit in legitima partium magnitudine: Discretum vero in debito earum numero.
units.tr: 6. The essential complete is said to be the whole consisting of matter and form. The continuous complete consists in the proper magnitude of its parts; the discrete, however, in the due number of them.

units.la: 7. Incompletum quibus modis capiatur, ex acceptionibus completi liquet. Tribuitur autem vel parti uni seorsim acceptae; quomodo corpus humanum & mens, sigillatim si sumantur, incompleta dicuntur. Quae satis frequens est acceptio: Atque ita quemadmodum completum nihil aliud est, quam totum, ita incompletum idem est, quod pars. Quare sicut ideo pars ratione Entitatis non est in se imperfectum quid, licet accedente respectu quodam ad totum ordinetur; ita tali modo incompletum non est aliquid in se imperfectum: sed potius eo ipso quia Ens est, debitâ sibi persectione gaudet.
units.tr: 7. In what ways "incomplete" is taken is clear from the senses of "complete". It is ascribed either to a single part taken on its own, as the human body and the mind, if they are taken separately, are said to be incomplete; and this is a fairly common usage. And so, just as the complete is nothing other than the whole, the incomplete is the same as the part. Hence, just as a part, as regards its entity, is not in itself something imperfect, although by a certain added relation it is ordered to the whole, so in this way the incomplete is not something imperfect in itself; rather, by the very fact that it is a being, it enjoys the perfection due to it.

units.la: 8. Vel incompletum tribuitur toti, idque vel in fieri, vel in facto esse. Incompletum in fieri dicitur totum, quâtenus ipsi adhuc quædam partes sunt adjungendæ; ita incompletus est tractatus, cui nondum extrema manus est addita: Estque sic idem quod inchoatum.
units.tr: 8. Or "incomplete" is ascribed to the whole, and this either as being in process or as being in a finished state. A whole is said to be incomplete in process insofar as some parts are still to be added to it; thus a treatise is incomplete when the finishing touch has not yet been put to it; and in this sense it is the same as "begun".

units.la: 9. Incompletum in facto esse dicitur totum, cui partes quædam desunt per privationem, quæ adesse debebant; Atque ita idem est, quod mutilum, mancum, defectuosum, truncatum &c. sive illæ partes ab ipso ortu desint, sive postmodum fuerint sublatæ.
units.tr: 9. A whole is said to be incomplete in a finished state when certain parts are lacking to it through a privation, since they ought to be present; and in this sense it is the same as maimed, crippled, defective, truncated, and so on, whether those parts are missing from its very origin or were removed afterwards.

units.la: 10. Estque hoc duplex, reparabile, vel irreparabile; Prout illæ partes ordinario naturæ cursu restitui & suppleri possunt, vel secus; Quorum exempla passim obvia. Et hæc de completo & incompleto.
units.tr: 10. This is twofold: reparable or irreparable, according as those parts can be restored and supplied by the ordinary course of nature or not. Examples of both are everywhere to be met with. And so much for the complete and the incomplete.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. DE Subjecto & Adjuncto.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI. On the Subject and the Adjunct.

units.la: 1. Sequuntur nunc affectiones, ex Relationibus externis orta; Sunt autem dua tales relationes Appositio & Circumstantia.
units.tr: 1. Now follow the affections that arise from external relations. There are two such relations, apposition and circumstance.

units.la: 2. Appositio est unius ad alterum externa coordinatio. Quare hinc patet 1. In omni appositione esse duo; unum quod apponitur, & alterum cui apponitur. Unde fluit, idem sibi ipsi apponi non posse; quare cum judicium Appositionis species est, in eo nemo in propria causa judex esse potest.2. In omni appositione esse ordinem, adeo ut unum propter alterum adsit, & præcipuè appositum, propter id cui apponitur. Hinc vestimenta propter hominem, & non homo propter vestimenta. 3. Appositum esse extra essentiam ejus cui apponitur. Quod igitur rei pars est, id ejus adjunctum dici nequit. 4. In omni appositione esse cognationem & convenientiam quamdam. Atque hinc in omni possessione, convenientia requiritur inter possessorem & possessum. Convenientia autem illa vel est a natura, ut in familiâ, vel ab institutione, qualis est in hæreditate, donatione, contractu, occupatione, servitute &c. 5. Posito eo quod apponitur, etiam poni, id cui apponitur; ita positâ uxore, ponitur maritus; posito emente, ponitur vendens &c.
units.tr: 2. Apposition is the external coordination of one thing with another. From this it is clear: (1) In every apposition there are two things: one that is apposed, and another to which it is apposed. It follows that a thing cannot be apposed to itself; hence, since judgement is a species of apposition, no one can be judge in his own cause. (2) In every apposition there is an order, so that one exists for the sake of the other, and especially the apposed exists for the sake of that to which it is apposed. Hence clothes are for the man, and not the man for the clothes. (3) The apposed lies outside the essence of that to which it is apposed. What is a part of a thing therefore cannot be called its adjunct. (4) In every apposition there is some kinship and some agreement. Hence in every possession agreement is required between the possessor and the possessed. This agreement is either from nature, as in a family, or from institution, as in inheritance, gift, contract, occupation, slavery, and so on. (5) Given that which is apposed, that to which it is apposed is also posited. So, with a wife posited, the husband is posited; with a buyer posited, the seller is posited, and so on.

units.la: 3. Est autem duplex oppositio, simplex & connotata. Prior est nuda adjunctio unius ad aliud: Posterior verò est appositio cum intercedente functione, officio, aut operatione.
units.tr: 3. There is a twofold apposition, simple and connoted. The former is a bare joining of one thing to another; the latter is apposition with a function, office or operation intervening.

units.la: 4. Adjunctio varias habet species, v. gr.
units.tr: 4. Adjunction has various species, for example:

units.la: Adhæsionem, Appulsionem, Adjacentiam, accubationem, incubationem, impositionem, Assessionem, quas sigillatim explicare hujus non est loci; Saltem hoc explicandum, quod ipsis commune est, ipsum videlicet subjectum, & adjunctum.
units.tr: adhesion, appulsion, adjacency, reclining, incubation, imposition, and sitting upon. It is not the place to explain these one by one. It is enough to explain what they have in common, namely the subject and the adjunct themselves.

units.la: 5. Subjectum igitur hic est, cui aliquid præter essentiam extrinsecus adjungitur; inter hoc & ipsi oppositum adjunctum talis est relatio, ut quod modo subjectum dicitur, mox pro adjuncto haberi possit, & contra; Ex. gr. Vitrum subjectum dici potest Vini, tamquam adjuncti; & consimiliter Vinum subjectum & Vitrum adjunctum appellari potest. Usus tamen obtinet, ut illud subjectum dicamus, quod vel prius est, vel copiâ, & dignitate antecellit, vel alterum sustentat, & conservat.
units.tr: 5. The subject, then, here is that to which something is added from outside, beyond its essence. Between this and the adjunct opposed to it there is such a relation that what is now called the subject can soon be held to be the adjunct, and conversely.
