For example, a glass may be called the subject of wine, as the adjunct; and similarly wine may be called the subject and the glass the adjunct. Usage, however, has it that we call that the subject which is either prior, or surpasses in quantity and dignity, or sustains and preserves the other.

units.la: 6. Subjecti divisiones secundum diversas illas species, ob insignem earum varietatem dari non possunt; Accidentales, à communibus quibusdam fundamentis petitæ, hæ potissimum sunt 1. Subjectum est vel proprium, vel commune. Proprium est, cui adjunctum suum tantum adhæret; quale est homo vestium. Commune verò est, cujus adjunctum etiam aliis subjectis adhæret, quale est Aristoteles librorum.
units.tr: 6. Divisions of the subject according to those various species cannot be given, because of their remarkable variety. The accidental divisions, taken from certain common foundations, are chiefly these. (1) A subject is either proper or common. It is proper when its adjunct clings only to it, as a man to his clothes. It is common when its adjunct clings also to other subjects, as Aristotle to books.

units.la: 7. 2. Subjectum est vel totale, vel partiale: tuale : Illi fecundum omnes partes : huic vero fecundum hanc & illam tantum adjunctum adhæret: Ita totale subjectum est Petrus vestimentorum, at partiale ratione annuli, quem in digito tenet.
units.tr: 7. (2) A subject is either total or partial. The former has the adjunct clinging to it in all its parts; the latter has it clinging only in this or that part. Thus Peter is a total subject with respect to his clothes, but a partial one with respect to the ring he wears on his finger.

units.la: 8. 3. Subjectum est vel necessarium, vel contingens. Prius est, sine quo non est adjunctum, ut Respublica est Magistratus. Posterius vero sine quo est adjunctum, ut templum turris.
units.tr: 8. (3) A subject is either necessary or contingent. The former is that without which the adjunct does not exist, as the commonwealth is to the magistrate. The latter is that without which the adjunct may exist, as a building is to a tower.

units.la: 9. 4. Subjectum est vel per se, vel per accidens ; Quæ divisio, aliquando cum secunda videtur coincidere: At aliquando accipitur, ut subjectum per se dicatur, quod suâ natura ordinatum est ad adjunctum: Et per accidens, quod suâ natura non est ad illud destinatum. Ita studiosus est subjectum per se librorum, & per accidens gladii.
units.tr: 9. (4) A subject is either per se or per accidens. This division sometimes seems to coincide with the second. But sometimes it is taken so that a subject is called per se when by its nature it is ordered toward the adjunct, and per accidens when by its nature it is not destined for it. Thus a student is the subject per se of books, and per accidens of a sword.

units.la: 10. Adjunctum latè dictum significat, omne illud, quod præter essentiam rei adest; & sic quoque accidens sub se comprehendit: Presfius denotat omne appositum, & sic quoque objectum & signatum adjuncta dicuntur. Strictè quoque socium fortunarum denotat: Hic verò est, quod præter essentiam subjecto extrinsecè nudè apponitur: Et subjecto jam explicato oppònitur.
units.tr: 10. The adjunct, taken broadly, signifies everything that is present beyond the essence of a thing; in this sense it also includes accident under itself. In a narrower sense it denotes everything apposed, and in this sense objects and signified things are also called adjuncts. In the strictest sense it also denotes a companion in fortunes. But here it is that which is joined bare from outside to the subject, beyond its essence, and it is set in opposition to the subject, now explained.

units.la: 11. Ejus divisiones, ex iis, quæ de differentiis subjecti dicta sunt, haut magno negotio cognosci possunt. Et hæc de subjecto & adjuncto
units.tr: 11. Its divisions can be recognised without great difficulty from what has been said about the differences of the subject. And so much on the subject and the adjunct.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: DE Subjecto & Objecto.
units.tr: Of the Subject and the Object.

units.la: 1. Appositio connotata triplex est: 1. Occupatio. 2. Significatio. 3. Mensuratio. Occupatio inter Subjectum & Objectum: significatio inter Signum & Signatum: Mensuratio inter mensuram & mensuratum intercedit, de quibus nunc ordine agendum.
units.tr: 1. A connoted relation is threefold: (1) occupation; (2) signification; (3) measurement. Occupation lies between subject and object, signification between sign and signified, and measurement between measure and measured. These we must now take in order.

units.la: 2. Occupatio est appositio connotata, quâ unum circa alterum habet operationem; Unde patet 1. in omni occupatione esse duo, subjectum, quod operatur, & objectum, cui ista operatio applicatur. 2. Omne subjectum occupationis circa objectum esse; Unde nulla ars, aut scientia sine objecto esse potest; Quo fundamento Ramæi in perniciem Metaphysicæ abuntur. 3. Omne subjectum occupationis debere aliquid agere. 4. Posito objecto, poni subjectum, vid. in sensu composito; Dum enim ponitur patiens, poni debet & agens.
units.tr: 2. Occupation is a connoted relation by which one thing has an operation concerning another; Hence it is clear (1) that in every occupation there are two things: the subject, which operates, and the object, to which that operation is applied. (2) Every subject of an occupation is concerned with an object; hence no art or science can exist without an object. On this foundation the Ramists go to the ruin of Metaphysics. (3) Every subject of an occupation must do something. (4) When the object is posited, the subject is posited, see in the composite sense; for when the patient is posited, the agent must be posited too.

units.la: 3. Objectum hoc ratione communium differentiarum dividitur: 1. quod sit vel Materiale, vel formale. Primum est illud totum, circa cujus partem, vel accidens, vel aliud ad ipsum pertinens, agens est occupatum: Posterius verò est præcise illud, circa quod in in illo toto subjectum occupationem habet. Ita objectum materiale visus est paries, at formale ejus color. Atque ad hunc modum etiam subjectum dividi potest; ut materiale, sit totum suppositum agens, ut Petrus videns parietem: Et formale illa ratio, secundum quam agit, ut visus Petri circa parietem.
units.tr: 3. The object is divided in this way, according to the common differences: (1) it is either material or formal. The first is that whole, concerning some part, or accident, or other thing pertaining to it, of which the agent is occupied; the latter is precisely that about which the subject has its occupation within that whole. Thus the material object of sight is a wall, but its formal object is its colour. In this way the subject too can be divided: as material, it is the whole acting supposit, such as Peter seeing a wall; and as formal, it is that ground according to which it acts, such as the sight of Peter concerning the wall.

units.la: 4.. 2. Objectum est vel reciprocum, vel non reciprocum: Illud voco, quod suâ actione reagit in subjectum: hoc verò quod non reagit, sed tantum in se recipit actionem subjecti; ita qualitates contrariæ sibi mutuò sunt objecta reciproca, ita reus in foro objectum reciprocum est Actoris. At Advocatus sui clientis non reciprocum. Notandum tamen reciprocum objectum non reagere, ut objectum, sed ut subjectum; adeò ut ejus reactionis respectu, quod prius erat subjectum, nunc dicatur objectum.
units.tr: 4. 2. The object is either reciprocal or non-reciprocal. I call that reciprocal which by its action reacts upon the subject; the other, which does not react but only receives the action of the subject into itself, is non-reciprocal. Thus contrary qualities are reciprocal objects of one another, and the defendant in court is the reciprocal object of the plaintiff, but a client's advocate is not. It must be noted, however, that a reciprocal object reacts not as an object but as a subject; so that, with respect to its reaction, what was previously the subject is now called the object.

units.la: 5. 3. Objectum est vel proprium, vel commune; illud est, cui soli functio talis subjecti applicatur, ut est sapor gustus: Hoc verò, circa quod talis functio subjecti tantum non versatur, ut sunt Motus, magnitudo & figura, visus. Dicitur expresse functio talis; Diversas enim functiones si spectemus, vix dabitur Objectum proprium, circa quod alia etiam subjecta non sint occupata.
units.tr: 5. 3. The object is either proper or common. The former is that to which such a function of the subject is applied alone, as flavour is to taste. The latter is that with which such a function of the subject is hardly ever concerned, as motion, magnitude, and figure are to sight. The phrase "such a function" is stated expressly; for if we consider different functions, there will hardly be a proper object about which other subjects are not also occupied.

units.la: 6. 4. Objectum est vel per se, vel per accidens. Prius dicitur, circa quod quâ tale, subjectum quâ tale est occupatum; ideoque est formale objectum; circa quod agit formale subjectum, ut visus circa colorem. Posterius vero dicitur, quando refertur objectum materiale, ad subjectum formale, ut cum sapor dicitur gustare pomum; vel quando Subjectum materiale refertur ad objectum formale, ut cum homo videt colorem; vel quando utrumque est materiale, ut cum homo sentit ignem.
units.tr: 6. 4. The object is either per se or per accidens. The former is said to be that about which the subject, as such, is occupied as such; and so it is the formal object, the one about which the formal subject acts, as sight about colour. The latter is said to be when a material object is referred to a formal subject, as when flavour is said to taste an apple; or when a material subject is referred to a formal object, as when a man sees colour; or when both are material, as when a man feels fire.

units.la: 7. 5. Objectum est vel proximum vel remotum. Illud dicitur, cui proximè applicatur operatio agentis: Hoc verò, quod intercedente alio objecto. Ita ignis proximè versatur circa cibi calefactionem, remotè verò circa ejus coctionem. Ex quo patet, interobjecta etiam subordinationem esse; nec mirum hoc, quoniam ad illa requiritur actio, adeo ut subjectum semper sit causa aliqua, non quidem objecti semper, sed etiam alicujus in & circa ipsum. Nota tamen, objectum proximum, ratione remoti esse subjectum, non objectum.
units.tr: 7. 5. The object is either proximate or remote. The former is that to which the agent's operation is applied directly; the latter is that to which it is applied with another object intervening. Thus fire is directly concerned with the heating of food, but remotely with its cooking. From this it is clear that there is also a subordination among objects, and this is no surprise, since action is required for them; so that the subject is always some cause, not indeed of the object always, but of something in and about it. Note, however, that a proximate object, in relation to a remote one, is a subject, not an object.

units.la: 8. 6. Objectum est vel Principale, vel minus principale: Principale est, circa quod præcipuè versatur actio subjecti, ut Studiosus circa ea, quæ utilitatem afferunt in libris. Minus principale verò, circa quod popotissima cura non versatur, ut Studiosus circa inutilia utilibus permista.
units.tr: 8. 6. The object is either principal or less principal. The principal is that about which the action of the subject is chiefly engaged, as a student is with those things that bring profit from books. The less principal is that about which his main care is not engaged, as a student is with useless things mixed in with useful ones.

units.la: 9. Dividitur quoque aliquando Objectum, in objectum tractationis, operationis, & informationis. Sed 1. illa tantum in artibus obtinet. 2. Infiniti penè sunt modi, quibus unum circa aliud occupatū esse potest. 3. Et cum omne subjectum operetur, etiam omne objectum erit operationis, adeò ut secundum membrum reliqua includat; quoniam quod tractat & informat etiam operatur. Ex his autem divisionibus Objecti differentias Subjecti, ad objectum relati, facilè cognosces. Sint igitur hæc de Subjecto & Objecto.
units.tr: 9. The object is also sometimes divided into the object of treatment, of operation, and of information. But (1) the first of these holds only in the arts; (2) there are almost infinitely many ways in which one thing can be occupied about another; (3) and since every subject operates, every object will also be an object of operation, so that the second member includes the rest, since what treats and informs also operates. From these divisions of the object you will easily recognise the differences of the subject as related to the object. So much, then, on subject and object.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: DE Signo & Signato.
units.tr: OF THE SIGN AND THE SIGNIFIED.

units.la: 1. SEquitur Significatio, quæ est appositio connotata, quâ unum aliud aliquid indicat. Quare in omni significatione est indicans, quod Signum, & indicatum, quod signatum dicitur. Unde 1. nihil sui ipsius signum esse potest. 2. Signum aliquid alicui alteri significare debet, non sibi ipsi; Unde duplex oritur signi relatio, una ad rem significatam, quæ hic spectatur; altera ad potentiam, cui rem significat; quæ occupationis est species, quia illa potentia est signi objectum. 3. Signum indicat aliud cognoscenti, vel sensui vel intellectui: Quare sublato cognoscente signum formam amittit.
units.tr: 1. Next comes signification, which is a connoted application by which one thing indicates something else. Hence in every signification there is that which indicates, called the sign, and that which is indicated, called the signified. Hence, first, nothing can be a sign of itself. Second, a sign must signify something to someone else, not to itself. Hence a twofold relation of the sign arises: one to the thing signified, which is the one considered here; the other to the power to which it signifies the thing, which is a kind of occupation, since that power is the object of the sign. Third, a sign indicates something to a knower, either to the sense or to the intellect; hence, if the knower is removed, the sign loses its form.

units.la: 2. Sumitur autem signum quoad vocem 1. pro Argumento. 2. Pro vexillo, quod signum militare est. 3. Pro puncto in Geometria. 4. Pro certa stellarum constellatione in Astrologia. 5. Strictè pro admirando quodam opere, miraculo, in S. Scriptura. 6. Pro omni indicante, ut hic.
units.tr: 2. As to the word, signum is taken (1) for an argument; (2) for a standard, which is a military sign; (3) for a point in geometry; (4) for a certain constellation of the stars in astrology; (5) strictly, for a remarkable work, a miracle, in Holy Scripture; (6) for anything that indicates, as here.

units.la: 3. Definitur, Burgersdicio ex Goclenii Lexico Philos. quod se ipsum sensibus, & id cujus signum est, intellectui offert. At 1. Non omne signum sensui est obvium, ut satis ostendunt notiones secundae, quae signa rerum & conceptuum sunt in ipso intellectu, in quo sunt. 2. Non omne signum aliquid intellectui offert. Habent quippe & bruta animantia sua signa, ut in canibus manifestum, at intellectu carent. Sufficiat igitur generalis definitio, quod sit aliquid, a se distinctum aliud indicans.
units.tr: 3. Burgersdijk, following Goclenius's Philosophical Lexicon, defines it as that which presents itself to the senses, and that of which it is the sign, to the intellect. But (1) not every sign is obvious to the senses, as second notions sufficiently show; these are signs of things and concepts, and they lie within the intellect itself. (2) Not every sign presents something to the intellect. Brute animals too have their signs, as is plain in dogs, yet they lack intellect. A general definition will therefore suffice: that it is something, distinct from itself, which indicates another thing.

units.la: 4. Differentiae signorum variae sunt; Nam primo ratione efficientis, sunt vel naturalia, vel arbitraria. Illa sunt, quae sua natura indicant: Haec vero, quae ex instituto; Sive divino, ut Sacramenta: Sive humano, ut voces rerum. Naturalia porro signa majorem adhuc ad sua signata rerequirunt habitudinem. Nam signatorum vel causæ sunt, ut Lunæ ascensus ad meridianum æstus marini, vel effecta, ut actiones læsæ morborum; vel signum & signatum simul sunt concausæ tertii alicujus, ut ira est impotentis animi signum; vel sunt ejusdem causæ effecta, ut tonitru fulminis; vel signum est accidens proprium subjecti signati, ut nigredo faciei Æthiopis; vel est totum partis, ut animal cordis; Vel pars totius, ut ex conspectâ facie per fenestram judicatur totius præsentiâ.
units.tr: 4. The kinds of signs are various. First, by reason of the efficient cause, they are either natural or arbitrary. The former are those which indicate by their nature; the latter are those which do so by institution, either divine, as the sacraments, or human, as the words of languages. Natural signs further require a closer relation to what they signify. For the things signified are either causes, as the rising of the moon is a sign of the tides of the sea; or effects, as the symptoms of diseases are of the disease; or the sign and the signified are both co-causes of some third thing, as anger is a sign of an impotent mind; or they are effects of the same cause, as thunder is of lightning; or the sign is a proper accident of the subject signified, as the blackness of an Ethiopian's face; or it is the whole of which the signified is a part, as the animal is of the heart; or it is a part of a whole, as when the presence of the whole is judged from a face seen through a window.

units.la: 5. Secundò ratione ordinis, signum est vel proximum, quod immediatè rem significat, ut fumus combustionem; vel remotum, quod intercedente alio signo signatum indicat, ut species, vel phantasma, vel umbra fumi, combustionis est. Atque hinc patet, etiam in significatione esse quamdam subordinationem, quâ rectè statuitur, id quoque signum esse signati, quod est signum signi.
units.tr: 5. Second, by reason of order, a sign is either proximate, which signifies the thing immediately, as smoke signifies burning; or remote, which indicates the signified through another intervening sign, as the image, or appearance, or shadow of smoke is a sign of burning. From this it is clear that there is also a certain subordination in signification, by which it is rightly held that whatever is the sign of a sign is also the sign of the signified.

units.la: 6. Tertiò, ratione adjunctorum signati, signum vel est præsentis rei, diciturque διαγνωστικὸν & demonstrativum; vel absentis, sive futuræ, & προγνωστικὸν ac prænuntians appellatur; sive præteritæ, & ἀναμνηστικὸν, & recordans ac commemorans audit. Huic respondet divisio signi in antecedens, consequens & conjunctum. Antecedens quippe est διαγνωστικὸν, Consequens ἀναἀναμνησικόν; & Conjunctum διαγνωστικόν.
units.tr: 6. Third, by reason of the circumstances of the signified, a sign is either of a present thing, and is called demonstrative [διαγνωστικὸν]; or of an absent thing, whether future, when it is called prognostic [προγνωστικὸν] and foretelling; or past, when it is called reminiscent [ἀναμνηστικὸν] and is heard as recalling and commemorating. To this corresponds the division of a sign into antecedent, consequent and conjoined. The antecedent is demonstrative, the consequent reminiscent, and the conjoined demonstrative.

units.la: 7. Quartò, ratione nexus cum signato, est vel necessarium vel contingens. Illud est, quod semper indicat: Hoc verò quod non semper indicat; ita senectus est necessarium signum antegressæ juventutis: Sed juventus est contingens futuræ senectutis. Græci peculiari nomine necessaria signa πτωματα, & contingentia εικος appellant.
units.tr: 7. Fourth, by reason of its connection with the signified, a sign is either necessary or contingent. The former is that which indicates always; the latter that which indicates not always. Thus old age is a necessary sign of the youth that went before; but youth is a contingent sign of the old age to come. The Greeks give the special names necessary signs [πτωματα] and contingent signs [εικος].

units.la: 8. Quintò, eâdem ratione signum est vel proprium, vel commune. Illud est, quod solum illud signatum indicat, ut tussis assectum pulmonum; Hoc verò, quod etiam aliis commune est, ut dolor lateris pleuritidem indicat. Signa propria Medicis dicuntur πραγματικά, eô quod directè tantum illum affectum designant; Et p'erumque ex συνοδομή plurium signorum communium constituuntur.
units.tr: 8. Fifth, by the same reasoning, a sign is either proper or common. The former is that which indicates only that signified, as a cough indicates an affection of the lungs; the latter is that which is common to others also, as pain in the side indicates pleurisy. Physicians call proper signs pragmatic [πραγματικά], because they designate directly only that one affection; and they are commonly constituted from the concurrence [συνοδομή] of several common signs.

units.la: 9.Sextò,ratione officii, signum est vel indicans, vel indicans & obsignans;Indicans, si rei præsentis sit, Græcis γνώρισμα dicitur; Et si proprium fuerit, nota; licet quandoque & commune signum nota dicatur, id tamen minus commodè fieri judicandum est. Conditiones enim notarum requirunt, ut sint propriæ notato, ipso notiores, ac ab ipso inseparabiles: Ita pura doctrina & rectus usus sacramentorum sunt notæ veræ Ecclesiæ. Præterea si indicans fuerit rei præteritæ, dicitur Græcis μνημόσυνον, sive commonefaciens. Obsignantia signa (Græcis σφεγγίδες dicta) sunt, quæ signatum non tantum indicant, sive præsens, sive præteritum, sed etiam veritatem alicujus roborant. Huc ergo pertinent Sacramenta, Sigilla, Pignora, Arrha &c.
units.tr: 9. Sixth, by reason of function, a sign is either indicating, or indicating and sealing. An indicating sign, if it is of a present thing, is called by the Greeks a mark [γνώρισμα]; and if it is proper, a note. Although sometimes a common sign is also called a note, this is to be judged less appropriate. For the conditions of notes require that they be proper to the thing noted, more known than it, and inseparable from it. Thus the pure teaching and the right use of the sacraments are the true notes of the Church. Moreover, if the indicating sign is of a past thing, it is called by the Greeks a memorial [μνημόσυνον], or something that reminds. Sealing signs (called by the Greeks seals [σφεγγίδες]) are those which not only indicate the signified, whether present or past, but also confirm the truth of something. To this class therefore belong sacraments, seals, pledges, earnests, and the like.

units.la: 1ā. Septimò, Signum est vel indicans tantum, quod & materiale dicitur; Vel indicans & repræsentans, quod formale appellatur. Hujus generis sunt imagines, statuæ, picturæ, comœdia, notiones primæ & secundæ, species intelligibiles &c.
units.tr: 10. Seventh, a sign is either one that only indicates, which is also called material; or one that indicates and represents, which is called formal. Of this kind are images, statues, pictures, comedies, first and second notions, intelligible species, and so on.

units.la: 11. Plures differentias signorum apud Metaphysicos habere poteris, ut quod sit vel actuale vel potentiale doctrinale, vel non doctrinale; Proprium vel improprium; Theoricum & Practicum; σημαντικὸν vel μιλαδελικόν: Sed vel spuriæ, vel inutiles sunt, vel ad superiores reduci possunt. Atque hæc de Signo & Signato.
units.tr: 11. You may find several further differences of signs among the metaphysicians: that a sign is either actual or potential; doctrinal or not doctrinal; proper or improper; theoretical and practical; significative or mnemonic [σημαντικὸν vel μιλαδελικόν]. But these are either spurious or useless, or they can be reduced to the higher divisions. So much for sign and signified.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: DE. Mensurâ & Mensurato.
units.tr: OF Measure and the Measured.

units.la: 1. REstat inter appositionis species Mensuratio, quâ unum alterius magnitudinem, numerum, perfectionem aut durationem mensurat: ubi mensurans dicitur mensura, prout alterum mensuratum.
units.tr: 1. There remains, among the species of apposition, measuring, by which one thing measures the magnitude, number, perfection or duration of another. Here the measuring thing is called the measure, and the other the measured.

units.la: 2. Vox quidem mensura primo adhibita videtur, ad denotandam solam dimensionis magnitudinis regulam: Sed postea, non secus ac alii termini, usurpari cæpit, pro omni æstimatione partium, vel quasi partium, prout hic capitur.
units.tr: 2. The word measure seems first to have been used only for the rule of measuring dimension in magnitude. Later, like other terms, it began to be used for every estimation of parts, or quasi-parts, as it is taken here.

units.la: 3. Est autem mensura, quâ in quovis extenso & limitato partes æstimantur. Non igitur hic est ipsa extensi cujuscunque limitatio, (quia hæc modus est, ut superiori tractatu dictum:) sed ipsius limitationis æstimatio; in quovis extenso, videlicet nontantum in magnitudine, sed & in omni eo, in quo aliquo modo partes adesse concipiuntur.
units.tr: 3. A measure is that by which the parts of anything extended and limited are estimated. It is therefore not the limitation of an extended thing itself (since this is a mode, as was said in the previous treatise), but the estimation of that limitation. This holds for any extended thing, not only in magnitude but in anything in which parts are conceived to be present in some way.

units.la: 4. Id autem, quo extensi partes æstimantur, primò debet esse certum; id est, notum, ac minimè dubium; quoniam enim omnis æstimatio cognitionem præsupponit, & quidem certam, quomodo ex regulâ quâdam partes æstimari poterunt, nisi illa certa sit? Et quo pacto certitudo partium desumetur ex eo, quod certum non esset? Prout igitur signum semper debet esse notum, ita & mensura. 2. Debet id esse constans; Quia notum ac certum esse debet; omne autem certò notum non potest se aliter habere. Et mensura est regula mensurati, omnis autem regula firma esse debet, adeòque & constans. Mensura debet esse prima; juxta tritum hoc; Primum in unoquoque genere est mensura reliquorum. Ratio est, quia mensura quâ talis est incommensurabilis: At nihil est incommensurabile, nisi sit in unoquoque genere mensuratorum primum; posteriora enim omnia à primo mensurantur. 4. Mensura debet esse æqualis mensurato: Ratio est, quia æstimatio partium non fit per inæquale judicium: At inæqualis mensura inæquale judicium proferet. 5. Mensura debet esse indivisibilis. Ratio est, quia debet esse prima. At primum quâ tale in priora est individuum; Et si mensura debeat esse æqualis mensurato, etiam erit indivisibilis; factâ enim divisione minor evaderet. 6. Mensura & mensuratum ejusdem debent esse generis. Ratio est, quia primum & secundum ejusdem sunt generis: At mensura est prima. Et deinde quæ æqualia dicuntur, ejusdem debent esse generis: At mensura mensurato dicitur æqualis.
units.tr: 4. Now that by which the parts of an extended thing are estimated must first be certain; that is, known and least open to doubt. For since every estimation presupposes knowledge, and indeed certain knowledge, how could parts be estimated by some rule unless that rule were certain? And how could the certainty of the parts be derived from something that was not certain? Just as a sign must always be known, so too a measure. 2. It must be constant, because it must be known and certain, and what is certainly known cannot be otherwise. A measure is the rule of the measured, and every rule must be firm, and so constant. A measure must be first, according to the common saying: The first in each genus is the measure of the rest. The reason is that a measure, as such, is incommensurable; but nothing is incommensurable unless it is the first of the measured things in its genus, for all later things are measured by the first. 4. A measure must be equal to the measured. The reason is that the estimation of parts is not made by an unequal judgement, but an unequal measure would yield an unequal judgement. 5. A measure must be indivisible. The reason is that it must be first. But the first, as such, is an individual prior to others; and if a measure must be equal to the measured, it will also be indivisible, for if it were divided it would become smaller. 6. Measure and measured must be of the same kind. The reason is that the first and the second are of the same kind, and the measure is first. Further, things said to be equal must be of the same kind, and the measure is said to be equal to the measured.

units.la: 5. Sed ut planiora fiant hæc axiomata, discutienda breviter, quæ scrupulum hic movere possent. Ad primum igitur & secundum dici potest, mensuram sæpe ab arbitrio humano dependere, eoque mutari indies, prout in Monetis, ponderibus &c. res aperta est. Resp. Certitudo & constantia illa mensuræ consistit in debitâ exæquatione utriusque, quæ immutabilis est, licet secundum appellationem pro arbitrio mutetur mensura: Ea enim si in minorem, mutetur, non erit prioris mensurati mensura, sed quarumdam ejus partium; prout si in majorem excrescat, plures ad mensuratum partes requirit. Ex. grat. Sedecem unciæ Argenti libram constituunt; Manente autem eâdem argenti quantitate, manet quoque consimiliter ipsi respondens pondus: At si duodecem unciæ libram posteà efficiant, non erit tunc talis libra istius argenti mensura, sed aliquarum ejus partium; Manet igitur pondus & mensura, sed mutatur appellatio.
units.tr: 5. But to make these axioms clearer, let us briefly discuss the objections that might raise a doubt here. To the first and second it can be said that a measure often depends on human choice and so changes from day to day, as is plain in coins, weights and so on. Reply. The certainty and constancy of a measure consist in the due equation of the two, which is unchangeable, even though the measure may be changed at will by name. For if it were changed into a smaller one, it would not be the measure of the former measured thing, but of some of its parts; and if it grew into a larger one, it would require more parts for the measured thing. For example. Sixteen ounces of silver make a pound. While the same quantity of silver remains, the corresponding weight also remains. But if twelve ounces afterwards make a pound, that pound will not be the measure of this silver, but of some of its parts. So the weight and the measure remain, but the name changes.

units.la: 6. Ad tertium dici potest; Mensuram plerumque ex aliâ oriri mensurâ, prout ulna ex suis partibus, libra ex unciis, uncia ex dragmis &c. constituitur; At nullum ortum ex alio primum esse potest. Resp. Mensura prima in suo genere dicitur prout est mensura; adeoque ulna prima est in genere ulnarum, libra in genere librarum, uncia in genere unciarum, prout sunt mensuræ longitudinis ac ponderositatis tantæ; non quòd ipsæ absolutè sint primæ, nec ex aliis compositæ; id enim non requiritur, nisi & mensuratum absolutè tale sit.
units.tr: 6. To the third it can be said that a measure is generally derived from another measure: the ell is made up of its parts, the pound of ounces, the ounce of drachms, and so on. But nothing derived from another can be first. Reply. A measure is called first in its genus insofar as it is a measure. Thus the ell is first in the genus of ells, the pound in the genus of pounds, and the ounce in the genus of ounces, insofar as they are measures of such length and weight. This is not because they are absolutely first, or not composed of others; for that is not required unless the measured thing is itself absolutely such.

units.la: 7. Ad quartum dici potest, quod supra cap. 9. tb. 23. objiciebatur, voluntatem divinam sic non posse esse mensuram bonitatis Entium ; quoniam illa longè imò infinities, reliquorum Entium bonitatem superat. Sed & ibi dictum, illam æqualitatem in univocâ mensurâ, ubi videlicet mensura, non tantum quâ mensura, sed & quà res in se, ejusdem est generis cum mensurato, non in proportionali, ubi mensura quidem quâ talis, non autem quâ res, ejusdem cum mensurato est generis, locum habere. In hac quippe non convenientia, sed vel exorbitantia, vel desectus mensurati cum mensurâ æstimatur; ubi in illâ consideratur requisita convenientia ; Ita igitur rectum sui & obliqui, virtus sui & vitii, perfectio sui & impersectionis mensura est, non univoca, sed proportionalis, excessum, vel defectum æstimans. Vrgeri quoque potest, in extensivis minimum, in intensivis maximum, reliquorum esse mensuram, utpote quæ in illis prima sunt; At minimum & maximum non sunt æqualia mensurato. Resp. 1. Intelligi debet illa æqualitas adesse in convenienti mensurâ, non in illâ quæ proportionalis est, qualis est illa minimi & maximi, utpote quæ ostendunt, quomodo mensurata ab illis recedant. 2. Et omninò dum æqualis dicitur esse mensura mensurato, ideo & minima & maxima esse debet ; Si enim major aut minor diceretur, inæqualis foret ; ita ex. gr. libra rerespectu argenti ejusdem ponderis & minima & maxima est; quoniam ut sit mensura argento æqualis, neque major, neque minor esse potest. 3. Et cum minimum & maximum dicuntur mensuræ, hoc intelligi debet de mensurâ primâ absolutè, ad quam reliquæ omnes reducuntur, & æstimantur.
units.tr: 7. To the fourth it can be said, as was objected above at chapter 9, thesis 23, that the divine will cannot thus be the measure of the goodness of beings, since it exceeds the goodness of other beings not merely, but infinitely. But there it was also said that this equality holds in a univocal measure, where the measure is of the same genus as the measured both as measure and as thing in itself, and not in a proportional measure, where the measure is of the same genus as the measured as measure but not as thing. For in the proportional case what is estimated is not agreement but either the excess or the defect of the measured relative to the measure; whereas in the univocal case the required agreement is considered. Thus the straight is the measure of the straight and the crooked, virtue of itself and vice, perfection of itself and imperfection: the measure is not univocal but proportional, estimating excess or defect. It can also be urged that in extensive things the minimum, and in intensive things the maximum, is the measure of the rest, as being first in those kinds; but the minimum and maximum are not equal to the measured. Reply. 1. That equality must be understood as present in a suitable measure, not in the proportional measure, such as the minimum and maximum, which show how the measured things depart from them. 2. And generally, when a measure is said to be equal to the measured, it must be both minimum and maximum; for if it were said to be greater or less, it would be unequal. Thus, for example, a pound with respect to silver of the same weight is both minimum and maximum, since to be a measure equal to the silver it can be neither greater nor less. 3. And when the minimum and maximum are called measures, this must be understood of the absolutely first measure, to which all others are reduced and by which they are estimated.

units.la: 8. Ad quintum urgeri potest, omnem penè mensuram dividi, prout magnitudo & tempus in indefinitum, ulna in partes suas, pes in digitos, libra in uncias. Resp. Mensura prout est mensura dividi nequit: at prout ipsius partes, quas quâ res, non quâ mensura, obtinet, aliâ mensurâ mensurari possunt, ita quoque divisibilis sit, videlicet quâ res, non quâ mensura, prout hoc modo nec major nec minor esse potest.
units.tr: 8. To the fifth it can be urged that almost every measure is divided: magnitude and time into the indefinite, the ell into its parts, the foot into digits, the pound into ounces. Reply. A measure, as a measure, cannot be divided. But insofar as its parts, which it has as a thing and not as a measure, can be measured by another measure, it is also divisible, namely as a thing and not as a measure. In this way it can be neither greater nor less.

units.la: 2. Intelligi potest axioma de mensurâ in quocunque genere absolutè primâ, quæ ut sic indivisibilis esse debet. 3. Sed potius omni mensuræ tribuendum videtur, quæ eô ipso, quod mensuret mensuratum, illas partes indivisibiliter habere debet, quas habet mensuratum. Atque eodem modo capi debet, quod essentiæ rerum ratione indivisibilitatis, sint instar numerorum; ab his enim, licet quâ numeris divisibilibus, nihil auferri, nihilque iis addi potest, nisi alii atque alii fiant. Ita igitur indivisibilis mensura decem hominum est numerus denarius, quoniam si cum dividere tentes, è vestigio mensura esse desinet.
units.tr: 2. The axiom about measure may be understood as applying to what is absolutely first in any genus, which as such must be indivisible. 3. But it seems rather to be attributed to every measure, which, by the very fact that it measures the measured, must have indivisibly those parts which the measured has. In the same way it should be understood that the essences of things, with respect to indivisibility, are like numbers. From these, insofar as they are divisible numbers, nothing can be taken away and nothing added, unless other and other numbers are made. Thus the indivisible measure of ten men is the number ten, since if you try to divide it, at once it ceases to be the measure.

units.la: 9. Ad sextum itidem afferri potest, quod d. l. objectum fuit, voluntatem divinam esse mensuram omnis bonitatis creatae, cum tamen toto ab ipsa genere differt; prout & ulna panni mensura, quia lignea, ferrea, aut ossea est, toto genere à panno distat. Sed ibi responsum, homogeneitatem esse Mathematicam & in genere mensurae, non Metaphysicam & in genere Entium. Nam longitudo longitudine, latitudo latitudine, corpulentia trinâ dimensione, multitudo multitudine, motus motu, duratio duratione, perfectio perfectione mensurari debet. Dices: at intellectus apprehendendo objectum, dicitur ejusdem mensura: At intellectus non est objecto homogeneus. Resp. Actus intelligendi tunc spectatur concretè, cum objecto sumptus; Prout intellectio hominis, id est vera ejus ac actualis clara ac distincta apprehensio, mensura dicitur esse hominis, & cum eodem in genere mensurae, ejusdem generis est.
units.tr: 9. To the sixth likewise it can be said, as was objected in the same place, that the divine will is the measure of all created goodness, though it differs from it wholly in genus, just as the ell is the measure of cloth though it is made of wood, iron or bone and so differs wholly in genus from the cloth. But there it was answered that homogeneity is mathematical and belongs to the genus of measure, not metaphysical and belonging to the genus of beings. For length must be measured by length, breadth by breadth, bulk by three dimensions, number by number, motion by motion, duration by duration, and perfection by perfection. You will say: the intellect, in apprehending an object, is said to be the measure of that object, yet the intellect is not homogeneous with the object. Reply. The act of understanding is viewed concretely when taken together with its object. Thus the understanding of a man, that is his true, actual, clear and distinct apprehension, is said to be the measure of the man, and being in the same genus of measure, it is of the same genus as he is.

units.la: 10. Differentiae varias admittit mensura; & quidem 1. est vel univoca vel proportionalis; Prior dicitur, cum mensura, & quâ talis, & quâ res, ejusdem generis ac quantitatis est cum mensurato. At Proportionalem dico, in quâ mensura quidem quâ talis,non autem quâ res & quanta, ejusdem generis est cum mensurato. In hac igitur est ratione rei perpetuâ inæqualitas; Adeoque talis est vel excedens, cum ipsa superat mensuratum quantitate, vel deficiens, cum superatur à mensurato; Prioris exemplum est voluntas Divina ratione bonitatis Entium Creatorum; Posterioris, linea recta ratione curvæ.
units.tr: 10. Measure admits various differences. First, it is either univocal or proportional. The former is called so when the measure, both as such and as a thing, is of the same kind and quantity as what is measured. A proportional measure, however, I call one in which the measure, as such, but not as a thing and as a quantity, is of the same kind as what is measured. In this case, then, there is always an inequality in the ratio of the thing. Accordingly, it is either exceeding, when it surpasses what is measured in quantity, or deficient, when it is surpassed by what is measured. An example of the former is the divine will in respect of the goodness of created beings; of the latter, a straight line in respect of a curve.

units.la: 11. Mensura 2. ratione efficientis, vel est naturalis, vel arbitraria. Illam voco, quæ à natura ad mensuratum ordinata est, ut Lex Naturæ est vitæ & operationum humanarum, honesti & turpis: Hanc verò, quæ ab arbitrio hominis æstimat mensurati partes, ita gradus dignitatis inter homines, pretiosicatis in metallis, gemmis &c. mensura est arbitraria.
units.tr: 11. Second, a measure, with respect to its efficient cause, is either natural or arbitrary. I call that natural which is ordained by nature to what is measured, as the law of nature is the measure of human life and actions, of the honourable and the base. But that is arbitrary which, by the choice of man, assigns the parts of what is measured; thus the degrees of dignity among men, or of preciousness among metals, gems and so on, are an arbitrary measure.

units.la: 12. 3. Mensura est vel prima, vel orta. Illa est, quæ in eodem genere à nullâ aliâ mensuratur, sed ipsa mensurat reliquas; ita unitas in multitudine & numero prima est: Hæc verò, quæ in eodem genere ab aliâ mensuratâ mensuratur, ut numerus denarius ab unitate, & leges civiles à lege naturæ.
units.tr: 12. Third, a measure is either first or derived. The first is that which, in the same kind, is measured by nothing else, but itself measures the rest; thus unity is the first in multitude and number. The derived is that which, in the same kind, is measured by another measured thing, as the number ten is measured by unity, and civil laws by the law of nature.

units.la: 13. 4. Mensura est vel mensurans, vel mensurata. Prior dicitur illa forma, quâ partium fit æstimatio: Hæc verò sunt ipsæ partes mensuratæ. Attamen ultima hæc imimpropriè dicitur mēnsura; Mensuratum enim mensuræ opponitur, adeoque non nisi abusivè mensura dici potest. Ejusdem farinæ & explicationis est, ejus distinctio in actívam & passivam; Activa enim mensurans, & passiva mensurata dicitur.
units.tr: 13. Fourth, a measure is either measuring or measured. The former is called that form by which the estimation of parts is made; the latter are the parts themselves, which are measured. Yet this last is improperly called a measure, since the measured is opposed to the measure, and so it can be called a measure only in an abusive sense. Of the same kind and explanation is its division into active and passive; for the measuring is called active, and the measured passive.

units.la: 14. 5. Mensura est vel universalis, quæ ubique & semper eadem obtinet, ut lex naturæ; vel Particularis, quæ vel non ubique, vel non semper obtinet, ut lex ceremonialis, Pretium auri, Gemmarum &c.
units.tr: 14. Fifth, a measure is either universal, which holds everywhere and always, as the law of nature; or particular, which holds either not everywhere or not always, as the ceremonial law, or the price of gold, of gems, and so on.

units.la: 15. 6. Mensura est vel intrinseca vel extrinseca. Illa dicitur, quæ est in mensurato; hæc verò, quæ extra illud est; Quæ si ratione essentiæ intelligatur, inconvenienter censenda est; omnis enim mensura est extra essentiam mensurati: Atsi capiatur de loco, veritati non obstabit, si exempla proferantur intrinsecæ mensuræ.
units.tr: 15. Sixth, a measure is either intrinsic or extrinsic. The former is called that which is in the thing measured; the latter, that which is outside it. If this is understood with respect to essence, it is to be judged improper, for every measure is outside the essence of what is measured; but if it is taken with respect to place, it will not hinder the truth, if examples of an intrinsic measure are brought forward.

units.la: 16. 7. Ratione mensurati, tanquam in species dividi potest mensura, quod sit vel magnitudinis, vel multitudinis, vel Perfectionis; vel Durationis, vel Actionis. Mensura magnitudinis, vel est longitudinis, ut ulna, stadium, milliare; vel latitudinis: ut jugerum; vel corporeitatis, ut hemina, tonna &c. Mensura multitudinis est numerus. Mensura perfectionis Gradus dicitur, qui vel in virtutibus medicamentorum, vel in celeritate ac tarditate motus, vel in Gravitate & levitate, quorsum omnia spectant pondera, vel in dignitate ac præstantia, sive hominum, quæ nobilitas dicitur, sive aliarum rerum, quæ appellatur pretiositas. Mensura durationis est tempus, ut Annus, mensis, hora, &c. Mensura actionis est regula actionibus humanis præscripta, ut jus, lex &c. Quas species omnes enumerare, brevitas nostra vetat. Sint hæc igitur de Mensura & Mensurato.
units.tr: 16. Seventh, with respect to what is measured, measure can be divided into kinds, namely, of magnitude, of multitude, of perfection, of duration, or of action. The measure of magnitude is either of length, as the ell, the stadium, the mile; or of breadth, as the acre; or of bulk, as the hemina, the tun, and so on. The measure of multitude is number. The measure of perfection is called degree, which is found either in the virtues of medicines, or in the speed and slowness of motion, or in weight and lightness, to which all weights belong, or in dignity and excellence, whether of men, which is called nobility, or of other things, which is called preciousness. The measure of duration is time, as the year, month, hour, and so on. The measure of action is the rule prescribed for human actions, as right, law, and so on. Our brevity forbids us to enumerate all these kinds. Let these things stand, then, concerning measure and what is measured.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: DE Antiquo, Novo; Præterito, Præsente & Futuro.
units.tr: Of the Ancient and the New; the Past, the Present and the Future.

units.la: I. REstat tandem inter Relationes primas Circumstantia, quæ est relatio inter præsentiam unius Entis & præsentiam alterius; Quare non accipi debet pro ipsa præsentia loci vel temporis; nec quoque pro omni nudè apposito, prout à Burgerfdicio usurpatur; multò minus pro omni termino externo.
units.tr: I. Finally, among the primary relations there remains circumstance, which is the relation between the presence of one being and the presence of another. It must therefore not be taken as the presence of place or time itself, nor as any bare juxtaposition, as Burgersdijk uses it, and much less as any external boundary.

units.la: 2. Quoniam autem relatio determinatæ saltem est præsentiæ, ideo quoque non nisi Enti finito convenit, non infinito, utpote cui illæ denominationes tutò tribui nequeunt. Hic tamen explicandæ ejus denominationes, quia etiam per similitudinem quandoque ei tribuuntur.
units.tr: 2. Since, however, the relation concerns determinate presence at least, it therefore belongs to a finite being and not to an infinite one, to which these denominations cannot safely be attributed. Here, however, its denominations must be explained, since they are sometimes attributed to God by way of likeness.

units.la: 3. Quia vero vel loci, vel temporis est præsentia, ideò quoque relatio illa præsen& shy;tiarum, vel à loco, vel à tempore desumitur; adeo ut hinc diversæ oriantur denominationes, sive relatæ Entis affectiones. Et qui& shy;dem primò à præsentiâ temporis dicitur Ens Antiquum, Novum, item Præteritum, Præsens & Futurum.
units.tr: 3. But since presence is either of place or of time, the relation of those presences is likewise derived either from place or from time, so that different denominations arise from this, that is, relative affections of a being. And first, from the presence of time, a being is called ancient, new, and likewise past, present and future.

units.la: 4. Antiquum dicitur, quod quasi ante ævum præsentiam habuit, adeoque idem est, quod vetus ac priscum; Quare fundamentum Antiquitatis est diutina distantia ratione anterioris, ab eo, quod nunc durat.
units.tr: 4. Ancient is said of what has had presence, as it were, before the age, and so it is the same as old and primeval. Hence the foundation of antiquity is a long distance in respect of the earlier, from that which now endures.

units.la: 5. Novum dicitur, quod nuper fuit, aut incepit; estque idem quod recens; Fundamentum autem novitatis est exigua distantia ratione anterioris, ab eo quod nunc præsens est.
units.tr: 5. New is said of what lately was or began, and it is the same as recent. The foundation of newness, however, is a slight distance in respect of the earlier, from that which is now present.

units.la: 6. Præteritum dicitur, quodcunque ratione anterioris distat, ab eo quod nunc præsentiam obtinet. Prout Præsens, quod simul est cum eo, quod nunc est. Et futurum, quodcunque ratione posterioris distat.
units.tr: 6. Past is said of whatever is distant in respect of the earlier from that which now holds presence. Present is said of what is at the same time as that which now is. And future is said of whatever is distant in respect of the later.

units.la: 7. Ex quibus patet, differentias harum affectionum ratione ordinis & successionis alicujus in præsentiâ Entium desu& shy;mi debere. Ubi igitur nulla successio est, ut in præsentiâ Dei, ibi proprie hæ affectio­nes locum non habent. Et consimiliter, quæ illam successionem diutinam admittunt, ratione istius successionis, omnia haec attributa admittere possunt.
units.tr: 7. From these things it is clear that the differences of these affections must be derived from the order and some succession in the presence of beings. Where, therefore, there is no succession, as in the presence of God, these affections properly have no place. And similarly, those things which admit that long succession can, by reason of that succession, admit all these attributes.

units.la: 8. Atque has non nisi respectivas esse affectiones, patet, quod eidem diverso respectu attribui possint; Ita Adamus primis quinque creationis diebus futurus erat: sexto & reliquis suae vitae fuit praesens, nunc autem praeteritus dicitur.
units.tr: 8. That these affections are only relative is clear, since the same thing can be attributed to it under different respects. Thus Adam was future during the first five days of creation; on the sixth and the rest of his life he was present, but now he is called past.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: D E Praesente, Absente, Proximo & Remoto.
units.tr: Of the Present, the Absent, the Near and the Remote.

units.la: 1. DEinde de Praesentia & ubi, seu loci, Ens dicitur Praesens & Absens, & si absit, Proximum & Remotum.
units.tr: 1. Next, concerning presence and place, or location: a being is said to be present or absent, and if absent, near or remote.

units.la: 2. Praesens dicitur hic, quod ibi habet suum ubi, ubi etiam alia id habent. Quod ubi vel latius vel angustius extendi posse videtur; quoniam illud, quod domi absens, fori tamen, ac civitatis respectu, imo regionis, ut & orbis terrarum universi, praesens dici poterit. Potissimum tamen praesens dicitur, quod eodem cum altero communi loco continetur.
units.tr: 2. Here something is called present which has its own "where" in that place, where others also have theirs. This "where" can seemingly be taken more broadly or more narrowly; for what is absent from the home may still be called present with respect to the court and the city, indeed the region, and likewise the whole world. Chiefly, however, something is called present when it is contained in the same common place as another.

units.la: 3. Absens dicitur, quod alibi habet suum ubi, quam hoc ad quod refertur; Atque hoc etiam praesertim in corporibus, distans appellatur, eò quod inter hoc & alterum illud aliquod corpus intercedat. Atque hinc patet, quid sit illud distans, in quod agens agere nequit, quod supra notatum.
units.tr: 3. Something is called absent when it has its own "where" elsewhere than that to which it is referred. And this, especially in bodies, is called distant, because some body intervenes between this one and that other. From this it is clear what that distant thing is, to which an agent cannot act, as was noted above.

units.la: 4. Absens verò non aequali semper abest distantiâ, sed vel longius distat, atque tum remotum dicitur; vel proprius accedit diciturque propinquum, vel & proximum; Nisi hoc dicatur, quod immediatè accedit.
units.tr: 4. But what is absent is not always absent at an equal distance: it may be farther off, and then it is called remote; or it may come closer, and then it is called near, or even next; unless we say that which comes immediately close.

units.la: 5. Atque hinc patet, has denominationes relativas esse, quoniam eidem Enti diverso respectu tribui possunt; ita v. gr. Papa hic absens, Romæ præsens est; Hinc remotus, propinquus Patavio &c. dicitur.
units.tr: 5. From this it is clear that these are relative designations, since they can be attributed to the same being in different respects. Thus, for example, the Pope, who is absent here, is present at Rome; and from here he is called remote, from Padua near, and so on.

units.la: 6. Deo quoque hæ denominationes tribui nequeunt, quoniam finitam localitatem præsupponunt; sed solis creaturis attribuuntur; nisi Deus præsens dici posse existimes, quoniam hic & ubique totus est. At illa est omnipræsentia, quâ ita dicitur præsens, ut nullibi dicatur absens; Cum tamen, quod hic præsens dicitur, etiam alibi absit. Et hæc de Circumstantiâ.
units.tr: 6. These designations cannot be attributed to God either, since they presuppose a finite locality; they belong only to creatures. Unless you think God can be called present, since he is whole here and everywhere. But that is omnipresence, by which he is called present in such a way that he is nowhere called absent; whereas what is called present here is also absent elsewhere. And these are the points on circumstance.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: DE Convenientiâ & Disconvenientiâ.
units.tr: On Agreement and Disagreement

units.la: 1. FUerunt hactenus Affectiones respectiva a primis relationibus oriundæ, quæ sesequuntur nunc, quæ ab ortis relationibus desumuntur; Et quidem primò, quæ prosluunt à convenientiâ & disconvenientiâ.
units.tr: 1. Hitherto we have dealt with the respective affections arising from the primary relations. Now we come to those that follow, which are derived from the relations that arise from them. And first, those that flow from agreement and disagreement.

units.la: 2. Convenientia, quibusdam & cognatio, licet minus recte dicta, est consensus plurium in aliquo tertio: Prout & disconvenientia, sive distinctio & diversitas late dicta, est plurium in tertio dissensus.
units.tr: 2. Agreement, which some call kinship, though the name is less correct, is the consent of several things in some third thing. Likewise disagreement, or distinction and diversity taken in the wider sense, is the dissent of several things in a third.

units.la: 3. Dicitur esse consensus plurium, quoniam est relatio, quæ non est ejusdem cum seipso convenientia: sed semper inter duo, si non materialiter, saltem formaliter inter se distincta, intercedere debet, ut supra probatum. Dicitur in aliquo tertio, quod vel realiter distinguitur ab utroque conveniente, vel non; sufficit quippe si formaliter tertium, hoc est fundamentum convenientiæ, & disconvenientiæ, ab utroque extremo distinguatur.
units.tr: 3. It is called the consent of several things because it is a relation, and a relation of agreement cannot hold of a thing with itself. It must always lie between two things that are distinct, if not materially then at least formally, as was shown above. It is said to be in some third thing, which either is really distinct from each of the things agreeing or is not. For it is enough if the third thing, that is, the ground of agreement and disagreement, is formally distinct from each extreme.

units.la: 4. Vulgò definitur, affectio Entis, quâ plura, vel quasi plura uniuntur; At si unio quædam esset, & res convenientes partes fierent tertii alicujus; Nam & sic disconvenientia separatio quædam, hoc est istius unionis destructio foret. Definitur quoque, extremorum identificatio: At improprie admodum sumi debet vox identificatio, ut quæ proprie significat constitutionem in eâdem essentiâ, quia identitas proprie est in essentiâ convenientia; quâ non consentiunt, quæ causis externis, effectis, subjectis, adjunctis ac objectis tantum conveniunt.
units.tr: 4. It is commonly defined as an affection of being by which several things, or things almost several, are united. But if there were some union, and the agreeing things became parts of some whole, then disagreement would be a kind of separation, that is, the destruction of that union. It is also defined as the identification of the extremes. But the word identification must be taken very loosely, since properly it signifies being constituted in the same essence, because identity properly lies in agreement of essence; things that agree only in external causes, effects, subjects, adjuncts and objects do not thereby agree in that way.

units.la: 5. Dividitur convenientia in simplicem & analogicam. Prior dicitur convenientia unius cum alio, in eodem tertio; adeo ut sit ipsorum Entium: Posterior vero, quae & analogia dicitur, est convenientia plurium cum pluribus in eâdem habitudine; ideoque est habitudinis consensus. Atque hoc pacto etiâ disconvenientia in simplicem & analogicam dividi potest, ut illa sit diffinsus unius ab altero in eodem tertio, quomodo Petrus dissentit à Paulo, in essentiâ numericâ. At hæc, diffensus plurium à pluribus in habitudine, prout numerus binarius & quaternarius ratione mutuæ habitudinis, dissentiunt, à ternario & quinario.
units.tr: 5. Agreement is divided into simple and analogical. The former is called the agreement of one thing with another in the same third thing, so that it belongs to the beings themselves. The latter, which is also called analogy, is the agreement of several things with several in the same relation, and so it is the consent of relations. In this way disagreement too can be divided into simple and analogical: the former is the dissent of one thing from another in the same third thing, as Peter differs from Paul in numerical essence; the latter is the dissent of several things from several in a relation, as the number two and the number four, by reason of their mutual relation, differ from three and five.

units.la: 6. Deinde dividitur convenientia, quod sit vel realis vel rationis; Cujus divisionis termini variis modis accipiuntur. Mihi realis est, quae est à parte rei, citra intellectus, sive rationis, operationem; ut ita rationis sit, cujus nullum in re est fundamentum, sed nudè ab intellectus operatione dependet. Ut si intellectus fingat convenientiam inter res, quae nulla est in ipsis; qualis est inter Ens verum & figmentum; vel inter duo entia ficta.
units.tr: 6. Next, agreement is divided into real and of reason. The terms of this division are taken in various ways. For my part, real agreement is that which is on the side of the thing, apart from the operation of the intellect or of reason; so that agreement of reason is that which has no foundation in the thing but depends merely on the operation of the intellect. For example, if the intellect feigns an agreement between things where there is none in them, such as the agreement between a true being and a fiction, or between two fictitious beings.

units.la: 7. Atque ita realis convenientia duplex est, vel strictè, vel latè dicta. Illa est inter rem & seipsam, diversimode consideratam; adeo ut diversam considerationem, aliquid in ipsa re sibi respondens habentem pro fundamento habeat. Estque proin identitas stricte dicta: quia eadem in eâ praecise est essentia. Talis igitur inter Ens ejusque principia & affectiones absolutas; inter Deum, ejusque attributa, inter Petrum puerum & seipsum senem; inter partes & totum. Haec autem (latè dicta) est inter res diversas, ob fundamentum commune ipsis in re conveniens; Estque varia.
units.tr: 7. Real agreement is therefore twofold, taken either strictly or broadly. The former is between a thing and itself considered in different ways, so that it has as its ground something in the thing itself that answers to the different consideration. This is therefore identity in the strict sense, since precisely the same essence is in it. Such is the agreement between a being and its principles and absolute affections, between God and his attributes, between Peter as a boy and Peter as an old man, and between parts and the whole. The latter, however, taken broadly, is between different things, on account of a common ground that agrees in them in reality; and it is of various kinds.

units.la: 8. Est quippe vel interna vel externa: Prior est convenientia duarum rerum in fundamento ad essentiam pertinente; unde & essentialis & identitas latè dicta dici potest. Posterior verò est convenientia duarum rerum in fundamento ad essentiam non pertinente.
units.tr: 8. It is either internal or external. The former is the agreement of two things in a ground that belongs to the essence; whence it may also be called essential identity in the wider sense. The latter is the agreement of two things in a ground that does not belong to the essence.

units.la: 9. Interna est vel Generica, vel specisica; Generica est convenientia duarum rerum sub eodem genere; sive proximo, ut homo & brutum, sive remoto, ut homo & planta conveniunt. Specifica autem est convenientia duarum rerum sub eâdem specie; qualis est inter Petrum & Paulum. Numerica identitas, quae his communiter additur est ipsa convenientia realis stricte dicta. Dubitabis forsan, annon & alia detur species convenientiae internae, quâ res duae materiâ vel formâ, tanquam partibus essentialibus conveniant. Resp. Datur quidem illa, estque essentialis, sed non distincta à prioribus ; Nam quæ materiâ conveniunt, eâ quoque genere consentiunt; Et in quibus eadem est forma specisica, illa conveniunt specie.
units.tr: 9. Internal agreement is either generic or specific. Generic agreement is the agreement of two things under the same genus, whether the nearer genus, as man and brute agree, or the more remote, as man and plant agree. Specific agreement is the agreement of two things under the same species, such as that between Peter and Paul. Numerical identity, which is commonly added to these, is itself real agreement in the strict sense. You may perhaps doubt whether there is not also another kind of internal agreement, by which two things agree in matter or form as essential parts. I answer: there is indeed such a kind, and it is essential, but it is not distinct from the former. For things that agree in matter also agree in genus, and things in which the specific form is the same agree in species.

units.la: 10. Externa convenientia vel primaria est, vel secundaria; Illa est, quâ res conveniunt aliquâ specie dependentiæ; in quâ independens dependentis essentiam non ingreditur: Hæc verò est convenientia rerum in respectu externo.
units.tr: 10. External agreement is either primary or secondary. The former is that by which things agree in some kind of dependence, in which the independent thing does not enter into the essence of the dependent. The latter is the agreement of things in an external respect.

units.la: 11. Primaria igitur vel est causalis; vel effectiva, vel subjectiva, vel Accidentalis. Causalis dicitur, quando res conveniunt causâ externâ, efficiente & fine: Prout Cain & Abel efficiente causa, vestis & domus fine conveniunt. Effectiva est, cum res conveniunt effectis, ut duo artifices ὁμότεχνοι. Subjectiva est, quâ accidentia conveniunt subjecto, ut virtutes & vitia, quia ambo sunt in animo. Accidentalis denique est, quâ res conveniunt accidentibus, quantitate videlicet & qualitate. Convenientia autem in quantitate, si fuerit continua, dicitur æqualitas; si discreta, paritas: At in qualitate dicitur similitudo.
units.tr: 11. Primary agreement is therefore either causal, effective, subjective, or accidental. It is called causal when things agree in an external cause, efficient or final: thus Cain and Abel agree in their efficient cause, and clothing and a house in their final cause. It is effective when things agree in their effects, as two craftsmen of the same trade (homotechnoi). It is subjective when accidents agree in a subject, as virtues and vices agree because both are in the mind. Lastly, it is accidental when things agree in accidents, namely quantity and quality. Agreement in quantity, if it is continuous, is called equality; if discrete, parity. Agreement in quality is called similarity.

units.la: 12. Secundaria convenientia est vel adjunctiva, quâ res conveniunt eodem adjuncto, ut qui eodem feruntur navigio, sub eodem latitant pallio, actecto dormiunt; vel objectiva, cum res conveniunt objecto ut duo medici ejusdem ægroti, duo præceptores ejusdem discipuli curam gerentes; Vel circumstantialis, cum res conveniunt circumstantia loci & temporis, ut populares, contubernales, condomestici, commensales, contemporanei. Quibus si velis addere convenientiam in signo & mensurâ, poteris; Ego susque deque habebo, sive ad objectivam reducas, sive ab ipsâ distinguas.
units.tr: 12. Secondary agreement is either adjunctive, when things agree in the same adjunct, as those who sail in the same ship, shelter under the same cloak, or sleep under the same roof; or objective, when things agree in the same object, as two physicians of the same patient, or two tutors caring for the same pupil; or circumstantial, when things agree in the circumstances of place and time, as fellow-citizens, housemates, members of the same household, table-companions, and contemporaries. If you wish to add agreement in sign and measure, you may; I am indifferent whether you reduce it to the objective or distinguish it from it.

units.la: 13. Disconvenientia sive distinctio, ut dividenda sit, non constat inter Metaphysicos; solidissimè ac sufficientissimè eam præstitit, Clariss. Heereboord, Volum. 2. Disp. 29. & 30. quem per omnia sequi, hic non erubesco, modo id per momos liceat. Est igitur disconvenientia vel realis vel rationis. Illa est, quâ distinguuntur ipsa objecta, sive conceptus objectivi: Hæc vero, quâ tantum distinguuntur conceptus formales ejusdem rei & objecti.
units.tr: 13. Disagreement, or distinction, and how it should be divided, is not settled among the metaphysicians. The most solid and sufficient treatment of it was given by the most distinguished Heereboord, Vol. 2, Disp. 29 and 30, whom I am not ashamed to follow in everything, provided that this is allowed by the critics. Disagreement is therefore either real or of reason. The former is that by which the objects themselves, or objective concepts, are distinguished; the latter is that by which only the formal concepts of the same thing and object are distinguished.

units.la: 14. Realis igitur distinctio est 1. inter rem & rem 2. inter modum & modum oppositum, videlicet essendi, aut fiendi, non autem concipiendi. 3. inter rem & modum ejus separabilem. 4. inter Ens & non-Ens, adeoque & inter habitum & privationem. 5. inter Entia realia & rationis. Signa hujus sunt 1. Essentiæ diversitas; realiter enim distinguuntur, quorum diversæ essentiæ.
units.tr: 14. Real distinction therefore holds: (1) between thing and thing; (2) between a mode and an opposite mode, namely of being or of becoming, but not of conceiving; (3) between a thing and its separable mode; (4) between being and non-being, and so also between a habit and its privation; (5) between real beings and beings of reason. The signs of this are: (1) diversity of essence, for things whose essences are diverse are really distinct; (2) separability, for things that are really distinct can be separated from one another without contradiction; (3) opposition, as will be made clear in the following chapter; (4) in substances, cause and effect; in accidents, diversity of subject. For their reasons and examples see the said Heereboord, loc. cit.

units.la: 2. Separabilitas; nam quæ realiter distinguuntur, ea citrà contradictionem à seinvicem separari possunt. 3. Oppositio, prout seq. cap. patebit. 4. In subsistentiis efficiens & effectum: in accidentibus diversitas subjecti. Quorum rationes & exempla, vide apud d. Heereboord, d l.
units.tr: 15. But disagreement of reason holds: (1) between diverse modes and inadequate forms by which the same object is conceived, as between God and his attributes, or between a being and its principles and affections; (2) between diverse modes of conceiving the same being; (3) and between the divine attributes. It is judged (1) from subordination, (2) from different definition, (3) from what is conceived about God and about being in general. For reasons and examples, see the same passage.

units.la: 15. At rationis disconvenientia est 1. inter diversos modos & formas inadæquatas objectum idem concipiendi, ut inter Deum ejusque attributa, inter Ens ejusque principia & affectiones. 2. Inter diversos modos concipiendi idem Ens. 3. Et inter attributa divina; & judicatur 1. ex subordinatione. 2. diversa definitione. 3. ex iis quæ de Deo, & ente in genere sunt concepta. Rationes & exempla, vid. d. l.
units.tr: 15. But a disagreement of reason is: (1) between different modes and inadequate forms conceiving the same object, as between God and His attributes, and between Being and its principles and affections. (2) Between different modes of conceiving the same Being. (3) And between the divine attributes; and it is judged (1) from subordination, (2) from different definition, (3) from the things that are conceived about God and about being in general. For the reasons and examples, see the same place.

units.la: 16. Ex quibus patet 1. hanc rationis disconvenientiam opponi convenientiæ reali strictè dictæ, adeò ut ubi hæc sit disconvenientia, ibi sit illa realis convenientia.
units.tr: 16. From these things it is clear, first, that this disagreement of reason is opposed to real agreement strictly so called, so that where there is this disagreement, there is that real agreement.

units.la: 2. Hinc liquet, disconvenientiam realem opponi 1. convenientiæ rationis. 2. convenientia reali late dictæ: quoniam enim in hac duæ sunt res, etiam illæ realiter distingui debent.
units.tr: 2. From this it is clear that real disagreement is opposed (1) to agreement of reason, and (2) to real agreement taken broadly, since in the latter there are two things, and these too must be really distinguished.

units.la: 17. Realis porro distinctio, est vel essentialis, vel non-essentialis. Essentialis est, quâ res distinguuntur essentiis; adeoque & interna dici potest, prout & diversitas; Estque triplex, Generica, specifica, vel Numerica. Generica est, quâ res distinguuntur gegenere, sive summo, ut quæ sunt in diversis prædicamentis absolutis; sive medio, ut quæ sunt sub diverso genere unius prædicamenti, ut homo & aurum. Specifica est, quâ species opponuntur sub eodem genere; unde & differentia dicitur, ut &, si duæ sint species, contrarietas; ut homo & brutum. Numerica est, quâ singularia distinguuntur sub eâdem specie, ut Petrus, & Paulus, fortitudo Alexandri & Scipionis.
units.tr: 17. Real distinction is either essential or non-essential. Essential distinction is that by which things are distinguished by their essences. It can therefore also be called internal, as can diversity. It is threefold: generic, specific, or numerical. Generic distinction is that by which things are distinguished by genus, either the highest genus, as things that belong to different absolute categories, or an intermediate genus, as things that fall under different genera of one category, such as man and gold. Specific distinction is that by which species are opposed under the same genus; hence it is also called difference, and, if there are two species, contrariety, as with man and beast. Numerical distinction is that by which individuals are distinguished under the same species, as Peter and Paul, or the courage of Alexander and of Scipio.

units.la: 18. Non-essentialis, est quâ objecta non distinguuntur essentiâ; Estque suppositalis, vel non-suppositalis. Prior est tantum in S. S. Mysterio Trinitatis, ubi eadem singularis est essentia, sed res distinctæ personæ, sive ὑποστάσεις & suppositæ. Nonsuppositalis est illa, quæ convenientiæ externæ opponitur, adeòque secundum ipsius differentias dividitur, quòd sit vel Primaria, vel secundaria; ut Primaria iterum sit, vel causalis, vel effectiva, vel subjectiva, vel accidentalis; Et accidentalis denuò, vel inæqualitas, vel imparitas, vel dissimilitudo. Et secundaria, vel adjunctiva, vel objectiva, vel circumstantialis; quarum omnium definitiones, ex iis, quæ de convenientiæ externæ speciebus dicta sunt, facilè colligi possunt.
units.tr: 18. Non-essential distinction is that by which objects are not distinguished by essence. It is either supposital or non-supposital. The former occurs only in the holy mystery of the Trinity, where the essence is one and singular, but the things are distinct persons, or hypostases [ὑποστάσεις] and supposita. The non-supposital is that which is opposed to external agreement, and so it is divided according to its own differences into primary or secondary. The primary is again either causal, effective, subjective, or accidental; and the accidental is again either inequality, disparity, or dissimilitude. The secondary is either adjunctive, objective, or circumstantial. The definitions of all these can easily be gathered from what has been said about the kinds of external agreement.

units.la: 19. Disconvenientia rationis triplex est vel virtualis, vel formalis, vel modalis. Virtualis tualis est, quâ ratio idem distinguit à se ipso, ob diversos effectus, qualis est inter intellectum & voluntatem; inter justitiam, misericordiam & decreta Dei. Formalis est, quâ distinguuntur conceptu formali, quæ identicè planè sunt idem; quomodo distinguuntur universalia à singularibus, homo à Petro. Modalis distinctio est 1. inter rem & modum ejus inseparabilem. 2. inter modos non oppositos sibi. At hæc vix distinguitur à formali; nisi formalis dicatur ratione conceptus, & modalis ratione modi, quo id, quod illi conceptui respondet, per modum modi interni, ac incompleti apprehenditur; Vix enim aliam diversitatem observo; Nam Ens ejusque affectiones modaliter inter se distinguuntur, & formaliter quoque, quoniam in sensu identico idem sunt, ut supra hinc inde ostensum. Et hæc de Convenientiâ & Disconvenientiâ nientiâ.
units.tr: 19. Disagreement of reason is threefold: it is either virtual, formal, or modal. Virtual disagreement is that by which a reason distinguishes itself from itself on account of its different effects, as between the intellect and the will, or between justice, mercy and the decrees of God. Formal distinction is that by which things are distinguished by formal concept, though they are altogether identically the same; this is how universals are distinguished from singulars, or man from Peter. Modal distinction is (1) between a thing and its inseparable mode, and (2) between modes not opposed to one another. But this is hardly distinguished from the formal, unless the formal is named from the point of view of the concept and the modal from the point of view of the manner in which what corresponds to that concept is apprehended, through the mode of an internal and incomplete mode. For I scarcely observe any other diversity. Being and its affections are distinguished from one another modally, and also formally, since in an identical sense they are the same, as has been shown above on both sides. And these things concerning agreement and disagreement.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII. DE Oppositione.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII. ON OPPOSITION.

units.la: 1. QUoniam autem illa, quæ realiter disconveniunt, nec de se invicem, nec de eodem tertio dici possunt, etiam illa dicuntur opposita; prout illa disconvenientia oppositio, adeo ut hujus differentiæ tiæ, non nisi certi sint modi istius disconvenientiæ; etiam hic aliquid de oppositione dicendum.
units.tr: 1. Since those things which are really disagreeing (realiter disconveniunt) can be predicated neither of each other nor of the same third thing, these also are called opposites; and, as that disagreement is opposition, so the differences of this are nothing other than certain modes of that disagreement. Therefore something must also be said here about opposition.

units.la: 2. Est igitur oppositio, disconvenientia, quâ nec unum de altero, nec utrumque de eodem tertio prædicari potest. Intellige autem 1. unum & alterum quâ tale, hoc est, prout eâdem plane ratione consideTantur, seu ut communiter dicunt, eodem modo, & tempore, secundum idem & ad idem. 2. Intellige prædicationem veram ac affirmatam. Ut igitur oppositio realem arguit diversitatem, ita talis prædicationis negatio oppositionis est index. Quare licet de Petro dicatur, quod sit homo, & non asinus, erunt tamen homo & asinus opposita, quia homo affirmatè, asinus negatè de Petro prædicatur; Prout quoque erunt opposita, licet dicam, Petrus est homo, & Petrus est asinus, quia dum homo vere & proprie de Petro affirmatur, asinus vel falsè vel improprie, id est, non eodem modo de ipso dicitur. Consimiliter opposita censeri debent calor & frigus, licet Petrus calidus dicatur & frigidus, quoniam non secundum idem, seu eandem partem ipsi calor & frigus insunt. Idem judicandum de patre & filio, aliisque relationibus oppositis, quæ quidem de eodem dicuntur, sed non ad idem, sive ejusdem respectu.
units.tr: 2. Opposition, then, is a disagreement by which neither one can be predicated of the other, nor both of the same third thing. Understand, however, (1) that the one and the other are taken as such, that is, insofar as they are considered in precisely the same respect, or, as they commonly say, in the same way and time, according to the same thing and with regard to the same thing. (2) Understand a true and affirmative predication. Thus, just as opposition implies real diversity, so the denial of such a predication is a sign of opposition. Hence, although it is said of Peter that he is a man and not an ass, man and ass will nevertheless be opposed, because man is predicated of Peter affirmatively and ass negatively. In the same way they will be opposed even if I say, "Peter is a man" and "Peter is an ass," because while man is truly and properly affirmed of Peter, ass is said of him either falsely or improperly, that is, not in the same way. Similarly, heat and cold ought to be judged opposed, although Peter is said to be warm and cold, since heat and cold do not inhere in him according to the same thing or the same part. The same judgment holds for father and son and other opposed relations, which are indeed said of the same subject, but not with respect to the same thing, or not in the same respect.

units.la: 3.
