Proprietates oppositorum sunt, ut 1. sint simul natura, videlicet in sensu composito, hoc est quatenus sunt opposita; Cujus ratio est, quod oppositio sit relatio, in qua relata, qua talia, semper natura simul sunt. 2. Ut sint simul cognitione; Quae enim simul sunt natura, ea quoque simul cognitione sunt. 3. Ut juxta se invicem posita, magis elucescant. Cujus ratio est, quod simul sint cognitione. 4. Ut tot modis unum dicatur, quot modis alterum. Quod itidem in sensu composito & in actu signato, capiendum. 5. Ut oppositas habeant definitiones: Quia alias extremo utrique sua definitio non foret conveniens.
units.tr: 3. The properties of opposites are these: (1) they are simultaneous in nature, namely in the composite sense, that is, insofar as they are opposites; the reason is that opposition is a relation, and related things, as such, are always simultaneous in nature. (2) They are simultaneous in knowledge; for things that are simultaneous in nature are also simultaneous in knowledge. (3) Placed side by side, they stand out more clearly, because they are simultaneous in knowledge. (4) One is said in as many ways as the other. This too is to be understood in the composite sense and in actual signification. (5) They have opposed definitions; otherwise the definition proper to each extreme would not fit.

units.la: 4. Sunt autem oppositorum quinque genera, Contradicentia, Privantia, Contraria, Relata, & Disparata; quorum quatuor priora directè opposita dicuntur, eo quod eorum unum uni tantum e diametro opponatur; at ultimum genus indirectum dicitur, quod in ipso unum pluribus pariter opponatur. Et rursum, directè opposita vel sunt duo Entia, vel unum Ens, & alterum non-ens; Et haec dicuntur contradicentia, si illud non-ens absolutè, tale sit; at privantia, si saltem sit comparatè non-ens. Prout & illa dicuntur contraria, si utrumque Ens absolutum sit; & Relata, si unum sit alterius.
units.tr: 4. There are five kinds of opposites: contradictories, privatives, contraries, relatives, and disparates. Of these, the first four are called directly opposed, because one of each is opposed to only one other, whereas the last kind is called indirect, because in it one is opposed equally to many. Again, directly opposed things are either two beings, or one being and another non-being. The former are called contradictories if that non-being is absolutely non-being; but privatives if it is at least non-being in comparison. Likewise they are called contraries if each extreme is an absolute being, and relatives if one is of the other.

units.la: 5. Sunt autem contradicentia, duo op-posita, poposita, quorum unum simpliciter est negatio alterius. Additur simpliciter, ut denotetur contradicentium differentia à reliquis oppositorum speciebus, in quibus unum quidem negat alterum, ut homo brutum in contrariis, pater filium in relatis &c. sed non simpliciter; quoniam illa negatione aliquid ponitur, cum in simplici nihil ponatur, sed tantum aliquid tollatur, ut non homo negat hominem, sed nihil ponit.
units.tr: 5. Contradictories are two opposites, one of which is simply the negation of the other. The word "simply" is added to mark the difference of contradictories from the other species of opposites, in which one indeed negates the other (as man negates brute among contraries, or father negates son among relatives, etc.), but not simply; for in that negation something is posited, whereas in the simple negation nothing is posited but only something is removed. Thus "not-man" negates man, but posits nothing.

units.la: 6. Atque hinc patet, 1. Contradictionem esse oppositionem prorsus immediatam; Quia nihil intercedere potest inter rem, ejusque simplicem negationem. 2. Posito uno contradicentium, tolli alterum. 3. Si eorum unum sit Ens, alterum esse non ens. 4. Ipsam contradictionum esse maximam oppositionem, quoniam omne respuit medium. 5. Esse primam; quia nullam aliam praesupponit, ipsam vero omnes reliquae oppositiones involvunt. 6. Esse reliquarum mensuram; quia videlicet prima est; Atque hinc reliquae species magis vel minus oppositae sunt, prout magis minusve ad contradictionem accedunt.
units.tr: 6. From this it is evident: (1) that contradiction is an absolutely immediate opposition, since nothing can come between a thing and its simple negation; (2) that, once one of the contradictories is posited, the other is removed; (3) that if one of them is a being, the other is a non-being; (4) that contradiction itself is the greatest opposition, since it rejects every middle; (5) that it is the first, since it presupposes no other, whereas all the other oppositions involve it; (6) that it is the measure of the rest, namely because it is first; and hence the other species are more or less opposed according as they approach contradiction more or less closely.

units.la: 7. Est autem contradictio expressa, vel implicita. Prior est cum infinita & simplex illa negatio uni extremo additur, ut homo non-homo. Posterior vero, cum unum extremum alterum sine negationis nota addita evertit, ut Deus, mortalis; Corpus unum, & in pluribus locis; unde dicitur, contradictio in adjecto, & oppositum in appposito.
units.tr: 7. Contradiction is either expressed or implicit. The former occurs when the infinite and simple negation is added to one extreme, as man and not-man. The latter occurs when one extreme overturns the other without the addition of a sign of negation, as God and mortal, or one body and in several places; whence it is said: a contradiction in the adjective, and an opposite in the apposition.

units.la: 8. Privative opposita, five privantia, sunt duo opposita, quorum unum est negatio persectionis alicujus debita; intercedit itaque inter habitum, qui est ipsa debita perfectio; & privationem, quae est debitae istius persectionis negatio. Privantia proinde 1.circa idem sunt subjectum, quia eidem persectio debita est, de qua negari potest. 2.Non omne respuunt medium: quoniam ad minimum admittunt medium negationis. 3. Habent unum extremum prater naturam. Quae autem hic latius dici possent, ex supradictis cap.8. f. 3. tract. 1. repeti possunt.
units.tr: 8. Privatively opposed things, or privatives, are two opposites of which one is the negation of some perfection due to a thing. Thus there lies between the habit, which is the due perfection itself, and the privation, which is the negation of that due perfection. Privatives, therefore: (1) are about the same subject, since the same subject is due the perfection, of which the negation can be made; (2) do not reject every middle, since at least they admit a middle of negation; (3) have one extreme contrary to nature. What could be said more broadly here may be repeated from what was said above, chapter 8, section 3, tract. 1.

units.la: 9. Contraria dicuntur, duo opposita absoluta, quae sub eodem genere maxime distant. Dicuntur duo, ne sint disparata; absoluta, ut distinguantur a relatis. Sub eodem genere, vel Logico, ut duae species ejusdem generis proximi; vel Physico, quod subjectum est; ut qualitates contrariae inter fe opponuntur.
units.tr: 9. Contraries are said to be two absolute opposites which are most distant within the same genus. They are said to be "two" so that they are not disparates; "absolute," so that they are distinguished from relatives; "within the same genus," either the logical genus, as two species of the same proximate genus, or the physical genus, which is the subject; thus contrary qualities are opposed to each other.

units.la: 10. Contraria, licet ut reliqua, exceptis contradicentibus, opposita, medium negationis admittant, tamen & nonnulla ipsorum etiam participationis habent, quale est tepor inter calorem & frigus: quod ex miscela extremorum oritur.
units.tr: 10. Contraries, although like the rest (except contradictories) opposed, admit a middle of negation; nevertheless some of them also have a middle of participation, such as lukewarmness between heat and cold, which arises from a mixture of the extremes.

units.la: II. Relata, sive relativè opposita, sunt duo opposita, quorum unum negat alterum ob mutuum respectum, seu relationem intercedentem; Suntque proinde Relatum & correlatum, de quibus, ut & de ipsa relatione, supra, tract. I. sect. 3. cap. 4. fuit actum.
units.tr: 11. Relatives, or relatively opposed things, are two opposites of which one negates the other on account of a mutual respect, or the intervening relation; and they are therefore relate and correlate, concerning which, as well as the relation itself, it was treated above, tract. 1, sect. 3, chap. 4.

units.la: 12. Disparata sunt, quorum unum pluribus pariter & eodem modo opponitur; Suntque proinde 1. Plura individua speciei unius. 2 Species plures duabus ejusdem generis. 3. Plura entia diversorum generum; Et hæc de Oppositione.
units.tr: 12. Disparates are those of which one is opposed equally and in the same way to several things: they are therefore (1) several individuals of one species; (2) several species of one genus of two; (3) several beings of diverse genera. And this is what I have to say on opposition.

units.la: CAP. XXXIV.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIV.

units.la: DE Ordine.
units.tr: Concerning Order.

units.la: I. ORdo denique sequitur, ultima Relationum ortarum, unde Entia inter se ordinata ratione successionis dicuntur. Sumitur autem ordo 1. Pro statuto. 2. Pro enim relatione. 3. Pro relatione à successione ut hic.
units.tr: I. Order follows last of the relations that arise, whereby beings are said to be ordered among themselves by the principle of succession. Order is taken (1) for what is established, (2) for relation in general, and (3) for relation arising from succession, as here.

units.la: 2. In hujus consideratione videndum, 1. Quid sit? 2. Quodnam ejus subjectum? 3. Quomodo se id habeat? 4. Ejus divisiones. 5. Ejus oppositum. 6. Quænam ejus proprietates?
units.tr: 2. In considering it, we must examine: (1) What is it? (2) What is its subject? (3) How does it stand? (4) Its divisions. (5) Its opposite. (6) What are its properties?

units.la: 3. I. Ordo, vulgò definitur, habitudo inter priora, posteriora & simultanea; quæ ex enumeratione relatorum constat, quâ sine definiri potest, quod sit, relatio, quâ plura ad se invicem ratione successionis referuntur. Illa autem plura ratione formalis, & non semper materialis conceptus, hoc est realiter, distingui debent. Ratio successionis ordinem à reliquis relationum speciebus satis distinguit.
units.tr: 3. I. Order is commonly defined as "the relation among prior, posterior and simultaneous things." It consists in an enumeration of related items, and without these it can be defined thus: it is a relation by which several things are referred to one another by the principle of succession. These several things must be distinguished by formal concept, and not always by material concept, that is, really. The principle of succession sufficiently distinguishes order from the other kinds of relation.

units.la: 4. II. Subjectum ordinis per se nullum est, quoniam relatio subjectum non requirit. Fundamentaliter autem sunt illa ipsa plura, quæ tali modo ad se invicem referuntur, non enim differt relatio realiter à suo fundamento: Fundamentum autem ordinis est successio: At hæc à succedentibus realiter non differt.
units.tr: 4. II. The subject of order is in itself nothing, since a relation does not require a subject. But its foundation is the very several things that are referred to one another in this way, for a relation does not really differ from its foundation. The foundation of order, however, is succession, and this does not really differ from the things that succeed.

units.la: 5. III. Quare 1. nec ordo istis pluribus aliud aliquod Ens superaddit; quia sic ordinis daretur ordo 2. Nec privationem; quia ordo præsentiam, privatio absentiam infert. 2. Nec ens rationis, quia nemine cogitante, etiam adest ordo; Sed 4. denominationem externam; quoniam à termino externæ relationis desumitur. Obj. At essentia prior est existentiâ: Sed existentia essentiam extrinsecè non denominat. Resp. Negatur consequentia: Sequitur enim tantum, quod existentia, non sit denominatio externa essentiæ, quod verum est: Quæstio autem hîc est, an essentia, denominata à prioritate, quâ existentiam antecedere concipitur, denominetur extrinsecè? quod affirmandum; quia prioritas illa non est de esse essentiæ.
units.tr: 5. III. Hence (1) order adds no further being to those several things, for then there would be an order of order; (2) nor does it add a privation, since order implies presence and privation implies absence; (3) nor a being of reason, since order is present even when no one is thinking of it; but (4) an external denomination, since it is derived from the term of an external relation. Objection: essence is prior to existence, but existence does not extrinsically denominate essence. Reply: the consequence is denied. It follows only that existence is not an external denomination of essence, which is true. The question here, however, is whether essence, denominated from the priority by which it is conceived to precede existence, is extrinsically denominated. This must be affirmed, since that priority does not belong to the being of the essence.

units.la: Objic. 2. In S. S. Trinitate Pater prior est Filio: Sed non per denominationem externam. Resp. 1. Illa prioritas nobis plane est incomprehensibilis. 2. Nec proprie dicta illa est prioritas; quia nulla hîc adest successio, quoniam Pater & Filius ab æterno sunt.
units.tr: Objection 2: In the Most Holy Trinity the Father is prior to the Son, but not by external denomination. Reply: (1) that priority is wholly incomprehensible to us; (2) nor is it properly called priority, since there is no succession here, because the Father and the Son are from eternity.

units.la: 6. IV. Quoad differentias, ordo vel est Coordinatio, vel Subordinatio. Prior est inter ea, quæ connexa & simultanea dicuntur: Posterior verò inter Priora & Posteriora, sive Antecedentia & Consequentia: Nisi velis hæc de ordine temporis saltem accipere. Horum autem singula multis modis dicuntur; At ex differentiis unius de reliquis judicium fieri potest: Dividenda autem Prioritas.
units.tr: 6. IV. As to its differences, order is either coordination or subordination. The former obtains among things said to be connected and simultaneous; the latter among prior and posterior things, that is, antecedents and consequents, unless you wish to take these only in the order of time. Each of these is called by many names, but a judgment about the rest can be made from the differences of one. Priority must be divided.

units.la: 7. Est igitur prioritas vel Rei, vel Cognitionis. Illa est, quâ conceptus objectivus est ante alium: Hæc verò, quâ unum ante alterum cognoscitur.
units.tr: 7. Priority is therefore either of thing or of knowledge. The former is that by which one objective concept is before another; the latter is that by which one thing is known before another.

units.la: 8. Prioritas cognitionis est vel naturalis, vel arbitraria. Naturalis in subordinatiû locum habens, est vel distincta, vel confusa. Prior sequitur ordinem intellectus & naturæ generantis: At posterior inverso ordine procedens, ad ordinem sensuum ac naturæ intendentis instituitur. Arbitraria prioritas in coordinatis, & unius generis speciebus obtinet.
units.tr: 8. Priority of knowledge is either natural or arbitrary. Natural priority, which holds in subordinate things, is either distinct or confused. The former follows the order of the intellect and of generating nature; the latter, proceeding in the inverse order, is established by the order of the senses and of nature in its tendency. Arbitrary priority holds among coordinates and among species of one genus.

units.la: 9. Prioritas rei est vel essentia, vel existentia. Prioritas essentia, latè videlicet dictæ, est vel Metaphysica, vel Physica.
units.tr: 9. Priority of thing is either of essence or of existence. Priority of essence, taken broadly, is either metaphysical or physical.

units.la: 10. Prioritas Metaphysica est inter ea, quorum conceptus objectivi realiter non differunt: Quemadmodum Physica, inter ea, quæ realiter distinguuntur.
units.tr: 10. Metaphysical priority obtains among things whose objective concepts do not really differ, just as physical priority obtains among things that really are distinct.

units.la: 11. Metaphysica prioritas duplex est, vel secundum existendi consecutionem, vel secundum conceptuum originationem; Prior est, cum conceptus formales ita se habent, ut posito uno non necessariò ponatur alter, qualis est inter generalia & specialia, v.gr. inter Animal & hominem. Posterior est, cum conceptus formales ex se oriuntur, aut oriri, sibique ita succedere concipiuntur; Qualis est inter Ens ejusque principia, & affectiones; inter essentiam Dei, ejusque attributa.
units.tr: 11. Metaphysical priority is twofold: either according to the succession of existence, or according to the origination of concepts. It is prior when the formal concepts are so related that, once one is posited, the other is not necessarily posited; such is the case between genera and species, for example between animal and man. It is posterior when formal concepts arise from one another, or are conceived as succeeding one another; such is the case between being and its principles and affections, and between the essence of God and his attributes.

units.la: 12. Prioritas Physica, sive naturæ strictè dictæ, est vel generantis naturæ, vel intendentis. Priori ordine, simplicia compositis, causæ effectis, elementa mistis &c. priora sunt: At posteriori omnia secus habent, juxta supra adductum Axioma: Quod prius in intentione, id posterius in executione sive generatione.
units.tr: 12. Physical priority, or priority of nature strictly so called, is either of generating nature or of nature in its tendency. In the first order, simples are prior to composites, causes to effects, elements to mixed bodies, and so on; but in the second, everything is the other way round, according to the axiom cited above: what is prior in intention is posterior in execution or generation.

units.la: 13. Prioritas existentiæ vel loci, vel temporis est; Atque illa vel Physici loci est, diciturque dispositionis; vel Politici, quorsum spectat prioritas dignitatis & honoris. Temporis autem est, quâ unum ante aliud duravit, aut durare incepit.
units.tr: 13. Priority of existence is either of place or of time. The former is either of physical place, and is called priority of arrangement, or of political place, to which belongs priority of dignity and honour. Priority of time is that by which one thing has lasted, or has begun to last, before another.

units.la: 14. V. Ordini opponitur Confusio, quæ est ordinis perturbatio; Perturbatur autem ordo, quando vel posteriora non sequuntur, vel priora non præcedunt, vel simultanea præcedunt aut sequuntur. Quibus generalibus modis omnis confusio fieri debet.
units.tr: 14. V. Opposed to order is confusion, which is a disturbance of order. Order is disturbed when posterior things do not follow, or prior things do not precede, or simultaneous things precede or follow. All confusion must arise in these general ways.

units.la: 15. VI. Inter Proprietates, hæ potissimum observandæ 1. Quæ dependent ab una principio, illa sunt ordinata. 2. Quæ repugnant uni primo, illa sunt confusa. Ratio est, quia in omni ordine est aliquid primum. 3. Ordo dignior est confusione. 4. Quo quid magis accedit ad ordinem, eò dignius est. 5. Ordo est constantior confusione. &c.
units.tr: 15. VI. Among the properties, these are chiefly to be observed: (1) Those things which depend on one principle are ordered. (2) Those things which conflict with one first are confused; the reason being that in every order there is something first. (3) Order is more worthy than confusion. (4) The more a thing approaches order, the more worthy it is. (5) Order is more constant than confusion, etc.

units.la: 16. Atque ita, absoluta ordinis doctrinâ, de omnibus, quas propositueram, Entis affectionibus, pro modo institutionum, satis me dixisse arbitror; In quibus si quid desiderari, aut ipse observem, aut ab aliis Philosophiæ cultoribus, monear, id in Exercitationibus Metaphysicis, quas Deo volente, brevi exhibebo, supplebo.
units.tr: 16. Thus, with the doctrine of order complete, I think I have said enough, according to the manner of these Institutes, about all the affections of being that I proposed. If anything is found lacking in them, either I myself shall observe it or other lovers of philosophy shall warn me, and I shall supply it in the Metaphysical Exercises, which, God willing, I shall soon publish.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM METAPHYSICARUM, Tractatus Tertius, QVI EST DE Fructu consequente.
units.tr: OF THE METAPHYSICAL INSTITUTES, Third Treatise, Which Concerns the Consequent Fruit

units.la: 1. CUm omnis ars omnisque disciplina, ad defectus naturæ humanæ auferendos instituta sit, ea sanè, quæ universalis erit disciplina, omnibus defectibus suo modo prospicere tenetur. Quare Metaphysica, quæ generalis fundamenti officio perfungitur, prout generalis est scientia, ubique suam utilitatem edere debet. Metaphysici igitur est, illam usus universalitatem primò ostendere, ac deinde quomodo, ex eâ petenda sit, docere.
units.tr: 1. Since every art and every discipline is established to remove the defects of human nature, the discipline that is universal must surely make provision for all defects in its own way. Therefore Metaphysics, which discharges the office of a general foundation insofar as it is a general science, must display its usefulness everywhere. It is the task of the metaphysician, then, first to show this universal usefulness, and then to teach how it is to be drawn from it.

units.la: 2. Utilitas autem Metaphysicæ se extendit 1. ad Ϡεωρίαν & cognitionem τῶ ὄντων quâ ab intellectu ignorantia cum connexis ipsi vitiis auffertur. 2. Ad πρᾶξιν & operationem τῶν δεόντων, quâ voluntas, altera mentis potentia, quantum pote, perficitur.
units.tr: 2. The usefulness of Metaphysics extends (1) to theory and knowledge of beings [θεωρίαν; τῶν ὄντων], by which ignorance, together with the vices connected with it, is removed from the intellect; (2) to practice and the doing of what ought to be done [πρᾶξιν; τῶν δεόντων], by which the will, the other power of the mind, is perfected as far as possible.

units.la: 1 Ϡεωρίαν: Greek, "theoria"; τῶ ὄντων: Greek, "tōn ontōn" as printed.
units.tr: 1 Theory [θεωρίαν]: Greek, "theoria"; of beings [τῶν ὄντων]: Greek, "tōn ontōn" as printed.

units.la: 3. Cognitioni Entium duobus modis Metaphysica prodest. 1. Quàtenus ipsius notitiam ipsa aliquo modo tradit. 2. Quâtenus confert modo cognoscendi omnia, eumque promovet, ordinat ac fundat.
units.tr: 3. Metaphysics benefits knowledge of beings in two ways: (1) insofar as it hands down the knowledge of them in some way itself; (2) insofar as it contributes a method of knowing all things, and promotes, orders and grounds that method.

units.la: 4. Tradit autem omnium rerum notitiam, 1. dum ostendit universale uniuscujusque entis esse. 2. Dum generalia, quæ & prima dicuntur, ejus exhibet principia. 3. Dum universales promit affectiones. 4. Dum communes & maximè generales rerum pandit differentias.
units.tr: 4. Metaphysics hands down knowledge of all things, (1) while it shows the universal being of each entity; (2) while it sets forth the principles of the general things, which are also called first; (3) while it brings forth the universal affections; (4) while it lays open the common and most general differences of things.

units.la: 5. Ostendit autem 1. cujuscunque Entis esse, quia explicat in actu signato, quid sit illud esse, quod in exercitio omnibus & singulis convenit; Prout igitur, qui cognoscit, quid sit animal, etiam in genere, & quasi potentiâ, cognoscit, quid sit homo & brutum, quoniam hæc sub esse animalis continentur; ita consimiliter, qui novit, quid sit Ens, is quoque omnium, quæ sub ente continentur, generalem & quasi remotam habet notitiam.
units.tr: 5. It shows the being of any entity, because it explains in formal act what that being is, which belongs in actuality to all and each. Just as one who knows what an animal is, even in the genus, knows also, as it were potentially, what a human and a brute are, since these are contained under the being of animal, so likewise one who knows what Being is also has a general and, as it were, remote knowledge of all the things that are contained under being.

units.la: 6. Idque non tantum in entibus ipsis, sed & eorum affectionibus præstat, dum pro diversâ naturâ affectionum generalium, etiam speciales inter se distant, adeò ut speciales cum generalibus ejusdem sint naturæ, quare & illæ ex his æstimandæ erunt. Ita v. gr. cum principem esse respectiva sit hominis affectio, ea quoque summam aliquam relationem, quæ est appositio & relatio externa, præsupponit, quæ non nisi externam enti addit denominationem, facilè colligitur, quod principem esse non nisi externa sit denominatio, ad essentiam hominis non pertinens.
units.tr: 6. And it does this not only in beings themselves but also in their affections, insofar as, according to the differing nature of the general affections, the special ones too differ from one another, so that the special ones are of the same nature as the general ones, and therefore must be judged by them. Thus, for example, since being a prince is a relative affection of a man, it also presupposes some relation, which is an apposition and external relation, and which adds to the entity only an external denomination. From this it is easily gathered that being a prince is nothing but an external denomination, not pertaining to the essence of man.

units.la: 7. Ostendit II. cujusque entis principia, ex quibus ejus esse aliquatenus cognoscitur; cum principia ista sint ipsum esse, ac ostendant, quodcunque esse sibi proprium, ac ab aliis distinctum habere, in quo à se ipso est negativè constitutum, si ens sit infinitæ perfectionis: at ab alio quo externo, intercedente actione positivâ, prout omnes creaturæ, quæ finitâ tantum persectione gaudent: Et quoniam tale cujusvis entis est esse, qualia sunt ejusdem principia, & hæc pro modo constitutionis varia sunt, diversum quoque ipsum esse manifestum est.
units.tr: 7. It shows (II) the principles of each entity, from which its being is known in some measure; since these principles are the being itself, they show that whatever being is proper to a thing and distinct from others has, in that it is negatively constituted by itself, if the entity is of infinite perfection; but by something else, external to it, with a positive action intervening, as with all creatures, which enjoy only finite perfection. And since the being of any entity is such as its principles are, and these vary according to the mode of constitution, it is clear that the being itself is also diverse.

units.la: 8. Indicat præterea III. quænam sint affectiones generales, quæ debitè singulis entibus accommodatæ, ipsis propriæ evadunt. Unde investiganda eorum essentia, ex congruâ videlicet constitutione; unde profluat eorum unitas, & in quo ipsa consistat; quid sit ipsorum veritas, necessitas, quisque ipsius status ac gradus; Quæ & qualis ipsorum perfectio; quomodo existant, præsentia dicantur, ac quem usum conferant. Ad hæc omnes patefacit generales habitudines, & exinde ortas affectiones respectivas v, gr. quibus modis unum ab altero dependeat: quæ ad se invicem extrinsecus referantur. Adeo ut nihil in cujusvis entis notitia restet, quin hoc ex generalibus Metaphysicæ affectionibus suo modo profluat.
units.tr: 8. It indicates moreover (III) what are the general affections, which, suitably fitted to each entity, become proper to them. Hence their essence is to be investigated, namely from a congruent constitution; whence their unity flows and in what it consists; what their truth, necessity, and each one's status and degree are; what and of what kind their perfection is; how they exist, are said to be present, and what use they bring. Besides these, it lays open all the general relations and the respective affections arising from them, e.g. by what modes one depends on another, and which are referred to one another extrinsically. So that nothing remains in the knowledge of any entity which does not flow from the general affections of Metaphysics in its own way.

units.la: 9. IV. Exhibet quoque generales Entium differentias, quibus vel ratione essentiæ, vel perfectionum ac affectionum, à se mutuo discrepent. Fructus præ reliquis insignis, quem hic exemplo Dei & reliquorum entium, utpote per omnia ab ipso discrepantium, breviter applicabo.
units.tr: 9. (IV) It also sets forth the general differences of beings, by which they differ from one another either in essence or in perfections and affections. This is a fruit remarkable beyond the rest, which I shall briefly apply here by the example of God and the other beings, as differing from him in all respects.

units.la: 10. Primò igitur ratione constitutionis; Ens est vel negativè constitutum, ut Deus; vel positivè, à causâ efficiente positivâ ac reali productione productum, ut omnia reliqua præter Deum, vid. tract. 2. cap. 1. th. 2. & 4.
units.tr: 10. First, then, in respect of constitution: a being is either negatively constituted, as God; or positively, produced by an efficient cause and real production, as all the rest besides God; see Tract. 2, ch. 1, th. 2 and 4.

units.la: 11. Secundò ratione essentiæ; Ens habet essentiam actualem, quæ absque omni potentiâ est, ut Deus; vel potentialem, quæ potentiam ad non esse habet, ut creatura, vid. cap. 1. th. 19.
units.tr: 11. Second, in respect of essence: a being has an actual essence, which is without any potentiality, as God; or a potential essence, which has a potentiality for non-being, as a creature; see ch. 1, th. 19.

units.la: 12. Tertiò ab unitate; Ens est vel actu divisum à quovis alio, ut creatura; vel non semper actu divisum, sed tantum necessario indivisum in se, ut Deus, vid. cap. 2. th. 4.
units.tr: 12. Third, from unity: a being is either actually divided from every other, as a creature; or not always actually divided, but only necessarily undivided in itself, as God; see ch. 2, th. 4.

units.la: 13. Quartò, à modo unitatis; Ens vel adadmittit conceptum sui universalem, vel non admittit; Admittunt omnes creaturæ, nullâtenus Deus, vid. cap. 3. th. 21.
units.tr: 13. Fourth, from the mode of unity: a being either admits a universal concept of itself, or does not admit it. All creatures admit it; God in no way does; see ch. 3, th. 21.

units.la: 14. Quinto à simplicitate; Ens est vel absolutè simplex, sine aliquo ad compositionem ordine, ut Deus; vel est tantum comparatè simplex, ut multæ creaturarum, vid. cap. 4. th. 3. & 7. Item, vel est simplex omni carens multitudine, ut Deus, vel aliquam multitudinem involvens, ut creaturæ, vid. d. c. th. 6.
units.tr: 14. Fifth, from simplicity: a being is either absolutely simple, without any order to composition, as God; or is only comparatively simple, as many creatures are; see ch. 4, th. 3 and 7. Likewise, it is either simple, lacking all multitude, as God, or involving some multitude, as creatures; see d. c. th. 6.

units.la: 15. Sexto, à veritate; Ens verum æstimatur vel in ordine ad proprium tantum intellectum, ut Deus, quatenus conformis est conceptui, quem ipse habet de perfectissimo Ente; vel in ordine ad alium intellectum, ut creaturæ ad intellectum divinum, vid. cap. 5. th. 11.
units.tr: 15. Sixth, from truth: a true being is judged either in relation to its own intellect alone, as God, insofar as it conforms to the concept which he himself has of the most perfect Being; or in relation to another intellect, as creatures are to the divine intellect; see ch. 5, th. 11.

units.la: 16. Septimò à necessitate, sive gradu veritatis; Ens est vel absolutè necessarium, cujus non-esse implicat contradictionem, ut Deus; vel relatè tantum, cujus non-esse citra contradictionem dari potest, ut creaturæ, vid. cap. 6. th. 8. & 17.
units.tr: 16. Seventh, from necessity, or degree of truth: a being is either absolutely necessary, whose non-existence implies a contradiction, as God; or only relatively so, whose non-existence can be without contradiction, as creatures; see ch. 6, th. 8 and 17.

units.la: 17. Octavo, à statu veritatis; Ens est absolutè immutabile, nullum agnoscens desectum, ut Deus; vel mutabile, sive comparatè immutabile, defectum ex se agnoscens, ut creaturæ, vid. cap. 7. th. 3. 4. & 8.
units.tr: 17. Eighth, from the state of truth: a being is absolutely immutable, acknowledging no defect, as God; or mutable, or comparatively immutable, acknowledging defect from itself, as creatures; see ch. 7, th. 3, 4 and 8.

units.la: 18. Nono, à perspicuitate; Ens vel plane intellectui humano propter excessum imimproportionatum, ut Deus ; vel ipsi proportionatum, ut reliqua præter eum entia, vid. cap. 8. th. 8.
units.tr: 18. Ninth, from clarity: a being is either wholly beyond the human intellect because of its disproportionate excess, as God; or proportionate to it, as the other beings besides him; see ch. 8, th. 8.

units.la: 19. Decimò, à perfectione ; ens vel caret omni imperfectione, omnemque habet persectionem, ut Deus ; vel aliquam habet imperfectionem, & non omnem perfectionem, ut creatura, vid. cap. 9. th. 18.
units.tr: 19. Tenth, from perfection: a being either lacks all imperfection and has all perfection, as God; or has some imperfection and does not have all perfection, as a creature; see ch. 9, th. 18.

units.la: 20. Vndecimo, à mensurâ perfectionis, sive bonitate ; Ens est, vel bonum bonitate mensurante, ut Deus ; vel mensurata, ut creatura, vid. d. c. th. 21. 22. 23.
units.tr: 20. Eleventh, from the measure of perfection, or goodness: a being is either good with a measuring goodness, as God; or measured, as a creature; see d. c. th. 21, 22, 23.

units.la: 21. Duodecimò à modo perfectionis ; Ens est, vel infinitum, in quo infinitæ sunt & illimitatæ, mensuræque adæquatæ persectiones, ut Deus ; vel finitum & limitatum, à mensura deficientes habens persectiones, ut creatura, vid. cap. 9. th. 28. & cap. 10. th. 4. & passim per totum caput.
units.tr: 21. Twelfth, from the mode of perfection: a being is either infinite, in which the perfections are infinite, unlimited, and of adequate measure, as God; or finite and limited, having perfections that fall short of the measure, as a creature; see ch. 9, th. 28, and ch. 10, th. 4, and throughout the whole chapter.

units.la: 22. Decimò tertio, à conditione ; Ens est vel absolutum, & à conditione quacunque liberum, ut Deus ; vel conditionatum, conditionem suæ præsentiæ ac perfectionis requirens ; ut creatura, vid. cap. 11. th. 3. 4.
units.tr: 22. Thirteenth, from condition: a being is either absolute, and free from any condition, as God; or conditioned, requiring a condition for its presence and perfection, as a creature; see ch. 11, th. 3, 4.

units.la: 23. Decimò quarto, à distinctione ; Ens est vel necessario positive distinctum ab aliis, ut creatura ; vel negative, & non necessario positive, ut Deus, vid. cap. 12. th. 4.
units.tr: 23. Fourteenth, from distinction: a being is either necessarily positively distinct from others, as a creature; or negatively, and not necessarily positively, as God; see ch. 12, th. 4.

units.la: 24. Decimo quinto, ab existentia ; Ens consiliderari potest, ut non existens, ut creatura ; vel non potest cogitari, ut non-existens, ut Deus, vid.cap.12.th.11. & 14. Item, Ens vel habet existentiam permanentem, ut Deus; vel successivam, ut creatura, d. c.th.25. & 29.
units.tr: 24. Fifteenth, from existence: a being can be considered as not existing, as a creature; or it cannot be thought of as not existing, as God; see ch. 12, th. 11 and 14. Likewise, a being has existence either permanent, as God; or successive, as a creature; see ibid., th. 25 and 29.

units.la: 25. Decimo sexto, ab ubietate; Ens ubietatem habet vel infinitam, quâ ubicunque est, totum, est & totu extra, & totum in quocunque assignabili, ut Deus; vel finitam, quâ non est totum extra, nec totum in quocunque assignabili, ut creatura, vid. cap.13. th.7. 8.
units.tr: 25. Sixteenth, from ubiety: a being has ubiety either infinite, by which it is wholly wherever it is, wholly outside everything and wholly in any assignable place, as God; or finite, by which it is not wholly outside, nor wholly in any assignable place, as a creature; see ch. 13, th. 7, 8.

units.la: 26. Decimo septimo, à duratione; Ens habet durationem infinitam, permanentem, ac æternam, ut Deus; vel finitam, successivam, & non æternam, ut creatura, vid. cap.14. th.4.5.
units.tr: 26. Seventeenth, from duration: a being has duration either infinite, permanent and eternal, as God; or finite, successive and not eternal, as a creature; see ch. 14, th. 4, 5.

units.la: 27. Decimo octavo, ab actu; Ens habet actum absolutum ac purissimum, cui nulla potentia respondet, ut Deus; vel respectivum ac impurum, quo potentia aliqua perficitur, ut creatura, vid. cap.15. th.7.
units.tr: 27. Eighteenth, from act: a being has an act that is absolute and most pure, to which no potency corresponds, as God; or one that is relative and impure, by which some potency is perfected, as a creature; see ch. 15, th. 7.

units.la: 28. Decimo nono, ab utilitate; Ens est vel summum & absolutè bonum, omnibus reliquis usum præbens, ut Deus; vel est medium, & comparatè tale, ut Creatura, vid. cap.16. th.12. & 13.
units.tr: 28. Nineteenth, from usefulness: a being is either the highest and absolutely good, providing use for all the rest, as God; or it is a means and good only comparatively, as a creature; see ch. 16, th. 12 and 13.

units.la: 29. Vigesimo, à dependentiâ; Ens est vel absolutè independens, & omnis dependentis causa, ut Deus; vel dependens, aut non nisi comparatè independens, ut creatura, vid. cap.17. th.8. 11.
units.tr: 29. Twentieth, from dependence: a being is either absolutely independent, and the cause of all that depends, as God; or dependent, or independent only comparatively, as a creature; see ch. 17, th. 8, 11.

units.la: 30. Vigesimo primo, à causa; Ens vel est tantum causa, & nunquam causatum, ut, Deus, vel est quoque causatum, licet alicujus respectu causa dicatur, ut creatura, vid. cap. 19. th. 12.
units.tr: 30. Twenty-first, from cause: a being is either only a cause, and never caused, as God; or it is also caused, although it may be called a cause with respect to something, as a creature; see ch. 19, th. 12.

units.la: 31. Vigesimo secundo, à subordinatione efficientium; Ens est vel absolutè prima efficiens, ut Deus; vel secunda, & non nisi in certo genere prima, ut Creatura, vid. cap. 20. th. 10. Item, Ens vel est efficiens omnipotens, vel non-omnipotens, vid. ib. th. 11. Item; Ens vel potest esse efficiens partialis, ut creatura, vel non potest, ut Deus, vid. ib. th. 13. Item ens est causa absolutè libera, ut Deus; vel secundum quid tantum, ut creatura, vid. ib. th. 24.
units.tr: 31. Twenty-second, from the subordination of efficient causes: a being is either absolutely the first efficient cause, as God; or a second one, and first only within a certain kind, as a creature; see ch. 20, th. 10. Likewise, a being is either an omnipotent efficient cause or a non-omnipotent one; see ibid., th. 11. Likewise, a being either can be a partial efficient cause, as a creature, or cannot, as God; see ibid., th. 13. Likewise, a being is a cause that is absolutely free, as God; or free only in a certain respect, as a creature; see ibid., th. 24.

units.la: 32. Vigesimo tertio, à fine; Ens est, vel propter quod reliqua omnia sunt, ipsum ob nullum aliud, ut Deus; vel quod propter aliud est, ut creatura, vid. cap. 21. th. 16. 22.
units.tr: 32. Twenty-third, from the end: a being is either that for the sake of which all other things are, itself for no other reason, as God; or one that exists for the sake of another, as a creature; see ch. 21, th. 16, 22.

units.la: 33. Vigesimo quarto, ab inhærentia; Ens vel potest esse subjectum accidentis, ut creaturæ; vel non potest, ut Deus, vid. cap. 23. th. 8.
units.tr: 33. Twenty-fourth, from inherence: a being either can be the subject of an accident, as a creature; or cannot, as God; see ch. 23, th. 8.

units.la: 34. Vigesimo quinto, à circumstantia; Enti vel proprie conveniunt denominationes à circumstantia loci & temporis desumtæ, ut creaturis; vel non proprie conveniunt, ut Deo, vid. cap. 30. th. 2. 7. & cap. 31. th. 6.
units.tr: 34. Twenty-fifth, from circumstance: names taken from the circumstances of place and time belong properly to a being, as to creatures; or they belong not properly, as to God; see ch. 30, th. 2, 7, and ch. 31, th. 6.

units.la: 35. Patet igitur Entium differentiaş, ex Metaphysica desumi posse, ac proinde ipipsam ad ipsorum Entium cognitionem, non tantum conferre, sed & summopere necessariam esse. Nunc videndum, quomodo modum cognoscendi adjuvet?
units.tr: 35. It is therefore clear that the differences of beings can be drawn from Metaphysics, and that it is not only helpful but absolutely necessary for the knowledge of those beings themselves. Now we must see how it helps us to know the method.

units.la: 36. Ad modum singula cognoscendi confert Metaphysica, dum Logices præcepta non tantum ordinat ac disponit, sed & fundat; Adeò ut Logica solam formam addendo, Metaphysica materiam generalem suggerat, eamque debito ordine ad speciale deducere doceat. Quod ordine & per partes ostendendum. Consistit autem modus cognoscendi & intellectum dirigendi, partim in propriâ intellectus informatione, partim in acquisitæ cognitionis communicatione, Burgersdic. lib. 1. Log. cap. 1. Theor. 1. §. 7. Et utramque adjuvat Metaphysica.
units.tr: 36. Metaphysics contributes to the method of knowing each thing, since it not only orders and arranges the precepts of Logic but also grounds them. Thus, while Logic supplies only the form, Metaphysics supplies the general matter and teaches how to derive it in due order into the specific. This must be shown in order and part by part. The method of knowing, and of directing the intellect, consists partly in the intellect's own formation, and partly in the communication of acquired knowledge; see Burgersdijk, Logic, bk. 1, ch. 1, Theor. 1, §7. Metaphysics helps with both.

units.la: 37. Propriam intellectus informationem valdè ope ac cognitione Metaphysicæ promoveri, in genere certum esse potest, quod tam procul admirationem arceat. Nihil quippe admirari, Philosophiæ finem esse, alibi, ex Pythagora & Aristotele constitui; At Metaphysica peculiari quodam jure σοφίας titulum meretur, quod ab omnibus admirationem fugat. Nam 1. fœda est admiratio, ex primarum causarum ignoran-tiâ prodiens; at illam Metaphysica tollit, non tantum quid sint illæ, sed & quæ sint explicans, vid. cap. 20. th. 10. 11. 2. Peversa est admirationis sublatio,
units.tr: 37. That the intellect's own formation is greatly advanced by the knowledge of Metaphysics can be certain in general, because it so effectively keeps away wonder. For that to wonder at nothing is the end of philosophy has been laid down elsewhere, on the authority of Pythagoras and Aristotle; yet Metaphysics deserves the title of wisdom by a special right, since it drives wonder away from everything. For 1. wonder is a defective state, arising from ignorance of the first causes; but Metaphysics removes it by explaining not only what those causes are but also what they are like; see ch. 20, th. 10, 11. 2. The removal of wonder is perverse when

units.la: quā ex comparatione tantum similium, non quidem re, sed exi-stimatione, illa auffertur, satis tamen frequens est. Solent quippe homines de ente ignotiori ita philosophari, ut de altero magis noto; Unde & similes de Deo conceptus formant, quales de Creaturâ; & de intelligentiis, quales de corporibus, ut Anthropomorphitæ & quicunque Angelis corpora tribuunt, dilucidè ostendunt. At Metaphysica aliter fieri debere ostendit, dum 1. infinitam inter Deum & Creaturas discrepantiam passim adstruit. 2. Dum unicuique propriam tribuit essentiam, per quam ens est, talesque habet affectiones & operationes, qualis est ipsa essentia, vid. cap. 1. th. 31. 32. Adeo ut simplicium simplices, compositorum compositæ, finitorum finitæ sint essentiæ, adeoque & affectiones, quibus consimiles conceptus respondere debent.
units.tr: it is taken away merely by comparing like things, not in reality but in opinion, though this is quite a common occurrence. For people are accustomed to reason about a less known being as if about one that is better known. Hence they also form concepts of God like those they have of a creature, and of spirits like those they have of bodies; as the Anthropomorphites, and all who ascribe bodies to angels, clearly show. But Metaphysics shows that it must be done otherwise, since 1. it everywhere asserts an infinite difference between God and creatures; 2. it assigns to each thing its own essence, through which it is what it is, and has such affections and operations as the essence itself is; see ch. 1, th. 31, 32. So that simple things have simple essences, compound things compound essences, and finite things finite essences, and so too their affections, to which correspondingly similar concepts ought to answer.

units.la: 31. Deinde & in specie, informatur intellectus, vel proprio marte, & ex ingenti universi volumine, vel ex libris; dictis scriptisve aliorum. Priori modo inservit Metaphysica, dum 1. ostendit reductionem cujuscunque cognoscibilis ad suprema sua genera. 2. Confert ad æstimationem dignitatis ac præstantiæ, cujuscunque rei. 3. Ejus exhibet divisiones ac abstractiones. 4. Ad definiendum summopere necessaria est. 5. Ad plura cognoscenda, viam æternit.
units.tr: 31. Next, the intellect is formed in particular, either by its own effort and from the vast volume of the universe, or from books, that is, from the words or writings of others. Metaphysics serves the former way, since 1. it shows the reduction of any knowable thing to its highest genera; 2. it contributes to the estimation of the dignity and excellence of any thing; 3. it supplies its divisions and abstractions; 4. it is absolutely necessary for defining; 5. it opens the way to knowing more things.

units.la: 39. I. Quoniam igitur nullius intelligibilis plenam ac adæquatam notitiam habemus, si sola propria ac specialia attributa, quæ definitio per differentiam exprimit ac infert, cognoscamus; cum & præterea requiratur, ut communia quoque & generalia prædicata, quæ per genus in definitione significantur, exactè teneamus, quia hæc non minus quam illa, ad essentiam rei, definitione repræsentatam, spectant. Genus enim proximum in definitione positum, omnia genera remotiora & superiora, omnesque eorum differentias in se continet: Sed illa ratio optimè, imò tantum è primæ Philosophiæ eruitur fundamentis; Nam quum per essentiam Ens sit, & sit id quod est, facilè intelligitur, eum qui essentiam inquirit, non tantum id per quod est, id est differentiam, investigare oportere, sed etiam illud omne, per quod quovis modo est, quo genera etiam remotissima, qualia sunt Metaphysica, necessariò pertinent.
units.tr: 39. I. Since we do not have full and adequate knowledge of anything intelligible if we know only the proper and special attributes that a definition expresses and implies through the difference, and since we must also hold firmly to the common and general predicates signified by the genus in the definition, because these pertain to the essence of the thing represented in the definition no less than the others do. For the proximate genus placed in a definition contains within itself all the more remote and higher genera and all their differences. But this principle is drawn very well, indeed only, from the foundations of first philosophy. For since a thing is through its essence and is what it is, it is easily understood that one who inquires into an essence must investigate not only that through which it is, that is, the difference, but also everything through which it is in any way, to which even the most remote genera, such as those of Metaphysics, necessarily belong.

units.la: 40. Et quoniam brevitatem debitam in definitionibus Logici requirunt, omninò vetant, aliquid ad esse generis spectans, speciei definitionem ingredi; Quare nisi summa teneamus genera, aut data cujuscunque speciei definitio nihil proderit, aut certè lex illa Logicorum vitianda erit.
units.tr: 40. And since logicians require due brevity in definitions, and utterly forbid the definition of a species to include anything that belongs to the being of the genus, unless we hold the highest genera, the definition of any given species will be of no use, or else that rule of the logicians must be abandoned.

units.la: Ex. gr. Si definiatur Homo, quod sit animal rationale; nihil proderit ignoranti, quid sit animal, vivens, corpus, substantia, ens; neque plene cognoscet, quid sit albedo, aut quid ad ejus essentiam requiratur, nisi noverit, quid sit color, qualitas, accidens, vid. cap. 23. th. 15.
units.tr: For example: if Man is defined as a rational animal, it will be of no use to someone ignorant of what an animal is, a living thing, a body, a substance, a being; nor will he fully know what whiteness is, or what is required for its essence, unless he knows what colour, quality and accident are; see ch. 23, th. 15.

units.la: 41. Hoc igitur argumento monemur, ne quid unquam in accuratà veritatis investigatione de re ullâ apprehendamus, nihil pronunciemus affirmando vel negando, nihil disputemus confirmando vel refutando, priusquam eam per genera sua, ad suprema usque excurrendo duxerimus. Hoc neglecto facilè se homines in difficultates conjiciunt inextricabiles, eoque saepe deveniunt, ut specialiorem naturæ gradum à generaliori, qui in re erant conjunctissimi, opinionis errore divellant; sicut Plato, dum Hominem Animali, Animal corpori, ut species suis generibus, subordinare neglexit, hominem esse Animam pronunciavit, nihilque corpus ad ejus essentiam pertinere. Ex adverso, qui reductioni dictæ gnaviter invigilat, facem sibi accendit, ad clarissimè videnda, in quibus alii hallucinati sunt turpissimè: v. gr. Intellectionem humanam ad Metaphysicum suum genus si reducamus, patebit ex cap. 15. th. 9. quod sit Actus immanens, quare intellectus erit potentia simul activa & passiva, quatenus eundem intelligendi
units.tr: 41. We are therefore warned by this argument never to grasp anything about any thing in an accurate investigation of the truth, never to pronounce anything by affirming or denying, never to dispute anything by confirming or refuting, before we have led it through its genera, running up to the highest. If this is neglected, people easily throw themselves into inextricable difficulties, and often come to tear a more specific grade of nature away from a more general one, which were most closely joined in reality, through an error of opinion; as Plato did, when he neglected to subordinate Man to Animal and Animal to body, as species to their genera, and pronounced that man is soul and that the body contributes nothing to his essence. On the other hand, one who diligently attends to the aforesaid reduction kindles a torch for himself, to see most clearly those points in which others have gone most shamefully astray. For example: if we reduce human intellection to its Metaphysical genus, it will be clear from ch. 15, th. 9 that it is an immanent act; hence the intellect will be a power both active and passive, insofar as it both produces the same act of understanding and receives the product into itself; in this sense one and the same intellect of ours is called agent and patient in different respects.

units.la: actum & producit, & productum in se recipit; quo sensu unus idemque intellectus noster diversa ratione Agens & patiens appellatur.
units.tr: of the same act and produces it, and receives the thing produced into itself. In this sense one and the same intellect of ours is called both agent and patient, under different aspects.

units.la: 42. H. Nec minus in æstimandâ præstantiâ rerum confert Metaphysica, oftendens, perfectionem rebus accedere aut decedere, ex majore minoreve recessu vel accessu ad ens vel non Ens, vid. cap. 9. th. 18. vel & relatione unius ad aliud, vid. cap. ult. facile n. hinc dijudicabimus inter Entia realia perfectiones. v. gr. quod Metallum perfectissimum, quæ animæ species nobilior, quis sensuum nobilissimus; & in practicis, in quo sit summum hominis bonum, an in virtute, nobilitate, divitiis, vel honore consistat? quæ virtutum regina, quæ amicitia perfectior? quæ forma Reip. præstantissima? In notionibus secundis, quodnam instrumentum Logicæ præstantissimum, quæ definitio, quis syllogismus perfectior? Et in Privationibus: ut cum duo cuilibet virtuti opponantur vitia, unum in excessu, alterum in defectu, utrum sit minus malum? an præstat principem esse callidum, vel plane obtusum? an melior & tolerabilior regni status, ubi consilarii, boni & sapientes, princeps vero ad Remp. minus idoneus; an vero is, ubi princes bonus & sapiens, consiliarii malitiosi & inepti.
units.tr: 42. II. Metaphysics is no less useful in judging the excellence of things, showing that perfection is added to or taken from things according to their greater or lesser approach to or withdrawal from being or non-being (see ch. 9, th. 18), or also by the relation of one thing to another (see the last chapter). From this we may easily judge the perfections among real beings: for example, which metal is most perfect, which kind of soul is nobler, which of the senses is the noblest. In practical matters, we may ask where the highest good of man lies: in virtue, nobility, riches, or honour? Which is queen of the virtues? Which friendship is more perfect? Which form of commonwealth is most excellent? Among second notions: which instrument of Logic is most excellent, which definition is better, which syllogism is more perfect? And among privations: since two vices are opposed to every virtue, one in excess and the other in deficiency, which is the lesser evil? Is it better for a prince to be shrewd or utterly dull? Is the state of a kingdom better and more tolerable where the counsellors are good and wise but the prince is less fit for government, or where the prince is good and wise but the counsellors are malicious and incompetent?

units.la: 43. III. Egregium in ostendendis convenientiis ac difconvenientiis cognofcibilium inter fe affert Metaphysica emolumentum; Fluit enim id ipsum exipfiffima Metaphysicæ naturâ, quæ talis est, ut communitates omnium rerum mentis oculis proponat, & generaliffimas intelligibilium diversitates exponat, ut supra visum. Res certe jucunditatis plena est, scire quid tenuiffimus quisque acarus aut vermiculus commune habeat, cum Entiû omnium præftantiffimo; Cum eo enim convenire, convenientia utriusque in uno tertio manifestat; Hoc enim pacto Substantiarum & Accidentium cap. 23. th. 7. Materialium & immaterialium, cap. 1. th. 24. convenientias differentiasque ex Metaphysica depromere licet. Quibus susque deque habitis, absurdæ ac ridiculæ oriuntur hominum opiniones; id toties quoties in Cardano notat Illuftriff. Scaliger; Ita quippe Exerc. 360. ubi Cardanus exiftimârat, majorem esse differentiam inter ftrenuiffimum equum & ignaviffimum, quam inter verum & pictum, ita eum excipit Scaliger: Ergo Equi ignavia formam abjecerit Ac longe minus quam non equus erit: fi ejus natura longè est inferior eâ, quæ neutiquam equus est. Quare fi mihi effet imperium in eum, qui ista prodidit atque profitetur, equo pisto vehi juberem per bibernos pulveres Mediolanenfes. ·
units.tr: 43. III. Metaphysics also offers an outstanding advantage in showing the agreements and disagreements among knowable things. This follows from the very nature of Metaphysics, which is such that it sets before the eyes of the mind the commonalities of all things and sets out the most general differences among intelligible things, as was shown above. It is certainly a pleasant thing to know what the most slender mite or little worm has in common with the most excellent of all beings. For by agreeing with it, the agreement of each with the other is shown in a third thing; in this way, through Metaphysics, one may draw out the agreements and differences of substances and accidents (cap. 23. th. 7.), of material and immaterial things (cap. 1. th. 24.). When these are treated carelessly, absurd and ridiculous opinions of men arise; the Illustrious Scaliger notes this as often as he deals with Cardano. Thus, in Exerc. 360., where Cardano had held that the difference between a most vigorous horse and a most lazy one is greater than that between a true thing and a painted one, Scaliger answers him: Therefore the laziness of a horse has cast off its form, and it will be far less than a non-horse, if its nature is so far inferior to that which is not a horse at all. Wherefore, if I had power over the man who has put forth and professes these things, I would order him to be carried on a painted horse through the wintry dust of Milan.

units.la: 44. Tradens autem rerum ratione effentiæ inter se convenientias,ac difconvenientias, Fundamenta simul omnis distinctionis ac divisionis promit; qui usus ratione necessitatis se extendit, quousque distinctio, id est ad omnia. Plurimorum enim & ubivis occurrentium mater errorum est, quòd multorum intellectui deest facultas abstrahendi, & quæ vel in se, vel & in unâ eâdemque re multa ac diversa adunantur, distinguendi. Quales v. gr. sunt, qui cum Diogene Mensam & Cyathum vident, menseitatem & cyathitatem non vident, quoniam oculis Philosophicis, ut Plato de Diogene ajebat carent. Sunt qui discrimen reale nullum possunt agnoscere, nisi inter ea, quæ manifeste divulsa vident; quemadmodum Flacius, peccatum originis ad substantiam hominis pertinere putavit, quia ab eâ nequeat abesse. Sic nonulli in physicis gustum & tactum eumdem esse sensum arbitrantur; quòd ille sine tactu aliquo non perficiatur. Hujus vitio & defectu complures in moralibus & politicis non distinguunt Beatitudinem à felicitate, Remp. à Civitate & urbe, familiam à domo, alterationem à Mutatione Rerum Pub. in Theologiâ justificationem & sanctificationem, luctum irregenitorum & regenitorum, & sic in cæteris. Et sane quanti sint abstractiones & distinctiones critis nobis proverbiis satis com-
units.tr: 44. In setting out the agreements and disagreements among things according to the reason of their essence, Metaphysics at the same time supplies the foundations of all distinction and division. This use extends, by the necessity of the case, as far as distinction does, that is, to all things. For the mother of very many errors, which occur everywhere, is that many people lack the ability to abstract and to distinguish the many and diverse things that are united either in themselves or in one and the same thing. Such are, for example, those who, when they see a table and a cup with Diogenes, do not see tablehood and cuphood, since they lack the philosophical eyes of which Plato spoke concerning Diogenes. Some can recognise no real difference except between things they see plainly separated; thus Flacius thought original sin pertained to the substance of man, because it could not be absent from it. So some in physics think taste and touch are the same sense, because the former is not completed without some touch. Through this fault and defect, many in moral and political matters do not distinguish blessedness from happiness, the commonwealth from the state and city, the household from the house, alteration from change of public affairs; in theology they do not distinguish justification from sanctification, or the mourning of the unregenerate from that of the regenerate, and so on in other cases. And indeed, how great abstractions and distinctions are is sufficiently commended to us by proverbs of this kind: He who distinguishes well teaches well; the abstracting of things is not lying. Hence the learned define being learned as knowing the differences of things, and a philosopher as one who knows how to abstract. The usefulness and necessity of distinction are therefore very great, but its difficulty is no less: to divide things into their own parts [τὸ γὰρ διαιρεῖσθαι εἰς τὰ πρὸς ἑαυτὰ], but this belongs to the learned and wise. Metaphysics lessens this difficulty by its use: for it gives those philosophical eyes which the brothers of Diogenes lack; through its study the most useful habit of abstracting is awakened in us. And since the same thing is the measure of right and of wrong, it therefore rejects and banishes into exile all frivolous distinctions (which are commonly, but undeservedly, said to be their cause), since they lack a foundation in the nature of things, are empty concepts and masks of the mind, and offer only smoke to the hearer.

units.la: commendatur, qualia sunt, Qui bene distinguit,bene docet;abstrahentium non est mendaciū.Hinc eruditū esse eruditi definiunt nōsse rerū differentias, &Philosophū esse qui abstrahere novit. Maxima proinde distinctionis est utilitas & necessitas, sed non minor difficultas, τὸ γὰρ διαιρεῖσθαι εἰς τὰ προϲ ἑαυτὰ, sed doctorum & Sapientum. Verum difficultatem minuit per hunc usum Metaphysica: Hæc enim donat oculis illis Philosophicis, quibus Diogenis fratres destituuntur; hujus studio utilissimus abstrahendi habitus in nobis excitatur. Et quia idem est mensura recti & obliqui, exinde rejicit, & exilio damnat frivolas omnes (quarum quidem vulgò, sed immeritò causa audit) distinctiunculas, quum fundamento in rerum natura careant, inanes conceptūs ac mentis larvæ sint, meros fumos objicientes audienti.
units.tr: commended, such as these: He who distinguishes well teaches well; the abstracting of things is not lying. Hence the learned define being learned as knowing the differences of things, and a philosopher as one who knows how to abstract. The usefulness and necessity of distinction are therefore very great, but its difficulty is no less: to divide things into their own parts [τὸ γὰρ διαιρεῖσθαι εἰς τὰ πρὸς ἑαυτὰ], but this belongs to the learned and wise. Metaphysics lessens this difficulty by its use: for it gives those philosophical eyes which the brothers of Diogenes lack; through its study the most useful habit of abstracting is awakened in us. And since the same thing is the measure of right and of wrong, it therefore rejects and banishes into exile all frivolous distinctions (which are commonly, but undeservedly, said to be their cause), since they lack a foundation in the nature of things, are empty concepts and masks of the mind, and offer only smoke to the hearer.

units.la: 4s. IV. Quantum rerum accuratæ definitiones præstent, nemini non obvium esse puto, sed nec minus quam difficulter & periculosè constituantur ipsæ: Verum, vix facilis, tuta & accurata obscurioris rei, dabitur definitio, nisi metaphysicæ auxilio: utpote quæ rerum tradit attributa communia, quæ vice generis in definitione funguntur; & dum differentias earum exhibet, simul propria suggerit attributa, aut ad ea indaganda viam sternit; Et magis, dum inferius & cognoscibilis genus proximum, omnia remotiora, eorumque differentias includit, eorum quoque præsupponit notitiam, quî igitur poterit generis proximi convenientia debitè æstimari, nisi & summum quoque genus pernoscatur? Quin & examine à superiori facto deprehendi potest, quodnam unicuique rei sit genus conveniens; Exempli gr. Quod in Dei ejusve attributorum descriptione vice generis & differentiæ ponatur, haberi potest tum ex Entis divisione, tum ex affectionum Entis doctrinâ, nec aliunde id potest Theologia Naturalis arcessere. Habentur inde Creaturæ in genere ejusque affectionum communissimarum genera & differentiæ; facilè investigatur genus proximum corporis, Angeli, Temporis, motus &c. Hinc & recte Philosophus Reipublicæ genus constituit τάξιν, hoc est ordinem, sive ordinationem, quia ipsi in Metaphysicis opponitur confusio. Hinc ea quæ Reip. opponuntur rectè per confusionem definiuntur, sic Tyrannis est confusio Civitatis, sic ochlocratia, &c. vid. cap. 34.
units.tr: 45. IV. I think it is obvious to everyone how much accurate definitions of things are worth, but how difficult and dangerous it is to frame them. Yet a definition of an obscure thing can hardly be easy, sound and accurate without the help of Metaphysics, since it sets out the common attributes of things, which serve in the place of genus in a definition; and while it shows their differences, it at the same time suggests their proper attributes or prepares the way for investigating them. Moreover, since the nearest knowable genus includes all the more remote things and their differences, it presupposes knowledge of them too. How, then, could the agreement of the nearest genus be duly estimated unless the highest genus also is thoroughly known? Indeed, by the method stated above, it can be grasped what genus is suited to each thing. For example, what is placed in the place of genus and difference in the description of God or of his attributes can be had both from the division of being and from the doctrine of the affections of being; natural theology cannot draw it from anywhere else. From these one obtains the genera and differences of creatures in general and of their most general affections; the proximate genus of body, of angel, of time, of motion, and so on, is easily investigated. Hence the Philosopher rightly made the genus of the commonwealth to be order [τάξιν], that is, arrangement or ordering, since confusion is opposed to it in Metaphysics. Hence things opposed to the commonwealth are rightly defined through confusion: thus tyranny is the confusion of a state, and so is mob rule, and so on (see ch. 34).

units.la: 46. V. Ad plura cognoscenda viam sternit, dum 1. Ordinem inter illa commonstrat. 2. Eorum scientiis mirificè proderit.
units.tr: 46. V. It prepares the way for knowing many things, since 1. it shows the order among them, and 2. it is of wonderful help to their sciences.

units.la: 47. I. Ordinem monstrat, dum à generalioribus ad specialia processum inchoat, cum. eumque facilem, certum, ac naturæ consentaneum passim ostendit, quo non tantum confert memoriæ, (cum quæ ordine tenentur, tanquam continuatâ chordâ, longè felicius memoriæ mandentur, retineantur, atque ex eâ suggerantur: ) sed & laborisgravitatem ac prolixitatem valde imminuit. Etenim Scientiarum omnium officium est & propria virtus, monente Verulamio, ut experientiæ ambages & itinera longa quantum veritatis ratio permittit, abbrevient, ac proinde remedium veteri querelæ de vita brevi, arte longa, adferant. Et sanè eam ob causam omnes artes & disciplinas constitutas esse, inductione constat. Eccur enim de homine in communi tractatio instituitur? ut compendiose ea habeamus, quæ in singulis individuis cognoscere infinitum & impossibile fuisset. Cur de Animali in genere agitur? quia infinitum & vitæ humanæ impossibile, communia attributa Animalium in omnibus & singulis cognoscere speciebus & individuis. Cur de viventibus in genere docetur? ne sit opus ea quæ Plantis, Bestiis & hominibus communiter insunt, in singulis seorsim contemplari, quod & operosum & tædiosum nimis. Quo verò scientiæ sunt universaliores & superiores, eò magis dictum officium præstant, ut ex allatis exemplis patet; Cum igitur certum sit, Metaphyficam omnium esse generalissimam & supremam ; maximè illum usum ab ipsâ, præstari conspicuum erit: Nulla quippe est scientia , quæ de pluribus nos erudiat rebus, nulla, quæ hoc præceptis faciat pauci-oribus.
units.tr: 47. I. Monstrates order, in that it begins the progress from the more general to the special, and everywhere shows this to be easy, certain and in agreement with nature, by which it not only helps the memory (since things held in order are committed to memory and retained far more happily, as if on one continuous string, and are recalled from it), but also greatly lessens the weight and tedium of labour. Indeed, as Verulam warns, it is the duty and proper virtue of all sciences to shorten the detours and long roads of experience, as far as the reason of truth allows, and so to offer a remedy to the old complaint about life being short, art being long. And it is clear from induction that all arts and disciplines were established for this reason. For why is a treatment of man in general undertaken? So that we may have in compendium those things which it would have been infinite and impossible to know in each individual. Why is there a discussion of animal in general? Because it is infinite and impossible for human life to know the common attributes of animals in all and each of their species and individuals. Why is teaching given about living things in general? So that there is no need to contemplate separately in each case what is common to plants, beasts and men, which is both laborious and all too tedious. Now the more universal and higher the sciences are, the more fully they perform this duty, as is clear from the examples given. Since it is therefore certain that Metaphysics is the most general and highest of all, that use of it will be seen to be most conspicuous: for there is no science that teaches us about more things, and none that makes this with fewer precepts.

units.la: 48. 2. Scientiis, ad quas plura illa cognoscenda pertinere possunt, Metaphysica prodest, dum primo, eas inter se unit ac connectit: Secundò eis subjecta præscribit. Tertio, earum defendit principia. Quarto, earum affectiones, in ipsis de subjecto demonstrandas, tradit.
units.tr: 48. 2. Metaphysics is useful to the sciences to which those many things to be known may belong, in that first, it unites them and connects them with one another; secondly, it prescribes their subjects to them; thirdly, it defends their principles; fourthly, it sets out their affections, which are to be demonstrated of the subject within them.

units.la: 49. Primò, reliquas scientias inter se unit. Quam noxia in corpore humano est continuitatis solutio, tam perniciosum in disciplinis vulgare illud vitium, quo peculiaria sibi quisque in suâ scientiâ regna figit, quasi nullum illa ad aliam scientiam respectum includat, aut sine omni alterius ope subsistere possit. Noxium inquam illud est vitium; Ut enim unius disciplinæ partes & axiomata facilè destruuntur, & corruunt, si seorsim singula & non omnia inter se connexa & cohærentia tradideris, ita nec disciplinæ & scientiæ singulæ sartæ tectæ permanere queunt, nisi unionis & communionis vinculo continéantur: Omninò ut Sagittæ illius Scythæ senis singulæ seorsim facilè à filiis frangi poterant, conjunctæ in fasciculo non poterant. At hoc inindissolubile omnium disciplinarum vinculum Metaphysica maximè monstrat. Nam quicquid per Entis divisionem distinctis considerandum scientiis tribuitur, id in iis, quæ sunt ante entis divisiones, est unum & individuum. Etenim sicut corpora sublunaria omnia unam communem materiam habent, quæ ita est eorum mater, uttamen formam informantem sibi peculiarem singula teneant: Ita cunctæ artes ac scientiæ, unius illius Entis, quod Metaphysica considerat, partem sibi aliquam abscindunt, de unâ illâ materiâ omnes partici- pant, etiamsi formas ei diversas imprimant, & secundum diversas rationes illam tractent. Unit ergo Metaphysica pulchro vinculo reliquas disciplinas, & secum & inter se.
units.tr: 49. First, it unites the remaining sciences with one another. Just as division of continuity is harmful to the human body, so the common vice in the disciplines is harmful, by which each person fixes peculiar kingdoms for himself in his own science, as if it included no relation to another science or could stand without the help of any other. I say that this vice is harmful. For just as the parts and axioms of one discipline are easily destroyed and collapse if you teach them separately and not all connected and cohering with one another, so the individual disciplines and sciences cannot remain sound and whole unless they are held together by the bond of union and fellowship. It is like the arrows of that old Scythian: each one could easily be broken by his sons when taken singly, but when bound together in a bundle they could not be broken. Metaphysics most clearly shows this indissoluble bond of all the disciplines. For whatever is assigned to the distinct sciences to be considered through the division of being is, in those things which come before the divisions of being, one and undivided. Indeed, just as all sublunary bodies have one common matter, which is their mother, yet each keeps its own peculiar informing form, so all the arts and sciences cut off for themselves some part of that one Being which Metaphysics considers. All of them share in that one matter, even if they impress different forms on it and treat it according to different aspects. Metaphysics therefore unites the other disciplines with itself and with one another by a fine bond.

units.la: §0. Secundo Metaphysica nostra reliquis disciplinis subjecta præscribit, easque hoc pacto, constituit, ac inter se discernit. Quemadmodum ubi Physica definit Medicina incipit; ubi Politica finit, Jurisprudentia orditur: ita ubi prima Philosophia subsistit cæteræ disciplinæ inchoantur: ipsa quippe secat res, ut autem res secantur, ita scientias secari æquum est.
units.tr: §0. Second, our Metaphysics prescribes subjects to the other disciplines, and in this way constitutes them and distinguishes them from one another. Just as Medicine begins where Physics ends, and Jurisprudence starts where Politics finishes, so the other disciplines begin where first Philosophy stops. For it cuts things, and just as things are cut, so it is fitting that the sciences be cut.

units.la: §1. Tertio, Principia aliarum scientiarum defendit, quoniam illa aut demonstrat, aut immediatè ex conceptibus educit. Contra negantem principia disputandum non esse, vulgò dicimus, quoniam ex eorum concessione saltem procedit conclusio: At cum cujuscunque scientiæ non sit suâ demonstrare principia, utpote quæ præsupponit, aut fluctuabunda semper erit, & potius opinio, quam certa scientia, nisi auxilio illis corroborandis ac clarissimè probandis suggereret Metaphysica; ita v. gr. non poterit Physicus Materiæ sive corporis probare productionem ac finitatem tàm essentiæ, quam durationis, nisi Metaphysicis subsultus principiis.
units.tr: §1. Third, it defends the principles of the other sciences, since those sciences either demonstrate them or derive them immediately from concepts. We commonly say that one should not argue against a person who denies principles, since the conclusion at least proceeds from their concession. But since no science can demonstrate its own principles, because it presupposes them, it will always be wavering and be opinion rather than certain knowledge, unless Metaphysics supplies help to strengthen and most clearly prove those principles. For example, the natural philosopher cannot prove the production and finitude of matter or body, both in its essence and in its duration, unless he is supported by Metaphysical principles.

units.la: 52. Quarto;Nec minus attributa istorum Subjectorum, inferioribus scientiis jam assignatorum, ipsa Metaphysica ostendit, & ad illa invenienda viam monstrat. Nam si ducamus illa inferiora subjecta per omnia Entis generalia, seu metaphysica attributa, perquirendo, quomodo singula in his inserioribus subjectis determinentur, eisdemque applicentur, habebimus attributa propria & affectiones speciales; quam ad rem præter generalem attributorum doctrinam, etiam Divisio Entis prima, ex omnibus attributis educta, plurimum facit.
units.tr: 52. Fourth, Metaphysics itself likewise shows the attributes of those subjects already assigned to the inferior sciences, and points out the way to discover them. For if we lead those inferior subjects through all the general attributes of Being, or metaphysical attributes, by inquiring how each is determined in these inferior subjects and applied to them, we will have proper attributes and special affections. For this purpose, besides the general doctrine of attributes, the first division of Being, drawn from all the attributes, is of great help.

units.la: 53. Atque ita ex parte ostensus Metaphysicæ usus, circa propriam intellectus informationem, ex vasto mundi volumine, non habito respectu ad alios, rerum notitiam venditantes; Ex quibus similiter comparanda rerum cognitioni, insignes præstat commoditates. Comparatur autem exscriptis aliorum rerum cognitio, r. Veri sensus investigatione, ac perceptione. 2. Iudicio de veritate vel falsitate ejusdem; Et utrobique emolumentum haut mediocre confert.
units.tr: 53. And so the use of Metaphysics has been shown in part: it serves the proper formation of the intellect, out of the vast volume of the world, without regard to others who offer knowledge of things. From these the knowledge of things is likewise to be acquired, and Metaphysics offers remarkable advantages. Knowledge of things is acquired from the writings of others in two ways: first, by investigating the true sense and perceiving it; second, by judging the truth or falsity of it. In both respects it brings no small benefit.

units.la: 54. I. Verus sensus investigatur, partim ex legitimâ terminorum simplicium perceptione; partim ex eorum cohaesione. Ad simplicium terminorum perceptionem conferre Metaphysicam notissimum est; Etenim primo, extra omnem dubitationis aleam est, nullos alicujus disciplinae terminos toties in omni sermone ac scripto occurrere, quoties communissimi & generalissimi primae Philosophiae; nihil enim loquimur, vel scribimus, nisi de aliquo, de uno. de Ente, & non-Ente, de causa &c Et si specialia velimus attingere, adhibentur ejus termini in quaestionibus & disputationibus: v. gr. Optics, an color sit Ens reale? quae distinctio, lumen, lucis, radii? &c. In Physicis, an temperamentum sit relatio, vel harmonia an ignis & anima sit substantia vel accidens? In Theologicis, an voluntarium sit de essentia peccati, quae norma bonorum operum? quae notae ecclesiae? &c. In his quippe aliisque innumeris necessaria est terminorum praecognitio, priusquam affirmes vel neges, propugnes vel oppugnes, tum ne turpem elenchi ignorationem committas, aut in logomachiam tandem Disputatio terminetur.
units.tr: 54. I. The true sense is investigated, partly from the proper perception of the simple terms, and partly from their cohesion. It is well known that Metaphysics contributes to the perception of simple terms. For, first, it is beyond all doubt that no terms of any discipline occur as often in every speech and writing as the most common and most general terms of first Philosophy. For we say or write nothing except about something, about one thing, about Being and non-Being, about cause, and so on. And if we wish to touch on special matters, the terms of Metaphysics are used in questions and disputations. For example, in optics: whether colour is a real being; what is the distinction between light, luminous and rays, etc. In physics: whether temperament is a relation or a harmony; whether fire and soul are substance or accident. In theology: whether the voluntary belongs to the essence of sin; what is the rule of good works; what are the marks of the Church, etc. In these and countless other matters, prior knowledge of the terms is necessary before you affirm or deny, defend or attack, so that you do not commit the shameful fallacy of ignorance of the argument, or let the disputation finally end in a war of words.

units.la: §5.
