Secundo, & speciales termini singulárum disciplinarum adgenerales istos Metaphyficos & revocandi, & exiis, ut pote primis, aliquatenus mensurandi ac æstimandi sunt; Quidquid enim inest generi, id quoque inest speciebus; unde quod generalibus istis terminis inest, id quoque specialibus suo modo inesse par est. Ita igitur entia ex generali ente, affectiones ex affectionibus, habitudines ex habitudinibus, potentiæ ex potentiis generalibus deducuntur. V. gr. Homo ut ens, ex Entis Metaphysicâ contemplatione illustratur; ut Rsibilis, ex potentiâ activâ; ut pater ex dependentiâ; ut cives ex unione; ut subditus, Maritus &c. ex appositione. &c.
units.tr: §5. Second, the special terms of the individual disciplines must be traced back to these general metaphysical terms, and, as to first terms, must be measured and valued to some extent by them. For whatever is in the genus is also in the species. Hence what belongs to these general terms must also belong to the special terms in its own way. Thus beings are derived from general Being, affections from affections, relations from relations, powers from general powers. For example, man as a being is illuminated from the metaphysical contemplation of Being; as risible, from active power; as father, from dependence; as citizen, from union; as subject, husband, etc., from apposition, etc.

units.la: §6. Cohæsio terminorum ex mutuo respectu percipitur, qui semper in respectu Metaphysico fundatus est; unde maximè Metaphysica confert ad axiomatum & enunciatorum Metaphysicorum extra Metaphysicam occurrentium genuinum sensum rectè intelligendum, eumdemque ab abusu contra Pseudographemata vindicandum. Creberrima est principiorum Metaphysicorum detorsio, perversa interpretatio, & vitiosa accommodatio: at Metaphysica ea rectè explicans, teipsum à tali vitio præstabit immunem, & præterea efficiet, ut aliorum erroribus sanâ & congruâ principiorum interpretatione
units.tr: §6. The cohesion of terms is perceived from their mutual relation, which is always founded on a metaphysical relation. Hence Metaphysics above all contributes to rightly understanding the genuine sense of the axioms and metaphysical statements that occur outside Metaphysics, and to defending that sense from abuse against spurious writings. The twisting of metaphysical principles, their perverse interpretation, and their faulty application are very common. But Metaphysics, by explaining them rightly, will keep you yourself free from such a fault, and will also enable you to meet the errors of others with a sound and fitting interpretation of the principles.

units.la: Metaphysica, in the tract's sense of the Metaphysics of the disciplines. occurras. Ita cum ex eo, quod perfecto nihil possit addi, vid. cap. 9. th. 18. Soc息niani probant, à λόγῳ non potuisse carnem assumi, id ineptissimè detorqueri percipies, cum axioma de solâ perfectione loquatur essentiali, quæ multò minus ab Ente primo excludit accessum extraessentialem in unione hypostatica, quam ab Ente secundo, accessum accidentis in unione accidentali; Idem in infinitis aliis observabis.
units.tr: Metaphysica, in the tract's sense of the Metaphysics of the disciplines. occurras. So when the Socinians prove, from the fact that nothing can be added to what is perfect (see chap. 9, th. 18), that the flesh could not be assumed by the Word, you will perceive how absurdly this is twisted. For the axiom speaks only of essential perfection, which excludes an extra-essential addition from the First Being in the hypostatic union far less than it excludes the addition of an accident from a Second Being in an accidental union. You will observe the same in countless other cases.

units.la: §7. Hinc etiam, non obscurè elucescit, quantum valeat in ferendo judicio, de veritate & falsitate congruitate & incongruitate dicti scripti vel alterius; Cum enim judicium ante legitimam perceptionem temerarium, & calumniantis animi sit indicium, prius terminorum, eorumque cohæsionis probè gnarus esse debet, qui ad judicandum animum applicat. Et magis, cum veritas quælibet specialis generalem præsupponat veritatem, quam Metaphysicæ est suggerere, illa ad hanc, tanquam ad lydium lapidem, exigenda erit; Cum prima veritas (loquor de iis, quæ naturali lumine cognoscuntur:) omnis reliquæ sit mensura. Quare non saltem Autorum sententiæ, v. gr. de communicatione propriorum, accidentium extra subjectum existentiâ, corporum penetratione & polytopiâ, salsitatis damnandæ sunt, sed & proverbia ac dicteria familiari passim sermone trita exaexaminari possunt. Quæ in tantum falsa aut vera æstimari debent, quatenus axiomata Metaphysica dissentientia aut consentientia habent. Ex. gr. Omni veritati repugnans est sententia, quam ad salvandum absurdum transsubstantiationis dogma, proponunt Conimbric. 1. Phys. c. 9. qu. 5. art. 3. circa difficultatem, ut ajunt, de constitutione vermis, enati ex speciebus sacræ Eucharistiæ; Neque enim ille fieri poterit ex incorruptibili & gloriosó Salvatoris corpore, in quod realiter transmutatam ajunt hostiâ, quâ loco panis utuntur: Neque ex nihilo: neque ex putrefactâ hostiâ, ut autumant; Quare hunc in modum huic ictui prospicere nituntur: Dicendum breviter est, in eo eventu receptis primum in quantitate dispositionibus ad formam vermis, ipso generationis momento subjici a Dea materiam, vel denuo creatam, vel aliunde ascitam, vel potius eandemmet quæ evanuerat, reproductam, ex quâ simul cum formâ vermis componatur. Nam 1. quantitatem, quæ accidens est, esse sine subjecto, repugnat huic axiomati, nullum inhærens est sine eo cui inhæreat; & huic: Nullum inhærens est extra illud cui inhæreat, vid. cap. 23. th. 2. II. Recipi dispositiones in quantitate illâ accidentariâ, repugnat huic axiomati: Subjectum toto genere dignius est accidente; Et huic, Omne subjectum accidentis est substantiâ ; vid. d.c.th. 7. III. Quantitatem illam, quæ prius fuit hostiæ, postea fieri vermis, repugnat huic axiomati: Nullum inhærens potest transire, ex eo cui inhæret in aliud, vid. d. c.th. 2. IV. A Deo isti productioni materiam immediatè subjici per extraordinariam & miraculosam actionem, repugnat Axiomati: Essentia non sunt multiplicanda præter necessitatem, vid.cap. 1.th. 28. Adeoque nec multiplicanda, nulla urgente necessitate, ut hoc in negotio, miracula. V. Illam materiam denuò ex nihilo creari, repugnat huic: Frustrà fit per plura, quod æquè bene fieri potest per pauciora, cujus ratio est Axioma modo allegatum: Essentia non sunt multiplicanda præter necessitatem. VI. Eamdemmet, quæ evanuerat, hoc est annihilata erat, reproduci, repugnat ipsius singularitati, quâ omne ens suum esse semel habet: at bis haberet illa materia, si ejus nullâ parte reliquâ, denuò reproducenda foret, vid.cap. 3.th. 5. 8.
units.tr: §7. Hence it also shines out clearly how much it is worth in forming a judgement about the truth and falsity, the agreement and disagreement, of a written work or of anything else. For since a judgement made before proper perception is rash and is a sign of a calumnious mind, whoever applies his mind to judging must first be well acquainted with the terms and their cohesion. And all the more so, since any special truth presupposes a general truth, which it is the task of Metaphysics to suggest; that truth must be tested by this one, as by a touchstone, since the first truth (I speak of those known by natural light) is the measure of all the rest. Therefore not only the opinions of authors, for example about the communication of properties, the existence of accidents outside a subject, the penetration of bodies and multilocation, are to be condemned as false, but also proverbs and sayings worn smooth by everyday speech can be examined. These should be judged true or false to the extent that they agree or disagree with metaphysical axioms. For example, the opinion which the Conimbricenses propose, to save the absurd transubstantiation dogma, in their commentary on the Physics (book 1, chap. 9, question 5, article 3, on the difficulty, as they say, about the constitution of a worm born from the species of the sacred Eucharist, is entirely contrary to truth. For it could not come from the incorruptible and glorified body of the Saviour, into which they say the host is really changed, which they use in place of bread; nor from nothing; nor from the rotting host, as they assert. Hence they try to meet this blow in the following way: It must be said briefly that in that event, with the dispositions in quantity received first for the form of a worm, at the very moment of generation matter is placed under it by God, either newly created, or taken from elsewhere, or rather the very same matter which had vanished, reproduced, out of which it is composed together with the form of the worm. For: (1) that quantity, which is an accident, should exist without a subject contradicts this axiom, nothing inhering is without that in which it inheres, and this one, nothing inhering is outside that in which it inheres (see chap. 23, th. 2). (2) That dispositions should be received in that accidental quantity contradicts this axiom, the subject is by its whole genus more worthy than the accident, and this one, every subject of an accident is a substance (see the same chap., th. 7). (3) That the quantity which first belonged to the host should afterwards become a worm contradicts this axiom, nothing inhering can pass from that in which it inheres into another (see the same chap., th. 2). (4) That matter should be placed under this production immediately by God through an extraordinary and miraculous action contradicts the axiom, essences are not to be multiplied beyond necessity (see chap. 1, th. 28). Hence miracles, which no pressing necessity demands in this matter, should not be multiplied either. (5) That this matter should be created again out of nothing contradicts this one, it is vain to do by more what can equally well be done by fewer, the reason for which is the axiom just cited, essences are not to be multiplied beyond necessity. (6) That the very same matter which had vanished, that is, had been annihilated, should be reproduced contradicts its very singularity, by which every being has its existence only once; for that matter would then have existence twice, if it were to be reproduced with no part of it remaining (see chap. 3, th. 5, 8).

units.la: §8. Hoc ipso facto in omnibus sententiis familiari passim sermone tritis; observat Metaphysicus, quasdem esse veras & exactè quadrantes, alias non exactè; ac proinde non nisi contingenter esse veras. Quoniam multæ sæpe earum sub uno axiomate Metaphysico continentur. Ita v. gr. sub isto axiomate Metaphysico: Plura requiruntur ad esse, quam ad non esse; Quod cap. 1. th. 7. ut ex primo fluens, omissum est, hæc continentur, & ex eo expendi debent, vulgata: Perditur in puncto, quod non revocatur in anno. Facilis descensus Averni: at revocare gradum, superasque evadere ad auras, hoc opus, hic labor est. Ardua quæ pulchra: Pulchrum enim est magis Ens, deforme quasi non ens. Item ex hoc; nihil est in dependente quod non prius sit in independente, cap. 17. th.9. hæc oriuntur: Discefed à doctis: SusMinervam: qui non habet, non dabit: Concionator frigidus, sine flammis auditor: Qualis cognitio, talis curatio: Cœcus cœco dux, & consimilia plura. Quis itaque eorum, qui circa investigationem & analysin occupati sunt, ut Theologi, Iurisconsulti, aliique Metaphysicæ utilitatibus carere poterit?
units.tr: §8. By this same fact, in all the sentences that are worn smooth by everyday talk, the Metaphysician observes that some are true and exactly so, others not exactly, and therefore that some are true only contingently. For many of them are often contained under a single metaphysical axiom. Thus, for example, under this metaphysical axiom, More is required for being than for non-being, which was omitted from ch. 1, th. 7 as following from the first, these sayings are contained and must be weighed by it: the common saying Time lost in a moment is not recovered in a year. The descent to Avernus is easy; but to retrace one's steps and climb up to the upper air, this is the task, this is the labour. Hard are the things that are beautiful. For the beautiful is more being, and the ugly is as it were non-being. Likewise from this, nothing is in the dependent that is not first in the independent, ch. 17, th. 9, arise these: Do not teach the learned: a pig to Minerva; he who has not will not give; a cold preacher makes a listener without flames; as the diagnosis, so the cure; a blind man is a guide to a blind man; and many similar sayings. Who, then, among those who are occupied with investigation and analysis, such as theologians, jurists, and others, could do without the uses of Metaphysics?

units.la: 59. Nec minus emolumentum præstat, in docendo & informando alios prima Philosophia, quod ex hisce quatuor dilucidè apparet, 1. quod ,sine ipsa nullum Thema simplex debitè pertractari queat, 2. Loca communia non possint conscribi. 3. Nullus tractatus de quâvis materiâ concipi aut describi, possit. 4. Denique quod sine ipsâ impossibile sit, debitè de quâcunque re differere.
units.tr: 59. Nor does first philosophy give less advantage in teaching and instructing others, which is clear from these four points: (1) that without it no simple theme can be properly treated; (2) common places cannot be written up; (3) no treatise on any matter can be conceived or described; (4) finally, that without it it is impossible to discourse properly on any subject whatever.

units.la: 60. Etenim I. ad tractationem Thematis omninò requiritur, ut ipsum ad genus suum revoces, ejus causas & affectiones omnes enumeres, sed utrumque neutiquam sine ope Metaphysicæ, præstabis. Hæc enim summa genera rerum, & quomodo ad ea inseriora reduci debeant, summasque rerum causas & affectiones, ex quibus speciliores deducuntur, pandit; quemadmodum id jam ostendi.
units.tr: 60. For, first, for the treatment of a theme it is altogether required that you refer it to its genus and list all its causes and affections; but you will do neither without the help of Metaphysics. For this sets out the highest kinds of things, and how the lower ones ought to be reduced to them, and the highest causes and affections of things, from which the more specific ones are deduced, as I have already shown.

units.la: 61. II. Porro quemadmodum Alphabetum literarum omnium enumeratione, certâque digestione, hunc inter alios usum habet, ut Lexicographi juxta id vocabula omnia in Dictionariis ordine disponere, aliique alia numerare atque ordinatè dirigere possint: ita ipsa Metaphysica, realium præcipuè attributorum plena enumeratione, rectâque dispositione, hunc inter alios usum obtinet, ut omnia de omni re cognoscenda aut dicenda plenè enumeremus ac ordine digeramus, quare directam & compendiosam viam docendi exhibet: ostendit&q; quomodo secundum illam omnia in unum fasciculum colligi possint, quæ alii de re eadem divisim, diffuse & confuse prodiderunt.
units.tr: 61. (2) Further, just as the alphabet, by the enumeration and fixed arrangement of all letters, serves among other uses to let lexicographers arrange all words in dictionaries in order, and others to count and direct them in order, so Metaphysics, by the full enumeration and right arrangement of the real attributes especially, serves among other uses to let us list fully and arrange in order everything that is to be known or said about any thing. Hence it offers a direct and compendious way of teaching; and it shows how, according to it, all those things can be gathered into one bundle which others have set forth separately, diffusely and confusedly about the same matter.

units.la: 62. III. Ad scribendum de aliquâ materiâ tractatum, prodest Metaphysica, utpote 1. terminorum, non tantum generalium, sed & specialium perceptionem procreans. 2. Definitionibus & divisionibus constituendis inserviens. 3. Axiomata generalia tradens. 4. Ordinem legitimum instituens: Quæ omnia ad quemcunque tractatum quam maxime requiruntur. In specie id ostendere, nunc brevitati inservire volens, supersedeo.
units.tr: 62. (3) For writing a treatise on any matter, Metaphysics is useful, since it (1) produces a grasp not only of general but also of special terms; (2) serves in framing definitions and divisions; (3) delivers general axioms; (4) establishes a lawful order. All of these are very greatly required for any treatise whatever. To show this in particular I now refrain, wishing to serve brevity.

units.la: 63. IV. De objecta quácunque materia bene differendi facultatem Logicæ communiter vendicamus, nec male; Est enim illa ipsa facultas, ars, aut modus quidam, dirigendi mentem in rerum cognitione: Verum Logica saltem formam ac modum suppeditat, at materiam aliunde emendicatum venit; Eam autem constituunt axiomata ac principia complexa, quæ quidem cuil.bet-disciplinæ propria, vernacula ac domestica sunt, at præterea etiam communia quædam, & quidem nulla frequentiora, quam Metaphysicæ, veluti communissimæ ac supremæ cognoscendæ veritatis normæ. Hinc scilicet factum est, ut multa Metaphysicorum propria axiomata, à Dialecticis ad Topica translata sint: Quidquid enim in his est optimum & fructosissimum, in Metaphysicis agris natum fuit. Enunciata autem & Axiomata Metaphysica in omnigeno discursu obvia sunt, sed partim expressè posita, partim suppressè infixa. Si quæ autem tacitè vim suam effundant, in iis eruendis sedulo aciem intendere debes; Major enim propositio, ut Syllogismi semper ponit fundamentum, ita sæpissimè generali Metaphysices axiomati, aut definitioni innititur. Ita in Catechefi nostrā Heidelbergensi; quast. 30. Catechumeni Reformatorum adversus Pontificios ita argumentantur: Qui est perfectus servator, in eo fideles omnia possident, quæ ad salutem requiruntur: At Iesus est perfectus servator. Ergo. Introspice hujus Syllogismi majorem, & videbis ipsam in definitione Metaphysicā perfecti fundari: Possem hic campum latissimum aperire, ut quisque ea Metaphysicæ Axiomata opportunè posset venari, ut iis abundet: Verum non patitur nobis proposita brevitas: Reservandum ergo id peculiaribus Lectionibus, de usu Metaphysicæ applicando institutis. Usus autem Metaphysicæ in docendo diò clarius hinc patescit: Simulque, nihil ad totam Theoriam τ ὄντων requiri, quod non ex solā Metaphysicā, tamquam fonte desumi possit.
units.tr: 63. (4) We commonly and not wrongly claim for Logic the faculty of discoursing well on any matter whatever. For that faculty is itself an art or method of directing the mind in the knowledge of things. But Logic supplies only the form and manner, while the matter comes from elsewhere, begged in. The matter is made up of axioms and complex principles, which are indeed proper to each discipline, native and domestic to it, but also some that are common, and none more frequent than those of Metaphysics, as the most common and supreme norms of the truth to be known. Hence it has come about that many proper axioms of the Metaphysicians have been transferred by the Dialecticians to the Topics; for whatever is best and most fruitful in these was born in the Metaphysical fields. Metaphysical statements and axioms are met with in every kind of discourse, some expressly set down, some implied and built in. If any work their force silently, you ought to apply your attention diligently to bringing them out. For the major premise, as always in a syllogism, lays the foundation, and so very often rests on some general Metaphysical axiom or definition. So in our Heidelberg Catechism, question 30, the catechumens of the Reformed argue against the Papists thus: He who is the perfect Saviour, in him the faithful possess all things that are required for salvation; but Jesus is the perfect Saviour; therefore... Look into the major of this syllogism, and you will see that it is founded on the definition of the perfect in Metaphysics. I could open here a very broad field, so that anyone might fittingly hunt out those Metaphysical axioms and abound in them. But the brevity we have proposed does not allow it. That is therefore to be reserved for the special Lectures set up on applying the use of Metaphysics. The use of Metaphysics in teaching becomes clearer from this; and at the same time, that nothing is required for the whole theory of beings [τῶν ὄντων] which cannot be drawn from Metaphysics alone, as from a fountain.

units.la: 64. Emolumentum quoque præstat Metaphysica, in περὶ ξεῖς τῶν ὄντων, præscribens regulas & leges agendi, operandi, vivendi, quàtenus communissimæ in naturâ notiones, ut mensuræ & regulæ assumi possunt, ad ea mensuranda & regulanda, quæ à creaturâ rationali producí debent: Et simul patefaciens normam, ex quâ facta, mores, studia hominum ad decreta Metaphysicæ exigi possunt; videndo, an illa his respondeant & consentiant, an verò ab iis deflectant & dissentiant, non faciendo, vel praticè abnegando, quod generalissimæ notiones affirmando quasi jubent. Quod ut patefiat, breviter ostendendum, 1. Quomodo leges civiles plerumque axiomatibus Metaphysicis superstruantur. 2. Quo pasto in ipsâ vitâ degendâ specialiter utilis sit.
units.tr: 64. Metaphysics also gives advantage in concerning the state of beings [περὶ ξεῖς τῶν ὄντων], prescribing the rules and laws of acting, working and living, insofar as the most common notions in nature can be taken as measures and rules, to measure and regulate those things which ought to be produced by the rational creature. And at the same time it lays open the norm by which the deeds, morals and pursuits of men can be brought under the decrees of Metaphysics; by seeing whether these correspond and agree with them, or rather deviate from and dissent from them, by not doing, or by practically denying, what the most general notions, by affirming, as it were command. So that this may become plain, it must be shown briefly: (1) how civil laws are for the most part built upon Metaphysical axioms; (2) in what way it is specially useful in living life itself.

units.la: 65. I. Leges Civiles. axiomatibus Metaphysicis inniti, patebit, si breviter ex titul. D. de R. I. quædam ad illa reducantur. Igitur l. 1. Regula est, quæ rem, quæ est breviter enarrat. Quæ definitio colligitur ex tribus prioribus proprietatibus Mensuræ. Enarrat enim rem quæ est, quia mensura certa & constans esse debet; & breviter, quia mensura prima est, cap. 29. th. 4. Item l. 2. Mulieres ab omnibus officiis civilibus, vel publicis remotæ sunt &c. §. 1. Item, impubes omnibus officiis civilibus debet abstinere. Fluit ex eo, quod inter subjectum & adjunctum requiratur proportio & convenientia, cap. 26. th. 2. l. 3. Ejus est nôlle, qui potest velle. Cujus ratio est, quod contraria sint sub eodem subjecto, Cap. 33. th. 9. l. 6. Non vult hæres esse, qui ad alium transferre voluit hæreditatem; Ratio est, quia à se removet constitutionem hæredis, adeoque & esse, juxta Axioma: Cujus nullum est esse, ejus nulla constitutio, cap. 1. th 7. l. 7. Ius nostrum non patitur, eundem in paganis & testato & intestato decessisse (Addita ratione) quod earum rerum natura liter inter se pugnassit, juxta definitionem oppositorum, quæ de eodem tertio dici nequeunt, Secundum naturam est, commoda cuiusque rei eum sequi, quem sequuntur incommoda, quoniam privatio & habitus ejusdem sunt subiecti, cap. 33. th. 8. l. 11. Id quod nostrum est sine facto nostro ad alium transferri non potest; Quoniam, nihil deferente independente & causa, nihil acquiritur dependenti & causato, cap. 17. th. 10. l. 12. In testamentis plenius voluntates testantium interpretantur; Quia primum in unoquoque genere est mensura reliquorum, cap. 29. th. 4. l. 16. Imaginaria vendicio non est pretio accedente; Quia posita constitutione ponitur esse, cap. 1 th. 7. Et quod habet omnia requisita id perfectum est, cap. 9. th. 6. l. 35. Nihil tam naturale est, quam eo genere quidve dissolvere, quo colligatum est, Quia qualis est alicujus constitutio, talis quoque est essentia, talesque ejus affectiones reliquæ, adeoque & talis duratio, cap. 1. th. 7. l. 37. Nemo qui condemnare potest, absolvere non potest. Ratio est, quia habitus & privatio ejusdem subjecti sunt, cap. 33 th. 8. Unde & tales actus, quorum unus est alterius quasi privatio, ejusdem sunt subjecti. l. 40. Furiosi, vel ejus, cui bonis interdictum est, nulla voluntas est. Quia deficiente judicio deficit voluntatis consensus, ut in furioso; Et subilatâ indifferentiâ, & factâ determi-na-
units.tr: 65. I. That civil laws rest on Metaphysical axioms will be clear if some of them are briefly reduced to those axioms from the title De regulis iuris. So: l. 1. A rule is that which briefly describes the thing that is. This definition is gathered from the three first properties of a measure. For it describes the thing that is, because a measure must be certain and constant; and briefly, because the first measure is, ch. 29, th. 4. Likewise l. 2. Women are removed from all civil or public offices, etc., §1. Likewise, a minor ought to abstain from all civil offices. It follows from this that between subject and adjunct a proportion and agreement is required, ch. 26, th. 2, l. 3. It is characteristic of him who can will to be unwilling. The reason is that contraries are under the same subject, ch. 33, th. 9, l. 6. He does not wish to be heir who has wished to transfer the inheritance to another; the reason is that he removes from himself the constitution of heir, and so also his being, according to the axiom: Whose there is no being, his there is no constitution, ch. 1, th. 7, l. 7. Our law does not allow that the same person has died both testate and intestate in respect of the same goods (the reason added) because the very nature of those things fights between them, according to the definition of opposites, which cannot be said of the same third thing. It is according to nature that the advantages of anything follow him whom its disadvantages follow, since privation and habit are of the same subject, ch. 33, th. 8, l. 11. What is ours cannot be transferred to another without our act; since, nothing being conveyed by the independent and cause, nothing is acquired by the dependent and caused, ch. 17, th. 10, l. 12. In wills the intentions of the testators are interpreted more fully. Because the first in each genus is the measure of the rest, ch. 29, th. 4, l. 16. An imaginary sale is not made without the price being added; because the constitution being posited, being is posited, ch. 1, th. 7. And what has all the requisites is perfect, ch. 9, th. 6, l. 35. Nothing is so natural as to dissolve a thing in the same kind in which it is bound, because as is the constitution of anything, so too is its essence, and so its remaining affections, and so too its duration, ch. 1, th. 7, l. 37. Whoever cannot condemn cannot absolve. The reason is that habit and privation are of the same subject, ch. 33, th. 8. Hence also such acts, one of which is as it were the privation of the other, are of the same subject. l. 40. A madman, or one whose goods have been interdicted, has no will. Because when judgment is lacking, the consent of the will is lacking, as in a madman; and once indifference is removed and determination made to the opposite

units.la: 1 th. natione ad oppositum, perit voluntas, cap. 2o. th. 19. l. 45. Neque pignus, neque depositum, neque precarium, neque emtio, neque locatio rei suae consistere potest. Quia omnis relatio est inter duo, tract. 1. f. 3. c. 4. th. 7. Unde & in appositione duo sunt, tract. 2. c. 26. th. 2. l. 54. Nemo plus juris ad alium transferre potest, quam ipse habeat, Quoniam nisi in dependente, quod non prius fuerit in independente, cap. 17. th. 9. l. 56. Semper in dubiis benigniora, praeferenda sunt; Quia plura requiruntur ad esse, quam ad non esse, cum ad esse requiratur constitutio, ad non esse nihil, Cap. 1. th. 7. at benignitas magis conservat esse, quam rigor. l. 73. §. 3 Quae in testamento ita sunt scripta, ut intelligi nequeant, perinde sunt, ac si scripta non essent, Nullum quippe est signum, quod cognoscenti nihil indicare potest, cap. 28. th. 7.
units.tr: 1 th. Neither a pledge, nor a deposit, nor a precarious loan, nor a purchase, nor a lease of one's own property can stand, because every relation is between two things, tract. 1, f. 3, c. 4, th. 7. Hence also in apposition there are two terms, tract. 2, c. 26, th. 2, l. 54. No one can transfer to another more right than he himself has, since nothing is in the dependent that was not first in the independent, c. 17, th. 9, l. 56. In doubtful matters the more lenient course is to be preferred, because more is required for a thing to be than for it not to be, since being requires a constitution, while not-being requires nothing, c. 1, th. 7; and leniency preserves existence more than strictness does, l. 73, §3. Those provisions in a will which are so written that they cannot be understood are just as if they had not been written, for there is no sign which can indicate nothing to one who knows it, c. 28, th. 7.

units.la: 66. L. 80. In toto jure generi per speciem de- rogatur.
units.tr: 66. L. 80. In the whole of the law, the genus is derogated by the species.

units.la: Quoniam Genus in una specie conservari nequit, cap. 24 th. 12. L. 83. Non videtur rem amittere, quibus propria non fuit, Quia Privatio praesupponit habitum, utpote, quia ejusdem cum ipsa est subjecti, cap. 33. th. 8. L. 100. Omnia quae jure contrahuntur, contrario jure pereunt; vid. allegatam ad l. 35. h. t. rationem. L. 143. In toto & partes continentur; Quia totum est aliquo modo multum & unum, a partibus, bus, quâ talibus, reipsa non distinctum, cap. 24. th. 3. L. 120. Nemo plus commodi heredi suo relinquit, quam ipse habuit; Quoniam nihil est in dependente, quâ tali, quod non sit prius in independente, cap. 17. th. 9. L. 123. §. 1. Temporaria permutatio jus provinciæ non innovat. Quia ejus manet essentia, ut quæ non tollitur extrinseca, & reparabili mutatione, cap. 7. th. 5. 6. L. 129. §. 1. Cum principalis causa non consistit, nec ea quidem quæ sequuntur locum habent; Quia efficientes minus principales, sine principali aliqua effectum producere non possunt, cap. 20. th. 26. L. 141. §. 1. Vni duo pro solido hæredes esse non possunt. Ratio est, quia cujuslibet entis una est constitutio in esse, unaque essentia, cap. 1. th. 27. L. 147. Semper specialia generalibus insunt; Quia totum aliquo modo multum esse debet, & ex unione plurium, sive partium constat, cap. 24. th. 3. L. 175. §. 1. Quod quis sibi velit habere non potest, id repudiare non potest. Quia privatio præsupponit habitum, ut quæ non est, nisi debita persectionis negatio, cap. 33. th. 8. L. 175. §. 1. Non debeo melioris conditionis esse, quam auctor meus fuit; Quoniam nihil est in dependente, quod non prius sit in independente, cap. 17. th. 9. L. 182. Quod nullius esse potest, id ut alicujus fieret, nulla obligatio valet efficere; quia in omni appositione est ordo ac convenientia quædam, cap. 26. th. 2. Eådem ratione stabilitur l. 185. Impossibilium nulla est obligatio. L. 208. Non potest videri desisse habere, qui nunquam habuit, ob rationem ad l. 17. §. 1. modo allatam, &c.
units.tr: Since the genus cannot be preserved in one species, c. 24, th. 12, l. 83. It does not seem that one loses a thing to which one never had a proper claim, because privation presupposes a habit, inasmuch as it belongs to the same subject as that habit, c. 33, th. 8, l. 100. All things that are acquired by law perish by the contrary law; see the reason given at l. 35 of this title, l. 143. The whole contains its parts; because the whole is in some way many and one, distinct from its parts as such, but not really distinct, c. 24, th. 3. l. 120. No one leaves more advantage to his heir than he himself had, since nothing is in the dependent, as such, that is not first in the independent, c. 17, th. 9. l. 123, §1. A temporary exchange does not alter the right of a province, because its essence remains, as that which is not taken away by an external and reparable change, c. 7, th. 5, 6. l. 129, §1. When the principal cause does not exist, neither do those things which follow from it have any place, because less principal efficient causes cannot produce an effect without some principal cause, c. 20, th. 26. l. 141, §1. Two persons cannot be heirs in full to one estate. The reason is that each being has one constitution in existence and one essence, c. 1, th. 27. l. 147. Special provisions always stand within general ones, because the whole must in some way be many, and consists of the union of several parts or pieces, c. 24, th. 3. l. 175, §1. What someone cannot wish to have, he cannot renounce, because privation presupposes a habit, since it is nothing but the denial of a due perfection, c. 33, th. 8. l. 175, §1. I ought not to be in a better condition than my author was, since nothing is in the dependent that is not first in the independent, c. 17, th. 9. l. 182. What cannot belong to anyone, no obligation can make belong to someone, because in every apposition there is a certain order and agreement, c. 26, th. 2. By the same reasoning l. 185 is established: There is no obligation to impossible things. l. 208. He who never had something cannot be seen to have ceased to have it, for the reason just given at l. 17, §1, etc.

units.la: 67. II. In vitâ degendâ specialiter utilem esse Metaphysicam, breviter uno atque altero axiomate ostendam. Sit itaque 1. pro Exemplo hoc Axioma Metaphysicum: Primum & perfectissimum in unoquoque genere est mensura reliquorum, cap. 29. th. 4. Optimè notárunt illud axioma Sapientes & principes Ahasueri, quando Reginæ Vasthi superbiam ideo puniendam decrevere, ne omnes fœminæ factum Reginæ imitando, maritos suos spernant, sed honorem ut ipsis tribuant. Hinc in scripturis toties nobis vita, actiones, mores Christi, ut regulæ vitæ nostræ proponuntur. Hinc cum beatorum Angelorum erga Deum officia sint præstantissima, in genere officiorum à creaturis præstitorum, petimus quotidie: fiat voluntas tua, ut in cælo, sic & in terra. Et cum sontes S. Scripturæ perfectissimè nobis mentem Dei declarent, hinc versiones omnes ad eos exigere debemus: Consimiliter in Oeconomicis & Politicis, usum habet: Ita in omni virtute ad summum fastigium tendendum est Patrifamiliâs, quia ipsius virtus exemplar esse debet, ad quod se omnis tiorem esse, d.c.tb. 18 nonne monet ne unquam rebus utaris sublimibus, ad humilia bona consequenda, ut faciunt, v.gr. qui scientiam & bona animi expetunt, propter eminentiam, aliorum oppressionem, honorem, opes, aliaque fortunae bona. Denique dum prima Philosophia dicit, qui intendit finem, intendit etiam media fini cohaerentia, ibid. nonne monet, ut, si tibi propositueris fructus diligentiae & laboris, diligens quoque & laboris patiens sis? Etsi fines expetas honestos, uti expetere debes, ut adhibeas media honesta.
units.tr: 67. II. I will show briefly, by one or two axioms, that Metaphysics is especially useful in living one's life. Let the first, by way of example, be this metaphysical axiom: The first and most perfect thing in each kind is the measure of the rest, c. 29, th. 4. The wise men and princes of Ahasuerus well understood this axiom when they decided that the pride of Queen Vashti should be punished, so that all women, imitating the queen's deed, would not despise their husbands but would give them honour. Hence in Scripture the life, actions and manners of Christ are so often set before us as the rules of our life. Hence, since the services of the blessed angels towards God are most excellent among the services rendered by creatures, we pray daily: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. And since the sacred writings most perfectly declare to us the mind of God, we ought to direct all translations to them. It holds similarly in economics and politics. So in every virtue the head of a household must strive for the highest summit, because his own virtue ought to be the pattern to which everyone under him conforms. Does it not warn us, [to be] more sublime, d.c.tb. 18, not to use lofty things to obtain lowly goods, as those do who seek learning and gifts of mind for the sake of eminence, the oppression of others, honour, wealth and other goods of fortune? Finally, since First Philosophy says that whoever intends an end also intends the means that belong to that end, does it not warn, ibid., that if you have set yourself the fruit of diligence and labour, you should also be diligent and patient of labour? If you seek honest ends, you must likewise seek honest means.

units.la: 70. Vicissim dum asserit Metaphysica, omne bonum sui diffusivum & communicativum esse, nonne te excitat ad Eleemosynas largiendas, & ut approbes illud Ciceronis é Platone dictum: Non solum nobis nati sumus: Ortus nostri partem patria vendicat, partem amici.
units.tr: 70. Conversely, since Metaphysics asserts that every good is diffusive of itself and communicative, does it not stir you to give alms generously, and to approve that saying of Cicero, taken from Plato: We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, and our friends a part.

units.la: 71. Item dum ostendit Metaphysica, nihil existere, quin producat aliquid, aut productum in se recipiat, scias, non esse tibi otium sectandum, sed semper aliquid agendum, aliquid patiendum; Semper operis aliquid facito, inquit Augustinus, ut te diabolus inveniat occupatum.
units.tr: 71. Again, since Metaphysics shows that nothing exists which does not produce something, or receive something produced in itself, know that you must not pursue idleness, but must always be doing something and suffering something. Always do some work, says Augustine, so that the devil may find you occupied.

units.la: 72. Nullum Effectum excedere causæ suæ virtutem, docet Metaphysica; Hinc nihil ultra vires suscipies, nihil invitâ dices faciesve minervâ. Hinc Concionator si ipse frigeat, auditores nihil flammarum concipiunt; nec pios concitat affectus in aliis, nisi prius ipse pie affectus fuerit.
units.tr: 72. Metaphysics teaches that no effect exceeds the power of its cause. Hence you will undertake nothing beyond your powers, and you will say or do nothing against the grain of Minerva. Hence, if the preacher himself is cold, his hearers conceive no flames; nor does he stir up pious affections in others unless he has first been piously affected himself.

units.la: 73. Ex definitione perfecti, cognoscis, quid ad perfecti operis absolutionem requiratur; Curare nimirum debes, ne quid desit, ne quid superfit, ne quid addi, vel demi possit.
units.tr: 73. From the definition of the perfect you learn what is required for the completion of a perfect work: namely, you must take care that nothing is lacking, that nothing is superfluous, and that nothing can be added or taken away.

units.la: 74. Plura ad esse, quam non esse requiri, docet Metaphysica; Ergo imperii clavum tenens, illa Regum & principum facta imitaberis, quorum haec sunt dicta; Conservare magis cupio, quam perdere plebem; malo unum servare civem, quam mille hostes perdere. Inde quoque festinationem novercam prudentiae scies in moralibus; nec non in rebus aliis, si quid praeclarum & singulare futurum sit, lente festinandum esse, memineris.
units.tr: 74. Metaphysics teaches that more is required for being than for not-being. Therefore, holding the helm of government, you will imitate the deeds of kings and princes, of whom these words are recorded: I desire to preserve the people rather than destroy them; I prefer to save one citizen than to destroy a thousand enemies. From this too you will learn that haste is the stepmother of prudence in moral matters; and you should remember that in other matters too, if something is to be excellent and unique, it must be hastened slowly.

units.la: 75. Iustinus, lib. 8. sub initio, inquit, Graeciae Civitates in mutuum exitium sine modo ruentes, omnibus perire, quod singulae amitterent, non nisi oppressae, senserunt: Non ergo memores fuerunt Axiomatis Metaphysici; Quod competit omnibus & singulis alicujus multitudinis unitatibus, id competit etiam ipsi multitudini. cap. 24. th. 3.
units.tr: 75. Justin, book 8 at the beginning, says that the Greek cities, rushing without measure into mutual destruction, felt only when they were overpowered that all of them would perish through what each one lost. They were therefore not mindful of the metaphysical axiom: What belongs to all and each of the unities of some multitude belongs also to the multitude itself, c. 24, th. 3.

units.la: 76. Quod si in primaria Entis divisione in Infinitum & finitum, homo sese intuitu Creatoris, tanquam in speculo voluerit contemplari atque examinare, vitæ practicæ reperiet fœcundum fontem, habebit τὸ γνῶθι θεόν, τὸ γνῶθι σεαυτόν ; Experietur-que, utut in aliis scientiis superbiendi occasionem habere queant homines, aut obrepere iis possit oblivio Dei, in Metaphysicâ tamen seriò inspectâ, fieri id nequâquam posse.
units.tr: 76. If in the primary division of being into infinite and finite, a man chooses to contemplate and examine himself in the sight of the Creator, as in a mirror, he will find a fruitful source of practical life, and will have know God [τὸ γνῶθι θεόν] and know yourself [τὸ γνῶθι σεαυτόν]. And he will experience that, although in other sciences men may have occasion for pride, or forgetfulness of God may creep upon them, yet in Metaphysics, if it is seriously studied, this can by no means happen.

units.la: 7. Denique Metaphysica dum rerum perfectionem & dignitatem ponderat, atque suo pretio æstimat, multum facit ad deliberationes & consultationes ritè instituendas ; docet quid eligere, quid sugere debeas ; Ex. gr. in Herculis bivio constitutum, ex alterâ parte voluptate, ex alterâ virtute adstante, utrum eligere conveniat, Metaphysica te docebit, si voluptatis&virtutis generalissima attributa fueris contemplatus, quæ in Entis doctrinâ occurrunt ; plus enim realitatis in virtute, quam in voluptate comperies. In ducendâ uxore digniora semper bona indignioribus præferenda esse, Oeconomica prudentia præscribit ; Eadem requisita uxoris enumerat, cerras animi corporisque dotes, & bona externa. Quæ autem ex his digniora sint, ex communissimis primæ Philosophiæ principiis erui potest. Si ex necessitate successionis optio detur in Republica, inter principem callidum & obtusum plane, quaeritur uter eligendus? Cum autem Metaphysic⁴ physica doceat, id præferendum esse, quod Enti vicinius, & calliditas vicinior fit vero Enti (prudentiæ) callidum obtuso præferes. Plura adderem, sed me charta de sermonis fine monet, ubi vix officinam utilitatum practicarum aperueram? Dicta autem copiose satis patefaciunt, quam insignem usum præstet vitæ degendæ & τὰ ἀπὸ ἀ-ξι τῶ ὄντων Metaphysica. Et cum nec minorem antea in cognitione &Σωφίας τῶ ὄντων oftenderinus, ubique utilis Prima Philosophia dignoscitur.
units.tr: 7. Finally, when Metaphysics weighs the perfection and worth of things and sets their price, it does much to help us make deliberations and consultations rightly. It teaches what we ought to choose and what we ought to avoid. For example, if someone stands at the crossroads of Hercules, with pleasure on one side and virtue standing by on the other, and asks which he should choose, Metaphysics will teach him, provided he has considered the most general attributes of pleasure and virtue that occur in the doctrine of being. For he will find more reality in virtue than in pleasure. In choosing a wife, household prudence prescribes that the better goods should always be preferred to the worse. The same prudence lists the qualities required in a wife: certain gifts of mind and body, and external goods. Which of these are the better can be drawn from the most common principles of first philosophy. If, from the necessity of succession, a choice is offered in a commonwealth between a prince who is clever and one who is plainly dull, the question is which of the two should be chosen. Since Metaphysics teaches that what is closer to being is to be preferred, and cleverness is closer to true being (prudence), you will prefer the clever to the dull. I could add more, but the paper warns me about the end of my discourse, when I have hardly opened the workshop of practical usefulness. Yet what has been said is clear enough to show what remarkable use Metaphysics offers for the living of life, and [the things that come from the worth of beings]. And since I have shown that it is no less useful in the knowledge of [the wisdom of beings], First Philosophy is recognised everywhere as useful.

units.la: 78. Luculenta adeo cum sint hæc Metaphysicæ commoda, merito suspecta esse debent, quæcunque à malevolis adversus ipsam, ejusque utilitates in medium adducuntur; & vel sponte suâ corruunt: Quidquid autem roboris habeant, expendendum nunc esset, sed deficit charta, id itaque in ipsis Exercitationibus præstabitur; Hoc tamen obter teneri poterit, ipsos Metaphysicos aliquâ ex parte in culpâ esse, quòd vulgò divina hæc Scientia tam male audiat; Etenim plurima abipsis planè neglecta fuerunt; ipsam Metaphysicam à Logicâ non sufficienter distinxerunt, generalia (specialibus accommodare, & ex specialibus generalia excitare, parum aut non curarunt; Generalissimas notiones, ut faciliores ac notiores, quam utiis accuratius cognoscendis, & usui applicandis, tempus & opera sint impendenda, omiserunt; unde incauti impegere in illa, quæ tamquam notissima adspicere dedignati sunt. Et denique plurimi Metaphysicam potius in subtilitate quæstionum, quam utilitate ad alias disciplinas positam æxistimârunt; quo præjudicio gravati, de usu ne cogitârunt quidem. His inquam aliisque vitiis Metaphysici suam scientiam suspectam reddiderunt.
units.tr: 78. These advantages of Metaphysics are so evident that whatever is brought forward against it and its usefulness by ill-disposed people ought rightly to be viewed with suspicion, and such objections collapse of their own accord. Yet the strength they may have would have to be weighed now, but the paper is failing, so this will be done in the Exercises themselves. Still, this can be granted: the Metaphysicians themselves are partly to blame for the fact that this divine science is so ill spoken of by the common people. For very many things have been wholly neglected by them. They did not sufficiently distinguish Metaphysics from Logic. They cared little or not at all for adapting general things to particular ones and for drawing general things out of particular ones. They omitted to spend time and effort on the most general notions, which are easier and better known, but which need to be understood more accurately and applied in use. So the unwary have run into those things that they disdained to look at as though they were most well known. And finally, very many have judged Metaphysics to be placed more in the subtlety of questions than in its usefulness for other disciplines. Burdened by this prejudice, they did not even think of its use. By these and other faults, I say, the Metaphysicians have made their own science suspect.

units.la: ATque ita, per Dei gratiam, absolvi hocce triplici tractatu constans Metaphysicarum Institutionum Ἀντρωπολογία iisdem penè verbis ac sententiis conscriptum, ac typis excusum, quibus, ita suggerente memoriâ, illud in privato Collegio Discipulis proposuerâ, nihil minus tum quam ejus editionem, aut etiam conscriptionem cogitans; Pleniores quippe Exercitationes moliebar, ex quibus postea institutiones formari possent. Verius itaque ahortivus quâ legitimus fœtus, hac festinatione, partim Discipulorum continuâ petitione, partim, & quam maximè, serio quorum in me est non exigua autoritas, hortatu, dicam an imperio, præcipitatâ, exclusus, vel me ipso Judice, æstimabitur.
units.tr: And so, by the grace of God, these Metaphysical Institutes, consisting of this three-part treatise, have been completed. They were written and printed in almost the same words and opinions with which, as memory suggested, I had set them before my students in a private class, without thinking at all about their publication or even their composition. Indeed, I was working on fuller Exercises, from which institutes could be formed later. Therefore this work, hurried along partly by the continual request of my students, and partly, and very much so, by the earnest exhortation (shall I say command?) of those whose authority over me is not small, will be judged, even by my own verdict, to be an abortion rather than a lawful offspring.

units.la: Nam nec ubique eadem ἀκεβέα, nec eadem brevitas aut prolixitas ; Alicubi ab institutionibus declinator ad elenchtica, alicubi hæc prorsus declino ; Nec mirum, currente prælo, non minus ac calamo, animo etiam aliis intento, omnia pene prodiere : Solam evidentiam ac claritatem dictorum, quantum potui ubique tentavi, quam an assecutus sim, tuo (Lector) stabit judicio. Cæterum quot capita, tot sententias & hic experiere in quibusdam, licet sedulò omnis immutationis, quantum possibile fuit, speciem evitare conatus sim : Novi quippe probé χαλεπὸν εἶναι συνήθειαν μα- χρὸν ἰάσασθαι. Contentiones ac inanes rixas evitavi, ut quibus non tantum carere possumus, sed & ipsa Veritas, ejusque utilitas non parum detrimenti capit. In refutando sententias, absque ullâ calumniâ in Authores placidum me gessi : Ita quippe fert animus, incolumem etiam servare amicitiam, licet diversum sentiamus ; Quid enim ad me, quod alius aliter statuat : Fruatur ille suo ingenio, & me meo frui, ne deneget. Turpius nihil existimo, quam diversum sententes aut tabificâ invidiâ, aut vatiniano odio prosequi ; nonne qui id facit, seipsum macerat, ne dicam enecat? Id igitur præstiti, ut potius sententias, quas à vero deviare autumabam, in ordinem cogerem, quam ut authores earum traducerem. Si erravero aut in aliquo lapsus fuero, (quisquis enim est, qui non saepius aberrat:) memor sis humanae sortis, & Christianae charitatis; quarum illâ ab indignatione, hac verò à contumelâ liberaberis: Sciens sanè & volens non erravi, unicè hoc exoptans, ut voto & fructui Discipulorum meorum satisfacerem; Gloriam non exspectavi, probè gnarus, plura ac praestantiora ad illam requiri, quam hisce chartis continentur; quare nec te adspexisse, nisi Bibliopolae quaestum suum in iis quaesiissent. Si, dum forte per otium hasce pagellas inspicere libuerit, aliquid quod in usum tuum convertas, reperieris, eo utere ac fruere: Sin quod displiceat, expunge, contemne, refuta, nam & tale quid si observavero, in posterioribus cogitationibus, non benigniorem à meipso exspectabit fortem. Interim velim sis monitus, me Vocabula Constitutionis & Distinctionis, quibus illud, quod per modum prioris inadaequatè de Ente concipimus, expressi, in amplâ satis, ac forte non satis trita significatione usurpâsse; Sed deërant alia; Neque hoc aegrè feres, dum in pluribus aliis idem fieri à Metaphysicis passim observas; Longe quippe angustior significatio in vulgari usu Dependentiae, Inhaerentiae, Unionis, &c. quam quae est in usu Metaphysicorum. Scilicet vulgari linguâ loquendum, etiam de iis, quæ ne quidem vulgus cogitat. Exspectares forsan, longiorem Meisneri, Scheibleri, & inprimis Calovii inter Lutheranos; Suarezii, Conimbricenfium, aliorumque inter Iesuitas refutationem; Sed elenchtica prolixiora inter didactica tradere non duxi consultum; & magis quoniam Exercitationes Metaphysicas, si Deo ita visum, brevi , quibus inter alia hoc præstabo, ut Maccovium, Timplerum, Keckermannum, Burgersdicium, a'iosque Reformatæ Religionis Metaphysicos ab eorum injuriis vindicem. Hæ si tibi gratæ videantur, unâ precare mecum Ἀρχιφιλόσοφον, ut conatus meos alina sua benedictione largiter velit promovere; ad sui nominis gloriam, ac animarum nostrarum salutem. Vale.
units.tr: For the accuracy [ἀκριβεία] is not the same everywhere, nor is the brevity or the length. In some places I have turned from the institutes to refutations, and in others I have avoided these altogether. It is no wonder that almost everything came out while the press was running, no less than the pen, with my mind also occupied with other things. I have tried, as far as I could, everywhere to attain clarity and evidence in what I say. Whether I have succeeded will rest with your judgment, Reader. Moreover, you will find here, in some places, as many opinions as there are heads, although I have tried carefully to avoid any appearance of change so far as possible. For I know well that "it is difficult to cure a long-standing habit" [χαλεπὸν εἶναι συνήθειαν μακρὸν ἰάσασθαι]. I have avoided contentions and empty quarrels, since we can not only do without them, but truth itself and its usefulness suffer no small harm from them. In refuting opinions, I have behaved calmly towards the authors, without any slander. For that is how my mind is inclined: to keep friendship intact even when we think differently. What does it matter to me that another thinks otherwise? Let him enjoy his own talent, and let him not begrudge me mine. I think nothing more shameful than to pursue those who think differently with consuming envy or Vatinian hatred. Does not the one who does this waste himself, not to say destroy himself? I have therefore taken care to bring to order the opinions that I thought strayed from the truth, rather than to slander their authors. If I have erred or slipped in anything (for who is there who does not err more often?), remember human frailty and Christian charity, of which the first will free you from indignation and the second from insult. I did not err knowingly and willingly; I desired only one thing, to satisfy the wish and the profit of my students. I have not looked for glory, being well aware that more and greater things are required for it than are contained in these pages. Therefore you should not have looked at them either, unless the bookseller had sought his gain in them. If, by chance, when you have leisure, you care to look over these little pages and find something that you can turn to your use, use it and enjoy it. But if something displeases you, delete it, despise it, refute it. For if I notice any such thing in my later thoughts, I shall not expect a kinder fate from myself. Meanwhile, I would like you to be warned that I have used the terms Constitution and Distinction, by which I expressed what we conceive inadequately of being in the manner of a prior thing, in a fairly broad and perhaps not very common meaning. But other words were lacking. Nor will you take this badly, since you notice the same being done in many other places by the Metaphysicians. For the meaning of Dependence, Inherence, Union, and so on, in common usage is far narrower than in the usage of the Metaphysicians. Clearly we must speak in ordinary language even about things that the common people do not even think of. You might perhaps expect a longer refutation of Meisner, Scheibler, and above all Calov among the Lutherans, and of Suárez, the Conimbricenses, and others among the Jesuits. But I did not think it advisable to put lengthy refutations among the teaching texts. The more so since, if God so wills, I shall shortly produce Metaphysical Exercises, in which, among other things, I will do this: defend Maccovius, Timpler, Keckermann, Burgersdijk, and other Metaphysicians of the Reformed Religion from their injuries. If these seem welcome to you, pray with me to the Archphilosopher [Ἀρχιφιλόσοφος], that He may be pleased to advance my efforts generously with His own blessing, to the glory of His name and the salvation of our souls. Farewell.
